Even in the midst of its resurgence as a vital tradition, many sociologists have viewed the current form of the powwow, a ceremonial gathering of native Americans, as a sign that tribal culture is in decline. Focusing on the dances and rituals that have recently come to be shared by most tribes, they suggest that an intertribal movement is now in ascension and claim the inevitable outcome of this tendency is the eventual dissolution of tribes and the complete assimilation of native Americans into Euroamerican society. Proponents of this "Pan-Indian" theory point to the greater frequency of travel and communication between reservations, the greater urbanization of native Americans, and, most recently, their increasing politicization in response to common grievances as the chief causes of the shift toward intertribalism.

Indeed, the rapid diffusion of dance styles, outfits, and songs from one reservation to another offers compelling evidence that intertribalism has been increasing. However, these sociologists have failed to note the concurrent revitalization of many traditions unique to individual tribes. Among the Lakota, for instance, the Sun Dance was revived, after a forty-year hiatus, during the 1950s. Similarly, the Black Legging Society of the Kiowa and the Hethuska Society of the Ponca—both traditional groups within their respective tribes—have gained new popularity. Obviously, a more complex societal shift is taking place than the theory of Pan-Indianism can account for.

An examination of the theory's underpinnings may be critical at this point, especially given that native Americans themselves chafe most against the Pan-Indian classification. Like other assimilationist theories with which it is associated, the Pan-Indian view is predicated upon an a priori assumption about the nature of cultural contact: that upon contact minority societies immediately begin to succumb in every respect—biologically, linguistically, and culturally—to the majority society. However, there is no evidence that this is happening to native American groups.

Yet the fact remains that intertribal activities are a major facet of native American culture today. Certain dances at powwows, for instance, are announced as intertribal, others as traditional. Likewise, speeches given at the beginnings of powwows are often delivered in English, while the prayer that follows is usually spoken in a native language. Cultural borrowing is, of course, old news. What is important to note is the conscious distinction native Americans make between tribal and intertribal tendencies.

Tribalism, although greatly altered by modern history, remains a potent force among native Americans. It forms a basis for tribal identity, and aligns music and dance with other social and cultural activities important to individual tribes. Intertribal activities, on the other hand, reinforce native American identity along a broader front, where this identity is directly threatened by outside influences.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the position it intends to dismantle. The Sociologists look at the modern powwow, a ceremonial gathering of native Americans, and read the dances and rituals now shared across tribes as a sign of cultural decline, predicting that tribes will dissolve and native Americans will be absorbed into Euroamerican society. Their label for the trend is Pan-Indianism, and they trace it to easier travel and communication between reservations, growing urbanization, and political organizing around shared grievances. Notice that this position is being reported rather than endorsed, and that the word 'inevitable' in their forecast is exactly what the rest of the passage will test.

The Author grants the sociologists their evidence before turning it around: styles, outfits, and songs really do spread quickly from one reservation to another, so intertribalism is genuinely on the rise. What the sociologists missed is what was happening alongside it, since traditions belonging to single tribes were reviving at the same time. The Lakota Sun Dance returned in the 1950s after a forty-year gap, and tribe-specific groups such as the Kiowa Black Legging Society and the Ponca Hethuska Society have grown popular again. The conclusion drawn is deliberately modest: something more complicated is under way than Pan-Indianism can account for.

Having shown the theory to be incomplete, the author goes after its foundations, noting first that native Americans themselves object most strongly to the Pan-Indian label. The assumption underneath the theory, shared with other assimilationist accounts, is taken on faith rather than demonstrated: that on contact a minority society immediately begins giving way on every front at once, biologically, linguistically, and culturally. The author's rejection is flat and evidentiary rather than theoretical, since nothing of the sort can be observed among native American groups. Watch that this attacks the premise the sociologists start from, not the data they collected.

A concession follows, and it matters that the author makes it. Intertribal activity genuinely is a major part of native American life now, and the examples given are ordinary ones: some powwow dances are announced as intertribal and others as traditional, and an opening speech may be delivered in English while the prayer after it is spoken in a native language. Cultural borrowing, the author adds, is hardly news. The point worth holding onto is a different one, namely that native Americans consciously distinguish tribal from intertribal, which means the two strands are being kept apart rather than blended.

The closing paragraph resolves the tension the passage has been building. Instead of one force replacing another, two operate at once on different levels. Tribalism, much altered by modern history but still potent, supplies tribal identity and ties music and dance to the other social and cultural activities that matter within a particular tribe. Intertribal activity works on a wider front, strengthening a shared native American identity precisely where outside influences press against it. The author's answer to Pan-Indianism is therefore not denial but reframing: intertribalism responds to external threat rather than marking a stage on the road to assimilation.
overall_html: The passage argues that the spread of shared intertribal practices at powwows is not evidence that native American tribal culture is dissolving into the majority society, since tribe-specific traditions are reviving at the same time and native Americans themselves draw a conscious line between tribal and intertribal activity. The author's purpose is corrective, moving from a statement of the Pan-Indian theory, to counterevidence, to an attack on the assimilationist assumption underlying it, to a concession about how prominent intertribalism really is, and finally to a reframing in which tribalism grounds tribal identity while intertribal activity defends a broader native American identity against outside influence. The viewpoints to keep apart are the sociologists who advance Pan-Indianism and the author who reinterprets it.

Scientists typically advocate the analytic method of studying complex systems: systems are divided into component parts that are investigated separately. But nineteenth-century critics of this method claimed that when a system's parts are isolated its complexity tends to be lost. To address the perceived weaknesses of the analytic method these critics put forward a concept called organicism, which posited that the whole determines the nature of its parts and that the parts of a whole are interdependent.

Organicism depended upon the theory of internal relations, which states that relations between entities are possible only within some whole that embraces them, and that entities are altered by the relationships into which they enter. If an entity stands in a relationship with another entity, it has some property as a consequence. Without this relationship, and hence without the property, the entity would be different—and so would be another entity. Thus, the property is one of the entity's defining characteristics. Each of an entity's relationships likewise determines a defining characteristic of the entity.

One problem with the theory of internal relations is that not all properties of an entity are defining characteristics: numerous properties are accompanying characteristics—even if they are always present, their presence does not influence the entity's identity. Thus, even if it is admitted that every relationship into which an entity enters determines some characteristic of the entity, it is not necessarily true that such characteristics will define the entity; it is possible for the entity to enter into a relationship yet remain essentially unchanged.

The ultimate difficulty with the theory of internal relations is that it renders the acquisition of knowledge impossible. To truly know an entity, we must know all of its relationships; but because the entity is related to everything in each whole of which it is a part, these wholes must be known completely before the entity can be known. This seems to be a prerequisite impossible to satisfy.

Organicists' criticism of the analytic method arose from their failure to fully comprehend the method. In rejecting the analytic method, organicists overlooked the fact that before the proponents of the method analyzed the component parts of a system, they first determined both the laws applicable to the whole system and the initial conditions of the system; proponents of the method thus did not study parts of a system in full isolation from the system as a whole. Since organicists failed to recognize this, they never advanced any argument to show that laws and initial conditions of complex systems cannot be discovered. Hence, organicists offered no valid reason for rejecting the analytic method or for adopting organicism as a replacement for it.
explanation_html:
Two camps are set against each other immediately. The Scientists favor the analytic method: divide a complex system into its component parts and investigate each part separately. The Organicists, nineteenth-century critics of that approach, objected that isolating the parts destroys the very complexity you were trying to explain, and proposed instead that a whole determines the nature of its parts and that those parts are interdependent. Track both positions carefully from here, because the passage will lay out organicism sympathetically for two paragraphs before taking it apart. Nothing yet reveals where The Author stands.

The machinery underneath organicism is unpacked next, and it has a name: the theory of internal relations. Its claim is that things can be related only inside some larger whole that contains them, and that entering a relation changes the things related. The reasoning runs as a short chain. Standing in a relation gives an entity a property; without the relation it would lack that property; lacking it, the entity would be a different entity; so the property helps define what the entity is. Generalize the chain and every relationship an entity enters fixes one of its defining characteristics. Follow the links closely, since the objections coming attack specific ones.

The first objection targets the move from property to defining characteristic. Some properties are merely accompanying: they may be present at all times and still do no work in making the entity the thing it is. Grant the organicists that every relationship produces some characteristic and their conclusion still does not follow, because the characteristic produced may be incidental, leaving the entity essentially unchanged by the relation. Notice the concessive shape of the argument, which the author uses more than once here, conceding the weaker premise and then denying that the strong conclusion follows from it.

A heavier objection follows, and the author flags it as the ultimate one: internal relations make knowledge unobtainable. If knowing an entity requires knowing all of its relations, and the entity is related to everything within each whole it belongs to, then those wholes would have to be known completely before the entity could be known at all. That is a prerequisite nobody can satisfy. Watch what the two objections accomplish together, since the theory has now been shown to be logically unnecessary and practically unusable, which clears the ground for the diagnosis in the final paragraph.

The closing paragraph explains why the organicists went wrong in the first place: they never fully understood the method they were rejecting. Proponents of the analytic method do not begin with isolated parts at all. They first determine the laws applicable to the whole system and the initial conditions of that system, so the parts are examined inside that frame rather than apart from it. Because the organicists missed this, they never even attempted the argument they needed, which would have had to show that such laws and initial conditions cannot be discovered. The verdict is unqualified: no valid reason was given for rejecting analysis or for installing organicism in its place.
overall_html: The passage examines organicism, the nineteenth-century objection that studying a complex system part by part destroys its complexity, and concludes that the doctrine fails on every count: the theory of internal relations it depends on confuses incidental properties with defining ones and makes knowledge of anything impossible, while the criticism itself misreads a method that actually starts from the laws and initial conditions of the whole system. The author's purpose is evaluative and ultimately dismissive, setting out the organicist position and its supporting theory before raising two objections and closing with a diagnosis of the underlying mistake. Keep apart the scientists who use the analytic method, the organicists who attack it, and the author, who sides with the scientists.

Opponents of compulsory national service claim that such a program is not in keeping with the liberal principles upon which Western democracies are founded. This reasoning is reminiscent of the argument that a tax on one's income is undemocratic because it violates one's right to property. Such conceptions of the liberal state fail to take into account the intricate character of the social agreement that undergirds our liberties. It is only in the context of a community that the notion of individual rights has any application; individual rights are meant to define the limits of people's actions with respect to other people. Implicit in such a context is the concept of shared sacrifice. Were no taxes paid, there could be no law enforcement, and the enforcement of law is of benefit to everyone in society. Thus, each of us must bear a share of the burden to ensure that the community is protected.

The responsibility to defend one's nation against outside aggression is surely no less than the responsibility to help pay for law enforcement within the nation. Therefore, the state is certainly within its rights to compel citizens to perform national service when it is needed for the benefit of society.

It might be objected that the cases of taxation and national service are not analogous: While taxation must be coerced, the military is quite able to find recruits without resorting to conscription. Furthermore, proponents of national service do not limit its scope to only those duties absolutely necessary to the defense of the nation. Therefore, it may be contended, compulsory national service oversteps the acceptable boundaries of governmental interference in the lives of its citizens.

By responding thus, the opponent of national service has already allowed that it is a right of government to demand service when it is needed. But what is the true scope of the term "need"? If it is granted, say, that present tax policies are legitimate intrusions on the right to property, then it must also be granted that need involves more than just what is necessary for a sound national defense. Even the most conservative of politicians admits that tax money is rightly spent on programs that, while not necessary for the survival of the state, are nevertheless of great benefit to society. Can the opponent of national service truly claim that activities of the military such as quelling civil disorders, rebuilding dams and bridges, or assisting the victims of natural disasters—all extraneous to the defense of society against outside aggression—do not provide a similar benefit to the nation? Upon reflection, opponents of national service must concede that such a broadened conception of what is necessary is in keeping with the ideas of shared sacrifice and community benefit that are essential to the functioning of a liberal democratic state.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by stating a position and answering it in the same breath. The Opponents of compulsory national service say the program clashes with the liberal principles Western democracies rest on. The Author likens this to calling an income tax undemocratic because it violates a right to property, and the comparison carries the whole argument: rights only make sense inside a community, since their function is to mark the limits of how people may act toward one another. Built into that arrangement is shared sacrifice. With no taxes there is no law enforcement, and law enforcement benefits everyone, so each person must carry part of the burden.

A compact two-step inference does the work here, and it is short enough to skim past. Defending the nation against outside aggression is at least as weighty a responsibility as paying for law enforcement within it; therefore the state acts within its rights when it compels citizens to serve where society needs them. Recognize that the passage's actual conclusion has already arrived by this point. Everything that follows exists to handle resistance to it rather than to build it further.

An objection is now voiced on the opponents' behalf, and the author states it fairly rather than weakening it. The two cases may not be parallel: taxes have to be coerced, whereas the military can fill its ranks with volunteers and needs no conscription. Worse, supporters of national service do not confine it to duties strictly necessary for defense. On that reading, compulsory service crosses the line between legitimate government and intrusion into citizens' lives. Keep straight that this paragraph belongs to the opponents; the author has not changed position, only paused to let the strongest reply be heard.

The reply turns that objection into a concession. By arguing about scope, the opponents have already granted that government may demand service when it is genuinely needed, so the live question becomes how far 'need' extends. If present tax policy counts as a legitimate intrusion on property, need already reaches past bare national defense, since even the most conservative politicians accept spending on programs the state could survive without. The author then asks whether quelling civil disorders, rebuilding dams and bridges, and assisting disaster victims deliver a comparable benefit, treating the answer as obvious and the broadened sense of necessity as exactly what shared sacrifice implies.
overall_html: The passage defends compulsory national service against the charge that it violates liberal principles, arguing by analogy with taxation that individual rights exist only within a community founded on shared sacrifice, and that the wide benefit conferred by service justifies the state in requiring it. The author's purpose is persuasive rather than descriptive, moving from the opponents' objection and the taxation parallel, to a brief statement of the conclusion, to a fairly presented counterobjection about voluntary recruitment and excessive scope, and finally to a reply that converts that counterobjection into an admission about how broadly need must be understood. The two viewpoints in play are the opponents of national service and the author who answers them.

James Porter (1905–1970) was the first scholar to identify the African influence on visual art in the Americas, and much of what is known about the cultural legacy that African-American artists inherited from their African forebears has come to us by way of his work. Porter, a painter and art historian, began by studying African-American crafts of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. This research revealed that many of the household items created by African-American men and women—walking sticks, jugs, and textiles—displayed characteristics that linked them iconographically to artifacts of West Africa. Porter then went on to establish clearly the range of the cultural territory inherited by later African-American artists.

An example of this aspect of Porter's research occurs in his essay "Robert S. Duncanson, Midwestern Romantic-Realist." The work of Duncanson, a nineteenth-century painter of the Hudson River school, like that of his predecessor in the movement, Joshua Johnston, was commonly thought to have been created by a Euro-American artist. Porter proved definitively that both Duncanson and Johnston were of African ancestry. Porter published this finding and thousands of others in a comprehensive volume tracing the history of African-American art. At the time of its first printing in 1943, only two other books devoted exclusively to the accomplishments of African-American artists existed. Both of these books were written by Alain LeRoy Locke, a professor at the university where Porter also taught. While these earlier studies by Locke are interesting for being the first to survey the field, neither addressed the critical issue of African precursors; Porter's book addressed this issue, painstakingly integrating the history of African-American art into the larger history of art in the Americas without separating it from those qualities that gave it its unique ties to African artisanship. Porter may have been especially attuned to these ties because of his conscious effort to maintain them in his own paintings, many of which combine the style of the genre portrait with evidence of an extensive knowledge of the cultural history of various African peoples.

In his later years, Porter wrote additional chapters for later editions of his book, constantly revising and correcting his findings, some of which had been based of necessity on fragmentary evidence. Among his later achievements were his definitive reckoning of the birth year of the painter Patrick Reason, long a point of scholarly uncertainty, and his identification of an unmarked grave in San Francisco as that of the sculptor Edmonia Lewis. At his death, Porter left extensive notes for an unfinished project aimed at exploring the influence of African art on the art of the Western world generally, a body of research whose riches scholars still have not exhausted.
explanation_html:
Everything in the opening establishes why Porter matters and how his research proceeded. He was the first scholar to identify African influence on visual art in the Americas, which makes his work the source of most of what is now known about the legacy African-American artists inherited from African forebears. His route to that conclusion began small, with eighteenth- and nineteenth-century African-American crafts: walking sticks, jugs, textiles, ordinary household objects whose iconography, meaning the imagery and motifs worked into them, matched artifacts from West Africa. From that narrow base he went on to map the wider cultural territory later artists drew on. Note the direction of travel, from particular objects to a broad claim about inheritance.

The Duncanson essay is offered as an illustration of that broader mapping. Duncanson painted with the Hudson River school, and both he and an earlier figure in the movement, Joshua Johnston, had commonly been assumed to be Euro-American; Porter established definitively that both were of African ancestry. That finding was one of thousands published in his 1943 history of African-American art, and its significance emerges from the comparison that follows. Only two books on the subject existed, both by Alain LeRoy Locke, a colleague at Porter's university, and while they were pioneering surveys neither took up African precursors. Porter's book did, integrating African-American art into the larger history of art in the Americas without cutting it off from its African ties, a balance The Author links to Porter's own portraits, which combine genre style with deep knowledge of African cultural history.

Late career and unfinished business close the passage. Porter kept adding chapters to later editions and revising conclusions he had originally drawn from fragmentary evidence, presented here as a strength rather than a lapse, since the scholarship corrected itself as better material appeared. Two specific results stand in for the rest: settling the long-disputed birth year of the painter Patrick Reason, and identifying an unmarked San Francisco grave as that of the sculptor Edmonia Lewis. The notes he left for a project on African art's influence on Western art generally give the passage a forward-looking ending, since the author reports that scholars have still not exhausted that research.
overall_html: The passage presents James Porter as the scholar who first traced the African roots of visual art in the Americas, following him from his early study of African-American crafts and their West African iconography, through the 1943 history in which he corrected the record on painters such as Duncanson and Johnston and supplied the African precursors that Locke's earlier surveys had omitted, to his late revisions and the unfinished project he left behind. The author's purpose is appreciative and largely narrative, organizing the material chronologically around Porter's widening scope. No competing viewpoints are developed; the only evaluative voice is the author's own, which treats Porter's integration of African-American art into the wider history of art in the Americas as his central achievement.

Between June 1987 and May 1988, the bodies of at least 740 bottlenose dolphins out of a total coastal population of 3,000 to 5,000 washed ashore on the Atlantic coast of the United States. Since some of the dead animals never washed ashore, the overall disaster was presumably worse; perhaps 50 percent of the population died. A dolphin die-off of this character and magnitude had never before been observed; furthermore, the dolphins exhibited a startling range of symptoms. The research team that examined the die-off noted the presence of both skin lesions and internal lesions in the liver, lung, pancreas, and heart, which suggested a massive opportunistic bacterial infection of already weakened animals.

Tissues from the stricken dolphins were analyzed for a variety of toxins. Brevetoxin, a toxin produced by the blooming of the alga Ptychodiscus brevis, was present in eight out of seventeen dolphins tested. Tests for synthetic pollutants revealed that polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were present in almost all animals tested.

The research team concluded that brevetoxin poisoning was the most likely cause of the illnesses that killed the dolphins. Although P. brevis is ordinarily not found along the Atlantic coast, an unusual bloom of this organism—such blooms are called "red tides" because of the reddish color imparted by the blooming algae—did occur in the middle of the affected coastline in October 1987. These researchers believe the toxin accumulated in the tissue of fish and then was ingested by dolphins that preyed on them. The emaciated appearance of many dolphins indicated that they were metabolizing their blubber reserves, thereby reducing their buoyancy and insulation (and adding to overall stress) as well as releasing stores of previously accumulated synthetic pollutants, such as PCBs, which further exacerbated their condition. The combined impact made the dolphins vulnerable to opportunistic bacterial infection, the ultimate cause of death.

For several reasons, however, this explanation is not entirely plausible. First, bottlenose dolphins and P. brevis red tides are both common in the Gulf of Mexico, yet no dolphin die-off of a similar magnitude has been noted there. Second, dolphins began dying in June, hundreds of miles north of and some months earlier than the October red tide bloom. Finally, the specific effects of brevetoxin on dolphins are unknown, whereas PCB poisoning is known to impair functioning of the immune system and liver and to cause skin lesions; all of these problems were observed in the diseased animals. An alternative hypothesis, which accounts for these facts, is that a sudden influx of pollutants, perhaps from offshore dumping, triggered a cascade of disorders in animals whose systems were already heavily laden with pollutants. Although brevetoxin may have been a contributing factor, the event that actually precipitated the die-off was a sharp increase in the dolphins' exposure to synthetic pollutants.
explanation_html:
The opening is pure setup, laying out the event the rest of the passage will try to explain. Between June 1987 and May 1988 at least 740 bottlenose dolphins washed ashore on the U.S. Atlantic coast, out of a coastal population of three to five thousand, and since not every carcass reaches land the true toll may have been half the population. Two features make the episode unusual: nothing of this character or scale had been recorded before, and the symptoms varied startlingly. The Research Team found lesions on the skin and inside the liver, lung, pancreas, and heart, a pattern suggesting bacterial infection that took hold in animals already weakened by something else.

Short and purely factual, this stretch supplies the two findings the competing explanations will fight over. Tissue from the stricken dolphins was screened for a range of toxins. Brevetoxin, a poison released when the alga Ptychodiscus brevis blooms, appeared in eight of the seventeen animals tested. Screening for synthetic pollutants turned up polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, in almost every animal examined. Hold on to the proportions rather than just the names, because the gap between eight of seventeen and nearly all of them is doing quiet work in the argument still to come.

The research team's explanation is a chain worth following link by link. They identified brevetoxin poisoning as the likely cause, supported by an unusual bloom of P. brevis in the middle of the affected coastline in October 1987, a red tide, so called for the reddish color blooming algae give the water. Fish absorbed the toxin and dolphins preying on them ingested it. Emaciated animals were burning their blubber reserves, which cost them buoyancy and insulation, added to their overall stress, and released PCBs previously stored in the fat. The accumulated damage left them open to the opportunistic bacterial infection that actually killed them.

The Author now dismantles that chain with three objections and offers a replacement. Dolphins and P. brevis red tides are both common in the Gulf of Mexico with no comparable die-off recorded there; the deaths began in June, months earlier than the October bloom and hundreds of miles north of it; and while brevetoxin's specific effects on dolphins are simply unknown, PCB poisoning is documented to impair the immune system and liver and to cause skin lesions, all of which the diseased animals showed. The alternative fits those facts: a sudden influx of pollutants, perhaps from offshore dumping, overwhelmed animals already heavily laden with chemicals. Brevetoxin is allowed a contributing role, nothing more.
overall_html: The passage recounts an unprecedented die-off of Atlantic bottlenose dolphins, presents the research team's conclusion that brevetoxin from a red tide weakened the animals until bacterial infection killed them, and then rejects that account in favor of a sudden influx of synthetic pollutants as the precipitating cause. The author's purpose is to evaluate a proposed explanation and substitute a stronger one, moving from the facts of the event, to the toxicological findings, to the team's causal chain, and finally to three objections concerning the Gulf of Mexico, the mismatch in timing and location, and the documented effects of PCBs. The two voices to keep apart are the research team and the author who overturns their conclusion.

In England before 1660, a husband controlled his wife's property. In the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with the shift from land-based to commercial wealth, marriage began to incorporate certain features of a contract. Historians have traditionally argued that this trend represented a gain for women, one that reflects changing views about democracy and property following the English Restoration in 1660. Susan Staves contests this view; she argues that whatever gains marriage contracts may briefly have represented for women were undermined by judicial decisions about women's contractual rights.

Sifting through the tangled details of court cases, Staves demonstrates that, despite surface changes, a rhetoric of equality, and occasional decisions supporting women's financial power, definitions of men's and women's property remained inconsistent—generally to women's detriment. For example, dower lands (property inherited by wives after their husbands' deaths) could not be sold, but "curtesy" property (inherited by husbands from their wives) could be sold. Furthermore, comparatively new concepts that developed in conjunction with the marriage contract, such as jointure, pin money, and separate maintenance, were compromised by peculiar rules. For instance, if a woman spent her pin money (money paid by the husband according to the marriage contract for the wife's personal items) on possessions other than clothes she could not sell them; in effect they belonged to her husband. In addition, a wife could sue for pin money only up to a year in arrears—which rendered a suit impractical. Similarly, separate maintenance allowances (stated sums of money for the wife's support if husband and wife agreed to live apart) were complicated by the fact that if a couple tried to agree in a marriage contract on an amount, they were admitting that a supposedly indissoluble bond could be dissolved, an assumption courts could not recognize. Eighteenth-century historians underplayed these inconsistencies, calling them "little contrarieties" that would soon vanish. Staves shows, however, that as judges gained power over decisions on marriage contracts, they tended to fall back on pre-1660 assumptions about property.

Staves' work on women's property has general implications for other studies about women in eighteenth-century England. Staves revises her previous claim that separate maintenance allowances proved the weakening of patriarchy; she now finds that an oversimplification. She also challenges the contention by historians Jeanne and Lawrence Stone that in the late eighteenth century wealthy men married widows less often than before because couples began marrying for love rather than for financial reasons. Staves does not completely undermine their contention, but she does counter their assumption that widows had more money than never-married women. She points out that jointure property (a widow's lifetime use of an amount of money specified in the marriage contract) was often lost on remarriage.
explanation_html:
Set the historical baseline first: before 1660 an English husband simply controlled his wife's property. As wealth shifted from land to commerce over the following century and a half, marriage took on some of the features of a contract, and Traditional Historians have read that shift as a gain for women, tied to new post-Restoration thinking about democracy and property. Staves arrives as the dissenting voice, and her claim is narrower than a flat denial: whatever gains marriage contracts briefly represented were then undone by judicial decisions about women's contractual rights. The disagreement is not over whether marriage contracts appeared, but over what they actually delivered once judges got hold of them.

The bulk of the passage is Staves' evidence, and one pattern runs through it: property definitions stayed inconsistent in ways that fell against women. Dower land, inherited by a widow, could not be sold, while curtesy property, inherited by a widower, could. Newer contractual devices came hedged with odd rules of their own. Pin money, the allowance a husband paid for his wife's personal purchases, bought possessions she could not resell unless they were clothes, so in effect they were his, and arrears could be claimed only a year back, which made suing pointless. Separate maintenance hit a deeper contradiction, since agreeing in advance on payments for living apart conceded that an indissoluble bond could dissolve. Eighteenth-Century Historians brushed all this aside as little contrarieties soon to vanish; Staves shows judges reverting to pre-1660 assumptions as their power grew.

Widening out, the final paragraph shows what Staves' findings do to neighboring scholarship, including her own. She retracts an earlier position, no longer treating separate maintenance allowances as proof that patriarchy was weakening, and now calls that reading an oversimplification. She also takes on Jeanne and Lawrence Stone, who explain the late-eighteenth-century decline in wealthy men marrying widows by a turn toward marrying for love rather than money. Notice how precisely the author limits the disagreement: Staves does not refute them outright, but she does undercut their assumption that widows had more money than never-married women, since jointure, a widow's lifetime use of a sum set in the marriage contract, was often lost on remarriage.
overall_html: The passage lays out Susan Staves' argument that the contractual features English marriage acquired after 1660 did not in fact improve women's property position, because inconsistent judicial definitions and awkward rules attached to devices such as dower, pin money, separate maintenance, and jointure repeatedly worked to women's disadvantage as judges fell back on older assumptions. The author's purpose is expository, setting Staves' thesis against the traditional historical view, working through her court-case evidence, and finally showing how her conclusions revise both her own earlier claim and the Stones' account of declining remarriage to widows. The viewpoints to track are the traditional historians, the eighteenth-century historians who minimized the inconsistencies, the Stones, and Staves herself.

The expansion of mass media has led to an explosion in news coverage of criminal activities to the point where it has become virtually impossible to find citizens who are unaware of the details of crimes committed in their communities. Since it is generally believed that people who know the facts of a case are more likely than those who do not to hold an opinion about the case, and that it is more desirable to empanel jurors who do not need to set aside personal prejudices in order to render a verdict, empaneling impartial juries has proven to be a daunting task in North American courts, particularly in trials involving issues or people of public interest.

Judges rely on several techniques to minimize partiality in the courtroom, including moving trials to new venues and giving specific instructions to juries. While many judges are convinced that these techniques work, many critics have concluded that they are ineffective. Change of venue, the critics argue, cannot shield potential jurors from pretrial publicity in widely reported cases. Nor, they claim, can judges' instructions to juries to ignore information learned outside the courtroom be relied upon; one critic characterizes such instruction as requiring of jurors "mental contortions which are beyond anyone's power to execute."

The remedy for partiality most favored by judges is voir dire, the questioning of potential jurors to determine whether they can be impartial. But critics charge that this method, too, is unreliable for a number of reasons. Some potential jurors, they argue, do not speak out during voir dire (French for "to speak the truth") because they are afraid to admit their prejudices, while others confess untruthfully to having prejudices as a way of avoiding jury duty. Moreover, some potential jurors underestimate their own knowledge, claiming ignorance of a case when they have read about it in newspapers or discussed it with friends. Finally, the critics argue, judges sometimes phrase questions in ways that indicate a desired response, and potential jurors simply answer accordingly.

These criticisms have been taken seriously enough by some countries that rely on juries, such as Canada and Great Britain, that they have abandoned voir dire except in unusual circumstances. But merely eliminating existing judicial remedies like voir dire does not really provide a solution to the problem of impartiality. It merely recognizes that the mass media have made total ignorance of criminal cases among jurors a virtual impossibility. But if a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community's collective experience; today, this experience includes exposure to mass media. Impartiality does not reside in the mind of any one juror; it instead results from a process of deliberation among the many members of a panel of informed, curious, and even opinionated people.
explanation_html:
The problem is framed as a collision between one fact and two assumptions. The fact is that media coverage of crime has become so thorough that virtually no citizen is unaware of the details of cases in their own community. The assumptions are that people who know the facts are likelier to have formed an opinion, and that jurors carrying no personal prejudice are preferable to jurors who must set one aside. Together they make impartial juries extremely hard to empanel, especially where the issues or the people involved attract public interest. Keep an eye on the second assumption, because the closing paragraph is going to overturn it.

Two remedies arrive together with the disagreement they provoke. The Judges move trials to new venues and instruct juries to disregard what they learned outside the courtroom, and many of them are convinced these measures work. The Critics conclude that they do not. A change of venue cannot outrun publicity in a widely reported case, and telling jurors to set aside outside information demands what one critic calls mental contortions no one can perform. Note the shape of this exchange, since the critics offer no replacement of their own; they argue only that the existing tools fail, and the same pattern repeats immediately.

Voir dire, the questioning of potential jurors about whether they can be impartial, is the remedy judges favor most and it draws the fullest attack. The critics list four ways it goes wrong. Some jurors will not admit prejudices they actually hold; others claim prejudices they lack in order to escape jury duty; some underestimate their own exposure, professing ignorance of a case they have read about or discussed with friends; and judges occasionally phrase questions so that the wanted answer is obvious, and receive it. Every objection concerns the reliability of what jurors say, whether the distortion comes from fear, self-interest, poor self-knowledge, or the questioner.

The final paragraph accepts the criticisms and then moves past them, which is where The Author finally speaks directly. Canada and Great Britain have found them persuasive enough to abandon voir dire except in unusual circumstances, but removing a remedy is not a solution; it merely concedes that total ignorance of criminal cases is no longer achievable. The positive claim reverses the assumption from the opening: a truly impartial jury should consist of informed citizens representing the community's collective experience, and that experience now includes exposure to mass media. Impartiality belongs to no individual juror, arising instead from deliberation among many informed, curious, even opinionated people.
overall_html: The passage argues that jury impartiality should be understood as a product of collective deliberation rather than as the absence of knowledge or opinion in any individual juror. The author's purpose is to reframe a problem, first explaining why saturating media coverage makes traditionally impartial juries nearly impossible to assemble, then reporting the critics' case that the judges' remedies of changed venue, cautionary instruction, and voir dire are all unreliable, and finally rejecting the response of simply abandoning those remedies. The viewpoints to track are the judges who trust their techniques, the critics who dismiss them without proposing a replacement, and the author, who accepts much of the criticism but draws a constructive conclusion from it.

Personal names are generally regarded by European thinkers in two major ways, both of which deny that names have any significant semantic content. In philosophy and linguistics, John Stuart Mill's formulation that "proper names are meaningless marks set upon . . . persons to distinguish them from one another" retains currency; in anthropology, Claude Lévi-Strauss's characterization of names as being primarily instruments of social classification has been very influential. Consequently, interpretation of personal names in societies where names have other functions and meanings has been neglected. Among the Hopi of the southwestern United States, names often refer to historical or ritual events in order both to place individuals within society and to confer an identity upon them. Furthermore, the images used to evoke these events suggest that Hopi names can be seen as a type of poetic composition.

Throughout life, Hopis receive several names in a sequence of ritual initiations. Birth, entry into one of the ritual societies during childhood, and puberty are among the name-giving occasions. Names are conferred by an adult member of a clan other than the child's clan, and names refer to that name giver's clan, sometimes combining characteristics of the clan's totem animal with the child's characteristics. Thus, a name might translate to something as simple as "little rabbit," which reflects both the child's size and the representative animal.

More often, though, the name giver has in mind a specific event that is not apparent in a name's literal translation. One Lizard clan member from the village of Oraibi is named Lomayayva, "beautifully ascended." This translation, however, tells nothing about either the event referred to—who or what ascended—or the name giver's clan. The name giver in this case is from Badger clan. Badger clan is responsible for an annual ceremony featuring a procession in which masked representations of spirits climb the mesa on which Oraibi sits. Combining the name giver's clan association with the receiver's home village, "beautifully ascended" refers to the splendid colors and movements of the procession up the mesa. The condensed image this name evokes—a typical feature of Hopi personal names—displays the same quality of Western Apache place names that led one commentator to call them "tiny imagist poems."

Hopi personal names do several things simultaneously. They indicate social relationships—but only indirectly—and they individuate persons. Equally important, though, is their poetic quality; in a sense they can be understood as oral texts that produce aesthetic delight. This view of Hopi names is thus opposed not only to Mill's claim that personal names are without inherent meaning but also to Lévi-Strauss's purely functional characterization. Interpreters must understand Hopi clan structures and linguistic practices in order to discern the beauty and significance of Hopi names.
explanation_html:
A field's default assumptions are laid out so that they can be overturned. European Thinkers treat personal names in two ways, and both deny that names carry meaning: Mill's formulation, still current in philosophy and linguistics, makes proper names meaningless marks that distinguish one person from another, while Lévi-Strauss's influential anthropological account makes them instruments of social classification. The cost of these positions is that names with other functions have gone uninterpreted. The Author puts the Hopi forward as the counterexample, since their names refer to historical or ritual events, at once placing a person within society and conferring an identity, and the imagery involved makes them a kind of poetry.

The mechanics of naming come first, and they are more specific than they might seem. A Hopi receives several names across a lifetime, each tied to a ritual initiation such as birth, entry into a ritual society in childhood, or puberty. The giver is always an adult from a clan other than the child's, and the name refers back to the giver's clan, often blending a characteristic of that clan's totem animal with a characteristic of the child. A name meaning little rabbit works exactly this way, catching the child's size and the representative animal together. Treat this as the simple case, because the paragraph that follows presents the more usual one.

Most names conceal more than they reveal, and this example shows how much interpretive work they demand. Lomayayva, borne by a Lizard clan member from the village of Oraibi, translates as beautifully ascended, which on its own identifies neither what ascended nor which clan supplied the name. The giver belongs to Badger clan, which stages an annual ceremony where masked representations of spirits climb the mesa Oraibi sits on. Combine the giver's clan with the receiver's village and the name turns out to evoke the colors and movement of that procession. The author calls such compression typical and connects it to Western Apache place names once described as tiny imagist poems.

Everything is gathered in the closing paragraph, where the argument is stated outright. Hopi names do indicate social relationships, though only indirectly, and they do individuate people, which is what the European accounts would lead you to expect. What those accounts cannot accommodate is the third function, the poetic one, since these names operate as short oral texts that produce aesthetic delight. That makes the author's position a rejection of both earlier views at once, Mill's denial of inherent meaning and Lévi-Strauss's purely functional reading. A practical consequence follows: an interpreter must know Hopi clan structure and linguistic practice before a name's beauty becomes visible.
overall_html: The passage argues that Hopi personal names carry real semantic and poetic content, referring to historical or ritual events through condensed images that only knowledge of clan structure and language can unpack. The author's purpose is to challenge two established European positions, Mill's view that proper names are meaningless marks and Lévi-Strauss's view that they are instruments of social classification, moving from those claims to the mechanics of Hopi ritual naming, then to a worked example in which beautifully ascended proves to describe a Badger clan procession up the mesa at Oraibi, and finally to the conclusion that such names are best read as oral poetry. The viewpoints in play are the European thinkers and the author who answers them.

Homing pigeons can be taken from their lofts and transported hundreds of kilometers in covered cages to unfamiliar sites and yet, when released, be able to choose fairly accurate homeward bearings within a minute and fly home. Aside from reading the minds of the experimenters (a possibility that has not escaped investigation), there are two basic explanations for the remarkable ability of pigeons to "home": the birds might keep track of their outward displacement (the system of many short-range species such as honeybees); or they might have some sense, known as a "map sense," that would permit them to construct an internal image of their environment and then "place" themselves with respect to home on some internalized coordinate system.

The first alternative seems unlikely. One possible model for such an inertial system might involve an internal magnetic compass to measure the directional leg of each journey. Birds transported to the release site wearing magnets or otherwise subjected to an artificial magnetic field, however, are only occasionally affected. Alternately, if pigeons measure their displacement by consciously keeping track of the direction and degree of acceleration and deceleration of the various turns, and timing the individual legs of the journey, simply transporting them in the dark, with constant rotations, or under complete anesthesia ought to impair or eliminate their ability to orient. These treatments, however, have no effect. Unfortunately, no one has yet performed the crucial experiment of transporting pigeons in total darkness, anesthetized, rotating, and with the magnetic field reversed all at the same time.

The other alternative, that pigeons have a "map sense," seems more promising, yet the nature of this sense remains mysterious. Papi has posited that the map sense is olfactory: that birds come to associate odors borne on the wind with the direction in which the wind is blowing, and so slowly build up an olfactory map of their surroundings. When transported to the release site, then, they only have to sniff the air en route and/or at the site to know the direction of home. Papi conducted a series of experiments showing that pigeons whose nostrils have been plugged are poorly oriented at release and home slowly.

One problem with the hypothesis is that Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips failed to detect any ability in pigeons to distinguish natural air (presumably laden with olfactory map information) from pure, filtered air. Papi's experimental results, moreover, admit of simpler, nonolfactory explanations. It seems likely that the behavior of nostril-plugged birds results from the distracting and traumatic nature of the experiment. When nasal tubes are used to bypass the olfactory chamber but allow for comfortable breathing, no disorientation is evident. Likewise, when the olfactory epithelium is sprayed with anesthetic to block smell-detection but not breathing, orientation is normal.
explanation_html:
The puzzle and the two candidate answers arrive together. Carry a homing pigeon hundreds of kilometers in a covered cage to a place it has never seen, release it, and within a minute it chooses a fairly accurate bearing for home. Setting aside the possibility that the birds read the experimenters' minds, which the author notes drily has actually been investigated, either a pigeon keeps track of its outward displacement as it travels, the method short-range species such as honeybees use, or it has a map sense, an internal image of its environment that lets it place itself relative to home on some internal coordinate system. The passage takes these in turn.

Displacement tracking is dismissed, and the reasoning is entirely experimental. If a bird measured the direction of each leg with an internal magnetic compass, then fitting it with magnets or subjecting it to an artificial magnetic field ought to disrupt it, and only occasionally does. If instead it consciously registered turns, accelerations, decelerations, and elapsed time, then carrying it in darkness, rotating it constantly, or anesthetizing it should impair its orientation, and none of these treatments has any effect. The author ends on an honest caveat rather than a flourish: nobody has yet combined darkness, anesthesia, rotation, and a reversed magnetic field in a single crucial experiment.

Attention shifts to the more promising option, though notice that the author calls the map sense mysterious rather than established. Papi supplies the leading version of it, an olfactory map: birds come to associate odors carried on the wind with the direction that wind blows from, gradually assembling a smell-based picture of their surroundings. On that account a displaced pigeon need only sample the air along the way or at the release site to work out where home lies. Papi's supporting work is a series of experiments showing that pigeons with plugged nostrils orient poorly on release and take a long time to get home.

The Author raises two difficulties, and the second does the real damage. First, Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips could detect no ability in pigeons even to distinguish natural air, supposedly loaded with olfactory map information, from pure filtered air. Second, Papi's own results admit of a simpler explanation having nothing to do with smell, since plugging a bird's nostrils is distracting and traumatic in itself. Two controls make that case: nasal tubes that bypass the olfactory chamber while allowing comfortable breathing produce no disorientation, and anesthetic sprayed on the olfactory epithelium to block smell without blocking breathing leaves orientation normal.
overall_html: The passage examines how homing pigeons navigate from unfamiliar release sites, weighs the two available explanations, and finds neither established: tracking the outward journey is ruled out by experiments in which magnets, darkness, rotation, and anesthesia leave the birds unaffected, while the more promising map sense remains poorly understood. The author's purpose is to evaluate competing hypotheses, and the second half concentrates on Papi's proposal that the map is built from odors carried on the wind, undercut both by the failure of Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips to show that pigeons distinguish natural from filtered air and by controls suggesting nostril-plugged birds are merely traumatized. The viewpoints are Papi's and the author's skeptical assessment of it.

Freud's essay on "The Uncanny" can be said to have defined, for our century, what literary criticism once called the Sublime. This apprehension of a beyond or of a dæmonic—a sense of transcendence—appears in literature or life, according to Freud, when we feel that something uncanny is being represented, or conjured up, or at least intimated. Freud locates the source of the uncanny in our tendency to believe in the "omnipotence of thought," that is, in the power of our own or of others' minds over the natural world. The uncanny is, thus, a return to animistic conceptions of the universe, and is produced by the psychic defense mechanisms Freud called repression.

It would have seemed likely for Freud to find his literary instances of the uncanny, or at least some of them, in fairy tales, since as much as any other fictions they seem to be connected with repressed desires and archaic forms of thought. But Freud specifically excluded fairy tales from the realm of the uncanny. "Who would be so bold," Freud asks, "as to call it an uncanny moment, for instance, when Snow White opens her eyes once more?" Why not? Because, he goes on to say, in those stories everything is possible, so nothing is incredible, and, therefore, no conflicts in the reader's judgment are provoked. Thus Freud, alas, found fairy tales to be unsuited to his own analysis.

However, the psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim, with a kind of wise innocence, has subjected fairy tales to very close, generally orthodox, and wholly reductive Freudian interpretations. Bettelheim's book, although written in apparent ignorance of the vast critical traditions of interpreting literary romance, is nevertheless a splendid achievement, brimming with useful ideas and insights into how young children read and understand.

Bruno Bettelheim's major therapeutic concern has been with autistic children, so inevitably his interpretive activity is directed against a child's tendency to withdraw defensively or abnormally. According to Bettelheim, a child's desperate isolation, loneliness, and inarticulate anxieties are addressed directly by fairy tales. By telling the child such stories themselves, parents strengthen the therapeutic effect of fairy tales, for in the telling, parents impart to the child their approval of the stories.

But why should fairy tales, in themselves, be therapeutic? Bettelheim's answer depends on the child's being an interpreter: "The fairy tale is therapeutic because children find their own solutions, through contemplating what the story seems to imply about their inner conflicts at this moment in their lives." Bettelheim proceeds on the basis of two complementary assumptions: that children will interpret a story benignly, for their own good; and that Freudian interpretations will yield an accurate account of children's interpretations. The child, questing for help, and the analyst, attempting to find helpful patterns in the stories, thus read alike, though in different vocabularies.
explanation_html:
The opening establishes Freud's claim and what it displaced. His essay on the uncanny, we are told, gave this century its version of what criticism once called the Sublime, a sense of something beyond or demonic, an apprehension of transcendence. For Freud that sensation arises in life or literature whenever something uncanny is represented, conjured, or merely intimated, and its source is a lingering belief in the omnipotence of thought, the notion that minds can act on the natural world. The uncanny is therefore a return to animistic ways of seeing the universe, produced by the defense mechanism Freud named repression.

Fairy tales look like Freud's obvious material, since they connect as directly as any fiction to repressed desires and archaic forms of thought, and The Author raises that expectation on purpose before reporting that Freud specifically excluded them. Freud's own instance is Snow White opening her eyes, which he declines to call an uncanny moment. His reason is that in such stories anything is possible, so nothing seems incredible and no conflict of judgment is provoked in the reader. The author's 'alas' is the tell here, marking the exclusion as a loss and opening the space the rest of the passage will fill.

Bettelheim steps into exactly that space, doing to fairy tales what Freud declined to do. His readings are close, orthodox in their Freudianism, and, in the author's own word, wholly reductive, and he seems unaware of the long critical tradition of interpreting literary romance. The verdict nonetheless comes out generous: the book is called a splendid achievement, full of useful ideas and insights into how young children read and understand. Hold on to that mixed assessment, since the praise and the reservation are being offered together, and the paragraphs following set out what Bettelheim actually argues.

Bettelheim's clinical history is offered as the key to his approach. He has worked chiefly with autistic children, so his interpretation is aimed against a child's tendency to withdraw defensively or abnormally. On his account fairy tales speak directly to a child's desperate isolation, loneliness, and anxieties the child cannot articulate. A second element of the therapy is easy to skim past, namely the telling itself: when parents tell these stories to the child, they convey their approval of them, and that approval strengthens whatever therapeutic work the stories do.

The question left hanging is pressed here, since it is not obvious why the stories themselves should heal anything. Bettelheim's answer turns the child into an interpreter, finding personal solutions by contemplating what a story seems to imply about the conflicts alive in that child at that moment. The author then exposes the two assumptions propping the answer up: that children will read a story benignly, for their own good, and that Freudian interpretation accurately captures what children make of it. The result is a neat symmetry, with child and analyst reading alike while speaking different vocabularies.
overall_html: The passage moves from Freud's account of the uncanny as a return of animistic belief in the omnipotence of thought, through his refusal to count fairy tales as uncanny on the grounds that their unlimited possibility provokes no conflict of judgment, to Bettelheim's thoroughly Freudian reading of that very material as therapy for children's unspoken anxieties. The author's purpose is expository and evaluative, presenting Bettelheim's work as a valuable if reductive achievement resting on two assumptions, that children interpret stories for their own good and that Freudian analysis captures what children actually do. The three positions to keep apart are Freud's, Bettelheim's, and the author's mixed assessment of both.

Some Native American tribes have had difficulty establishing their land claims because the United States government did not recognize their status as tribes; therefore during the 1970s some Native Americans attempted to obtain such recognition through the medium of U.S. courts. In presenting these suits, Native Americans had to operate within a particular sphere of U.S. government procedure, that of its legal system, and their arguments were necessarily interpreted by the courts in terms the law could understand: e.g., through application of precedent or review of evidence. This process brought to light some of the differing perceptions and definitions that can exist between cultures whose systems of discourse are sometimes at variance.

In one instance, the entire legal dispute turned on whether the suing community—a group of Mashpee Wampanoag in the town of Mashpee, Massachusetts—constituted a tribe. The area had long been occupied by the Mashpee, who continued to have control over land use after the town's incorporation. But in the 1960s, after an influx of non-Mashpee people shifted the balance of political power in the town, the new residents were able to buy Mashpee-controlled land from the town and develop it for commercial or private use. The Mashpee's 1976 suit claimed that these lands were taken in violation of a statute prohibiting transfers of land from any tribe of Native Americans without federal approval. The town argued that the Mashpee were not a tribe in the sense intended by the statute and so were outside its protection. As a result, the Mashpee were required to demonstrate their status as a tribe according to a definition contained in an earlier ruling: a body of Native Americans "governing themselves under one leadership and inhabiting a particular territory."

The town claimed that the Mashpee were not self-governing and that they had no defined territory: the Mashpee could legally be self-governing, the town argued, only if they could show written documentation of such a system, and could legally inhabit territory only if they had precisely delineated its boundaries and possessed a deed to it. The Mashpee marshaled oral testimony against these claims, arguing that what the town perceived as a lack of evidence was simply information that an oral culture such as the Mashpee's would not have recorded in writing. In this instance, the disjunction between U.S. legal discourse and Mashpee culture—exemplified in the court's inability to "understand" the Mashpee's oral testimony as documentary evidence—rendered the suit unsuccessful. Similar claims have recently met with greater success, however, as U.S. courts have begun to acknowledge that the failure to accommodate differences in discourse between cultures can sometimes stand in the way of guaranteeing the fairness of legal decisions.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out a procedural trap. Some Native American tribes could not press land claims because the federal government did not recognize them as tribes, so during the 1970s several went to court to win that recognition. Going to court meant entering one particular arena of U.S. government procedure, where a claim only counts once it is restated in the terms the law handles — precedent, documentary evidence, formal definition. The Author is not simply narrating litigation; the thesis is that this translation exposes real differences in perception and definition between cultures whose systems of discourse do not line up.

The Mashpee case makes that abstract point concrete, and the whole dispute reduces to one question: were the Mashpee a tribe? They had long occupied the area and kept control over land use even after the town of Mashpee was incorporated. In the 1960s an influx of newcomers tipped the town's political balance, and those residents bought Mashpee-controlled land from the town and developed it. The 1976 suit invoked a statute barring transfers of tribal land without federal approval. The Town replied that the Mashpee were not a tribe in the statute's sense, which shifted the burden onto them to satisfy an earlier ruling's definition: self-governing under one leadership, inhabiting a particular territory.

The closing paragraph shows the definition being applied in a way the Mashpee could not meet. The Town read both halves of it as demands for paper, arguing that self-government required written documentation and that inhabiting territory required delineated boundaries and a deed. The Mashpee answered with oral testimony, pointing out that the missing records were exactly what an oral culture would never have produced in writing. Because the court could not treat that testimony as documentary evidence, the suit failed. The author closes on movement rather than defeat: similar claims have fared better as courts begin to recognize that ignoring differences in discourse can compromise fairness.
overall_html: The passage uses the Mashpee Wampanoag land suit to argue that when a claim from an oral culture is forced into the categories of the U.S. legal system, the mismatch between systems of discourse can itself determine the outcome. The author's purpose is illustrative and mildly critical, moving from the general problem of court-sought tribal recognition, to the specific dispute over whether the Mashpee met a legal definition of tribe, to the evidentiary demand for written proof that an oral culture could not supply, and finally to a note that courts have since grown more accommodating. The positions to track are the Mashpee, the Town, and the author's own framing of the clash as one of discourse rather than fact.

Long after the lava has cooled, the effects of a major volcanic eruption may linger on. In the atmosphere a veil of fine dust and sulfuric acid droplets can spread around the globe and persist for years. Researchers have generally thought that this veil can block enough sunlight to have a chilling influence on Earth's climate. Many blame the cataclysmic eruption of the Indonesian volcano Tambora in 1815 for the ensuing "year without a summer" of 1816—when parts of the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada were hit by snowstorms in June and frosts in August.

The volcano-climate connection seems plausible, but, say scientists Clifford Mass and David Portman, it is not as strong as previously believed. Mass and Portman analyzed global temperature data for the years before and after nine volcanic eruptions, from Krakatau in 1883 to El Chichón in 1982. In the process they tried to filter out temperature changes caused by the cyclic weather phenomenon known as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, which warms the sea surface in the equatorial Pacific and thereby warms the atmosphere. Such warming can mask the cooling brought about by an eruption, but it can also mimic volcanic cooling if the volcano happens to erupt just as an El Niño-induced warm period is beginning to fade.

Once El Niño effects had been subtracted from the data, the actual effects of the eruptions came through more clearly. Contrary to what earlier studies had suggested, Mass and Portman found that minor eruptions have no discernible effect on temperature. And major, dust-spitting explosions, such as Krakatau or El Chichón, cause a smaller drop than expected in the average temperature in the hemisphere (Northern or Southern) of the eruption—only half a degree centigrade or less—with a correspondingly smaller drop in the opposite hemisphere.

Other researchers, however, have argued that even a small temperature drop could result in a significant regional fluctuation in climate if its effects were amplified by climatic feedback loops. For example, a small temperature drop in the northeastern U.S. and southeastern Canada in early spring might delay the melting of snow, and the unmelted snow would continue to reflect sunlight away from the surface, amplifying the cooling. The cool air over the region could, in turn, affect the jet stream. The jet stream tends to flow at the boundary between cool northern air and warm southern air, drawing its power from the sharp temperature contrast and the consequent difference in pressure. An unusual cooling in the region could cause the stream to wander farther south than normal, allowing more polar air to come in behind it and deepen the region's cold snap. Through such a series of feedbacks a small temperature drop could be blown up into a year without a summer.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the standard picture. After an eruption ends, a veil of fine dust and sulfuric acid droplets can circle the globe and hang there for years, and researchers have generally held that this veil blocks enough sunlight to cool the planet. The example supplied is the one the passage will eventually return to: Tambora's enormous 1815 eruption in Indonesia, widely blamed for the 1816 'year without a summer', when the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada got snow in June and frost in August. Treat this paragraph as the claim under review rather than the author's own position.

The challenge arrives immediately. Mass and Portman accept that the volcano-climate link is plausible but argue it is weaker than previously believed, and the paragraph is mostly about their method, which matters for the result. They examined global temperature data before and after nine eruptions, from Krakatau in 1883 to El Chichon in 1982, and worked to strip out the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a cyclic warming of the equatorial Pacific sea surface that warms the atmosphere with it. Notice why this cuts both ways: such warming can hide an eruption's cooling, and a fading warm period can also imitate cooling that the volcano did not cause.

With El Nino subtracted, the numbers shift in two ways, both of them deflating. Minor eruptions turn out to have no detectable effect on temperature at all, which contradicts what earlier studies had suggested. Even the big dust-throwing explosions like Krakatau and El Chichon produce less than expected, dropping the average temperature by only about half a degree centigrade or less in their own hemisphere, and by less still in the other one. The finding is quantitative rather than absolute: volcanoes do cool the climate, but by an amount too small to carry the weight the opening paragraph's story placed on it.

A rebuttal closes the passage. Other researchers grant the small drop but argue that climatic feedback loops can amplify it into a large regional swing. The worked example follows the causal chain carefully. A slight early-spring chill in the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada delays snowmelt, and the lingering snow reflects sunlight away, deepening the cooling. The cooler air then reaches the jet stream, which runs along the boundary between cool northern and warm southern air and is driven by that temperature contrast; unusual cooling pushes it farther south, letting polar air follow. Stack those effects and a half-degree becomes a year without a summer.

The positions to keep distinct are the researchers who generally credited the volcano-climate link, Mass and Portman, and the other researchers who invoke amplification.
