Countee Cullen (Countee Leroy Porter, 1903–1946) was one of the foremost poets of the Harlem Renaissance, the movement of African American writers, musicians, and artists centered in the Harlem section of New York City during the 1920s. Beginning with his university years, Cullen strove to establish himself as an author of romantic poetry on abstract, universal topics such as love and death. Believing poetry should consist of "lofty thoughts beautifully expressed," Cullen preferred controlled poetic forms. He used European forms such as sonnets and devices such as quatrains, couplets, and conventional rhyme, and he frequently employed classical allusions and Christian religious imagery, which were most likely the product both of his university education and of his upbringing as the adopted son of a Methodist Episcopal reverend.

Some literary critics have praised Cullen's skill at writing European-style verse, finding, for example, in "The Ballad of the Brown Girl" an artful use of diction and a rhythm and sonority that allow him to capture the atmosphere typical of the English ballad form of past centuries. Others have found Cullen's use of European verse forms and techniques unsuited to treating political or racial themes, such as the themes in "Uncle Jim," in which a young man is told by his uncle of the different experiences of African Americans and whites in United States society, or "Incident," which relates the experience of an eight-year-old child who hears a racial slur. One such critic has complained that Cullen's persona as expressed in his work sometimes seems to vacillate between aesthete and spokesperson for racial issues. But Cullen himself rejected this dichotomy, maintaining that his interest in romantic poetry was quite compatible with his concern over racial issues. He drew a distinction between poetry of solely political intent and his own work, which he believed reflected his identity as an African American. As the heartfelt expression of his personality accomplished by means of careful attention to his chosen craft, his work could not help but do so.

Explicit references to racial matters do in fact decline in Cullen's later work, but not because he felt any less passionately about these matters. Rather, Cullen increasingly focused on the religious dimension of his poetry. In "The Black Christ," in which the poet imagines the death and resurrection of a rural African American, and "Heritage," which expresses the tension between the poet's identification with Christian traditions and his desire to stay close to his African heritage, Cullen's thoughts on race were subsumed within what he conceived of as broader and more urgent questions about the suffering and redemption of the soul. Nonetheless, Cullen never abandoned his commitment to the importance of racial issues, reflecting on one occasion that he felt "actuated by a strong sense of race consciousness" that "grows upon me, I find, as I grow older."
explanation_html:
The first paragraph establishes who Cullen was and what he was after. A leading poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the 1920s flowering of African American writing, music and art centered in Harlem, Cullen set out from his university years to write romantic poetry on universal abstractions such as love and death. His conception of the art, poetry as lofty thoughts beautifully expressed, drew him toward controlled forms, so he worked in European sonnets and used quatrains, couplets and conventional rhyme. The classical allusions and Christian imagery running through the work are traced to two sources, his university education and his upbringing as the adopted son of a Methodist Episcopal reverend.

A critical debate occupies the middle, and it holds three positions that need keeping apart. Some critics admire his handling of European verse, praising the diction, rhythm and sonority of 'The Ballad of the Brown Girl' for catching the atmosphere of the old English ballad. Other critics judge those inherited forms unsuited to political or racial subjects, of the sort found in a poem about an uncle explaining how differently African Americans and whites are treated, or another about a child who hears a racial slur, and one such critic complains that Cullen's persona wavers between aesthete and racial spokesperson. Cullen rejected that dichotomy outright, insisting his romantic interests and his racial concerns were compatible and separating poetry of purely political intent from work that expressed his identity because it expressed his personality with craft.

What remains is a fact that could look like retreat, and the last paragraph explains it away. Explicit references to race do decline in the later poetry, but not, the passage insists, because Cullen's feeling had cooled; the cause is an increasing focus on religion. In 'The Black Christ', which imagines the death and resurrection of a rural African American, and 'Heritage', which sets his attachment to Christian tradition against his pull toward African origins, racial thought is folded into larger questions of suffering and redemption. The closing remark blocks the wrong inference, since Cullen described a race consciousness that only grew as he aged.
overall_html: The passage presents Countee Cullen as a Harlem Renaissance poet committed to traditional European forms and universal romantic subjects, sets out the critical dispute over whether such forms can carry racial themes, and argues that his later turn toward religious subject matter absorbed rather than abandoned his racial concerns. The author's purpose is to characterize and defend a poet's development, moving from his formative influences and formal preferences, to the divided critical response and Cullen's own rejection of the aesthete-versus-spokesperson dichotomy, and finally to evidence that his commitment to racial issues persisted to the end. Keep Cullen, the critics who admire his craft, and the critics who question his forms distinct.

The following passage was written in the mid-1990s.

The demand for electricity in certain countries has been projected recently to grow by 50 percent by the year 2010. Unfortunately, the increased use of fossil fuels to generate this electricity may ultimately damage human and environmental health. For example, emissions of air pollutants in these countries are expected to double over the next 25 years, even if energy is used efficiently, so that local urban air quality will likely deteriorate. Renewable sources of electricity, such as solar radiation, wind, and waterpower, are possible solutions to the problems caused by increasing demand for electricity. Unlike fossil fuels, renewable energy sources are available in virtually all geographic regions, and they allow electricity production without dangerous environmental pollutants. Additionally, these sources can usually be located closer to consumers than can plants that use fossil fuels, thus reducing transmission and distribution costs. Technologies for the successful long-term exploitation of these resources, however, are not always implemented successfully.

In rural Brazil, for example, millions of citizens do not have electricity, and the lack of necessary infrastructure has limited efforts to provide it. In 1992, an energy agency from the United States developed a joint project with two Brazilian states to install 800 household solar electrical systems and train local personnel to service them. Under the project's terms, local utilities install, maintain, and own the systems, and collect fees from users. Backers hoped the project would attract enough private investment for substantial expansion throughout Brazil. But the project directors rejected the relatively high bids of local Brazilian companies to produce the solar collectors and thus missed an opportunity to stimulate local production. Consequently, a short-term savings in start-up costs precluded the long-term benefits deriving from the development of local production capacity and technological skill, which eventually would have led to independence from costly foreign expertise. As a result, participating utilities can generate only enough income to cover operating and maintenance costs, which makes further investment and expansion unlikely. Thus, the movement toward a sustainable, rural electricity system in Brazil remains stalled.

But some efforts have avoided these pitfalls. In the mid-1980s, a Danish energy agency helped agencies in India build three modern wind turbine plants and gradually develop local technical capacity. Local participants were trained in planning, operation, maintenance, and construction of turbines. Indian firms subsequently began manufacturing turbines and, as more locally manufactured equipment became available, Indian utilities were able to increase their use of wind energy profitably. The success of these small projects spurred enthusiasm; Indian utilities were soon ordering more equipment and private investment in wind energy surged. Because the Danish agency, unlike its U.S. counterpart, recognized the importance of local involvement at all levels, the project has a good chance of remaining competitive and profitable for the long run.
explanation_html:
The opening frames a problem and its proposed solution before hinting at the passage's real subject. Electricity demand in certain countries is projected to rise by half by 2010, and meeting that with fossil fuels threatens human and environmental health, with pollutant emissions expected to double over twenty-five years even where energy is used efficiently. Renewables such as sunlight, wind and waterpower answer several difficulties at once, being available in virtually every region, producing power without dangerous pollutants, and sitting nearer consumers so that transmission and distribution cost less. Watch the pivot in the last sentence, since what follows is not about the technologies themselves but about whether they get implemented well.

Brazil supplies the negative case. Millions of rural Brazilians have no electricity and little infrastructure to deliver it, so in 1992 a United States energy agency joined with two Brazilian states to install 800 household solar systems and train local people to service them, with local utilities owning, installing and maintaining the equipment and collecting fees. The hope was that private investment would follow and the model would spread. The damaging decision was to reject the relatively high bids from Brazilian firms to make the solar collectors. Saving money at the start cost the country a domestic manufacturing base and the technical skill that would eventually have ended its dependence on costly foreign expertise, and utilities now earn only enough to cover operations, so expansion has stalled.

India supplies the contrast, and the comparison is the whole point. In the mid-1980s a Danish agency helped Indian agencies build three modern wind turbine plants while deliberately developing local capability, training participants in planning, operation, maintenance and construction. Indian firms then began manufacturing turbines themselves, and as domestically made equipment became available utilities could expand wind power profitably, which brought further orders and a surge of private investment. The verdict is stated outright and names the difference: because the Danish agency, unlike its United States counterpart, recognized that local involvement mattered at every level, the project stands a good chance of remaining competitive and profitable.
overall_html: The passage argues that renewable sources can meet rising electricity demand without the health and environmental damage of fossil fuels, but that whether such projects last depends on building local manufacturing and technical capacity rather than merely installing equipment. The author's purpose is to draw that practical lesson by comparison, opening with the case for renewables and the caveat that the technologies are not always implemented successfully, then setting a failed solar project in rural Brazil, where cheaper foreign collectors displaced local producers and expansion stalled, against a Danish-assisted wind program in India that trained local participants and prompted domestic manufacture, investment and growth. The evaluation throughout is the author's own.

Although philanthropy—the volunteering of private resources for humanitarian purposes—reached its apex in England in the late nineteenth century, modern commentators have articulated two major criticisms of the philanthropy that was a mainstay of England's middle-class Victorian society. The earlier criticism is that such philanthropy was even by the later nineteenth century obsolete, since industrialism had already created social problems that were beyond the scope of small, private voluntary efforts. Indeed, these problems required substantial legislative action by the state. Unemployment, for example, was not the result of a failure of diligence on the part of workers or a failure of compassion on the part of employers, nor could it be solved by well-wishing philanthropists.

The more recent charge holds that Victorian philanthropy was by its very nature a self-serving exercise carried out by philanthropists at the expense of those whom they were ostensibly serving. In this view, philanthropy was a means of flaunting one's power and position in a society that placed great emphasis on status, or even a means of cultivating social connections that could lead to economic rewards. Further, if philanthropy is seen as serving the interests of individual philanthropists, so it may be seen as serving the interests of their class. According to this "social control" thesis, philanthropists, in professing to help the poor, were encouraging in them such values as prudence, thrift, and temperance, values perhaps worthy in themselves but also designed to create more productive members of the labor force. Philanthropy, in short, was a means of controlling the labor force and ensuring the continued dominance of the management class.

Modern critics of Victorian philanthropy often use the words "amateurish" or "inadequate" to describe Victorian philanthropy, as though Victorian charity can only be understood as an antecedent to the era of state-sponsored, professionally administered charity. This assumption is typical of the "Whig fallacy": the tendency to read the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present. If most Victorians resisted state control and expended their resources on private, voluntary philanthropies, it could only be, the argument goes, because of their commitment to a vested interest, or because the administrative apparatus of the state was incapable of coping with the economic and social needs of the time.

This version of history patronizes the Victorians, who were in fact well aware of their vulnerability to charges of condescension and complacency, but were equally well aware of the potential dangers of state-managed charity. They were perhaps condescending to the poor, but—to use an un-Victorian metaphor—they put their money where their mouths were, and gave of their careers and lives as well.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by naming its target: two criticisms modern commentators level at Victorian philanthropy, meaning the middle-class habit of volunteering private resources for humanitarian ends, which peaked in late nineteenth-century England. The earlier critics hold that the practice was already obsolete by that point, since industrialism had produced social problems far too large for small voluntary efforts and demanding substantial legislation instead. Unemployment is the example, and notice how carefully it is framed: it arose neither from workers lacking diligence nor from employers lacking compassion, so no amount of goodwill from philanthropists could have solved it.

The second charge cuts harder because it questions motive rather than adequacy. The recent critics treat Victorian philanthropy as self-serving, a way of flaunting power and position in a society preoccupied with status, or of cultivating connections that paid off economically. Their argument then scales up from the individual to the class. On the social control thesis, urging prudence, thrift and temperance on the poor, whatever those virtues are worth in themselves, conveniently manufactured a more productive workforce, so charity worked as a means of controlling labor and keeping the management class dominant.

Here the author starts pushing back, and the target is the assumption underneath the criticism rather than any particular claim within it. Describing Victorian charity as amateurish or inadequate presumes it can only be judged as a rough draft of today's professional, state-administered welfare. The author gives that habit a name, the Whig fallacy, the tendency to read the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present. Under that assumption, Victorian resistance to state control must be explained away as devotion to a vested interest or as the state's administrative incapacity, never as a position arrived at deliberately.

Judgment comes in the short closing paragraph. Such history patronizes the Victorians, who were entirely conscious of how they might look, alive both to the charges of condescension and complacency they invited and to the dangers of charity managed by the state. The concession is genuine, since the author grants that they probably were condescending toward the poor, but the defense is that they backed their convictions with their money and with their careers and lives as well. What distinguishes them from their critics, on this account, is commitment rather than sophistication.
overall_html: The passage sets out two modern criticisms of Victorian philanthropy, that it was obsolete against industrial-scale social problems and that it was a self-serving instrument of social control, and then defends the Victorians by attacking the assumption underlying such criticism. The author's purpose is corrective: after presenting each charge in its own terms, the argument identifies the Whig fallacy, the habit of reading the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present, and points out that Victorians consciously weighed the dangers of state-managed charity and committed their money, careers and lives to the alternative. Keep the earlier critics, the recent critics with their social control thesis, and the author's defense separate.

Most of what has been written about Thurgood Marshall, a former United States Supreme Court justice who served from 1967 to 1991, has just focused on his judicial record and on the ideological content of his earlier achievements as a lawyer pursuing civil rights issues in the courts. But when Marshall's career is viewed from a technical perspective, his work with the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) reveals a strategic and methodological legacy to the field of public interest law. Though the NAACP, under Marshall's direction, was not the first legal organization in the U.S. to be driven by a political and social agenda, he and the NAACP developed innovations that forever changed the landscape of public interest law: during the 1940s and 1950s, in their campaign against state-sanctioned racial segregation, Marshall and the NAACP, instead of simply pursuing cases as the opportunity arose, set up a predetermined legal campaign that was meticulously crafted and carefully coordinated.

One aspect of this campaign, the test case strategy, involved sponsoring litigation of tactically chosen cases at the trial court level with careful evaluation of the precedential nuances and potential impact of each decision. This allowed Marshall to try out different approaches and discover which was the best to be used. An essential element in the success of this tactic was the explicit recognition that in a public interest legal campaign, choosing the right plaintiff can mean the difference between success and failure. Marshall carefully selected cases with sympathetic litigants, whose public appeal, credibility, and commitment to the NAACP's goals were unsurpassed.

In addition, Marshall used sociological and psychological statistics—presented in expert testimony, for example, about the psychological impact of enforced segregation—as a means of transforming constitutional law by persuading the courts that certain discriminatory laws produced public harms in violation of constitutional principles. This tactic, while often effective, has been criticized by some legal scholars as a pragmatic attempt to give judges nonlegal material with which to fill gaps in their justifications for decisions where the purely legal principles appear inconclusive.

Since the time of Marshall's work with the NAACP, the number of public interest law firms in the U.S. has grown substantially, and they have widely adopted his combination of strategies for litigation, devoting them to various public purposes. These strategies have been used, for example, in consumer advocacy campaigns and, more recently, by politically conservative public interest lawyers seeking to achieve, through litigation, changes in the law that they have not been able to accomplish in the legislature. If we focus on the particular content of Marshall's goals and successes, it might seem surprising that his work has influenced the quest for such divergent political objectives, but the techniques that he honed—originally considered to be a radical departure from accepted conventions—have become the norm for U.S. public interest litigation today.
explanation_html:
Notice how the opening carves out a niche. Previous Commentators writing about Thurgood Marshall, a United States Supreme Court justice from 1967 to 1991, have concentrated on his judicial record and on the ideological content of his earlier civil rights work as a lawyer. The Author proposes a different lens, a technical one, under which his years directing the NAACP reveal a strategic and methodological legacy to public interest law. The claim is carefully limited, since the NAACP was not the first legal organization in the country driven by a political and social agenda. What was new, in the campaign against state-sanctioned racial segregation during the 1940s and 1950s, was replacing opportunistic case-by-case litigation with a meticulously crafted and coordinated plan.

The first component of that plan gets a paragraph of its own. Under the test case strategy, the NAACP sponsored tactically chosen cases at the trial court level, evaluating in advance the precedential nuances and potential impact of each decision, which let Marshall try out different approaches and discover which worked best. One element of the tactic is singled out as essential, and it is more practical than doctrinal: in a public interest campaign the choice of plaintiff can decide success or failure, so Marshall selected litigants whose public appeal, credibility and commitment to the organization's goals were unsurpassed.

The second component shifts from who brings the case to what kind of evidence it carries. Marshall introduced sociological and psychological statistics, presented for example as expert testimony about the psychological impact of enforced segregation, in order to persuade courts that particular discriminatory laws produced public harms violating constitutional principles. The author calls the tactic often effective and then reports pushback, the only dissenting note in the passage. Some Legal Scholars treat it as a pragmatic maneuver that hands judges nonlegal material to fill gaps in their justifications where the purely legal principles look inconclusive.

The legacy gets measured last, and the measure is deliberately uncomfortable. Public interest law firms in the United States have grown substantially in number since Marshall's NAACP years, and they have widely adopted his combination of litigation strategies while aiming them at all sorts of purposes, from consumer advocacy to, more recently, politically conservative campaigns seeking through the courts what they could not obtain in the legislature. Focus on the particular content of Marshall's goals and that spread looks surprising; focus instead, as the author urges, on technique, and it follows naturally, since methods once seen as a radical departure from convention have become the norm.
overall_html: The passage sets aside the usual attention to Thurgood Marshall's judicial record and ideology in order to argue that his lasting bequest to public interest law was technical, a deliberately planned and tightly coordinated style of litigation built on tactically selected test cases, sympathetic plaintiffs and social-scientific evidence. The author's purpose is to reframe a familiar figure, moving from the neglected angle, through the two signature tactics, to the observation that these once-radical methods now count as standard and serve political ends as divergent as consumer advocacy and conservative law reform. Three voices appear: Previous Commentators, whose emphasis the author redirects, Some Legal Scholars, who question the use of nonlegal material, and The Author's own appraisal.

The painter Roy Lichtenstein helped to define pop art—the movement that incorporated commonplace objects and commercial-art techniques into paintings—by paraphrasing the style of comic books in his work. His merger of a popular genre with the forms and intentions of fine art generated a complex result: while poking fun at the pretensions of the art world, Lichtenstein's work also managed to convey a seriousness of theme that enabled it to transcend mere parody.

That Lichtenstein's images were fine art was at first difficult to see, because, with their word balloons and highly stylized figures, they looked like nothing more than the comic book panels from which they were copied. Standard art history holds that pop art emerged as an impersonal alternative to the histrionics of abstract expressionism, a movement in which painters conveyed their private attitudes and emotions using nonrepresentational techniques. The truth is that by the time pop art first appeared in the early 1960s, abstract expressionism had already lost much of its force. Pop art painters weren't quarreling with the powerful early abstract expressionist work of the late 1940s but with a second generation of abstract expressionists whose work seemed airy, high-minded, and overly lyrical. Pop art paintings were full of simple black lines and large areas of primary color. Lichtenstein's work was part of a general rebellion against the fading emotional power of abstract expressionism, rather than an aloof attempt to ignore it.

But if rebellion against previous art by means of the careful imitation of a popular genre were all that characterized Lichtenstein's work, it would possess only the reflective power that parodies have in relation to their subjects. Beneath its cartoonish methods, his work displayed an impulse toward realism, an urge to say that what was missing from contemporary painting was the depiction of contemporary life. The stilted romances and war stories portrayed in the comic books on which he based his canvases, the stylized automobiles, hot dogs, and table lamps that appeared in his pictures, were reflections of the culture Lichtenstein inhabited. But, in contrast to some pop art, Lichtenstein's work exuded not a jaded cynicism about consumer culture, but a kind of deliberate naivete, intended as a response to the excess of sophistication he observed not only in the later abstract expressionists but in some other pop artists. With the comics—typically the domain of youth and innocence—as his reference point, a nostalgia fills his paintings that gives them, for all their surface bravado, an inner sweetness. His persistent use of comic-art conventions demonstrates a faith in reconciliation, not only between cartoons and fine art, but between parody and true feeling.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining both a movement and a puzzle. Pop art brought commonplace objects and commercial-art techniques into painting, and Roy Lichtenstein helped define it by paraphrasing the style of comic books. The second sentence sets the agenda: the result was complex, because the work pokes fun at the pretensions of the art world and still conveys enough seriousness of theme to transcend mere parody. That two-sidedness is what the rest of the passage exists to explain, so keep both halves live as you read. The Author is committed to the second half in particular, and each later paragraph works to show that the comic-book surface is not the whole story.

A correction follows, aimed squarely at the received account. Lichtenstein's images were hard to recognize as fine art at first, since word balloons and highly stylized figures made them look like the panels they were copied from. Standard Art History explains pop art as an impersonal alternative to the histrionics of abstract expressionism, the movement whose painters conveyed private attitudes and emotions through nonrepresentational technique. The author disputes both the timing and the target. By the early 1960s abstract expressionism had already lost much of its force, and the pop painters were not quarreling with the powerful early work of the late 1940s but with a second generation whose canvases struck them as airy, high-minded and overly lyrical. The conclusion inverts the standard reading, making Lichtenstein part of a rebellion against a fading movement rather than an aloof attempt to ignore it.

The seriousness promised at the outset arrives last. If careful imitation of a popular genre were all Lichtenstein offered, his work would carry only the reflective power any parody has toward its subject. Beneath the cartoonish method, though, the author finds an impulse toward realism, an insistence that contemporary painting had stopped depicting contemporary life; the stilted romances and war stories, the automobiles, hot dogs and table lamps, reflected the culture he actually inhabited. Unlike some pop art, his work exudes no jaded cynicism about consumer culture but a deliberate naivete, a response to the excess of sophistication he saw in later abstract expressionists and in some fellow pop artists. Because comics belong to youth and innocence, nostalgia fills the paintings and lends them an inner sweetness beneath the surface bravado, evidence of a faith in reconciliation between cartoons and fine art, and between parody and true feeling.
overall_html: The passage argues that Lichtenstein's comic-derived paintings amount to far more than parody, joining a joke at the art world's expense to a genuine realism about contemporary life and an unfashionable sweetness of feeling. The author's purpose is interpretive and partly corrective, first stating the complexity of the work, then challenging Standard Art History's account of pop art as an impersonal alternative to abstract expressionism by placing Lichtenstein inside a rebellion against that movement's weakened second generation, and finally reading his deliberate naivete and nostalgia as faith in reconciliation between cartoon and fine art. Two viewpoints matter here: Standard Art History, which the author revises, and The Author's own admiring reading of the paintings.

Because the market system enables entrepreneurs and investors who develop new technology to reap financial rewards from their risk of capital, it may seem that the primary result of this activity is that some people who have spare capital accumulate more. But in spite of the fact that the profits derived from various technological developments have accrued to relatively few people, the developments themselves have served overall as a remarkable democratizing force. In fact, under the regime of the market, the gap in benefits accruing to different groups of people has been narrowed in the long term.

This tendency can be seen in various well-known technological developments. For example, before the printing press was introduced centuries ago, few people had access to written materials, much less to scribes and private secretaries to produce and transcribe documents. Since printed materials have become widely available, however, people without special position or resources—and in numbers once thought impossible—can take literacy and the use of printed texts for granted. With the distribution of books and periodicals in public libraries, this process has been extended to the point where people in general can have essentially equal access to a vast range of texts that would once have been available only to a very few. A more recent technological development extends this process beyond printed documents. A child in school with access to a personal computer and modem—which is becoming fairly common in technologically advanced societies—has computing power and database access equal to that of the best-connected scientists and engineers at top-level labs of just fifteen years ago, a time when relatively few people had personal access to any computing power. Or consider the uses of technology for leisure. In previous centuries only a few people with abundant resources had the ability and time to hire professional entertainment, and to have contact through travel and written communication—both of which were prohibitively expensive—with distant people. But now broadcast technology is widely available, and so almost anyone can have an entertainment cornucopia unimagined in earlier times. Similarly, the development of inexpensive mail distribution and telephone connections and, more recently, the establishment of the even more efficient medium of electronic mail have greatly extended the power of distant communication.

This kind of gradual diffusion of benefits across society is not an accident of these particular technological developments, but rather the result of a general tendency of the market system. Entrepreneurs and investors often are unable to maximize financial success without expanding their market, and this involves structuring their prices to the consumers so as to make their technologies genuinely accessible to an ever-larger share of the population. In other words, because market competition drives prices down, it tends to diffuse access to new technology across society as a result.
explanation_html:
Start with the concession, since the paragraph is built as one. Because the market system lets entrepreneurs and investors who develop new technology profit from risking capital, it can look as though the main result is that people with spare capital accumulate more of it. The Author grants the premise, that profits from various technological developments have gone to relatively few people, and rejects the conclusion drawn from it. Those developments have served overall as a remarkable democratizing force, and under the regime of the market the gap in benefits accruing to different groups has narrowed in the long term. Note the phrase carrying the weight, in the long term, and note also that the claim is about benefits rather than about who ends up rich.

Examples fill the entire middle, arranged so that each repeats the same movement, from a privileged few to nearly everyone. Before the printing press, written material was scarce and only those with position or resources had scribes and private secretaries; printed texts made literacy and the use of documents ordinary, and public libraries pushed the process further, giving people in general essentially equal access to a range of texts once available to very few. Computing repeats the pattern more recently, since a schoolchild with a personal computer and modem holds the computing power and database access that only the best-connected scientists at top laboratories commanded fifteen years earlier. Leisure follows the same arc, since hired entertainment, travel and correspondence with distant people were once prohibitively expensive, while broadcast technology now offers almost anyone an entertainment cornucopia, and cheap mail, telephones and electronic mail have extended distant communication broadly.

The mechanism comes last, and it is what converts a list of examples into an argument. This gradual diffusion is not an accident of these particular inventions but the result of a general tendency in the market system. The reasoning runs through incentives: entrepreneurs and investors usually cannot maximize financial success without expanding their market, and expanding it means structuring prices so that an ever-larger share of the population can genuinely afford the technology. Competition drives prices down, and falling prices spread access across society. That closes the loop on the objection raised at the start, since the same profit motive that concentrates the gains in few hands also disperses the technology itself.
overall_html: The passage maintains that although the profits from new technology accrue to relatively few people, the technologies themselves act as a powerful democratizing force, narrowing over the long term the gap in benefits available to different groups. The author's purpose is to defend that counterintuitive claim, opening with the appearance it must overcome, filling the middle with parallel examples running from printing and public libraries to personal computers, broadcasting and electronic mail, and closing with the mechanism that makes the pattern systematic, namely that profit-seeking firms must expand their markets and competition pushes prices down. The Author is the only viewpoint developed, and the opening impression is raised only in order to be corrected.

Neurobiologists once believed that the workings of the brain were guided exclusively by electrical signals; according to this theory, communication between neurons (brain cells) is possible because electrical impulses travel from one neuron to the next by literally leaping across the synapses (gaps between neurons). But many neurobiologists puzzled over how this leaping across synapses might be achieved, and as early as 1904 some speculated that electrical impulses are transmitted between neurons chemically rather than electrically. According to this alternative theory, the excited neuron secretes a chemical called a neurotransmitter that binds with its corresponding receptor molecule in the receiving neuron. This binding of the neurotransmitter renders the neuron permeable to ions, and as the ions move into the receiving neuron they generate an electrical impulse that runs through the cell; the electrical impulse is thereby transmitted to the receiving neuron.

This theory has gradually won acceptance in the scientific community, but for a long time little was known about the mechanism by which neurotransmitters manage to render the receiving neuron permeable to ions. In fact, some scientists remained skeptical of the theory because they had trouble imagining how the binding of a chemical to a receptor at the cell surface could influence the flow of ions through the cell membrane. Recently, however, researchers have gathered enough evidence for a convincing explanation: that the structure of receptors plays the pivotal role in mediating the conversion of chemical signals into electrical activity.

The new evidence shows that receptors for neurotransmitters contain both a neurotransmitter binding site and a separate region that functions as a channel for ions; attachment of the neurotransmitter to the binding site causes the receptor to change shape and so results in the opening of its channel component. Several types of receptors have been isolated that conform to this structure, among them the receptors for acetylcholine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glycine, and serotonin. These receptors display enough similarities to constitute a family, known collectively as neurotransmitter-gated ion channels.

It has also been discovered that each of the receptors in this family comes in several varieties so that, for example, a GABA receptor in one part of the brain has slightly different properties than a GABA receptor in another part of the brain. This discovery is medically significant because it raises the possibility of the highly selective treatment of certain brain disorders. As the precise effect on behavior of every variety of each neurotransmitter-gated ion channel is deciphered, pharmacologists may be able to design drugs targeted to specific receptors on defined categories of neurons that will selectively impede or enhance these effects. Such drugs could potentially help ameliorate any number of debilitating conditions, including mood disorders, tissue damage associated with stroke, or Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a theory that turned out to be wrong, and that is worth marking, because what follows is the history of a correction. Early Neurobiologists held that the brain works by electrical signals alone, with impulses literally leaping across the synapses, the gaps between neurons. Nobody could explain how such a leap would happen, and as early as 1904 some researchers proposed that the transfer is chemical instead. On that alternative account, an excited neuron secretes a chemical called a neurotransmitter, the chemical binds to its corresponding receptor molecule on the receiving neuron, the binding makes that neuron permeable to ions, and the ions moving in generate an electrical impulse that runs through the cell.

The theory's fortunes come next, along with the gap that stayed open. The chemical account gradually won acceptance in the scientific community, yet for a long time nobody knew by what mechanism a neurotransmitter renders the receiving neuron permeable to ions. That missing step kept The Skeptics in play, since they had trouble imagining how a chemical binding at the cell surface could influence the flow of ions through the membrane. Then comes the pivot the rest of the passage develops: researchers have recently gathered enough evidence for a convincing explanation, and it turns on the structure of the receptors themselves.

That explanation is structural and pleasingly simple. A receptor contains two parts, a site where the neurotransmitter binds and a separate region that functions as a channel for ions, and attachment of the neurotransmitter to the binding site changes the receptor's shape so that the channel opens. That is the entire mechanism, and it dissolves precisely the difficulty The Skeptics raised. Several receptors conforming to this design have been isolated, among them those for acetylcholine, gamma-aminobutyric acid, known as GABA, glycine and serotonin, and their similarities are close enough for the group to be treated as a family, the neurotransmitter-gated ion channels.

A refinement closes the passage, followed by what it might be good for. Each receptor in the family comes in several varieties, so a GABA receptor in one part of the brain has slightly different properties from a GABA receptor elsewhere. The medical significance rests on that variation. Once the precise effect on behavior of every variety is deciphered, pharmacologists may be able to design drugs aimed at specific receptors on defined categories of neurons, selectively impeding or enhancing those effects. Watch the hedged phrasing, since help for mood disorders, tissue damage from stroke and Alzheimer's disease is offered as a potential result rather than an accomplished one.
overall_html: The passage recounts how neurobiology moved from a purely electrical picture of communication between neurons to a chemical one, then explains the structural discovery that finally supplied the missing mechanism, receptors combining a neurotransmitter binding site with a separate ion channel that opens when the receptor changes shape. The author's purpose is expository, tracing a problem and its resolution in four steps, from the old electrical theory and its chemical rival, through the doubts that lingered while the mechanism was unknown, to the receptor family called neurotransmitter-gated ion channels, and finally to the prospect of drugs targeted at particular receptor varieties. No live dispute remains; Early Neurobiologists and The Skeptics figure as stages the evidence has moved past.

The accumulation of scientific knowledge regarding the environmental impact of oil well drilling in North America has tended to lag behind the actual drilling of oil wells. Most attempts to regulate the industry have relied on hindsight: the need for regulation becomes apparent only after undesirable events occur. The problems associated with oil wells' potential contamination of groundwater—fresh water within the earth that supplies wells and springs—provide a case in point.

When commercial drilling for oil began in North America in the mid-nineteenth century, regulations reflected the industry's concern for the purity of the wells' oil. In 1893, for example, regulations were enacted specifying well construction requirements to protect oil and gas reserves from contamination by fresh water. Thousands of wells were drilled in such a way as to protect the oil, but no thought was given to the possibility that the groundwater itself might need protection until many drinking-water wells near the oil well sites began to produce unpotable, oil-contaminated water.

The reason for this contamination was that groundwater is usually found in porous and permeable geologic formations near the earth's surface, whereas petroleum and unpotable saline water reservoirs are generally found in similar formations but at greater depths. Drilling a well creates a conduit connecting all the formations that it has penetrated. Consequently, without appropriate safeguards, wells that penetrate both groundwater and oil or saline water formations inevitably contaminate the groundwater. Initial attempts to prevent this contamination consisted of sealing off the groundwater formations with some form of protective barrier to prevent the oil flowing up the well from entering or mixing with the natural groundwater reservoir. This method, which is still in use today, initially involved using hollow trees to seal off the groundwater formations; now, however, large metal pipe casings, set in place with cement, are used.

Regulations currently govern the kinds of casing and cement that can be used in these practices; however, the hazards of insufficient knowledge persist. For example, the long-term stability of this way of protecting groundwater is unknown. The protective barrier may fail due to corrosion of the casing by certain fluids flowing up the well, or because of dissolution of the cement by these fluids. The effects of groundwater bacteria, traffic vibrations, and changing groundwater chemistry are likewise unassessed. Further, there is no guarantee that wells drilled in compliance with existing regulations will not expose a need for research in additional areas: on the west coast of North America, a major disaster recently occurred because a well's location was based on a poor understanding of the area's subsurface geology. Because the well was drilled in a channel accessing the ocean, not only was the area's groundwater completely contaminated, but widespread coastal contamination also occurred, prompting international concern over oil exploration and initiating further attempts to refine regulations.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph states a thesis and then narrows to a test case. The author claims that scientific understanding of what oil drilling does to the environment has consistently trailed the drilling itself, so regulation in North America has been written backward, arriving only once something has already gone wrong. Groundwater contamination is offered as the illustration, and the definition supplied there matters for the rest of the passage: groundwater is fresh water held underground that feeds wells and springs. Expect the following paragraphs to walk through this example chronologically and to keep confirming the hindsight pattern.

History bears the claim out, and the irony is the point. When commercial drilling started in the middle of the nineteenth century, the rules that existed were written to protect the oil, not the water; the 1893 construction requirements were designed to keep fresh water from spoiling oil and gas reserves. Thousands of wells were built to that standard, with nobody considering that the traffic might run the other way. The problem announced itself only when drinking-water wells near drilling sites began delivering oil-tainted water that people could not drink, which is precisely the hindsight the opening described.

Here the passage pauses the narrative to explain the underlying geology, and the mechanism is simple once laid out. Groundwater sits in porous, permeable rock fairly near the surface, while petroleum and undrinkable salty water occupy comparable formations much deeper down. Drilling punches a channel through everything it passes, so a well reaching both layers will contaminate the fresh water unless something blocks the path. The fix has always been a barrier sealing off the groundwater formation so oil rising up the well cannot mix with it. Notice the continuity across the centuries: hollow trees originally, and today large metal casings cemented into place.

The closing paragraph returns to the thesis, arguing that current rules governing casing and cement have not cured the deeper problem of insufficient knowledge. Nobody knows how long these barriers last, since fluids moving up a well can corrode the casing or dissolve the cement, and the influence of groundwater bacteria, traffic vibrations and shifting groundwater chemistry has not been assessed at all. Worse, compliance guarantees nothing about unknown risks. The west coast disaster makes the point, where poor understanding of subsurface geology put a well in a channel opening to the ocean, contaminating groundwater and the coast and prompting yet another round of regulatory refinement.
overall_html: The passage argues that knowledge of drilling's environmental effects has always lagged behind the drilling itself, so oil regulation in North America is written only after damage appears, and it uses groundwater contamination as the sustained example. The author's purpose is to demonstrate that pattern, moving from early rules that protected oil from water rather than water from oil, to the geology that makes contamination inevitable without a barrier, to the casing-and-cement solution, and finally to the gaps that persist in current regulation, including a west coast disaster caused by a misjudged well location. There are no competing camps here; the argument is carried entirely by the author's own analysis.

In many bilingual communities of Puerto Rican Americans living in the mainland United States, people use both English and Spanish in a single conversation, alternating between them smoothly and frequently even within the same sentence. This practice—called code-switching—is common in bilingual populations. While there are some cases that cannot currently be explained, in the vast majority of cases subtle factors, either situational or rhetorical, explain the use of code-switching.

Linguists say that most code-switching among Puerto Rican Americans is sensitive to the social contexts, which researchers refer to as domains, in which conversations take place. The main conversational factors influencing the occurrence of code-switching are setting, participants, and topic. When these go together naturally they are said to be congruent; a set of three such congruent factors constitutes a conversational situation. Linguists studying the choice between Spanish and English among a group of Puerto Rican American high school students classified their conversational situations into five domains: family, friendship, religion, education, and employment. To test the effects of these domains on code-switching, researchers developed a list of hypothetical situations made up of two of the three congruent factors, or of two incongruent factors, approximating an interaction in one of the five domains. The researchers asked the students to determine the third factor and to choose which mix of language—on a continuum from all English to all Spanish—they would use in that situation. When given two congruent factors, the students easily supplied the third congruent factor and strongly agreed among themselves about which mix they would use. For instance, for the factors of participants "parent and child" and the topic "how to be a good son or daughter," the congruent setting chosen was "home" and the language mix chosen was Spanish only. In contrast, incongruent factors such as the participants "priest and parishioner" and the setting "beach" yielded less agreement on the third factor of topic and on language choice.

But situational factors do not account for all code-switching; it occurs even when the domain would lead one not to expect it. In these cases, one language tends to be the primary one, while the other is used only sparingly to achieve certain rhetorical effects. Often the switches are so subtle that the speakers themselves are not aware of them. This was the case with a study of a family of Puerto Rican Americans in another community. Family members believed they used only English at home, but their taped conversations occasionally contained some Spanish, with no change in situational factors. When asked what the presence of Spanish signified, they commented that it was used to express certain attitudes such as intimacy or humor more emphatically.
explanation_html:
The opening describes a behavior and then promises an explanation for it. In many Puerto Rican American communities on the mainland, speakers move between English and Spanish within a single conversation and even within one sentence, a practice linguists call code-switching and find throughout bilingual populations. The last sentence is the one to hold onto, since it lays out the passage's plan: a few instances still resist explanation, but the great majority are accounted for by subtle factors that are either situational or rhetorical. That two-part distinction sets up the two paragraphs that follow, one for each kind of factor.

Situational factors come first, and the vocabulary needs unpacking. Linguists hold that most switching responds to the social context, or domain, of a conversation, shaped by three things: setting, participants, and topic. When those three fit together naturally they are congruent, and a congruent trio makes up a conversational situation. Studying high school students, researchers sorted situations into the domains of family, friendship, religion, education, and employment, then handed the students two factors and asked them to supply the third and to pick a language mix ranging from all English to all Spanish. Given congruent pairs the students agreed readily; parent and child discussing how to be a good son or daughter produced home and Spanish only. Incongruent pairs, such as a priest and parishioner at the beach, scattered their answers.

The final paragraph turns to the other half of the explanation announced at the start. Switching also happens where the domain gives no reason to expect it, and in those cases one language clearly dominates while the other appears only in small doses for rhetorical effect, often so quietly that the speakers do not notice they have done it. A study of one Puerto Rican American family supplies the evidence: they were convinced they spoke only English at home, yet recordings caught occasional Spanish with no change in setting, participants or topic. Asked about it, they explained that the Spanish gave attitudes such as intimacy or humor more emphasis.
overall_html: The passage explains that code-switching between English and Spanish in Puerto Rican American communities is not random but driven by two identifiable kinds of factors, situational ones tied to the domain of a conversation and rhetorical ones used for emphasis even when the situation does not call for a switch. The author's purpose is expository, first defining the practice and announcing the two-part explanation, then reporting the domain study of high school students in which congruent combinations of setting, participants and topic produced strong agreement about language choice, and finally presenting the family study that illustrates unconscious switching for effect. The findings belong to the linguists; the author reports them without dispute.

Reader-response theory, a type of literary theory that arose in reaction to formalist literary criticism, has endeavored to shift the emphasis in the interpretation of literature from the text itself to the contributions of readers to the meaning of a text. According to literary critics who endorse reader-response theory, the literary text alone renders no meaning; it acquires meaning only when encountered by individual readers, who always bring varying presuppositions and ways of reading to bear on the text, giving rise to the possibility—even probability—of varying interpretations. This brand of criticism has met opposition from the formalists, who study the text alone and argue that reader-response theory can encourage and even validate fragmented views of a work, rather than the unified view acquired by examining only the content of the text. However, since no theory has a monopoly on divining meaning from a text, the formalists' view appears unnecessarily narrow.

The proponents of formalism argue that their approach is firmly grounded in rational, objective principles, while reader-response theory lacks standards and verges on absolute subjectivity. After all, these proponents argue, no author can create a work that is packed with countless meanings. The meaning of a work of literature, the formalists would argue, may be obscure and somewhat arcane; yet, however hidden it may be, the author's intended meaning is legible within the work, and it is the critic's responsibility to search closely for this meaning. However, while a literary work is indeed encoded in various signs and symbols that must be translated for the work to be understood and appreciated, it is not a map. Any complicated literary work will invariably raise more questions than it answers. What is needed is a method that enables the critic to discern and make use of the rich stock of meanings created in encounters between texts and readers.

Emphasizing the varied presuppositions and perceptions that readers bring to the interpretations of a text can uncover hitherto unnoticed dimensions of the text. In fact, many important works have received varying interpretations throughout their existence, suggesting that reader-based interpretations similar to those described by reader-response theory had been operating long before the theory's principles were articulated. And while in some cases critics' textual interpretations based on reader-response theory have unfairly burdened literature of the past with contemporary ideologies, legitimate additional insights and understandings continue to emerge years after an ostensibly definitive interpretation of a major work has been articulated. By regarding a reader's personal interpretation of literary works as not only valid but also useful in understanding the works, reader-response theory legitimizes a wide range of perspectives on these works and thereby reinforces the notion of them as fluid and lively forms of discourse that can continue to support new interpretations long after their original composition.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph does three jobs at once, so separate them as you read. It defines reader-response theory, which grew up against formalist criticism and relocates meaning from the text to what readers contribute: on this view a text by itself means nothing until a reader, carrying particular assumptions and habits of reading, meets it, which makes divergent interpretations likely rather than merely possible. It then gives the formalists their objection, that attending to readers licenses fragmented readings instead of the unified one a text's own content yields. The last sentence is the author stepping in: since no theory owns the route to meaning, the formalist position looks unnecessarily narrow.

The middle paragraph puts the formalists' best case first and then answers it. Their claim is one of rigor, that formalism rests on rational objective principles while reader-response theory has no standards and slides toward pure subjectivity, since no author can load a work with limitless meanings; however buried or arcane the intended meaning may be, it is legible in the work and the critic's task is to dig it out. The author's reply grants the premise and rejects the conclusion. A literary work is indeed encoded in signs and symbols needing translation, but it is not a map, and any complex work raises more questions than it settles, which is why criticism needs a method for using the meanings generated when texts meet readers.

The final paragraph builds the positive case, and notice that the author's argument is largely historical. Foregrounding what readers bring can expose dimensions of a text nobody had noticed, and the fact that major works have been read differently across their lifetimes suggests reader-based interpretation was already at work long before the theory named it. A concession follows, that some reader-response criticism has unfairly saddled older literature with present-day ideologies, but the author holds that genuine insights keep surfacing even after a supposedly definitive reading. Treating a reader's own interpretation as valid and useful legitimizes many perspectives and keeps literary works alive as discourse still open to new readings.
overall_html: The passage defends reader-response theory, which locates a text's meaning in the encounter between text and reader, against the formalist objection that such an approach abandons objective standards and fragments works that should be read as unified wholes. The author's purpose is evaluative and clearly partisan, first laying out both positions and calling formalism narrow, then presenting the formalists' rigor argument in order to answer it, and finally arguing from the long history of shifting interpretations that reader-based reading uncovers real insights and keeps literature open to new understanding. Keep three voices separate: the reader-response critics, the formalists who oppose them, and the author, who sides with the former while conceding the theory's occasional abuses.

Faculty researchers, particularly in scientific, engineering, and medical programs, often produce scientific discoveries and invent products or processes that have potential commercial value. Many institutions have invested heavily in the administrative infrastructure to develop and exploit these discoveries, and they expect to prosper both by an increased level of research support and by the royalties from licensing those discoveries having patentable commercial applications. However, although faculty themselves are unlikely to become entrepreneurs, an increasing number of highly valued researchers will be sought and sponsored by research corporations or have consulting contracts with commercial firms. One study of such entrepreneurship concluded that "if universities do not provide the flexibility needed to venture into business, faculty will be tempted to go to those institutions that are responsive to their commercialized desires." There is therefore a need to consider the different intellectual property policies that govern the commercial exploitation of faculty inventions in order to determine which would provide the appropriate level of flexibility.

In a recent study of faculty rights, Patricia Chew has suggested a fourfold classification of institutional policies. A supramaximalist institution stakes out the broadest claim possible, asserting ownership not only of all intellectual property produced by faculty in the course of their employment while using university resources, but also for any inventions or patent rights from faculty activities, even those involving research sponsored by nonuniversity funders. A maximalist institution allows faculty ownership of inventions that do not arise either "in the course of the faculty's employment [or] from the faculty's use of university resources." This approach, although not as all-encompassing as that of the supramaximalist university, can affect virtually all of a faculty member's intellectual production. A resource-provider institution asserts a claim to faculty's intellectual product in those cases where "significant use" of university time and facilities is employed. Of course, what constitutes significant use of resources is a matter of institutional judgment.

As Chew notes, in these policies "faculty rights, including the sharing of royalties, are the result of university benevolence and generosity. [However, this] presumption is contrary to the common law, which provides that faculty own their inventions." Others have pointed to this anomaly and, indeed, to the uncertain legal and historical basis upon which the ownership of intellectual property rests. Although these issues remain unsettled, and though universities may be overreaching due to faculty's limited knowledge of their rights, most major institutions behave in the ways that maximize university ownership and profit participation.

But there is a fourth way, one that seems to be free from these particular issues. Faculty-oriented institutions assume that researchers own their own intellectual products and the rights to exploit them commercially, except in the development of public health inventions or if there is previously specified "substantial university involvement." At these institutions industry practice is effectively reversed, with the university benefiting in far fewer circumstances.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph builds a problem that the rest of the passage will answer with a taxonomy. Faculty in the sciences, engineering and medicine generate discoveries and inventions worth money, and universities have spent heavily on the administrative machinery to develop them, counting on more research support and on royalties from licensing whatever can be patented. The pressure point is mobility: professors rarely turn entrepreneur themselves, but the valuable ones get recruited by research corporations or sign consulting contracts, and a quoted study warns that inflexible universities will lose them. Hence the question the passage sets itself, which policy on faculty inventions strikes the right level of flexibility.

Three of four categories arrive here, from most grasping to least, and it is worth fixing the order. Chew, whose classification the passage adopts, defines a supramaximalist institution as one claiming everything, not just intellectual property produced in the course of employment using university resources but inventions and patent rights from any faculty activity, including research funded by outsiders. A maximalist institution lets faculty keep only what arises neither from their employment nor from university resources, which in practice still sweeps in nearly all of their output. A resource-provider institution claims a share only where significant use was made of university time and facilities, though the university itself decides what counts as significant.

Before the fourth category comes an evaluation of these three. Chew's objection, quoted here, is that such policies treat any rights faculty retain, royalties included, as gifts from a generous university, whereas common law actually assigns inventions to their faculty inventors. Others have flagged the same anomaly and the shaky legal and historical footing of intellectual property ownership generally. The passage leaves the underlying question open, notes that universities may be overreaching because faculty do not know their rights, and reports the practical upshot without endorsement: most major institutions still act to maximize their own ownership and share of the profits.

The closing paragraph delivers the fourth option and a quiet verdict on it. Faculty-oriented institutions begin from the opposite presumption, that researchers own their intellectual products and the right to commercialize them, carving out only public health inventions and cases where substantial university involvement was specified in advance. The effect is to invert standard industry practice, leaving the university to benefit in far fewer situations. Read the opening phrase carefully, since it is the closest thing to an authorial judgment in the passage: this way seems free of the problems Chew identified, which marks it as the answer to the flexibility question raised at the start.
overall_html: The passage surveys the policies universities use to claim ownership of faculty inventions, adopting Chew's fourfold classification and moving from the supramaximalist and maximalist institutions that claim almost everything, through the resource-provider standard, to the faculty-oriented approach that presumes researchers own what they create. The author's purpose is to identify which policy offers the flexibility universities need to keep valuable researchers, framing the survey with that question, pausing to relay Chew's point that current practice treats faculty rights as university generosity even though common law grants faculty ownership, and closing by presenting the faculty-oriented model as apparently free of those problems. Chew supplies the framework and the critique; the author reports and mildly endorses.

The Canadian Auto Workers' (CAW) Legal Services Plan, designed to give active and retired autoworkers and their families access to totally prepaid or partially reimbursed legal services, has been in operation since late 1985. Plan members have the option of using either the plan's staff lawyers, whose services are fully covered by the cost of membership in the plan, or an outside lawyer. Outside lawyers, in turn, can either sign up with the plan as a "cooperating lawyer" and accept the CAW's fee schedule as payment in full, or they can charge a higher fee and collect the balance from the client. Autoworkers appear to have embraced the notion of prepaid legal services: 45 percent of eligible union members were enrolled in the plan by 1988. Moreover, the idea of prepaid legal services has been spreading in Canada. A department store is even offering a plan to holders of its credit card.

While many plan members seem to be happy to get reduced-cost legal help, many lawyers are concerned about the plan's effect on their profession, especially its impact on prices for legal services. Some point out that even though most lawyers have not joined the plan as cooperating lawyers, legal fees in the cities in which the CAW plan operates have been depressed, in some cases to an unprofitable level. The directors of the plan, however, claim that both clients and lawyers benefit from their arrangement. For while the clients get ready access to reduced-price services, lawyers get professional contact with people who would not otherwise be using legal services, which helps generate even more business for their firms. Experience shows, the directors say, that if people are referred to a firm and receive excellent service, the firm will get three to four other referrals who are not plan subscribers and who would therefore pay the firm's standard rate.

But it is unlikely that increased use of such plans will result in long-term client satisfaction or in a substantial increase in profits for law firms. Since lawyers with established reputations and client bases can benefit little, if at all, from participation, the plans function largely as marketing devices for lawyers who have yet to establish themselves. While many of these lawyers are no doubt very able and conscientious, they will tend to have less expertise and to provide less satisfaction to clients. At the same time, the downward pressure on fees will mean that the full-fee referrals that proponents say will come through plan participation may not make up for a firm's investment in providing services at low plan rates. And since lowered fees provide little incentive for lawyers to devote more than minimal effort to cases, a "volume discount" approach toward the practice of law will mean less time devoted to complex cases and a general lowering of quality for clients.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph is pure setup, so get the mechanics straight before the argument starts. Since late 1985 the Canadian Auto Workers' Legal Services Plan has given autoworkers, retirees and their families legal help that is either fully prepaid or partly reimbursed. Members may use the plan's own staff lawyers, whose work membership covers entirely, or go outside, and an outside lawyer either signs on as a cooperating lawyer accepting the plan's fee schedule as full payment or charges more and bills the client for the difference. Uptake has been strong, with 45 percent of eligible members enrolled by 1988, and prepaid plans are spreading in Canada.

Two opposed assessments fill the middle paragraph. Concerned lawyers worry about the effect on their profession and particularly on prices, observing that even though most lawyers have stayed out of the plan, fees in cities where it operates have fallen, sometimes below a profitable level. The plan's directors answer that the arrangement serves both sides: clients get cheap access, and lawyers meet people who would never otherwise hire them, which feeds the firm more work. Their supporting claim is specific and worth noting, since a satisfied plan client reportedly generates three or four further referrals who are not subscribers and who pay standard rates.

Only now does the author speak, and the verdict goes against the directors on both of their promises. The reasoning starts from who actually joins: established lawyers with reputations and clients gain nothing, so the plans work mainly as marketing for newcomers, who may be able and conscientious but bring less expertise and leave clients less satisfied. The referral argument then fails on arithmetic, because falling fees mean full-price referrals may not cover what a firm sinks into low-rate plan work. Worse, cheap fees reward minimal effort, so a volume discount approach starves complex cases of time and drags quality down.
overall_html: The passage examines the CAW's prepaid legal services plan and concludes that wider use of such plans is unlikely to deliver either lasting client satisfaction or real profit for law firms, because they attract mainly inexperienced lawyers, depress fees below what referrals can recoup, and reward minimal effort on demanding cases. The author's purpose is evaluative, first explaining how the plan works and how quickly it has caught on, then setting the worries of concerned lawyers about depressed fees against the directors' claim that plan work generates full-rate referrals, and finally rejecting that defense point by point. Three positions are in play: the concerned lawyers, the plan's directors, and the author's skeptical judgment.
