One of the foundations of scientific research is that an experimental result is credible only if it can be replicated—only if performing the experiment a second time leads to the same result. But physicists John Sommerer and Edward Ott have conceived of a physical system in which even the least change in the starting conditions—no matter how small, inadvertent, or undetectable—can alter results radically. The system is represented by a computer model of a mathematical equation describing the motion of a particle placed in a particular type of force field.

Sommerer and Ott based their system on an analogy with the phenomena known as riddled basins of attraction. If two bodies of water bound a large landmass and water is spilled somewhere on the land, the water will eventually make its way to one or the other body of water, its destination depending on such factors as where the water is spilled and the geographic features that shape the water's path and velocity. The basin of attraction for a body of water is the area of land that, whenever water is spilled on it, always directs the spilled water to that body.

In some geographical formations it is sometimes impossible to predict, not only the exact destination of the spilled water, but even which body of water it will end up in. This is because the boundary between one basin of attraction and another is riddled with fractal properties; in other words, the boundary is permeated by an extraordinarily high number of physical irregularities such as notches or zigzags. Along such a boundary, the only way to determine where spilled water will flow at any given point is actually to spill it and observe its motion; spilling the water at any immediately adjacent point could give the water an entirely different path, velocity, or destination.

In the system posited by the two physicists, this boundary expands to include the whole system: i.e., the entire force field is riddled with fractal properties, and it is impossible to predict even the general destination of the particle given its starting point. Sommerer and Ott make a distinction between this type of uncertainty and that known as "chaos"; under chaos, a particle's general destination would be predictable but its path and exact destination would not.

There are presumably other such systems because the equation the physicists used to construct the computer model was literally the first one they attempted, and the likelihood that they chose the only equation that would lead to an unstable system is small. If other such systems do exist, metaphorical examples of riddled basins of attraction may abound in the failed attempts of scientists to replicate previous experimental results—in which case, scientists would be forced to question one of the basic principles that guide their work.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by naming the principle it will eventually put at risk. Science treats a result as credible only when repeating the experiment produces the same outcome. Against that, Sommerer and Ott have devised a physical system in which even a change too small, accidental or invisible to notice in the starting conditions sends the results somewhere completely different. The system is not a laboratory setup but a computer model of an equation describing how a particle moves inside a particular kind of force field. Keep the replication principle in mind, since the last paragraph returns to it.

Rather than explain the physics directly, the authors of the model reach for an analogy, and the next two paragraphs build it. Picture a large landmass with a body of water on either side. Spill water anywhere on the land and it eventually drains into one body or the other, with the destination set by where it was spilled and by the terrain shaping its route and speed. A basin of attraction is simply the stretch of land from which every spill ends up in one particular body of water. Nothing unpredictable has entered yet; this is the orderly baseline.

Unpredictability arrives now. In certain terrain you cannot say where the water will end up, and not merely which precise spot but which body of water entirely. The reason is that the boundary between neighboring basins is riddled with fractal properties, meaning it is packed with an enormous number of small irregularities, notches and zigzags. Along a boundary like that the only way to learn where water goes is to pour it and watch, because spilling at a point right beside it can produce a different path, a different speed and a different destination.

The analogy now maps onto the model, and the crucial move is one of scale. What was a thin boundary in the landscape becomes the entire system: the whole force field carries those fractal properties, so nothing about the particle's destination can be predicted from where it starts. The physicists then draw a distinction you should hold onto, separating this from chaos. Under chaos you could still say roughly where a particle would end up, only not by what route or exactly where; here even the general destination is beyond reach.

The closing paragraph extends the finding outward and delivers the payoff. Because the equation used was simply the first one tried, it would be a remarkable coincidence if it were the only equation capable of producing such instability, so comparable systems probably exist. If they do, then some of the failures scientists have had in reproducing earlier experimental results may be riddled basins of attraction in metaphorical form. Note the conditional framing throughout, and note where it leads: scientists would have to reconsider the replication principle the passage began with.
overall_html: The passage presents Sommerer and Ott's computer model of a particle in a force field so thoroughly riddled with fractal properties that the smallest undetectable change in starting conditions makes even the particle's general destination unpredictable, a stronger uncertainty than chaos. The author's purpose is expository, defining replication as the principle at stake, developing the riddled basins of attraction analogy in stages from an orderly baseline to fractal boundaries, applying it to the model, and closing on the conditional implication that similar systems probably exist and that failures to replicate experiments might reflect them. The only viewpoint developed is that of the two physicists, reported in the author's neutral voice.

The work of South African writer Ezekiel Mphahlele has confounded literary critics, especially those who feel compelled to draw a sharp distinction between autobiography and fiction. These critics point to Mphahlele's best-known works—his 1959 autobiography Down Second Avenue and his 1971 novel The Wanderers—to illustrate the problem of categorizing his work. While his autobiography traces his life from age five until the beginning of his self-imposed 20-year exile at age thirty-eight, The Wanderers appears to pick up at the beginning of his exile and go on from there. Critics have variously decried the former as too fictionalized and the latter as too autobiographical, but those who focus on traditional labels inevitably miss the fact that Mphahlele manipulates different prose forms purely in the service of the social message he advances.

Even where critics give him a favorable reading, all too often their reviews carry a negative subtext. For example, one critic said of The Wanderers that if anger, firsthand experiences, compassion, and topicality were the sole requirements for great literature, the novel might well be one of the masterpieces of this declining part of the twentieth century. And although this critic may not have meant to question the literary contribution of the novel, there are those who are outright dismissive of The Wanderers because it contains an autobiographical framework and is populated with real-world characters. Mphahlele briefly defends against such charges by pointing out the importance of the fictional father-son relationship that opens and closes the novel. But his greater concern is the social vision that pervades his work, though it too is prone to misunderstandings and underappreciation. Mphahlele is a humanist and an integrationist, and his writings wonderfully articulate his vision of the future; but critics often balk at this vision because Mphahlele provides no road maps for bringing such a future about.

Mphahlele himself shows little interest in establishing guidelines to distinguish autobiography from fiction. Though he does refer to Down Second Avenue as an autobiography and The Wanderers as a novel, he asserts that no novelist can write complete fiction or absolute fact. It is the nature of writing, at least the writing he cares about, that the details must be drawn from the writer's experiences, and thus are in some sense fact, but conveyed in such a way as to maximize the effectiveness of the social message contained in the work, and thus inevitably fiction. As he claims, the whole point of the exercise of writing has nothing to do with classification; in all forms writing is the transmission of ideas, and important ideas at that: "Whenever you write prose or poetry or drama you are writing a social criticism of one kind or another. If you don't, you are completely irrelevant—you don't count."
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph sets up a conflict between a writer and the categories used to read him. The critics who insist on a firm line between autobiography and fiction have found Mphahlele's work hard to place, and the two books they cite show why: his 1959 autobiography covers his life from five to thirty-eight, when his self-imposed twenty-year exile began, and his 1971 novel seems to take up at that same point and continue. Their verdicts pull in opposite directions, the autobiography faulted as too fictionalized and the novel as too autobiographical. The author supplies the thesis in the final clause: preoccupation with labels misses that he uses prose forms in whatever way serves his social message.

The second paragraph shows the criticism operating even where it seems friendly. One reviewer allowed that if anger, firsthand experience, compassion and topicality were all great literature required, the novel might be a masterpiece of the century's decline, a compliment built around a withheld judgment. Others dismiss the novel outright for its autobiographical framework and real-world characters. Mphahlele answers only briefly, pointing to the invented father-son relationship that frames the book, because what he cares about is his social vision. Note where the resistance lies: he is a humanist and integrationist whose writing articulates a future, and critics balk because he offers no route to reaching it.

The last paragraph hands the argument to Mphahlele himself and resolves the categorization question by dissolving it. He will use the labels loosely, calling one book an autobiography and the other a novel, while denying that any novelist writes complete fiction or absolute fact. His reasoning is that the details of the writing he values must come from lived experience, which makes them factual, yet they are shaped to make the social message land, which makes them fictional. Classification is therefore beside the point, since writing exists to transmit ideas, and as he puts it, prose that is not social criticism does not count.
overall_html: The passage argues that critics who insist on classifying Ezekiel Mphahlele's books as either autobiography or fiction have misread him, because he treats prose forms as instruments for delivering a social message and denies that any writing is wholly factual or wholly invented. The author's purpose is corrective and defensive, moving from the critics' contradictory complaints about his autobiography and his novel, to the negative subtext running even through favorable reviews and their discomfort with a vision that offers no road map, and finally to Mphahlele's own position that writing exists to transmit ideas. The viewpoints to keep apart are the critics, Mphahlele, and the sympathetic author.

A vigorous debate in astronomy centers on an epoch in planetary history that was first identified by analysis of rock samples obtained in lunar missions. Scientists discovered that the major craters on the Moon were created by a vigorous bombardment of debris approximately four billion years ago—the so-called late heavy bombardment (LHB). Projectiles from this bombardment that affected the Moon should also have struck Earth, a likelihood with profound consequences for the history of Earth since, until the LHB ended, life could not have survived here.

Various theoretical approaches have been developed to account for both the evidence gleaned from samples of Moon rock collected during lunar explorations and the size and distribution of craters on the Moon. Since the sizes of LHB craters suggest they were formed by large bodies, some astronomers believe that the LHB was linked to the disintegration of an asteroid or comet orbiting the Sun. In this view, a large body broke apart and peppered the inner solar system with debris. Other scientists disagree and believe that the label "LHB" is in itself a misnomer. These researchers claim that a cataclysm is not necessary to explain the LHB evidence. They claim that the Moon's evidence merely provides a view of the period concluding billions of years of a continuous, declining heavy bombardment throughout the inner solar system. According to them, the impacts from the latter part of the bombardment were so intense that they obliterated evidence of earlier impacts. A third group contends that the Moon's evidence supports the view that the LHB was a sharply defined cataclysmic cratering period, but these scientists believe that because of its relatively brief duration, this cataclysm did not extend throughout the inner solar system. They hold that the LHB involved only the disintegration of a body within the Earth-Moon system, because the debris from such an event would have been swept up relatively quickly.

New support for the hypothesis that a late bombardment extended throughout the inner solar system has been found in evidence from the textural features and chemical makeup of a meteorite that has been found on Earth. It seems to be a rare example of a Mars rock that made its way to Earth after being knocked from the surface of Mars. The rock has recently been experimentally dated at about four billion years old, which means that, if the rock is indeed from Mars, it was knocked from the planet at about the same time that the Moon was experiencing the LHB. This tiny piece of evidence suggests that at least two planetary systems in the inner solar system experienced bombardment at the same time. However, to determine the pervasiveness of the LHB, scientists will need to locate many more such rocks and perhaps obtain surface samples from other planets in the inner solar system.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by establishing the phenomenon that the rest of it will argue about. Analysis of rocks brought back from the Moon showed that its major craters were produced by an intense bombardment of debris roughly four billion years ago, an episode named the late heavy bombardment. The step that makes this more than lunar geology comes next: whatever struck the Moon should have struck Earth as well. Note the consequence the author draws, since it explains why the debate matters at all. If the bombardment reached Earth, life here could not have survived until it stopped.

Three positions are then set out, and the efficient way to hold them apart is to ask what each says about the event's cause and its reach. The solar system cataclysm group reads the large crater sizes as the work of big bodies and links the bombardment to an asteroid or comet that broke up in orbit and scattered debris through the inner solar system. The gradual decline group calls the label itself a misnomer, arguing that no catastrophe is needed: the Moon simply records the tail end of billions of years of steadily diminishing bombardment, with the late impacts so fierce that they erased the traces of earlier ones. The local cataclysm group accepts a sharply defined cratering episode but confines it to the Earth-Moon system, reasoning that its brief duration fits debris from a body that broke up nearby and was swept up quickly.

New evidence arrives in the final paragraph, and it supports one of those three positions rather than settling the dispute. A meteorite found on Earth, identified by its texture and chemistry as a rare piece of Mars knocked loose from that planet's surface, has been dated experimentally to about four billion years. If the identification holds, Mars was being struck at the same time the Moon was, which points to at least two planetary systems bombarded simultaneously and thus to the solar-system-wide view. Notice how heavily the author qualifies the finding, calling it tiny and requiring more such rocks and surface samples from other planets.
overall_html: The passage explains the astronomical debate over the late heavy bombardment, the episode of intense cratering about four billion years ago recorded in lunar rock, and reports new meteorite evidence that a similar bombardment reached Mars. The author's purpose is expository rather than partisan, first establishing the phenomenon and its implication that life on Earth could not have survived until it ended, then laying out three competing accounts, and finally presenting evidence that tips toward one of them while stressing how much more is needed. Keep the three groups distinct: those positing a solar-system-wide cataclysm, those denying any cataclysm, and those confining it to the Earth-Moon system.

Specialists in international communications almost unanimously assert that the broadcasting in developing nations of television programs produced by industrialized countries amounts to cultural imperialism: the phenomenon of one culture's productions overwhelming another's, to the detriment of the flourishing of the latter. This assertion assumes the automatic dominance of the imported productions and their negative effect on the domestic culture. But the assertion is polemical and abstract, based on little or no research into the place held by imported programs in the economies of importing countries or in the lives of viewers. This is not to deny that dominance is sometimes a risk in relationships between cultures, but rather to say that the assertion lacks empirical foundation and in some cases goes against fact. For one example, imported programs rarely threaten the economic viability of the importing country's own television industry. For another, imported programs do not uniformly attract larger audiences than domestically produced programs; viewers are not part of a passive, undifferentiated mass but are individuals with personal tastes, and most of them tend to prefer domestically produced television over imported television.

The role of television in developing nations is far removed from what the specialists assert. An anthropological study of one community that deals in part with residents' viewing habits where imported programs are available cites the popularity of domestically produced serial dramas and points out that, because viewers enjoy following the dramas from day to day, television in the community can serve an analogous function to that of oral poetry, which the residents often use at public gatherings as a daily journal of events of interest.

An empirical approach not unlike that of anthropologists is needed if communications specialists are to understand the impact of external cultural influences on the lives of people in a society. The first question they must investigate is: Given the evidence suggesting that the primary relationship of imported cultural productions to domestic ones is not dominance, then what model best represents the true relationship? One possibility is that, rather than one culture's productions dominating another's, the domestic culture absorbs the imported productions and becomes enriched. Another is that the imported productions fuse with domestic culture only where the two share common aspects, such as the use of themes, situations, or character types that are relevant and interesting to both cultures.

Communications researchers will also need to consider how to assess the position of the individual viewer in their model of cultural relationships. This model must emphasize the diversity of human responses, and will require engaging with the actual experiences of viewers, taking into account the variable contexts in which productions are experienced, and the complex manner in which individuals ascribe meanings to those productions.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a consensus position the author immediately puts under pressure. The Specialists in international communications hold that when developing nations broadcast programs made in industrialized countries, the result is cultural imperialism, one culture's output swamping another's and stunting it. That claim, the author points out, assumes both that imported shows automatically dominate and that they damage the domestic culture. The rebuttal is about evidence rather than principle: the assertion is polemical, abstract, and built on almost no research. The author concedes dominance can be a genuine risk between cultures, then offers two counterfacts, since imports seldom endanger a domestic television industry and viewers, being individuals with tastes, usually prefer home-grown programming.

Evidence of the kind the author says is missing arrives next. An anthropological study of a single community where imported programs are available found that domestically produced serial dramas were the popular ones. The interesting move is the analogy that follows: because residents enjoy following a drama from day to day, television in that community works much as oral poetry does at public gatherings, serving as a running daily journal of events people care about. Read this as an illustration of television taking on a local social function, not as a claim that imports never matter anywhere.

Having cleared the ground, the author turns prescriptive. If communications specialists want to understand external cultural influence on people's lives, they need the empirical habits of anthropologists, and the first question is which model actually fits, given evidence that dominance is not the primary relationship. Two candidates are floated without a verdict: the domestic culture may absorb imported productions and be enriched by them, or the two may fuse only where they already overlap, sharing themes, situations or character types that interest both cultures. Keep these as possibilities the author raises rather than conclusions the author settles on.

A second task for the model closes the passage, which is locating the individual viewer inside it. The author's requirement is diversity: human responses vary, so researchers must engage with what viewers actually experience, allow for the variable contexts in which a program is watched, and account for the complex ways individuals ascribe meaning to what they see. Notice this circles back to the first paragraph's point that audiences are not a passive, undifferentiated mass, turning that objection into a design constraint on future research.
overall_html: The passage disputes the near-unanimous claim that broadcasting industrialized countries' television in developing nations amounts to cultural imperialism, arguing that the claim is polemical and unsupported by research into how imported programs actually function in importing economies and in viewers' lives. The author's purpose is first corrective and then programmatic: after undercutting the dominance assumption with counterexamples and an anthropological illustration of television serving a community much as oral poetry does, the author sets out what better research would require, namely a model that captures the real relationship between imported and domestic productions and takes the individual viewer seriously. The viewpoints to track are the specialists the author criticizes and the author's own empirical alternative.

Computers have long been utilized in the sphere of law in the form of word processors, spreadsheets, legal research systems, and practice management systems. Most exciting, however, has been the prospect of using artificial intelligence techniques to create so-called legal reasoning systems—computer programs that can help to resolve legal disputes by reasoning from and applying the law. But the practical benefits of such automated reasoning systems have fallen short of optimistic early predictions and have not resulted in computer systems that can independently provide expert advice about substantive law. This is not surprising in light of the difficulty in resolving problems involving the meaning and applicability of rules set out in a legal text.

Early attempts at automated legal reasoning focused on the doctrinal nature of law. They viewed law as a set of rules, and the resulting computer systems were engineered to make legal decisions by determining the consequences that followed when its stored set of legal rules was applied to a collection of evidentiary data. Such systems underestimated the problems of interpretation that can arise at every stage of a legal argument. Examples abound of situations that are open to differing interpretations: whether a mobile home in a trailer park is a house or a motor vehicle, whether a couple can be regarded as married in the absence of a formal legal ceremony, and so on. Indeed, many notions invoked in the text of a statute may be deliberately left undefined so as to allow the law to be adapted to unforeseen circumstances. But in order to be able to apply legal rules to novel situations, systems have to be equipped with a kind of comprehensive knowledge of the world that is far beyond their capabilities at present or in the foreseeable future.

Proponents of legal reasoning systems now argue that accommodating reference to, and reasoning from, cases improves the chances of producing a successful system. By focusing on the practice of reasoning from precedents, researchers have designed systems called case-based reasoners, which store individual example cases in their knowledge bases. In contrast to a system that models legal knowledge based on a set of rules, a case-based reasoner, when given a concrete problem, manipulates the cases in its knowledge base to reach a conclusion based on a similar case. Unfortunately, in the case-based systems currently in development, the criteria for similarity among cases are system dependent and fixed by the designer, so that similarity is found only by testing for the presence or absence of predefined factors. This simply postpones the apparently intractable problem of developing a system that can discover for itself the factors that make cases similar in relevant ways.
explanation_html:
The passage sets up a gap between promise and delivery. Computers have long handled routine legal work through word processors, spreadsheets, research systems and practice management tools, but the exciting prospect was artificial intelligence: legal reasoning systems, programs that resolve disputes by reasoning from the law and applying it. The author's verdict arrives early and is negative, since practical benefits have fallen short of optimistic early predictions and no system independently supplies expert advice on substantive law. The explanation offered is the difficulty of settling what rules in a legal text mean and when they apply. Treat that interpretive problem as the passage's organizing theme, because both remaining paragraphs are versions of it.

Attention turns to the first generation of attempts, which treated law as doctrine, a set of rules. Those systems were engineered to reach decisions by applying their stored rules to a body of evidentiary data, and their weakness, in the author's account, is that they underestimated how much interpretation every stage of a legal argument demands. The examples are deliberately homely: whether a mobile home in a trailer park counts as a house or a motor vehicle, whether a couple can be regarded as married without a formal ceremony. Worse, statutes often leave notions undefined on purpose so the law can stretch to unforeseen circumstances. Applying rules to novel situations would therefore require something like comprehensive knowledge of the world, which the author says is far beyond these systems now and for the foreseeable future.

The successor approach and the passage's second viewpoint arrive together at the end. The Proponents of legal reasoning systems now argue that building in reference to cases improves the odds, and researchers have accordingly designed case-based reasoners, which store individual example cases and, given a concrete problem, manipulate them to reach a conclusion drawn from a similar case rather than from rules. The author's objection is that the improvement is only apparent. In the systems currently under development, what counts as similarity is system dependent and fixed by the designer, so a match is found merely by testing for predefined factors. That postpones rather than solves the apparently intractable problem of getting a system to discover for itself which factors make cases relevantly alike.
overall_html: The passage argues that legal reasoning systems have underdelivered because the interpretation of legal language, not the mechanical application of rules, is the heart of legal work. The author's purpose is critical and diagnostic, tracing the field's two generations in turn: rule-based systems that ignored how much interpretive judgment each step of an argument requires and would need implausibly broad world knowledge to handle novel situations, and the case-based reasoners now favored by proponents, whose similarity criteria are fixed in advance by their designers and so merely defer the same intractable problem. The only developed viewpoints are the proponents' renewed optimism and the author's consistent skepticism about both approaches.

Many critics agree that the primary characteristic of Senegalese filmmaker Ousmane Sembène's work is its sociopolitical commitment. Sembène was trained in Moscow in the cinematic methods of socialist realism, and he asserts that his films are not meant to entertain his compatriots, but rather to raise their awareness of the past and present realities of their society. But his originality as a filmmaker lies most strikingly in his having successfully adapted film, originally a Western cultural medium, to the needs, pace, and structures of West African culture. In particular, Sembène has found within African oral culture techniques and strategies that enable him to express his views and to reach both literate and nonliterate Senegalese viewers.

A number of Sembène's characters and motifs can be traced to those found in traditional West African storytelling. The tree, for instance, which in countless West African tales symbolizes knowledge, life, death, and rebirth, is a salient motif in Emitaï. The trickster, usually a dishonest individual who personifies antisocial traits, appears in Borom Sarret, Mandabi, and Xala as a thief, a corrupted civil servant, and a member of the elite, respectively. In fact, most of Sembène's characters, like those of many oral West African narratives, are types embodying collective ideas or attitudes. And in the oral tradition, these types face archetypal predicaments, as is true, for example, of the protagonist of Borom Sarret, who has no name and is recognizable instead by his trade—he is a street merchant—and by the difficulties he encounters but is unable to overcome.

Moreover, many of Sembène's films derive their structure from West African dilemma tales, the outcomes of which are debated and decided by their audiences. The open-endedness of most of his plots reveals that Sembène similarly leaves it to his viewers to complete his narratives: in such films as Borom Sarret, Mandabi, and Ceddo, for example, he provides his spectators with several alternatives as the films end. The openness of his narratives is also evidenced by his frequent use of freeze-frames, which carry the suggestion of continued action.

Finally, like many West African oral tales, Sembène's narratives take the form of initiatory journeys that bring about a basic change in the worldview of the protagonist and ultimately, Sembène hopes, in that of the viewer. His films denounce social and political injustice, and his protagonists' social consciousness emerges from an acute self-consciousness brought about by the juxtaposition of opposites within the films' social context: good versus evil, powerlessness versus power, or poverty versus wealth. Such binary oppositions are used analogously in West African tales, and it seems likely that these dialectical elements are related to African oral storytelling more than, as many critics have supposed, to the Marxist components of his ideology.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up a contrast worth marking immediately. The critics largely agree that sociopolitical commitment is the defining feature of Sembène's work, and there is support for that in his Moscow training in socialist realism and in his own statement that his films exist to raise his compatriots' awareness rather than to entertain them. Then comes the turn that carries the author's thesis: what is most original about him is not the politics but the adaptation of film, a Western medium, to West African needs, pace, and structures. The mechanism named is oral culture, which lets him reach literate and nonliterate viewers alike.

Evidence begins with the smallest units, character and motif. The tree, a stock symbol of knowledge, life, death, and rebirth across West African tales, is prominent in one film; the trickster, the figure who personifies antisocial traits, turns up in three others as a thief, a corrupt civil servant, and a member of the elite. The larger claim is that his characters work the way oral-narrative characters do, functioning as types that embody collective ideas rather than as individuals, and facing archetypal predicaments. The unnamed street merchant, identified only by his trade and by difficulties he cannot overcome, is the clean example.

Structure supplies the second parallel, and the word moreover tells you the argument is accumulating rather than shifting ground. West African dilemma tales hand their outcomes to the audience to debate and decide, and Sembène's plots are said to do the same, since several of his films close by laying out alternatives instead of settling on one. His frequent freeze-frames get read the same way, as images that imply the action continues beyond the ending. Keep the division clear: the previous paragraph was about what his narratives contain, this one about the shape they take.

The third parallel arrives with the argumentative payoff attached. Sembène's films are built as initiatory journeys that transform the protagonist's worldview and, he hopes, the viewer's, and that transformation runs on stark oppositions between good and evil, powerlessness and power, poverty and wealth, which push the protagonist from self-consciousness into social consciousness. Because West African tales use the same device, the author concludes that these dialectical elements derive from oral storytelling rather than from the Marxist strand in his ideology. That is a direct reply to the critics, whose reading the first paragraph had set up precisely so it could be corrected here.
overall_html: Against the critical consensus that Ousmane Sembène's work is defined above all by its sociopolitical commitment, the passage argues that his real originality lies in adapting film, a Western medium, to the techniques of West African oral storytelling. The author's purpose is to establish and defend that thesis, and the macro-structure is a single claim followed by three cumulative parallels: characters and motifs drawn from traditional tales, plots that leave resolution to the audience as dilemma tales do, and initiatory journeys built on binary oppositions. The last parallel answers the critics directly by tracing Sembène's dialectical elements to oral tradition rather than to the Marxist component of his thinking.

Passage A

Readers, like writers, need to search for answers. Part of the joy of reading is in being surprised, but academic historians leave little to the imagination. The perniciousness of the historiographic approach became fully evident to me when I started teaching. Historians require undergraduates to read scholarly monographs that sap the vitality of history; they visit on students what was visited on them in graduate school. They assign books with formulaic arguments that transform history into an abstract debate that would have been unfathomable to those who lived in the past. Aimed so squarely at the head, such books cannot stimulate students who yearn to connect to history emotionally as well as intellectually.

In an effort to address this problem, some historians have begun to rediscover stories. It has even become something of a fad within the profession. This year, the American Historical Association chose as the theme for its annual conference some putative connection to storytelling: "Practices of Historical Narrative." Predictably, historians responded by adding the word "narrative" to their titles and presenting papers at sessions on "Oral History and the Narrative of Class Identity," and "Meaning and Time: The Problem of Historical Narrative." But it was still historiography, intended only for other academics. At meetings of historians, we still encounter very few historians telling stories or moving audiences to smiles, chills, or tears.

Passage B

Writing is at the heart of the lawyer's craft, and so, like it or not, we who teach the law inevitably teach aspiring lawyers how lawyers write. We do this in a few stand-alone courses and, to a greater extent, through the constraints that we impose on their writing throughout the curriculum. Legal writing, because of the purposes it serves, is necessarily ruled by linear logic, creating a path without diversions, surprises, or reversals. Conformity is a virtue, creativity suspect, humor forbidden, and voice mute.

Lawyers write as they see other lawyers write, and, influenced by education, profession, economic constraints, and perceived self-interest, they too often write badly. Perhaps the currently fashionable call for attention to narrative in legal education could have an effect on this. It is not yet exactly clear what role narrative should play in the law, but it is nonetheless true that every case has at its heart a story—of real events and people, of concerns, misfortunes, conflicts, feelings. But because legal analysis strips the human narrative content from the abstract, canonical legal form of the case, law students learn to act as if there is no such story.

It may well turn out that some of the terminology and public rhetoric of this potentially subversive movement toward attention to narrative will find its way into the law curriculum, but without producing corresponding changes in how legal writing is actually taught or in how our future colleagues will write. Still, even mere awareness of the value of narrative could perhaps serve as an important corrective.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens in the voice of the historian, who treats a professional habit as harmful rather than merely dull. Reading, the claim goes, depends on surprise and on searching for answers, and academic history leaves no room for either. Teaching is what made the problem vivid: undergraduates are assigned monographs that drain the vitality out of the subject, because instructors simply inflict on students what graduate school inflicted on them. Note the charge, since it returns later — formulaic argument converts the past into an abstract debate that the people who lived it would find unintelligible. Such books reach only the intellect, and students want an emotional connection too.

A concession appears and is then withdrawn. Some historians have begun rediscovering stories, enough for the historian to call it a fad, and the profession's main association even built its annual conference around historical narrative. The response was cosmetic: the word narrative added to titles, papers delivered in sessions that were still historiography and still aimed at other academics. The closing sentence gives you the test being applied throughout, which is effect rather than vocabulary — at these meetings almost nobody actually tells a story or moves an audience to smiles, chills, or tears.

Passage B moves to legal education and a second speaker, the law teacher, but the shape of the complaint is recognizably the same. Law schools teach students to write like lawyers whether they mean to or not, partly through a few dedicated courses and far more through constraints imposed across the entire curriculum. The description of legal writing is the heart of the paragraph: linear logic, a path free of diversions, surprises, or reversals, and a value system in which conformity counts as a virtue, creativity draws suspicion, humor is forbidden, and personal voice vanishes. Set that beside the historian's objection about imagination.

Cause and possible cure occupy this paragraph. Lawyers write badly, the argument runs, because they imitate the bad writing around them, with education, professional norms, economic pressure, and self-interest reinforcing the habit. The law teacher then raises the same fashionable remedy Passage A examined, the current call for attention to narrative, while treating its proper role in law as genuinely unsettled. The reason it might matter is stated plainly: every case starts as a story of real people, events, conflicts, and feelings, but legal analysis strips that human content away to leave an abstract canonical form, training students to act as though no story existed.

The close is a prediction with a small hedge attached. The law teacher expects the terminology and public rhetoric of the narrative movement to seep into the curriculum while the actual teaching of legal writing, and the writing future lawyers produce, stay exactly as they are. That is the same hollow adoption the historian described in the history profession, which is why the two passages feel like one argument told twice. The final sentence is where the tone diverges slightly, since awareness of narrative's value is allowed to count, on its own, as an important corrective.
overall_html: Both passages are insider critiques of how a profession trains its members to write, and both weigh the same fashionable remedy. The historian of Passage A argues that academic historiography drains history of surprise and emotion and that the discipline's new interest in narrative has produced little beyond relabeled conference papers; the law teacher of Passage B argues that legal writing enforces linear logic and suppresses creativity, humor, and voice, and that legal analysis strips the human story out of every case. The relationship is close agreement across different fields, with each writer doubting that the turn to narrative will change practice, though the law teacher ends by granting that mere awareness of narrative's value could still serve as a corrective.

Traditional theories of animal behavior assert that animal conflict within a species is highly ritualized and does not vary from contest to contest. This species-specific model assumes that repetitive use of the same visual and vocal displays and an absence of escalated fighting evolved to prevent injury. The contestant that exhibits the "best" display wins the contested resource. Galápagos tortoises, for instance, settle contests on the basis of height: the ritualized display consists of two tortoises facing one another and stretching their necks skyward; the tortoise perceived as being "taller" wins.

In populations of the spider Agelenopsis aperta, however, fighting behavior varies greatly from contest to contest. In addition, fighting is not limited to displays: biting and shoving are common. Susan Riechert argues that a recently developed model, evolutionary game theory, provides a closer fit to A. aperta territorial disputes than does the species-specific model, because it explains variations in conflict behavior that may result from varying conditions, such as differences in size, age, and experience of combatants. Evolutionary game theory was adapted from the classical game theory that was developed by von Neumann and Morgenstern to explain human behavior in conflict situations. In both classical and evolutionary game theory, strategies are weighed in terms of maximizing the average payoff against contestants employing both the same and different strategies. For example, a spider may engage in escalated fighting during a dispute only if the disputed resource is valuable enough to warrant the risk of physical injury. There are, however, two major differences between the classical and evolutionary theories. First, whereas in classical game theory it is assumed that rational thought is used to determine which action to take, evolutionary game theory assumes that instinct and long-term species advantage ultimately determine the strategies that are exhibited. The other difference is in the payoffs: in classical game theory, the payoffs are determined by an individual's personal judgment of what constitutes winning; in evolutionary game theory, the payoffs are defined in terms of reproductive success.

In studying populations of A. aperta in a grassland habitat and a riparian habitat, Riechert predicts that such factors as the size of the opponents, the potential rate of predation in a habitat, and the probability of winning a subsequent site if the dispute is lost will all affect the behavior of spiders in territorial disputes. In addition, she predicts that the markedly different levels of competition for web sites in the two habitats will affect the spiders' willingness to engage in escalated fighting. In the grassland, where 12 percent of the habitat is available for occupation by A. aperta, Riechert predicts that spiders will be more willing to engage in escalated fighting than in the riparian habitat, where 90 percent of the habitat is suitable for occupation.
explanation_html:
Begin with the model the passage exists to complicate. Traditional theories hold that conflict between members of the same species is ritualized and essentially identical from one contest to the next, on the reasoning that repeating fixed visual and vocal displays, and never escalating into real fighting, evolved to keep animals from getting hurt. Whichever contestant produces the best display takes the resource. The tortoise case makes that abstraction concrete: two animals face each other, stretch their necks upward, and the one perceived as taller wins without any contact. This is the species-specific model, and the passage keeps that label, so hold onto it.

A counterexample arrives and brings a rival framework with it. In one spider species, fighting differs sharply from contest to contest and includes biting and shoving, not just display. Susan Riechert argues that evolutionary game theory fits these territorial disputes better than the species-specific model does, because it accounts for variation produced by conditions such as a combatant's size, age, and experience. The rest of the paragraph explains the theory through its parent. Classical game theory, built to model human conflict, and its offshoot both judge a strategy by the average payoff it earns against opponents using the same and different strategies, so a spider escalates only when the resource justifies the risk. Two differences separate them: classical theory assumes rational deliberation while the newer version substitutes instinct and long-term species advantage, and classical payoffs reflect an individual's own judgment of winning while evolutionary payoffs are measured as reproductive success.

Prediction is what the closing paragraph adds, converting the framework into expectations that could be checked in the field. Riechert expects an opponent's size, the rate of predation in a habitat, and the chance of securing another web site after a loss all to shape how a spider handles a dispute. The sharper prediction concerns scarcity. Only about a tenth of the grassland is available for occupation, against nearly all of the riparian habitat, so competition for sites is far more intense in the grassland and spiders there should be readier to escalate. Notice that this is exactly the context-driven variation the species-specific model has no room for.
overall_html: The passage sets two accounts of animal conflict against each other: the traditional species-specific model, on which contests within a species are invariant rituals of display that evolved to prevent injury, and evolutionary game theory, which Susan Riechert argues better explains the highly variable and often physically rough territorial disputes of one spider species. The author's purpose is expository rather than argumentative, first laying out the older model with the tortoise example, then introducing Riechert's alternative and distinguishing it from the classical game theory it was adapted from, and finally reporting her predictions about how habitat scarcity and other local conditions should govern a spider's willingness to escalate. The positions to keep apart are the traditional theories and Riechert's.

Most people acknowledge that not all governments have a moral right to govern and that there are sometimes morally legitimate reasons for disobeying the law, as when a particular law prescribes behavior that is clearly immoral. It is also commonly supposed that such cases are special exceptions and that, in general, the fact that something is against the law counts as a moral, as well as legal, ground for not doing it; i.e., we generally have a moral duty to obey a law simply because it is the law. But the theory known as philosophical anarchism denies this view, arguing instead that people who live under the jurisdiction of governments have no moral duty to those governments to obey their laws. Some commentators have rejected this position because of what they take to be its highly counterintuitive implications: (1) that no existing government is morally better than any other (since all are, in a sense, equally illegitimate), and (2) that, lacking any moral obligation to obey any laws, people may do as they please without scruple. In fact, however, philosophical anarchism does not entail these claims.

First, the conclusion that no government is morally better than any other does not follow from the claim that nobody owes moral obedience to any government. Even if one denies that there is a moral obligation to follow the laws of any government, one can still evaluate the morality of the policies and actions of various governments. Some governments do more good than harm, and others more harm than good, to their subjects. Some violate the moral rights of individuals more regularly, systematically, and seriously than others. In short, it is perfectly consistent with philosophical anarchism to hold that governments vary widely in their moral stature.

Second, philosophical anarchists maintain that all individuals have basic, nonlegal moral duties to one another—duties not to harm others in their lives, liberty, health, or goods. Even if governmental laws have no moral force, individuals still have duties to refrain from those actions that constitute crimes in the majority of legal systems (such as murder, assault, theft, and fraud). Moreover, philosophical anarchists hold that people have a positive moral obligation to care for one another, a moral obligation that they might even choose to discharge by supporting cooperative efforts by governments to help those in need. And where others are abiding by established laws, even those laws derived from mere conventions, individuals are morally bound not to violate those laws when doing so would endanger others. Thus, if others obey the law and drive their vehicles on the right, one must not endanger them by driving on the left, for, even though driving on the left is not inherently immoral, it is morally wrong to deliberately harm the innocent.
explanation_html:
The setup arrives in stages, so track them separately. Most people accept that some governments lack the moral right to govern and that a clearly immoral law may be disobeyed, but treat those as special exceptions to a general moral duty to obey a law simply because it is the law. Philosophical anarchism denies that general duty outright: living under a government's jurisdiction creates no moral obligation to obey its laws. Some commentators reject the theory for two implications they find impossible to swallow, that no government could be morally better than any other since all are equally illegitimate, and that with no duty to obey, people may do as they please. The last sentence states the author's thesis, and it is narrow — the theory entails neither implication.

The first rebuttal pulls apart two questions the commentators had run together. Denying that anyone owes a government obedience says nothing about whether governments can be compared morally, since their policies and actions remain open to evaluation on independent grounds. Some do more good than harm to their subjects and some the reverse; some violate individual rights more regularly, more systematically, and more seriously than others. Philosophical anarchism is therefore perfectly consistent with holding that governments differ widely in moral stature, which is all the author needs to defeat the first objection.

The second rebuttal does the heavier work, and it operates by relocating morality outside the law. Individuals owe one another basic nonlegal duties not to damage another person's life, liberty, health, or goods, and those duties already rule out murder, assault, theft, and fraud whether or not statutes carry moral force. Added to them is a positive obligation of mutual care, which someone might even discharge by backing government efforts to help the needy. The last move covers merely conventional rules: where others are already following an established law, breaking it puts them in danger, so you are morally bound to comply. Driving on the left is not wrong in itself, but doing it among right-hand drivers harms the innocent, and that is what makes it wrong.
overall_html: The passage defends philosophical anarchism, the view that people living under a government have no moral duty to obey its laws, against critics who dismiss it for two supposedly unacceptable implications. The author's purpose is to rebut those objections rather than to prove the theory correct, and the structure is a single thesis followed by the two answers in order: governments can still be ranked morally by the good and harm their policies do, and individuals still owe each other nonlegal duties, including a duty not to endanger people by flouting conventional laws everyone else observes. Keep three positions apart as you read: the common view of legal obligation, the commentators' objections, and the anarchist position the author is clearing.

Asian American poetry from Hawaii, the Pacific island state of the United States, is generally characterizable in one of two ways: either as portraying a model multicultural paradise, or as exemplifying familiar Asian American literary themes such as generational conflict. In this light, the recent work of Wing Tek Lum in Expounding the Doubtful Points is striking for its demand to be understood on its own terms. Lum offers no romanticized notions of multicultural life in Hawaii, and while he does explore themes of family, identity, history, and literary tradition, he does not do so at the expense of attempting to discover and retain a local sensibility. For Lum such a sensibility is informed by the fact that Hawaii's population, unlike that of the continental U.S., has historically consisted predominantly of people of Asian and Pacific island descent, making the experience of its Asian Americans somewhat different than that of mainland Asian Americans.

In one poem, Lum meditates on the ways in which a traditional Chinese lunar celebration he is attending at a local beach both connects him to and separates him from the past. In the company of new Chinese immigrants, the speaker realizes that while ties to the homeland are comforting and necessary, it is equally important to have "a sense of new family" in this new land of Hawaii, and hence a new identity—one that is sensitive to its new environment. The role of immigrants in this poem is significant in that, through their presence, Lum is able to refer both to the traditional culture of his ancestral homeland as well as to the flux within Hawaiian society that has been integral to its heterogeneity. Even in a laudatory poem to famous Chinese poet Li Po (701–762 A.D.), which partly serves to place Lum's work within a distinguished literary tradition, Lum refuses to offer a stereotypical nostalgia for the past, instead pointing out the often elitist tendencies inherent in the work of some traditionally acclaimed Chinese poets.

Lum closes his volume with a poem that further points to the complex relationships between heritage and local culture in determining one's identity. Pulling together images and figures as vastly disparate as a famous Chinese American literary character and an old woman selling bread, Lum avoids an excessively romantic vision of U.S. culture, while simultaneously acknowledging the dream of this culture held by many newly arrived immigrants. The central image of a communal pot where each person chooses what she or he wishes to eat but shares with others the "sweet soup / spooned out at the end of the meal" is a hopeful one; however, it also appears to caution that the strong cultural emphasis in the U.S. on individual drive and success that makes retaining a sense of homeland tradition difficult should be identified and responded to in ways that allow for a healthy new sense of identity to be formed.
explanation_html:
Start by noticing that the passage opens with a category Lum is about to escape. Conventional Criticism reads Asian American poetry from Hawaii in one of two ways, either as a portrait of a model multicultural paradise or as a vehicle for familiar Asian American themes such as generational conflict. Against that backdrop The Author presents Wing Tek Lum's recent collection as striking, precisely because it demands to be understood on its own terms. Lum offers no romanticized multiculturalism, and although he does write about family, identity, history and literary tradition, he does not sacrifice a local sensibility to do it. That sensibility rests on a demographic fact the author spells out: Hawaii's population has historically been predominantly of Asian and Pacific island descent, so the Asian American experience there differs from the mainland one.

Evidence arrives next, two poems read for the same quality. In the first, the speaker attends a traditional Chinese lunar celebration at a local beach and finds that it both connects him to the past and separates him from it; among new Chinese immigrants he realizes that ties to the homeland are comforting and necessary, yet a sense of new family in Hawaii matters equally, yielding an identity sensitive to its new environment. The immigrants do double duty here, pointing back to the ancestral culture and forward to the flux that has made Hawaiian society heterogeneous. The second poem praises the classical poet Li Po and so places Lum within a distinguished tradition, but even there he declines stereotypical nostalgia, noting instead the elitist tendencies in some traditionally acclaimed Chinese poetry.

The volume's closing poem gets the last paragraph, and the author reads it as the fullest statement of the tension tracked throughout, between inherited heritage and local culture in shaping identity. Lum yokes together strikingly unlike figures, a famous Chinese American literary character and an old woman selling bread, refusing an excessively romantic vision of United States culture while still acknowledging the dream that many newly arrived immigrants attach to it. The image of a communal pot, where each person takes what she or he wishes but shares the sweet soup at the end, reads as hopeful. The author hears a warning inside the hope, though: the strong American emphasis on individual drive and success makes homeland tradition hard to retain, and that pressure must be identified and answered before a healthy new identity can form.
overall_html: The passage presents Wing Tek Lum's poetry as work that escapes the two standard readings of Asian American writing from Hawaii, neither idealizing multicultural life nor reducing itself to familiar generational themes, and instead holding ancestral heritage and a distinctly local sensibility in deliberate tension. The author's purpose is appreciative interpretation rather than plain description, opening with the conventional categories Lum refuses, then reading a lunar-celebration poem and a tribute to Li Po as evidence, and closing with the volume's final poem and its image of a shared pot. The only developed viewpoints are Conventional Criticism, invoked briefly as a foil, and the author's own admiring assessment of Lum.

passage_html:
In England the burden of history weighs heavily on common law, that unwritten code of time-honored laws derived largely from English judicial custom and precedent. Students of contemporary British law are frequently required to study medieval cases, to interpret archaic Latin maxims, or to confront doctrinal principles whose validity is based solely on their being part of the "timeless reason" of the English legal tradition. Centuries-old custom serves as the basis both for the divisions of law school subject matter and for much of the terminology of legal redress. Connected not only with legal history but also with the cultural history of the English people, common law cannot properly be understood without taking a long historical view.

Yet the academic study of jurisprudence has seldom treated common law as a constantly evolving phenomenon rooted in history; those interpretive theories that do acknowledge the antiquity of common law ignore the practical contemporary significance of its historical forms. The reasons for this omission are partly theoretical and partly political. In theoretical terms, modern jurisprudence has consistently treated law as a unified system of rules that can be studied at any given moment in time as a logical whole. The notion of jurisprudence as a system of norms or principles deemphasizes history in favor of the coherence of a system. In this view, the past of the system is conceived as no more than the continuous succession of its states of presence. In political terms, believing in the logic of law is a necessary part of believing in its fairness; even if history shows the legal tradition to be far from unitary and seldom logical, the prestige of the legal institution requires that jurisprudence treat the tradition as if it were, in essence, the application of known rules to objectively determined facts. To suggest otherwise would be dispiriting for the student and demoralizing for the public.

Legal historian Peter Goodrich has argued, however, that common law is most fruitfully studied as a continually developing tradition rather than as a set of rules. Taking his cue from the study of literature, Goodrich sees common law as a sort of literary text, with history and tradition serving as the text's narrative development. To study the common law historically, says Goodrich, is to study a text in which fiction is as influential as analysis, perception as significant as rule, and the play of memory as strong as the logic of argument. The concept of tradition, for Goodrich, implies not only the preservation and transmission of existing forms, but also the continuous rewriting of those forms to adapt them to contemporary legal circumstances.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph makes a claim about what common law is and how it has to be studied. Common law is the unwritten body of English law built out of judicial custom and precedent, and history sits heavily on it: British law students read medieval cases, parse archaic Latin maxims, and meet doctrines whose validity rests on nothing but their place in the timeless reason of the tradition. Even the way law school subjects are divided and the vocabulary of legal redress descend from centuries-old custom. The Author draws the conclusion plainly, that because common law is bound up with the cultural history of the English people as well as with legal history, it cannot properly be understood without taking a long historical view.

A pivot on 'Yet' identifies the gap the passage exists to expose. Academic jurisprudence has seldom treated common law as a phenomenon that evolves in history, and the interpretive theories that do concede its antiquity still ignore what its historical forms mean in practice today. Two explanations follow. Theoretically, Modern Jurisprudence treats law as a unified system of rules examinable at any moment as a logical whole, which shrinks the past into a mere succession of present states. Politically, believing in law's logic is part of believing in its fairness, so the prestige of the institution requires that the tradition be presented as known rules applied to objectively determined facts, since conceding otherwise would dispirit students and demoralize the public.

The alternative arrives last and belongs to Goodrich, a legal historian whose approach the author reports approvingly. Study common law as a continually developing tradition, he argues, not as a set of rules. Taking his cue from literary study, he treats it as a kind of text whose narrative development is its history and tradition, so that on this reading fiction weighs as much as analysis, perception as much as rule, and memory as much as the logic of argument. Notice how neatly this answers the theoretical objection raised just before it. Tradition in Goodrich's sense means not only preserving and transmitting inherited forms but continuously rewriting them to suit contemporary legal circumstances, which is exactly the evolving quality Modern Jurisprudence leaves out.
overall_html: The passage holds that common law is inseparable from its history yet has rarely been studied that way, and it presents Goodrich's proposal to treat common law as a continually developing tradition, read much as one reads a literary text, rather than as a fixed system of rules. The author's purpose is to diagnose an omission and point toward a remedy, moving from the weight of history on common law, to the theoretical and political reasons jurisprudence has set that history aside, to Goodrich's alternative. Three viewpoints are in play: The Author, who insists on the long historical view, Modern Jurisprudence, which treats law as a logical whole, and Goodrich, whose approach the author presents as more fruitful.

passage_html:
The passages discuss relationships between business interests and university research.

Passage A

As university researchers working in a "gift economy" dedicated to collegial sharing of ideas, we have long been insulated from market pressures. The recent tendency to treat research findings as commodities, tradable for cash, threatens this tradition and the role of research as a public good.

The nurseries for new ideas are traditionally universities, which provide an environment uniquely suited to the painstaking testing and revision of theories. Unfortunately, the market process and values governing commodity exchange are ill suited to the cultivation and management of new ideas. With their shareholders impatient for quick returns, businesses are averse to wide-ranging experimentation. And, what is even more important, few commercial enterprises contain the range of expertise needed to handle the replacement of shattered theoretical frameworks.

Further, since entrepreneurs usually have little affinity for adventure of the intellectual sort, they can buy research and bury its products, hiding knowledge useful to society or to their competitors. The growth of industrial biotechnology, for example, has been accompanied by a reduction in the free sharing of research methods and results—a high price to pay for the undoubted benefits of new drugs and therapies.

Important new experimental results once led university scientists to rush down the hall and share their excitement with colleagues. When instead the rush is to patent lawyers and venture capitalists, I worry about the long-term future of scientific discovery.

Passage B

The fruits of pure science were once considered primarily a public good, available for society as a whole. The argument for this view was that most of these benefits were produced through government support of universities, and thus no individual was entitled to restrict access to them.

Today, however, the critical role of science in the modern "information economy" means that what was previously seen as a public good is being transformed into a market commodity. For example, by exploiting the information that basic research has accumulated about the detailed structures of cells and genes, the biotechnology industry can derive profitable pharmaceuticals or medical screening technologies. In this context, assertion of legal claims to "intellectual property"—not just in commercial products but in the underlying scientific knowledge—becomes crucial.

Previously, the distinction between a scientific "discovery" (which could not be patented) and a technical "invention" (which could) defined the limits of industry's ability to patent something. Today, however, the speed with which scientific discoveries can be turned into products and the large profits resulting from this transformation have led to a blurring of both the legal distinction between discovery and invention and the moral distinction between what should and should not be patented.

Industry argues that if it has supported—either in its own laboratories or in a university—the makers of a scientific discovery, then it is entitled to seek a return on its investment, either by charging others for using the discovery or by keeping it for its own exclusive use.
explanation_html:
Passage A speaks in the first person, and you should register that voice immediately. The University Researcher describes academic science as a gift economy, a culture of collegial sharing that has long kept researchers insulated from market pressure. The recent habit of treating findings as commodities tradable for cash is framed as a threat both to that tradition and to research as a public good. This is a position statement rather than a neutral survey, so expect argument in what follows.

The case for universities comes next. They are the nurseries of new ideas because they supply conditions suited to slow, painstaking testing and revision of theories, and the values governing commodity exchange fit that work badly. Two reasons are offered: shareholders impatient for quick returns make firms averse to wide-ranging experimentation, and, the point The University Researcher calls more important still, few commercial enterprises hold the breadth of expertise needed when an entire theoretical framework shatters and must be replaced.

A second objection follows, this one about secrecy rather than capability. Entrepreneurs with little affinity for intellectual adventure can buy research and bury its products, withholding knowledge useful to society or to competitors. Industrial biotechnology supplies the illustration, since its growth has coincided with less free sharing of research methods and results. Notice the concession folded into the sentence, since the new drugs and therapies are called undoubted benefits; the complaint concerns the price paid for them.

Passage A closes by trading argument for image. Important results once sent university scientists rushing down the hall to share the excitement with colleagues, and now the rush is toward patent lawyers and venture capitalists. Nothing further is proved here; the register turns personal and ends on worry about the long-term future of scientific discovery. Read this as a value judgment about a change in culture, not as a claim that discovery itself has stopped.

Passage B opens on the same transformation in a detached, explanatory voice with no personal stake. The fruits of pure science, it notes, were once considered primarily a public good available to society as a whole. The justification for that older view turned on funding: most of those benefits were produced through government support of universities, so no individual was entitled to restrict access to them. Watch how carefully this is presented as a past consensus rather than as the writer's own commitment.

Now the shift. Because science is critical to the modern information economy, what was previously seen as a public good is being transformed into a market commodity. Biotechnology reappears as the example, though the use differs from Passage A's; here it shows how basic research on the detailed structures of cells and genes gets converted into profitable pharmaceuticals and medical screening technologies. In that context, legal claims to intellectual property become crucial, and the important detail is that such claims now reach the underlying scientific knowledge, not merely the commercial products.

The relevant legal history is spelled out next. Patents were once bounded by a distinction between a scientific discovery, which could not be patented, and a technical invention, which could. Speed and money have eroded that boundary: discoveries turn into products quickly and the resulting profits are large, so both the legal line between discovery and invention and the moral line about what should be patentable have blurred. Passage B records the blurring without pronouncing it regrettable.

The final paragraph hands the argument to Industry, and the reasoning is straightforward. Where a company has supported the makers of a scientific discovery, whether in its own laboratories or in a university, it claims entitlement to a return on that investment, either by charging others for use of the discovery or by keeping it for its exclusive use. The position is reported rather than assessed, which is precisely what separates this passage from the first.
overall_html: Both passages address the same development, the conversion of scientific knowledge from a shared public good into privately held property, but they handle it very differently. Passage A is an argument, in which The University Researcher defends the academic gift economy on the grounds that market values suit neither long-term theoretical work nor open sharing, closing on worry about the future of discovery. Passage B is an explanation, tracing how the role of science in the information economy has made intellectual property claims central and blurred the old legal and moral line between discovery and invention, and ending with Industry's own justification for seeking a return. In short, Passage A evaluates the shift that Passage B analyzes neutrally.
