In an experiment, two strangers are given the opportunity to share $100, subject to the following constraints: One person—the "proposer"—is to suggest how to divide the money and can make only one such proposal. The other person—the "responder"— must either accept or reject the offer without qualification. Both parties know that if the offer is accepted, the money will be split as agreed, but if the offer is rejected, neither will receive anything.

This scenario is called the Ultimatum Game. Researchers have conducted it numerous times with a wide variety of volunteers. Many participants in the role of the proposer seem instinctively to feel that they should offer 50 percent to the responder, because such a division is "fair" and therefore likely to be accepted. Two-thirds of proposers offer responders between 40 and 50 percent. Only 4 in 100 offer less than 20 percent. Offering such a small amount is quite risky; most responders reject such offers. This is a puzzle: Why would anyone reject an offer as too small? Responders who reject an offer receive nothing, so if one assumes—as theoretical economics traditionally has—that people make economic decisions primarily out of rational self-interest, one would expect that an individual would accept any offer.

Some theorists explain the insistence on fair divisions in the Ultimatum Game by citing our prehistoric ancestors' need for the support of a strong group. Small groups of hunter-gatherers depended for survival on their members' strengths. It is counterproductive to outcompete rivals within one's group to the point where one can no longer depend on them in contests with other groups. But this hypothesis at best explains why proposers offer large amounts, not why responders reject low offers.

A more compelling explanation is that our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups, where it is hard to keep secrets. Our emotions are therefore not finely tuned to one-time, strictly anonymous interactions. In real life we expect our friends and neighbors to notice our decisions. If people know that someone is content with a small share, they are likely to make that person low offers. But if someone is known to angrily reject low offers, others have an incentive to make that person high offers. Consequently, evolution should have favored angry responses to low offers; if one regularly receives fair offers when food is divided, one is more likely to survive. Because one-shot interactions were rare during human evolution, our emotions do not discriminate between one-shot and repeated interactions. Therefore, we respond emotionally to low offers in the Ultimatum Game because we instinctively feel the need to reject dismal offers in order to keep our self-esteem. This self-esteem helps us to acquire a reputation that is beneficial in future encounters.
explanation_html:
Read the opening paragraph as a rulebook, since every later argument depends on getting the setup exactly right. Two strangers can share one hundred dollars under tight constraints. One of them, the proposer, suggests a split and gets only that single attempt. The other, the responder, must take the offer as it stands or refuse it outright, with no bargaining permitted. Both know the stakes in advance: acceptance means the money is divided as proposed, refusal means neither person receives anything at all. Note that the anonymity and the one-shot structure become crucial once the explanations begin.

Naming the experiment as the Ultimatum Game, the author reports what actually happens and then extracts a puzzle from it. Proposers tend to feel that half is the fair share and therefore the likely one to be accepted, and the numbers bear that instinct out, with two-thirds offering between forty and fifty percent and only four in a hundred going below twenty. The genuinely surprising result is on the other side, since stingy offers are usually rejected. On the traditional economic assumption that people act from rational self-interest, any offer beats nothing, so refusing it should not happen.

The first attempted answer is evolutionary, and the author dispatches it quickly. Some theorists trace the insistence on fairness to prehistoric life in small hunter-gatherer bands, where survival depended on the strengths of the other members. On that account it is self-defeating to beat your own group's members so thoroughly that you can no longer rely on them when your group faces another. Notice how narrowly the objection is aimed rather than sweeping: the hypothesis may well explain why proposers hand over large shares, but it leaves the actual puzzle, the responder's refusal, untouched.

The explanation the author endorses keeps the evolutionary frame but relocates the mechanism in emotion and reputation. Feelings were shaped over millions of years in small groups where secrets were hard to keep, so they are not calibrated for anonymous one-off encounters. Where neighbors observe your decisions, being known to accept scraps invites low offers while being known to react angrily invites generous ones, so evolution favored anger at low offers and the better food shares that follow. Since one-shot situations were rare, our emotions do not distinguish them, and the rejection in the laboratory is that reputation-protecting instinct firing out of context.
overall_html: The passage sets out the Ultimatum Game and the puzzle it produces, that responders reject small offers even though refusing leaves them with nothing, and argues that the best explanation is an emotional apparatus shaped by small-group life in which rejecting insulting offers protected one's reputation and future share. The author's purpose is to weigh explanations and endorse one, moving from the rules, to the experimental results and their conflict with the assumption of rational self-interest, to a group-strength hypothesis rejected as explaining only proposers, and finally to the reputation account. The viewpoints to separate are traditional economics, some theorists, and the author.

Over the past 50 years, expansive, low-density communities have proliferated at the edges of many cities in the United States and Canada, creating a phenomenon known as suburban sprawl. Andres Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, and Jeff Speck, a group of prominent town planners belonging to a movement called New Urbanism, contend that suburban sprawl contributes to the decline of civic life and civility. For reasons involving the flow of automobile traffic, they note, zoning laws usually dictate that suburban homes, stores, businesses, and schools be built in separate areas, and this separation robs people of communal space where they can interact and get to know one another. It is as difficult to imagine the concept of community without a town square or local pub, these town planners contend, as it is to imagine the concept of family independent of the home.

Suburban housing subdivisions, Duany and his colleagues add, usually contain homes identical not only in appearance but also in price, resulting in a de facto economic segregation of residential neighborhoods. Children growing up in these neighborhoods, whatever their economic circumstances, are certain to be ill prepared for life in a diverse society. Moreover, because the widely separated suburban homes and businesses are connected only by "collector roads," residents are forced to drive, often in heavy traffic, in order to perform many daily tasks. Time that would in a town center involve social interaction within a physical public realm is now spent inside the automobile, where people cease to be community members and instead become motorists, competing for road space, often acting antisocially. Pedestrians rarely act in this manner toward each other. Duany and his colleagues advocate development based on early-twentieth-century urban neighborhoods that mix housing of different prices and offer residents a "gratifying public realm" that includes narrow, tree-lined streets, parks, corner grocery stores, cafes, small neighborhood schools, all within walking distance. This, they believe, would give people of diverse backgrounds and lifestyles an opportunity to interact and thus develop mutual respect.

Opponents of New Urbanism claim that migration to sprawling suburbs is an expression of people's legitimate desire to secure the enjoyment and personal mobility provided by the automobile and the lifestyle that it makes possible. However, the New Urbanists do not question people's right to their own values; instead, they suggest that we should take a more critical view of these values and of the sprawl-conducive zoning and subdivision policies that reflect them. New Urbanists are fundamentally concerned with the long-term social costs of the now-prevailing attitude that individual mobility, consumption, and wealth should be valued absolutely, regardless of their impact on community life.
explanation_html:
The main viewpoint arrives right after the phenomenon is defined. Suburban sprawl names the expansive, low-density communities that have spread at the edges of North American cities over the past fifty years. The New Urbanists, a movement represented here by three prominent town planners, contend that sprawl erodes civic life and civility. Their reasoning begins with zoning: because rules written around the flow of automobile traffic place homes, stores, businesses, and schools in separate areas, residents lose the communal spaces where they would otherwise meet and come to know one another. The analogy they offer makes the claim vivid, since a community without a town square or local pub is said to be as hard to imagine as a family without a home.

The case expands here, and it helps to track it as three linked harms. Subdivision houses tend to be identical in price as well as appearance, so neighborhoods become economically segregated in practice and the children raised in them, at any income level, grow up unready for a diverse society. Because homes and businesses are joined only by collector roads, ordinary daily tasks require driving, and hours that a town center would fill with contact in a public realm are instead spent in traffic, where people stop acting as community members and start acting as motorists competing for road space, often antisocially, in a way pedestrians rarely do to one another. The remedy follows directly: neighborhoods modeled on early-twentieth-century ones, mixing price levels and putting narrow tree-lined streets, parks, corner groceries, cafes, and small schools within walking distance, so that different sorts of people meet and develop mutual respect.

A counterargument finally appears, and it is answered rather than dismissed. Opponents of New Urbanism hold that moving to sprawling suburbs expresses a legitimate desire for the enjoyment and personal mobility a car provides and for the life it makes possible. Watch precisely what is conceded and what is refused. The New Urbanists do not challenge anyone's right to hold those values; they ask that the values, and the zoning and subdivision policies built to serve them, be viewed more critically. The closing sentence states their underlying worry, which is the long-term social cost of treating individual mobility, consumption, and wealth as absolute goods whatever happens to community life.
overall_html: The passage lays out the New Urbanist critique of suburban sprawl, on which zoning that separates homes from stores, workplaces, and schools strips away the shared public space communities need, segregates neighborhoods by income, and replaces face-to-face contact with time spent driving. The author's purpose is to present that position together with its proposed alternative, walkable mixed-price neighborhoods modeled on early-twentieth-century urban ones, and then to report how its proponents answer their critics. The two viewpoints to keep apart are the New Urbanists, represented by Duany and his colleagues, and the opponents who defend suburban life as a legitimate choice about personal mobility, a right the New Urbanists grant while still questioning the values behind it.

Passage A

In ancient Greece, Aristotle documented the ability of foraging honeybees to recruit nestmates to a good food source. He did not speculate on how the communication occurred, but he and naturalists since then have observed that a bee that finds a new food source returns to the nest and "dances" for its nestmates. In the 1940s, von Frisch and colleagues discovered a pattern in the dance. They observed a foraging honeybee's dance, deciphered it, and thereby deduced the location of the food source the bee had discovered. Yet questions still remained regarding the precise mechanism used to transmit that information.

In the 1960s, Wenner and Esch each discovered independently that dancing honeybees emit low-frequency sounds, which we now know to come from wing vibrations. Both researchers reasoned that this might explain the bees' ability to communicate effectively even in completely dark nests. But at that time many scientists mistakenly believed that honeybees lack hearing, so the issue remained unresolved. Wenner subsequently proposed that smell rather than hearing was the key to honeybee communication. He hypothesized that honeybees derive information not from sound, but from odors the forager conveys from the food source.

Yet Gould has shown that foragers can dispatch bees to sites they had not actually visited, something that would not be possible if odor were in fact necessary to bees' communication. Finally, using a honeybee robot to simulate the forager's dance, Kirchner and Michelsen showed that sounds emitted during the forager's dance do indeed play an essential role in conveying information about the food's location.

Passage B

All animals communicate in some sense. Bees dance, ants leave trails, some fish emit high-voltage signals. But some species—bees, birds, and primates, for example—communicate symbolically. In an experiment with vervet monkeys in the wild, Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler found that prerecorded vervet alarm calls from a loudspeaker elicited the same response as did naturally produced vervet calls alerting the group to the presence of a predator of a particular type. Vervets looked upward upon hearing an eagle alarm call, and they scanned the ground below in response to a snake alarm call. These responses suggest that each alarm call represents, for vervets, a specific type of predator.

Karl von Frisch was first to crack the code of the honeybee's dance, which he described as "language." The dance symbolically represents the distance, direction, and quality of newly discovered food. Adrian Wenner and others believed that bees rely on olfactory cues, as well as the dance, to find a food source, but this has turned out not to be so.

While it is true that bees have a simple nervous system, they do not automatically follow just any information. Biologist James Gould trained foraging bees to find food in a boat placed in the middle of a lake and then allowed them to return to the hive to indicate this new location. He found that hive members ignored the foragers' instructions, presumably because no pollinating flowers grow in such a place.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with the long history of a single question. Aristotle recorded that a foraging honeybee finding food can recruit nestmates, and naturalists ever since have watched the returning bee dance without knowing how the dance works. Von Frisch and his colleagues supplied the breakthrough in the 1940s, detecting a pattern in the dance and reading it well enough to deduce where the food lay. Note the loose end the paragraph deliberately leaves, because it drives everything after: knowing that the dance encodes a location did not reveal the mechanism by which the information gets transmitted.

Two candidate mechanisms enter, and the paragraph is really about why the question stalled. Wenner and Esch found independently in the 1960s that dancing bees emit low-frequency sounds, now known to come from wing vibrations, and both took this to explain how bees manage to communicate in a completely dark nest. The obstacle was a mistaken belief, common at the time, that honeybees cannot hear, which left the sound explanation unresolved. Wenner then changed position and proposed odor instead, arguing that nestmates take their information from smells the forager carries back from the food.

Resolution arrives in two strokes. Gould showed that foragers can dispatch bees to sites the foragers themselves had never visited, which odor alone could not accomplish, so smell cannot be necessary to the communication. Kirchner and Michelsen then built a robot bee to simulate the dance and demonstrated that the sounds produced during it really do carry essential information about the food's location. Wenner's odor hypothesis is set aside and the sound account confirmed, completing the arc the first paragraph promised.

Passage B begins somewhere else entirely, with a general claim about animal communication. Every animal communicates in some fashion, but a few species communicate symbolically, meaning a signal stands for something in particular. The vervet monkey study supplies the evidence: recorded alarm calls played through a loudspeaker drew the same reactions as genuine ones, with the monkeys looking upward at an eagle call and scanning the ground at a snake call. Because each response matches a specific predator, each call appears to represent that predator to the animals.

Bees now appear as a second instance of the same phenomenon, and notice how differently the shared research gets used. Von Frisch is credited with cracking the code of the dance and with calling it language, and what this author emphasizes is symbolic content, since the dance stands for the distance, direction, and quality of the food. Wenner's olfactory proposal receives a single dismissive clause saying it turned out not to be so. Passage A devoted two paragraphs to that dispute; here it is a detail inside an argument about symbols.

The closing paragraph adds a claim Passage A never makes, that bees assess what they are told. Their nervous system is simple, but they do not automatically act on just any information. Gould trained foragers to feed from a boat anchored in the middle of a lake and let them return to report the location, and the hive ignored the instructions, presumably because no pollinating flowers grow in open water. The dance is therefore treated not as an automatic trigger but as a message its recipients weigh against what they already know.
overall_html: Both passages draw on the same honeybee research but put it to different uses. Passage A traces a scientific question about mechanism, running from Aristotle through von Frisch's decoding of the dance to the contest between Wenner's odor hypothesis and the sound hypothesis, which Gould and then Kirchner and Michelsen's robot bee settled in favor of sound. Passage B is not concerned with mechanism at all: it argues that certain species communicate symbolically, offering vervet alarm calls and the bee dance as examples, and closes with Gould's lake experiment to show that bees evaluate the messages they receive. The relationship is one of different scope over shared evidence, with the two agreeing only that Wenner's odor explanation was wrong.

Most scholars of Mexican American history mark César Chávez's unionizing efforts among Mexican and Mexican American farm laborers in California as the beginning of Chicano political activism in the 1960s. By 1965, Chávez's United Farm Workers Union gained international recognition by initiating a worldwide boycott of grapes in an effort to get growers in California to sign union contracts. The year 1965 also marks the birth of contemporary Chicano theater, for that is the year Luis Valdez approached Chávez about using theater to organize farm workers. Valdez and the members of the resulting Teatro Campesino are generally credited by scholars as having initiated the Chicano theater movement, a movement that would reach its apex in the 1970s.

In the fall of 1965, Valdez gathered a group of striking farm workers and asked them to talk about their working conditions. A former farm worker himself, Valdez was no stranger to the players in the daily drama that was fieldwork. He asked people to illustrate what happened on the picket lines, and the less timid in the audience delighted in acting out their ridicule of the strikebreakers. Using the farm workers' basic improvisations, Valdez guided the group toward the creation of what he termed "actos," skits or sketches whose roots scholars have traced to various sources that had influenced Valdez as a student and as a member of the San Francisco Mime Troupe. Expanding beyond the initial setting of flatbed-truck stages at the fields' edges, the acto became the quintessential form of Chicano theater in the 1960s. According to Valdez, the acto should suggest a solution to the problems exposed in the brief comic statement, and, as with any good political theater, it should satirize the opposition and inspire the audience to social action. Because actos were based on participants' personal experiences, they had palpable immediacy.

In her book El Teatro Campesino, Yolanda Broyles-González rightly criticizes theater historians for having tended to credit Valdez individually with inventing actos as a genre, as if the striking farm workers' improvisational talent had depended entirely on his vision and expertise for the form it took. She traces especially the actos' connections to a similar genre of informal, often satirical shows known as carpas that were performed in tents to mainly working-class audiences. Carpas had flourished earlier in the twentieth century in the border area of Mexico and the United States. Many participants in the formation of the Teatro no doubt had substantial cultural links to this tradition and likely adapted it to their improvisations. The early development of the Teatro Campesino was, in fact, a collective accomplishment; still, Valdez's artistic contribution was a crucial one, for the resulting actos were neither carpas nor theater in the European tradition of Valdez's academic training, but a distinctive genre with connections to both.
explanation_html:
The opening does historical scene-setting, anchoring two movements to the same year. Most scholars of Mexican American history treat Cesar Chavez's unionizing of farm laborers in California as the start of Chicano political activism in the 1960s, and by 1965 his union had drawn international attention with a worldwide grape boycott aimed at forcing growers to sign contracts. That same year Luis Valdez approached Chavez about using theater to organize workers, and the group that followed, Teatro Campesino, is generally credited with launching the Chicano theater movement. Nothing is contested yet; the author is laying out the standard account, and the credit given to Valdez is exactly what the last paragraph will complicate.

The middle paragraph reconstructs how the form was actually built. Valdez, a former farm worker himself, gathered striking laborers and asked them to describe their conditions and then act out what happened on the picket lines, with the bolder ones relishing the chance to ridicule strikebreakers. Out of those rough improvisations he shaped what he called actos, short comic skits whose sources scholars trace to influences he absorbed as a student and as a member of a mime troupe. Two ingredients are already in play here: the workers' raw material and Valdez's shaping. By his own standard, an acto should expose a problem and suggest a solution, satirize the opposition, and move the audience to act, drawing its force from lived experience.

The closing paragraph adds a corrective and then the author's own balance. Yolanda Broyles-Gonzalez faults theater historians for treating actos as Valdez's individual invention, as though the workers' improvisational talent depended entirely on his vision, and she connects the form instead to carpas, informal and often satirical tent shows played to working-class audiences in the Mexico-United States border region earlier in the century. The author calls that criticism right and grants that many participants likely carried the carpa tradition into their improvising. Then comes the qualification: the Teatro's early development was genuinely collective, yet Valdez's artistic contribution was crucial, since the actos were neither carpas nor European-style theater but a distinct genre tied to both.
overall_html: The passage recounts the birth of Chicano theater in 1965, when Luis Valdez turned striking farm workers' improvisations into actos, and then weighs how much credit for that form belongs to Valdez alone. The author's purpose is partly narrative and partly evaluative: two paragraphs of history and description set up a final paragraph that endorses Broyles-Gonzalez's objection to the individual-genius account while insisting that Valdez's shaping still mattered. Keep three viewpoints apart, namely the scholars and theater historians who credit Valdez individually, Broyles-Gonzalez, who traces the actos to the carpa tradition, and the author, who calls the achievement collective yet defends Valdez's distinctive role.

In October 1999, the Law Reform Commission of Western Australia (LRCWA) issued its report, "Review of the Civil and Criminal Justice System." Buried within its 400 pages are several important recommendations for introducing contingency fees for lawyers' services into the state of Western Australia. Contingency-fee agreements call for payment only if the lawyer is successful in the case. Because of the lawyer's risk of financial loss, such charges generally exceed regular fees.

Although there are various types of contingency-fee arrangements, the LRCWA has recommended that only one type be introduced: "uplift" fee arrangements, which in the case of a successful outcome require the client to pay the lawyer's normal fee plus an agreed-upon additional percentage of that fee. This restriction is intended to prevent lawyers from gaining disproportionately from awards of damages and thus to ensure that just compensation to plaintiffs is not eroded. A further measure toward this end is found in the recommendation that contingency-fee agreements should be permitted only in cases where two conditions are satisfied: first, the contingency-fee arrangement must be used only as a last resort when all means of avoiding such an arrangement have been exhausted; and second, the lawyer must be satisfied that the client is financially unable to pay the fee in the event that sufficient damages are not awarded.

Unfortunately, under this recommendation, lawyers wishing to enter into an uplift fee arrangement would be forced to investigate not only the legal issues affecting any proposed litigation, but also the financial circumstances of the potential client and the probable cost of the litigation. This process would likely be onerous for a number of reasons, not least of which is the fact that the final cost of litigation depends in large part on factors that may change as the case unfolds, such as strategies adopted by the opposing side.

In addition to being burdensome for lawyers, the proposal to make contingency-fee agreements available only to the least well-off clients would be unfair to other clients. This restriction would unjustly limit freedom of contract and would, in effect, make certain types of litigation inaccessible to middle-income people or even wealthy people who might not be able to liquidate assets to pay the costs of a trial. More importantly, the primary reasons for entering into contingency-fee agreements hold for all clients. First, they provide financing for the costs of pursuing a legal action. Second, they shift the risk of not recovering those costs, and of not obtaining a damages award that will pay their lawyer's fees, from the client to the lawyer. Finally, given the convergence of the lawyer's interest and the client's interest under a contingency-fee arrangement, it is reasonable to assume that such arrangements increase lawyers' diligence and commitment to their cases.
explanation_html:
The passage begins as a plain report before it turns into an argument. In 1999 the Law Reform Commission of Western Australia published a long review of the state's civil and criminal justice system, and tucked inside it were recommendations to introduce contingency fees. Make sure the term is clear: under such an agreement the lawyer is paid only if the case succeeds, and because the lawyer absorbs the risk of getting nothing, the fee charged on a win normally runs higher than an ordinary one. Nothing evaluative has happened yet; the author is simply setting up the proposal that the second half of the passage will attack.

Details of the recommendation follow, and they matter because every later objection targets them. Of the various possible contingency arrangements, the Commission would permit only the uplift kind, in which a winning client pays the lawyer's normal fee plus an agreed additional percentage of it. The stated aim is to stop lawyers taking a disproportionate share of a damages award so that plaintiffs keep their compensation intact. Two further conditions narrow things further: the arrangement may be used only as a last resort once every alternative has been exhausted, and the lawyer must be satisfied that the client could not pay if the damages awarded proved insufficient.

'Unfortunately' marks the pivot, and from here the author is arguing rather than reporting. The first complaint is practical. A lawyer wanting an uplift agreement would have to investigate not only the legal merits of the case but also the client's financial circumstances and the probable cost of the litigation. That last task is the weak point, since what a case finally costs turns largely on factors that shift while it unfolds, such as the strategies the opposing side adopts. The screening requirement, in short, asks lawyers to forecast something that cannot be forecast reliably.

The closing objection moves from inconvenience to fairness. Limiting contingency agreements to the least well-off, the author argues, is unjust to everyone else, since it restricts freedom of contract and effectively puts some litigation out of reach for middle-income or even wealthy people who cannot liquidate assets to fund a trial. Weightier still is the claim that the reasons for entering such agreements hold for all clients: they finance the costs of pursuing an action, they shift the risk of never recovering those costs from client to lawyer, and, by aligning the two parties' interests, they can be expected to sharpen a lawyer's diligence and commitment.
overall_html: The passage sets out the Law Reform Commission of Western Australia's proposal to permit contingency fees only in the restricted uplift form and only for clients who cannot otherwise pay, then argues that those restrictions are both burdensome and unfair. The author's purpose is critical: the first two paragraphs report the recommendation neutrally, and the last two attack it, first on the practical ground that lawyers cannot reliably gauge a client's means or a case's eventual cost, then on the principled ground that the benefits of contingency arrangements, namely financing, risk transfer, and sharper lawyer commitment, belong to clients at every income level. Only two viewpoints are in play, the Commission's and the author's.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), approved by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948, was the first international treaty to expressly affirm universal respect for human rights. Prior to 1948 no truly international standard of humanitarian beliefs existed. Although Article 1 of the 1945 UN Charter had been written with the express purpose of obligating the UN to "encourage respect for human rights and for fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion," there were members of delegations from various small countries and representatives of several nongovernmental organizations who felt that the language of Article 1 was not strong enough, and that the Charter as a whole did not go far enough in its efforts to guarantee basic human rights. This group lobbied vigorously to strengthen the Charter's human rights provisions and proposed that member states be required "to take separate and joint action and to co-operate with the organization for the promotion of human rights." This would have implied an obligation for member states to act on human rights issues. Ultimately, this proposal and others like it were not adopted; instead, the UDHR was commissioned and drafted.

The original mandate for producing the document was given to the UN Commission on Human Rights in February 1946. Between that time and the General Assembly's final approval of the document, the UDHR passed through an elaborate eight-stage drafting process in which it made its way through almost every level of the UN hierarchy. The articles were debated at each stage, and all 30 articles were argued passionately by delegates representing diverse ideologies, traditions, and cultures. The document as it was finally approved set forth the essential principles of freedom and equality for everyone—regardless of sex, race, color, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status. It also asserted a number of fundamental human rights, including among others the right to work, the right to rest and leisure, and the right to education.

While the UDHR is in many ways a progressive document, it also has weaknesses, the most regrettable of which is its nonbinding legal status. For all its strong language and high ideals, the UDHR remains a resolution of a purely programmatic nature. Nevertheless, the document has led, even if belatedly, to the creation of legally binding human rights conventions, and it clearly deserves recognition as an international standard-setting piece of work, as a set of aspirations to which UN member states are intended to strive, and as a call to arms in the name of humanity, justice, and freedom.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph sets the UDHR against what came before it and quietly plants the criticism the passage will return to. Approved in 1948, it was the first international treaty to affirm universal respect for human rights outright, where previously no truly international humanitarian standard existed. The 1945 UN Charter had aimed at the same goal, obligating the UN to encourage respect for rights and freedoms without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion, but the reformers, delegates from various small countries together with representatives of nongovernmental organizations, judged that language too weak. Their proposal would have required member states themselves to act on human rights, separately and jointly. Watch what becomes of it: the binding obligation was dropped and a drafted declaration commissioned instead.

Having explained why the document exists, the passage turns to how it was made and what it says. The mandate went to the UN Commission on Human Rights in early 1946, and the text then moved through an elaborate eight-stage drafting process that reached nearly every level of the UN hierarchy, with all thirty articles argued passionately by delegates from sharply different ideologies, traditions and cultures. The approved result set out freedom and equality for everyone regardless of sex, race, color, language, religion, opinion, origin, property, birth or status, and asserted specific entitlements including rights to work, to rest and leisure, and to education. The detail is doing legitimacy work, establishing breadth of participation and breadth of coverage.

Judgment arrives in the closing paragraph, and the author is the one delivering it. The verdict is split but finally favorable. On the debit side, and named the most regrettable weakness, the UDHR binds no one legally; for all its strong language and high ideals it remains a resolution of purely programmatic character, which is the direct consequence of the choice recorded at the start. The nevertheless then carries the paragraph: the declaration did eventually lead to legally binding human rights conventions, and it earns recognition as international standard-setting work, as a set of aspirations member states are meant to strive toward, and as a call to arms. The criticism is conceded in order to be outweighed.
overall_html: The passage presents the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the first international instrument expressly affirming universal human rights, explaining that it emerged only after a push to write binding obligations into the UN Charter failed, describing its long multi-stage drafting and the breadth of what it proclaims, and then assessing it. The author's purpose is evaluative, moving from historical background to composition and content and finally to a verdict that concedes the document's lack of legal force while insisting on its value as a standard-setter and as the spur to the binding conventions that followed. The author is the only judging voice; the reformers who wanted a stronger Charter appear as background that sets up the closing complaint.

It is commonly assumed that even if some forgeries have aesthetic merit, no forgery has as much as an original by the imitated artist would. Yet even the most prominent art specialists can be duped by a talented artist turned forger into mistaking an almost perfect forgery for an original. For instance, artist Han van Meegeren's The Disciples at Emmaus (1937)—painted under the forged signature of the acclaimed Dutch master Jan Vermeer (1632–1675)—attracted lavish praise from experts as one of Vermeer's finest works. The painting hung in a Rotterdam museum until 1945, when, to the great embarrassment of the critics, van Meegeren revealed its origin. Astonishingly, there was at least one highly reputed critic who persisted in believing it to be a Vermeer even after van Meegeren's confession.

Given the experts' initial enthusiasm, some philosophers argue that van Meegeren's painting must have possessed aesthetic characteristics that, in a Vermeer original, would have justified the critics' plaudits. Van Meegeren's Emmaus thus raises difficult questions regarding the status of superbly executed forgeries. Is a forgery inherently inferior as art? How are we justified, if indeed we are, in revising downwards our critical assessment of a work unmasked as a forgery? Philosopher of art Alfred Lessing proposes convincing answers to these questions.

A forged work is indeed inferior as art, Lessing argues, but not because of a shortfall in aesthetic qualities strictly defined, that is to say, in the qualities perceptible on the picture's surface. For example, in its composition, its technique, and its brilliant use of color, van Meegeren's work is flawless, even beautiful. Lessing argues instead that the deficiency lies in what might be called the painting's intangible qualities. All art, explains Lessing, involves technique, but not all art involves origination of a new vision, and originality of vision is one of the fundamental qualities by which artistic, as opposed to purely aesthetic, accomplishment is measured. Thus Vermeer is acclaimed for having inaugurated, in the seventeenth century, a new way of seeing, and for pioneering techniques for embodying this new way of seeing through distinctive treatment of light, color, and form.

Even if we grant that van Meegeren, with his undoubted mastery of Vermeer's innovative techniques, produced an aesthetically superior painting, he did so about three centuries after Vermeer developed the techniques in question. Whereas Vermeer's origination of these techniques in the seventeenth century represents a truly impressive and historic achievement, van Meegeren's production of The Disciples at Emmaus in the twentieth century presents nothing new or creative to the history of art. Van Meegeren's forgery therefore, for all its aesthetic merits, lacks the historical significance that makes Vermeer's work artistically great.
explanation_html:
A widely held assumption opens the passage, namely that a forgery can never match an original by the imitated artist in aesthetic merit, and the van Meegeren episode is produced immediately to strain it. Passed off under Vermeer's signature, The Disciples at Emmaus drew lavish praise from the experts as one of the Dutch master's finest works and hung in a Rotterdam museum until van Meegeren admitted authorship in 1945. Pay attention to the last detail, since it sharpens the puzzle: one highly reputed critic went on believing the picture was a Vermeer even after the confession.

The second paragraph turns the anecdote into a philosophical problem. Because the experts were genuinely enthusiastic, some philosophers conclude the painting must have had qualities that would have justified such praise had Vermeer produced it, which forces three questions: what status superb forgeries hold, whether forgery is inherently inferior as art, and how a downward revision of a work's rating can ever be justified once it is unmasked. Watch the last sentence closely, because in calling Lessing's answers convincing the author quietly takes a side before the argument has even been presented.

Lessing's answer is a distinction, and getting it straight is the whole passage. He agrees the forgery is inferior as art, but denies the shortfall lies in aesthetic qualities strictly defined, meaning what is perceptible on the picture's surface; van Meegeren's composition, technique and color are flawless, even beautiful. The deficiency sits instead in intangible qualities. Every work of art involves technique, but only some involve originating a new vision, and that originality is a fundamental measure of artistic as opposed to merely aesthetic accomplishment, which is why Vermeer is credited with inaugurating a new way of seeing.

The closing paragraph applies the distinction to the case and lands the conclusion. Grant van Meegeren everything, including mastery of Vermeer's innovative techniques and even an aesthetically superior painting, and one fact remains: he worked roughly three centuries after those techniques were invented. Vermeer's origination of them was an impressive and historic achievement, while a twentieth-century imitation contributes nothing new or creative to the history of art. The forgery therefore lacks historical significance, and that absence, not any flaw you could see on the canvas, is what keeps it from artistic greatness.
overall_html: The passage argues, following Lessing, that a forgery is inferior as art not because it looks worse but because artistic greatness depends on originality of vision and historical significance, qualities a copy cannot possess however aesthetically accomplished it is. The author's purpose is to explain and endorse a solution to a puzzle, moving from the van Meegeren case that fooled the experts, to the philosophical questions it raises, to Lessing's distinction between aesthetic and artistic merit, and finally to that distinction applied back to the forgery. The positions to track are the experts who praised the fake, the philosophers who infer real aesthetic quality from that praise, and Lessing, whose answers the author explicitly accepts.

Passage A

One function of language is to influence others' behavior by changing what they know, believe, or desire. For humans engaged in conversation, the perception of another's mental state is perhaps the most common vocalization stimulus.

While animal vocalizations may have evolved because they can potentially alter listeners' behavior to the signaler's benefit, such communication is—in contrast to human language—inadvertent, because most animals, with the possible exception of chimpanzees, cannot attribute mental states to others. The male Physalaemus frog calls because calling causes females to approach and other males to retreat, but there is no evidence that he does so because he attributes knowledge or desire to other frogs, or because he knows his calls will affect their knowledge and that this knowledge will, in turn, affect their behavior. Research also suggests that, in marked contrast to humans, nonhuman primates do not produce vocalizations in response to perception of another's need for information. Macaques, for example, give alarm calls when predators approach and coo calls upon finding food, yet experiments reveal no evidence that individuals were more likely to call about these events when they were aware of them but their offspring were clearly ignorant; similarly, chimpanzees do not appear to adjust their calling to inform ignorant individuals of their own location or that of food. Many animal vocalizations whose production initially seems goal-directed are not as purposeful as they first appear.

Passage B

Many scientists distinguish animal communication systems from human language on the grounds that the former are rigid responses to stimuli, whereas human language is spontaneous and creative.

In this connection, it is commonly stated that no animal can use its communication system to lie. Obviously, a lie requires intention to deceive: to judge whether a particular instance of animal communication is truly prevarication requires knowledge of the animal's intentions. Language philosopher H. P. Grice explains that for an individual to mean something by uttering x, the individual must intend, in expressing x, to induce an audience to believe something and must also intend the utterance to be recognized as so intended. But conscious intention is a category of mental experience widely believed to be uniquely human. Philosopher Jacques Maritain's discussion of the honeybee's elaborate "waggle-dance" exemplifies this view. Although bees returning to the hive communicate to other bees the distance and direction of food sources, such communication is, Maritain asserts, merely a conditioned reflex: animals may use communicative signs but lack conscious intention regarding their use.

But these arguments are circular: conscious intention is ruled out a priori and then its absence taken as evidence that animal communication is fundamentally different from human language. In fact, the narrowing of the perceived gap between animal communication and human language revealed by recent research with chimpanzees and other animals calls into question not only the assumption that the difference between animal and human communication is qualitative rather than merely quantitative, but also the accompanying assumption that animals respond mechanically to stimuli, whereas humans speak with conscious understanding and intent.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a functional account of language: one of its jobs is to change what other people know, believe or desire, and thereby their behavior. Add the second sentence and you get the benchmark the rest of the passage will apply, since for humans in conversation the usual prompt for speaking is reading someone else's mental state. Short as it is, this paragraph is doing setup work, defining the standard against which animal calls are about to be measured.

The comparison follows, and the key word is inadvertent. Animal vocalizations may well have evolved because they shift a listener's behavior to the signaler's advantage, but on the Author of Passage A's account most animals cannot attribute mental states at all, chimpanzees possibly excepted, so no intention to inform is involved. The male Physalaemus frog calls because calling draws females and repels rival males, with no evidence he credits other frogs with knowledge or desire. Experiments make the same point with primates: macaques do not call more readily when they know of a predator or food and their offspring plainly do not, and chimpanzees do not adjust calls to inform the ignorant.

Passage B begins by reporting the received distinction rather than asserting it. Many scientists, it says, separate animal communication from human language by treating the first as rigid response to stimuli and the second as spontaneous and creative. Keep the attribution firmly in mind, because everything through the next paragraph is a summary of the view B intends to dismantle, and mistaking summary for endorsement will scramble your reading of the passage.

The lying test is offered as the standard test case: no animal, it is said, can use its system to deceive. That claim depends on intention, since a lie requires an intent to deceive, so settling it means knowing an animal's intentions. Grice supplies the demanding standard, that meaning something by an utterance requires intending to induce a belief and intending the utterance to be recognized as so intended, and conscious intention is widely believed to be uniquely human. Maritain illustrates the resulting verdict, calling the honeybee's waggle-dance, which conveys distance and direction of food, a mere conditioned reflex.

Now the objection arrives, and it targets the reasoning rather than the facts. The Author of Passage B charges the arguments with circularity: conscious intention is excluded from animals in advance, and then its absence is treated as proof that their communication differs fundamentally from human language. Recent work with chimpanzees and other animals has narrowed the perceived gap, which puts pressure on two assumptions at once, that the difference is qualitative rather than merely one of degree, and that animals react mechanically while humans speak with understanding and intent.
overall_html: Both passages examine whether animal communication differs in kind from human language, and they come down on opposite sides: Passage A holds that animal vocalizations are inadvertent because most animals cannot attribute mental states, citing frog calls and primate experiments in which callers ignore what listeners need to know, while Passage B argues that the standard case for such a divide is circular, assuming animals lack conscious intention and then treating that assumption as evidence. The purposes differ accordingly, A presenting empirical findings to support the qualitative distinction and B critiquing the logic behind it. Track the Author of Passage A, the many scientists whose view Passage B reports through Grice and Maritain, and the Author of Passage B, who rejects it.

In contrast to the mainstream of U.S. historiography during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, African American historians of the period, such as George Washington Williams and W. E. B. DuBois, adopted a transnational perspective. This was true for several reasons, not the least of which was the necessity of doing so if certain aspects of the history of African Americans in the United States were to be treated honestly.

First, there was the problem of citizenship. Even after the adoption in 1868 of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which defined citizenship, the question of citizenship for African Americans had not been genuinely resolved. Because of this, emigrationist sentiment was a central issue in black political discourse, and both issues were critical topics for investigation. The implications for historical scholarship and national identity were enormous. While some black leaders insisted on their right to U.S. citizenship, others called on black people to emigrate and find a homeland of their own. Most African Americans were certainly not willing to relinquish their claims to the benefits of U.S. citizenship, but many had reached a point of profound pessimism and had begun to question their allegiance to the United States.

Mainstream U.S. historiography was firmly rooted in a nationalist approach during this period; the glorification of the nation and a focus on the nation-state as a historical force were dominant. The expanding spheres of influence of Europe and the United States prompted the creation of new genealogies of nations, new myths about the inevitability of nations, their "temperaments," their destinies. African American intellectuals who confronted the nationalist approach to historiography were troubled by its implications. Some argued that imperialism was a natural outgrowth of nationalism and its view that a state's strength is measured by the extension of its political power over colonial territory; the scramble for colonial empires was a distinct aspect of nationalism in the latter part of the nineteenth century.

Yet, for all their distrust of U.S. nationalism, most early black historians were themselves engaged in a sort of nation building. Deliberately or not, they contributed to the formation of a collective identity, reconstructing a glorious African past for the purposes of overturning degrading representations of blackness and establishing a firm cultural basis for a shared identity. Thus, one might argue that black historians' internationalism was a manifestation of a kind of nationalism that posits a diasporic community, which, while lacking a sovereign territory or official language, possesses a single culture, however mythical, with singular historical roots. Many members of this diaspora saw themselves as an oppressed "nation" without a homeland, or they imagined Africa as home. Hence, these historians understood their task to be the writing of the history of a people scattered by force and circumstance, a history that began in Africa.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by staking a contrast. While mainstream U.S. historiography of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries looked inward, early African American historians such as Williams and DuBois worked transnationally, looking beyond the borders of the United States. Several reasons lay behind this, and the one flagged as most important is necessity: certain parts of African American history simply could not be treated honestly within a national frame. Read this as a thesis paragraph promising an explanation, and expect the reasons to arrive in order.

The first reason is the unsettled status of citizenship. Although the Fourteenth Amendment had defined citizenship in 1868, the question remained genuinely unresolved for African Americans, which pushed emigration to the center of black political discourse and made both citizenship and emigration urgent subjects of research with large consequences for scholarship and national identity. Notice the split the paragraph records: some leaders pressed their claim to U.S. citizenship while others urged departure and a homeland elsewhere, and even those unwilling to surrender the benefits of citizenship had grown deeply pessimistic and were questioning their allegiance.

Attention shifts to what the mainstream was doing, supplying the second reason. Historiography of the era was nationalist through and through, glorifying the nation and treating the nation-state as the engine of history, and the expanding reach of Europe and the United States generated fresh genealogies of nations along with myths about their inevitability, temperaments and destinies. African American intellectuals found the implications disturbing, and some drew a direct line from nationalism to imperialism, since a doctrine that measures a state's strength by political power extended over colonies makes the scramble for empire a natural outgrowth rather than an aberration.

A complication closes the passage, signaled by that opening yet. For all their distrust of U.S. nationalism, these historians were engaged in nation building of their own, reconstructing a glorious African past in order to overturn degrading images of blackness and ground a shared identity. So their internationalism can be read as its own nationalism, one that posits a diasporic community holding a single culture, however mythical, with common roots but no sovereign territory or official language. Members of that diaspora saw themselves as an oppressed nation without a homeland, or imagined Africa as home, which made their task a history of a scattered people that begins in Africa.
overall_html: The passage explains why early African American historians departed from the nationalist mainstream of their era and wrote transnationally, pointing to the unresolved citizenship of African Americans and the emigration debate it fueled, and to their objection that nationalist historiography carried imperialism within it. Its purpose is analytic rather than evaluative: the author sets up the contrast, supplies the reasons behind it, and then closes with a paradox, arguing that these historians practiced a nationalism of their own by constructing a diasporic people with a glorious African past and a shared culture. The viewpoints to keep straight are the early African American historians, the nationalist mainstream they resisted, and the author's own qualified reading of their internationalism.

To study centuries-old earthquakes and the geologic faults that caused them, seismologists usually dig trenches along visible fault lines, looking for sediments that show evidence of having shifted. Using radiocarbon dating, they measure the quantity of the radioactive isotope carbon 14 present in wood or other organic material trapped in the sediments when they shifted. Since carbon 14 occurs naturally in organic materials and decays at a constant rate, the age of organic materials can be reconstructed from the amount of the isotope remaining in them. These data can show the location and frequency of past earthquakes and provide hints about the likelihood and location of future earthquakes.

Geologists William Bull and Mark Brandon have recently developed a new method, called lichenometry, for detecting and dating past earthquakes. Bull and Brandon developed the method based on the fact that large earthquakes generate numerous simultaneous rockfalls in mountain ranges that are sensitive to seismic shaking. Instead of dating fault-line sediments, lichenometry involves measuring the size of lichens growing on the rocks exposed by these rockfalls. Lichens—symbiotic organisms consisting of a fungus and an alga—quickly colonize newly exposed rock surfaces in the wake of rockfalls, and once established they grow radially, flat against the rocks, at a slow but constant rate for as long as 1,000 years if left undisturbed. One species of North American lichen, for example, spreads outward by about 9.5 millimeters each century. Hence, the diameter of the largest lichen on a boulder provides direct evidence of when the boulder was dislodged and repositioned. If many rockfalls over a large geographic area occurred simultaneously, that pattern would imply that there had been a strong earthquake. The location of the earthquake's epicenter can then be determined by mapping these rockfalls, since they decrease in abundance as the distance from the epicenter increases.

Lichenometry has distinct advantages over radiocarbon dating. Radiocarbon dating is accurate only to within plus or minus 40 years, because the amount of the carbon 14 isotope varies naturally in the environment depending on the intensity of the radiation striking Earth's upper atmosphere. Additionally, this intensity has fluctuated greatly during the past 300 years, causing many radiocarbon datings of events during this period to be of little value. Lichenometry, Bull and Brandon claim, can accurately date an earthquake to within ten years. They note, however, that using lichenometry requires careful site selection and accurate calibration of lichen growth rates, adding that the method is best used for earthquakes that occurred within the last 500 years. Sites must be selected to minimize the influence of snow avalanches and other disturbances that would affect normal lichen growth, and conditions like shade and wind that promote faster lichen growth must be factored in.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the established technique, which functions as the baseline the new method will be measured against. To study earthquakes from centuries past, seismologists dig trenches along visible faults and look for sediments that shifted. Radiocarbon dating then supplies the timing: organic material such as wood caught in those sediments contains carbon 14, which occurs naturally and decays at a fixed rate, so the amount left indicates age. The purpose is forward-looking as well as historical, since knowing where past earthquakes struck and how often they recurred offers hints about future ones.

A new alternative is introduced, and its logic is worth following step by step. Bull and Brandon reasoned from the fact that large earthquakes trigger many rockfalls at once in mountains sensitive to shaking. Rather than dating sediments, their method measures lichens, the fungus-and-alga organisms that quickly colonize freshly exposed rock and then spread outward flat against it at a slow but steady rate for up to a thousand years, one North American species widening by about nine and a half millimeters a century. The largest lichen on a boulder therefore dates the fall. Widespread simultaneous rockfalls indicate a strong earthquake, and because rockfalls thin out with distance, mapping them locates the epicenter.

The final paragraph evaluates, and the balance of it matters more than the headline. Radiocarbon dating is accurate only to within forty years either way, because atmospheric radiation striking the Earth makes the natural quantity of carbon 14 vary, and that intensity has swung sharply over the last three hundred years, leaving many datings from that period nearly worthless. Against this, Bull and Brandon claim accuracy within ten years. Note that they supply the limits themselves: sites must be chosen to exclude avalanches and similar disturbances, growth rates must be calibrated for conditions like shade and wind, and the method suits earthquakes of the last five hundred years.
overall_html: The passage introduces lichenometry, a method of dating past earthquakes by measuring the lichens growing on rocks exposed by earthquake-triggered rockfalls, and presents it as a more precise alternative to the radiocarbon dating of fault-line sediments. The author's purpose is expository and comparative rather than argumentative, first describing the traditional trenching and radiocarbon technique, then explaining how Bull and Brandon's method works and how mapping rockfalls locates an epicenter, and finally weighing its tenfold gain in accuracy against the conditions it requires, including careful site selection, calibrated growth rates, and a limit of roughly five hundred years. The only viewpoint developed is that of Bull and Brandon.

While courts have long allowed custom-made medical illustrations depicting personal injury to be presented as evidence in legal cases, the issue of whether they have a legitimate place in the courtroom is surrounded by ongoing debate and misinformation. Some opponents of their general use argue that while illustrations are sometimes invaluable in presenting the physical details of a personal injury, in all cases except those involving the most unusual injuries, illustrations from medical textbooks can be adequate. Most injuries, such as fractures and whiplash, they say, are rather generic in nature—certain commonly encountered forces act on particular areas of the body in standard ways—so they can be represented by generic illustrations.

Another line of complaint stems from the belief that custom-made illustrations often misrepresent the facts in order to comply with the partisan interests of litigants. Even some lawyers appear to share a version of this view, believing that such illustrations can be used to bolster a weak case. Illustrators are sometimes approached by lawyers who, unable to find medical experts to support their clients' claims, think that they can replace expert testimony with such deceptive professional illustrations. But this is mistaken. Even if an unscrupulous illustrator could be found, such illustrations would be inadmissible as evidence in the courtroom unless a medical expert were present to testify to their accuracy.

It has also been maintained that custom-made illustrations may subtly distort the issues through the use of emphasis, coloration, and other means, even if they are technically accurate. But professional medical illustrators strive for objective accuracy and avoid devices that have inflammatory potential, sometimes even eschewing the use of color. Unlike illustrations in medical textbooks, which are designed to include the extensive detail required by medical students, custom-made medical illustrations are designed to include only the information that is relevant for those deciding a case. The end user is typically a jury or a judge, for whose benefit the depiction is reduced to the details that are crucial to determining the legally relevant facts. The more complex details often found in textbooks can be deleted so as not to confuse the issue. For example, illustrations of such things as veins and arteries would only get in the way when an illustration is supposed to be used to explain the nature of a bone fracture.

Custom-made medical illustrations, which are based on a plaintiff's X rays, computerized tomography scans, and medical records and reports, are especially valuable in that they provide visual representations of data whose verbal description would be very complex. Expert testimony by medical professionals often relies heavily on the use of technical terminology, which those who are not specially trained in the field find difficult to translate mentally into visual imagery. Since, for most people, adequate understanding of physical data depends on thinking at least partly in visual terms, the clearly presented visual stimulation provided by custom-made illustrations can be quite instructive.
explanation_html:
The passage frames a live dispute and immediately gives the other side the floor. Courts have long admitted custom-made medical illustrations of personal injury, yet debate and misinformation persist about whether they belong there. The first complaint from the opponents is that custom work is usually unnecessary: illustrations can be invaluable for showing physical detail, but except for genuinely unusual injuries, textbook illustrations would do. Their reasoning is that most injuries, fractures and whiplash among them, are generic, since familiar forces act on particular body parts in standard ways, so generic pictures can represent them. Notice this objection goes unanswered for now.

A second objection concerns honesty rather than necessity, and here the author answers directly. The worry is that custom illustrations bend the facts to serve whichever litigant paid for them, a belief some lawyers share, imagining that a picture can prop up a weak case. The passage confirms the temptation is real, since lawyers who cannot find supportive medical experts sometimes approach illustrators hoping deceptive images will substitute for testimony. The rebuttal is procedural rather than moral: even if a dishonest illustrator existed, such an illustration could not be admitted as evidence unless a medical expert testified to its accuracy.

The third objection is subtler, alleging that emphasis, coloration and similar choices can skew the issues even in a technically accurate image, and the author's answer is the longest in the passage. Professional illustrators aim at objective accuracy and steer clear of inflammatory devices, sometimes dropping color altogether. The stronger point turns the first objection on its head: textbook illustrations carry the exhaustive detail medical students need, while custom images are built for a judge or jury and pared down to what determines the legally relevant facts. Veins and arteries would merely obscure a picture meant to explain a fracture.

Having cleared the objections, the author closes with the affirmative case. Custom illustrations are constructed from the plaintiff's own X rays, scans, records and reports, and their value lies in turning data whose verbal description would be forbiddingly complex into something visible. Expert testimony leans on technical vocabulary that untrained listeners struggle to convert into mental pictures, which is the real obstacle in the courtroom. Since most people need at least some visual thinking to grasp physical data properly, the clear visual stimulation these illustrations supply is genuinely instructive rather than merely persuasive.
overall_html: The passage defends the use of custom-made medical illustrations as courtroom evidence, answering the charges that textbook images would suffice, that custom work misrepresents facts for partisan advantage, and that even accurate images distort through emphasis and color, before arguing positively that such illustrations make complex physical data comprehensible to judges and juries who cannot easily visualize technical testimony. The author's purpose is persuasive, and the structure is objection-and-response across three paragraphs followed by an affirmative case. Two viewpoints are in play, the opponents whose three lines of complaint organize the passage, and the author, who rebuts the second and third directly.

Passage A

Because dental caries (decay) is strongly linked to consumption of the sticky, carbohydrate-rich staples of agricultural diets, prehistoric human teeth can provide clues about when a population made the transition from a hunter-gatherer diet to an agricultural one. Caries formation is influenced by several factors, including tooth structure, bacteria in the mouth, and diet. In particular, caries formation is affected by carbohydrates' texture and composition, since carbohydrates more readily stick to teeth.

Many researchers have demonstrated the link between carbohydrate consumption and caries. In North America, Leigh studied caries in archaeologically derived teeth, noting that caries rates differed between indigenous populations that primarily consumed meat (a Sioux sample showed almost no caries) and those heavily dependent on cultivated maize (a Zuni sample had 75 percent carious teeth). Leigh's findings have been frequently confirmed by other researchers, who have shown that, in general, the greater a population's dependence on agriculture is, the higher its rate of caries formation will be.

Under some circumstances, however, nonagricultural populations may exhibit relatively high caries rates. For example, early nonagricultural populations in western North America who consumed large amounts of highly processed stone-ground flour made from gathered acorns show relatively high caries frequencies. And wild plants collected by the Hopi included several species with high cariogenic potential, notably pinyon nuts and wild tubers.

Passage B

Archaeologists recovered human skeletal remains interred over a 2,000-year period in prehistoric Ban Chiang, Thailand. The site's early inhabitants appear to have had a hunter-gatherer-cultivator economy. Evidence indicates that, over time, the population became increasingly dependent on agriculture.

Research suggests that agricultural intensification results in declining human health, including dental health. Studies show that dental caries is uncommon in pre-agricultural populations. Increased caries frequency may result from increased consumption of starchy-sticky foodstuffs or from alterations in tooth wear. The wearing down of tooth crown surfaces reduces caries formation by removing fissures that can trap food particles. A reduction of fiber or grit in a diet may diminish tooth wear, thus increasing caries frequency. However, severe wear that exposes a tooth's pulp cavity may also result in caries.

The diet of Ban Chiang's inhabitants included some cultivated rice and yams from the beginning of the period represented by the recovered remains. These were part of a varied diet that also included wild plant and animal foods. Since both rice and yams are carbohydrates, increased reliance on either or both should theoretically result in increased caries frequency.

Yet comparisons of caries frequency in the Early and Late Ban Chiang Groups indicate that overall caries frequency is slightly greater in the Early Group. Tooth wear patterns do not indicate tooth wear changes between Early and Late Groups that would explain this unexpected finding. It is more likely that, although dependence on agriculture increased, the diet in the Late period remained varied enough that no single food dominated. Furthermore, there may have been a shift from sweeter carbohydrates (yams) toward rice, a less cariogenic carbohydrate.
explanation_html:
Passage A establishes the principle everything after it depends on. Dental caries, ordinary tooth decay, is tightly linked to the sticky, carbohydrate-heavy foods that agriculture supplies, so prehistoric teeth can indicate when a population shifted from hunting and gathering to farming. The author is careful not to make decay a simple function of diet, listing tooth structure and oral bacteria alongside it. Within diet, the detail that matters is texture and composition, because some carbohydrates cling to teeth more readily than others.

Evidence for the link comes next, moving from one striking case to a general rule. Leigh examined teeth recovered archaeologically in North America and found the rates diverging sharply by diet, with a largely meat-eating Sioux sample showing almost no caries and a maize-dependent Zuni sample showing three-quarters of teeth decayed. The paragraph then widens the claim: other researchers have repeatedly confirmed Leigh's result, so that in general the more a population depends on agriculture, the higher its caries rate. Hold onto the phrase in general, because the next paragraph qualifies it.

The qualification arrives right on schedule and keeps A from overstating its own rule. Some populations that never farmed still show relatively high caries rates, and two examples make the point. Early nonagricultural groups in western North America ate large quantities of finely stone-ground acorn flour, a highly processed carbohydrate, and their caries frequencies are correspondingly high. Wild plants gathered by the Hopi included several with strong decay-causing potential, notably pinyon nuts and wild tubers. The lesson is that processing and plant type, not farming as such, drive the effect.

Passage B narrows from principle to a single excavation. Human remains buried over a two-thousand-year span were recovered at prehistoric Ban Chiang in Thailand, and the earliest inhabitants appear to have combined hunting, gathering and cultivation. The one trend B establishes here is that the population grew steadily more dependent on agriculture over that span. Notice how neatly this site fits the framework A supplied, since an increasing reliance on farming is precisely the condition under which caries rates are expected to climb.

Before reporting results, B lays out the expectations and the mechanisms in play. Research generally indicates that intensifying agriculture worsens human health, dental health included, and that caries is uncommon before farming. Two possible causes are distinguished: more starchy, sticky food, or changes in how teeth wear down. The wear mechanism runs both ways and repays close reading. Wearing away the crown surface removes the fissures that trap food and so reduces decay, meaning less fiber or grit increases caries, yet wear severe enough to expose the pulp cavity causes caries too.

The Ban Chiang diet is then specified, sharpening the prediction. Cultivated rice and yams were present from the very start of the period covered by the remains, but they formed part of a mixed diet that also drew on wild plants and animals. Since both rice and yams are carbohydrates, the theory just outlined predicts that leaning more heavily on either or both should push caries frequency up. That prediction is stated explicitly so the finding in the last paragraph registers as a genuine surprise.

The results contradict the prediction, and the closing paragraph works through why. Caries frequency is slightly higher in the Early Group than the Late Group, the reverse of what increasing agriculture should produce, and the wear patterns show no change between the groups that could account for it. Two explanations are offered, both tentative. The Late diet may have stayed varied enough that no single food dominated, and there may have been a move away from sweeter yams toward rice, a carbohydrate less likely to cause decay.
overall_html: Both passages concern what dental caries reveals about ancient diets, and the relationship is one of general rule applied to a particular site, with the application producing an unexpected result. Passage A establishes that caries rates rise with dependence on agriculture while noting that heavily processed or naturally cariogenic wild plants can raise them too; Passage B examines two thousand years of remains from Ban Chiang, where reliance on farming increased yet caries frequency was slightly higher in the earlier group, and explains this by a persistently varied diet and a possible shift from yams to less cariogenic rice. Each passage reports researchers' findings in a single expository voice.
