Passage A

Law enforcement agencies can effectively nullify particular laws, or particular applications of law, simply by declining to prosecute violators. This power appears to be exercised frequently and I attempt here to explain why.

Rules of law are almost always overinclusive: read literally, they forbid some conduct that the legislature that formulated the rule did not want to forbid. The costs of precisely tailoring a rule to the conduct intended to be forbidden would be prohibitive given the limitations of human foresight and the inherent ambiguities of language. The more particularly the legislature tries to describe the forbidden conduct, the more loopholes it will create. Enforcing an overinclusive rule to the letter could impose very heavy social costs. The effect would be like punishing an innocent person in order to reduce the probability of acquitting a guilty one. Of course, the danger of punishing the innocent is not a decisive blow against the use of a particular method of law enforcement; the danger must be traded off against the costs of alternative methods that would reduce it. But there is a technique—discretionary nonenforcement—by which the costs of overinclusion can be reduced without a corresponding increase in underinclusion (loopholes).

Of course, allowing discretionary nonenforcement does not determine the principle by which the law enforcement agency will select its cases. Conceivably the agency could concentrate its resources on those areas of conduct that had been brought inadvertently within the scope of the rule. But this seems unlikely. Capricious enforcement is not unknown (or even rare) but it does not appear to be the central tendency since legislative oversight assures that the agency does not stray too far from the intended, as distinct from the enacted, regulation being enforced.

Passage B

The newspaper reported that 231,000 water customers in the city are late paying their bills—some by months, others by decades. In all, these water delinquents owe the city more than $625 million in overdue bills and penalties. So officials are planning to selectively cut the water to a few residences with outstanding bills to show that they are serious about collecting those debts. Officials plan to target only high-income neighborhoods, to make examples of a few privileged residents who will be in no position to complain since they were caught stiffing the system.

But property owners are responsible for water bills. So why not just do what every other property-related creditor or tax authority does—attach a lien to the property? The money owed would automatically be available whenever a property was sold, and the threat of negative credit implications would be a powerful incentive to keep current with one's water obligations.

Well, here's an answer: a loophole prohibits debts other than taxes from being subject to liens by the city, and, technically, water charges are not taxes. But if the problem is with the law, then why not change the law? Wouldn't that be easier, and politically smarter, than shutting off people's water?
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a claim and a promise. The legal theorist writing it observes that enforcement agencies can effectively nullify a law, or particular applications of one, simply by declining to prosecute, and that the power gets used often. What follows is offered as an explanation of why, so read the rest of this passage as justification rather than complaint.

The explanation rests on a structural fact about rules: they are nearly always overinclusive, forbidding on their face conduct the legislature never meant to reach. Drafting precisely enough to avoid that would cost too much, given the limits of human foresight and the ambiguity of language, and each added specification opens another loophole. Enforcing an overinclusive rule to the letter would carry heavy social costs, which the theorist likens to punishing an innocent person to reduce the chance of acquitting a guilty one. The payoff comes last: discretionary nonenforcement cuts the costs of overinclusion without widening the loopholes that finer drafting would create.

A gap in that argument gets acknowledged before anyone else can press it. Permitting discretion says nothing about which cases an agency will actually drop; in principle it could focus on conduct the rule captured inadvertently, but the theorist doubts agencies are that careful. The concession is real, since capricious enforcement is described as neither unknown nor even rare. What keeps caprice from being the central tendency is legislative oversight, which holds agencies reasonably close to the regulation the legislature intended as distinct from the one it actually enacted.

Passage B abandons theory and reports a case. A newspaper found that 231,000 water customers in one city are behind on their bills, some by decades, owing the city more than $625 million in charges and penalties. Officials plan to cut service at a few homes to demonstrate seriousness, and to pick those homes in high-income neighborhoods, on the theory that wealthy residents caught stiffing the system will be in no position to object. That is selective enforcement of exactly the kind Passage A described, now attached to real consequences.

An alternative follows, framed as an obvious question rather than a legal argument. Since property owners are the ones responsible for water bills, the city could simply do what other property-related creditors and tax authorities do and attach a lien to the property. The debt would then be collected automatically whenever the property was sold, and the prospect of damaged credit would give owners a strong reason to stay current, all without anyone's water being shut off.

The answer turns out to be a technicality, and the commentator declines to accept it as a reason. City liens may cover taxes only, and water charges do not technically qualify as taxes, so the lien route is closed by a loophole. The closing questions carry the argument: if the law is the problem, change the law, which would be easier and politically smarter than shutting off people's water. Where Passage A treats enforcement discretion as a sensible accommodation to imperfect rules, this ending insists that the rule itself be repaired.
overall_html: Passage A argues that selective nonenforcement is a rational response to the fact that legal rules are inevitably overinclusive, since drafting them precisely would be prohibitively costly and would only create more loopholes, with legislative oversight keeping agencies roughly aligned with what the legislature intended. Passage B reports a city preparing to cut water service to a few wealthy delinquents as an example to 231,000 debtors, notes that liens would collect the money automatically, and objects that a technicality blocking liens ought to be fixed by amending the law. The relationship is theory met with a troubling case: B supplies a concrete instance of the discretion A defends and treats changing the rule, rather than enforcing it selectively, as the right remedy.

The prevailing trend in agriculture toward massive and highly mechanized production, with its heavy dependence on debt and credit as a means of raising capital, has been linked to the growing problem of bankruptcy among small farms. African American horticulturalist Booker T. Whatley has proposed a comprehensive approach to small farming that runs counter to this trend. Whatley maintains that small farms can operate profitably despite these economic obstacles, and he provides guidelines that he believes will bring about such profitability when combined with smart management and hard work.

Whatley emphasizes that small farms must generate year-round cash flow. To this end, he recommends growing at least ten different crops, which would alleviate financial problems should one crop fail completely. To minimize the need to seek hard-to-obtain loans, the market for the farm products should be developed via a "clientele membership club" (CMC), whereby clients pay in advance for the right to go to the farm and harvest what they require. To help guarantee small farmers a market for all of their crops, Whatley encourages them to grow only crops that clients ask for, and to comply with client requests regarding the use of chemicals.

Whatley stresses that this "pick-your-own" farming is crucial for profitability because 50 percent of a farmer's production cost is tied up with harvesting, and using clients as harvesters allows the farmer to charge 60 percent of what supermarkets charge and still operate the farm at a profit. Whatley's plan also affords farmers the advantage of selling directly to consumers, thus eliminating distribution costs. To realize profits on a 25-acre farm, for example, Whatley suggests that a CMC of about 1,000 people is needed. The CMC would consist primarily of people from metropolitan areas who value fresh produce.

The success of this plan, Whatley cautions, depends in large part on a farm's location: the farm should be situated on a hard-surfaced road within 40 miles of a population center of at least 50,000 people, as studies suggest that people are less inclined to travel any greater distances for food. In this way, Whatley reverses the traditional view of hard-surfaced roads as farm-to-market roads, calling them instead "city-to-farm" roads. The farm should also have well-drained soil and a ready water source for irrigation, since inevitably certain preferred crops will not be drought resistant. Lastly, Whatley recommends carrying liability insurance upwards of $1 million to cover anyone injured on the farm. Adhering to this plan, Whatley contends, will allow small farms to exist as a viable alternative to sprawling corporate farms while providing top-quality agricultural goods to consumers in most urban areas.
explanation_html:
Start with the problem the proposal is meant to answer. Agriculture has moved toward huge, heavily mechanized operations that raise capital through debt and credit, and that trend has been linked to rising bankruptcy among small farms. Against it, the horticulturalist Booker T. Whatley sets a comprehensive alternative, insisting that small farms can operate profitably despite those pressures if they follow his guidelines and combine them with smart management and hard work. Notice that the author is reporting Whatley's position rather than endorsing it, so treat everything that follows as a set of claims belonging to Whatley.

The first plank of the plan is steady income. Whatley wants year-round cash flow, which is why he recommends growing at least ten different crops, so that one total failure cannot sink the operation. To avoid loans that small farmers find hard to obtain, he would have them build their market through a clientele membership club, an arrangement in which customers pay in advance for the right to come to the farm and harvest what they need. Two further requirements follow from that setup: grow only the crops clients actually ask for, and comply with their requests about chemical use, so nothing is produced without a buyer already waiting.

Why this pick-your-own arrangement carries so much weight becomes clear here, and the reasoning is arithmetical. Harvesting accounts for half of a farmer's production cost, so shifting that labor onto the clients lets the farm charge only about sixty percent of supermarket prices and still turn a profit. Selling directly to the people who eat the food removes distribution costs as well. Whatley also puts numbers on scale, estimating that a twenty-five acre farm needs a club of roughly a thousand members, drawn mainly from metropolitan areas by the appeal of fresh produce.

The closing paragraph gathers the practical conditions and delivers the payoff. Location matters most, in Whatley's warning: a hard-surfaced road, and a population center of at least fifty thousand within forty miles, since studies suggest people will not travel farther for food. Watch the conceptual flip embedded in that requirement, because Whatley recasts roads traditionally seen as carrying produce from farm to market as roads carrying city dwellers out to the farm. He adds well-drained soil, a ready water source for irrigation given that some favored crops are not drought resistant, and heavy liability insurance for injured visitors. Follow all of it, he contends, and small farms remain a viable alternative to sprawling corporate ones.
overall_html: The passage lays out Booker T. Whatley's blueprint for keeping small farms profitable in an era of large, debt-financed, mechanized agriculture: diversify into at least ten crops, sell through a prepaid clientele membership club whose members do their own harvesting, and site the farm close enough to a city that customers will actually make the drive. The author's purpose is expository rather than evaluative, moving from the problem, to the marketing and cost logic of the club, to the physical and legal conditions the plan demands, and ending with Whatley's claim that such farms can stand as a genuine alternative to corporate agriculture. Whatley's is the only viewpoint developed in the passage.

When Jayne Hinds Bidaut saw her first tintype, she was so struck by its rich creamy tones that she could hardly believe this photographic process had been abandoned. She set out to revive it. Bidaut had been searching for a way to photograph insects from her entomological collection, but paper prints simply seemed too flat to her. The tintype, an image captured on a thin, coated piece of iron (there is no tin in it), provided the detail and dimensionality she wanted. The image-containing emulsion can often create a raised surface on the plate.

For the photographer Dan Estabrook, old albumen prints and tintypes inspired a fantasy. He imagines planting the ones he makes in flea markets and antique shops, to be discovered as "originals" from a bygone time that never existed.

On the verge of a filmless, digital revolution, photography is moving forward into its past. In addition to reviving the tintype process, photographers are polishing daguerreotype plates, coating paper with egg whites, making pinhole cameras, and mixing emulsions from nineteenth-century recipes in order to coax new expressive effects from old photographic techniques. So diverse are the artists returning to photography's roots that the movement is more like a groundswell.

The old techniques are heavily hands-on and idiosyncratic. That is the source of their appeal. It is also the prime reason for their eclipse. Most became obsolete in a few decades, replaced by others that were simpler, cheaper, faster, and more consistent in their results. Only the tintype lasted as a curiosity into the twentieth century. Today's artists quickly discover that to exploit the past is to court the very uncertainty that early innovators sought to banish. Such unpredictability attracted Estabrook to old processes. His work embraces accident and idiosyncrasy in order to foster the illusion of antiquity. In his view, time leaches meaning from every photograph and renders it a lost object, enabling us to project onto it our sentiments and associations. So while the stains and imperfections of prints made from gum bichromate or albumen coatings would probably have been cropped out by a nineteenth-century photographer, Estabrook retains them to heighten the sense of nostalgia.

This preoccupation with contingency offers a clue to the deeper motivations of many of the antiquarian avant-gardists. The widely variable outcome of old techniques virtually guarantees that each production is one of a kind and bears, on some level, the indelible mark of the artist's encounter with a particular set of circumstances. At the same time, old methods offer the possibility of recovering an intimacy with photographic communication that mass media have all but overwhelmed.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a single practitioner rather than a thesis. Jayne Hinds Bidaut encountered a tintype, was captivated by its rich creamy tones, and could hardly believe such a process had been abandoned, so she set out to revive it. Her motive was concrete: she wanted to photograph insects from her entomological collection, and ordinary paper prints looked flat to her. A tintype, an image captured on a thin coated sheet of iron despite what the name suggests, gave her the detail and dimensionality she wanted, partly because the emulsion can leave a raised surface on the plate.

A second practitioner arrives with a very different motive, and the brevity of this paragraph is doing structural work rather than signaling unimportance. Where Bidaut wanted a physical quality that the old process delivers, Dan Estabrook is drawn to a fantasy about how such pictures might be received. He imagines planting his own albumen prints and tintypes in flea markets and antique shops so that someone will discover them as originals from a bygone time that never actually existed.

Only now does the author name the general phenomenon these two exemplify, and it is framed as a paradox: just as a filmless digital revolution arrives, photography is moving forward into its past. Beyond the tintype, artists are polishing daguerreotype plates, coating paper with egg whites, building pinhole cameras, and mixing emulsions from nineteenth-century recipes, all in pursuit of expressive effects the old methods yield. The final sentence is about scale, since the sheer diversity of artists involved makes this less a narrow revival than a groundswell.

Here the author explains both what these processes offer and why they disappeared, and the answer turns out to be the same in each case. The techniques are hands-on and idiosyncratic, which is their appeal and also why nearly all were displaced within decades by methods that were simpler, cheaper, faster and more consistent, with only the tintype surviving into the twentieth century as a curiosity. Reviving them means courting the very uncertainty early innovators tried to banish, and that is exactly what drew Estabrook. He embraces accident to manufacture an illusion of age, reasoning that time drains meaning from a photograph and leaves a lost object onto which viewers project their own sentiments, so he keeps the stains a nineteenth-century photographer would have cropped out.

The closing paragraph generalizes from Estabrook's taste for accident to the motives of the whole movement, whose members the author calls the antiquarian avant-gardists. Two payoffs are named. Because the outcomes of old techniques vary so widely, each production is effectively one of a kind and bears the mark of one artist's encounter with one particular set of circumstances. Beyond that, these methods offer a way of recovering an intimacy with photographic communication that mass media have all but overwhelmed, which is the deeper motive beneath the technical curiosity described earlier.
overall_html: The passage documents a contemporary movement of photographers reviving obsolete nineteenth-century processes and argues that their deeper motive is the unpredictability those processes guarantee, which makes each print one of a kind and restores an intimacy that mass media have eroded. The author's purpose is explanatory: two individual cases, Bidaut chasing the tintype's depth and Estabrook chasing the aura of a fabricated past, lead into a statement of the trend, then an account of why the old techniques both appeal and once died out, and finally the motivation shared across the movement. The viewpoints in play are those of the two photographers and the author's own diagnosis of what unites them.

Passage A is from a 2007 article on the United States patent system; passage B is from a corporate statement.

Passage A

Theoretically, the patent office is only supposed to award patents for "nonobvious" inventions, and the concept of translating between an Internet address and a telephone number certainly seems obvious. Still, a court recently held that a technology company had infringed on patents covering computer servers that perform these translations.

In an ideal world, patents would be narrow enough that companies could "invent around" others' patents if licensing agreements cannot be reached. Unfortunately, the patent system has departed from this ideal. In recent decades, the courts have dramatically lowered the bar for obviousness. As a result, some patents being granted are so broad that inventing around them is practically impossible.

Large technology companies have responded to this proliferation of bad patents with the patent equivalent of nuclear stockpiling. By obtaining hundreds or even thousands of patents, a company can develop a credible deterrent against patent lawsuits: if someone sues it for patent infringement, it can find a patent the other company has infringed and countersue. Often, however, a fundamental mistake is made: not joining this arms race. As a result, a company can find itself defenseless against lawsuits.

Software patents are particularly ripe for abuse because software is assembled from modular components. If the patent system allows those components to be patented, it becomes almost impossible to develop a software product without infringing numerous patents. Moreover, because of the complexity of software, it is often prohibitively expensive to even find all the patents a given software product might in principle be infringing. So even a software maker that wanted to find and license all of the patents relevant to its products is unlikely to be able to do so.

Passage B

Software makers like ours have consistently taken the position that patents generally impede innovation in software development and are inconsistent with open-source/free software. We will continue to work to promote this position and are pleased to join our colleagues in the open-source/free software community, as well as those proprietary vendors who have publicly stated their opposition to software patents.

At the same time, we are forced to live in the world as it is, and that world currently permits software patents. A small number of very large companies have amassed large numbers of software patents. We believe such massive software patent portfolios are ripe for misuse because of the questionable nature of many software patents generally and because of the high cost of patent litigation.

One defense against such misuse is to develop a corresponding portfolio of software patents for defensive purposes. Many software makers, both open-source and proprietary, pursue this strategy. In the interests of our company and in an attempt to protect and promote the open-source community, we have elected to adopt this same stance. We do so reluctantly because of the perceived inconsistency with our stance against software patents; however, prudence dictates this position.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens on a mismatch between rule and practice. The patent office is only supposed to award patents for nonobvious inventions, yet translating an Internet address into a telephone number looks like an obvious idea, and a court nonetheless held that a technology company had infringed patents covering servers that perform exactly that translation. The example is doing argumentative work rather than merely reporting news, since the author offers it as a specimen of the standards problem that the next paragraph diagnoses.

Now comes the diagnosis, framed as the gap between an ideal and the actual system. Ideally patents would be narrow enough that a company unable to reach a licensing agreement could simply invent around them. Instead, the author of Passage A argues, courts have dramatically lowered the bar for obviousness in recent decades, so patents now issue that are broad enough to make inventing around them practically impossible. Hold on to the causal chain here, because a loose obviousness standard produces bad patents, and bad patents produce the corporate behavior described next.

The consequence is an arms race, and the chosen metaphor is deliberately martial. Large technology companies have answered the flood of bad patents with the patent equivalent of nuclear stockpiling, amassing hundreds or thousands of patents so that any firm suing them can be countersued over something in the pile. The author treats staying out of this race as a fundamental mistake rather than a principled abstention, since a company without a stockpile has no deterrent and can find itself defenseless against infringement suits.

The last paragraph of Passage A narrows to software and explains why the problem bites hardest there. Software is assembled from modular components, so once those components can be patented, almost any product will infringe numerous patents at once. Complexity compounds the trouble, because identifying every patent a program might infringe is often prohibitively expensive, which means even a maker genuinely willing to find and license everything relevant is unlikely to manage it. Notice that this shuts off the obvious remedy of simply complying with the system.

Passage B shifts from outside analysis to a first-person position statement by a software maker. Its declared view is that patents generally impede innovation in software development and are inconsistent with open-source and free software. The company says it will keep working to promote that position and is pleased to stand alongside the open-source community as well as those proprietary vendors who have publicly opposed software patents. Read this paragraph as the principled commitment against which the rest of the passage has to be measured.

A concession follows, and its signal phrase matters: the company is forced to live in the world as it is, and that world currently permits software patents. It observes that a small number of very large companies have amassed large software patent portfolios, and it regards those portfolios as ripe for misuse for two stated reasons, the questionable nature of many software patents and the high cost of patent litigation. The reasoning here converges closely with what Passage A said about stockpiling and bad patents.

The closing paragraph delivers the reluctant decision. One defense against the misuse just described is to build a corresponding portfolio of software patents purely for defensive purposes, a strategy many software makers of both kinds already pursue. The software maker announces that it is adopting the same stance, in its own interest and, as it frames the matter, to protect and promote the open-source community. Watch the admission attached to the announcement, since the company concedes the perceived inconsistency with its opposition to software patents and says prudence, not principle, dictates the move.
overall_html: Passage A argues that courts have lowered the standard for obviousness so far that patents are now too broad to invent around, pushing large technology firms into defensive stockpiling, a problem worst in software because modular components and sheer complexity make infringement unavoidable and comprehensive licensing impractical. Passage B is a software maker's position statement that opposes software patents in principle yet announces, reluctantly and as a matter of prudence, that it will assemble a defensive portfolio of its own. The relationship is diagnosis and response: Passage B accepts the picture of a dysfunctional, misuse-prone system that Passage A analyzes from the outside, and then acts out that arms-race logic in the first person.

Calvaria major is a rare but once-abundant tree found on the island of Mauritius, which was also home to the dodo, a large flightless bird that became extinct about three centuries ago. In 1977 Stanley Temple, an ecologist whose investigation of Calvaria major was a sidelight to his research on endangered birds of Mauritius, proposed that the population decline of Calvaria major was linked to the demise of the dodo, a hypothesis that subsequently gained considerable currency. Temple had found only thirteen Calvaria major trees on Mauritius, all overmature and dying, and all estimated by foresters at over 300 years old. These trees produced fruits that appeared fertile but that Temple assumed could no longer germinate, given his failure to find younger trees.

The temporal coincidence between the extinction of the dodo and what Temple considered the last evidence of natural germination of Calvaria major seeds led him to posit a causal connection. Specifically, he hypothesized that the fruit of Calvaria major had developed its extremely thick-walled pit as an evolutionary response to the dodo's habitual consumption of those fruits, a trait enabling the pits to withstand the abrasive forces exerted on them in the birds' digestive tracts. This defensive thickness, though, ultimately prevented the seeds within the pits from germinating without the thinning caused by abrasion in the dodo's gizzard. What had once been adaptive, Temple maintained, became a lethal imprisonment for the seeds after the dodo vanished.

Although direct proof was unattainable, Temple did offer some additional findings in support of his hypothesis, which lent his argument a semblance of rigor. From studies of other birds, he estimated the abrasive force generated within a dodo's gizzard. Based on this estimate and on test results determining the crush-resistant strength of Calvaria major pits, he concluded that the pits could probably have withstood a cycle through a dodo's gizzard. He also fed Calvaria major pits to turkeys, and though many of the pits were destroyed, ten emerged, abraded yet intact. Three of these sprouted when planted, which he saw as vindicating his hypothesis.

Though many scientists found this dramatic and intriguing hypothesis plausible, Temple's proposals have been strongly challenged by leading specialists in the field. Where Temple had found only thirteen specimens of Calvaria major, Wendy Strahm, the foremost expert on the plant ecology of Mauritius, has identified hundreds, many far younger than three centuries. So Calvaria major seeds have in fact germinated, and the tree's reproductive cycle has thus continued, since the dodo's disappearance. Additional counterevidence comes from horticultural research by Anthony Speke, which shows that while only a minority of unabraded Calvaria major seeds germinate, the number is still probably sufficient to keep this species from becoming extinct. The population decline, while clearly acute, could easily be due to other factors, including disease and damage done by certain nonindigenous animals introduced onto Mauritius in the past few centuries.
explanation_html:
The opening supplies the two facts a famous hypothesis was built on: Calvaria major, a once-abundant and now rare tree on Mauritius, and the dodo, a flightless bird of the same island that died out about three centuries ago. In 1977 the ecologist Stanley Temple, who studied the tree only as a sideline to research on endangered birds, proposed that the tree's decline was linked to the dodo's demise, and the idea caught on widely. His evidence base was thin, which is worth registering early: thirteen trees, all overmature and dying, all estimated at over three hundred years old, bearing fruit that looked fertile but that he assumed could no longer germinate, since he found nothing younger.

The causal story grows out of that coincidence in timing. Temple reasoned that the fruit's unusually thick-walled pit had evolved in response to the dodo's habit of eating it, the thickness protecting the seed from the abrasive forces inside the bird's digestive tract. Then comes the twist that makes the hypothesis memorable: the same armor became a trap, because without the thinning a dodo's gizzard supplied, the seed could not germinate at all. What had once been adaptive, on Temple's account, turned into a lethal imprisonment the moment the bird disappeared.

Supporting evidence follows, and the author's framing deserves attention, since these findings are said to lend the argument only a semblance of rigor. Direct proof was unattainable, so Temple estimated the abrasive force inside a dodo's gizzard from studies of other birds, measured how much crushing the pits could withstand, and concluded they would probably have survived a pass through. He also fed pits to turkeys: many were destroyed, ten emerged abraded but intact, and three of those sprouted once planted, a result he treated as vindication.

The closing paragraph turns the passage against Temple. Many scientists found the hypothesis dramatic and plausible, but leading specialists have challenged it strongly. Wendy Strahm, the foremost expert on the plant ecology of Mauritius, has identified hundreds of these trees rather than thirteen, many of them far younger than three centuries, and that finding alone breaks the argument, since the seeds have plainly germinated and the reproductive cycle has continued since the dodo vanished. Anthony Speke's horticultural research adds that while only a minority of unabraded seeds germinate, the number is probably still enough to keep the species going. The decline is real, the author allows, but disease and introduced animals could easily account for it.
overall_html: The passage reconstructs Stanley Temple's much-repeated hypothesis that Calvaria major stopped reproducing because the extinct dodo's gizzard was needed to abrade its thick-walled pits, and then presents the specialist evidence that dismantles it. The author's purpose is critical: three paragraphs lay out the hypothesis, its evolutionary logic, and the indirect support Temple assembled, before a final paragraph in which Strahm's discovery of hundreds of trees, many well under three centuries old, and Speke's germination research show that unabraded seeds sprout often enough to sustain the species. Keep three things apart here, namely Temple's position, the specialists who refute it, and the author's own consistently skeptical framing.

An organism is considered to have an infection when a disease-causing agent, called a pathogen, establishes a viable presence in the organism. This can occur only if the pathogenic agent is able to reproduce itself in the host organism. The only agents believed until recently to be responsible for infections—viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites—reproduce and regulate their other life processes by means of genetic material, composed of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA). It was thus widely assumed that all pathogens contain such genetic material in their cellular structure.

This assumption has been challenged, however, by scientists seeking to identify the pathogen that causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a degenerative form of dementia in humans. CJD causes the brain to become riddled with tiny holes, like a sponge (evidence of extensive nerve cell death). Its symptoms include impaired muscle control, loss of mental acuity, memory loss, and chronic insomnia. Extensive experiments aimed at identifying the pathogen responsible for CJD have led surprisingly to the isolation of a disease agent lacking nucleic acid and consisting mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. Researchers coined the term "prion" for this new type of protein pathogen.

Upon further study, scientists discovered that prions normally exist as harmless cellular proteins in many of the body's tissues, including white blood cells and nerve cells in the brain; however, they possess the capability of converting their structures into a dangerous abnormal shape. Prions exhibiting this abnormal conformation were found to have infectious properties and the ability to reproduce themselves in an unexpected way, by initiating a chain reaction that induces normally shaped prions to transform themselves on contact, one after another, into the abnormal, pathogenic conformation. This cascade of transformations produces a plaque, consisting of thread-like structures, that collects in the brain and ultimately destroys nerve cells. Because prions, unlike other pathogens, occur naturally in the body as proteins, the body does not produce an immune response when they are present. And in the absence of any effective therapy for preventing the cascade process by which affected prions reproduce themselves, CJD is inevitably fatal, though there are wide variations in pre-symptomatic incubation times and in how aggressively the disease progresses.

Although the discovery of the link between prions and CJD was initially received with great skepticism in the scientific community, subsequent research has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogens. Furthermore, it is now believed that a similar process of protein malformation may be involved in other, more common degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. This possibility has yet to be fully explored, however, and the exact mechanisms by which prions reproduce themselves and cause cellular destruction have yet to be completely understood.
explanation_html:
Definitions come first, and they set up the assumption the rest of the passage overturns. An organism counts as infected when a pathogen, meaning a disease-causing agent, establishes a viable presence in it, which can happen only if the agent is able to reproduce inside the host. Until recently the only agents believed capable of this were viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, all of which reproduce and regulate their life processes using genetic material made of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. From that shared feature came a widely held inference: every pathogen must contain such genetic material in its cellular structure.

The challenge arrives through research on one specific disease. Scientists hunting the pathogen behind Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a degenerative dementia that leaves the brain riddled with tiny holes where nerve cells have died and that brings impaired muscle control, loss of mental acuity, memory loss and chronic insomnia, found something the standing assumption did not allow for. Extensive experiments isolated a disease agent that lacks nucleic acid entirely and consists mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. Researchers coined the term prion for this new kind of protein pathogen, and the coinage itself signals that an existing category could not accommodate the find.

How something without genetic material reproduces is the puzzle solved here. Prions normally exist as harmless cellular proteins in many tissues, including white blood cells and nerve cells in the brain, but they can convert their structure into a dangerous abnormal shape, and prions in that conformation prove to be infectious. Reproduction works by contact rather than by copying instructions: an abnormal prion induces a normally shaped one it touches to transform, which then does the same to the next, in a chain reaction. The cascade produces a plaque of thread-like structures that collects in the brain and destroys nerve cells. Two consequences follow, both grim, since the body mounts no immune response against proteins that occur in it naturally, and with no therapy able to interrupt the cascade the disease is inevitably fatal.

The closing paragraph reports how the finding was received and how far its implications now stretch. Great skepticism greeted the link between prions and the disease at first, but subsequent research has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogen. Beyond that, a similar process of protein malformation is now thought to be involved in more common degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Watch the hedging in the final sentence, because the author is careful to note that this possibility is not yet fully explored and the exact mechanisms of prion reproduction and cell destruction remain incompletely understood.
overall_html: The passage traces how the search for the cause of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease overturned the long-standing assumption that every pathogen must contain nucleic acid, since the agent isolated proved to be a protein, the prion, that reproduces by inducing normally shaped proteins to refold into an abnormal, plaque-forming conformation. The author's purpose is expository, moving from the standard definition of infection, to the anomalous discovery, to the mechanism that explains how a pathogen without genetic material propagates and why the resulting disease resists immune response and treatment, and finally to broader implications for conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The voice is neutral scientific reporting, with no competing viewpoints beyond the early skepticism later research overcame.

One of the more striking developments in modern North American dance was African American choreographer Katherine Dunham's introduction of a technique known as dance-isolation, in which one part of the body moves in one rhythm while other parts are kept stationary or are moved in different rhythms. The incorporation of this technique into North American and European choreography is relatively recent, although various forms of the technique have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures. Dunham's success in bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques from those cultures into the mainstream of modern North American dance is due in no small part to her training in both anthropological research and choreography.

As an anthropologist in the 1930s, Dunham was one of the pioneers in the field of dance ethnology. Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry. Moreover, no other social scientist at that time was sufficiently trained in dance to be able to understand dance techniques, while experts in dance were not trained in the methods of social research.

Starting in 1935, Dunham conducted a series of research projects into traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture. Especially critical to her success was her approach to research, which diverged radically from the methodology that prevailed at the time. Colleagues in anthropology advised her not to become too closely involved in the dances she was observing, both because of the extreme physical demands of the dances, and because they subscribed to the long-standing view, now fortunately recognized as unrealistic, that effective data gathering can and must be conducted from a position of complete detachment. But because of her interest and her skill as a performer, she generally eschewed such caution and participated in the dances herself. Through prolonged immersion of this kind, Dunham was able not only to comprehend various dances as complex cultural practices, but also to learn the techniques well enough to teach them to others and incorporate them into new forms of ballet.

Between 1937 and 1945, Dunham developed a research-to-performance method that she used to adapt Caribbean dance forms for use in theatrical performance, combining them with modern dance styles she learned in Chicago. The ballets she created in this fashion were among the first North American dances to rectify the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance. Her work was thus crucial in establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right, making possible future companies such as Arthur Mitchell's Dance Theater of Harlem.
explanation_html:
The opening defines the technique and then explains why one particular person was able to import it. Dance-isolation means moving one part of the body in one rhythm while other parts stay stationary or move in rhythms of their own, and although its incorporation into North American and European choreography is relatively recent, forms of it have long been essential to traditional dances in certain African, Caribbean and Pacific-island cultures. Katherine Dunham is credited with carrying it into the mainstream, and the explanation offered is the one the whole passage develops: she was trained both in anthropological research and in choreography.

Background follows on why the field she entered was so empty. Working as an anthropologist in the 1930s, Dunham was a pioneer of dance ethnology, an area that barely existed because dance had been neglected as a subject of social research. Two causes are given for that neglect. Most social scientists gravitated toward topics their peers would recognize as scientifically rigorous and therefore legitimate, which left dance looking unserious, and there was a plain skills gap as well, since no social scientist of the period was trained enough in dance to understand its techniques, while experts in dance knew nothing of research methods.

Her method is the heart of the passage, and it is presented as a deliberate break with orthodoxy. From 1935 Dunham conducted research into traditional Caribbean dance forms and their origins in African culture, and what proved critical was her refusal of the prevailing methodology. Colleagues in anthropology advised her against becoming too closely involved, partly because the dances were physically demanding and partly because they held the long-standing view, which the author calls unrealistic, that effective data gathering must be conducted from complete detachment. Her own interest and her skill as a performer led her to dance the dances herself instead. That prolonged immersion paid off twice over, letting her grasp the dances as complex cultural practices and letting her learn them well enough to teach them and build them into new ballets.

The closing paragraph converts research into legacy. Between 1937 and 1945 Dunham developed a research-to-performance method for adapting Caribbean dance forms to theatrical use, combining them with the modern dance styles she had learned in Chicago. The ballets she made this way were among the first North American dances to correct the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance. The author's final claim concerns lasting consequence rather than personal achievement, since this work was crucial in establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right and made later companies such as Arthur Mitchell's Dance Theater of Harlem possible.
overall_html: The passage credits Katherine Dunham with bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques into mainstream North American dance, arguing that her dual training as anthropologist and choreographer, and above all her willingness to participate in the dances she studied, made that transfer possible. The author's purpose is appreciative and explanatory, moving from the technique and its cultural sources, to the neglected state of dance ethnology when she began, to the immersive method that broke with her colleagues' insistence on detachment, and finally to the ballets and the legacy they left. The one real clash of viewpoints is between Dunham's approach and the anthropological orthodoxy urging distance, a norm the author treats as discredited.

Passage A

Research concerning happiness and wealth reveals a paradox: at any one time richer people report higher levels of happiness than poorer people in the same society report, and yet over time advanced societies have not grown happier as they have grown richer. Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income. Two phenomena—habituation and rivalry—push up the norm.

When our living standards increase, we love it initially but then we adjust and it makes little difference. For example, if we ask people with different incomes what income they consider sufficient, the "required income" correlates strongly with their actual income: a rise in actual income causes a roughly equivalent rise in required income. We can also look at reported happiness over time. Job satisfaction depends little on the absolute level of wages but rises if wages rapidly increase.

We do not have the same experience with other aspects of our lives. We do not foresee how we adjust to material possessions, so we overinvest in acquiring them, at the expense of leisure.

Now consider the phenomenon of rivalry. In a study conducted by Solnick and Hemenway, people were asked to choose between two options, with all prices held constant:

A. You earn $50,000 a year while everyone else earns $25,000;

B. You earn $100,000 a year while others make $200,000.

The majority chose the first. They were happy to be poorer, provided their relative position improved.

And indeed, how people compare to their "reference group"—those most like them—is crucial for happiness. In East Germany, for example, living standards have soared since 1990, but the level of happiness has plummeted because people now compare themselves with West Germans, rather than with people in other Soviet bloc countries.

Passage B

Does the Solnick and Hemenway study mean that we care most about one-upmanship? Perhaps out of our primeval past comes the urge to demonstrate our superiority in order to help ensure mating prospects, keeping our genetic lines going. Still programmed like this, we get unexplainable pleasure from having a bigger house than our neighbors.

This theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not the explanation best supported by the evidence. Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.

If two people feel equally successful, they will be equally happy even if their incomes differ greatly. Of course, people who earn more generally view themselves as successful. But it is the success—not the money per se—that provides the happiness. We use material wealth to show not just that we are prosperous, but that we are prosperous because we create value.

What scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society. It is a bonus that it also brings happiness.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a paradox worth committing to memory: within one society at one moment, richer people report more happiness than poorer people, yet as whole advanced societies grow richer over decades, average happiness does not climb. The resolution offered is that people judge their income against a norm rather than against an absolute figure, and that norm rises along with actual income. Two forces are named as the drivers of the rising norm, habituation and rivalry, and the rest of the passage takes them up in exactly that order.

Habituation gets the first treatment. The claim is that a higher living standard thrills you briefly and then becomes the new baseline, so it stops registering. Two pieces of support follow. Ask people what income they would consider sufficient and the answer tracks whatever they currently earn, rising almost one-for-one when actual income rises. Job satisfaction shows the same signature: the absolute level of wages barely matters, but a rapid increase does lift satisfaction, which is what you would expect if only change, rather than level, is actually felt.

A brief but consequential extension follows. Adjustment of this kind does not govern every part of life, and, more importantly, we fail to anticipate it. Because people do not foresee how quickly a new possession stops feeling new, they overinvest in acquiring things and underinvest in leisure. Notice that this is the point where the author stops merely describing a mechanism and starts drawing a critical conclusion about how people misallocate their own lives, which is the first evaluative move in the passage.

With habituation covered, the author pivots to the second force, rivalry, and hands the argument over to evidence rather than assertion. The framing of the Solnick and Hemenway study is what matters here, so read it carefully: respondents choose between two income scenarios with all prices held constant. That last condition is the whole design, since fixing prices strips purchasing power out of the comparison and leaves relative standing as the only thing that varies between the two options.

The first option describes a low-absolute, high-relative world: you take home fifty thousand a year while everyone around you takes home half that. Hold on to the structure rather than the figures. Your own purchasing power here is modest, but you sit comfortably at the top of your comparison group. Because prices are held constant across both options, choosing this scenario can express only one thing, a preference about where you stand relative to other people rather than about what your money can buy.

The second option reverses both variables: your income doubles to a hundred thousand, but everyone else is earning twice what you do. In straightforward material terms you are far better off here than in the first scenario, so anyone who cared only about absolute living standards would take this one without hesitating. The pair is constructed so that absolute wealth and relative rank point in opposite directions, which forces respondents to reveal which of the two they actually weigh more heavily when made to choose.

The result arrives in a single sentence, and it is the payoff the setup was built for. Most respondents took the first option, accepting genuinely lower purchasing power in exchange for outranking the people around them. The author's gloss is precise and worth borrowing: they were happy to be poorer as long as their relative position improved. That is rivalry demonstrated rather than merely asserted, and it delivers the second half of the explanation promised at the end of the opening paragraph.

Rivalry is then sharpened into something more specific than generalized competition. What matters is not humanity at large but one's reference group, the people most like oneself, and that group can shift. East Germany supplies the case: living standards soared after 1990 while reported happiness dropped, because the comparison moved from other Soviet bloc populations to West Germans. The example closes the passage by showing that a rising norm can outrun a rising income and leave people materially better off but subjectively worse off.

Passage B opens by taking the same Solnick and Hemenway result and asking what it actually demonstrates. The author of B first lays out the popular reading, an evolutionary drive toward one-upmanship: ancestors who displayed superiority secured better mating prospects and kept their genetic lines going, and we are still running that program, which is why a house bigger than the neighbor's produces pleasure we cannot quite explain. Read this paragraph as a position being set up for evaluation, not as one the author endorses.

The turn comes immediately. The theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not what the evidence best supports. In its place the author offers a different reading of the same data: earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel successful, that they have created value. Notice exactly what kind of move this is. It does not deny that comparison drives the result; it reinterprets what the comparison is measuring, substituting a judgment about achievement for a competitive instinct.

The success interpretation is then tested against the cases that would separate it from a simple money explanation. Two people who feel equally successful end up equally happy even when their incomes differ greatly, which is the crucial dissociation, and income tracks happiness only because high earners generally do regard themselves as successful. On this account wealth functions as evidence rather than as cause, and what people display with material goods is not merely that they are prosperous but that their prosperity came from creating value.

The closing paragraph flips the moral verdict. Scholars routinely treat wanting more than others as an ignoble tendency, but on this reading it is the visible surface of a desire to create value, and creating value benefits society at large. Happiness, the author adds almost dismissively, is a bonus rather than the point. Set this against Passage A, which treats comparison as a trap that prevents rising societies from becoming happier; the same comparative instinct is recast here as socially productive rather than self-defeating.
overall_html: Both passages ask why relative rather than absolute income drives happiness, and they read the same evidence to opposite ends. Passage A explains the paradox that richer individuals are happier while richer societies are not, arguing that habituation and rivalry with a shifting reference group push up the norm against which income is judged, so real gains cancel out; its purpose is diagnostic, identifying a trap. Passage B accepts the Solnick and Hemenway finding but rejects the evolutionary one-upmanship interpretation of it, arguing that relative prosperity pleases people because it signals successful value creation, a tendency it defends as socially beneficial. The two agree on the data and disagree about what it means.

It is generally believed that while in some cases government should intervene to protect people from risk—by imposing air safety standards, for example—in other cases, such as mountain climbing, the onus should be on the individual to protect himself or herself. In the eyes of the public at large, the demarcation between the two kinds of cases has mainly to do with whether the risk in question is incurred voluntarily. This distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk may in fact be the chief difference between lay and expert judgments about risk. Policy experts tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake; laypeople care a great deal whether a risk is undertaken voluntarily. However, judgments about whether a risk is "involuntary" often stem from confusion and selective attention, and the real reason for such judgments frequently lies in an antecedent judgment of some other kind. They are thus of little utility in guiding policy decisions.

First, it is not easy to determine when a risk is voluntarily incurred. Although voluntariness may be entirely absent in the case of an unforeseeable collision with an asteroid, with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, it is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree. Risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash. But they can choose airlines on the basis of safety records or choose not to fly. In characterizing the risks as involuntary, people focus on a small part of a complex interaction, not the decision to fly, but the accident when it occurs.

Second, people often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. It is unlikely that people would want to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, even if the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved were quite good. By contrast, people would probably not object to spending enormous resources on improving the safety of firefighters, even though the decision to become a firefighter is voluntary. In short, there is no special magic in notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary." Therefore, regulatory policy should be guided by a better understanding of the factors that underlie judgments about voluntariness.

In general, the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction. Departures from this principle should be justified not by invoking the allegedly voluntary or involuntary nature of a particular risk, but rather by identifying the more specific considerations for which notions of voluntariness serve as proxies.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by laying out a distinction it intends to dismantle. Government sometimes intervenes to protect people from risk, as with air safety standards, and sometimes leaves protection to the individual, as with mountain climbing, and the public sorts cases by asking whether the risk was incurred voluntarily. The Author identifies this as the main split between policy experts, who focus on aggregate lives at stake, and laypeople, who care enormously about voluntariness. The thesis lands at the end of the paragraph and is blunt: such judgments stem from confusion and selective attention, usually stand in for some other judgment, and are therefore of little use in guiding policy.

The first of two supporting arguments attacks the coherence of the category itself. Voluntariness is rarely all or nothing; for most environmental, occupational and social risks it comes in degrees, with an unforeseeable asteroid collision as the rare pure case. Air travel makes the point concrete. Passengers are said to face involuntary risk because they cannot control whether the plane crashes, yet they can choose airlines by safety record or decline to fly at all. The author's diagnosis is that people fix on one narrow slice of a complex interaction, the accident itself, while ignoring the decision that led to it.

The second argument is sharper, because it exposes what the label is actually doing. People call a risk voluntary when they disapprove of the purpose for which it is run. Taxpayers would not pour resources into making skydiving safer even at a favorable ratio of dollars to lives saved, yet they would not object to large sums spent protecting firefighters, though becoming a firefighter is just as much a choice. The pair is matched so that approval of the activity is the only difference left. Hence the flat verdict that there is no special magic in these notions, and the call to understand what really underlies them.

Having cleared the ground, the author states the positive rule. Government should save as many lives as it can within the limited resources devoted to risk reduction, and departures from that principle need genuine justification rather than an appeal to how voluntary a risk was. Read the final phrase carefully, because it softens the attack in a useful way: voluntariness serves as a proxy for more specific considerations. The concept is not empty, then, but a crude substitute that should be replaced by the particular factors hiding behind it.
overall_html: The passage argues that the public's distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk, though it is the chief difference between lay judgments and those of policy experts who count aggregate lives, is too confused to guide regulation. The author's purpose is first critical and then prescriptive: one argument shows that voluntariness is a matter of degree that people assess by attending to a single slice of a longer interaction, a second shows that the label really tracks approval of the activity's purpose, and the closing paragraph substitutes a straightforward lives-saved standard while conceding that voluntariness functions as a proxy for more specific considerations worth identifying directly.

African American painter Sam Gilliam (b. 1933) is internationally recognized as one of the foremost painters associated with the Washington Color School, a group of Color Field style painters practicing in Washington, D.C. during the 1950s and 1960s. The Color Field style was an important development in abstract art that emerged after the rise of abstract expressionism. It evolved from complex and minimally representational abstractions in the 1950s to totally nonrepresentational, simplified works of bright colors in the 1960s.

Gilliam's participation in the Color Field movement was motivated in part by his reaction to the art of his African American contemporaries, much of which was strictly representational and was intended to convey explicit political statements. Gilliam found their approach to be aesthetically conservative: the message was unmistakable, he felt, and there was little room for the expression of subtlety or ambiguity or, more importantly, the exploration of new artistic territory through experimentation and innovation. For example, one of his contemporaries worked with collage, assembling disparate bits of images from popular magazines into loosely structured compositions that depicted the period's political issues—themes such as urban life, the rural South, and African American music. Though such art was quite popular with the general public, Gilliam was impatient with its straightforward, literal approach to representation. In its place he sought an artistic form that was more expressive than a painted figure or a political slogan, more evocative of the complexity of human experience in general, and of the African American experience in particular. In this he represented a view that was then rare among African American artists.

Gilliam's highly experimental paintings epitomized his refusal to conform to the public's expectation that African American artists produce explicitly political art. His early experiments included pouring paint onto stained canvases and folding canvases over onto themselves. Then around 1965 Gilliam became the first painter to introduce the idea of the unsupported canvas. Partially inspired by the sight of neighbors hanging laundry on clotheslines, Gilliam began to drape huge pieces of loose canvas along floors and fold them up and down walls, even suspending them from ceilings, giving them a third dimension and therefore a sculptural quality. These efforts demonstrate a sensitivity to the texture of daily experience, as well as the ability to generate tension by juxtaposing conceptual opposites—such as surface and depth or chaos and control—to form a cohesive whole. In this way, Gilliam helped advance the notion that the deepest, hardest-to-capture emotions and tensions of being African American could not be represented directly, but were expressed more effectively through the creation of moods that would allow these emotions and tensions to be felt by all audiences.
explanation_html:
Context comes first, and the paragraph is almost entirely factual. Sam Gilliam, born in 1933, is internationally recognized as a leading painter of the Washington Color School, a group of Color Field artists working in Washington, D.C. through the 1950s and 1960s. The author sketches what that style was: an important development in abstract art that emerged after abstract expressionism and changed shape across two decades, starting as complex work that still carried faint traces of representation and ending as wholly nonrepresentational, simplified painting in bright color. Nothing is being argued yet. You are being handed the movement Gilliam belonged to so that the next paragraph can explain why he joined it.

The motive arrives next, defined entirely by opposition. Gilliam's participation in Color Field grew partly from his reaction against the work of his African American contemporaries, most of it strictly representational and built to deliver explicit political statements. He judged that approach aesthetically conservative: the message was unmistakable, leaving little space for subtlety or ambiguity and, more important to him, little room to experiment. The example given is a contemporary who assembled magazine fragments into loose collages about political themes such as urban life, the rural South, and African American music. That work was popular with the public, but Gilliam had no patience for its literalism and wanted a form more expressive than a painted figure or a slogan, one answering to the complexity of human experience generally and African American experience in particular. Such a view, the author notes, was then rare.

The closing paragraph shows the position turning into practice. Gilliam's highly experimental paintings amounted to a refusal of the public's expectation that African American artists produce explicitly political work. Early on he poured paint onto stained canvases and folded canvases back onto themselves; then, around 1965, he became the first painter to introduce the unsupported canvas, prompted partly by the sight of neighbors hanging laundry on clotheslines. He draped enormous loose canvases across floors, folded them up and down walls, and suspended them from ceilings, giving them a third dimension and a sculptural quality. Two achievements are read into this: a sensitivity to the texture of daily experience, and an ability to generate tension by holding conceptual opposites, surface against depth or chaos against control, in one coherent work. The larger claim is that the hardest emotions of African American life resist direct representation and travel better as moods any audience can feel.
overall_html: The passage presents Sam Gilliam as a Color Field painter whose abstraction was a deliberate answer to the strictly representational, overtly political art of his African American contemporaries, work he found aesthetically conservative and closed to experiment. The author's purpose is expository and admiring, moving from the movement Gilliam belonged to, to the artistic quarrel that drew him into it, to the experiments that followed, culminating in the unsupported draped canvas that gave painting a sculptural dimension. Two viewpoints matter, Gilliam's and that of the contemporaries whose literal, message-driven work he rejected, and the author endorses his conviction that the deepest tensions of African American experience are conveyed through mood rather than direct depiction.

passage_html:
Passage A is from a source published in 2004 and passage B is from a source published in 2007.

Passage A

Millions of people worldwide play multiplayer online games. They each pick, say, a medieval character to play, such as a warrior. Then they might band together in quests to slay magical beasts; their avatars appear as tiny characters striding across a Tolkienesque land.

The economist Edward Castronova noticed something curious about the game he played: it had its own economy, a bustling trade in virtual goods. Players generate goods as they play, often by killing creatures for their treasure and trading it. The longer they play, the wealthier they get.

Things got even more interesting when Castronova learned about the "player auctions." Players would sometimes tire of the game and decide to sell off their virtual possessions at online auction sites.

As Castronova stared at the auction listings, he recognized with a shock what he was looking at. It was a form of currency trading! Each item had a value in the virtual currency traded in the game; when it was sold on the auction site, someone was paying cold hard cash for it. That meant that the virtual currency was worth something in real currency. Moreover, since players were killing monsters or skinning animals to sell their pelts, they were, in effect, creating wealth.

Passage B

Most multiplayer online games prohibit real-world trade in virtual items, but some actually encourage it, for example, by granting participants intellectual property rights in their creations.

Although it seems intuitively the case that someone who accepts real money for the transfer of a virtual item should be taxed, what about the player who only accumulates items or virtual currency within a virtual world? Is "loot" acquired in a game taxable, as a prize or award is? And is the profit in a purely in-game trade or sale for virtual currency taxable? These are important questions, given the tax revenues at stake, and there is pressure on governments to answer them, given that the economies of some virtual worlds are comparable to those of small countries.

Most people's intuition probably would be that accumulation of assets within a game should not be taxed even though income tax applies even to noncash accessions to wealth. This article will argue that income tax law and policy support that result. Loot acquisitions in game worlds should not be treated as taxable prizes and awards, but rather should be treated like other property that requires effort to obtain, such as fish pulled from the ocean, which is taxed only upon sale. Moreover, in-game trades of virtual items should not be treated as taxable barter.

By contrast, tax doctrine and policy counsel taxation of the sale of virtual items for real currency, and, in games that are intentionally commodified, even of in-world sales for virtual currency, regardless of whether the participant cashes out. This approach would leave entertainment value untaxed without creating a tax shelter for virtual commerce.
explanation_html:
Passage A begins in plain descriptive mode, building the setting before any argument arrives. Millions of people worldwide play multiplayer online games, each choosing a character such as a medieval warrior and then banding together with others on quests to slay magical beasts, their avatars appearing as tiny figures striding across a Tolkienesque landscape. There is no thesis here at all; the paragraph exists so that the economic observations coming next have something concrete to attach themselves to.

The economist Edward Castronova enters as the observer whose realization organizes the rest of Passage A. Playing one of these games himself, he noticed something curious, namely that it contained an economy of its own with a bustling trade in virtual goods. The mechanism is straightforward: players generate goods in the course of play, often by killing creatures for their treasure and trading what they collect, so the longer someone plays, the wealthier that player becomes.

A second observation raises the stakes, and notice that Passage A is advancing in deliberate steps rather than stating its conclusion outright. Castronova then learned about player auctions, the practice by which players who tire of a game sell off their accumulated virtual possessions at online auction sites. Hold on to the crucial detail, which is that these sales take place outside the game itself, since that is exactly what makes the recognition in the next paragraph possible.

Now the realization lands. Staring at the auction listings, Castronova saw with a shock that he was looking at a form of currency trading, because each item had a value in the game's virtual currency and was simultaneously changing hands for real money on the auction site. That link means the virtual currency is worth something in real currency. The broader inference closes Passage A: players killing monsters or skinning animals for pelts are not merely amusing themselves, they are in effect creating wealth.

Passage B switches genre completely, opening a legal article about taxation rather than a narrative of discovery. Its first move is a factual distinction that will matter at the end: most multiplayer online games prohibit real-world trade in virtual items, while some actively encourage it, for example by granting participants intellectual property rights in their creations. That split between commodified and non-commodified games underlies the conclusion the article eventually reaches.

The questions the article exists to answer are posed here. Taxing someone who accepts real money for transferring a virtual item seems intuitively right, but harder cases follow. Should a player who only accumulates items or virtual currency inside a virtual world be taxed, is in-game loot taxable the way a prize or award is, and is profit from a purely in-game trade taxable? The author of Passage B stresses that these are not idle puzzles, since substantial tax revenue is at stake and the economies of some virtual worlds are comparable to those of small countries, which puts real pressure on governments to answer.

The thesis follows, and it sides with common intuition while grounding that intuition in doctrine. Most people assume accumulating assets within a game should not be taxed, even though income tax reaches noncash accessions to wealth, and Passage B argues that tax law and policy genuinely support that result. Loot acquired in a game world should not be treated as a taxable prize or award; the better analogy is property that takes effort to obtain, such as fish pulled from the ocean, which is taxed only upon sale. In-game trades of virtual items, similarly, should not count as taxable barter.

The closing paragraph draws the other half of the line. Where a virtual item is sold for real currency, tax doctrine and policy do counsel taxation, and in games that are intentionally commodified, the ones flagged at the start of Passage B, even in-world sales for virtual currency should be taxed regardless of whether the participant ever cashes out. The stated payoff of drawing the boundary in that place is that entertainment value stays untaxed while virtual commerce does not become a tax shelter.
overall_html: Passage A recounts the economist Edward Castronova's realization that multiplayer online games contain functioning economies whose virtual currency carries real exchange value, so that players killing monsters and selling the proceeds are in effect creating wealth. Passage B, a tax law article, takes that reality as its starting point and asks what ought to be taxed, arguing that loot and in-game trades should be left alone, on the analogy of fish taxed only when sold, while sales for real money and in-world sales in intentionally commodified games should be taxed. The relationship is description followed by application: A establishes that virtual wealth is economically real, and B works out the legal consequences that A never addresses.
