In certain fields of human endeavor, such as music, chess, and some athletic activities, the performance of the best practitioners is so outstanding, so superior even to the performance of other highly experienced individuals in the field, that some people believe some notion of innate talent must be invoked to account for this highest level of performance. Certain psychologists have supported this view with data concerning the performance of prodigies and the apparent heritability of relevant traits. They have noted, for example, that most outstanding musicians are discovered by the age of six, and they have found evidence that some of the qualities necessary for exceptional athletic performance, including superior motor coordination, speed of reflexes, and hand-eye coordination, can be inborn.

Until recently, however, little systematic research was done on the topic of superior performance, and previous estimates of the heritability of traits relevant to performance were based almost exclusively on random samples of the general population rather than on studies of highly trained superior performers as compared with the general population. Recent research in different domains of excellence suggests that exceptional performance arises predominantly from acquired complex skills and physiological adaptations, rather than from innate abilities. For example, it has been found that the most accomplished athletes show a systematic advantage in reaction time or perceptual discrimination only in their particular fields of performance, not in more general laboratory tests for these factors. Similarly, superior chess players have exceptional memory for configurations of chess pieces, but only if those configurations are typical of chess games.

The vast majority of exceptional adult performers were not exceptional as children, but started instruction early and improved their performance through sustained high-level training. Only extremely rarely is outstanding performance achieved without at least ten years of intensive, deliberate practice. With such intensive training, chess players who may not have superior innate capacities can acquire skills that circumvent basic limits on such factors as memory and the ability to process information. Recent research shows that, with the clear exception of some traits such as height, a surprisingly large number of anatomical characteristics, including aerobic capacity and the percentage of muscle fibers, show specific changes that develop from extended intense training.

The evidence does not, therefore, support the claim that a notion of innate talent must be invoked in order to account for the difference between good and outstanding performance, since it suggests instead that extended intense training, together with that level of talent common to all reasonably competent performers, may suffice to account for this difference. Since sustained intense training usually depends on an appropriate level of interest and desire, and since those who eventually become superior performers more often show early signs of exceptional interest than early evidence of unusual ability, motivational factors are more likely to be effective predictors of superior performance than is innate talent.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the position it will spend the rest of its length undermining. In fields such as music, chess and certain athletic activities, the very best performers so far outstrip even highly experienced rivals that some people conclude an innate talent must be invoked to explain the gap. Certain psychologists support that conclusion with two kinds of data, evidence about prodigies and evidence about heritability: most outstanding musicians are discovered by the age of six, and qualities that matter athletically, among them superior motor coordination, speed of reflexes and hand-eye coordination, can be inborn. Notice that the author is reporting this case rather than making it.

The pivot arrives with 'however', and it comes in two parts. First a methodological complaint: until recently superior performance was barely studied systematically, and heritability estimates rested almost entirely on random samples of the general population rather than on comparisons between highly trained superior performers and everyone else. Then the substantive counterclaim, drawn from recent research across several domains, that exceptional performance arises predominantly from acquired complex skills and physiological adaptations rather than innate abilities. Both examples turn on specificity: elite athletes show their advantage in reaction time or perceptual discrimination only within their own sport, not on general laboratory tests, and strong chess players have exceptional memory only for configurations typical of real games.

Evidence for the training account accumulates here. The vast majority of exceptional adult performers were not exceptional children; what they had was an early start and years of sustained high-level instruction, and outstanding performance almost never appears without at least ten years of intensive, deliberate practice. Two findings extend the point. Chess players who lack superior innate capacities can nonetheless acquire skills that circumvent ordinary limits on memory and information processing, and, with the clear exception of traits such as height, a surprisingly large number of anatomical characteristics, including aerobic capacity and the percentage of muscle fibers, change measurably under extended intense training. Even the body, on this evidence, is partly made rather than simply given.

The conclusion follows in two steps, both carefully hedged. First, the evidence does not support the claim that innate talent must be invoked to explain the difference between good and outstanding performance, since extended intense training combined with the level of talent common to all reasonably competent performers may suffice. Second, and more interesting for where the passage ends up, the author redirects attention to motivation: sustained intense training depends on an appropriate level of interest and desire, and those who eventually become superior performers more often show early signs of exceptional interest than early evidence of unusual ability, which makes motivational factors the better predictor. Watch the modest phrasing, because the author claims sufficiency rather than proof.
overall_html: The passage challenges the view that innate talent must be invoked to explain the gap between good performers and outstanding ones, arguing instead that acquired skills, physiological adaptations built through training, and motivation account for it. The author's purpose is to rebut: the talent position and the psychological data behind it come first, then a methodological criticism and research showing that elite advantages are domain-specific and that even anatomical traits respond to prolonged practice, before a closing paragraph that proposes early interest as a better predictor of excellence than early ability. Keep the psychologists who favor innate talent distinct from the author, who favors extended deliberate training together with motivational factors.

Physicists are often asked why the image of an object, such as a chair, appears reversed left-to-right rather than, say, top-to-bottom when viewed in a mirror. Their answer is simply that an image viewed in a mirror appears reversed about the axis around which the viewer rotates his or her field of sight in turning from the object to its reflected image. That is, the reversal in question is relative to the position and orientation of the observer when the object is viewed directly. Since we ordinarily rotate our field of sight about a vertical axis, mirror images usually appear reversed left-to-right. This is the field-of-sight explanation.

However, some physicists offer a completely different explanation of what mirrors "do," suggesting that mirrors actually reverse things front-to-back. If we place a chair in front of a mirror we can envision how its reflected image will appear by imagining another chair in the space "inside" the mirror. The resulting reflection is identical to, and directly facing, the original chair. The most notable thing about this explanation is that it is clearly based on a false premise: the chair "inside" the mirror is not real, yet the explanation treats it as though it were as real and three dimensional as the original chair.

This explanation appeals strongly to many people, however, because it is quite successful at explaining what a mirror does—to a point. It seems natural because we are accustomed to dealing with our mental constructs of objects rather than with the primary sense perceptions on which those constructs are based. In general, we can safely presume a fairly reliable equation between our perceptions and their associated mental constructs, but mirrors are an exception. They present us with sense perceptions that we naturally construe in a way that is contrary to fact. Indeed, mirrors are "designed" to make a two-dimensional surface appear to have depth. Note, for example, that mirrors are among the few objects on which we almost never focus our eyes; rather, we look into them, with our focal lengths adjusted into the imagined space.

In addition to its intuitive appeal, the front-to-back explanation is motivated in part by the traditional desire in science to separate the observer from the phenomenon. Scientists like to think that what mirrors do should be explainable without reference to what the observer does (e.g., rotating a field of sight). However, questions about the appearances of images can be properly answered only if we consider both what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors. If we remove the observer from consideration, we are no longer addressing images and appearances, because an image entails an observer and a point of view.
explanation_html:
The passage begins with a familiar puzzle and the standard answer to it. Asked why a mirror flips an object left to right rather than top to bottom, the field-of-sight physicists reply that the image is reversed about whichever axis you rotate your field of sight around as you turn from the object to its reflection. The load-bearing phrase is that the reversal is relative to where the observer stood and how the observer was oriented when viewing the object directly. Since we ordinarily swivel around a vertical axis, the flip ordinarily looks like a left-right one. Keep this account in view, because the author will end up defending it.

A rival account follows, and the verdict on it arrives immediately. Some physicists hold that mirrors actually reverse things front to back, and the way to picture it is to set a chair before a mirror and imagine a second chair occupying the space inside the glass, identical to the first and directly facing it. The objection is blunt: this explanation is clearly built on a false premise, since the chair inside the mirror is not real, yet the account treats it as though it were as solid and three dimensional as the chair standing in the room.

Having called the rival explanation false, the author turns to the more interesting question of why it nonetheless convinces so many people. It works up to a point, and it feels natural because we habitually deal with our mental constructs of objects rather than with the primary sense perceptions those constructs rest on. Usually that substitution is safe, since construct and perception line up reliably, but mirrors are the exception, handing us perceptions we instinctively construe in a way contrary to fact. A mirror is effectively designed to make a two-dimensional surface appear to have depth, and the everyday detail offered as evidence is telling: we almost never focus our eyes on a mirror itself, but look into it, adjusting our focal length into a space that is not really there.

The closing paragraph identifies a second motive behind the rival view and then rejects it on principle. Part of the front-to-back account's appeal is the traditional scientific desire to separate the observer from the phenomenon, so that what a mirror does can be described without reference to anything the viewer does, such as rotating a field of sight. The author's reply is that the instinct misfires in this case. Questions about how images appear can be answered properly only by considering both what mirrors do and what happens when we look into them, because once the observer is removed you are no longer discussing images or appearances at all, an image being something that entails a viewer and a point of view.
overall_html: The passage sets two physicists' explanations of mirror reversal against each other and defends the first, arguing that the field-of-sight account, which makes the reversal relative to the axis the observer turns through, is sound, while the popular front-to-back account depends on treating an imaginary chair inside the mirror as if it were real. The author's purpose is corrective, moving from the accepted explanation, to the rival and its false premise, to a diagnosis of why that rival feels so natural given our habit of substituting mental constructs for raw perceptions, and finally to the scientific motive behind it. The governing principle at the close is that an image cannot be described with the observer removed.

In the last half-century, firefighters in North America have developed a powerful system for fighting wildfires using modern technology. But at the same time, foresters and ecologists are increasingly aware that too much firefighting can be worse than none at all. Over the millennia, many forest ecosystems have evolved in such a way that they are dependent on periodic fires for renewal and for limiting damage when fires do occur. Ancient ponderosa forests, for example, were stable in part because low-intensity fires maintained open forests with low levels of fuel for future fires. These fires burned lightly around the bases of mature trees, leaving these trees alive and clearing the understory of brush and young trees. Scientists can easily count the regular recurrence of fires in these forests over the centuries by examining the scars left on trunks; the typical interval between fires could be as short as 5 years and rarely extended beyond 25 years.

If fires are kept out of forests, however, deadwood and other fuels build up; then, when fire is sparked by lightning or some other cause, what results is a fire so large that it leaves total devastation. Such fires often kill off wildlife that might escape low-intensity fires, and they also reach the crowns of centuries-old trees, destroying them and ultimately enabling rains to erode the unprotected topsoil. Because of the relative success of fire-suppression efforts, many forests, including ponderosa forests, have now been free of fire for 50 years or longer, leaving them vulnerable to these devastating crown fires. It is therefore increasingly necessary for land managers in North America to strive to manage rather than eliminate fires; land management policies should recognize the essential role that fire plays in many ecosystems.

Fire behavior depends on the complex interaction of three factors—topography, weather, and fuel—and since topography is fixed and weather is unpredictable, fuel is the only element that land managers can control. Land managers should therefore focus their efforts on fuel. A new kind of wildfire management that is designed to simulate the natural role of fire through a combination of selective harvesting and prescribed fires is the most promising method for controlling fuel. Selective timber harvesting focuses on smaller trees—markets for this smaller material do exist—leaving the larger, fire-tolerant trees on the land and thinning the forest, thereby re-creating the conditions that allow for low-intensity burns. Prescribed fire management includes both the intentional lighting of controlled burns and the policy of allowing fires set by lightning to burn when the weather is damp enough to reduce the risk of extensive damage. Once fuels are reduced by these fires, maintenance burns at 15- to 20-year intervals will be needed. When wildfires inevitably occur, they will be more easily controlled and do much less damage.
explanation_html:
A technological success and an ecological complication are set against each other from the start. North American firefighters have built a powerful modern suppression system, yet foresters and ecologists increasingly recognize that too much firefighting can be worse than none, because many forest ecosystems evolved to depend on periodic fire for renewal and for limiting the damage fires do. Ancient ponderosa forests are the illustration to hold on to: frequent low-intensity fires kept them open and low in fuel, burning lightly around the bases of mature trees, leaving those trees alive and clearing brush and young growth from the understory. Scars on the trunks let scientists count the intervals, which could be as short as five years and rarely ran beyond twenty-five.

The consequences of removing that cycle occupy the second paragraph. Keep fire out and deadwood and other fuels accumulate, so that when lightning or some other source finally ignites them the resulting fire is large enough to leave total devastation. Follow the chain of damage: wildlife that would survive a light burn is killed, flames climb into the crowns of centuries-old trees and destroy them, and rain then erodes topsoil left without protection. Because suppression has largely succeeded, many forests including ponderosa have gone fifty years or more without fire, which is precisely what leaves them open to crown fires. The recommendation follows, that managers manage fire rather than eliminate it.

Having established the principle, the closing paragraph supplies the method. Fire behavior depends on topography, weather and fuel, and since the first is fixed and the second unpredictable, fuel is the only element managers can control, so that is where effort belongs. The proposed approach imitates the natural fire regime with two complementary tools. Selective harvesting removes smaller trees, for which markets exist, thinning the stand while leaving the larger fire-tolerant trees and restoring conditions suited to low-intensity burning. Prescribed fire management covers deliberately lit burns and letting lightning fires run in damp weather, after which maintenance burns every fifteen to twenty years keep fuel loads down.
overall_html: The passage argues that aggressive fire suppression has made North American forests more dangerous rather than safer, because ecosystems such as ponderosa pine evolved with frequent low-intensity fires that kept fuel loads low, and decades without burning have set up catastrophic crown fires. The author's purpose is to recommend a policy shift from eliminating fire to managing it, and the structure moves from the ecological role of natural fire, through the destruction that follows its removal, to a concrete program of selective harvesting of smaller trees and prescribed burns with maintenance burns every fifteen to twenty years. The only viewpoint developed is the author's, aligned with the foresters and ecologists cited at the outset.

The government of Mali passed a law against excavating and exporting the wonderful terra-cotta sculptures from the old city of Djenne-jeno, but it could not enforce it. And it certainly could not afford to fund thousands of archaeological excavations. The result was that many fine Djenne-jeno terra-cotta sculptures were illicitly excavated in the 1980s and sold to foreign collectors who rightly admired them. Because these sites were looted, much of what we would most like to know about this culture—much that we could have learned had the sites been preserved by careful archaeology—may now never be known.

It has been natural to condemn such pillaging. And, through a number of declarations from UNESCO and other international bodies, a protective doctrine has evolved concerning the ownership of many forms of cultural property (the "UNESCO doctrine"). Essentially the doctrine provides that cultural artifacts should be regarded as the property of the culture. For an individual belonging to that culture, such works are, using UNESCO's terminology, part of an "artistic and cultural patrimony." Further, a number of countries have strengthened the UNESCO doctrine by declaring all antiquities that originate within their borders to be state property that cannot be freely exported.

Accordingly, it seems reasonable that the government of Mali, within whose borders the Djenne-jeno antiquities are buried, be the one to regulate excavating Djenne-jeno and to decide where the statues should go. Regrettably, and this is a painful irony, regulations prohibiting export and requiring repatriation can discourage recording and preserving information about cultural antiquities, one of the key reasons for the UNESCO regulations. For example, if someone in London sells a figure from Djenne-jeno with documentation that it came out of the ground there after the regulations were implemented, then the authorities committed to the restitution of objects taken illegally out of Mali have the very evidence they need to seize the figure.

Suppose that from the beginning, Mali had been helped by UNESCO to exercise its trusteeship of the Djenne-jeno terra-cotta sculptures by licensing excavations and educating people to recognize that such artifacts have greater value when they are removed carefully from the earth with accurate records of location. Suppose Mali had required that objects be recorded and registered before leaving the excavation site, and had imposed a tax on exported objects to fund acquisitions of important pieces for the national museum. The excavations encouraged by such a system may have been less well conducted and less informative than proper, professionally administered excavations by accredited archaeologists. Some people would still have avoided the rules. But would this not have been better than what actually happened?
explanation_html:
A case study opens the passage, and its job is to establish a loss. Mali outlawed the excavation and export of the terra-cotta sculptures of the old city of Djenne-jeno but could not enforce the ban, and it could not afford to fund thousands of archaeological digs either. Looting followed through the 1980s, with fine pieces dug out illicitly and sold to foreign collectors whom the author pointedly says admired them rightly. The cost is what matters here: because the sites were plundered rather than carefully excavated, what archaeology could have told us about this culture may never be recovered.

The response to such losses is laid out next, in a neutral register. Condemning the pillaging has been the natural reaction, and declarations from UNESCO and other international bodies have produced a protective framework, the UNESCO doctrine, whose core provision is that cultural artifacts should count as the property of the culture that made them, part of what UNESCO calls an artistic and cultural patrimony for the people who belong to it. Some countries have gone further still, declaring every antiquity originating inside their borders to be state property that cannot be freely exported. No objection appears yet; the position is simply being set out.

Now the author's own view emerges, first as a concession and then as a complication. Since the Djenne-jeno antiquities lie within Mali's borders, it seems reasonable for Mali to regulate the digging and decide where the statues end up. The irony that follows, and the author calls it painful, is that export bans and repatriation rules can discourage the recording and preservation of information that motivated the rules in the first place. Trace the example carefully: a Djenne-jeno figure offered in London with documentation showing it came out of the ground after the regulations took effect gives the authorities exactly the evidence needed to seize it.

A counterfactual closes the passage and carries the author's proposal. Suppose UNESCO had helped Mali exercise trusteeship from the beginning by licensing excavations and teaching people that artifacts removed carefully, with accurate records of location, are worth more; suppose objects had to be recorded and registered before leaving the site, with a tax on exports funding purchases for the national museum. Notice that the concessions come before the conclusion, since such digs would have been less skilled and less informative than professional archaeology and some people would have evaded the rules regardless. The closing rhetorical question does the arguing: even so, this would have beaten what actually occurred.
overall_html: Using the looting of Djenne-jeno as its case, the passage argues that strict prohibitions on excavating and exporting antiquities can defeat their own purpose, since a government unable to enforce them or to fund excavations gets neither preservation nor documentation, and rules requiring repatriation give collectors a reason to hide an object's provenance. The author's purpose is to propose a workable alternative, moving from the loss at Djenne-jeno, to the UNESCO doctrine that artifacts belong to their culture, to the irony that doctrine produces, and finally to a licensed and taxed excavation regime offered through a closing rhetorical question. The UNESCO doctrine and the author's qualified critique of it are the positions to track.

The following passage is based on an article published in 1987.

Medical practitioners are ethically required to prescribe the best available treatments. In ordinary patient-physician interactions, this obligation is unproblematic, but when physicians are clinical researchers in comparative studies of medical treatments, special issues arise. Comparative clinical trials involve withholding one or more of the treatments from at least one group of patients. Traditionally, most physicians and ethicists have agreed that in testing a new treatment on a patient population for which there exists a currently accepted treatment, the participating physicians should have no opinion as to which treatment is clinically superior—a state of mind usually termed "equipoise."

Unfortunately, the conception of equipoise that is typically employed—which I will term "theoretical equipoise"—may be too strict. Theoretical equipoise exists only when the overall evidence for each of two treatment regimens is judged by each clinical researcher to be exactly balanced—an ideal hardly attainable in practice. Clinical researchers commonly have some preference for one of the treatments being tested, an intuitive preference perhaps, or one based on their interpretation and balancing of various sources of evidence. Even if researchers judged the evidence to be balanced at the start of a comparative clinical trial, such a balance would be extremely fragile, liable to be "tipped" by small accretions of evidence as the study progresses. Consequently, if the standard of theoretical equipoise is adhered to, few comparative clinical trials could commence and even fewer could proceed to completion.

These difficulties associated with theoretical equipoise suggest that a different notion of equipoise should be developed, one that I will label "clinical equipoise." Clinical equipoise would impose rigorous ethical standards on comparative clinical trials without unreasonably constricting them. One reason for conducting comparative clinical trials is to resolve a current or imminent conflict in the expert clinical community over what treatment is to be preferred for patients with a given illness. It could be that the standard treatment is A but new evidence suggests that B will be superior. Medical experts may be divided as to which treatment is better, with each side recognizing that opposing experts can differ honestly in their interpretation of the evidence.

The very absence of consensus within the expert clinical community is what makes clinical equipoise possible. One or more of a comparative clinical trial's researchers may have a decided treatment preference based on their assessments of the evidence. But that is no ethical bar to participation in the trial. The clinical researchers must simply each recognize that their less-favored treatment is preferred by a sizable constituency within the medical profession as a whole.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting up an ethical collision. Doctors are obliged to give patients the best available treatment, which is simple in ordinary care but awkward in a comparative clinical trial, since trials work precisely by withholding a treatment from some group of patients. The traditional resolution, endorsed by most physicians and ethicists, is equipoise: a researcher may ethically run the trial only if they hold no view about which treatment is clinically better. Keep that definition close, because the rest of the passage is The Author arguing that the standard version of it is unworkable and needs replacing.

The critique arrives immediately. The usual conception, which The Author names theoretical equipoise, demands that each researcher judge the evidence for the two treatments to be exactly balanced, and that is an ideal almost nobody actually occupies. Researchers normally lean one way, whether from intuition or from how they weigh the evidence, and even a genuine balance would be delicate enough to tip as data accumulate mid-study. The consequence is practical rather than abstract: hold researchers to theoretical equipoise and very few trials could ever start, and fewer still finish. Notice that the objection is about feasibility, not about ethics being unimportant.

Having dismantled the strict version, The Author proposes a replacement, clinical equipoise, pitched as keeping rigorous ethical standards without strangling research. The supporting reasoning shifts the unit of judgment away from the individual researcher and toward the profession. One reason trials exist at all is to settle a live disagreement in the expert clinical community about which treatment to prefer; the standard is A, new evidence hints at B, and The Medical Experts are split, each side granting that honest people can read the same evidence differently. That split is the raw material the new standard will use.

The closing paragraph delivers the payoff. Because consensus is absent among The Medical Experts, clinical equipoise becomes possible, and an individual researcher's private preference stops being disqualifying. A researcher may firmly favor one treatment on their own reading of the evidence and still participate ethically. The single requirement is modest and clearly stated: each must acknowledge that the treatment they favor less is preferred by a substantial constituency within the profession. Watch how the burden has moved from the individual mind, where balance was unattainable, to the community, where genuine disagreement is easy to verify.
overall_html: The passage argues that the traditional standard governing comparative clinical trials, theoretical equipoise, is too strict to be workable, because it requires each researcher to see the evidence for two treatments as exactly balanced, and proposes clinical equipoise in its place, which locates the required uncertainty in genuine disagreement among expert clinicians rather than in any individual's mind. The Author's purpose is to diagnose a problem and offer a solution, moving from the ethical dilemma trials create, to the failure of the standard remedy, to the definition and justification of a replacement. The only developed viewpoint is The Author's, with The Medical Experts appearing as the divided community whose disagreement makes the new standard function.

Passage A

In 1994, Estonia became the first country to introduce a "flat tax" on personal and corporate income. Income is taxed at a single uniform rate of 26 percent: no schedule of rates, no deductions. So far eight countries have followed Estonia's example. An old idea that for decades elicited the response, "Fine in theory, just not practical in the real world," seems to be working as well in practice as it does on the blackboard.

Practical types who said that flat taxes cannot work offer a further instant objection, once they are shown such taxes working, namely, that they are unfair. Enlightened countries, it is argued, have "progressive" tax systems, requiring high-income earners to forfeit a bigger share of their incomes in tax than low-income earners have to pay. A flat tax seems to rule this out in principle.

Not so. A flat tax on personal incomes combines a threshold (that is, an exempt amount) with a single rate of tax on all income above it. The extent to which such a system is progressive can be varied within wide limits using just these two variables. Under the systems operating in most developed countries, the incentives for high-income earners to avoid tax (legally or otherwise) are enormous; and the opportunities to do so, which arise from the very complexity of the codes, are commensurately large. So it is unsurprising that high-income earners usually pay about as much tax under new flat-tax regimes as they would have paid under the previous codes.

Passage B

A lot of people don't understand graduated, as opposed to "flat," taxes. They think that if you make more money you pay a higher rate on your entire earnings, which seems unfair. Actually, graduated progressive taxes treat all taxpayers equally. Every taxpayer pays the same rate on equivalent layers of income. People in higher brackets don't pay the higher rate on their entire income, only on the portion of income over a specified amount. People, not dollars, are treated equally.

All people are created equal, but not all dollars are created equal. Earnings of the working poor go almost entirely for survival expenses such as food, shelter, and clothing. At that level, every dollar is critical; even a small difference causes tremendous changes in quality of life. Middle-income earners are still very conscious of expenses, but have much greater flexibility in absorbing small fluctuations in income.

Even some of the flat tax proposals recognize this, and want to exempt a primary layer from the tax system. So, since they recognize that survival dollars are different from discretionary dollars, why go suddenly from one extreme (paying no taxes) to the other (paying the top rate)? Since flat tax proposals are supposed to bring in the same total amount of tax revenue, if the working poor are going to pay less and the high-income earners are going to pay less, it is naturally going to fall on the middle class to make up the difference.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a fact meant to settle an old argument. Estonia adopted a flat tax in 1994, meaning one uniform rate on personal and corporate income with no rate schedule and no deductions, and eight countries have since copied it. The rhetorical work is in the last sentence: a proposal long dismissed as fine on paper but unworkable in reality now appears to work in reality too. The Author of A is writing as an advocate, and the opening is designed to clear away the practicality objection before the fairness objection is taken up.

The second paragraph stages the objection The Author of A wants to answer. The Practical Types, having lost the argument that flat taxes cannot function, fall back on the claim that they are unfair. Their reasoning rests on progressivity: an enlightened system makes high earners surrender a larger share of income than low earners do, and a single rate seems to make that impossible by definition. Notice this paragraph states the opposing case rather than endorsing it, and the phrase 'seems to rule this out' is already flagging where the rebuttal will land.

'Not so' delivers the rebuttal. A flat tax pairs a single rate with a threshold of exempt income, and adjusting those two numbers can produce a wide range of progressivity, so the objection confuses one rate with no progressivity. The Author of A then adds a practical argument: existing codes are so complex that high earners have both strong incentives and abundant opportunities to avoid tax, which is why high earners in flat-tax countries end up paying roughly what they paid before. The defense is thus both theoretical and empirical.

Passage B opens by correcting a misunderstanding running the other direction. The Author of B says many people wrongly imagine that moving into a higher bracket means paying the higher rate on everything they earn, which would indeed look unfair. In fact a graduated system applies the same rate to the same layer of income for everyone, and the higher rate touches only the portion above a set amount. The formulation to hold onto is the closing one: people are treated equally, dollars are not. That distinction is the hinge of the entire passage.

The next paragraph supplies the moral reasoning behind that distinction. For the working poor, nearly every dollar goes to food, shelter and clothing, so each one is essential and a small loss produces a large drop in quality of life. Middle-income earners still watch expenses but can absorb minor swings. The argument is about the differing real value of a dollar at different income levels, and it explains why The Author of B thinks equal rates on unequal dollars would not in fact be equal treatment.

The close turns that principle against flat-tax proposals on their own terms. The Author of B points out that some such proposals already exempt a base layer of income, which concedes that survival dollars differ from discretionary dollars; if so, jumping straight from a zero rate to the top rate makes no sense. Then comes the arithmetic objection: since flat taxes are meant to raise the same total revenue, cutting what the working poor and high earners pay leaves the middle class to cover the shortfall. Note this directly contests the reassurance offered at the end of Passage A.
overall_html: Passage A defends the flat tax against the charge of unfairness, arguing that a threshold plus a single rate can deliver as much progressivity as desired and that high earners already pay about the same under flat regimes as under complex ones, while Passage B defends graduated taxation on the grounds that equal treatment of people requires unequal treatment of dollars, since income spent on survival differs in kind from discretionary income. The two disagree directly on fairness and on who bears the burden, with The Author of B closing on the claim that a revenue-neutral flat tax shifts cost onto the middle class. A's purpose is to rebut The Practical Types; B's is to explain and justify progressivity.

Charles Darwin objected to all attempts to reduce his theory of evolution to its doctrine of natural selection. "Natural selection has been the main but not the exclusive means of modification," he declared. Nonetheless, a group of self-proclaimed strict constructionist Darwinians has recently risen to prominence by reducing Darwin's theory in just this way. These theorists use the mechanism of natural selection to explain all biological phenomena; they assert that natural selection is responsible for every aspect of every species' form and behavior, and for the success or failure of species in general.

Natural selection is generally held to result in adaptation, the shaping of an organism's form and behavior in response to environmental conditions to achieve enhanced reproductive success. If the strict constructionists are right, the persistence of every attribute and the survival of every species are due to such adaptation. But in fact, nature provides numerous examples of attributes that are not adaptations for reproductive success and of species whose success or failure had little to do with their adaptations.

For example, while it is true that some random mutations of genetic material produce attributes that enhance reproductive success and are thus favored by natural selection, and others produce harmful attributes that are weeded out, we now know from population genetics that most mutations fall into neither category. Research has revealed that neutral, nonadaptive changes account to a large extent for the evolution of DNA. Most substitutions of one unit of DNA for another within a population have no effect on reproductive success. These alterations often change the attributes of species, but their persistence from one generation to the next is not explainable by natural selection.

Additionally, the study of mass extinctions in paleontology has undermined the strict constructionist claim that natural selection can account for every species' success or failure. The extinction of the dinosaurs some 65 million years ago was probably caused by the impact of an extraterrestrial body. Smaller animal species are generally better able to survive the catastrophic changes in climate that we would expect to follow from such an impact, and mammals in the Cretaceous period were quite small because they could not compete on the large scale of the dominant dinosaurs. But while this scenario explains why dinosaurs died off and mammals fared relatively well, it does not conform to the strict constructionist view of the adaptive reasons for the success of species. For that view assumes that adaptations are a response to conditions that are already in place at the time the adaptations occur, and mammals could not have adapted in advance to conditions caused by the impact. In a sense, their success was the result of dumb luck.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting Darwin himself against people who claim his authority. Darwin resisted every attempt to reduce his theory of evolution to its doctrine of natural selection, insisting that selection was the main but not the exclusive means of modification. Nonetheless a group of self-proclaimed strict constructionist Darwinians has recently gained prominence by performing exactly that reduction, using natural selection to explain all biological phenomena, from every aspect of a species' form and behavior to the success or failure of species in general. That final extension is the broadest claim on the table, and it is the one the last paragraph goes after.

Definitions and a roadmap arrive together here. Natural selection is generally held to produce adaptation, meaning form and behavior shaped in response to environmental conditions so as to improve reproductive success. If the strict constructionists are right, then every attribute that persists and every species that survives does so because of such adaptation. The author denies both halves in a single sentence, promising examples of attributes that are not adaptations for reproductive success and of species whose success or failure had little to do with their adaptations. Expect the two paragraphs that follow to take those two promises in order.

The first counterexample comes from genetics and answers the claim about attributes. Some random mutations do produce traits that enhance reproductive success and are favored by selection, and others produce harmful traits that get weeded out, but population genetics has shown that most mutations fall into neither category. Neutral, nonadaptive change accounts to a large extent for the evolution of DNA, since most substitutions of one unit of DNA for another have no effect on reproductive success. Then comes the payoff: these alterations often do change a species' attributes, yet their persistence from one generation to the next simply is not explainable by natural selection.

The second counterexample comes from paleontology and answers the claim about species. Dinosaurs probably died out some sixty-five million years ago because an extraterrestrial body struck the earth, and smaller animals are generally better placed to survive the catastrophic climate change such an impact would bring; Cretaceous mammals happened to be small precisely because they could not compete on the scale the dinosaurs dominated. That story explains the outcome, but watch where it fails the strict constructionists. Their view assumes adaptations respond to conditions already in place when the adaptation occurs, and no mammal could have adapted in advance to a catastrophe that had not yet happened. Their success, in the author's phrase, was dumb luck.
overall_html: The passage argues against strict constructionist Darwinians who treat natural selection as the explanation of every biological phenomenon, siding with Darwin's own insistence that selection was the main but not the exclusive means of modification. The author's purpose is refutation, and the structure is tidy: the opposing position is stated, narrowed to two testable claims about the persistence of attributes and the fate of species, and then answered with one counterexample each, neutral DNA substitutions that endure without affecting reproductive success, and the mass extinction in which mammals survived because of a size they could not have acquired in anticipation of the impact. Track three positions here, Darwin's, the strict constructionists', and the author's.

From a critical discussion of the work of Victorian photographer Julia Margaret Cameron.

What Cameron called her "fancy-subject" pictures—photographs in which two or more costumed sitters enacted, under Cameron's direction, scenes from the Bible, mythology, Shakespeare, or Tennyson—bear unmistakable traces of the often comical conditions under which they were taken. In many respects they have more connection to the family album pictures of recalcitrant relatives who have been herded together for the obligatory group picture than they do to the masterpieces of Western painting. In Raphael and Giotto there are no infant Christs whose faces are blurred because they moved, or who are looking at the viewer with frank hatred. These traces, of course, are what give the photographs their life and charm. If Cameron had succeeded in her project of making seamless works of illustrative art, her work would be among the curiosities of Victorian photography—like Oscar Gustave Rejlander's extravagantly awful The Two Ways of Life—rather than among its most vital images.

It is precisely the camera's realism—its stubborn obsession with the surface of things—that has given Cameron's theatricality and artificiality its atmosphere of truth. It is the truth of the sitting, rather than the fiction which all the dressing up was in aid of, that wafts out of these wonderful and strange, not-quite-in-focus photographs. They are what they are: pictures of housemaids and nieces and husbands and village children who are dressed up as Mary Madonnas and infant Jesuses and John the Baptists and Lancelots and Guineveres and trying desperately hard to sit still. The way each sitter endures his or her ordeal is the collective action of the photograph, its "plot" so to speak. When we look at a narrative painting we can suspend our disbelief; when we look at a narrative photograph we cannot. We are always aware of the photograph's doubleness—of each figure's imaginary and real personas. Theater can transcend its doubleness, can make us believe (for at least some of the time) that we are seeing only Lear or Medea. Still photographs of theatrical scenes can never escape being pictures of actors.

What gives Cameron's pictures of actors their special quality—their status as treasures of photography of an unfathomably peculiar sort—is their singular combination of amateurism and artistry. In The Passing of Arthur, for example, the mast and oar of the makeshift boat representing a royal barge are obviously broomsticks and the water is white muslin drapery. But these details are insignificant. For once, the homely truth of the sitting gives right of place to the romantic fantasy of its director. The picture, a night scene, is magical and mysterious. While Cameron's fancy-subject pictures have been compared to poor amateur theatricals, The Passing of Arthur puts one in mind of good amateur theatricals one has seen, and recalls with shameless delight.
explanation_html:
Before any argument begins, the passage identifies what it is: material drawn from a critical discussion of the Victorian photographer Julia Margaret Cameron. That framing should shape your expectations, since a critical discussion promises evaluation rather than biography, and what follows will judge particular photographs and account for their effect. Read everything after this line as one critic's sustained assessment of Cameron's staged pictures, with the critic's own voice supplying the passage's single developed viewpoint.

The subject narrows to Cameron's fancy-subject pictures, staged scenes in which costumed sitters enacted episodes from the Bible, mythology, Shakespeare or Tennyson under her direction. The opening judgment is deflating and meant to be: these images carry unmistakable traces of the comical conditions in which they were made, and they resemble the obligatory family group portrait of unwilling relatives far more than the masterpieces of Western painting they imitate. Raphael and Giotto offer no blurred infant Christs and no babies staring out with frank hatred. Then comes the reversal that governs the whole passage, because those very traces are what give the photographs their life and charm; had Cameron achieved the seamless illustrative art she wanted, her work would be a Victorian curiosity rather than one of the period's most vital bodies of images.

Now the critic explains why the failure works, and the reasoning turns on something the camera cannot help doing. Because photography is stubbornly obsessed with the surface of things, Cameron's theatricality takes on an atmosphere of truth, though the truth in question is that of the sitting rather than the fiction all the dressing up was meant to serve. What you see are housemaids, nieces, husbands and village children costumed as Madonnas and Lancelots, all trying desperately to hold still, and the way each endures that ordeal becomes the real plot of the picture. The principle follows: a narrative painting lets you suspend disbelief while a narrative photograph never does, since you stay aware of each figure's imaginary and real persona at once, and unlike theater a photograph cannot stop being a picture of actors.

The closing paragraph names the quality that makes these pictures treasures, a singular combination of amateurism and artistry, and tests it on one image. In The Passing of Arthur the mast and oar of the makeshift royal barge are obviously broomsticks and the water is white muslin drapery, yet the critic dismisses such details as insignificant. Something unusual happens in this photograph: for once the homely truth of the sitting yields right of place to the romantic fantasy of its director, and the night scene becomes magical and mysterious. Notice that the final sentence refines an earlier insult rather than dropping it, since the fancy-subject pictures have been likened to poor amateur theatricals while this one recalls a good amateur theatrical, remembered with shameless delight.
overall_html: The passage is a critic's appreciation of Julia Margaret Cameron's staged fancy-subject photographs, arguing that their visible failures as illustration, the blurring, the restless sitters, the makeshift props, are exactly what makes them vital, because the camera records the truth of the sitting rather than the fiction being enacted. The purpose is evaluative, running from a deflating comparison with family album snapshots and Renaissance painting, through the principle that a narrative photograph never permits the suspension of disbelief that painting and theater allow, to a single example, The Passing of Arthur, in which fantasy briefly prevails. The only developed viewpoint is the critic's, with Cameron's own intentions serving as the thing measured.

Some critics of advertising have assumed that the creation of false needs in consumers is the principal mechanism underlying what these critics regard as its manipulative and hegemonic power. Central to this type of critique are the writings of political theorist Herbert Marcuse, who maintained that modern people succumb to oppression by believing themselves satisfied in spite of their living in an objectively unsatisfying world. This process occurs because in mass market culture the powerful psychological techniques of advertising create "needs" that are false and whose satisfaction thus contributes, not to the genuine well-being of consumers, but rather to the profit—and thereby the disproportionate power—of corporations.

Marcuse supposed that we all have certain real needs, both physical and psychological. Advertising appropriates these needs for its own purposes, forging psychological associations between them and consumer items, e.g., between sex and perfume, thereby creating a false "need" for these items. Since the quest for fulfillment is thus displaced from its true objects to consumer items, the implicit promises of advertisements are never really fulfilled and the consumer remains at some level unsatisfied.

Unfortunately, the distinction between real and false needs upon which this critique depends is extremely problematic. If Marcusians are right, we cannot, with any assurance, separate our real needs from the alleged false needs we feel as a result of the manipulation of advertisers. For, in order to do so, it would be necessary to eliminate forces of persuasion that are so prevalent in society that they have come to inform our instinctive judgments about things.

But, in fact, Marcusians make a major mistake in assuming that the majority of consumers who respond to advertising do not do so autonomously. Advertising techniques are unable to induce unwilling behavior in rational, informed adults, and regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising claims. Moreover, evidence suggests that most adults understand and recognize the techniques used and are not merely passive instruments. If there is a real need for emotional fulfillment, and if we can freely and authentically choose our means of obtaining it, then free, informed individuals may choose to obtain it through the purchase of commodities or even through the enjoyment occasionally provided by advertisements themselves. It is no doubt true that in many—perhaps even most—cases the use of an advertised product does not yield the precise sort of emotional dividend that advertisements seem to promise. This does not mean, however, that consumers do not freely and intentionally use the product as a means to another sort of fulfillment, or even that its genuine fulfillment of needs must be less than the advertisement suggests.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by laying out the position it intends to dismantle. Some critics of advertising assume that advertising's manipulative and hegemonic power works chiefly by manufacturing false needs, and the theorist at the center of that view is Herbert Marcuse, who held that modern people succumb to oppression precisely by believing themselves satisfied while living in an objectively unsatisfying world. The proposed mechanism is worth stating plainly: in mass market culture, the psychological techniques of advertising create needs that are not real, and satisfying them serves corporate profit and the disproportionate power that comes with it rather than any genuine well-being.

Marcuse's account is spelled out in more detail here so that it can be tested later. He supposed that people have certain real needs, physical and psychological alike, which advertising then appropriates by forging associations between those needs and particular consumer items, the standard illustration being the link built between sex and perfume. Because the quest for fulfillment is displaced from its true objects onto purchasable goods, the promise implicit in an advertisement is never really kept, so the consumer remains unsatisfied at some level. Note that permanent dissatisfaction is a prediction of the theory, which matters once the author starts pushing back.

'Unfortunately' introduces the first objection, and it strikes at the foundation of the critique rather than its conclusions. The whole argument depends on separating real needs from false ones, and the author contends that this distinction is extremely problematic. If the Marcusians are right about how pervasive advertising's persuasion has become, then that persuasion has already shaped our instinctive judgments about things, and telling the authentic apart from the manufactured would require eliminating forces that saturate the society we do our judging in.

The second objection is stronger, and it targets the theory's picture of consumers. Marcusians make a major mistake, the author argues, in assuming that people who respond to advertising are not acting autonomously. Advertising cannot induce unwilling behavior in rational, informed adults, regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising, and evidence suggests most adults recognize the techniques used on them rather than absorbing them passively. From there the argument turns constructive. If the need for emotional fulfillment is real and people can freely choose how to pursue it, then buying an advertised product, or even enjoying the advertisement itself, can be a genuine choice. The author grants that products often fail to deliver the precise emotional dividend implied, but denies that this makes consumers dupes rather than people deliberately using a product toward some other satisfaction.
overall_html: The passage attacks the Marcusian claim that advertising dominates consumers by manufacturing false needs whose satisfaction feeds corporate profit rather than genuine well-being. The author's purpose is refutation, and the structure falls into two halves: the first two paragraphs present Marcuse's theory sympathetically and in enough detail to be tested, while the last two dismantle it, first by arguing that the distinction between real and false needs cannot be drawn in a society already saturated with persuasion, then by arguing that informed adults recognize advertising techniques and may freely choose commodities as a route to real emotional fulfillment. Keep the Marcusians and the author's own position firmly apart.

Passage A

There are two principles that are fundamental to a theory of justice regarding property. The principle of justice in acquisition specifies the conditions under which someone can legitimately come to own something that was previously not owned by anyone. The principle of justice in transfer specifies the conditions under which the transfer of property from one person to another is justified.

Given such principles, if the world were wholly just, the following definition would exhaustively cover the subject of justice regarding property:

1. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in acquisition is entitled to that property.

2. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in transfer, from someone else who is entitled to the property, is entitled to the property.

3. No one is entitled to any property except by (repeated) applications of 1 and 2.

However, not all actual situations are generated in accordance with the principles of justice in acquisition and justice in transfer. Some people steal from others or defraud them, for example. The existence of past injustice raises the issue of the rectification of injustice. If past injustice has shaped present ownership in various ways, what, if anything, ought to be done to rectify that injustice? A principle of rectification would use historical information about previous situations and injustices done in them, and information about the actual course of events that flowed from these injustices, to produce a description of the property ownership that should have resulted. Actual ownership of property must then be brought into conformity with this description.

Passage B

In 1790, the United States Congress passed the Indian Nonintercourse Act, which requires that all transfers of lands from Native Americans to others be approved by the federal government. The law has not been changed in any relevant respect, and it remains in effect today. Its purpose is clear. It was meant to guarantee security to Native Americans against fraudulent acquisition by others of the Native Americans' land holdings. Several suits have been initiated by Native American tribes for recovery of lands held by them when the Nonintercourse Act took effect.

One natural (one might almost say obvious) way of reasoning about Native American claims to land in North America is this: Native Americans were the first human occupants of this land. Before the European invasion of North America, the land belonged to them. In the course of that invasion and its aftermath, the land was illicitly taken from them. The current owners lack a well-founded right to the land, which now lies illicitly in their hands. Ideally, the land should be restored to its rightful owners. This may be impractical; compromises might have to be made. But the original wrong can most easily be righted by returning the land to them—or by returning it wherever that is feasible.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by naming the two building blocks of its theory of justice regarding property. The principle of justice in acquisition specifies how someone may legitimately come to own something that nobody owned before, and the principle of justice in transfer specifies when passing property from one person to another is justified. Everything that follows is assembled out of these two ideas, so fix them now: one governs original ownership, the other governs the movement of what is already owned.

A conditional frames the list that follows, and it is doing real work rather than serving as filler. Given those two principles, the claim is that if the world were wholly just, the definition about to be offered would exhaustively cover the subject of justice regarding property. Register that qualifier immediately, because the assumption of a wholly just world is exactly what the last paragraph of Passage A takes back.

The first clause of the definition simply converts the acquisition principle into an entitlement: a person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in acquisition is entitled to that property. Think of this as the ground floor of the system, since it covers the original taking of something previously unowned, and every later holding will have to trace back eventually to a step of this kind.

The second clause does the same work for transfers, with one condition attached that is easy to skim past. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in transfer is entitled to it, but only when the property came from someone who was already entitled to it. That requirement is what makes the whole chain of ownership matter, since a properly conducted transfer still fails to confer entitlement if the person handing the property over had no legitimate claim to it.

The third clause closes the system rather than adding anything new to it. No one is entitled to any property except through repeated applications of the first two clauses, which means every legitimate holding must be traceable back through a series of just transfers to a just original acquisition. Nothing outside that chain can generate an entitlement, and this exclusivity is what gives the theory its bite when real cases are examined.

Reality now intrudes on the ideal, and the earlier qualifier is cashed in. Actual situations are not all generated in accordance with the two principles, since some people steal from others or defraud them, which raises the further issue of rectifying injustice. If past injustice has shaped present ownership, the question is what ought to be done about it. The remedy proposed is historical in method, drawing on information about previous situations, the injustices done in them, and the actual course of events that followed, in order to describe the ownership that should have resulted, after which real ownership must be brought into conformity with that description.

Passage B moves from theory to a concrete legal case. In 1790 the United States Congress passed the Indian Nonintercourse Act, which requires that all transfers of land from Native Americans to others be approved by the federal government, and the law remains in effect today without relevant change. Its purpose was protective, meant to guarantee Native Americans security against fraudulent acquisition of their land holdings by others. The final sentence supplies the live consequence, since several tribes have initiated suits for recovery of lands they held when the Act took effect.

The closing paragraph sets out the line of reasoning it calls natural, almost obvious, and its shape should look familiar after Passage A. Native Americans were the first human occupants of the land, so before the European invasion it belonged to them; in the course of that invasion and its aftermath the land was illicitly taken; the current owners therefore lack a well-founded right to what now lies in their hands. The conclusion is that ideally the land should be restored to its rightful owners. Notice the concession attached, since the argument allows that this may be impractical and that compromises might be needed, while insisting the original wrong is most easily righted by returning land wherever doing so is feasible.
overall_html: Passage A sets out an entitlement theory of property built from principles of just acquisition and just transfer, observes that those alone would settle the subject only in a wholly just world, and therefore adds a principle of rectification that uses historical information to describe the ownership that should have resulted had past injustices not occurred. Passage B applies exactly that kind of reasoning to a real case, describing the Indian Nonintercourse Act and the tribal suits brought under it before sketching the natural argument that land illicitly taken from its first occupants should be given back. The relationship is theory and application, with B supplying a concrete historical injustice of the sort A's rectification principle is designed to address.

Given the amount of time and effort that curators, collectors, dealers, scholars, and critics spend on formulating judgments of taste in relation to oil paintings, it seems odd that so few are prepared to apply some of the same skills in exploring works of art that stimulate another sense altogether: that of smell. Why is great perfume not taken more seriously? While art professionals are very serious about many branches of literature, architecture, and music, I have yet to find a curatorial colleague who regularly beats a path to the fragrance counter in search of, say, Joy Parfum, the 1930 masterpiece by Henri Alméras.

And yet, the parallels between what ought to be regarded as sister arts are undeniable. Painters combine natural and, these days, synthetic pigments with media such as oils and resins, much as the perfumer carefully formulates natural and synthetic chemical compounds. The Old Masters deployed oil paint across the color spectrum, and applied layers on a determining ground and various kinds of underpainting, slowly building up to the surface, completing their work with thin glazes on top. Thus various types of mashed-up earth and vegetable suspended in linseed or poppy oil are brushed over a stretch of woven fabric. They begin to dry, and a picture is born. Its appearance changes over time, because the tendency of oil paint is to become gradually more transparent.

So, too, talented "noses" experiment with complex configurations of olfactory elements and produce in symphonic combination many small sensations, at times discordant, sweet, bitter, melancholy, or happy, as the case may be. These combinations change and develop in sequence or in unison as the substance and its constituents evaporate at different rates, some quickly, others slowly, thanks to the warmth of our skin. A brilliant perfumer may thus devise an imaginary world no less powerful, or intimate, than that of a great composer or painter, and in calling on our capacity to discover there some memory of childhood or of a long-forgotten experience, perfumers are in the same business as the artist who creates the illusion of life on canvas.

Perhaps one reason that truly great smells are so often undervalued is that perfumes are today made and distributed under the not particularly watchful gaze of a few large corporations. The cynical bean counters in Paris and Zurich do not hesitate to tamper with old formulas, insisting on the substitution of cheap chemical compounds that approximately resemble rarer, better ingredients in an effort to increase profits. They do not tell their customers when or how they do this; indeed, they presume their customers won't notice the difference. Consequently, fine perfume is now hopelessly entangled with the international cosmetic dollar, and ill-served by marketing and public relations.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a complaint dressed up as a puzzle. Enormous effort goes into formulating judgments of taste about oil painting, yet almost no one applies those same skills to an art addressed to smell. The Author is writing from inside the art world about his own colleagues, and the tone is pointed rather than neutral: professionals take branches of literature, architecture and music seriously, but no curatorial colleague regularly visits the fragrance counter. Calling a 1930 perfume a masterpiece and naming its creator is doing argumentative work, since masterpiece and named author are precisely the vocabulary reserved for recognized art.

Having posed the question, the author starts building the case that these are sister arts, and the method is a sustained technical parallel. Painters combine natural and now synthetic pigments with media such as oils and resins, much as a perfumer formulates natural and synthetic chemical compounds. The account of Old Master practice is deliberately concrete and unglamorous, layers built over a determining ground and various underpainting, finished with thin glazes, so that a painting turns out to be mashed earth and vegetable matter suspended in oil and brushed across woven fabric. The closing detail carries the most weight: because oil paint grows gradually more transparent, the work keeps changing after it is finished.

The comparison now runs in the other direction, and the shared feature turns out to be change over time. Talented noses experiment with complex configurations that yield many small sensations in symphonic combination, at times discordant, sweet, bitter or melancholy, and those combinations develop in sequence or together as different constituents evaporate at different rates on warm skin. That is the olfactory counterpart of a painting's shifting surface. The paragraph then makes the boldest claim in the passage: a perfumer can devise an imaginary world no less powerful than a composer's or a painter's, and in summoning a long-forgotten memory does the same work as an artist creating the illusion of life on canvas.

The closing paragraph offers an explanation for the neglect described at the start, and it shifts the blame away from the audience. A new profile appears, the corporations that now make and distribute perfume, whose accountants tamper with old formulas without hesitation, substituting cheap chemical compounds that only approximate rarer and better ingredients, and who assume customers will never notice the difference. The causal claim matters more than the contempt: because fine perfume is now hopelessly entangled with the international cosmetics trade and handled by marketing and public relations, it has become difficult to see as art at all.
overall_html: The passage argues that great perfume deserves the same serious critical attention given to painting, music and literature, and that its neglect reflects a failure of the art world rather than any limitation of the medium. The author's purpose is persuasive: after opening on the oddity that curators who scrutinize oil paintings ignore fragrance entirely, the two middle paragraphs construct a detailed parallel between the painter's layered materials and the perfumer's evaporating compounds, both of which change over time and both of which conjure an imaginary world out of memory, before the final paragraph attributes the undervaluation to corporations that quietly debase formulas and to the marketing that now surrounds them.

"Stealing thunder" is a courtroom strategy that consists in a lawyer's revealing negative information about a client before that information is revealed or elicited by an opposing lawyer. While there is no point in revealing a weakness that is unknown to one's opponents or that would not be exploited by them, many lawyers believe that if the weakness is likely to be revealed in opposing testimony, it should be volunteered; otherwise, the hostile revelation would be more damaging.

Although no empirical research has directly tested the effectiveness of stealing thunder in actual trials, studies involving simulated trial situations have suggested that the technique is, in fact, effective, at least within a reasonably broad range of applications. Lawyers' commonly held belief in the value of stealing thunder is not only corroborated by those experimental findings; it is also supported by several psychological explanations of why the technique should work. For one thing, volunteering damaging information early may create an image of credibility. Psychological research suggests that people who reveal information that appears to be against their own best interest are likely to be perceived as more credible and thus may be more persuasive. Stealing thunder may also provide juries with an impetus for critical assessment by previewing, and thus alerting them to, testimony that the opposition plans to present. In psychological experiments, audiences that were previously warned of an upcoming attempt at persuasion became more resistant to the persuasive attempt, forming counterarguments based on the warning. Also, the value placed on a persuasive message is probably much like the value placed on any commodity; the scarcer the commodity, the more valuable it is. A persuasive message will thus increase in value and effectiveness to the extent that it is seen as scarce. In the courtroom, a piece of evidence brought by both the prosecution and the defense, as when thunder is stolen, may be seen as less scarce—becoming "old news." Thus, unless that evidence is of overriding consequence, it should carry less weight than if it had been included only in hostile testimony.

Finally, stealing thunder may work because the lawyer can frame the evidence in his or her own terms and downplay its significance, just as politicians sometimes seek to put their "spin" on potentially damaging information. However, it may therefore be effective only when the negative information can be framed positively. Jurors, who often initially have little information about a case, are usually eager to solidify their position regarding the case. They can therefore be expected to use the early positive framing to guide their subsequent analysis of the trial information. But this also suggests limitations on the use of the technique: when information is very damaging, stealing thunder may create an early negative impression that forms a cognitive framework for jurors, who then filter subsequent information through this schema.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining its subject precisely, and the definition carries a built-in condition. Stealing thunder is a lawyer's disclosure of damaging information about a client before the opposing lawyer can reveal or elicit it. Notice the qualification attached immediately: there is no point volunteering a weakness the other side does not know about or would not exploit. The strategy applies only where the damaging fact is likely to surface in opposing testimony anyway, and the belief held by many lawyers is that in exactly that situation a hostile revelation would do more damage than a voluntary one.

The second paragraph establishes that the tactic works and then explains why, and its structure is a list of separate causes worth keeping apart. No empirical research has tested actual trials, but simulated trial studies suggest the technique is effective within a reasonably broad range of applications, and psychological theory supports what lawyers already believe. Three mechanisms follow. Volunteering harmful information builds credibility, since people who say things apparently against their own interest are perceived as more believable and so persuade more effectively. Previewing the opposition's evidence also functions as a warning, and warned audiences in experiments resist persuasion better because they begin forming counterarguments in advance. The third mechanism treats a persuasive message as a commodity subject to scarcity: evidence brought by both sides becomes old news rather than a scarce revelation, so unless it is of overriding consequence it should carry less weight than it would have in hostile testimony alone.

A fourth mechanism arrives, and with it the passage's turn toward limits. Going first lets the lawyer frame the evidence in his or her own terms and downplay its significance, much as politicians put a spin on damaging news. That advantage is conditional in a way the earlier three were not, since it works only when the negative information can be framed positively at all. The reasoning about jurors then cuts both ways. Because they usually start with little information and are eager to solidify a position, they take the early positive framing as a guide to everything that follows. That same eagerness is the danger: when the information is very damaging, the early disclosure hardens into a negative cognitive framework through which jurors filter the rest of the trial.
overall_html: The passage explains and largely supports stealing thunder, the courtroom practice of disclosing a client's damaging information before an opponent can, holding that simulated-trial research and four psychological mechanisms corroborate the belief lawyers already hold, while a final limitation constrains its use. The author's purpose is explanatory rather than adversarial, moving from a careful definition with its own built-in condition, through the credibility, forewarning and scarcity effects, to the framing advantage, whose dependence on jurors' eagerness to settle on a position also explains why very damaging information can backfire by fixing an early negative schema. The only viewpoints in play are the author's analysis and the common lawyerly belief it vindicates.
