Physicists posit that at first our universe was infinitesimally small and infinitely hot and dense. It then underwent a period of extremely rapid, massive inflation (the Big Bang), and it has since continued to expand and cool.

According to physicists Sean Carroll and Jennifer Chen, the Big Bang was not a unique event; events like it happen periodically over an incredibly vast time scale. This is based on the suggestion of some physicists that the Big Bang was the beginning of our universe as we know it, but not the beginning of a larger Universe—or “multiverse"—that encompasses everything, including that which we can never see because it is beyond our "cosmic bubble."

Carroll and Chen were initially interested in why time flows in only one direction. In physics the flow of time is captured by the second law of thermodynamics, which implies that entropy—a measure of total disorder—naturally increases with time. Entropy increases because there are more ways for a system to be disordered than for it to be ordered. Therefore, if change occurs, it is more likely to be change toward greater disorder. For example, in a moderately orderly room, if one moves an object in the room randomly, there are many more places one can put it that will make the room less orderly than there are places that will make it more orderly. So if, over time, objects in the room are continually moved randomly, it is most likely that the room will get increasingly disordered.

While the Big Bang process and what followed obey the second law of thermodynamics, it is a mystery why there should have been a small, hot, and dense universe to begin with. Such a low entropy universe is an extremely unlikely configuration, not what scientists would expect from a randomly occurring initial condition. Carroll and Chen's innovation is to argue that the most common initial condition is actually likely to resemble cold, empty space—not an obviously favorable starting point for the onset of inflation.

Recent research has shown that even empty space has faint traces of energy that fluctuate on the subatomic scale. Physicists Jaume Garriga and Alexander Vilenkin have suggested that these fluctuations can generate their own big bangs in tiny areas widely separated in time and space. Carroll and Chen take our universe, and others, to be such fluctuations in a high entropy multiverse.

On this view, while the initial state that produced our universe would appear to be, taken by itself, a highly improbable one, in the vastness of the multiverse the creation of our universe is not that unlikely. Indeed it is likely not even a unique event.
explanation_html:
The opening lays down the standard picture in three strokes so that later paragraphs have something to modify. Our universe began vanishingly small, unimaginably hot and packed to extraordinary density; it then blew up in a burst of enormously rapid expansion, the Big Bang; and it has been spreading out and cooling ever since. Nothing controversial is being claimed yet. Hold onto the starting condition in particular, because the puzzle the passage eventually poses is about why the universe began in that state at all.

The first real claim arrives with names attached. Carroll and Chen argue that the Big Bang was not a one-off but one of a recurring series, spaced out over stretches of time beyond ordinary imagining. This rests on a proposal already circulating among physicists, that our Big Bang started our universe without starting everything, since a larger multiverse contains regions we could never observe, lying outside the cosmic bubble we inhabit. Keep the distinction between our universe and that wider whole in view.

A detour follows, and it is worth seeing that it is not a detour at all. The pair began with a different question, namely why time runs one way, which physics handles through the second law of thermodynamics: entropy, the amount of disorder in a system, tends to rise. The reason offered is purely a matter of counting, since disordered arrangements vastly outnumber ordered ones, so random change is far likelier to make things messier. The tidy room is the illustration — move things at random for long enough and the room degrades.

Now the problem this sets up. The Big Bang and everything after it are consistent with the second law, but the starting point is not explained by it, because a tiny, hot, dense universe is a low-entropy arrangement and therefore wildly improbable as a random initial condition. That is the mystery the counting argument leaves behind. Carroll and Chen's contribution is to reverse the expectation: the ordinary condition to expect is cold, empty space, which on the face of it is the last place inflation would get started.

The apparent dead end is opened up by borrowing a result from elsewhere. Empty space turns out not to be entirely empty, carrying faint energy that flickers at subatomic scale, and Garriga and Vilenkin have proposed that such flickers can set off big bangs of their own in small pockets far apart in both space and time. Carroll and Chen adopt this, treating our universe and others as exactly these fluctuations occurring within a high-entropy multiverse.

The closing paragraph collects the payoff, and the logic is about the difference between a single case and an enormous sample. Judged on its own, the state that launched our universe looks like a freak occurrence; set against the sheer extent of the multiverse, something like it happening is not improbable at all. The last sentence loops back to where the argument started, since on this account our universe's origin was probably not unique.
overall_html: The passage explains how Sean Carroll and Jennifer Chen account for an oddity the standard Big Bang picture leaves unexplained — why the universe should have begun in an extraordinarily improbable low-entropy state — by arguing that the ordinary condition is cold, empty space whose subatomic energy fluctuations, as Garriga and Vilenkin proposed, can spawn big bangs, so that our universe is one fluctuation among many in a high-entropy multiverse and its origin is neither improbable nor unique. The author's purpose is expository rather than evaluative, building from the accepted account, through entropy and the arrow of time, to the puzzle and then the proposed resolution, with Carroll and Chen as the developed viewpoint.

Most writings on the subject of motion pictures, including those scrutinizing the structural characteristics, aesthetic qualities, and effects of motion pictures on audiences, have traditionally been relatively abstract and have not considered what a film's audiences actually see. In fact, various external factors intervene between the filmmaker's intent and the audience's experience, often altering the qualities of a film and, consequently, the viewer's perception of it.

In the process of distribution, a film can be mutilated in many ways. The damage is most obvious when films in one language are shown to audiences that speak a different language. Subtitling may be simply incompetent, full of mistakes, or used for actual censorship. Dubbing—a significantly more profound intervention—can be even more damaging. Some films are reedited to render them "more understandable" by their target audiences, while others are given new titles rather than translations of their original titles, a practice that often creates false expectations and distorts the work's intent.

When a film is shown on television or video, it suffers the most extensive deformations. In addition to causing a loss of image size and definition, current mass-market television and video technology is harmful in other ways. These intrusions include advertisements that break the intended continuity, the superimposition of images—such as station identifications and weather bulletins—over parts of the picture, and spoken announcements over parts of the soundtrack considered by programmers to be "unimportant." Some alterations, such as a subtle increase in the projection speed of a televised movie to obtain more commercial time, are almost imperceptible but nonetheless detrimental to the integrity of a film.

It seems that audiences and even most film critics have tacitly accepted this situation—they rarely speak about it. This may be partly because of the special nature of film. In many other arts it is obvious that reproductions of a work are not the work itself, and they are not treated as such. However, the very nature of film makes it an exactly reproducible art form; under ideal conditions, each print is not merely a reproduction but is in fact another instance of the work itself. But we tend to overlook how rarely the ideal conditions apply, and this is disturbing for two reasons. First, professional analysis, interpretation, and evaluation may be unfair to filmmakers when—as is surprisingly often the case—they are based on a version that has already been seriously altered. Second, when critics' comments are based on original, uncompromised versions of the films, they may raise false expectations with regard to the more or less faulty versions that are often available to viewers.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by identifying a blind spot rather than a controversy. Writing about film, whether it examines how films are built, how good they are, or what they do to audiences, has tended to stay abstract and to skip the question of what viewers are actually looking at. The second sentence gives the author's thesis and the plan of what follows: a gap opens between what the filmmaker meant to make and what reaches the audience, because outside forces get in between, changing the film and with it the viewer's impression of it.

The first category of interference is distribution, and the examples escalate. Trouble is easiest to see when a film crosses a language barrier. Subtitles may be sloppy or plainly wrong, or may be turned into a tool for censorship, and dubbing counts as a deeper intrusion still because it replaces rather than accompanies the original. Beyond translation, films get recut so a new audience will supposedly follow them better, and get renamed rather than translated, which the author points out can set up expectations the film never intended.

Television and video are treated as the worst offenders, and the paragraph piles up the reasons. Start with the picture itself, smaller and less sharp than intended. Then come the interruptions broadcasting adds: commercials that sever the flow the director built, station logos and weather bulletins pasted over the image, and announcements talked over stretches of soundtrack that a programmer has decided do not matter. The last example makes the strongest point, since quietly speeding up a film to free up advertising time is almost impossible to notice and damages the work anyway.

The closing paragraph asks why nobody objects, and the explanation turns on what a film is. With most art forms, a reproduction is obviously not the original and nobody confuses the two, whereas film is exactly reproducible, so in ideal conditions a print is not a copy of the work but another instance of it. That is precisely what lulls people, because we forget how seldom the conditions are ideal. Two consequences trouble the author, and note that they cut in opposite directions: criticism built on an already altered version treats filmmakers unfairly, while criticism built on the pristine version promises viewers something the damaged versions available to them will not deliver.
overall_html: The passage argues that writing about film ignores a practical fact — that distribution and broadcast routinely alter what audiences actually see, through bad or censoring subtitles, dubbing, reediting, retitling, reduced image quality, interruptions, and even imperceptible speed changes — and that this passes almost unremarked because film's exact reproducibility makes each print seem to be the work itself. The author's purpose is corrective, moving from the neglected question, through two catalogues of damage, to an explanation of the silence and its costs: criticism based on altered versions is unfair to filmmakers, while criticism based on intact ones misleads viewers who will see something worse. The only viewpoint developed is the author's.

A recent worldwide decline of ocean fishery stocks has stimulated rapid growth in cultivated production of fish and shellfish, usually known as fish farming. Between 1987 and 1997, for example, global fish production from farming doubled. Fish farming produces a quarter of all fish and shellfish eaten by humans, and, as global population increases, fish farming will probably become even more important in supplying human protein needs. Some experts even argue that in addition to helping to compensate for the decline in ocean harvests, fish farming will restore wild populations by relieving pressure on ocean fisheries. There is, however, little if any evidence that fish farming will restore ocean fishery stocks. The complexity of production systems leads to an underlying paradox: fish farming is a possible solution, but also a potential contributing factor, to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide.

In the first place, the more intensive forms of fish farming, oriented toward high-volume production, threaten the sustainability of ocean fisheries through water pollution and ecological disruption. Intensive fish farming usually involves the enclosure of fish in a secure system; population densities are typically high, resulting in the generation of large amounts of waste and increased potential for the spread of pathogens. Habitat destruction through the spread of untreated waste, the escape of species not native to the farm's region, or contamination by new pathogens can all ensue, seriously damaging ocean and coastal resources and, ultimately, wild fishery stocks.

Even more important, intensive farming of many species of fish requires large inputs of fish meal and fish oil in order to supply fatty acids that vegetable matter lacks or essential amino acids that it inadequately supplies, like lysine and methionine. For the ten species of fish most commonly farmed, an average of 1.9 kilograms of wild fish is required for every kilogram of fish produced. Of the ten species, only three—catfish, milkfish, and carp—require less fish input than is eventually harvested, while the farming of carnivorous species like salmon has a very high input-to-output ratio. Although some defenders of fish farming contend that predatory carnivores in the wild consume even more fish than they would on a farm, farming of such carnivorous species requires up to 5 kilograms of wild fish for every kilogram of fish produced.

Expanding farm production does have the potential to alleviate some of the pressure on wild fishery stocks. For example, increasing the farm production of fish like salmon can reduce prices, deterring investment in fishing fleets and, over time, reducing fishing efforts. Similarly, other farmed fish like tilapia and channel catfish provide alternatives to ocean fish like cod and haddock. Nonetheless, even these benefits may in the end be lost because niche markets have started to develop for several species of wild-caught fish, causing their catch rates to remain high even as the production of viable farmed substitutes has increased.
explanation_html:
The opening moves from a trend to a thesis, so track where the reporting stops. Ocean stocks are falling worldwide, and farming of fish and shellfish has grown fast in response, doubling globally between 1987 and 1997 and now supplying a quarter of what people eat, with more likely as population grows. Some experts go further, claiming farming will actually rebuild wild populations by taking pressure off the oceans. The author answers that there is little or no evidence for this and states the paradox that organizes the passage: fish farming may be both a remedy for the decline of ocean stocks and a cause of it.

The first supporting argument concerns pollution and ecological damage, and it applies specifically to intensive, high-volume operations rather than farming in general. Penning large numbers of fish together in an enclosed system concentrates their waste and makes disease easy to spread. Three consequences follow: untreated waste can wreck habitat, farmed species can escape into regions where they do not belong, and new pathogens can be introduced. Each degrades coastal and ocean resources, and through them the wild stocks that farming was supposed to protect.

The author flags the second argument as the weightier one, and it is a matter of arithmetic. Many farmed fish need feed made of fish meal and oil, because plant matter cannot supply the fatty acids and supplies certain essential amino acids poorly. Across the ten most farmed species, producing a kilogram of fish consumes on average almost two kilograms of wild fish, and only catfish, milkfish and carp come out ahead. Notice how the defenders' reply is handled: granting that wild carnivores eat more than farmed ones does not touch the figure that farming a carnivore like salmon can burn five kilograms of wild fish per kilogram produced.

The final paragraph gives the other half of the paradox its due before withdrawing it. Farming can genuinely ease pressure on wild stocks in two ways, by pushing prices down so that investment in fishing fleets becomes less attractive and effort declines over time, and by offering substitutes, tilapia and channel catfish standing in for cod and haddock. The concluding turn is a market observation rather than a biological one: specialty demand for particular wild-caught species has emerged, keeping catch rates high even where a farmed alternative exists, so the benefit may not survive.
overall_html: The passage rejects the optimistic claim that fish farming will replenish depleted ocean fisheries, arguing instead a paradox: farming is at once a partial solution and a contributor to the decline, since intensive operations pollute habitat, release non-native species and spread pathogens, and since feeding farmed fish consumes on average nearly two kilograms of wild fish per kilogram produced, and up to five for carnivores like salmon. The author's purpose is evaluative, setting out the growth of the industry and the experts' hopeful case, then two arguments against it, and finally conceding the genuine price and substitution benefits before noting that niche markets for wild-caught fish may cancel them. The competing viewpoints are the optimistic experts and defenders of farming against the author's qualified skepticism.

Criminal courts frequently rely on accomplice witnesses (witnesses who testify regarding the role of an alleged co-conspirator in a crime) and jailhouse informants (witnesses who provide testimony based on information obtained while incarcerated) for prosecutorial information. Typically the testimony provided by such cooperating witnesses includes information garnered through the witnesses' conversations with the accused, which can include a purported confession to the crime.

Information from a cooperating witness is often provided in exchange for a reduced sentence or some other incentive. This kind of inducement creates a situation that is highly conducive to evidence fabrication on the part of the cooperating witness. In fact, one recent study concluded that lying informants are rarely prosecuted and therefore have much to gain and little to lose by testifying falsely.

While courts have recognized the unreliable nature of evidence obtained through bartered testimony, they have held that safeguards are in place to adequately protect the accused against a conviction based on false testimony. These safeguards allow effective cross-examination of a cooperating witness and enable the jury to consider a witness’s motivations. However, these safeguards do not always provide protection. There are cases in which prosecutors merely imply to cooperating witnesses that they will receive an incentive in exchange for testimony. In such cases, the exchange between prosecution and witness does not have to be disclosed to the jury.

In addition, psychological research on confession testimony—confessions obtained by investigators directly from the accused—reveal further problems with bartered testimony. This research indicates that jurors give undue weight to confession evidence when rendering guilt decisions. This effect is especially notable in cases where jurors are aware that a defendant has been offered an incentive in exchange for a confession. This is particularly relevant here because if people have difficulty realizing the effect that an incentive can have on a defendant’s behavior, they may also fail to realize the effect that an incentive may have on a cooperating witness’s behavior.

A common psychological phenomenon may account for jurors’ superficial examination of confession evidence. Studies show that people tend to explain the behavior of others in terms of internal dispositions or attitudes as opposed to external, situational factors. In one study, regardless of whether confession evidence was obtained via negative pressure (threats of worse treatment and/or harsher punishment) or positive pressure (promises of better treatment and/or leniency), mock jurors viewed a confession as evidence that the defendant committed the crime because “only a guilty person would confess to such a crime.” The same logic can be applied to the testimony of cooperating witnesses: jurors may presuppose that accomplice witnesses and jailhouse informants offer their testimony as atonement rather than deducing that external factors made it expedient to give the testimony.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by defining its terms, and the two categories are worth separating. An accomplice witness testifies about what a supposed co-conspirator did; a jailhouse informant testifies about what they learned while locked up. Criminal courts lean on both for evidence, and what these cooperating witnesses typically deliver is the content of conversations they had with the accused, sometimes including a claimed confession. Nothing critical is said yet, but notice that the whole category rests on one person reporting another's private words.

Now the weakness. Cooperating witnesses are usually paid in something valuable, most often a lighter sentence, and the author argues that this arrangement is close to an invitation to invent evidence. The supporting study makes the incentive structure explicit by looking at the downside rather than the upside: prosecution of informants who lie is rare, so a false witness stands to gain a great deal and risks almost nothing.

The response from the courts is acknowledged fairly before it is challenged. Judges are aware that bartered testimony is shaky, but hold that existing protections suffice, since the defense can cross-examine the witness thoroughly and the jury can weigh what the witness stands to gain. The author's counter is narrow and concrete rather than sweeping: prosecutors sometimes only hint at a reward instead of promising one, and an implied bargain need not be revealed to the jury, so there is nothing for the jury to weigh.

A second line of attack arrives from psychology, and the argument here is by analogy, so follow the transfer carefully. Research on confessions given directly to investigators shows that jurors weigh such evidence too heavily, and the effect is especially pronounced when jurors know the defendant was offered an incentive in exchange. The author draws the parallel: if people cannot properly discount the pull an incentive exerts on a defendant, they are unlikely to discount its pull on a cooperating witness either.

The closing paragraph supplies the underlying mechanism, which is what makes the analogy more than a guess. People habitually explain what others do by reference to character and attitude rather than the pressures of the situation. The study cited shows the effect at full strength, since mock jurors treated a confession as proof of guilt whether it was extracted by threats or coaxed by promises of leniency, reasoning that only the guilty confess. Applied to cooperating witnesses, the same bias leads jurors to read testimony as an act of atonement instead of a calculated response to what was on offer.
overall_html: The passage argues that testimony from accomplice witnesses and jailhouse informants is dangerously unreliable because it is bought with sentence reductions and other incentives, and that the safeguards courts rely on do not cure the problem: implied bargains never reach the jury, and psychological research shows jurors overvalue confession-type evidence even when they know an incentive was involved. The author's purpose is critical and diagnostic, moving from a definition of cooperating witnesses, to the incentive to fabricate, to the courts' confidence in cross-examination and why it falls short, and finally to the tendency to explain behavior by disposition rather than situation, which leads jurors to mistake bought testimony for atonement. The courts' position and the author's critique are the viewpoints to keep apart.

Passage A is adapted from a book by a music historian, and passage B from an anthropology journal.

Passage A

Many commentators have described the blues musician of the United States as an extension of the griot of West Africa, yet one could hardly find two performers with less in common from a sociological perspective. Griots were the historians of their communities, representatives of time-honored traditions, the preservers of lore and cultural identity. They took these traditions and transformed them into song, and as a result often enjoyed great status in their communities. In societies that lacked libraries and museums, official documents and archives, the griot's song filled many of the roles that these institutions serve in other societies.

The blues musician, in contrast, honed a music of personal expression, often reflecting a lack of connection to the broader streams of society, evoking feelings of alienation and anomie. Slavery caused this terrible disjunction. Slavery destroyed in large part the traditional social fabric, the communal values, the historical continuities that made the griot's art possible. Blues music was, in many ways, a response to this deprivation.

And here we encounter the fundamental tragedy of the blues and one of the sources of its unparalleled symbolic power. For the music sings of small, everyday details of individual lives. But behind this facade always sits a larger reality, invariably unspoken, but no less present for this silence. Separated from the social institutions that gave life its meaning and resonance within their traditional societies, African Americans struggled to find substitutes for what was lost within the smaller cosmos of their personal relationships and daily life. Blues music reflected this dynamic, gave it powerful poetic expression. From this perspective, the perennial themes of blues music—heartache and hardships—capture in a personal dimension the larger social truth.

Passage B

Fifteenth-century Portuguese explorers observed a stratified social hierarchy in the Wolof culture of Senegal, with a high-status noble sector (géer) and low-status caste groups (ñeeño). Wolof elites of the day ranked ñeeño in six subcastes, the lowest of which was griot.

Griots alone specialized in the spoken word. Raising one's voice in public was considered inappropriate for socially prominent people, but griots, considered unmarriageable outside their caste, shouted and sang their patrons' praises to crowds of people, often with a drum, and always with great eloquence.

At community gatherings, griots accompanied their patrons, with whom they had usually inherited a close relationship through generations of service. Reciting vivid histories about the brave deeds of their patrons' family ancestors and singing praises about their exemplary work and daily conduct, griots used their music to sway public opinion in favor of their patrons. Their songs invoked specific public values and described their patrons' adherence to them, making the griot a blend of community historian, storyteller, spokesperson, and ultimately, guardian of norms and culture. Despite the griots' public loudness, these performances and the prestige they brought their patrons required griots to be sensitive to Wolof community values and conceptions of correct social conduct.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by picking a fight with a received comparison. Author A notes that many commentators treat the American blues musician as a descendant of the West African griot, then denies the two have anything in common socially. The rest of the paragraph builds the griot side of the contrast: the griot kept the community's history, carried its inherited traditions, and preserved its lore and sense of itself, turning all of that into song and often gaining high standing for it. Where there were no libraries, archives or museums, the griot's song did their work.

The other half of the contrast follows, and it is drawn in opposite terms point for point. Blues is personal rather than communal, expressing disconnection from the wider society and a sense of alienation and rootlessness. Author A then supplies a cause rather than leaving the difference as mere description, and the causal claim is the important one: slavery tore apart the social fabric, shared values and unbroken historical memory that the griot's art depended on. Blues, on this account, grew out of what had been taken away.

The argument now converts the contrast into an interpretation of how blues works. Its lyrics stay with the small particulars of one person's life, but a larger reality sits behind them, never named and never absent, and that gap between surface and background is what Author A calls the music's tragedy and the root of its symbolic force. The reasoning connects back to the previous paragraph: cut off from the institutions that once gave life meaning, African Americans looked for replacements in private relationships and everyday life, so the familiar blues subjects of heartache and hardship register a social truth in personal form.

Passage B drops the argument entirely and gives you social history, so read it for facts that bear on Passage A rather than for a thesis. Portuguese explorers in the fifteenth century found the Wolof of Senegal organized in a rigid hierarchy, nobles known as géer above low-status caste groups known as ñeeño. The detail that matters most comes last, since the elites sorted ñeeño into six subcastes and placed griots at the very bottom.

What set griots apart was their monopoly on public speech. Wolof norms held that prominent people should not raise their voices in public, and griots, who could not marry outside their caste, did exactly the opposite, shouting and singing the praises of their patrons before crowds, usually with a drum and always with great skill. Notice the shape of this arrangement, in which low social rank and an indispensable public function belong to the same people.

The final paragraph fills in what griots actually did with that function. Attached to patron families through relationships inherited over generations, they appeared at community gatherings reciting the brave deeds of a patron's ancestors and praising the patron's own conduct, which worked to move public opinion in the patron's favor. Because those songs named particular community values and measured the patron against them, the griot ended up part historian, part storyteller, part spokesperson and finally a guardian of shared norms, and doing the job well required close attention to what the community counted as proper behavior.
overall_html: Passage A argues that the widespread comparison between the blues musician and the West African griot fails sociologically, since the griot was an honored keeper of communal history while blues grew from the alienation slavery produced by destroying exactly that communal fabric, giving personal expression to a larger unspoken social loss. Passage B offers no thesis at all, describing instead the griot's actual position in Wolof society: the lowest of six low-status subcastes, yet uniquely licensed to speak in public and functioning as historian, spokesperson and guardian of norms. The two stand in a relationship of detail complicating generalization, since Passage B supports Author A's picture of the griot's cultural role while unsettling the claim that griots enjoyed great status.

Complex societies flourished on the central plateau of southern Africa from the ninth through sixteenth centuries. Their regional political centers, called zimbabwes, were city-states enclosed within stone walls, which still exist as archaeological monuments. Great Zimbabwe, the largest of these, was the product of a highly stratified society whose ruling class wielded political authority over the whole plateau. By the fourteenth century, the inhabitants of Great Zimbabwe enjoyed notable prosperity, obtaining luxury goods such as Chinese glazed pottery and Near Eastern glass from distant trading emporia on Africa's east coast. Scholars often maintain that this prosperity was primarily attributable to Great Zimbabwe's control over gold mining on the plateau and the export of gold to the coastal markets. However, it is instead the agricultural basis for the zimbabwe economic system that is actually the most crucial element in understanding Great Zimbabwe's achievements.

During the fourteenth century, the population of Great Zimbabwe probably exceeded 10,000. This was an extraordinary size for a city at that time in an environment of typical African savanna woodland, because the only system of crop cultivation these soils could support was one that involved long fallow periods between plantings, a pattern typically resulting in low population densities and considerable mobility. Moreover, there were no carts or draft animals for transporting grain in bulk to large population centers, nor could grain be stored in large quantities for any length of time. The alternative agricultural system that Great Zimbabwe practiced was a complex cattle economy that exploited enormous areas of land for grazing. The population of Great Zimbabwe relied heavily on beef for food. In summer, cattle grazed on grass at higher elevations; in winter, the cattle were moved to lower regions unsuitable for grazing in summer because of the risk to the cattle of disease carried by the tsetse fly. This economy demanded large-scale coordinated efforts to control distant pastures and to move and protect the cattle as large herds. This favored a pattern of centralized control over the society, with cattle becoming the property of a ruling class.

Ordinary people were given use of individual cattle as an act of royal patronage. Because cattle exchange was an essential element in marriage contracts, the power of the royal class reached deep into everyone's lives. Similarly, the crucial role of cattle also explains Great Zimbabwe's successful mining industry. Gold is found in scattered deposits throughout the region. Some gold could simply be washed from the sand and gravel of rivers that cut through the deposits, and its recovery was a relatively undemanding seasonal village industry. However, the actual mining of the gold deposits was dangerous, required considerable labor, and might produce only small yields. It was through its use of cattle as a powerful incentive to laborers that royalty was able to muster the human resources necessary for large-scale gold mining.
explanation_html:
Two things happen in the opening paragraph, and the second matters more. The setup comes first: from the ninth through sixteenth centuries, complex societies on southern Africa's central plateau built stone-walled city-states called zimbabwes, and the largest, Great Zimbabwe, was ruled by a highly stratified society with authority over the whole plateau, prosperous enough by the fourteenth century to import Chinese glazed pottery and Near Eastern glass from east-coast trading ports. Then comes the pivot. Scholars credit that prosperity chiefly to control of plateau gold mining and gold exports, while the Author insists the agricultural basis of the economy is the crucial element instead. Everything after this defends that reversal.

The argument begins with a puzzle of scale. A fourteenth-century population above 10,000 was extraordinary in savanna woodland, since those soils supported only cultivation with long fallow periods, a pattern that normally produces thin, mobile populations, and there were no carts, draft animals or long-term storage to concentrate grain in a city. Crops therefore cannot explain the city. The alternative was a cattle economy exploiting enormous grazing areas, with beef a dietary mainstay and herds moved seasonally between higher summer pasture and lower winter ground that tsetse-borne disease made unusable in summer. Follow the causal chain to its end: that movement demanded coordinated control of distant pastures, which favored centralized rule, with cattle owned by a ruling class.

Economic control becomes social and industrial power in the final paragraph. Ordinary people received the use of individual cattle as royal patronage, and because cattle exchange was essential to marriage contracts, royal authority reached deep into everyone's private life. The same lever explains the mining industry. Gold sat in scattered deposits, and some could simply be washed from river sand and gravel, an undemanding seasonal village activity, but working the deposits themselves was dangerous, labor-intensive and often meagre in yield. Cattle supplied the incentive that let royalty muster a workforce on that scale, completing the Author's reversal of the Scholars: gold wealth was a product of the cattle economy rather than its foundation.
overall_html: Against the common scholarly view that Great Zimbabwe's prosperity rested chiefly on controlling and exporting plateau gold, the passage argues that the true foundation was agricultural, specifically a centralized cattle economy that alone could sustain a city of more than 10,000 people in savanna woodland where crop cultivation could not. The author's purpose is corrective, opening with the historical setting and the Scholars' gold thesis, then supplying the cattle-based alternative and the centralized rule it required, and finally showing that even the mining industry depended on cattle, since only royal cattle patronage could recruit labor for dangerous deep extraction. The contest is between the Scholars' explanation and the Author's own.

passage_html:
Passage A

The path a historical novelist has to tread is clearly beset by dangers. One cannot have medieval characters using correct period language because no one would find the speech readable. Similarly, in depicting the lives of real individuals, authors must invent dialogue, as well as other details missing from the historical record; otherwise characters will remain two-dimensional and never develop. In effect, the creation of a good narrative requires the telling of lies.

Nonetheless there is a clear and important distinction between telling lies and making mistakes. A lie is intentional and purposeful; a mistake is accidental and often unforgivable. The spectrum of historical fiction is therefore not as simple as "accurate equals good" and "inaccurate equals bad." It depends on whether the inaccuracies are constructive lies or accidental mistakes. Effective lies add to the story; mistakes detract from it.

Of course, some lies go too far and alienate the reader. Some are too obvious. But some lying is necessary, and to get away with it, one has to be both subtle and convincing. Shakespeare is a good model in this respect. He distorted the facts freely and knowingly conflated historical characters in historical plays. Yet such distortion makes the drama of human lives meaningful and memorable.

Passage B

As a writer of autobiographical texts, I'm always astonished at how falsely I remember things, astonished at how unreliable memory is. And even when I know a memory is incorrect, part of my brain cleaves to the wrong, imagined memory. I hold two memories in my head, and the false one is more vivid and more emotionally significant to me than the actual one. Which, then, is the truest memory?

It's convenient when the actual events adequately convey the emotional experience, but sometimes they don't and the writer has to choose. While I wouldn't be so disingenuous as to argue that a false memory is valid simply because it is vivid, I would argue that there must be a subjective truth to it, an emotional truth.

Ultimately, lying is all but inescapable for a writer attempting to create an artistically coherent autobiography. One reads an autobiography to see how the writer experienced and evaluates his or her own life, and a biography to find a more objective view. If false memories have an emotional power for the person who creates them, it's arguably more misleading to omit them than it is to include them.

My argument grows strained and my tone shrill because I'm unhappy with the patently illogical and unethical position that practical experience has led me to. Nonetheless, the trust a reader brings to reading an autobiography is a trust in a convincingly told tale, not the trust one brings to a newspaper article or a history of Assyria, in which aesthetics are secondary to factual accuracy. Autobiography dances on the shifting middle ground between fact and fiction, and different writers will draw their lines on that ground in different places.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by laying out the historical novelist's dilemma as a set of unavoidable compromises. Genuine period speech would be unreadable, so medieval characters must talk in language they never used; the record leaves gaps in the lives of real people, so dialogue and detail have to be invented or the characters stay two-dimensional. Author A states the conclusion in deliberately provocative terms, that good narrative requires telling lies, and that word choice is the hinge the next two paragraphs turn on.

A distinction immediately narrows what the provocation means. Lies are intentional and purposeful, mistakes are accidental, and Author A treats the accident as the graver fault. The consequence for judging historical fiction is that accuracy is the wrong yardstick: the question is not whether a book departs from the record but whether the departures are constructive lies or careless errors. Effective lies add to the story while mistakes detract from it. Hold on to that criterion, since it is Author A's real standard.

Limits arrive next, followed by a model. Not every lie works, because some go too far and alienate the reader and some are simply too obvious, so the necessary lying has to be subtle and convincing. Shakespeare is offered as the example, distorting facts freely and knowingly conflating historical characters, yet producing drama that makes human lives meaningful and memorable. Author A finishes where the passage started, with invention defended as a craft skill rather than excused as a lapse.

Passage B opens in the first person and shifts the problem from invention to memory. Writing autobiographical work, Author B is astonished at how unreliable recollection is, and at something stranger still: even when a memory is known to be wrong, part of the mind clings to it, so two versions coexist and the false one feels more vivid and more emotionally significant than the accurate one. The paragraph closes on a genuine question rather than an answer, which memory counts as the truest.

That question receives a qualified answer. Sometimes the actual events convey the emotional experience adequately and no conflict arises, but when they do not, the writer has to choose. Author B declines the easy claim that a false memory is valid merely because it is vivid, while maintaining that such a memory carries a subjective, emotional truth. Notice the hedging in the phrasing; this is a writer arguing for something they are not fully comfortable defending, and the final paragraph will say so outright.

The case is then pushed to its conclusion. Lying, Author B claims, is all but inescapable for anyone trying to build an artistically coherent autobiography, and the genre's purpose supports the claim: readers come to autobiography for how a writer experienced and evaluates his or her own life, and to biography for a more objective view. Given that purpose, omitting false memories that hold real emotional power for the person who created them may mislead a reader more than including them would.

Unusually, the closing paragraph turns on its own argument. Author B concedes that the reasoning has grown strained and the tone shrill, and admits unhappiness with a position that looks illogical and unethical yet is exactly where practical experience leads. The defense rests on what readers expect: trust in an autobiography is trust in a convincingly told tale, not the trust owed to a newspaper article or a history, where aesthetics come second to factual accuracy. Autobiography occupies shifting middle ground, and each writer draws the line in a different place.
overall_html: Both passages defend deliberate departures from fact as necessary to good writing, but they differ in scope and in confidence: Passage A treats invented speech and detail as a craft requirement of historical fiction and supplies a clean standard, that purposeful lies serving the story are legitimate while careless mistakes are not, whereas Passage B works from inside autobiography, where the falsehoods are the writer's own vivid false memories, and arrives at a comparable conclusion with open discomfort. Passage A moves from dilemma to criterion to model, while Passage B moves from a personal puzzle about memory to a claim about emotional truth and then to a candid admission of strain. Author A and Author B agree that such lying is unavoidable and part company over how easily it can be justified.

For nearly a century after the discovery in the 1880s that a bacterium, Vibrio cholerae, causes cholera, scientists believed that it traveled to new geographic regions only via human hosts and that epidemics typically occurred when the bacteria spread through contamination, by human waste, of food and unchlorinated water supplies. But scientists wondered where the bacteria went during the many years between epidemics. How could the disease arise seemingly spontaneously around the world, often where it was thought to have been eradicated?

In the 1970s, microbiologist Rita Colwell's claim that she had isolated V. cholerae from the Chesapeake Bay in the eastern United States met with great skepticism, as no biologists believed V. cholerae could persist without a human host, and no cholera outbreaks were occurring anywhere near the Chesapeake. Indeed, there had been no cholera epidemics anywhere in the United States since 1911. But, noting that most historic cholera outbreaks have happened along seacoasts, Colwell suspected that V. cholerae could somehow survive in seawater and that perhaps the bacteria were not always detectable by traditional culture methods—that is, that they could not always be cultured (i.e., grown) in a petri dish. Later that decade, a small cholera outbreak near New Orleans in the southern United States allowed Colwell to test this hypothesis. She used a new detection method on water from the local bayous from which people with cholera had eaten crab. This method uses an antibody that latches onto a key component of the bacterium's cell membrane. Linked to that antibody is a molecule that fluoresces bright green under ultraviolet light if the V. cholerae bacterium is present. Her tests showed that the bacteria were in the bayous. Furthermore, in a study in Asia, Colwell's antibody test detected the bacteria in 51 of 52 suspect water samples, whereas culture techniques found them in only 7 of the same 52 samples.

Colwell's further studies revealed that V. cholerae, like some other bacteria, goes into a dormant, sporelike state when environmental conditions do not favor reproduction; in this state, the bacterium's metabolic rate plummets and the bacterium shrinks some 15- to 300-fold. It stops reproducing and therefore cannot be cultured. This "viable but nonculturable" state, says Colwell, functions as a survival mechanism, enabling V. cholerae to persist in a wide range of conditions and habitats far from human hosts. Though no one knows exactly what conditions awaken V. cholerae from dormancy, Colwell notes that seasonal peaks in sea-surface temperatures in the Bay of Bengal in south Asia correlate closely with peaks in that region's cholera cases. If, as Colwell believes, the bacteria are persisting in the water all along, it is possible that changes in seawater temperature or salinity are what enable them to spread among humans again.
explanation_html:
Begin with the consensus and the hole in it. For roughly a century after the 1880s discovery that the bacterium Vibrio cholerae causes cholera, the Scientists held that it reached new regions only inside human hosts and that epidemics began when human waste contaminated food or unchlorinated water. The paragraph closes on the anomaly that consensus could not absorb: if the bacterium depends on people, where does it go during the long stretches between epidemics, and how does the disease surface again, seemingly from nowhere, in places thought to have been rid of it? That unanswered question is the problem the rest of the passage solves.

Colwell enters as the challenger, and her 1970s claim to have isolated V. cholerae from Chesapeake Bay met skepticism on two counts: no biologist thought the bacterium could persist without a human host, and there was no cholera nearby, indeed none in the country since 1911. Her reasoning was that most historic outbreaks occurred along seacoasts, so the bacterium might survive in seawater while escaping notice, since standard identification meant growing it in a petri dish. A small outbreak near New Orleans gave her a test. Using an antibody that latches onto the cell membrane and carries a molecule that fluoresces green under ultraviolet light, she found the bacteria in the bayous, and an Asian study using the same test detected them in 51 of 52 samples where culturing managed only 7.

The mechanism comes last, and it explains the anomaly raised at the start. Colwell's later work showed that V. cholerae can enter a dormant, sporelike state when conditions do not favor reproduction, its metabolic rate plummeting and its body shrinking dramatically; because it stops reproducing, it cannot be cultured, which is exactly why it appeared to vanish. She calls this viable but nonculturable state a survival mechanism that lets the bacterium persist across many habitats far from human hosts. What wakes it remains unknown, though seasonal sea-surface temperature peaks in the Bay of Bengal track that region's cholera peaks closely, suggesting to Colwell that shifts in temperature or salinity return the ever-present bacteria to people.
overall_html: The passage recounts how a century-old belief that cholera bacteria travel only in human hosts gave way to Rita Colwell's finding that V. cholerae persists in coastal waters in a dormant, viable but nonculturable state that traditional culture methods could not reveal. The author's purpose is expository, moving from the old consensus and the puzzle it left unsolved, through Colwell's contested hypothesis and the antibody-based tests that supported it, to the dormancy mechanism that accounts for both the bacterium's invisibility between epidemics and its apparently spontaneous reappearance. The two viewpoints to track are the Scientists' earlier orthodoxy and Colwell's revision of it, with the author reporting the shift rather than arguing against either side.

In the absence of international statutes prohibiting nations from causing each other environmental damage, scholars of international environmental law typically focus on trying to identify and clarify norms of "customary international law": that body of commonly accepted—but not formalized—legal principles that is manifest in the behavior of nations toward one another. Two environmental principles are often held to be established norms of customary international law. One of these principles proscribes transboundary harm: nations should prohibit activities within their borders that cause significant environmental harm beyond those borders. The other is the closely allied precautionary principle, which requires nations to exercise due care to avoid putting other nations at significant risk of environmental harm.

In debating whether a given principle should be classified as a norm of customary international law for the purposes of deciding international cases, scholars of international environmental law generally accept an established criterion: principles are norms only if nations customarily abide by the principles in actual practice rather than merely affirming them as desirable standards. In fact, however, many purported "norms" of customary international environmental law, including the duty to prevent transboundary harm and the precautionary principle, do not reflect the actual behavior of many nations. Although systematic empirical studies are lacking, experience shows that harmful pollutants constantly cross most international borders, and that nations have only rarely attempted to remedy this situation.

Even though nations only rarely abide by these environmental "norms," they nevertheless routinely profess to accept them. Similarly, while scholars discussing customary international law claim to focus on what nations do, their debates are almost invariably based on what nations profess. In reality, international environmental "norms" primarily reflect the evaluative standards that nations use to justify their own actions and criticize those of other nations. Hence these environmental "norms" are not properly classifiable as norms of customary international law. They might more accurately be characterized as an ideological system, since they merely represent some collective ideals of the international community.

In light of this fact, those scholars who seek in customary international law a firm grounding for decisions in international environmental cases are misdirecting their efforts. This is especially true given that international treaties and direct negotiations, rather than international court decisions, are now the principal means of resolving international environmental disputes. It would be more productive for scholars to study such disputes from perspectives more consonant with this trend. Specifically, attention should be directed toward how the affirmation of core environmental principles can contribute to negotiations and treaty formation. This approach would promote progress toward agreements that could effectively hold nations to appropriate standards of environmental conduct.
explanation_html:
Set the stage before any argument begins. With no international statutes forbidding nations from damaging each other's environments, the Scholars of international environmental law work instead on customary international law, the body of widely accepted but uncodified principles supposedly visible in how nations actually treat one another. Two environmental principles are usually treated as established norms of that kind: a ban on transboundary harm, meaning a nation should stop activities inside its borders that seriously damage the environment beyond them, and the closely allied precautionary principle, which demands due care so other nations are not placed at significant risk. Nothing critical yet, only the terms you will need.

The criterion arrives next, and it belongs to the Scholars themselves: a principle counts as a norm only if nations customarily follow it in practice, not merely affirm it as a desirable standard. The Author then turns that test against them. Neither the duty to prevent transboundary harm nor the precautionary principle matches the behavior of many nations. The evidence is admittedly loose, since systematic empirical studies are lacking, but experience shows harmful pollutants crossing most international borders constantly with only rare attempts at remedy. Watch the structure of this move, because the Author is defeating the Scholars' conclusion with the Scholars' own standard.

Having exposed the gap between conduct and profession, the Author explains what these principles really are. Nations seldom obey the norms yet routinely declare their acceptance of them, and the Scholars, while claiming to study what nations do, in practice debate what nations say. The norms therefore function as the evaluative standards states invoke to justify their own actions and criticize the actions of others. The conclusion follows directly: they are not properly classifiable as norms of customary international law, and are better described as an ideological system expressing collective ideals of the international community. That relabeling is the passage's central claim.

Critique becomes advice in the closing paragraph. If the norms are ideals rather than law, Scholars searching customary international law for a firm grounding for environmental decisions are misdirecting their effort, and a practical trend reinforces the point, since disputes are now settled mainly through treaties and direct negotiation rather than through international court decisions. The recommendation is to study how affirming core environmental principles can contribute to negotiation and treaty formation instead. Notice that the principles are never dismissed as worthless; they are relocated from adjudication to diplomacy, where the Author expects them to produce agreements that actually hold nations to standards.
overall_html: Applying the standard the field itself accepts, that a principle qualifies as customary international law only when nations actually follow it, the passage argues that the supposed environmental norms barring transboundary harm and requiring precaution fail that test, and are better understood as an ideological system of collective ideals that states invoke to justify themselves and condemn others. The author's purpose is critical and then prescriptive, moving from the terms and the criterion, to evidence of the gap between profession and practice, to a reclassification of the norms, and finally to the recommendation that scholars examine how such principles aid treaty formation and negotiation. The clash to track is between the Scholars and the Author.

The following passage is adapted from a 2001 article by a film historian.

In exhibiting works of art—whether in a gallery, a cinema, or anywhere else—the primary question usually is: which works should be exhibited together? In many exhibitions the selection is often tied to the creator of the works. For example, we might have an exhibition of Rembrandt's paintings. Another reasonable method might be to choose paintings with a particular theme or of a particular historical period, for example, Modernism. In all cases the aim is to select a series of works with something in common. In the world of cinema, this notion of "collecting the similar" has its analogue in the retrospective. This involves collecting together and screening several examples of the work of a particular director, star, studio, etc. In recent years a rediscovery of early (pre-1915) nonfiction film has been taking place, and such films have been the subject of some notable retrospectives.

But I would argue that the philosophy of "collecting the similar" is often inappropriate for screening early film, especially nonfiction, because it means showing several films of the same type one after the other in the same sitting, which would never have been the practice at the time the films were made. Gathering together several short films (and in the early 1910s most films were under fifteen minutes) by the same maker or studio, while useful for historians and academics, is often profoundly dull for the viewer. With some exceptions, nonfiction films have always been supporting films, not main attractions. Early cinemagoers never saw a collection of similar films screened together; they almost always saw a program that was a mix of everything from dramas and comedies to travelogues and news. Even into the 1920s a mixed program was the norm.

Film archives and retrospective festivals often behave as if the production of the films were the only side of the coin. Film archives spend vast amounts of time and effort in restoring films as they supposedly were when originally produced. These restorations are presented with great fanfare as authentic versions, or "directors' cuts." Yet as far as the exhibition side is concerned, authenticity is sometimes allowed to go out the window. Films are presented in an inauthentic setting, utterly shorn of the program that once gave these films life and context, a setting that allowed particular films to shine, but also to balance and react against other kinds of films. Film presenters discovered the magic of programming in the early years of the twentieth century, or more likely inherited it from the vaudeville tradition. It ill behooves us alleged early film lovers to forsake their insights today.
explanation_html:
The opening builds an analogy the argument will need. Exhibiting art turns on a single question, which works belong together, and the familiar answers group by creator, by theme, or by historical period, all of them versions of collecting the similar. Cinema's counterpart is the retrospective, where films by one director, star or studio are gathered and screened as a set, and the paragraph narrows to the case at issue, the rediscovery of pre-1915 nonfiction film and the notable retrospectives devoted to it. Read this as neutral setup: it defines the practice the passage will attack, and defines it in that practice's own favorable terms, as a reasonable method with a sensible aim.

The pivot is signaled by a first-person objection, which introduces the Author as a participant rather than a reporter. Collecting the similar suits early film badly, nonfiction especially, because it means watching several films of one type in a row, something no audience of the period ever did. Grouping short films, and in the early 1910s most ran under fifteen minutes, by maker or studio serves historians and academics while being profoundly dull to sit through. Two historical facts back this up: nonfiction films were, with few exceptions, supporting items rather than main attractions, and early cinemagoers saw mixed programs of dramas, comedies, travelogues and news, a norm that lasted into the 1920s.

The charge sharpens into an inconsistency at the close. Film Archives and retrospective festivals behave as though production were the only side of the coin, pouring effort into restoring films to their supposed original state and presenting the results with fanfare as authentic versions or directors' cuts. On the exhibition side, however, that same commitment to authenticity is dropped, since the films appear stripped of the program that once gave them life and context, a program that let individual films shine while balancing and reacting against other kinds. The Author ends on inherited wisdom: presenters discovered the magic of programming early in the twentieth century, probably from vaudeville, and abandoning that insight ill suits anyone claiming to love early film.
overall_html: The passage argues that the retrospective's guiding principle of collecting the similar is wrong for early film, especially nonfiction, because such films were originally supporting items inside mixed programs of dramas, comedies, travelogues and news, and screening them in same-type blocks is both historically false to the period and dull for the viewer. The author's purpose is corrective, first defining the grouping principle that governs art and film exhibition, then objecting to its use on early cinema, and finally exposing an inconsistency in Film Archives that restore production with painstaking authenticity while presenting the restorations in a setting authenticity has been allowed to leave. The only developed viewpoint is the Author's, aimed squarely at archives and festival programmers.
