By the mid-fourteenth century, professional associations of canon lawyers (legal advocates in Christian ecclesiastical courts, which dealt with cases involving marriage, inheritance, and other issues) had appeared in most of Western Europe, and a body of professional standards had been defined for them. One might expect that the professional associations would play a prominent role in enforcing these standards of conduct, as other guilds often did, and as modern professional associations do, but that seems not to have happened. Advocates' professional organizations showed little fervor for disciplining their erring members. Some even attempted to hobble efforts at enforcement. The Florentine guild of lawyers, for example, forbade its members to play any role in disciplinary proceedings against other guild members. In the few recorded episodes of disciplinary enforcement, the initiative for disciplinary action apparently came from a dissatisfied client, not from fellow lawyers.

At first glance, there seem to be two possible explanations for the rarity of disciplinary proceedings. Medieval canon lawyers may have generally observed the standards of professional conduct scrupulously. Alternatively, it is possible that deviations from the established standards of behavior were not uncommon, but that canonical disciplinary mechanisms were so inefficient that most delinquents escaped detection and punishment.

Two considerations make it clear that the second of these explanations is more plausible. First, the English civil law courts, whose ethical standards were similar to those of ecclesiastical courts, show many more examples of disciplinary actions against legal practitioners than do the records of church courts. This discrepancy could well indicate that the disciplinary mechanisms of the civil courts functioned more efficiently than those of the church courts. The alternative inference, namely, that ecclesiastical advocates were less prone to ethical lapses than their counterparts in the civil courts, seems inherently weak, especially since there was some overlap of personnel between the civil bar and the ecclesiastical bar.

Second, church authorities themselves complained about the failure of advocates to measure up to ethical standards and deplored the shortcomings of the disciplinary system. Thus the Council of Basel declared that canon lawyers failed to adhere to the ethical prescriptions laid down in numerous papal constitutions and directed Cardinal Cesarini to address the problem. In England, where medieval church records are extraordinarily rich, similar complaints about the failure of the disciplinary system to reform unethical practices were very common.

Such criticisms seem to have had a paradoxical result, for they apparently reinforced the professional solidarity of lawyers at the expense of the enforcement of ethical standards. Thus the profession's critics may actually have induced advocates to organize professional associations for self-defense. The critics' attacks may also have persuaded lawyers to assign a higher priority to defending themselves against attacks by nonprofessionals than to disciplining wayward members within their own ranks.
explanation_html:
Everything in the opening builds an expectation and then frustrates it. By the mid-fourteenth century canon lawyers, the advocates who argued in church courts over matters such as marriage and inheritance, had professional associations across most of Western Europe and an agreed body of professional standards. You would expect those associations to enforce the standards, as other guilds did and as modern professional bodies do, and The Author notes that they did not. Some actively obstructed: the Florentine guild barred its members from taking any part in disciplinary proceedings against another member. In the few recorded cases, a dissatisfied client rather than a fellow lawyer set the process in motion.

A clean either/or is set up, and defining the two options fairly is this paragraph's only job. Either medieval canon lawyers really did observe the standards scrupulously, leaving little to punish, or violations were common and the canonical disciplinary machinery was so inefficient that most offenders were never caught. Note the hedge 'at first glance', which signals that the author does not intend to leave the choice open; the next two paragraphs argue for the second option, each opening with one numbered consideration.

The first consideration is comparative. English civil law courts worked to ethical standards much like those of the ecclesiastical courts, yet their records show far more disciplinary action against legal practitioners. The natural reading is that civil court machinery simply functioned better. The author then closes off the competing reading, that church advocates were less prone to ethical lapses, calling it inherently weak and backing that with a telling detail, since some of the same individuals practiced at both bars and the two groups can hardly have differed in character. Watch how the argument works by eliminating the alternative inference rather than by direct proof.

The second consideration comes from inside the church rather than from comparison, which makes it hard to dismiss as an outsider's complaint. Church authorities said themselves that advocates fell short of ethical standards and that the disciplinary system was failing. The Council of Basel declared that canon lawyers were ignoring prescriptions laid down in numerous papal constitutions and handed the problem to Cardinal Cesarini, and England, whose medieval church records survive in unusual richness, yields many similar complaints that discipline was not reforming unethical practice. Taken with the previous paragraph, this settles the earlier choice in favor of an ineffective system.

The final paragraph turns from evidence to consequence, and the consequence runs opposite to what the critics wanted. Instead of producing reform, sustained criticism seems to have tightened professional solidarity at the expense of enforcement. The author suggests that outside attacks may have been part of why advocates organized associations at all, as a defensive measure, and that the same pressure led lawyers to rank self-defense against nonprofessionals above disciplining wayward colleagues. Notice how heavily hedged the language stays here, since the author is proposing an explanation for the paradox rather than claiming to have demonstrated it.
overall_html: The passage asks why the professional associations of medieval canon lawyers so rarely disciplined their own members, and concludes that the disciplinary system was ineffective rather than the profession unusually scrupulous. The author's purpose is to argue for one of two competing explanations, first posing the alternatives, then supporting the second with a comparison to English civil courts that disciplined practitioners far more often and with the church authorities' own complaints about enforcement, and finally proposing the paradox that outside criticism strengthened lawyers' solidarity and made discipline less likely still. The only sustained viewpoint is the author's; church authorities appear as corroborating witnesses rather than as an opposing position.

Many birds that form flocks compete through aggressive interaction for priority of access to resources such as food and shelter. The result of repeated interactions between flock members is that each bird gains a particular social status related to its fighting ability, with priority of access to resources increasing with higher status. As the number and intensity of interactions between birds increase, however, so increase the costs to each bird in terms of energy expenditure, time, and risk of injury. Thus, birds possessing attributes that reduce the number of costly interactions in which they must be involved, without leading to a reduction in status, are at an advantage. An external signal, such as a plumage type, announcing fighting ability and thereby obviating the actual need to fight, could be one such attribute.

The zoologist Rohwer asserted that plumage variations in "Harris sparrows" support the status signaling hypothesis (SSH). He reported that almost without exception birds with darker throats win conflicts with individuals having lighter plumage. He claimed that even among birds of the same age and sex the amount of dark plumage predicts relative dominance status.

However, Rohwer's data do not support his assertions: in one of his studies darker birds won only 57 out of 75 conflicts; within another, focusing on conflicts between birds of the same age group or sex, darker birds won 63 and lost 62. There are indications that plumage probably does signal broad age-related differences in status among Harris sparrows: adults, usually dark throated, have higher status than juveniles, who are usually light throated; moreover, juveniles dyed to resemble adults are dominant over undyed juveniles. However, the Harris sparrows' age-related plumage differences do not signal the status of individual birds within an age class, and thus cannot properly be included under the term "status signaling."

The best evidence for status signaling is from the greater titmouse. Experiments show a strong correlation between the width of the black breast-plumage stripe and status as measured by success in aggressive interactions. An analysis of factors likely to be associated with breast-stripe width (sex, age, wing length, body weight) has demonstrated social status to be the only variable that correlates with stripe width when the other variables are held constant.

An ingenious experiment provided further evidence for status signaling in the greater titmouse. One of three stuffed titmouse dummies was mounted on a feeding tray. When a live bird approached, the dummy was turned by radio control to face the bird and present its breast stripe in "display." When presented with a dummy having a narrower breast stripe than their own, birds approached closely and behaved aggressively. However, when presented with a dummy having a broader breast stripe than their own, live birds acted submissive and did not approach.
explanation_html:
The opening builds the logic that everything after it will test. Flocking birds compete aggressively for food and shelter, and repeated encounters sort each bird into a social status matching its fighting ability, with higher status bringing earlier access to resources. Fighting is expensive, though, costing energy and time and risking injury, and those costs rise as encounters multiply. Any trait that reduces the number of fights without lowering a bird's status therefore pays off. A visible signal of fighting ability, such as a plumage type, would do exactly that, and whether plumage really works this way is the status signaling hypothesis at issue.

Rohwer enters as the hypothesis's advocate, and his case rests on Harris sparrows. He reported that darker-throated birds beat lighter-plumaged ones almost without exception, then went further, claiming that even among birds matched for age and sex the amount of dark plumage predicts which will dominate. That second claim is the demanding one, since it says plumage marks the status of individual birds rather than merely separating broad classes of bird. Hold on to the distinction, because the objection coming next turns entirely on it.

The Author checks Rohwer's numbers against his conclusions and finds a mismatch. In one study darker birds won 57 of 75 conflicts, well short of the near-exceptionless pattern claimed, and in the study restricted to birds of the same age group or sex they won 63 and lost 62, essentially a coin flip. What plumage does track is age, since adults are usually dark throated and outrank light-throated juveniles, and juveniles dyed to resemble adults dominate undyed ones. But a broad age marker is not a signal of an individual bird's standing, so the sparrow evidence does not qualify as status signaling at all.

Having cleared away the weak case, the author supplies a strong one, so read this shift as support for the hypothesis rather than for Rohwer. In the greater titmouse, the width of the black stripe on the breast correlates closely with success in aggressive interactions. The decisive step is the control: sex, age, wing length, and body weight were all tested as possible drivers of stripe width, and with those held constant social status alone still tracks it. That isolates exactly the individual-level correlation the hypothesis requires and the Harris sparrow data failed to deliver.

The closing experiment adds behavior to correlation, and its design is worth appreciating. A stuffed titmouse was mounted on a feeding tray and turned by radio control to face any live bird that approached, presenting its breast stripe as though displaying. Birds confronted with a narrower stripe than their own came in close and behaved aggressively; birds confronted with a broader one held back and acted submissive. Since a dummy can do nothing but display, the stripe by itself was governing how the live birds behaved, which is the conclusion the author has been building toward throughout.
overall_html: The passage evaluates the status signaling hypothesis, the idea that a visible feature such as plumage advertises a bird's fighting ability and so spares it the cost of fighting, and concludes that the hypothesis holds even though the evidence most often cited for it does not support it. The author's purpose is first corrective and then constructive, setting out the logic of the hypothesis, showing that Rohwer's Harris sparrow data are far weaker than he claimed and reflect age classes rather than individual status, and finally presenting the greater titmouse breast stripe, with its controlled correlation and the radio-controlled dummy experiment, as genuine support. The viewpoints to keep separate are Rohwer's and the author's.

In The Dynamics of Apocalypse, John Lowe attempts to solve the mystery of the collapse of the Classic Mayan civilization. Lowe bases his study on a detailed examination of the known archaeological record. Like previous investigators, Lowe relies on dated monuments to construct a step-by-step account of the actual collapse. Using the erection of new monuments as a means to determine a site's occupation span, Lowe assumes that once new monuments ceased to be built, a site had been abandoned. Lowe's analysis of the evidence suggests that construction of new monuments continued to increase between A.D. 672 and 751, but that the civilization stopped expanding geographically; new construction took place almost exclusively in established settlements. The first signs of trouble followed. Monument inscriptions indicate that between 751 and 790, long-standing alliances started to break down. Evidence also indicates that between 790 and 830, the death rate in Classic Mayan cities outstripped the birthrate. After approximately 830, construction stopped throughout the area, and within a hundred years, the Classic Mayan civilization all but vanished.

Having established this chronology, Lowe sets forth a plausible explanation of the collapse that accommodates the available archaeological evidence. He theorizes that Classic Mayan civilization was brought down by the interaction of several factors, set in motion by population growth. An increase in population, particularly within the elite segment of society, necessitated ever more intense farming. Agricultural intensification exerted stress on the soil and led to a decline in productivity (the amount of food produced through each unit of labor invested). At the same time, the growth of the elite class created increasing demands for ceremonial monuments and luxuries, diverting needed labor from the fields. The theory holds that these stresses were communicated—and amplified—throughout the area as Mayan states engaged in warfare to acquire laborers and food, and refugees fled impoverished areas. The most vulnerable states thus began to break down, and each downfall triggered others, until the entire civilization collapsed.

If there is a central flaw in Lowe's explanation, it is that the entire edifice rests on the assumption that the available evidence paints a true picture of how the collapse proceeded. However, it is difficult to know how accurately the archaeological record reflects historic activity, especially of a complex civilization such as the Mayans', and a hypothesis can be tested only against the best available data. It is quite possible that our understanding of the collapse might be radically altered by better data. For example, Lowe's assumption about monument construction and the occupation span of a site might well be disproved if further investigations of Classic Mayan sites established that some remained heavily settled long after the custom of carving dynastic monuments had ceased.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out both what Lowe is trying to explain and how he goes about it, so keep his method separate from his findings. The subject is the collapse of Classic Mayan civilization, the source is the known archaeological record, and, like earlier investigators, he builds a step-by-step chronology from dated monuments. One working assumption carries a lot of weight: he treats the erection of new monuments as marking a site's occupation, so when new monuments stop appearing he takes the site to have been abandoned. The resulting sequence has four stages, with construction rising between 672 and 751 while geographic expansion halted, alliances breaking down between 751 and 790, deaths outrunning births between 790 and 830, and building ceasing entirely after 830, the civilization all but gone within a century.

With the sequence fixed, Lowe supplies a cause, and his theory is a chain reaction set off by population growth. More people, especially among the elite, forced more intensive farming, which stressed the soil and lowered productivity, meaning less food returned for each unit of labor invested. At the same time a growing elite demanded more ceremonial monuments and luxuries, pulling workers away from the fields just as the fields were yielding less. Warfare between Mayan states to seize laborers and food, together with refugees fleeing impoverished areas, transmitted these pressures across the region and amplified them. The weakest states broke down first, and each collapse triggered further ones. Notice that the author presents all of this as plausible and consistent with the evidence.

The critique that follows is narrower and gentler than it first sounds. The Author places the central flaw not in Lowe's reasoning but in its foundation, since the whole structure assumes the available evidence gives a true picture of how the collapse proceeded. Two qualifications immediately soften the charge: nobody can say how accurately the archaeological record reflects the activity of a civilization as complex as the Maya, and a hypothesis can only be tested against the best data on hand. The real objection, then, is that better evidence could change the picture entirely, and the example is precise. If further work showed that some sites stayed heavily settled after dynastic monument carving stopped, Lowe's assumption about occupation spans would collapse.
overall_html: The passage summarizes John Lowe's account of the Classic Mayan collapse, in which dated monuments yield a chronology running from continued building without expansion, through the breakdown of alliances and a death rate exceeding the birthrate, to the end of construction after 830, and in which population growth sets off a chain of agricultural stress, labor diverted to elite building, warfare, and refugee movement. The author's purpose is to present and then qualify that explanation, granting its plausibility and its fit with the evidence before observing that it stands or falls with the accuracy of the archaeological record, particularly Lowe's assumption that a site was abandoned once new monuments ceased. The two voices are Lowe's theory and the author's measured reservation.

The expansion of mass media has led to an explosion in news coverage of criminal activities to the point where it has become virtually impossible to find citizens who are unaware of the details of crimes committed in their communities. Since it is generally believed that people who know the facts of a case are more likely than those who do not to hold an opinion about the case, and that it is more desirable to empanel jurors who do not need to set aside personal prejudices in order to render a verdict, empaneling impartial juries has proven to be a daunting task in North American courts, particularly in trials involving issues or people of public interest.

Judges rely on several techniques to minimize partiality in the courtroom, including moving trials to new venues and giving specific instructions to juries. While many judges are convinced that these techniques work, many critics have concluded that they are ineffective. Change of venue, the critics argue, cannot shield potential jurors from pretrial publicity in widely reported cases. Nor, they claim, can judges' instructions to juries to ignore information learned outside the courtroom be relied upon; one critic characterizes such instruction as requiring of jurors "mental contortions which are beyond anyone's power to execute."

The remedy for partiality most favored by judges is voir dire, the questioning of potential jurors to determine whether they can be impartial. But critics charge that this method, too, is unreliable for a number of reasons. Some potential jurors, they argue, do not speak out during voir dire (French for "to speak the truth") because they are afraid to admit their prejudices, while others confess untruthfully to having prejudices as a way of avoiding jury duty. Moreover, some potential jurors underestimate their own knowledge, claiming ignorance of a case when they have read about it in newspapers or discussed it with friends. Finally, the critics argue, judges sometimes phrase questions in ways that indicate a desired response, and potential jurors simply answer accordingly.

These criticisms have been taken seriously enough by some countries that rely on juries, such as Canada and Great Britain, that they have abandoned voir dire except in unusual circumstances. But merely eliminating existing judicial remedies like voir dire does not really provide a solution to the problem of impartiality. It merely recognizes that the mass media have made total ignorance of criminal cases among jurors a virtual impossibility. But if a jury is to be truly impartial, it must be composed of informed citizens representative of the community's collective experience; today, this experience includes exposure to mass media. Impartiality does not reside in the mind of any one juror; it instead results from a process of deliberation among the many members of a panel of informed, curious, and even opinionated people.
explanation_html:
The problem is framed as a collision between one fact and two assumptions. The fact is that media coverage of crime has become so thorough that virtually no citizen is unaware of the details of cases in their own community. The assumptions are that people who know the facts are likelier to have formed an opinion, and that jurors carrying no personal prejudice are preferable to jurors who must set one aside. Together they make impartial juries extremely hard to empanel, especially where the issues or the people involved attract public interest. Keep an eye on the second assumption, because the closing paragraph is going to overturn it.

Two remedies arrive together with the disagreement they provoke. The Judges move trials to new venues and instruct juries to disregard what they learned outside the courtroom, and many of them are convinced these measures work. The Critics conclude that they do not. A change of venue cannot outrun publicity in a widely reported case, and telling jurors to set aside outside information demands what one critic calls mental contortions no one can perform. Note the shape of this exchange, since the critics offer no replacement of their own; they argue only that the existing tools fail, and the same pattern repeats immediately.

Voir dire, the questioning of potential jurors about whether they can be impartial, is the remedy judges favor most and it draws the fullest attack. The critics list four ways it goes wrong. Some jurors will not admit prejudices they actually hold; others claim prejudices they lack in order to escape jury duty; some underestimate their own exposure, professing ignorance of a case they have read about or discussed with friends; and judges occasionally phrase questions so that the wanted answer is obvious, and receive it. Every objection concerns the reliability of what jurors say, whether the distortion comes from fear, self-interest, poor self-knowledge, or the questioner.

The final paragraph accepts the criticisms and then moves past them, which is where The Author finally speaks directly. Canada and Great Britain have found them persuasive enough to abandon voir dire except in unusual circumstances, but removing a remedy is not a solution; it merely concedes that total ignorance of criminal cases is no longer achievable. The positive claim reverses the assumption from the opening: a truly impartial jury should consist of informed citizens representing the community's collective experience, and that experience now includes exposure to mass media. Impartiality belongs to no individual juror, arising instead from deliberation among many informed, curious, even opinionated people.
overall_html: The passage argues that jury impartiality should be understood as a product of collective deliberation rather than as the absence of knowledge or opinion in any individual juror. The author's purpose is to reframe a problem, first explaining why saturating media coverage makes traditionally impartial juries nearly impossible to assemble, then reporting the critics' case that the judges' remedies of changed venue, cautionary instruction, and voir dire are all unreliable, and finally rejecting the response of simply abandoning those remedies. The viewpoints to track are the judges who trust their techniques, the critics who dismiss them without proposing a replacement, and the author, who accepts much of the criticism but draws a constructive conclusion from it.

Personal names are generally regarded by European thinkers in two major ways, both of which deny that names have any significant semantic content. In philosophy and linguistics, John Stuart Mill's formulation that "proper names are meaningless marks set upon . . . persons to distinguish them from one another" retains currency; in anthropology, Claude Lévi-Strauss's characterization of names as being primarily instruments of social classification has been very influential. Consequently, interpretation of personal names in societies where names have other functions and meanings has been neglected. Among the Hopi of the southwestern United States, names often refer to historical or ritual events in order both to place individuals within society and to confer an identity upon them. Furthermore, the images used to evoke these events suggest that Hopi names can be seen as a type of poetic composition.

Throughout life, Hopis receive several names in a sequence of ritual initiations. Birth, entry into one of the ritual societies during childhood, and puberty are among the name-giving occasions. Names are conferred by an adult member of a clan other than the child's clan, and names refer to that name giver's clan, sometimes combining characteristics of the clan's totem animal with the child's characteristics. Thus, a name might translate to something as simple as "little rabbit," which reflects both the child's size and the representative animal.

More often, though, the name giver has in mind a specific event that is not apparent in a name's literal translation. One Lizard clan member from the village of Oraibi is named Lomayayva, "beautifully ascended." This translation, however, tells nothing about either the event referred to—who or what ascended—or the name giver's clan. The name giver in this case is from Badger clan. Badger clan is responsible for an annual ceremony featuring a procession in which masked representations of spirits climb the mesa on which Oraibi sits. Combining the name giver's clan association with the receiver's home village, "beautifully ascended" refers to the splendid colors and movements of the procession up the mesa. The condensed image this name evokes—a typical feature of Hopi personal names—displays the same quality of Western Apache place names that led one commentator to call them "tiny imagist poems."

Hopi personal names do several things simultaneously. They indicate social relationships—but only indirectly—and they individuate persons. Equally important, though, is their poetic quality; in a sense they can be understood as oral texts that produce aesthetic delight. This view of Hopi names is thus opposed not only to Mill's claim that personal names are without inherent meaning but also to Lévi-Strauss's purely functional characterization. Interpreters must understand Hopi clan structures and linguistic practices in order to discern the beauty and significance of Hopi names.
explanation_html:
A field's default assumptions are laid out so that they can be overturned. European Thinkers treat personal names in two ways, and both deny that names carry meaning: Mill's formulation, still current in philosophy and linguistics, makes proper names meaningless marks that distinguish one person from another, while Lévi-Strauss's influential anthropological account makes them instruments of social classification. The cost of these positions is that names with other functions have gone uninterpreted. The Author puts the Hopi forward as the counterexample, since their names refer to historical or ritual events, at once placing a person within society and conferring an identity, and the imagery involved makes them a kind of poetry.

The mechanics of naming come first, and they are more specific than they might seem. A Hopi receives several names across a lifetime, each tied to a ritual initiation such as birth, entry into a ritual society in childhood, or puberty. The giver is always an adult from a clan other than the child's, and the name refers back to the giver's clan, often blending a characteristic of that clan's totem animal with a characteristic of the child. A name meaning little rabbit works exactly this way, catching the child's size and the representative animal together. Treat this as the simple case, because the paragraph that follows presents the more usual one.

Most names conceal more than they reveal, and this example shows how much interpretive work they demand. Lomayayva, borne by a Lizard clan member from the village of Oraibi, translates as beautifully ascended, which on its own identifies neither what ascended nor which clan supplied the name. The giver belongs to Badger clan, which stages an annual ceremony where masked representations of spirits climb the mesa Oraibi sits on. Combine the giver's clan with the receiver's village and the name turns out to evoke the colors and movement of that procession. The author calls such compression typical and connects it to Western Apache place names once described as tiny imagist poems.

Everything is gathered in the closing paragraph, where the argument is stated outright. Hopi names do indicate social relationships, though only indirectly, and they do individuate people, which is what the European accounts would lead you to expect. What those accounts cannot accommodate is the third function, the poetic one, since these names operate as short oral texts that produce aesthetic delight. That makes the author's position a rejection of both earlier views at once, Mill's denial of inherent meaning and Lévi-Strauss's purely functional reading. A practical consequence follows: an interpreter must know Hopi clan structure and linguistic practice before a name's beauty becomes visible.
overall_html: The passage argues that Hopi personal names carry real semantic and poetic content, referring to historical or ritual events through condensed images that only knowledge of clan structure and language can unpack. The author's purpose is to challenge two established European positions, Mill's view that proper names are meaningless marks and Lévi-Strauss's view that they are instruments of social classification, moving from those claims to the mechanics of Hopi ritual naming, then to a worked example in which beautifully ascended proves to describe a Badger clan procession up the mesa at Oraibi, and finally to the conclusion that such names are best read as oral poetry. The viewpoints in play are the European thinkers and the author who answers them.

Homing pigeons can be taken from their lofts and transported hundreds of kilometers in covered cages to unfamiliar sites and yet, when released, be able to choose fairly accurate homeward bearings within a minute and fly home. Aside from reading the minds of the experimenters (a possibility that has not escaped investigation), there are two basic explanations for the remarkable ability of pigeons to "home": the birds might keep track of their outward displacement (the system of many short-range species such as honeybees); or they might have some sense, known as a "map sense," that would permit them to construct an internal image of their environment and then "place" themselves with respect to home on some internalized coordinate system.

The first alternative seems unlikely. One possible model for such an inertial system might involve an internal magnetic compass to measure the directional leg of each journey. Birds transported to the release site wearing magnets or otherwise subjected to an artificial magnetic field, however, are only occasionally affected. Alternately, if pigeons measure their displacement by consciously keeping track of the direction and degree of acceleration and deceleration of the various turns, and timing the individual legs of the journey, simply transporting them in the dark, with constant rotations, or under complete anesthesia ought to impair or eliminate their ability to orient. These treatments, however, have no effect. Unfortunately, no one has yet performed the crucial experiment of transporting pigeons in total darkness, anesthetized, rotating, and with the magnetic field reversed all at the same time.

The other alternative, that pigeons have a "map sense," seems more promising, yet the nature of this sense remains mysterious. Papi has posited that the map sense is olfactory: that birds come to associate odors borne on the wind with the direction in which the wind is blowing, and so slowly build up an olfactory map of their surroundings. When transported to the release site, then, they only have to sniff the air en route and/or at the site to know the direction of home. Papi conducted a series of experiments showing that pigeons whose nostrils have been plugged are poorly oriented at release and home slowly.

One problem with the hypothesis is that Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips failed to detect any ability in pigeons to distinguish natural air (presumably laden with olfactory map information) from pure, filtered air. Papi's experimental results, moreover, admit of simpler, nonolfactory explanations. It seems likely that the behavior of nostril-plugged birds results from the distracting and traumatic nature of the experiment. When nasal tubes are used to bypass the olfactory chamber but allow for comfortable breathing, no disorientation is evident. Likewise, when the olfactory epithelium is sprayed with anesthetic to block smell-detection but not breathing, orientation is normal.
explanation_html:
The puzzle and the two candidate answers arrive together. Carry a homing pigeon hundreds of kilometers in a covered cage to a place it has never seen, release it, and within a minute it chooses a fairly accurate bearing for home. Setting aside the possibility that the birds read the experimenters' minds, which the author notes drily has actually been investigated, either a pigeon keeps track of its outward displacement as it travels, the method short-range species such as honeybees use, or it has a map sense, an internal image of its environment that lets it place itself relative to home on some internal coordinate system. The passage takes these in turn.

Displacement tracking is dismissed, and the reasoning is entirely experimental. If a bird measured the direction of each leg with an internal magnetic compass, then fitting it with magnets or subjecting it to an artificial magnetic field ought to disrupt it, and only occasionally does. If instead it consciously registered turns, accelerations, decelerations, and elapsed time, then carrying it in darkness, rotating it constantly, or anesthetizing it should impair its orientation, and none of these treatments has any effect. The author ends on an honest caveat rather than a flourish: nobody has yet combined darkness, anesthesia, rotation, and a reversed magnetic field in a single crucial experiment.

Attention shifts to the more promising option, though notice that the author calls the map sense mysterious rather than established. Papi supplies the leading version of it, an olfactory map: birds come to associate odors carried on the wind with the direction that wind blows from, gradually assembling a smell-based picture of their surroundings. On that account a displaced pigeon need only sample the air along the way or at the release site to work out where home lies. Papi's supporting work is a series of experiments showing that pigeons with plugged nostrils orient poorly on release and take a long time to get home.

The Author raises two difficulties, and the second does the real damage. First, Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips could detect no ability in pigeons even to distinguish natural air, supposedly loaded with olfactory map information, from pure filtered air. Second, Papi's own results admit of a simpler explanation having nothing to do with smell, since plugging a bird's nostrils is distracting and traumatic in itself. Two controls make that case: nasal tubes that bypass the olfactory chamber while allowing comfortable breathing produce no disorientation, and anesthetic sprayed on the olfactory epithelium to block smell without blocking breathing leaves orientation normal.
overall_html: The passage examines how homing pigeons navigate from unfamiliar release sites, weighs the two available explanations, and finds neither established: tracking the outward journey is ruled out by experiments in which magnets, darkness, rotation, and anesthesia leave the birds unaffected, while the more promising map sense remains poorly understood. The author's purpose is to evaluate competing hypotheses, and the second half concentrates on Papi's proposal that the map is built from odors carried on the wind, undercut both by the failure of Schmidt-Koenig and Phillips to show that pigeons distinguish natural from filtered air and by controls suggesting nostril-plugged birds are merely traumatized. The viewpoints are Papi's and the author's skeptical assessment of it.

Freud's essay on "The Uncanny" can be said to have defined, for our century, what literary criticism once called the Sublime. This apprehension of a beyond or of a dæmonic—a sense of transcendence—appears in literature or life, according to Freud, when we feel that something uncanny is being represented, or conjured up, or at least intimated. Freud locates the source of the uncanny in our tendency to believe in the "omnipotence of thought," that is, in the power of our own or of others' minds over the natural world. The uncanny is, thus, a return to animistic conceptions of the universe, and is produced by the psychic defense mechanisms Freud called repression.

It would have seemed likely for Freud to find his literary instances of the uncanny, or at least some of them, in fairy tales, since as much as any other fictions they seem to be connected with repressed desires and archaic forms of thought. But Freud specifically excluded fairy tales from the realm of the uncanny. "Who would be so bold," Freud asks, "as to call it an uncanny moment, for instance, when Snow White opens her eyes once more?" Why not? Because, he goes on to say, in those stories everything is possible, so nothing is incredible, and, therefore, no conflicts in the reader's judgment are provoked. Thus Freud, alas, found fairy tales to be unsuited to his own analysis.

However, the psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim, with a kind of wise innocence, has subjected fairy tales to very close, generally orthodox, and wholly reductive Freudian interpretations. Bettelheim's book, although written in apparent ignorance of the vast critical traditions of interpreting literary romance, is nevertheless a splendid achievement, brimming with useful ideas and insights into how young children read and understand.

Bruno Bettelheim's major therapeutic concern has been with autistic children, so inevitably his interpretive activity is directed against a child's tendency to withdraw defensively or abnormally. According to Bettelheim, a child's desperate isolation, loneliness, and inarticulate anxieties are addressed directly by fairy tales. By telling the child such stories themselves, parents strengthen the therapeutic effect of fairy tales, for in the telling, parents impart to the child their approval of the stories.

But why should fairy tales, in themselves, be therapeutic? Bettelheim's answer depends on the child's being an interpreter: "The fairy tale is therapeutic because children find their own solutions, through contemplating what the story seems to imply about their inner conflicts at this moment in their lives." Bettelheim proceeds on the basis of two complementary assumptions: that children will interpret a story benignly, for their own good; and that Freudian interpretations will yield an accurate account of children's interpretations. The child, questing for help, and the analyst, attempting to find helpful patterns in the stories, thus read alike, though in different vocabularies.
explanation_html:
The opening establishes Freud's claim and what it displaced. His essay on the uncanny, we are told, gave this century its version of what criticism once called the Sublime, a sense of something beyond or demonic, an apprehension of transcendence. For Freud that sensation arises in life or literature whenever something uncanny is represented, conjured, or merely intimated, and its source is a lingering belief in the omnipotence of thought, the notion that minds can act on the natural world. The uncanny is therefore a return to animistic ways of seeing the universe, produced by the defense mechanism Freud named repression.

Fairy tales look like Freud's obvious material, since they connect as directly as any fiction to repressed desires and archaic forms of thought, and The Author raises that expectation on purpose before reporting that Freud specifically excluded them. Freud's own instance is Snow White opening her eyes, which he declines to call an uncanny moment. His reason is that in such stories anything is possible, so nothing seems incredible and no conflict of judgment is provoked in the reader. The author's 'alas' is the tell here, marking the exclusion as a loss and opening the space the rest of the passage will fill.

Bettelheim steps into exactly that space, doing to fairy tales what Freud declined to do. His readings are close, orthodox in their Freudianism, and, in the author's own word, wholly reductive, and he seems unaware of the long critical tradition of interpreting literary romance. The verdict nonetheless comes out generous: the book is called a splendid achievement, full of useful ideas and insights into how young children read and understand. Hold on to that mixed assessment, since the praise and the reservation are being offered together, and the paragraphs following set out what Bettelheim actually argues.

Bettelheim's clinical history is offered as the key to his approach. He has worked chiefly with autistic children, so his interpretation is aimed against a child's tendency to withdraw defensively or abnormally. On his account fairy tales speak directly to a child's desperate isolation, loneliness, and anxieties the child cannot articulate. A second element of the therapy is easy to skim past, namely the telling itself: when parents tell these stories to the child, they convey their approval of them, and that approval strengthens whatever therapeutic work the stories do.

The question left hanging is pressed here, since it is not obvious why the stories themselves should heal anything. Bettelheim's answer turns the child into an interpreter, finding personal solutions by contemplating what a story seems to imply about the conflicts alive in that child at that moment. The author then exposes the two assumptions propping the answer up: that children will read a story benignly, for their own good, and that Freudian interpretation accurately captures what children make of it. The result is a neat symmetry, with child and analyst reading alike while speaking different vocabularies.
overall_html: The passage moves from Freud's account of the uncanny as a return of animistic belief in the omnipotence of thought, through his refusal to count fairy tales as uncanny on the grounds that their unlimited possibility provokes no conflict of judgment, to Bettelheim's thoroughly Freudian reading of that very material as therapy for children's unspoken anxieties. The author's purpose is expository and evaluative, presenting Bettelheim's work as a valuable if reductive achievement resting on two assumptions, that children interpret stories for their own good and that Freudian analysis captures what children actually do. The three positions to keep apart are Freud's, Bettelheim's, and the author's mixed assessment of both.

Until recently, many biologists believed that invertebrate "schools" were actually transient assemblages, brought together by wind, currents, waves, or common food sources. Jellyfish groupings, for example, cannot be described as schools—cohesive social units whose members are evenly spaced and face the same way. However, recent research has found numerous cases in which crustaceans and other invertebrates form schools as fish do. Schooling crustaceans such as krill regularly collect in such massive numbers that they provide abundant food for fish, seabirds, and whales.

Like schooling fish, invertebrates with sufficient mobility to school will swim in positions that are consistent relative to fellow school members, and are neither directly above nor directly below a neighbor. The internal structure of such a school changes little with external physical disruption but dramatically with the advent of a predator.

Since schooling is an active behavior, researchers assume that it must bring important benefits. True, schooling would appear to make animals more visible and attractive to predators. However, schooling leaves vast tracts of empty water, thereby reducing a predator's chances of picking up the school's trail. A large group maintains surveillance better than an individual can, and may discourage predation by appearing to be one massive animal. And although an attacking predator may eat some of the invertebrates, any individual school member has a good probability of escaping.

In addition to conferring passive advantages, schooling permits the use of more active defense mechanisms. When a predator is sighted, the school compacts, so that a predator's senses may be unable to resolve individuals, or so that the school can execute escape maneuvers, such as freezing to foil predators that hunt by detecting turbulence. If the predator attacks, the school may split, or may employ "flash expansion"—an explosive acceleration of animals away from the school's center. When large predators threaten the entire school, the school may attempt to avoid detection altogether or to reduce the density of the school at the point of attack; when small predators threaten the margins, school members may put on dazzling and confusing displays of synchronized swimming.

Schooling may also enable invertebrates to locate food—when one group member finds food, other members observe its behavior and flock to the food source. On the other hand, competition within the school for food may be intense: some mysids circle around to the back of the school in order to eat food particles surreptitiously. Schooling can facilitate the search for mates, but as a school's numbers rise, food may become locally scarce and females may produce smaller clutches of eggs, or adults may start to feed on the young. Thus, circumstances apparently dictate the optimal size of a school; if that size is exceeded, some of the animals will join another school.
explanation_html:
A superseded view opens the passage and gives the new findings something to correct. Many biologists once held that invertebrate groupings were only temporary assemblages, thrown together by wind, currents, waves, or a shared food source. Jellyfish clusters make the point, since they lack what defines a real school: a cohesive social unit whose members keep even spacing and face the same direction. Recent research overturned that assumption by finding crustaceans and other invertebrates that school just as fish do. Krill are the striking case, collecting in numbers large enough to feed fish, seabirds, and whales.

Two structural facts confirm that these are schools rather than crowds. Any invertebrate mobile enough to school keeps a consistent position relative to its fellow members, and never sits directly above or directly below a neighbor. More telling is how the arrangement answers to disturbance, since external physical disruption barely alters the internal structure while the appearance of a predator changes it dramatically. That contrast carries the paragraph's real point, because it shows the formation is actively maintained by the animals themselves rather than imposed on them by the water.

Since schooling takes active effort, researchers infer that it must bring important benefits, and the passive ones are weighed here against an obvious cost. Grouping does make animals more visible and more attractive to predators. Set against that, a school leaves vast stretches of water empty, so a predator is less likely to pick up its trail at all; a large group keeps watch better than any individual can; and the mass may deter attack by looking like one enormous animal. Even a successful attack takes only a few members, leaving any given individual good odds of escape.

Beyond those passive advantages the school can act, and the responses are matched to the threat. On sighting a predator the school compacts, either so the hunter's senses cannot resolve individual bodies or so the group can execute escape maneuvers, including freezing in place to defeat predators that hunt by detecting turbulence. Under attack it may split, or use flash expansion, an explosive acceleration of animals away from the center. Threat size shapes the tactic: large predators menacing the whole school prompt attempts to avoid detection or to thin the school where the attack lands, while small predators nibbling at the margins are met with dazzling synchronized swimming.

Costs and benefits are balanced in the closing paragraph, which arrives at a limit. Schooling helps with finding food, since one member's discovery is watched by the others, who flock to the source, though competition inside the group can be intense and some mysids circle to the back of the school to feed unobserved. Finding mates gets easier too. But as numbers rise, food grows locally scarce, females produce smaller clutches, and adults may begin feeding on the young. Circumstances therefore set an optimal size, and once it is exceeded some animals leave to join another school.
overall_html: The passage establishes that many invertebrates genuinely school, correcting the older belief that their groupings were transient assemblages produced by currents or shared food, and then explains what schooling does for them. The author's purpose is explanatory rather than argumentative, moving from that corrected assumption and the structural criteria that identify a true school, to the passive antipredator benefits of grouping, to the active defensive maneuvers such as compacting, splitting, and flash expansion, and finally to the mixed effects on feeding and reproduction that impose an optimal size beyond which members depart. No competing viewpoints are developed beyond the superseded belief noted at the start.

Many of us can conceive of penalties that seem disproportionate to the crimes they are intended to punish. A sentence of probation for a person convicted of a brutal murder is one example of such an imbalance. At the other extreme is a sentence of twenty years in prison for shoplifting. But what is the source of these commonsense intuitions about the appropriateness of punishments?

There are two main rationales for punishing criminals. The first rationale justifies a punishment in terms of its benefit to society. Society is said to benefit whenever the fear of punishment deters a person from committing a crime, or when a convicted criminal is removed from contact with society at large. The second rationale is that a punishment is justified by the severity of the crime, independent of any benefit to society. This rationale is controversial because some find it difficult to see how a punishment can be justified if it brings no societal benefit; without such benefit, punishment would appear to be little more than retribution. But from the retributivist point of view, the question to be asked about punishment is not whether it is beneficial, but whether it is just—that is, appropriate.

One problem with the social-benefit rationale is that it is possible that very harsh penalties even for minor offenses may have great benefit to society. For example, if shoplifters faced twenty-year jail sentences, shoplifting might be deterred. Yet something leads us to say that in such cases the penalty far outweighs the crime. That is, there appears to be something intuitively wrong, or unjust, about these punishments. And it would seem that this intuition can only find support in a retributive conception of punishment, under which certain types of punishments are inherently more appropriate than others. The notion of appropriateness is absent from the first rationale, which could conceivably allow for any sort of punishment as long as it benefits society. Retributive considerations, on the other hand, allow for proportionality between punishments and crimes. This is what fuels our notion of just (as opposed to beneficial) punishment.

However, it can be argued that our intuition of the injustice of an overly harsh punishment is based on our sense that such a punishment is more harmful to the criminal than beneficial to society; and, similarly, that our intuition that a punishment is just is based on our sense that this punishment fairly balances societal benefit against harm to the criminal. In this way the second rationale can be seen as grounded in the first and its retributive nature disappears. Thus it seems that even our so-called intuitive notions of the appropriateness of punishments have their basis in the concept of benefit.
explanation_html:
A puzzle is posed before any theory arrives. Most of us can recognize a penalty that fails to fit its crime, whether it is probation for a brutal murder at one extreme or twenty years in prison for shoplifting at the other. Nothing here resolves those reactions; the paragraph simply names them as commonsense intuitions and asks where they come from. Treat that closing question as the passage's organizing problem, since everything after it attempts to trace the intuitions to a source, and the answer does not settle until the passage's final sentence.

Two justifications for punishment are laid out, and the distinction between them governs everything that follows. The first grounds punishment in benefit to society, delivered when fear of punishment deters someone from offending or when a convicted criminal is removed from contact with the public. The second grounds it in the severity of the crime alone, with no reference to benefit, which is why it attracts controversy: punishment that helps no one starts to look like plain retribution. The Retributivists reply that the right question is not whether a punishment is beneficial but whether it is just, meaning appropriate to what was done.

Pressure now falls on the social-benefit rationale, and the shoplifting example does the work. Very harsh penalties for minor offenses might well serve society, since twenty-year sentences would presumably deter shoplifting, and yet the punishment still strikes us as wildly out of proportion. Where can that judgment come from? Only, it appears, from a retributive conception in which certain punishments are inherently more appropriate than others, because benefit by itself contains no notion of appropriateness and would license anything that worked. Proportionality between crime and penalty belongs to retribution, and proportionality is what our sense of just punishment rests on.

Everything just concluded is reversed here, so read the previous paragraph as a position being built up rather than endorsed. The counterargument reinterprets the same intuitions: judging a harsh punishment unjust may simply express a sense that it harms the criminal more than it helps society, and judging a punishment just may express a sense that it balances the two fairly. On that reading the retributive rationale turns out to rest on the social-benefit rationale, and its distinctly retributive character dissolves. The passage ends deliberately at this point, with even our intuitions about appropriateness traced back to benefit.
overall_html: The passage asks where commonsense intuitions about proportionate punishment come from, entertains the retributive answer, and concludes that those intuitions rest on the concept of social benefit after all. The author's purpose is to work through a philosophical problem rather than to survey a debate, opening with penalties that plainly do not fit their crimes, distinguishing the social-benefit rationale from the retributive one, arguing that only retribution seems able to explain why a harsh but effective deterrent feels unjust, and then overturning that argument by recasting the same intuitions as judgments about harm to the criminal weighed against benefit to society. The retributivist position and the author's own conclusion are the two to keep apart.

Despite the great differences among the cultures from which we spring, there is a trait shared by many Hispanic-American writers: the use of a European language, Spanish, transplanted to the Western hemisphere. This fact has marked our literature profoundly and radically. We Hispanic Americans who write in Spanish have attempted from the beginning to break the ties of dependency that linked us with the literature of Spain. We have pursued this goal of ever-increasing independence through a twofold movement, seeking to adopt the literary forms and styles in vogue in other European and North American literatures, and endeavoring to describe the nature of the United States and give voice to the Hispanic peoples who live there. These often conflicting tactics can be described as cosmopolitanism and nativism, respectively.

The opposition between cosmopolitanism and nativism has divided the Hispanic-American literary consciousness for generations. For example, the work of one Mexican-American novelist was praised by some Hispanic-American critics for its skillful adaptation of European literary techniques but criticized for its paucity of specifically Mexican-American settings or characters. On the other hand, a Cuban-American novel was admired by other Hispanic-American critics for the vivid portrayal of its characters' daily lives but faulted for its "roughness" of form and language.

Cosmopolitanism is the venturing forth into the public or mainstream culture; nativism, the return to the private or original culture. There are periods in which the outward-oriented sensibility predominates, and others in which tendencies toward self-absorption and introspection prevail. An example of the former was the rich period of the avant-garde between 1918 and 1930. This was a time of searching and experimentation, when successive European movements from expressionism to surrealism—movements that were also inspiring other North American writers—had a profound influence on many Hispanic-American poets and novelists. This phase, which produced a number of outstanding works of exceptional boldness of expression, was followed by another characterized by a return to our peoples and our colloquial dialects, by the creation of works less indebted to current trends in the mainstream culture. Throughout our history, a concern for novelty and experimentation has been followed by a return to origins.

We contemporary Hispanic-American writers who write in Spanish live somewhere between the European tradition and the reality of the Americas. Our roots may be European, but our horizon is the land and history of the Americas. This is the challenge that we confront each day: in order to appreciate the value of one's own culture, one must first venture forth into the public sphere; in order not to disappear into the mainstream, one must return to one's origins. In this way, we attempt to reconcile the opposing tendencies of cosmopolitanism and nativism.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a shared inheritance rather than a shared culture: Hispanic-American writers spring from very different places but write in Spanish, a European language carried across the Atlantic. The Author writes from inside this group, using 'we' throughout, and frames its whole history as a push to break literary dependence on Spain. Two tactics serve that single goal — importing the forms and styles in vogue in other European and North American literatures, and turning outward to describe the United States and give voice to the Hispanic peoples living there. Notice he names them at once as cosmopolitanism and nativism, and flags that they often conflict.

Two contrasting receptions show the split doing real work. Hispanic-American critics praised a Mexican-American novelist for skillfully adapting European literary techniques, then faulted the same work for offering few specifically Mexican-American settings or characters; other critics admired a Cuban-American novel for its vivid picture of daily life but objected to the roughness of its form and language. Watch the symmetry, because it is the point: each book earns credit on one axis and a penalty on the other. The author supplies these as illustration of a divided consciousness, not as a judgment about which side is right.

Here the two terms get proper definitions and a history. Cosmopolitanism is the venture outward into the public or mainstream culture; nativism is the return inward to the private or original one, and Hispanic-American writing has swung between them in alternating periods. The avant-garde years between 1918 and 1930 are the outward example, when European movements from expressionism to surrealism, which were also shaping North American writers, pressed hard on Hispanic-American poets and novelists and produced work of unusual boldness. The inward swing followed, rooted in the writers' own peoples and colloquial dialects. The rhythm is cyclical: experimentation, then a return to origins.

The close converts the opposition into a resolution rather than a choice. Contemporary Hispanic-American writers working in Spanish live between the European tradition and the reality of the Americas — European roots, but a horizon made of American land and history. The Author's own position is that the two tendencies require each other: you must venture into the public sphere before you can appreciate the value of your own culture, and you must return to your origins to avoid disappearing into the mainstream. That reciprocity, not a victory for either tendency, is how he claims Hispanic-American writers reconcile cosmopolitanism and nativism.
overall_html: The passage argues that Hispanic-American literature written in Spanish has been shaped by a long oscillation between cosmopolitanism, the outward turn toward European and North American forms, and nativism, the inward turn toward local peoples and speech, and that the two tendencies are finally complementary rather than exclusive. The Author's purpose is explanatory and reconciling: he identifies the shared linguistic inheritance and the drive for independence from Spain, illustrates the split through contrasting critical receptions, traces its alternating historical phases, then argues that each tendency depends on the other. The viewpoints to keep apart are The Author, writing as a member of the group, and the Hispanic-American critics whose divided verdicts dramatize the tension.

In the past, students of Renaissance women's education extolled the unprecedented intellectual liberty and equality available to these women, but recently scholars have presented a different view of Renaissance education and opportunity for women. Joan Gibson argues that despite more widespread education for privileged classes of women, Renaissance educational reforms also increased restrictions on women. Humanist education in the Renaissance was based on the classical division of the liberal arts into seven categories, including the three language arts: grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric. Although medieval monastic education, also based on the classical division, had stressed grammar and languages in preparation for a life devoted to meditation on religious literature, humanist education revived the classical emphasis on rhetoric—the art of persuasive and declamatory speech—in the context of training for public service in legal and political debate. All students began with elementary study of grammar and progressed to stylistics and literary criticism. But rhetorical training, which was increasingly undertaken only at the university level, could lead in different directions—to study of composition and oral expression or to study of persuasion, in conjunction with a dialectic concerned with broad principles of logic and argumentation. Male students routinely learned material through rhetorical, argumentative role-playing, and although many Renaissance authors expressed horror at their aggressive wrangling, such combativeness was thought still less appropriate for women, who were not supposed to need such preparation for public life.

Thus, humanist education for women encompassed literary grammatical studies in both classical and vernacular languages, while dialectic and rhetoric, the disciplines required for philosophy, politics, and the professions, were prohibited to women. Even princesses lacked instruction in political philosophy or the exercise of such public virtues as philanthropy. The prevailing attitude was that girls needed only a generalist education conducted in a family setting and directed toward private enjoyment and the eventual teaching of very young children. Unlike either dialectic or rhetoric, grammar training cast students in the role of an audience, striving to understand authors and teachers. Women were to form an audience, not seek one; for them, instruction in speaking was confined to books of courtesy.

The coupling of expanded linguistic and literary education for women with the lack of available social roles for educated women led to uneasy resolutions: exceptionally learned women were labelled as preternatural or essentially masculine, or were praised as virtuous only if they were too modest to make their accomplishments public. Some Italian humanist women gave fashionable oratorical performances, but these were ceremonial in nature rather than designed to influence public affairs. Renaissance women educated along humanist lines did not tend to write works of philosophy; instead they became most notable for literary achievements, particularly translations, poetry, and tales in the vernacular or correspondence and orations in Latin.
explanation_html:
The opening sets a revision against an older consensus. Earlier students of Renaissance women's education celebrated an unprecedented intellectual liberty and equality, while recent scholars, and Joan Gibson in particular, argue that the reforms which widened access also tightened restrictions. The rest of the paragraph supplies the machinery behind that claim. Humanist education kept the classical seven liberal arts, three of them language arts: grammar, dialectic and rhetoric. Where medieval monastic schooling had stressed grammar and languages as preparation for religious meditation, humanism revived rhetoric, the art of persuasive public speech, as training for legal and political service. Everyone began with grammar, but advanced rhetorical work, increasingly a university matter, ran on aggressive argumentative role-playing thought unsuitable for women, who were not expected to enter public life.

'Thus' signals consequence, and the consequence is a hard boundary. Women's humanist education stopped at literary and grammatical study in classical and vernacular languages, while dialectic and rhetoric — the disciplines that opened philosophy, politics and the professions — were closed to them. Even princesses went untaught in political philosophy or in public virtues such as philanthropy. The prevailing attitude held that a girl needed only a generalist education conducted at home, aimed at private enjoyment and at eventually teaching very young children. Keep hold of the distinction the paragraph turns on: grammar casts a student as an audience receiving an author, while dialectic and rhetoric train a student to command one.

The final paragraph traces what happens when learning outruns opportunity. The resolutions were uneasy, as Gibson's argument predicts: an exceptionally learned woman was labelled preternatural or essentially masculine, or was credited with virtue only if she stayed modest enough to keep her accomplishments out of public view. Some Italian humanist women did give fashionable oratorical performances, but those occasions were ceremonial and were not meant to influence public affairs. Output followed training. These women produced not philosophy, which required the forbidden disciplines, but translations, poetry and vernacular tales, along with correspondence and orations in Latin.
overall_html: The passage lays out the revisionist case, associated with Joan Gibson, that Renaissance humanist education broadened women's literary learning while simultaneously narrowing their prospects, because dialectic and rhetoric, the disciplines that led toward public life, were withheld from them. The author's purpose is expository rather than polemical, presenting the mechanism in three steps: the contrast between older celebratory scholarship and the newer view alongside the structure of humanist training, then the specific curricular boundary drawn around women, then the social awkwardness and the literary rather than philosophical achievements that followed. The viewpoints to keep separate are the earlier students of Renaissance women's education and the recent scholars represented by Joan Gibson.

Some Native American tribes have had difficulty establishing their land claims because the United States government did not recognize their status as tribes; therefore during the 1970s some Native Americans attempted to obtain such recognition through the medium of U.S. courts. In presenting these suits, Native Americans had to operate within a particular sphere of U.S. government procedure, that of its legal system, and their arguments were necessarily interpreted by the courts in terms the law could understand: e.g., through application of precedent or review of evidence. This process brought to light some of the differing perceptions and definitions that can exist between cultures whose systems of discourse are sometimes at variance.

In one instance, the entire legal dispute turned on whether the suing community—a group of Mashpee Wampanoag in the town of Mashpee, Massachusetts—constituted a tribe. The area had long been occupied by the Mashpee, who continued to have control over land use after the town's incorporation. But in the 1960s, after an influx of non-Mashpee people shifted the balance of political power in the town, the new residents were able to buy Mashpee-controlled land from the town and develop it for commercial or private use. The Mashpee's 1976 suit claimed that these lands were taken in violation of a statute prohibiting transfers of land from any tribe of Native Americans without federal approval. The town argued that the Mashpee were not a tribe in the sense intended by the statute and so were outside its protection. As a result, the Mashpee were required to demonstrate their status as a tribe according to a definition contained in an earlier ruling: a body of Native Americans "governing themselves under one leadership and inhabiting a particular territory."

The town claimed that the Mashpee were not self-governing and that they had no defined territory: the Mashpee could legally be self-governing, the town argued, only if they could show written documentation of such a system, and could legally inhabit territory only if they had precisely delineated its boundaries and possessed a deed to it. The Mashpee marshaled oral testimony against these claims, arguing that what the town perceived as a lack of evidence was simply information that an oral culture such as the Mashpee's would not have recorded in writing. In this instance, the disjunction between U.S. legal discourse and Mashpee culture—exemplified in the court's inability to "understand" the Mashpee's oral testimony as documentary evidence—rendered the suit unsuccessful. Similar claims have recently met with greater success, however, as U.S. courts have begun to acknowledge that the failure to accommodate differences in discourse between cultures can sometimes stand in the way of guaranteeing the fairness of legal decisions.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out a procedural trap. Some Native American tribes could not press land claims because the federal government did not recognize them as tribes, so during the 1970s several went to court to win that recognition. Going to court meant entering one particular arena of U.S. government procedure, where a claim only counts once it is restated in the terms the law handles — precedent, documentary evidence, formal definition. The Author is not simply narrating litigation; the thesis is that this translation exposes real differences in perception and definition between cultures whose systems of discourse do not line up.

The Mashpee case makes that abstract point concrete, and the whole dispute reduces to one question: were the Mashpee a tribe? They had long occupied the area and kept control over land use even after the town of Mashpee was incorporated. In the 1960s an influx of newcomers tipped the town's political balance, and those residents bought Mashpee-controlled land from the town and developed it. The 1976 suit invoked a statute barring transfers of tribal land without federal approval. The Town replied that the Mashpee were not a tribe in the statute's sense, which shifted the burden onto them to satisfy an earlier ruling's definition: self-governing under one leadership, inhabiting a particular territory.

The closing paragraph shows the definition being applied in a way the Mashpee could not meet. The Town read both halves of it as demands for paper, arguing that self-government required written documentation and that inhabiting territory required delineated boundaries and a deed. The Mashpee answered with oral testimony, pointing out that the missing records were exactly what an oral culture would never have produced in writing. Because the court could not treat that testimony as documentary evidence, the suit failed. The author closes on movement rather than defeat: similar claims have fared better as courts begin to recognize that ignoring differences in discourse can compromise fairness.
overall_html: The passage uses the Mashpee Wampanoag land suit to argue that when a claim from an oral culture is forced into the categories of the U.S. legal system, the mismatch between systems of discourse can itself determine the outcome. The author's purpose is illustrative and mildly critical, moving from the general problem of court-sought tribal recognition, to the specific dispute over whether the Mashpee met a legal definition of tribe, to the evidentiary demand for written proof that an oral culture could not supply, and finally to a note that courts have since grown more accommodating. The positions to track are the Mashpee, the Town, and the author's own framing of the clash as one of discourse rather than fact.
