Philosopher Denise Meyerson views the Critical Legal Studies (CLS) movement as seeking to debunk orthodox legal theory by exposing its contradictions. However, Meyerson argues that CLS proponents tend to see contradictions where none exist, and that CLS overrates the threat that conflict poses to orthodox legal theory.

According to Meyerson, CLS proponents hold that the existence of conflicting values in the law implies the absence of any uniquely right solution to legal cases. CLS argues that these conflicting values generate equally plausible but opposing answers to any given legal question, and, consequently, that the choice between the conflicting answers must necessarily be arbitrary or irrational. Meyerson denies that the existence of conflicting values makes a case irresolvable, and asserts that at least some such cases can be resolved by ranking the conflicting values. For example, a lawyer's obligation to preserve a client's confidences may entail harming other parties, thus violating moral principle. This conflict can be resolved if it can be shown that in certain cases the professional obligation overrides ordinary moral obligations.

In addition, says Meyerson, even when the two solutions are equally compelling, it does not follow that the choice between them must be irrational. On the contrary, a solution that is not rationally required need not be unreasonable. Meyerson concurs with another critic that instead of concentrating on the choice between two compelling alternatives, we should rather reflect on the difference between both of these answers on the one hand, and some utterly unreasonable answer on the other—such as deciding a property dispute on the basis of which claimant is louder. The acknowledgment that conflicting values can exist, then, does not have the far-reaching implications imputed by CLS; even if some answer to a problem is not the only answer, opting for it can still be reasonable.

Last, Meyerson takes issue with the CLS charge that legal formalism, the belief that there is a quasi-deductive method capable of giving solutions to problems of legal choice, requires objectivism, the belief that the legal process has moral authority. Meyerson claims that showing the law to be unambiguous does not demonstrate its legitimacy: consider a game in which participants compete to steal the item of highest value from a shop; while a person may easily identify the winner in terms of the rules, it does not follow that the person endorses the rules of the game. A CLS scholar might object that legal cases are unlike games, in that one cannot merely apply the rules without appealing to, and therefore endorsing, external considerations of purpose, policy, and value. But Meyerson replies that such considerations may be viewed as part of, not separate from, the rules of the game.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting up a dispute and naming the side it will follow. Meyerson reads the Critical Legal Studies movement as trying to discredit orthodox legal theory by exposing contradictions within it, then lodges two objections that structure everything after: CLS finds contradictions where none exist, and it overstates the damage conflict does to orthodox theory. Keep those two charges apart, since the paragraphs that follow work through her replies one at a time, and note that the passage is reporting her arguments rather than advancing the author's own.

The first reply attacks the inference CLS draws from conflicting values. On Meyerson's account, Critical Legal Studies holds that because law contains competing values, any legal question yields equally plausible opposing answers, so the choice between them can only be arbitrary or irrational. Her counter is that conflict does not automatically make a case unresolvable, because the competing values can often be ranked. The illustration is a lawyer's duty to preserve a client's confidences when doing so harms another party and offends ordinary morality; show that the professional obligation overrides the moral one in certain cases and the apparent contradiction dissolves.

The second reply concedes more ground and is the subtler move. Grant that two solutions really are equally compelling; it still does not follow that choosing between them is irrational, since an answer that reason does not require may nonetheless be reasonable. Agreeing with another critic, Meyerson recommends shifting the comparison: rather than weighing the two strong answers against each other, set both against a genuinely absurd one, such as settling a property dispute by which claimant is louder. The conclusion limits the damage instead of denying the premise, because admitting that values conflict does not carry the far-reaching implications CLS attaches to it.

The last reply targets a different CLS charge, that legal formalism, the belief that a quasi-deductive method can settle problems of legal choice, requires objectivism, the belief that the legal process has moral authority. Meyerson answers that showing the law to be unambiguous says nothing about its legitimacy, and offers a game in which players compete to steal the most valuable item from a shop: identifying the winner under the rules is not endorsing the rules. The paragraph then stages a CLS objection and her rejoinder, that if applying legal rules requires appeal to purpose, policy and value, those considerations can be treated as part of the rules rather than external to them.
overall_html: The passage presents Meyerson's case against the Critical Legal Studies claim that conflicting values in the law make legal decisions arbitrary and so undermine orthodox legal theory. The author's purpose is to report and lay out that critique, opening with her two charges against CLS and then giving three replies in turn: that conflicting values can often be ranked so the case resolves, that even a genuinely tied choice can be reasonable rather than rational, as the contrast with an absurd answer shows, and that establishing the law to be unambiguous is not the same as endorsing its moral authority. The two viewpoints tracked throughout are Meyerson's and CLS's, with the author staying outside the dispute.

While historians once propagated the myth that Africans who were brought to the New World as slaves contributed little of value but their labor, a recent study by Amelia Wallace Vernon helps to dispel this notion by showing that Africans introduced rice and the methods of cultivating it into what is now the United States in the early eighteenth century. She uncovered, for example, an 1876 document that details that in 1718 starving French settlers instructed the captain of a slave ship bound for Africa to trade for 400 Africans including some "who know how to cultivate rice." This discovery is especially compelling because the introduction of rice into what is now the United States had previously been attributed to French Acadians, who did not arrive until the 1760s.

Vernon interviewed elderly African Americans who helped her discover the locations where until about 1920 their forebears had cultivated rice. At the heart of Vernon's research is the question of why, in an economy dedicated to maximizing cotton production, African Americans grew rice. She proposes two intriguing answers, depending on whether the time is before or after the end of slavery. During the period of slavery, plantation owners also ate rice and therefore tolerated or demanded its "after-hours" cultivation on patches of land not suited to cotton. In addition, growing the rice gave the slaves some relief from a system of regimented labor under a field supervisor, in that they were left alone to work independently.

After the abolition of slavery, however, rice cultivation is more difficult to explain: African Americans had acquired a preference for eating corn, there was no market for the small amounts of rice they produced, and under the tenant system—in which farmers surrendered a portion of their crops to the owners of the land they farmed—owners wanted only cotton as payment. The labor required to transform unused land to productive ground would thus seem completely out of proportion to the reward—except that, according to Vernon, the transforming of the land itself was the point.

Vernon suggests that these African Americans did not transform the land as a means to an end, but rather as an end in itself. In other words, they did not transform the land in order to grow rice—for the resulting rice was scarcely worth the effort required to clear the land—but instead transformed the land because they viewed land as an extension of self and home and so wished to nurture it and make it their own. In addition to this cultural explanation, Vernon speculates that rice cultivation might also have been a political act, a next step after the emancipation of the slaves: the symbolic claiming of plantation land that the U.S. government had promised but failed to parcel off and deed to newly freed African Americans.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting new research against an old myth. Historians once claimed that Africans brought to the New World as slaves contributed nothing of value beyond their labor, and Vernon's study undercuts that by showing they introduced rice and its cultivation methods into what is now the United States in the early eighteenth century. Her key documentation is an 1876 record describing starving French settlers in 1718 instructing a slave-ship captain to trade for 400 Africans, some of whom knew how to grow rice. Notice why the find carries such force: credit for introducing rice had gone to French Acadians, who did not arrive until the 1760s.

Vernon's method and her central puzzle come next. She interviewed elderly African Americans to locate the places where their forebears had grown rice up to about 1920, which sets up the question driving the rest of the passage: in an economy built around maximizing cotton, why grow rice at all? Her answer divides by period. Under slavery, plantation owners ate rice themselves and so tolerated or demanded after-hours cultivation on patches unsuited to cotton. A second and subtler benefit accrued to the growers, since tending rice released them from regimented labor under a field supervisor and let them work independently.

After abolition the puzzle sharpens, and the paragraph is built to make the behavior look irrational before rescuing it. Every practical incentive had disappeared: these farmers now preferred corn, no market existed for their small harvests, and under the tenant system landowners would take only cotton as payment. Turning unused land into productive ground was punishing work for almost no return. Watch the pivot in the closing clause, where Vernon proposes that the labor was not out of proportion to the reward because transforming the land was itself the point.

The closing paragraph unpacks that reversal. On Vernon's reading, these African Americans treated the transformation of land as an end rather than a means; the rice scarcely justified the clearing, so the clearing must have carried its own value, grounded in a view of land as an extension of self and home, something to nurture and make one's own. She then adds a second layer beside the cultural one, suggesting the work may also have been political, a symbolic claiming of plantation land the federal government had promised to newly freed African Americans and never delivered. Note that she offers this as speculation rather than established fact.
overall_html: The passage presents Vernon's research as a corrective to the old claim that enslaved Africans contributed nothing but their labor, showing that they brought rice cultivation to what is now the United States and that their descendants kept growing it long after any economic reason for doing so had vanished. The author's purpose is to report and endorse her findings, moving from the documentary evidence that overturns the credit long given to French Acadians, to her explanations for rice growing under slavery, to the sharper puzzle of the period after abolition, and finally to her cultural and political readings of land transformation as an end in itself. Vernon's account stands against the Historians who propagated the older myth.

Of the more than one thousand people who published memoirs of the French Revolution of 1789, about eighty were women. And of these eighty women memoirists, two thirds were members of the upper class, a proportion that might be attributed solely to privilege—at the time of the Revolution, only half of all French citizens could read, and only members of the upper class were able to write easily. But there were also political reasons. Most of the memoirs were published decades after the Revolution, during the restored monarchy that came to power in 1815. Those written by royalists, who opposed the Revolution, were published under the monarchy's aegis; in contrast, republican memoirists, who supported the Revolution, risked political sanctions against their work.

Because the memoirs were written so long after the events they describe, some historians question their reliability. Certainly, memory is subject to the loss or confusion of facts and, more to the point in these partisan accounts, to the distortions of a mind intent on preserving its particular picture of the past. But other scholars have shown that close inspection of these documents resolves such doubts on two scores. First, for major public happenings, there are often multiple accounts, allowing for cross-verification. Second, regarding the truth of personal events known only to the author, more subjective guidelines must be used: Are there internal verifications within a text that suggest the author is describing a plausible sequence of events, and acting in accord with what is known of the writer's character? Or is the narrative voice so pervaded by self-justifications that it forfeits credibility?

Denis Bertholet, in a study of nineteenth-century French autobiography, states that the women memoirists of this period defined themselves "in relationship to their sex"—i.e., they conformed to socially prescribed feminine roles of the time, fulfilling obligations as daughters, wives, or mothers. Nonetheless, instances of social activism by women abounded during the Revolution. On the whole, women's memoirs during this period exhibit a variety of personalities and experiences, and describe how women participated, individually and collectively, in the events of the Revolution. For example, the imprisoned royalist Madame de La Villirouët details how she managed to liberate not only herself but her co-prisoners through an epistolary campaign, and how she subsequently saved her husband's life by pleading his case in court. In addition, in both royalist and republican camps, several women defied the ban against women serving as soldiers and bore arms for their causes. Bertholet's study attests to the credibility of these accounts on both factual and subjective grounds, making the memoirs written by women particularly significant because they embody a clearly feminist mode of discourse and experience that one would not expect to find until the French Feminist movement more than a century later.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with numbers and then explains them. Of more than a thousand memoirs of the 1789 Revolution, roughly eighty were written by women, and two thirds of those women came from the upper class. Privilege accounts for part of that, since only half of French citizens could read and writing easily was an upper-class accomplishment, but the author insists on a political factor as well. Most of these memoirs appeared decades later, under the monarchy restored in 1815, which meant royalist authors who had opposed the Revolution published with official approval while republican authors who had supported it risked sanctions against their work.

A dispute over reliability follows. Because so much time separated the writing from the events described, Some Historians doubt these memoirs, and the author grants real grounds for doubt, since memory loses and confuses facts and, in partisan accounts especially, bends toward preserving a favored picture of the past. Other Scholars answer that close inspection resolves the doubts in two ways. Major public events are often covered in several memoirs, so accounts can be cross-verified. Private events known only to the writer call for subjective tests instead: does the narrative hang together plausibly and match what is known of the author's character, or is it so saturated with self-justification that credibility is forfeited?

The final paragraph applies those tests and delivers the payoff. Bertholet finds that women memoirists of the period defined themselves in relation to their sex, fulfilling the prescribed roles of daughter, wife or mother. The author qualifies that immediately, pointing to abundant social activism and to memoirs displaying varied personalities and real participation in events: Madame de La Villirouet, imprisoned as a royalist, freed herself and her fellow prisoners through a letter-writing campaign and then saved her husband by pleading his case in court, while women in both camps defied the ban on female soldiers and bore arms. Because Bertholet's study supports their credibility, the author concludes these memoirs embody a feminist discourse arriving a century early.
overall_html: The passage argues that the memoirs of the French Revolution written by women are both credible and historically significant, embodying a feminist mode of discourse and experience that would not otherwise appear until the French feminist movement more than a century later. The author's purpose is to defend these documents and establish their importance, opening with an account of who wrote them and the mixed social and political pressures that shaped the sample, then weighing the doubts raised by Some Historians against the verification methods proposed by Other Scholars, and finally drawing on Bertholet along with examples of women's activism to show what the memoirs actually record. The concluding judgment is the author's own.

The paintings of Romare Bearden (1914–1988) represent a double triumph. At the same time that Bearden's work reflects a lifelong commitment to perfecting the innovative painting techniques he pioneered, it also reveals an artist engaged in a search for ways to explore the varieties of African-American experience.

By presenting scene, character, and atmosphere using a unique layered and fragmented style that combines elements of painting with elements of collage, Bearden suggested some of the ways in which commonplace subjects could be forced to undergo a metamorphosis when filtered through the techniques available to the resourceful artist. Bearden knew that regardless of individual painters' personal histories, tastes, or points of view, they must pay their craft the respect of approaching it through an acute awareness of the resources and limitations of the form to which they have dedicated their creative energies.

But how did Bearden, so passionately dedicated to solving the more advanced problems of his painting technique, also succeed so well at portraying the realities of African-American life? During the Great Depression of the 1930s, Bearden painted scenes of the hardships of the period; the work was powerful, the scenes grim and brooding. Through his depiction of the unemployed in New York's Harlem he was able to move beyond the usual "protest painting" of the period to reveal instances of individual human suffering. His human figures, placed in abstract yet mysteriously familiar urban settings, managed to express the complex social reality lying beyond the borders of the canvas without compromising their integrity as elements in an artistic composition. Another important element of Bearden's compositions was his use of muted colors, such as dark blues and purples, to suggest moods of melancholy or despair. While functioning as part of the overall design, these colors also served as symbols of the psychological effects of debilitating social processes.

During the same period, he also painted happier scenes—depictions of religious ceremony, musical performance, and family life—and instilled them with the same vividness that he applied to his scenes of suffering. Bearden sought in his work to reveal in all its fullness a world long hidden by the clichés of sociology and rendered cloudy by the simplifications of journalism and documentary photography. Where any number of painters have tried to project the "prose" of Harlem, Bearden concentrated on releasing its poetry—its family rituals and its ceremonies of affirmation and celebration. His work insists that we truly see the African-American experience in depth, using the fresh light of his creative vision. Through an act of artistic will, he created strange visual harmonies out of the mosaic of the African-American experience, and in doing so reflected the multiple rhythms, textures, and mysteries of life.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a thesis framed as a paradox to be explained. Bearden's paintings represent a double triumph, because he spent a lifetime perfecting the painting techniques he pioneered while also using the work to explore the varieties of African-American experience. Treat the author as a Profile from the start, since the tone is evaluative and admiring rather than neutral. The word to hold on to is double, because those two commitments, technical innovation and social truth, are ones a reader might expect to pull against each other, and the rest of the passage exists to show how Bearden held them together.

Technique gets a paragraph of its own. Bearden presented scene, character and atmosphere through a layered, fragmented manner that fused painting with collage, and the author's point about it is not decorative: the method showed how commonplace subjects can be transformed once a resourceful artist puts them through the right procedures. The paragraph then generalizes into a principle attributed to Bearden, that whatever a painter's personal history, taste or point of view, respecting the craft means working from an acute awareness of what the chosen form makes possible and what it forbids. Notice that only the first half of the double triumph is handled here.

The second half arrives as an explicit question, which is worth registering as a structural signal: how did an artist so absorbed in technical problems also portray African-American life so convincingly? The Depression paintings supply the answer. Working with grim, brooding scenes of hardship and of Harlem's unemployed, Bearden pushed past the era's conventional protest painting to individual human suffering, placing figures in urban settings at once abstract and mysteriously familiar so they carried a social reality beyond the canvas without ceasing to function as composition. His muted dark blues and purples do the same double duty, serving the design while symbolizing the psychological toll of debilitating social processes.

The closing paragraph completes the portrait by widening the subject matter. Alongside suffering Bearden painted religious ceremony, musical performance and family life with the same vividness, and the author's assessment of what that accomplished is the passage's culminating claim. Sociological cliche, journalistic simplification and documentary photography had obscured this world, and Bearden set out to reveal it whole. The contrast the author draws is the memorable one: where other painters projected the prose of Harlem, Bearden released its poetry, its family rituals and ceremonies of affirmation, building strange visual harmonies out of the mosaic of African-American experience.
overall_html: The passage celebrates Romare Bearden for achieving two things at once, the perfecting of an innovative layered style that combines painting and collage and the honest rendering of African-American life in its full range. The author's purpose is appreciative and explanatory, first stating that double achievement, then examining his technique and the craft principle behind it, then answering how so technically preoccupied an artist conveyed social reality with such force through his Depression-era scenes and his symbolic use of muted color, and finally turning to the depictions of ceremony and family life in which he released what the author calls the poetry of Harlem. The only viewpoint developed is the author's own admiring assessment.

Philosophers of science have long been uneasy with biology, preferring instead to focus on physics. At the heart of this preference is a mistrust of uncertainty. Science is supposed to be the study of what is true everywhere and for all times, and the phenomena of science are supposed to be repeatable, arising from universal laws, rather than historically contingent. After all, if something pops up only on occasional Tuesdays or Thursdays, it is not classified as science but as history. Philosophers of science have thus been fascinated with the fact that elephants and mice would fall at the same rate if dropped from the Tower of Pisa, but not much interested in how elephants and mice got to be such different sizes in the first place.

Philosophers of science have not been alone in claiming that science must consist of universal laws. Some evolutionary biologists have also acceded to the general intellectual disdain for the merely particular and tried to emulate physicists, constructing their science as a set of universal laws. In formulating the notion of a universal "struggle for existence" that is the engine of biological history or in asserting that virtually all DNA evolves at a constant clocklike rate, they have attempted to find their own versions of the law of gravity. Recently, however, some biologists have questioned whether biological history is really the necessary unfolding of universal laws of life, and they have raised the possibility that historical contingency is an integral factor in biology.

To illustrate the difference between biologists favoring universal, deterministic laws of evolutionary development and those leaving room for historical contingency, consider two favorite statements of philosophers (both of which appear, at first sight, to be universal assertions): "All planets move in ellipses" and "All swans are white." The former is truly universal because it applies not only to those planets that actually do exist, but also to those that could exist—for the shape of planetary orbits is a necessary consequence of the laws governing the motion of objects in a gravitational field.

Biological determinists would say that "All swans are white" is universal in the same way, since, if all swans were white, it would be because the laws of natural selection make it impossible for swans to be otherwise: natural selection favors those characteristics that increase the average rate of offspring production, and so traits that maximize flexibility and the ability to manipulate nature will eventually appear. Nondeterminist biologists would deny this, saying that "swans" is merely the name of a finite collection of historical objects that may happen all to be white, but not of necessity. The history of evolutionary theory has been the history of the struggle between these two views of swans.
explanation_html:
Start with the prejudice the passage is diagnosing. The Philosophers of Science have preferred physics to biology because they mistrust uncertainty: on their conception, science studies what holds everywhere and always, produced by universal laws rather than by the accidents of history. Anything that turns up only now and then gets filed as history, not science. The elephant-and-mouse image makes the split concrete — the rate at which the two would fall is a law-governed fact and therefore interesting, while how they came to differ in size is a historical question and therefore ignored. Notice that the author is describing this attitude, not yet endorsing it.

The complaint then widens. The prestige of physics has pulled some evolutionary biologists along too, and The Determinists among them have tried to build biology as a set of universal laws — a single struggle for existence driving all biological history, or DNA evolving at a constant clocklike rate. Those, the author suggests, are attempts at a biological law of gravity. The paragraph turns on 'Recently, however': The Nondeterminists have begun asking whether biological history really is the necessary unfolding of universal laws, and have raised historical contingency as an integral factor. The two camps set up here are what the rest of the passage contrasts.

To make that disagreement concrete, the author sets two sentences side by side that both look like universal claims: all planets move in ellipses, and all swans are white. Only the planetary case gets settled here. It counts as genuinely universal because it governs not merely the planets that happen to exist but any planet that could exist, an elliptical orbit being a necessary consequence of how objects move in a gravitational field. The swan sentence is deliberately left hanging, since whether it works the same way is precisely what the two camps disagree about. Read this paragraph as machinery for the argument rather than as an argument itself.

The swan case is where the split becomes explicit. The Determinists read 'all swans are white' as universal in the planetary sense: if every swan is white, that is because natural selection could not have permitted otherwise, favoring whatever raises the average rate of offspring production, so that traits maximizing flexibility and the ability to manipulate nature must eventually appear. The Nondeterminists reject the necessity — 'swans' merely names a finite collection of historical objects that happen to share a color. The last sentence tells you what everything has been building toward: the history of evolutionary theory is itself the struggle between these two readings of the swan.
overall_html: The passage uses a philosophical prejudice against biology — the demand that real science consist of universal, repeatable laws rather than historical accident — to frame a live dispute inside biology itself, between determinists who treat evolutionary outcomes as necessary consequences of natural selection and nondeterminists who treat them as contingent historical facts. The author's purpose is expository: to explain why the dispute exists and then to sharpen it, moving from the philosophers' bias, to the biologists who absorbed it, to a two-sentence test case whose planetary half is uncontroversial and whose swan half is not. The viewpoints to keep apart are The Philosophers of Science, The Determinists and The Nondeterminists.

Ronald Dworkin argues that judges are in danger of uncritically embracing an erroneous theory known as legal positivism because they think the only alternative is a theory that they (and Dworkin) see as clearly unacceptable—natural law. The latter theory holds that judges ought to interpret the law by consulting their own moral convictions, even if this means ignoring the letter of the law and the legal precedents for its interpretation. Dworkin regards this as an impermissible form of judicial activism that arrogates to judges powers properly reserved for legislators.

Legal positivism, the more popular of the two theories, holds that law and morality are wholly distinct. The meaning of the law rests on social convention in the same way as does the meaning of a word. Dworkin's view is that legal positivists regard disagreement among jurists as legitimate only if it arises over what the underlying convention is, and it is to be resolved by registering a consensus, not by deciding what is morally right. In the same way, disagreement about the meaning of a word is settled by determining how people actually use it, and not by deciding what it ought to mean. Where there is no consensus, there is no legal fact of the matter. The judge's interpretive role is limited to discerning this consensus, or the absence thereof.

According to Dworkin, this account is incompatible with the actual practice of judges and lawyers, who act as if there is a fact of the matter even in cases where there is no consensus. The theory he proposes seeks to validate this practice without falling into what Dworkin correctly sees as the error of natural law theory. It represents a kind of middle ground between the latter and legal positivism. Dworkin stresses the fact that there is an internal logic to a society's laws and the general principles they typically embody. An interpretation that conforms to these principles may be correct even if it is not supported by a consensus. Since these general principles may involve such moral concepts as justice and fairness, judges may be called upon to consult their own moral intuitions in arriving at an interpretation. But this is not to say that judges are free to impose their own morality at will, without regard to the internal logic of the laws.

The positivist's mistake, as Dworkin points out, is assuming that the meaning of the law can only consist in what people think it means, whether these people be the original authors of the law or a majority of the interpreter's peers. Once we realize, as Dworkin does, that the law has an internal logic of its own that constrains interpretation, we open up the possibility of improving upon the interpretations not only of our contemporaries but of the original authors.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out a forced choice and the danger in it. Dworkin claims judges drift into legal positivism uncritically, because they assume the only other option is natural law, a theory that they and Dworkin alike reject. Get the content of that rejected theory straight: natural law tells judges to interpret by consulting their own moral convictions, even where doing so overrides the letter of the law and the precedents built around it. Dworkin's objection is institutional rather than moral — that is judicial activism, judges taking on powers properly belonging to legislators. The passage is setting up a two-option trap it will later escape.

Now the more popular option gets spelled out. The Legal Positivists separate law from morality completely, treating a law's meaning as resting on social convention exactly as a word's meaning does. On Dworkin's reading of them, jurists may legitimately disagree only about what the underlying convention actually is, and such disagreement is settled by registering consensus, never by working out what is morally right — much as you settle a word's meaning by observing how people use it rather than by deciding what it ought to mean. The consequence is severe: where there is no consensus there is no legal fact of the matter, and the judge can only report its absence.

Objection and alternative arrive together. Dworkin holds that judges and lawyers actually behave as though there is a fact of the matter even without consensus, which positivism cannot accommodate, and his own theory is built to vindicate that practice while avoiding natural law's error — notice the author calls that error real, siding with Dworkin rather than merely reporting him. The middle ground rests on the claim that a society's laws carry an internal logic and embody general principles, so an interpretation faithful to those principles can be correct with no consensus behind it. Since principles like justice and fairness are moral, judges may consult moral intuition, but bounded by that internal logic rather than free to impose their own views.

The close names the single error underneath positivism: assuming a law can only mean what people think it means, whether those people are the ones who wrote it or a majority of the interpreter's peers. Drop that assumption, grant the law an internal logic that constrains how it can be read, and something new becomes possible — an interpretation can improve not only on what contemporaries say but on what the original authors themselves understood. The author's voice is fully aligned with Dworkin here, so treat this as a shared conclusion rather than a neutral summary of someone else's position.
overall_html: The passage presents Dworkin's case that judges face a false choice between natural law, which frees them to substitute personal morality for the letter of the law, and legal positivism, which reduces legal meaning to social convention and leaves no fact of the matter wherever consensus fails. Dworkin's alternative is a middle ground: a society's laws carry an internal logic and general principles that can make an interpretation correct without consensus, licensing a constrained appeal to moral intuition. The structure runs from the false dilemma, to positivism stated, to Dworkin's alternative, to the mistake it corrects, and the author's purpose is expository but plainly endorsing, so keep Dworkin, The Legal Positivists and natural law theory distinct while noting where the author stands.

Traditionally, members of a community such as a town or neighborhood share a common location and a sense of necessary interdependence that includes, for example, mutual respect and emotional support. But as modern societies grow more technological and sometimes more alienating, people tend to spend less time in the kinds of interactions that their communities require in order to thrive. Meanwhile, technology has made it possible for individuals to interact via personal computer with others who are geographically distant. Advocates claim that these computer conferences, in which large numbers of participants communicate by typing comments that are immediately read by other participants and responding immediately to those comments they read, function as communities that can substitute for traditional interactions with neighbors.

What are the characteristics that advocates claim allow computer conferences to function as communities? For one, participants often share common interests or concerns; conferences are frequently organized around specific topics such as music or parenting. Second, because these conferences are conversations, participants have adopted certain conventions in recognition of the importance of respecting each others' sensibilities. Abbreviations are used to convey commonly expressed sentiments of courtesy such as "pardon me for cutting in" ("pmfci") or "in my humble opinion" ("imho"). Because a humorous tone can be difficult to communicate in writing, participants will often end an intentionally humorous comment with a set of characters that, when looked at sideways, resembles a smiling or winking face. Typing messages entirely in capital letters is avoided, because its tendency to demand the attention of a reader's eye is considered the computer equivalent of shouting. These conventions, advocates claim, constitute a form of etiquette, and with this etiquette as a foundation, people often form genuine, trusting relationships, even offering advice and support during personal crises such as illness or the loss of a loved one.

But while it is true that conferences can be both respectful and supportive, they nonetheless fall short of communities. For example, conferences discriminate along educational and economic lines because participation requires a basic knowledge of computers and the ability to afford access to conferences. Further, while advocates claim that a shared interest makes computer conferences similar to traditional communities—insofar as the shared interest is analogous to a traditional community's shared location—this analogy simply does not work. Conference participants are a self-selecting group; they are drawn together by their shared interest in the topic of the conference. Actual communities, on the other hand, are "nonintentional": the people who inhabit towns or neighborhoods are thus more likely to exhibit genuine diversity—of age, career, or personal interests—than are conference participants. It might be easier to find common ground in a computer conference than in today's communities, but in so doing it would be unfortunate if conference participants cut themselves off further from valuable interactions in their own towns or neighborhoods.
explanation_html:
The setup is a definition plus a proposed substitute for it. A traditional community combines a shared location with a sense of necessary interdependence — mutual respect and emotional support among people who rely on one another. Modern life pulls against that: as societies grow more technological and more alienating, people put in less of the interaction their communities need in order to thrive. Into that gap comes the computer conference, where participants type comments that others read and answer immediately, however far apart they live. Note whose claim closes the paragraph. The Advocates, not the author, are the ones asserting that such conferences function as communities and can stand in for dealings with neighbors.

A question opens the paragraph, and the whole of it answers on the advocates' behalf rather than in the author's own voice. Two features are offered. Participants share interests, since conferences form around topics such as music or parenting. And because the exchanges are conversations, participants have developed conventions that protect each other's sensibilities — abbreviations standing in for courtesies, sideways faces marking a joke that plain text would flatten, and a ban on all-capital typing because it grabs the eye the way shouting grabs the ear. The advocates call this an etiquette and build a stronger claim on it: that genuine, trusting relationships grow from it, extending to advice and support through illness or bereavement. No objection has been raised yet, so read this as the strongest version of the position about to be tested.

'But' marks the turn, and the author now speaks directly: conferences may be respectful and supportive and still fall short of being communities. Two objections do the work. The first concerns access, since participation requires computer knowledge and the money to pay for it, so conferences sort people along educational and economic lines. The second dismantles the advocates' central analogy between a shared interest and a shared location. Conference participants select themselves by their interest in the topic, whereas actual communities are nonintentional, which is why the people in a town vary more widely in age, career and personal interests than conference participants do. The ending is a warning rather than a flat condemnation: common ground may be easier to find online, but it would be a loss if finding it there pulled people further from their own neighborhoods.
overall_html: Against advocates who present computer conferences as workable substitutes for traditional communities, the author concedes the courtesy and mutual support such conferences display but denies that they qualify as communities, since access is filtered by education and money and, more fundamentally, since a self-selected shared interest is not the equivalent of a nonintentional shared location and yields far less real diversity. The purpose is evaluative: the passage defines community, states The Advocates' case at its strongest across a full paragraph, then rebuts the core analogy and warns that easy online common ground may draw people further from their neighborhoods. Keep the advocates' claims separate from the author's own assessment, which arrives only at the end.

In Intellectual Culture in Elizabethan and Jacobean England, J. W. Binns asserts that the drama of Shakespeare, the verse of Marlowe, and the prose of Sidney—all of whom wrote in English—do not alone represent the high culture of Renaissance (roughly sixteenth- and seventeenth-century) England. Latin, the language of ancient Rome, continued during this period to be the dominant form of expression for English intellectuals, and works of law, theology, and science written in Latin were, according to Binns, among the highest achievements of the Renaissance. However, because many academic specializations do not overlap, many texts central to an interpretation of early modern English culture have gone unexamined. Even the most learned students of Renaissance Latin generally confine themselves to humanistic and literary writings in Latin. According to Binns, these language specialists edit and analyze poems and orations, but leave works of theology and science, law and medicine—the very works that revolutionized Western thought—to "specialists" in those fields, historians of science, for example, who lack philological training. The intellectual historian can find ample guidance when reading the Latin poetry of Milton, but little or none when confronting the more alien and difficult terminology, syntax, and content of the scientist Newton.

Intellectual historians of Renaissance England, by contrast with Latin language specialists, have surveyed in great detail the historical, cosmological, and theological battles of the day, but too often they have done so on the basis of texts written in or translated into English. Binns argues that these scholars treat the English-language writings of Renaissance England as an autonomous and coherent whole, underestimating the influence on English writers of their counterparts on the European Continent. In so doing they ignore the fact that English intellectuals were educated in schools and universities where they spoke and wrote Latin, and inhabited as adults an intellectual world in which what happened abroad and was recorded in Latin was of great importance. Writers traditionally considered characteristically English and modern were steeped in Latin literature and in the esoteric concerns of late Renaissance humanism (the rediscovery and study of ancient Latin and Greek texts), and many Latin works by Continental humanists that were not translated at the time into any modern language became the bases of classic English works of literature and scholarship.

These limitations are understandable. No modern classicist is trained to deal with the range of problems posed by a difficult piece of late Renaissance science; few students of English intellectual history are trained to read the sort of Latin in which such works were written. Yet the result of each side's inability to cross boundaries has been that each presents a distorted reading of the intellectual culture of Renaissance England.
explanation_html:
The passage runs on a book's argument, so track Binns as the source of nearly every claim. His first point is that the famous English-language writers — Shakespeare's drama, Marlowe's verse, Sidney's prose — do not by themselves constitute the high culture of Renaissance England, because Latin remained the dominant medium for English intellectuals and the Latin works of law, theology and science rank among the period's highest achievements. The rest explains why those works go unread, and the reason is disciplinary rather than intellectual. The Latin Specialists stay with humanistic and literary material, editing poems and orations while handing theology, science, law and medicine to subject specialists such as historians of science, who lack philological training. Hence the imbalance: ample guidance for Milton's Latin poetry, almost none for Newton's.

'By contrast' introduces the other half of the problem. The Intellectual Historians have covered the era's historical, cosmological and theological disputes in great detail, but they work from texts written in English or translated into it. On Binns's account this leads them to treat English-language writing as a self-contained, coherent body and so to underrate how much Continental work shaped it. The correction is biographical as much as textual: English intellectuals were schooled in Latin, spoke and wrote it, and lived in an adult world where what happened abroad and was recorded in Latin mattered. Writers taken as characteristically English and modern were steeped in Latin literature and in late Renaissance humanism, and Continental Latin works untranslated at the time became the bases of classic English books.

The close does two things at once. It first excuses both camps: no classicist is trained to unpick a difficult piece of late Renaissance science, and hardly any student of English intellectual history can read the Latin such science was written in, so the gaps follow from how training works rather than from carelessness. Then comes the reversal signalled by 'Yet'. Understandable or not, neither side crosses the boundary, and the consequence is that each produces a distorted reading of Renaissance English intellectual culture. Notice that the verdict falls on both groups equally, which is the balance the whole passage has been arranging.
overall_html: Summarizing Binns, the passage argues that the intellectual culture of Renaissance England cannot be understood from its English-language literature alone, because Latin remained the working language of law, theology and science and tied English writers to the Continent. Its purpose is diagnostic: it identifies a division of academic labor in which The Latin Specialists read only humanistic and literary texts while The Intellectual Historians read only English ones, so the revolutionary Latin works fall between the two. The structure moves from one camp's blind spot to the other's, concedes that the training gap makes both understandable, then delivers the verdict that each side's picture of the period comes out distorted.

Discussions of how hormones influence behavior have generally been limited to the effects of gonadal hormones on reproductive behavior and have emphasized the parsimonious arrangement whereby the same hormones involved in the biology of reproduction also influence sexual behavior. It has now become clear, however, that other hormones, in addition to their recognized influence on biological functions, can affect behavior. Specifically, peptide and steroid hormones involved in maintaining the physiological balance, or homeostasis, of body fluids also appear to play an important role in the control of water and salt consumption. The phenomenon of homeostasis in animals depends on various mechanisms that promote stability within the organism despite an inconstant external environment; the homeostasis of body fluids, whereby the osmolality (the concentration of solutes) of blood plasma is closely regulated, is achieved primarily through alterations in the intake and excretion of water and sodium, the two principal components of the fluid matrix that surrounds body cells. Appropriate compensatory responses are initiated when deviations from normal are quite small, thereby maintaining plasma osmolality within relatively narrow ranges.

In the osmoregulation of body fluids, the movement of water across cell membranes permits minor fluctuations in the concentration of solutes in extracellular fluid to be buffered by corresponding changes in the relatively larger volume of cellular water. Nevertheless, the concentration of solutes in extracellular fluid may at times become elevated or reduced by more than the allowed tolerances of one or two percent. It is then that complementary physiological and behavioral responses come into play to restore plasma osmolality to normal. Thus, for example, a decrease in plasma osmolality, such as that which occurs after the consumption of water in excess of need, leads to the excretion of surplus body water in the urine by inhibiting secretion from the pituitary gland of vasopressin, a peptide hormone that promotes water conservation in the kidneys. As might be expected, thirst also is inhibited then, to prevent further dilution of body fluids. Conversely, an increase in plasma osmolality, such as that which occurs after one eats salty foods or after body water evaporates without being replaced, stimulates the release of vasopressin, increasing the conservation of water and the excretion of solutes in urine. This process is accompanied by increased thirst, with the result of making plasma osmolality more dilute through the consumption of water. The threshold for thirst appears to be slightly higher than for vasopressin secretion, so that thirst is stimulated only after vasopressin has been released in amounts sufficient to produce maximal water retention by the kidneys—that is, only after osmotic dehydration exceeds the capacity of the animal to deal with it physiologically.
explanation_html:
Everything begins with a corrective to a narrow assumption. Work on hormones and behavior has mostly stopped at the gonadal hormones and reproduction, drawn by the economy of one set of chemicals running both the biology of reproduction and sexual behavior. The author widens the field: other hormones shape behavior too, and the case to follow is the peptide and steroid hormones that maintain homeostasis in body fluids and also govern how much water and salt an animal takes in. The remainder supplies vocabulary you will need. Homeostasis means holding conditions steady inside an organism while the outside world changes; for body fluids that means keeping plasma osmolality — the concentration of dissolved substances in blood — inside a narrow band, mainly by adjusting the intake and excretion of water and sodium. Corrections begin while the deviation is still small.

With the terms in place, the mechanism is laid out in order. The first line of defense is passive: water crosses cell membranes, so small swings in solute concentration outside cells are absorbed by the much larger reservoir of water inside them. Once a swing exceeds roughly one or two percent, physiological and behavioral responses take over together, and the two worked examples run in opposite directions. Drink more than you need and osmolality falls, the pituitary stops secreting vasopressin, the peptide hormone that makes the kidneys hold water, the surplus leaves in urine, and thirst shuts off. Eat salty food or lose water to evaporation and osmolality rises, vasopressin is released, water is conserved while solutes are excreted, and thirst rises so drinking dilutes the plasma. Watch the closing detail: thirst has the higher threshold, so behavior is recruited only once the kidneys have done all they can.
overall_html: The passage extends the study of hormones and behavior beyond its usual confine of gonadal hormones and reproduction, arguing that the peptide and steroid hormones which keep the body's fluids in balance also control drinking and salt intake. Its purpose is explanatory rather than argumentative: the first paragraph corrects the narrow assumption and defines homeostasis and plasma osmolality, while the second traces the regulatory mechanism through paired examples of plasma that is too dilute and plasma that is too concentrated, ending with the observation that thirst is triggered at a higher threshold than vasopressin release. No competing viewpoints are developed; the passage speaks throughout in a single expository voice.

With the elimination of the apartheid system, South Africa now confronts the transition to a rights-based legal system in a constitutional democracy. Among lawyers and judges, exhilaration over the legal tools soon to be available is tempered by uncertainty about how to use them. The changes in the legal system are significant, not just for human rights lawyers, but for all lawyers—as they will have to learn a less rule-bound and more interpretative way of looking at the law. That is to say, in the past, the parliament was the supreme maker and arbiter of laws; when judges made rulings with which the parliament disagreed, the parliament simply passed new laws to counteract their rulings. Under the new system, however, a constitutional court will hear arguments on all constitutional matters, including questions of whether the laws passed by the parliament are valid in light of the individual liberties set out in the constitution's bill of rights. This shift will lead to extraordinary changes, for South Africa has never before had a legal system based on individual rights—one in which citizens can challenge any law or administrative decision on the basis of their constitutional rights.

South African lawyers are concerned about the difficulty of fostering a rights-based culture in a multiracial society containing a wide range of political and personal beliefs simply by including a bill of rights in the constitution and establishing the means for its defense. Because the bill of rights has been drawn in very general terms, the lack of precedents will make the task of determining its precise meaning a bewildering one. With this in mind, the new constitution acknowledges the need to look to other countries for guidance. But some scholars warn that judges, in their rush to fill the constitutional void, may misuse foreign law—they may blindly follow the interpretations given bills of rights in other countries, not taking into account the circumstances in those countries that led to certain decisions. Nonetheless, these scholars are hopeful that, with patience and judicious decisions, South Africa can use international experience in developing a body of precedent that will address the particular needs of its citizens.

South Africa must also contend with the image of the law held by many of its citizens. Because the law in South Africa has long been a tool of racial oppression, many of its citizens have come to view obeying the law as implicitly sanctioning an illegitimate, brutal government. Among these South Africans the political climate has thus been one of opposition, and many see it as their duty to cheat the government as much as possible, whether by not paying taxes or by disobeying parking laws. If a rights-based culture is to succeed, the government will need to show its citizens that the legal system is no longer a tool of oppression but instead a way to bring about change and help further the cause of justice.
explanation_html:
The passage opens on a moment of institutional change and the mixed feelings it produces. With apartheid gone, South Africa is moving to a rights-based legal system, and lawyers and judges are excited about the new tools but unsure how to handle them. The shift touches every lawyer, not only those doing human rights work, because the job becomes less rule-bound and more interpretative. Contrast the two arrangements carefully. Previously parliament was supreme, so a ruling it disliked could simply be undone by fresh legislation. Now a constitutional court will decide all constitutional questions, including whether parliament's own laws survive against the liberties listed in the bill of rights, and citizens can for the first time challenge any law or administrative decision by invoking their constitutional rights.

Having described the machinery, the passage turns to doubts about it. South African Lawyers worry that a rights-based culture will not follow automatically from writing a bill of rights and creating the means to defend it, not in a multiracial society holding widely varying political and personal beliefs. The practical problem is that the bill is phrased in very general terms with no precedents to pin those terms down. The constitution's own answer is to look abroad, which prompts the warning carried by The Scholars: judges hurrying to fill the void may take over foreign interpretations without asking what local circumstances produced them. Notice that the scholars object to careless borrowing rather than to borrowing itself, since they end hopeful that patient, judicious use of international experience can build precedent fitted to South Africans.

A second obstacle, about attitudes rather than doctrine, closes the passage. Because the law in South Africa functioned for so long as an instrument of racial oppression, many citizens came to treat obedience as endorsement of an illegitimate and brutal government. That produced a politics of opposition in which cheating the state — evading taxes, ignoring parking rules — could feel like a duty. The final sentence states the condition on which everything described earlier depends: the government has to show its citizens that the legal system has stopped being a tool of oppression and has become a means of bringing about change and furthering justice.
overall_html: The passage examines what South Africa's move from parliamentary supremacy to a rights-based constitutional democracy actually demands, arguing that the new constitutional court and bill of rights are only a beginning, since the bill's general wording lacks precedent to fix its meaning and the country's long history of law as racial oppression has left many citizens treating obedience as complicity. Its purpose is analytical: one paragraph explains the structural change, one relays the worries of South African Lawyers and the caution of The Scholars about borrowing foreign interpretations, and one identifies the public attitude the government must change before a rights-based culture can take hold. The author reports these concerns sympathetically rather than choosing among them.

The jury trial is one of the handful of democratic institutions that allow individual citizens, rather than the government, to make important societal decisions. A crucial component of the jury trial, at least in serious criminal cases, is the rule that verdicts be unanimous among the jurors (usually twelve in number). Under this requirement, dissenting jurors must either be convinced of the rightness of the prevailing opinion, or, conversely, persuade the other jurors to change their minds. In either instance, the unanimity requirement compels the jury to deliberate fully and truly before reaching its verdict. Critics of the unanimity requirement, however, see it as a costly relic that extends the deliberation process and sometimes, in a hung (i.e., deadlocked) jury, brings it to a halt at the hands of a single, recalcitrant juror, forcing the judge to order a retrial. Some of these critics recommend reducing verdict requirements to something less than unanimity, so that one or even two dissenting jurors will not be able to force a retrial.

But the material costs of hung juries do not warrant losing the benefit to society of the unanimous verdict. Statistically, jury trials are relatively rare; the vast majority of defendants do not have the option of a jury trial or elect to have a trial without a jury—or they plead guilty to the original or a reduced charge. And the incidence of hung juries is only a small fraction of the already small fraction of cases that receive a jury trial. Furthermore, that juries occasionally deadlock does not demonstrate a flaw in the criminal justice system, but rather suggests that jurors are conscientiously doing the job they have been asked to do. Hung juries usually occur when the case is very close—that is, when neither side has presented completely convincing evidence—and although the unanimity requirement may sometimes lead to inconclusive outcomes, a hung jury is certainly preferable to an unjust verdict.

Requiring unanimity provides a better chance that a trial, and thus a verdict, will be fair. Innocent people are already occasionally convicted—perhaps in some cases because jurors presume that anyone who has been brought to trial is probably guilty—and eliminating the unanimity requirement would only increase the opportunity for such mistakes. Furthermore, if a juror's dissenting opinion can easily be dismissed, an important and necessary part of the deliberation process will be lost, for effective deliberation requires that each juror's opinion be given a fair hearing. Only then can the verdict reached by the jury be said to represent all of its members, and if even one juror has doubts that are dismissed out of hand, society's confidence that a proper verdict has been reached would be undermined.
explanation_html:
Two positions go on the table, and only one of them is the author's. The paragraph first frames the jury trial as a rare democratic institution in which citizens rather than the government decide something important, then singles out the unanimity rule for serious criminal cases: a dissenting juror must either be won over or win the others over, and that pressure forces the panel to deliberate fully before it can return a verdict. Then comes the pivot. The Critics call unanimity a costly relic that drags deliberation out and sometimes halts it altogether when one stubborn juror hangs the jury and a retrial must be ordered, so some of them would lower the threshold enough that one or two dissenters could no longer force one.

The rebuttal begins with 'But' and meets the cost objection on its own terms. The Author answers first with arithmetic: jury trials are already uncommon, since most defendants either have no right to one, waive it, or plead guilty to the original or a reduced charge, and hung juries are a small fraction of that already small fraction, so the material cost is too slight to justify surrendering what unanimity buys. The second answer reinterprets the same evidence rather than disputing it. Deadlock is not a malfunction but a sign that jurors are taking the job seriously, and it tends to arise precisely where the case is close and neither side has presented convincing proof. A hung jury, the author concludes, beats an unjust verdict.

The closing paragraph moves from cost to fairness, which is the ground the author actually wants to fight on. Wrongful convictions already happen, possibly because jurors assume that anyone brought to trial is probably guilty, and loosening the verdict requirement would only widen the opening for such mistakes. The deeper point concerns the process itself: if a lone dissenter can simply be outvoted, deliberation loses the feature that makes it work, since every juror's view must get a genuine hearing before the verdict can be said to speak for the whole panel. Watch the final move from accuracy to legitimacy — doubts brushed aside would cost the public its confidence that a proper verdict was reached.
overall_html: The passage defends the requirement that juries in serious criminal cases reach unanimous verdicts, against critics who treat it as an expensive relic that lets a single holdout force a retrial. The author's purpose is rebuttal: after stating the critics' case, the passage answers it first on cost, noting that jury trials and hung juries alike are statistically rare and that deadlock signals conscientious jurors confronting a genuinely close case, and then on principle, arguing that a lower threshold would multiply wrongful convictions and would gut deliberation by letting a dissenter's doubts be dismissed, which would in turn undermine public confidence in verdicts. The two viewpoints to keep apart are The Critics and The Author.

Spurred by the discovery that a substance containing uranium emitted radiation, Marie Curie began studying radioactivity in 1897. She first tested gold and copper for radiation but found none. She then tested pitchblende, a mineral that was known to contain uranium, and discovered that it was more radioactive than uranium. Acting on the hypothesis that pitchblende must contain at least one other radioactive element, Curie was able to isolate a pair of previously unknown elements, polonium and radium. Turning her attention to the rate of radioactive emission, she discovered that uranium emitted radiation at a consistent rate, even if heated or dissolved. Based on these results, Curie concluded that the emission rate for a given element was constant. Furthermore, because radiation appeared to be spontaneous, with no discernible difference between radiating and nonradiating elements, she was unable to postulate a mechanism by which to explain radiation.

It is now known that radiation occurs when certain isotopes (atoms of the same element that differ slightly in their atomic structure) decay, and that emission rates are not constant but decrease very slowly with time. Some critics have recently faulted Curie for not reaching these conclusions herself, but it would have been impossible for Curie to do so given the evidence available to her. While relatively light elements such as gold and copper occasionally have unstable (i.e., radioactive) isotopes, radioactive isotopes of most of these elements are not available in nature because they have largely finished decaying and so have become stable. Conversely, heavier elements such as uranium, which decay into lighter elements in a process that takes billions of years, are present in nature exclusively in radioactive form.

Furthermore, we must recall that in Curie's time the nature of the atom itself was still being debated. Physicists believed that matter could not be divided indefinitely but instead would eventually be reduced to its indivisible components. Chemists, on the other hand, observing that chemical reactions took place as if matter was composed of atomlike particles, used the atom as a foundation for conceptualizing and describing such reactions—but they were not ultimately concerned with the question of whether or not such indivisible atoms actually existed.

As a physicist, Curie conjectured that radiating substances might lose mass in the form of atoms, but this idea is very different from the explanation eventually arrived at. It was not until the 1930s that advances in quantum mechanics overthrew the earlier understanding of the atom and showed that radiation occurs because the atoms themselves lose mass—a hypothesis that Curie, committed to the indivisible atom, could not be expected to have conceived of. Moreover, not only is Curie's inability to identify the mechanism by which radiation occurs understandable, it is also important to recognize that it was Curie's investigation of radiation that paved the way for the later breakthroughs.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph is straight narrative: what Curie did, in order. Prompted by the finding that a uranium-bearing substance gave off radiation, Curie began work in 1897, found nothing in gold or copper, and then found pitchblende more radioactive than the uranium it was known to contain. Reasoning that something else radioactive must be inside it, she isolated polonium and radium. She next examined the rate of emission, found uranium's unaffected by heating or dissolving, and concluded that each element emits at a fixed rate. The paragraph ends on a limitation rather than an achievement: radiation looked spontaneous, with radiating and nonradiating elements otherwise indistinguishable, so she could propose no mechanism for it.

Modern knowledge is now set against those conclusions, and then Curie is defended. We know today that radiation comes from the decay of certain isotopes — atoms of one element differing slightly in structure — and that emission rates fall very slowly rather than holding steady, which is why The Critics fault her for missing both points. The author's reply is that the evidence available to her made it impossible. Light elements such as gold and copper do sometimes have unstable isotopes, but nature no longer supplies them, since they have largely finished decaying into stable forms, while heavy elements such as uranium take billions of years to decay and therefore occur only in radioactive form. Her sample of the world was skewed by geology, not by carelessness.

'Furthermore' signals a second line of defense, this one about the intellectual climate rather than the specimens. In Curie's day what an atom even was remained unsettled. The Physicists held that matter cannot be divided forever and must bottom out in indivisible components. The Chemists treated matter as though it were built of atomlike particles because reactions behaved that way, but they used the atom as a working framework and were not ultimately concerned with whether such indivisible atoms actually existed. Keep the two positions apart, because the next paragraph turns on which of them Curie held.

The last paragraph closes both threads. Curie was a physicist, committed to the indivisible atom, and her conjecture that radiating substances lose mass as whole atoms follows from that commitment while differing sharply from the answer eventually reached. That answer waited for the 1930s, when quantum mechanics overturned the older picture of the atom and showed that radiation happens because atoms themselves lose mass. Since the necessary idea contradicted the atom she believed in, the author holds that she cannot be expected to have conceived it. The final sentence goes beyond defense to credit: her investigation of radiation is what opened the way for those later breakthroughs.
overall_html: The passage recounts Marie Curie's early work on radioactivity and then defends her against critics who fault her for concluding that emission rates are constant and for offering no mechanism for radiation. The author's purpose is exculpatory and finally appreciative: the second paragraph shows that naturally available samples could not have revealed slowly decaying isotopes, the third shows that the atom's nature was still disputed between The Physicists and The Chemists, and the fourth shows that the correct explanation had to wait for the quantum mechanics of the 1930s and contradicted the indivisible atom Curie accepted as a physicist. The passage ends by crediting her investigations with making those later breakthroughs possible.

Published in 1952, Invisible Man featured a protagonist whose activities enabled the novel's author, Ralph Ellison, to explore and to blend themes specifically tied to the history and plight of African Americans with themes, also explored by many European writers with whose works Ellison was familiar, about the fractured, evanescent quality of individual identity and character. For this thematic blend, Ellison received two related criticisms: that his allegiance to the concerns of the individual prevented him from directing his art more toward the political action that critics believed was demanded by his era's social and political state of affairs; and that his indulging in European fictional modes lessened his contribution to the development of a distinctly African American novelistic style.

Ellison found these criticisms to voice a common demand, namely that writers should censor themselves and sacrifice their individuality for supposedly more important political and cultural purposes. He replied that it demeans a people and its artists to suggest that a particular historical situation requires cultural segregation in the arts. Such a view characterizes all artists as incapable of seeing the world—with all its subtleties and complications—in unique yet expressive ways, and it makes the narrow assumption that audiences are capable of viewing the world only from their own perspectives.

Models for understanding Invisible Man that may be of more help than those employed by its critics can be found in Ellison's own love for and celebration of jazz. Jazz has never closed itself off from other musical forms, and some jazz musicians have been able to take the European-influenced songs of U.S. theater and transform them into musical pieces that are unique and personal but also expressive of African American culture. In like manner, Ellison avoided the mere recapitulation of existing literary forms as well as the constraints of artistic isolation by using his work to explore and express the issues of identity and character that had so interested European writers.

Further, jazz, featuring solos that, however daring, remain rooted in the band's rhythm section, provides a rich model for understanding the relationship of artist to community and parallels the ways the protagonist's voice in Invisible Man is set within a wider communal context. Ellison's explorations in the novel, often in the manner of loving caricature, of the ideas left him by both European and African American predecessors are a form of homage to them and thus ameliorate the sense of alienation he expresses through the protagonist. And even though Invisible Man's protagonist lives alone in a basement, Ellison proves that an individual whose unique voice is the result of the transmutation of a cultural inheritance can never be completely cut off from the community.
explanation_html:
Begin with the blend and the objections it drew. In Invisible Man, Ellison used his protagonist to fuse two sets of concerns: themes tied to African American history and hardship, and themes about the fractured, fleeting nature of individual identity that European writers he knew had also pursued. The Critics attacked the fusion from two angles, and the two complaints match the two halves of the blend. Devotion to the individual, they said, kept his art from the political action the era's social and political circumstances demanded, and his use of European fictional modes weakened his contribution to a distinctly African American style of novel.

Ellison's answer comes next, and notice that he treats both complaints as one. Underneath each, he says, lies a single demand that writers censor themselves and surrender their individuality for purposes claimed to matter more. His reply is that no historical situation legitimately requires cultural segregation in the arts, and that demanding it demeans both a people and its artists. Two assumptions get exposed along the way: that artists cannot see a subtle, complicated world in ways at once personal and communicable, and that audiences can grasp the world only from where they already stand.
