The accumulation of scientific knowledge regarding the environmental impact of oil well drilling in North America has tended to lag behind the actual drilling of oil wells. Most attempts to regulate the industry have relied on hindsight: the need for regulation becomes apparent only after undesirable events occur. The problems associated with oil wells' potential contamination of groundwater—fresh water within the earth that supplies wells and springs—provide a case in point.

When commercial drilling for oil began in North America in the mid-nineteenth century, regulations reflected the industry's concern for the purity of the wells' oil. In 1893, for example, regulations were enacted specifying well construction requirements to protect oil and gas reserves from contamination by fresh water. Thousands of wells were drilled in such a way as to protect the oil, but no thought was given to the possibility that the groundwater itself might need protection until many drinking-water wells near the oil well sites began to produce unpotable, oil-contaminated water.

The reason for this contamination was that groundwater is usually found in porous and permeable geologic formations near the earth's surface, whereas petroleum and unpotable saline water reservoirs are generally found in similar formations but at greater depths. Drilling a well creates a conduit connecting all the formations that it has penetrated. Consequently, without appropriate safeguards, wells that penetrate both groundwater and oil or saline water formations inevitably contaminate the groundwater. Initial attempts to prevent this contamination consisted of sealing off the groundwater formations with some form of protective barrier to prevent the oil flowing up the well from entering or mixing with the natural groundwater reservoir. This method, which is still in use today, initially involved using hollow trees to seal off the groundwater formations; now, however, large metal pipe casings, set in place with cement, are used.

Regulations currently govern the kinds of casing and cement that can be used in these practices; however, the hazards of insufficient knowledge persist. For example, the long-term stability of this way of protecting groundwater is unknown. The protective barrier may fail due to corrosion of the casing by certain fluids flowing up the well, or because of dissolution of the cement by these fluids. The effects of groundwater bacteria, traffic vibrations, and changing groundwater chemistry are likewise unassessed. Further, there is no guarantee that wells drilled in compliance with existing regulations will not expose a need for research in additional areas: on the west coast of North America, a major disaster recently occurred because a well's location was based on a poor understanding of the area's subsurface geology. Because the well was drilled in a channel accessing the ocean, not only was the area's groundwater completely contaminated, but widespread coastal contamination also occurred, prompting international concern over oil exploration and initiating further attempts to refine regulations.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph states a thesis and then narrows to a test case. The author claims that scientific understanding of what oil drilling does to the environment has consistently trailed the drilling itself, so regulation in North America has been written backward, arriving only once something has already gone wrong. Groundwater contamination is offered as the illustration, and the definition supplied there matters for the rest of the passage: groundwater is fresh water held underground that feeds wells and springs. Expect the following paragraphs to walk through this example chronologically and to keep confirming the hindsight pattern.

History bears the claim out, and the irony is the point. When commercial drilling started in the middle of the nineteenth century, the rules that existed were written to protect the oil, not the water; the 1893 construction requirements were designed to keep fresh water from spoiling oil and gas reserves. Thousands of wells were built to that standard, with nobody considering that the traffic might run the other way. The problem announced itself only when drinking-water wells near drilling sites began delivering oil-tainted water that people could not drink, which is precisely the hindsight the opening described.

Here the passage pauses the narrative to explain the underlying geology, and the mechanism is simple once laid out. Groundwater sits in porous, permeable rock fairly near the surface, while petroleum and undrinkable salty water occupy comparable formations much deeper down. Drilling punches a channel through everything it passes, so a well reaching both layers will contaminate the fresh water unless something blocks the path. The fix has always been a barrier sealing off the groundwater formation so oil rising up the well cannot mix with it. Notice the continuity across the centuries: hollow trees originally, and today large metal casings cemented into place.

The closing paragraph returns to the thesis, arguing that current rules governing casing and cement have not cured the deeper problem of insufficient knowledge. Nobody knows how long these barriers last, since fluids moving up a well can corrode the casing or dissolve the cement, and the influence of groundwater bacteria, traffic vibrations and shifting groundwater chemistry has not been assessed at all. Worse, compliance guarantees nothing about unknown risks. The west coast disaster makes the point, where poor understanding of subsurface geology put a well in a channel opening to the ocean, contaminating groundwater and the coast and prompting yet another round of regulatory refinement.
overall_html: The passage argues that knowledge of drilling's environmental effects has always lagged behind the drilling itself, so oil regulation in North America is written only after damage appears, and it uses groundwater contamination as the sustained example. The author's purpose is to demonstrate that pattern, moving from early rules that protected oil from water rather than water from oil, to the geology that makes contamination inevitable without a barrier, to the casing-and-cement solution, and finally to the gaps that persist in current regulation, including a west coast disaster caused by a misjudged well location. There are no competing camps here; the argument is carried entirely by the author's own analysis.

In many bilingual communities of Puerto Rican Americans living in the mainland United States, people use both English and Spanish in a single conversation, alternating between them smoothly and frequently even within the same sentence. This practice—called code-switching—is common in bilingual populations. While there are some cases that cannot currently be explained, in the vast majority of cases subtle factors, either situational or rhetorical, explain the use of code-switching.

Linguists say that most code-switching among Puerto Rican Americans is sensitive to the social contexts, which researchers refer to as domains, in which conversations take place. The main conversational factors influencing the occurrence of code-switching are setting, participants, and topic. When these go together naturally they are said to be congruent; a set of three such congruent factors constitutes a conversational situation. Linguists studying the choice between Spanish and English among a group of Puerto Rican American high school students classified their conversational situations into five domains: family, friendship, religion, education, and employment. To test the effects of these domains on code-switching, researchers developed a list of hypothetical situations made up of two of the three congruent factors, or of two incongruent factors, approximating an interaction in one of the five domains. The researchers asked the students to determine the third factor and to choose which mix of language—on a continuum from all English to all Spanish—they would use in that situation. When given two congruent factors, the students easily supplied the third congruent factor and strongly agreed among themselves about which mix they would use. For instance, for the factors of participants "parent and child" and the topic "how to be a good son or daughter," the congruent setting chosen was "home" and the language mix chosen was Spanish only. In contrast, incongruent factors such as the participants "priest and parishioner" and the setting "beach" yielded less agreement on the third factor of topic and on language choice.

But situational factors do not account for all code-switching; it occurs even when the domain would lead one not to expect it. In these cases, one language tends to be the primary one, while the other is used only sparingly to achieve certain rhetorical effects. Often the switches are so subtle that the speakers themselves are not aware of them. This was the case with a study of a family of Puerto Rican Americans in another community. Family members believed they used only English at home, but their taped conversations occasionally contained some Spanish, with no change in situational factors. When asked what the presence of Spanish signified, they commented that it was used to express certain attitudes such as intimacy or humor more emphatically.
explanation_html:
The opening describes a behavior and then promises an explanation for it. In many Puerto Rican American communities on the mainland, speakers move between English and Spanish within a single conversation and even within one sentence, a practice linguists call code-switching and find throughout bilingual populations. The last sentence is the one to hold onto, since it lays out the passage's plan: a few instances still resist explanation, but the great majority are accounted for by subtle factors that are either situational or rhetorical. That two-part distinction sets up the two paragraphs that follow, one for each kind of factor.

Situational factors come first, and the vocabulary needs unpacking. Linguists hold that most switching responds to the social context, or domain, of a conversation, shaped by three things: setting, participants, and topic. When those three fit together naturally they are congruent, and a congruent trio makes up a conversational situation. Studying high school students, researchers sorted situations into the domains of family, friendship, religion, education, and employment, then handed the students two factors and asked them to supply the third and to pick a language mix ranging from all English to all Spanish. Given congruent pairs the students agreed readily; parent and child discussing how to be a good son or daughter produced home and Spanish only. Incongruent pairs, such as a priest and parishioner at the beach, scattered their answers.

The final paragraph turns to the other half of the explanation announced at the start. Switching also happens where the domain gives no reason to expect it, and in those cases one language clearly dominates while the other appears only in small doses for rhetorical effect, often so quietly that the speakers do not notice they have done it. A study of one Puerto Rican American family supplies the evidence: they were convinced they spoke only English at home, yet recordings caught occasional Spanish with no change in setting, participants or topic. Asked about it, they explained that the Spanish gave attitudes such as intimacy or humor more emphasis.
overall_html: The passage explains that code-switching between English and Spanish in Puerto Rican American communities is not random but driven by two identifiable kinds of factors, situational ones tied to the domain of a conversation and rhetorical ones used for emphasis even when the situation does not call for a switch. The author's purpose is expository, first defining the practice and announcing the two-part explanation, then reporting the domain study of high school students in which congruent combinations of setting, participants and topic produced strong agreement about language choice, and finally presenting the family study that illustrates unconscious switching for effect. The findings belong to the linguists; the author reports them without dispute.

Reader-response theory, a type of literary theory that arose in reaction to formalist literary criticism, has endeavored to shift the emphasis in the interpretation of literature from the text itself to the contributions of readers to the meaning of a text. According to literary critics who endorse reader-response theory, the literary text alone renders no meaning; it acquires meaning only when encountered by individual readers, who always bring varying presuppositions and ways of reading to bear on the text, giving rise to the possibility—even probability—of varying interpretations. This brand of criticism has met opposition from the formalists, who study the text alone and argue that reader-response theory can encourage and even validate fragmented views of a work, rather than the unified view acquired by examining only the content of the text. However, since no theory has a monopoly on divining meaning from a text, the formalists' view appears unnecessarily narrow.

The proponents of formalism argue that their approach is firmly grounded in rational, objective principles, while reader-response theory lacks standards and verges on absolute subjectivity. After all, these proponents argue, no author can create a work that is packed with countless meanings. The meaning of a work of literature, the formalists would argue, may be obscure and somewhat arcane; yet, however hidden it may be, the author's intended meaning is legible within the work, and it is the critic's responsibility to search closely for this meaning. However, while a literary work is indeed encoded in various signs and symbols that must be translated for the work to be understood and appreciated, it is not a map. Any complicated literary work will invariably raise more questions than it answers. What is needed is a method that enables the critic to discern and make use of the rich stock of meanings created in encounters between texts and readers.

Emphasizing the varied presuppositions and perceptions that readers bring to the interpretations of a text can uncover hitherto unnoticed dimensions of the text. In fact, many important works have received varying interpretations throughout their existence, suggesting that reader-based interpretations similar to those described by reader-response theory had been operating long before the theory's principles were articulated. And while in some cases critics' textual interpretations based on reader-response theory have unfairly burdened literature of the past with contemporary ideologies, legitimate additional insights and understandings continue to emerge years after an ostensibly definitive interpretation of a major work has been articulated. By regarding a reader's personal interpretation of literary works as not only valid but also useful in understanding the works, reader-response theory legitimizes a wide range of perspectives on these works and thereby reinforces the notion of them as fluid and lively forms of discourse that can continue to support new interpretations long after their original composition.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph does three jobs at once, so separate them as you read. It defines reader-response theory, which grew up against formalist criticism and relocates meaning from the text to what readers contribute: on this view a text by itself means nothing until a reader, carrying particular assumptions and habits of reading, meets it, which makes divergent interpretations likely rather than merely possible. It then gives the formalists their objection, that attending to readers licenses fragmented readings instead of the unified one a text's own content yields. The last sentence is the author stepping in: since no theory owns the route to meaning, the formalist position looks unnecessarily narrow.

The middle paragraph puts the formalists' best case first and then answers it. Their claim is one of rigor, that formalism rests on rational objective principles while reader-response theory has no standards and slides toward pure subjectivity, since no author can load a work with limitless meanings; however buried or arcane the intended meaning may be, it is legible in the work and the critic's task is to dig it out. The author's reply grants the premise and rejects the conclusion. A literary work is indeed encoded in signs and symbols needing translation, but it is not a map, and any complex work raises more questions than it settles, which is why criticism needs a method for using the meanings generated when texts meet readers.

The final paragraph builds the positive case, and notice that the author's argument is largely historical. Foregrounding what readers bring can expose dimensions of a text nobody had noticed, and the fact that major works have been read differently across their lifetimes suggests reader-based interpretation was already at work long before the theory named it. A concession follows, that some reader-response criticism has unfairly saddled older literature with present-day ideologies, but the author holds that genuine insights keep surfacing even after a supposedly definitive reading. Treating a reader's own interpretation as valid and useful legitimizes many perspectives and keeps literary works alive as discourse still open to new readings.
overall_html: The passage defends reader-response theory, which locates a text's meaning in the encounter between text and reader, against the formalist objection that such an approach abandons objective standards and fragments works that should be read as unified wholes. The author's purpose is evaluative and clearly partisan, first laying out both positions and calling formalism narrow, then presenting the formalists' rigor argument in order to answer it, and finally arguing from the long history of shifting interpretations that reader-based reading uncovers real insights and keeps literature open to new understanding. Keep three voices separate: the reader-response critics, the formalists who oppose them, and the author, who sides with the former while conceding the theory's occasional abuses.

Faculty researchers, particularly in scientific, engineering, and medical programs, often produce scientific discoveries and invent products or processes that have potential commercial value. Many institutions have invested heavily in the administrative infrastructure to develop and exploit these discoveries, and they expect to prosper both by an increased level of research support and by the royalties from licensing those discoveries having patentable commercial applications. However, although faculty themselves are unlikely to become entrepreneurs, an increasing number of highly valued researchers will be sought and sponsored by research corporations or have consulting contracts with commercial firms. One study of such entrepreneurship concluded that "if universities do not provide the flexibility needed to venture into business, faculty will be tempted to go to those institutions that are responsive to their commercialized desires." There is therefore a need to consider the different intellectual property policies that govern the commercial exploitation of faculty inventions in order to determine which would provide the appropriate level of flexibility.

In a recent study of faculty rights, Patricia Chew has suggested a fourfold classification of institutional policies. A supramaximalist institution stakes out the broadest claim possible, asserting ownership not only of all intellectual property produced by faculty in the course of their employment while using university resources, but also for any inventions or patent rights from faculty activities, even those involving research sponsored by nonuniversity funders. A maximalist institution allows faculty ownership of inventions that do not arise either "in the course of the faculty's employment [or] from the faculty's use of university resources." This approach, although not as all-encompassing as that of the supramaximalist university, can affect virtually all of a faculty member's intellectual production. A resource-provider institution asserts a claim to faculty's intellectual product in those cases where "significant use" of university time and facilities is employed. Of course, what constitutes significant use of resources is a matter of institutional judgment.

As Chew notes, in these policies "faculty rights, including the sharing of royalties, are the result of university benevolence and generosity. [However, this] presumption is contrary to the common law, which provides that faculty own their inventions." Others have pointed to this anomaly and, indeed, to the uncertain legal and historical basis upon which the ownership of intellectual property rests. Although these issues remain unsettled, and though universities may be overreaching due to faculty's limited knowledge of their rights, most major institutions behave in the ways that maximize university ownership and profit participation.

But there is a fourth way, one that seems to be free from these particular issues. Faculty-oriented institutions assume that researchers own their own intellectual products and the rights to exploit them commercially, except in the development of public health inventions or if there is previously specified "substantial university involvement." At these institutions industry practice is effectively reversed, with the university benefiting in far fewer circumstances.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph builds a problem that the rest of the passage will answer with a taxonomy. Faculty in the sciences, engineering and medicine generate discoveries and inventions worth money, and universities have spent heavily on the administrative machinery to develop them, counting on more research support and on royalties from licensing whatever can be patented. The pressure point is mobility: professors rarely turn entrepreneur themselves, but the valuable ones get recruited by research corporations or sign consulting contracts, and a quoted study warns that inflexible universities will lose them. Hence the question the passage sets itself, which policy on faculty inventions strikes the right level of flexibility.

Three of four categories arrive here, from most grasping to least, and it is worth fixing the order. Chew, whose classification the passage adopts, defines a supramaximalist institution as one claiming everything, not just intellectual property produced in the course of employment using university resources but inventions and patent rights from any faculty activity, including research funded by outsiders. A maximalist institution lets faculty keep only what arises neither from their employment nor from university resources, which in practice still sweeps in nearly all of their output. A resource-provider institution claims a share only where significant use was made of university time and facilities, though the university itself decides what counts as significant.

Before the fourth category comes an evaluation of these three. Chew's objection, quoted here, is that such policies treat any rights faculty retain, royalties included, as gifts from a generous university, whereas common law actually assigns inventions to their faculty inventors. Others have flagged the same anomaly and the shaky legal and historical footing of intellectual property ownership generally. The passage leaves the underlying question open, notes that universities may be overreaching because faculty do not know their rights, and reports the practical upshot without endorsement: most major institutions still act to maximize their own ownership and share of the profits.

The closing paragraph delivers the fourth option and a quiet verdict on it. Faculty-oriented institutions begin from the opposite presumption, that researchers own their intellectual products and the right to commercialize them, carving out only public health inventions and cases where substantial university involvement was specified in advance. The effect is to invert standard industry practice, leaving the university to benefit in far fewer situations. Read the opening phrase carefully, since it is the closest thing to an authorial judgment in the passage: this way seems free of the problems Chew identified, which marks it as the answer to the flexibility question raised at the start.
overall_html: The passage surveys the policies universities use to claim ownership of faculty inventions, adopting Chew's fourfold classification and moving from the supramaximalist and maximalist institutions that claim almost everything, through the resource-provider standard, to the faculty-oriented approach that presumes researchers own what they create. The author's purpose is to identify which policy offers the flexibility universities need to keep valuable researchers, framing the survey with that question, pausing to relay Chew's point that current practice treats faculty rights as university generosity even though common law grants faculty ownership, and closing by presenting the faculty-oriented model as apparently free of those problems. Chew supplies the framework and the critique; the author reports and mildly endorses.

Is it necessary for defense lawyers to believe that the clients they defend are innocent of the charges against them? Some legal scholars hold that lawyers' sole obligation is to provide the best defense they are capable of, claiming that in democratic societies all people accused of crimes are entitled to the best possible legal representation. They argue that lawyers have no right to judge defendants because it is the job of the courts to determine guilt or innocence and the job of the lawyer to represent the defendant before the court. They believe that the lawyer's responsibility is to state those facts that will assist each client's case, construct sound arguments based on these facts, and identify flaws in the arguments of opposing counsel. According to these scholars, the lawyer's role is not to express or act on personal opinions but to act as an advocate, saying only what defendants would say if they possessed the proper training or resources with which to represent themselves.

But such a position overlooks the fact that the defense lawyer's obligation is twofold: to the defendant, certainly, but no less so to the court and, by extension, to society. For this reason, lawyers, great as their obligation to defendants is, should not, as officers of the court, present to the court assertions that they know to be false. But by the same principle, lawyers who are convinced that their clients are guilty should not undertake to demonstrate their innocence. Guilty defendants should not be entitled to false or insincere representation. When lawyers know with certainty that a defendant is guilty, it is their duty not to deny this. Rather, they should appraise the case as much as possible in their client's favor, after giving due consideration to the facts on the other side, and then present any extenuating circumstances and argue for whatever degree of leniency in sentencing they sincerely believe is warranted. In cases where it is uncertain whether the client is guilty but the lawyer sincerely believes the client may well be innocent, the lawyer should of course try to prove that the client is innocent.

The lawyer's obligation to the court and to society also ultimately benefits the defendant, because the "best defense" can only truly be provided by an advocate who, after a careful analysis of the facts, is convinced of the merits of the case. The fact that every client is entitled to a defense does not mean that defense lawyers should take every case they are offered. Lawyers should not be mere mouthpieces for a defendant but instead advocates for the rights of the defendant given the facts of the case.
explanation_html:
A question opens the passage, and the first answer belongs to someone else. Some legal scholars hold that a defense lawyer owes the client nothing but the strongest possible defense, on the democratic principle that anyone accused of a crime deserves first-rate representation. Judging the defendant is not the lawyer's business, they say, because determining guilt belongs to the court while representing the accused belongs to counsel. On this account the work is technical: marshal the helpful facts, build sound arguments from them, and expose the weaknesses in the other side's case. The lawyer is a pure advocate, voicing what clients would say for themselves if they had the training.

The 'but' signals the turn to the author, whose objection rests on a second obligation the scholars ignore, namely the lawyer's duty to the court and through it to society. From that duty several rules follow, and they are worth separating. As officers of the court, lawyers must not present claims they know to be false, and by the same logic a lawyer convinced of a client's guilt must not try to prove innocence, since guilty defendants have no entitlement to insincere representation. What the lawyer should do instead is appraise the case as favorably as the facts on both sides allow, then raise mitigating circumstances and press for whatever leniency the lawyer genuinely thinks the sentence should reflect. Where guilt is uncertain and innocence plausible, proving innocence remains the right course.

The close turns what looked like a restriction into a benefit for the defendant. A genuinely best defense, the author argues, can only come from an advocate who has studied the facts and believes in the case, so sincerity and effectiveness pull in the same direction rather than against each other. Two consequences follow. Everyone's entitlement to a defense does not oblige any particular lawyer to accept any particular case, and the lawyer's role is not to be a mouthpiece repeating whatever the client wants said, but to advocate for the defendant's rights within the limits the facts set.
overall_html: The passage argues that a defense lawyer's duty runs not only to the client but also to the court and to society, so lawyers should never assert what they know to be false and should not attempt to prove the innocence of a client they are convinced is guilty, arguing instead for mitigation and leniency. The author's purpose is to correct a position, first presenting the scholars who define the lawyer as a pure advocate obliged only to mount the strongest case, then setting out the twofold obligation and the rules it generates, and finally showing that sincere advocacy actually serves the defendant better. The two viewpoints to track are those legal scholars and the author's own counterposition.

Many educators in Canada and the United States advocate multicultural education as a means of achieving multicultural understanding. There are, however, a variety of proposals as to what multicultural education should consist of. The most modest of these proposals holds that schools and colleges should promote multicultural understanding by teaching about other cultures, teaching which proceeds from within the context of the majority culture. Students should learn about other cultures, proponents claim, but examination of these cultures should operate with the methods, perspectives, and values of the majority culture. These values are typically those of liberalism: democracy, tolerance, and equality of persons.

Critics of this first proposal have argued that genuine understanding of other cultures is impossible if the study of other cultures is refracted through the distorting lens of the majority culture's perspective. Not all cultures share liberal values. Their value systems have arisen in often radically different social and historical circumstances, and thus, these critics argue, cannot be understood and adequately appreciated if one insists on approaching them solely from within the majority culture's perspective.

In response to this objection, a second version of multicultural education has developed that differs from the first in holding that multicultural education ought to adopt a neutral stance with respect to the value differences among cultures. The values of one culture should not be standards by which others are judged; each culture should be taken on its own terms. However, the methods of examination, study, and explanation of cultures in this second version of multicultural education are still identifiably Western. They are the methods of anthropology, social psychology, political science, and sociology. They are, that is, methods which derive from the Western scientific perspective and heritage.

Critics of this second form of multicultural education argue as follows: The Western scientific heritage is founded upon an epistemological system that prizes the objective over the subjective, the logical over the intuitive, and the empirically verifiable over the mystical. The methods of social-scientific examination of cultures are thus already value laden; the choice to examine and understand other cultures by these methods involves a commitment to certain values such as objectivity. Thus, the second version of multicultural education is not essentially different from the first. Scientific discourse has a privileged place in Western cultures, but the discourses of myth, tradition, religion, and mystical insight are often the dominant forms of thought and language of non-Western cultures. To insist on trying to understand nonscientific cultures by the methods of Western science is not only distorting, but is also an expression of an attempt to maintain a Eurocentric cultural chauvinism: the chauvinism of science. According to this objection, it is only by adopting the (often nonscientific) perspectives and methods of the cultures studied that real understanding can be achieved.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by narrowing a broad agreement into a specific dispute. Educators across Canada and the United States back multicultural education as the road to multicultural understanding, but they disagree about what it should involve, and the first paragraph presents the least ambitious version. On this proposal, schools teach about other cultures from inside the majority culture, so students study those cultures using the majority culture's methods, perspectives and values. The values named are liberal ones, democracy, tolerance and equality of persons. Expect a pattern from here, since each proposal will be followed by an objection.

The objection arrives on schedule. The First Critics argue that filtering other cultures through the majority culture's outlook makes real understanding impossible, because that outlook works like a distorting lens. Their reasoning turns on a simple observation: liberal values are not universal, and other value systems grew out of social and historical circumstances that were often radically different. Judged from the majority perspective alone, such systems cannot be properly understood or appreciated. Notice that the complaint is about the perspective brought to the study, not about the subject matter chosen, which is exactly the gap the next proposal tries to close.

A second version of multicultural education answers that complaint by going neutral. Rather than measuring other cultures against the standards of one, this approach takes each culture on its own terms and declines to rank value systems at all. The paragraph then plants the weakness that the final objection will exploit, and you should mark it as it appears: the values may be neutral, but the methods are not culturally neutral in origin. Studying cultures through anthropology, social psychology, political science and sociology means studying them through disciplines that grow out of the Western scientific tradition.

The closing objection collapses the distinction the second proposal relied on. The Second Critics point out that Western science rests on an epistemology preferring the objective to the subjective, the logical to the intuitive, and the empirically verifiable to the mystical, so its methods already carry values, and choosing them commits you to values such as objectivity. Their conclusion is that the second version is not really different from the first. Since myth, tradition, religion and mystical insight often dominate non-Western thought, using scientific methods on nonscientific cultures both distorts them and expresses a chauvinism of science; only the studied culture's own methods yield understanding.
overall_html: The passage lays out a debate about what multicultural education should be, tracing a modest proposal that teaches other cultures from within the majority culture's liberal framework, the objection that this distorts what it studies, a second proposal that stays neutral about values, and the objection that its Western social-scientific methods are themselves value laden and so leave it no different from the first. The author's purpose is expository rather than argumentative, presenting each position and each criticism in turn without endorsing any of them or offering a resolution. Keep three sets of views apart: the proponents of each version of multicultural education, the First Critics, and the Second Critics, who would have cultures studied on their own methodological terms.

In studying the autobiographies of Native Americans, most scholars have focused on as-told-to life histories that were solicited, translated, recorded, and edited by non-Native American collaborators—that emerged from "bicultural composite authorship." Limiting their studies to such written documents, these scholars have overlooked traditional, preliterate modes of communicating personal history. In addition, they have failed to address the cultural constructs of the highly diverse Native American peoples, who prior to contact with nonindigenous cultures did not share with Europeans the same assumptions about self, life, and writing that underlie the concept of an autobiography—that indeed constitute the English word's root meaning.

The idea of self was, in a number of pre-contact Native American cultures, markedly inclusive: identity was not merely individual, but also relational to a society, a specific landscape, and the cosmos. Within these cultures, the expression of life experiences tended to be oriented toward current events: with the participation of fellow tribal members, an individual person would articulate, reenact, or record important experiences as the person lived them, a mode of autobiography seemingly more fragmented than the European custom of writing down the recollections of a lifetime. Moreover, expression itself was not a matter of writing but of language, which can include speech and signs. Oral autobiography comprised songs, chants, stories, and even the process whereby one repeatedly took on new names to reflect important events and deeds in one's life. Dance and drama could convey personal history; for example, the advent of a vision to one person might require the enactment of that vision in the form of a tribal pageant.

One can view as autobiographical the elaborate tattoos that symbolized a warrior's valorous deeds, and such artifacts as a decorated shield that communicated the accomplishments and aspirations of its maker, or a robe that was emblazoned with the pictographic history of the wearer's battles and was sometimes used in reenactments. Also autobiographical, and indicative of high status within the tribe, would have been a tepee painted with symbolic designs to record the achievements and display the dreams or visions of its owner, who was often assisted in the painting by other tribal members.

A tribe would, then, have contributed to the individual's narrative not merely passively, by its social codes and expectations, but actively by joining in the expression of that narrative. Such intracultural collaboration may seem alien to the European style of autobiography, yet any autobiography is shaped by its creator's ideas about the audience for which it is intended; in this sense, autobiography is justly called a simultaneous individual story and cultural narrative. Autobiographical expressions by early Native Americans may additionally have been shaped by the cultural perspectives of the people who transmitted them.
explanation_html:
The opening levels a two-part charge against existing work. Most scholars studying Native American autobiography have concentrated on as-told-to life histories, texts solicited, translated, recorded and edited by non-Native collaborators, what the passage calls bicultural composite authorship. Because they treat written documents as the whole field, they miss the traditional preliterate ways personal history was communicated. The second failing runs deeper: before contact, the many distinct Native American peoples did not share the European assumptions about self, life and writing that the very word autobiography is built from. Those three assumptions organize everything that follows, so keep them in view.

Self comes first, and the contrast is the point. In numerous pre-contact cultures identity was inclusive rather than purely individual, tying a person to a society, a particular landscape and the cosmos. Life experience was expressed as it happened, with other tribal members taking part while a person articulated, reenacted or recorded important events, which makes the practice look fragmented next to the European habit of writing down a lifetime's recollections late in life. Expression also meant language rather than writing, including speech and signs, so autobiography took the form of songs, chants, stories, successive names marking new deeds, and dance or drama such as a tribal pageant enacting one person's vision.

Objects extend the argument beyond performance, and the examples are cumulative rather than argumentative. Elaborate tattoos recording a warrior's brave acts count as autobiographical, as does a decorated shield announcing its maker's accomplishments and ambitions, or a robe carrying a pictographic record of the wearer's battles that could itself be used in reenactments. A tepee painted with symbolic designs did the same work, registering its owner's achievements and displaying dreams or visions while also signaling high standing in the tribe. Note the detail that closes the paragraph, since the next one depends on it: other tribal members often helped with the painting.

The final paragraph draws the conclusion the evidence was building toward. A tribe shaped an individual's narrative not just passively through its codes and expectations but actively, by taking part in expressing it. That intracultural collaboration may look foreign to European autobiography, yet the author argues the difference is smaller than it appears, since every autobiography is shaped by its author's sense of an audience, which makes the genre at once an individual story and a cultural narrative. The last sentence adds a further layer of shaping, noting that the people who transmitted early Native American self-expressions brought cultural perspectives of their own.
overall_html: The passage argues that scholars have defined Native American autobiography too narrowly by studying only written as-told-to life histories, and that recognizing pre-contact assumptions about a self bound to community, land and cosmos reveals a rich body of oral, performed and material self-expression, from songs and name-taking to painted shields, robes and tepees. The author's purpose is corrective, opening with what the scholars have overlooked, then documenting these alternative forms, and finally arguing that the collaboration they involved is less alien to European autobiography than it seems, since all autobiography is shaped by its intended audience. The positions to track are those of most scholars and the author's own broader account.

Most scientists who study the physiological effects of alcoholic beverages have assumed that wine, like beer or distilled spirits, is a drink whose only active ingredient is alcohol. Because of this assumption, these scientists have rarely investigated the effects of wine as distinct from other forms of alcoholic beverages. Nevertheless, unlike other alcoholic beverages, wine has for centuries been thought to have healthful effects that these scientists—who not only make no distinction among wine, beer, and distilled spirits but also study only the excessive or abusive intake of these beverages—have obscured.

Recently, a small group of researchers has questioned this assumption and investigated the effects of moderate wine consumption. While alcohol has been shown conclusively to have negative physiological effects—for example, alcohol strongly affects the body's processing of lipids (fats and other substances including cholesterol), causing dangerous increases in the levels of these substances in the blood, increases that are a large contributing factor in the development of premature heart disease—the researchers found that absorption of alcohol into the bloodstream occurs much more slowly when subjects drink wine than when they drink distilled spirits. More remarkably, it was discovered that deaths due to premature heart disease in the populations of several European countries decreased dramatically as the incidence of moderate wine consumption increased. One preliminary study linked this effect to red wine, but subsequent research has shown identical results whether the wine was white or red. What could explain such apparently healthful effects?

For one thing, the studies show increased activity of a natural clot-breaking compound used by doctors to restore blood flow through blocked vessels in victims of heart disease. In addition, the studies of wine drinkers indicate increased levels of certain compounds that may help to prevent damage from high lipid levels. And although the link between lipid processing and premature heart disease is one of the most important discoveries in modern medicine, in the past 20 years researchers have found several additional important contributing factors. We now know that endothelial cell reactivity (which affects the thickness of the innermost walls of blood vessels) and platelet adhesiveness (which influences the degree to which platelets cause blood to clot) are each linked to the development of premature heart disease. Studies show that wine appears to have ameliorating effects on both of these factors: it decreases the thickness of the innermost walls of blood vessels, and it reduces platelet adhesiveness. One study demonstrated a decrease in platelet adhesiveness among individuals who drank large amounts of grape juice. This finding may be the first step in confirming speculation that the potentially healthful effects of moderate wine intake may derive from the concentration of certain natural compounds found in grapes and not present in other alcoholic beverages.
explanation_html:
The opening identifies an assumption and hints that it has cost us something. Most scientists working on the physiology of alcoholic drinks have taken alcohol to be the only active ingredient in wine, exactly as it is in beer or spirits, and that premise has kept them from testing wine separately. Two further habits compound the problem: they lump the three drinks together, and they study only heavy or abusive consumption. Meanwhile wine has carried a centuries-old reputation for healthful effects, and notice how the paragraph ends, with the charge that this research tradition has obscured those effects rather than disproved them.

A challenge to that assumption organizes the middle paragraph, and the structure is concession followed by findings. A small group of researchers has taken up moderate wine drinking, and the passage first grants what is not in dispute: alcohol does real harm, notably by disrupting the body's handling of lipids, meaning fats and related substances such as cholesterol, and pushing their blood levels up in a way that contributes heavily to premature heart disease. Against that background come two results. Alcohol enters the bloodstream far more slowly from wine than from spirits, and in several European countries deaths from premature heart disease fell sharply as moderate wine drinking became more common. The color of the wine, initially thought to matter, turned out not to. The paragraph closes by asking what could explain this.

The answer occupies the final paragraph, which piles up mechanisms rather than arguing a case. Wine drinkers show more activity of a natural clot-dissolving compound that doctors use to reopen blocked vessels, and higher levels of compounds that may limit the damage high lipid levels do. The passage then widens the picture, noting that lipid processing is not the only route to premature heart disease; endothelial cell reactivity, which governs the thickness of vessels' inner walls, and platelet adhesiveness, which governs clotting, both matter too, and wine improves each. The closing detail is the important one, since grape juice also reduced platelet adhesiveness, pointing toward compounds in grapes rather than alcohol.
overall_html: The passage argues that by treating alcohol as wine's only active ingredient and studying only abusive drinking, mainstream researchers have obscured wine's apparent health benefits, which a smaller group investigating moderate consumption has begun to document. The author's purpose is to present and support that revisionist line, first identifying the assumption at fault, then reporting the slower absorption of alcohol from wine and the fall in premature heart disease deaths where moderate wine drinking rose, and finally surveying the mechanisms behind those effects, ending with the grape juice finding that suggests compounds in grapes rather than alcohol are responsible. Keep the assumptions of most scientists separate from the findings of the small group of researchers the author favors.

The Canadian Auto Workers' (CAW) Legal Services Plan, designed to give active and retired autoworkers and their families access to totally prepaid or partially reimbursed legal services, has been in operation since late 1985. Plan members have the option of using either the plan's staff lawyers, whose services are fully covered by the cost of membership in the plan, or an outside lawyer. Outside lawyers, in turn, can either sign up with the plan as a "cooperating lawyer" and accept the CAW's fee schedule as payment in full, or they can charge a higher fee and collect the balance from the client. Autoworkers appear to have embraced the notion of prepaid legal services: 45 percent of eligible union members were enrolled in the plan by 1988. Moreover, the idea of prepaid legal services has been spreading in Canada. A department store is even offering a plan to holders of its credit card.

While many plan members seem to be happy to get reduced-cost legal help, many lawyers are concerned about the plan's effect on their profession, especially its impact on prices for legal services. Some point out that even though most lawyers have not joined the plan as cooperating lawyers, legal fees in the cities in which the CAW plan operates have been depressed, in some cases to an unprofitable level. The directors of the plan, however, claim that both clients and lawyers benefit from their arrangement. For while the clients get ready access to reduced-price services, lawyers get professional contact with people who would not otherwise be using legal services, which helps generate even more business for their firms. Experience shows, the directors say, that if people are referred to a firm and receive excellent service, the firm will get three to four other referrals who are not plan subscribers and who would therefore pay the firm's standard rate.

But it is unlikely that increased use of such plans will result in long-term client satisfaction or in a substantial increase in profits for law firms. Since lawyers with established reputations and client bases can benefit little, if at all, from participation, the plans function largely as marketing devices for lawyers who have yet to establish themselves. While many of these lawyers are no doubt very able and conscientious, they will tend to have less expertise and to provide less satisfaction to clients. At the same time, the downward pressure on fees will mean that the full-fee referrals that proponents say will come through plan participation may not make up for a firm's investment in providing services at low plan rates. And since lowered fees provide little incentive for lawyers to devote more than minimal effort to cases, a "volume discount" approach toward the practice of law will mean less time devoted to complex cases and a general lowering of quality for clients.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph is pure setup, so get the mechanics straight before the argument starts. Since late 1985 the Canadian Auto Workers' Legal Services Plan has given autoworkers, retirees and their families legal help that is either fully prepaid or partly reimbursed. Members may use the plan's own staff lawyers, whose work membership covers entirely, or go outside, and an outside lawyer either signs on as a cooperating lawyer accepting the plan's fee schedule as full payment or charges more and bills the client for the difference. Uptake has been strong, with 45 percent of eligible members enrolled by 1988, and prepaid plans are spreading in Canada.

Two opposed assessments fill the middle paragraph. Concerned lawyers worry about the effect on their profession and particularly on prices, observing that even though most lawyers have stayed out of the plan, fees in cities where it operates have fallen, sometimes below a profitable level. The plan's directors answer that the arrangement serves both sides: clients get cheap access, and lawyers meet people who would never otherwise hire them, which feeds the firm more work. Their supporting claim is specific and worth noting, since a satisfied plan client reportedly generates three or four further referrals who are not subscribers and who pay standard rates.

Only now does the author speak, and the verdict goes against the directors on both of their promises. The reasoning starts from who actually joins: established lawyers with reputations and clients gain nothing, so the plans work mainly as marketing for newcomers, who may be able and conscientious but bring less expertise and leave clients less satisfied. The referral argument then fails on arithmetic, because falling fees mean full-price referrals may not cover what a firm sinks into low-rate plan work. Worse, cheap fees reward minimal effort, so a volume discount approach starves complex cases of time and drags quality down.
overall_html: The passage examines the CAW's prepaid legal services plan and concludes that wider use of such plans is unlikely to deliver either lasting client satisfaction or real profit for law firms, because they attract mainly inexperienced lawyers, depress fees below what referrals can recoup, and reward minimal effort on demanding cases. The author's purpose is evaluative, first explaining how the plan works and how quickly it has caught on, then setting the worries of concerned lawyers about depressed fees against the directors' claim that plan work generates full-rate referrals, and finally rejecting that defense point by point. Three positions are in play: the concerned lawyers, the plan's directors, and the author's skeptical judgment.

In the field of historiography—the writing of history based on a critical examination of authentic primary information sources—one area that has recently attracted attention focuses on the responses of explorers and settlers to new landscapes in order to provide insights into the transformations the landscape itself has undergone as a result of settlement. In this endeavor historiographers examining the history of the Pacific Coast of the United States have traditionally depended on the records left by European American explorers of the nineteenth century who, as commissioned agents of the U.S. government, were instructed to report thoroughly their findings in writing.

But in furthering this investigation some historiographers have recently recognized the need to expand their definition of what a source is. They maintain that the sources traditionally accepted as documenting the history of the Pacific Coast have too often omitted the response of Asian settlers to this territory. In part this is due to the dearth of written records left by Asian settlers; in contrast to the commissioned agents, most of the people who first came to western North America from Asia during this same period did not focus on developing a self-conscious written record of their involvement with the landscape. But because a full study of a culture's historical relationship to its land cannot confine itself to a narrow record of experience, these historiographers have begun to recognize the value of other kinds of evidence, such as the actions of Asian settlers.

As a case in point, the role of Chinese settlers in expanding agriculture throughout the Pacific Coast territory is integral to the history of the region. Without access to the better land, Chinese settlers looked for agricultural potential in this generally arid region where other settlers did not. For example, where settlers of European descent looked at willows and saw only useless, untillable swamp, Chinese settlers saw fresh water, fertile soil, and the potential for bringing water to more arid areas via irrigation. Where other settlers who looked at certain weeds, such as wild mustard, generally saw a nuisance, Chinese settlers saw abundant raw material for valuable spices from a plant naturally suited to the local soil and climate.

Given their role in the labor force shaping this territory in the nineteenth century, the Chinese settlers offered more than just a new view of the land. Their vision was reinforced by specialized skills involving swamp reclamation and irrigation systems, which helped lay the foundation for the now well-known and prosperous agribusiness of the region. That 80 percent of the area's cropland is now irrigated and that the region is currently the top producer of many specialty crops cannot be fully understood by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers as reconstructed from their interactions with that landscape.
explanation_html:
Begin with the definitions, since the passage assumes them afterward. Historiography means writing history from a critical reading of authentic primary sources, and one current line of work studies how explorers and settlers reacted to unfamiliar landscapes in order to understand how settlement changed those landscapes. For the Pacific Coast of the United States, traditional historiographers have leaned on one body of material: the accounts of nineteenth-century European American explorers, who wrote thoroughly because the government that commissioned them required detailed written reports. That last point is not incidental, since the reason those records exist is what makes their dominance so easy to explain.

The turn comes with a challenge to what counts as evidence. Revisionist historiographers argue that the accepted sources leave out how Asian settlers responded to the same territory, largely because few written records survive from them; unlike the commissioned agents, most people arriving from Asia in that period were not building a self-conscious written account of their dealings with the land. Rather than accept the gap, these historiographers widen the definition of a source, reasoning that a culture's historical relationship with its land cannot be captured by a narrow written record. Their proposed evidence is behavior, what Asian settlers actually did.

An extended example shows the method working. Chinese settlers were central to spreading agriculture across the Pacific Coast, and because they were shut out of the better land they went looking for potential in dry ground others dismissed. The paragraph makes the contrast through two paired perceptions, and the pairing is the point. Settlers of European descent saw willows and read the site as useless untillable swamp, while Chinese settlers read the same willows as fresh water, fertile soil and a source for irrigating drier land. Wild mustard likewise struck other settlers as a weed and Chinese settlers as raw material for valuable spices, well suited to local conditions.

The closing paragraph converts perception into consequence, which is what the argument needed. Chinese settlers were a large part of the labor force shaping the territory, and their way of seeing the land came with practical expertise in reclaiming swamp and building irrigation systems, work that underlies the region's prosperous agribusiness today. The final sentence ties the case back to the methodological claim: with 80 percent of the area's cropland irrigated and the region leading in specialty crops, historiographers cannot fully explain the present landscape unless they reconstruct the Chinese settlers' contribution from their interactions with it.
overall_html: The passage argues that historians of the Pacific Coast landscape must widen what they count as a source, because the written reports of commissioned European American explorers omit Asian settlers, whose relationship to the land has to be reconstructed from their actions instead. The author's purpose is to advocate that methodological shift and demonstrate its payoff, moving from the traditional reliance on written records, to the revisionist case for other evidence, to the example of Chinese settlers who saw water and fertile soil where others saw swamp, and finally to the irrigation expertise that shaped today's agribusiness. The traditional historiographers and the revisionists are the positions in play, with the author siding with the latter.

The survival of nerve cells, as well as their performance of some specialized functions, is regulated by chemicals known as neurotrophic factors, which are produced in the bodies of animals, including humans. Rita Levi-Montalcini's discovery in the 1950s of the first of these agents, a hormonelike substance now known as NGF, was a crucial development in the history of biochemistry, which led to Levi-Montalcini sharing the Nobel Prize for medicine in 1986.

In the mid-1940s, Levi-Montalcini had begun by hypothesizing that many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die. In order to confirm this theory, she conducted research that in 1949 found that, when embryos are in the process of forming their nervous systems, they produce many more nerve cells than are finally required, the number that survives eventually adjusting itself to the volume of tissue to be supplied with nerves. A further phase of the experimentation, which led to Levi-Montalcini's identification of the substance that controls this process, began with her observation that the development of nerves in chick embryos could be stimulated by implanting a certain variety of mouse tumor in the embryos. She theorized that a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth. To investigate this hypothesis, she used the then new technique of tissue culture, by which specific types of body cells can be made to grow outside the organism from which they are derived. Within twenty-four hours, her tissue cultures of chick embryo extracts developed dense halos of nerve tissue near the places in the culture where she had added the mouse tumor. Further research identified a specific substance contributed by the mouse tumors that was responsible for the effects Levi-Montalcini had observed: a protein that she named "nerve growth factor" (NGF).

NGF was the first of many cell-growth factors to be found in the bodies of animals. Through Levi-Montalcini's work and other subsequent research, it has been determined that this substance is present in many tissues and biological fluids, and that it is especially concentrated in some organs. In developing organisms, nerve cells apparently receive this growth factor locally from the cells of muscles or other organs to which they will form connections for transmission of nerve impulses, and sometimes from supporting cells intermingled with the nerve tissue. NGF seems to play two roles, serving initially to direct the developing nerve processes toward the correct, specific "target" cells with which they must connect, and later being necessary for the continued survival of those nerve cells. During some periods of their development, the types of nerve cells that are affected by NGF—primarily cells outside the brain and spinal cord—die if the factor is not present or if they encounter anti-NGF antibodies.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining the class of chemicals everything else depends on. Neurotrophic factors are substances produced naturally inside the bodies of animals, humans included, that govern whether nerve cells survive and whether they carry out their specialized jobs. Against that background the author places Rita Levi-Montalcini's discovery in the 1950s of NGF, the first such agent ever identified, framing it as a turning point in biochemistry important enough to earn her a share of the 1986 Nobel Prize for medicine. Nothing is being argued yet; you are simply being handed the subject and told why it matters.

The middle paragraph retraces the research itself, and the sequence of steps is what you should hold onto. Levi-Montalcini began in the mid-1940s from a hypothesis that sounds backwards, that many immature nerve cells are programmed to die, and her 1949 work supported it: developing embryos generate far more nerve cells than they finally need, the surviving number settling to match the volume of tissue requiring nerves. She then observed that implanting a certain mouse tumor into chick embryos stimulated nerve growth, and reasoned that a chemical from the tumor was responsible. Tissue culture, then a new technique for growing cells outside the organism, let her test that idea, and cultures of chick embryo extract sprouted dense halos of nerve tissue near the added tumor. Isolating the protein behind that effect gave her NGF.

The final paragraph moves from discovery to established knowledge, widening from one substance to a whole category. NGF proved to be the first of many cell-growth factors found in animal bodies, and later work showed it present across many tissues and biological fluids and especially concentrated in certain organs. Notice the two distinct jobs assigned to it: early on it steers developing nerve processes toward the specific target cells they must connect with, and afterwards it is required to keep those same cells alive. The closing detail underlines that dependence, since the nerve cells sensitive to NGF, mostly those outside the brain and spinal cord, die during certain developmental stages if the factor is missing or is blocked by antibodies.
overall_html: The passage recounts how Rita Levi-Montalcini identified nerve growth factor and explains what that substance does, building from a general definition of neurotrophic factors, through the experimental sequence that produced the discovery, to the current understanding of NGF's distribution and function. The author's purpose is expository rather than argumentative, informing the reader about a landmark in biochemistry and about the two roles NGF plays, first directing developing nerve processes to their target cells and then sustaining those cells afterwards. No competing viewpoints are developed here, so track the chronology and the chain of cause and effect rather than any clash of positions.

The proponents of the Modern Movement in architecture considered that, compared with the historical styles that it replaced, Modernist architecture more accurately reflected the functional spirit of twentieth-century technology and was better suited to the newest building methods. It is ironic, then, that the Movement fostered an ideology of design that proved to be at odds with the way buildings were really built.

The tenacious adherence of Modernist architects and critics to this ideology was in part responsible for the Movement's decline. Originating in the 1920s as a marginal, almost bohemian art movement, the Modern Movement was never very popular with the public, but this very lack of popular support produced in Modernist architects a high-minded sense of mission—not content merely to interpret the needs of the client, these architects now sought to persuade, to educate, and, if necessary, to dictate. By 1945 the tenets of the Movement had come to dominate mainstream architecture, and by the early 1950s, to dominate architectural criticism—architects whose work seemed not to advance the evolution of the Modern Movement tended to be dismissed by proponents of Modernism. On the other hand, when architects were identified as innovators—as was the case with Otto Wagner, or the young Frank Lloyd Wright—attention was drawn to only those features of their work that were "Modern"; other aspects were conveniently ignored.

The decline of the Modern Movement later in the twentieth century occurred partly as a result of Modernist architects' ignorance of building methods, and partly because Modernist architects were reluctant to admit that their concerns were chiefly aesthetic. Moreover, the building industry was evolving in a direction Modernists had not anticipated: it was more specialized and the process of construction was much more fragmented than in the past. Up until the twentieth century, construction had been carried out by a relatively small number of tradespeople, but as the building industry evolved, buildings came to be built by many specialized subcontractors working independently. The architect's design not only had to accommodate a sequence of independent operations, but now had to reflect the allowable degree of inaccuracy of the different trades. However, one of the chief construction ideals of the Modern Movement was to "honestly" expose structural materials such as steel and concrete. To do this and still produce a visually acceptable interior called for an unrealistically high level of craftmanship. Exposure of a building's internal structural elements, if it could be achieved at all, could only be accomplished at considerable cost—hence the well-founded reputation of Modern architecture as prohibitively expensive.

As Postmodern architects recognized, the need to expose structural elements imposed unnecessary limitations on building design. The unwillingness of architects of the Modern Movement to abandon their ideals contributed to the decline of interest in the Modern Movement.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up a contradiction the rest of the passage will unpack. The Modernists claimed their architecture surpassed the historical styles it displaced because it captured the functional spirit of twentieth-century technology and suited the newest building methods. The Author calls that claim ironic, since the design ideology the Movement produced turned out to be at odds with the way buildings are actually built. Two things are worth registering immediately: the author is not a neutral reporter here, and the complaint is practical rather than a matter of taste, aimed at the gap between Modernist theory and construction reality.

Stubbornness is named as a cause of the Movement's decline, and the paragraph then traces where that stubbornness came from. Beginning in the 1920s as a marginal, almost bohemian art movement, Modernism never won public affection, and the author argues that the absence of popular support bred a high-minded sense of mission in The Modernists: rather than simply interpreting a client's needs, they set out to persuade, educate, and if necessary dictate. By 1945 their tenets dominated mainstream architecture and by the early 1950s criticism too, so architects whose work did not advance the Movement were dismissed, while admired innovators were read selectively, with only their recognizably Modern features acknowledged.

Here the passage supplies its concrete reasons for the collapse, and this is where the central argument sits. The Author faults The Modernists both for ignorance of building methods and for refusing to admit that their real concerns were aesthetic. Meanwhile the industry moved the opposite way, splitting construction among many independent specialized subcontractors instead of a few trades, so a design had to accommodate a sequence of separate operations and allow for how much inaccuracy each trade permitted. Against that, the Movement insisted on honestly exposing steel and concrete, which demanded craftsmanship nobody could realistically supply, so exposure came only at great cost. Hence Modernism's well-earned reputation for being prohibitively expensive.

The brief closing paragraph delivers the verdict and brings in one more group. The Postmodernists recognized that the demand to expose structural elements imposed unnecessary limits on design, which retroactively confirms the complaint developed just before. The last sentence then restates the causal claim the passage has been assembling: because The Modernists would not abandon their ideals, interest in the Movement fell away. Watch how compact this is, since the author adds no fresh evidence and simply names the recognition that broke the ideology alongside the refusal that doomed it.
overall_html: The passage argues that the Modern Movement in architecture declined because its practitioners clung to an ideology of honestly exposed structure that ignored how buildings are really constructed and refused to concede its own aesthetic motives. The author's purpose is both explanatory and critical, moving from the irony buried in Modernism's founding claim, to the missionary dogmatism that grew out of its unpopularity, to its collision with an increasingly fragmented and specialized building industry, and finally to the Postmodern recognition that its demands were needless constraints. The clash to track is between the Author's practical critique and the Modernists' unyielding ideals, with the Postmodernists appearing briefly as the group that saw the problem.
