The following passage was written in the mid-1990s.

The demand for electricity in certain countries has been projected recently to grow by 50 percent by the year 2010. Unfortunately, the increased use of fossil fuels to generate this electricity may ultimately damage human and environmental health. For example, emissions of air pollutants in these countries are expected to double over the next 25 years, even if energy is used efficiently, so that local urban air quality will likely deteriorate. Renewable sources of electricity, such as solar radiation, wind, and waterpower, are possible solutions to the problems caused by increasing demand for electricity. Unlike fossil fuels, renewable energy sources are available in virtually all geographic regions, and they allow electricity production without dangerous environmental pollutants. Additionally, these sources can usually be located closer to consumers than can plants that use fossil fuels, thus reducing transmission and distribution costs. Technologies for the successful long-term exploitation of these resources, however, are not always implemented successfully.

In rural Brazil, for example, millions of citizens do not have electricity, and the lack of necessary infrastructure has limited efforts to provide it. In 1992, an energy agency from the United States developed a joint project with two Brazilian states to install 800 household solar electrical systems and train local personnel to service them. Under the project's terms, local utilities install, maintain, and own the systems, and collect fees from users. Backers hoped the project would attract enough private investment for substantial expansion throughout Brazil. But the project directors rejected the relatively high bids of local Brazilian companies to produce the solar collectors and thus missed an opportunity to stimulate local production. Consequently, a short-term savings in start-up costs precluded the long-term benefits deriving from the development of local production capacity and technological skill, which eventually would have led to independence from costly foreign expertise. As a result, participating utilities can generate only enough income to cover operating and maintenance costs, which makes further investment and expansion unlikely. Thus, the movement toward a sustainable, rural electricity system in Brazil remains stalled.

But some efforts have avoided these pitfalls. In the mid-1980s, a Danish energy agency helped agencies in India build three modern wind turbine plants and gradually develop local technical capacity. Local participants were trained in planning, operation, maintenance, and construction of turbines. Indian firms subsequently began manufacturing turbines and, as more locally manufactured equipment became available, Indian utilities were able to increase their use of wind energy profitably. The success of these small projects spurred enthusiasm; Indian utilities were soon ordering more equipment and private investment in wind energy surged. Because the Danish agency, unlike its U.S. counterpart, recognized the importance of local involvement at all levels, the project has a good chance of remaining competitive and profitable for the long run.
explanation_html:
The opening frames a problem and its proposed solution before hinting at the passage's real subject. Electricity demand in certain countries is projected to rise by half by 2010, and meeting that with fossil fuels threatens human and environmental health, with pollutant emissions expected to double over twenty-five years even where energy is used efficiently. Renewables such as sunlight, wind and waterpower answer several difficulties at once, being available in virtually every region, producing power without dangerous pollutants, and sitting nearer consumers so that transmission and distribution cost less. Watch the pivot in the last sentence, since what follows is not about the technologies themselves but about whether they get implemented well.

Brazil supplies the negative case. Millions of rural Brazilians have no electricity and little infrastructure to deliver it, so in 1992 a United States energy agency joined with two Brazilian states to install 800 household solar systems and train local people to service them, with local utilities owning, installing and maintaining the equipment and collecting fees. The hope was that private investment would follow and the model would spread. The damaging decision was to reject the relatively high bids from Brazilian firms to make the solar collectors. Saving money at the start cost the country a domestic manufacturing base and the technical skill that would eventually have ended its dependence on costly foreign expertise, and utilities now earn only enough to cover operations, so expansion has stalled.

India supplies the contrast, and the comparison is the whole point. In the mid-1980s a Danish agency helped Indian agencies build three modern wind turbine plants while deliberately developing local capability, training participants in planning, operation, maintenance and construction. Indian firms then began manufacturing turbines themselves, and as domestically made equipment became available utilities could expand wind power profitably, which brought further orders and a surge of private investment. The verdict is stated outright and names the difference: because the Danish agency, unlike its United States counterpart, recognized that local involvement mattered at every level, the project stands a good chance of remaining competitive and profitable.
overall_html: The passage argues that renewable sources can meet rising electricity demand without the health and environmental damage of fossil fuels, but that whether such projects last depends on building local manufacturing and technical capacity rather than merely installing equipment. The author's purpose is to draw that practical lesson by comparison, opening with the case for renewables and the caveat that the technologies are not always implemented successfully, then setting a failed solar project in rural Brazil, where cheaper foreign collectors displaced local producers and expansion stalled, against a Danish-assisted wind program in India that trained local participants and prompted domestic manufacture, investment and growth. The evaluation throughout is the author's own.

passage_html:
Although philanthropy—the volunteering of private resources for humanitarian purposes—reached its apex in England in the late nineteenth century, modern commentators have articulated two major criticisms of the philanthropy that was a mainstay of England's middle-class Victorian society. The earlier criticism is that such philanthropy was even by the later nineteenth century obsolete, since industrialism had already created social problems that were beyond the scope of small, private voluntary efforts. Indeed, these problems required substantial legislative action by the state. Unemployment, for example, was not the result of a failure of diligence on the part of workers or a failure of compassion on the part of employers, nor could it be solved by well-wishing philanthropists.

The more recent charge holds that Victorian philanthropy was by its very nature a self-serving exercise carried out by philanthropists at the expense of those whom they were ostensibly serving. In this view, philanthropy was a means of flaunting one's power and position in a society that placed great emphasis on status, or even a means of cultivating social connections that could lead to economic rewards. Further, if philanthropy is seen as serving the interests of individual philanthropists, so it may be seen as serving the interests of their class. According to this "social control" thesis, philanthropists, in professing to help the poor, were encouraging in them such values as prudence, thrift, and temperance, values perhaps worthy in themselves but also designed to create more productive members of the labor force. Philanthropy, in short, was a means of controlling the labor force and ensuring the continued dominance of the management class.

Modern critics of Victorian philanthropy often use the words "amateurish" or "inadequate" to describe Victorian philanthropy, as though Victorian charity can only be understood as an antecedent to the era of state-sponsored, professionally administered charity. This assumption is typical of the "Whig fallacy": the tendency to read the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present. If most Victorians resisted state control and expended their resources on private, voluntary philanthropies, it could only be, the argument goes, because of their commitment to a vested interest, or because the administrative apparatus of the state was incapable of coping with the economic and social needs of the time.

This version of history patronizes the Victorians, who were in fact well aware of their vulnerability to charges of condescension and complacency, but were equally well aware of the potential dangers of state-managed charity. They were perhaps condescending to the poor, but—to use an un-Victorian metaphor—they put their money where their mouths were, and gave of their careers and lives as well.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by naming its target: two criticisms modern commentators level at Victorian philanthropy, meaning the middle-class habit of volunteering private resources for humanitarian ends, which peaked in late nineteenth-century England. The earlier critics hold that the practice was already obsolete by that point, since industrialism had produced social problems far too large for small voluntary efforts and demanding substantial legislation instead. Unemployment is the example, and notice how carefully it is framed: it arose neither from workers lacking diligence nor from employers lacking compassion, so no amount of goodwill from philanthropists could have solved it.

The second charge cuts harder because it questions motive rather than adequacy. The recent critics treat Victorian philanthropy as self-serving, a way of flaunting power and position in a society preoccupied with status, or of cultivating connections that paid off economically. Their argument then scales up from the individual to the class. On the social control thesis, urging prudence, thrift and temperance on the poor, whatever those virtues are worth in themselves, conveniently manufactured a more productive workforce, so charity worked as a means of controlling labor and keeping the management class dominant.

Here the author starts pushing back, and the target is the assumption underneath the criticism rather than any particular claim within it. Describing Victorian charity as amateurish or inadequate presumes it can only be judged as a rough draft of today's professional, state-administered welfare. The author gives that habit a name, the Whig fallacy, the tendency to read the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present. Under that assumption, Victorian resistance to state control must be explained away as devotion to a vested interest or as the state's administrative incapacity, never as a position arrived at deliberately.

Judgment comes in the short closing paragraph. Such history patronizes the Victorians, who were entirely conscious of how they might look, alive both to the charges of condescension and complacency they invited and to the dangers of charity managed by the state. The concession is genuine, since the author grants that they probably were condescending toward the poor, but the defense is that they backed their convictions with their money and with their careers and lives as well. What distinguishes them from their critics, on this account, is commitment rather than sophistication.
overall_html: The passage sets out two modern criticisms of Victorian philanthropy, that it was obsolete against industrial-scale social problems and that it was a self-serving instrument of social control, and then defends the Victorians by attacking the assumption underlying such criticism. The author's purpose is corrective: after presenting each charge in its own terms, the argument identifies the Whig fallacy, the habit of reading the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present, and points out that Victorians consciously weighed the dangers of state-managed charity and committed their money, careers and lives to the alternative. Keep the earlier critics, the recent critics with their social control thesis, and the author's defense separate.

passage_html:
For decades, there has been a deep rift between poetry and fiction in the United States, especially in academic settings; graduate writing programs in universities, for example, train students as poets or as writers of fiction, but almost never as both. Both poets and writers of fiction have tended to support this separation, in large part because the current conventional wisdom holds that poetry should be elliptical and lyrical, reflecting inner states and processes of thought or feeling, whereas character and narrative events are the stock-in-trade of fiction.

Certainly it is true that poetry and fiction are distinct genres, but why have specialized education and literary territoriality resulted from this distinction? The answer lies perhaps in a widespread attitude in U.S. culture, which often casts a suspicious eye on the generalist. Those with knowledge and expertise in multiple areas risk charges of dilettantism, as if ability in one field is diluted or compromised by accomplishment in another.

Fortunately, there are signs that the bias against writers who cross generic boundaries is diminishing; several recent writers are known and respected for their work in both genres. One important example of this trend is Rita Dove, an African American writer highly acclaimed for both her poetry and her fiction. A few years ago, speaking at a conference entitled "Poets Who Write Fiction," Dove expressed gentle incredulity about the habit of segregating the genres. She had grown up reading and loving both fiction and poetry, she said, unaware of any purported danger lurking in attempts to mix the two. She also studied for some time in Germany, where, she observes, "Poets write plays, novelists compose libretti, playwrights write novels—they would not understand our restrictiveness."

It makes little sense, Dove believes, to persist in the restrictive approach to poetry and fiction prevalent in the U.S., because each genre shares in the nature of the other. Indeed, her poetry offers example after example of what can only be properly regarded as lyric narrative. Her use of language in these poems is undeniably lyrical—that is, it evokes emotion and inner states without requiring the reader to organize ideas or events in a particular linear structure. Yet this lyric expression simultaneously presents the elements of a plot in such a way that the reader is led repeatedly to take account of clusters of narrative details within the lyric flow. Thus while the language is lyrical, it often comes to constitute, cumulatively, a work of narrative fiction. Similarly, many passages in her fiction, though undeniably prose, achieve the status of lyric narrative through the use of poetic rhythms and elliptical expression. In short, Dove bridges the gap between poetry and fiction not only by writing in both genres, but also by fusing the two genres within individual works.
explanation_html:
The opening states the situation to be explained. In the United States, and above all inside universities, poetry and fiction have been held apart for decades, with graduate writing programs training a student as one or the other but almost never as both. Writers on both sides have largely endorsed the split, and the passage attributes that to a prevailing assumption about what each genre is for: poetry is supposed to be elliptical and lyrical, tracking inner states and the movement of thought and feeling, while character and narrative events are treated as the property of fiction.

A question drives the second paragraph, and it belongs to the author. Granting that these are genuinely distinct genres, why should a distinction produce separate training tracks and literary territoriality? The author offers a cultural explanation rather than a literary one, suggesting that American culture regards the generalist with suspicion, so anyone competent across several areas risks being called a dilettante, as though skill in one field must be diluted by accomplishment in another. The explanation is put forward tentatively, but it relocates the cause of the divide away from anything intrinsic to either genre.

Evidence that the bias is fading arrives next, concentrated in a single figure. Several recent writers are respected in both genres, and Rita Dove, acclaimed for her poetry and her fiction alike, is the passage's chief example. Speaking at a conference on poets who write fiction, she expressed gentle disbelief at the habit of segregating the two, recalling that she grew up reading and loving both and never suspected any danger in mixing them. Her study in Germany sharpens the contrast, since there poets write plays and novelists compose libretti, and the American restrictiveness would strike people as incomprehensible.

Why Dove thinks the division makes little sense occupies the close, and this is the most technical stretch of the passage. Her claim is that each genre already shares in the nature of the other, and her own poems demonstrate it as lyric narrative. The language is lyrical in the ordinary sense, evoking emotion and inner states without forcing the reader through a linear sequence, yet it simultaneously plants elements of a plot so that clusters of narrative detail keep surfacing within the lyric flow, and the poem accumulates into fiction. Her prose performs the reverse through poetic rhythm and elliptical expression. She therefore bridges the gap twice, by working in both genres and by fusing them inside single works.
overall_html: The passage explains the long-standing separation of poetry and fiction in American literary culture, attributes it less to any real difference between the genres than to a national suspicion of the generalist, and presents Rita Dove as evidence that the division is both weakening and unnecessary. The author's purpose is to diagnose the separation and then to challenge it, moving from the institutional split and the conventional wisdom supporting it, to a cultural explanation for its persistence, to Dove's incredulity and her German counterexample, and finally to an analysis of her lyric narrative, in which poems accumulate plot and prose takes on poetic rhythm. The viewpoints are the author's and Dove's, and they align.

The two passages discuss recent scientific research on music. They are adapted from two different papers presented at a scholarly conference.

Passage A

Did music and human language originate separately or together? Both systems use intonation and rhythm to communicate emotions. Both can be produced vocally or with tools, and people can produce both music and language silently to themselves.

Brain imaging studies suggest that music and language are part of one large, vastly complicated, neurological system for processing sound. In fact, fewer differences than similarities exist between the neurological processing of the two. One could think of the two activities as different radio programs that can be broadcast over the same hardware. One noteworthy difference, though, is that, generally speaking, people are better at language than music. In music, anyone can listen easily enough, but most people do not perform well, and in many cultures composition is left to specialists. In language, by contrast, nearly everyone actively performs and composes.

Given their shared neurological basis, it appears that music and language evolved together as brain size increased over the course of hominid evolution. But the primacy of language over music that we can observe today suggests that language, not music, was the primary function natural selection operated on. Music, it would seem, had little adaptive value of its own, and most likely developed on the coattails of language.

Passage B

Darwin claimed that since "neither the enjoyment nor the capacity of producing musical notes are faculties of the least [practical] use to man . . . they must be ranked amongst the most mysterious with which he is endowed." I suggest that the enjoyment of and the capacity to produce musical notes are faculties of indispensable use to mothers and their infants and that it is in the emotional bonds created by the interaction of mother and child that we can discover the evolutionary origins of human music.

Even excluding lullabies, which parents sing to infants, human mothers and infants under six months of age engage in ritualized, sequential behaviors, involving vocal, facial, and bodily interactions. Using face-to-face mother-infant interactions filmed at 24 frames per second, researchers have shown that mothers and infants jointly construct mutually improvised interactions in which each partner tracks the actions of the other. Such episodes last from one-half second to three seconds and are composed of musical elements—variations in pitch, rhythm, timbre, volume, and tempo.

What evolutionary advantage would such behavior have? In the course of hominid evolution, brain size increased rapidly. Contemporaneously, the increase in bipedality caused the birth canal to narrow. This resulted in hominid infants being born ever-more prematurely, leaving them much more helpless at birth. This helplessness necessitated longer, better maternal care. Under such conditions, the emotional bonds created in the premusical mother-infant interactions we observe in Homo sapiens today—behavior whose neurological basis essentially constitutes the capacity to make and enjoy music—would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with the question the whole set addresses, whether music and human language originated separately or together, and begins assembling the case for together. The similarities offered are functional rather than historical: both systems use intonation and rhythm to communicate emotion, both can be produced by voice or with tools, and both can be produced silently inside one's own head. Nothing has been concluded yet, but the direction of travel is clear, and each parallel is chosen to make a common origin look plausible.

Neurological evidence deepens the parallel and then introduces the wrinkle that will decide the argument. Brain imaging suggests that music and language belong to one large, vastly complicated system for processing sound, with fewer differences than similarities between them, an idea the passage captures with the image of two radio programs broadcast over the same hardware. Then comes the asymmetry to hold on to: generally speaking, people are better at language than at music. Anyone can listen easily enough, but most people perform poorly and many cultures leave composition to specialists, whereas nearly everyone actively performs and composes language.

The conclusion of Passage A draws on both preceding paragraphs at once. Shared neurology suggests that music and language evolved together as brain size increased over hominid evolution, while the observable primacy of language indicates that language, not music, was what natural selection actually operated on. Music, on this account, had little adaptive value of its own and most likely developed on the coattails of language, making it a by-product rather than a target of selection. That last claim is precisely what the second passage sets out to overturn.

Passage B opens by quoting Darwin, who ranked musical capacity among the most mysterious human faculties precisely because it seemed to serve no practical use. This author treats that as a problem to be solved rather than as a verdict, and answers with a thesis about one particular relationship: the enjoyment and production of musical notes are of indispensable use to mothers and their infants, and the evolutionary origins of human music lie in the emotional bonds their interaction creates. Notice what is and is not being disputed, since B says nothing against the neurology in A and everything against the claim that music lacked adaptive value.

Evidence for the thesis comes from observed behavior rather than from theory. Lullabies are set aside deliberately, since those are songs a parent chooses to sing, leaving the ritualized sequential exchanges of voice, face and body that mothers and infants under six months engage in on their own. Filmed at twenty-four frames per second, these prove to be jointly improvised, with each partner tracking the other, and they last from half a second to three seconds. The crucial claim is what they are made of, namely musical elements: variations in pitch, rhythm, timbre, volume and tempo.

The closing paragraph supplies the adaptive mechanism the thesis requires, and it does so by chaining physical changes together. Hominid brain size increased rapidly while growing bipedality narrowed the birth canal, so infants were born ever more prematurely and thus more helpless, which made longer and better maternal care necessary. Under those conditions the emotional bonds created in premusical mother-infant interaction would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage. Catch the definitional move planted mid-sentence, that the neurological basis of this behavior essentially constitutes the capacity to make and enjoy music, since that is how a claim about bonding becomes a claim about the origin of music.
overall_html: Both passages ask how human music originated, and they reach incompatible conclusions about whether it was ever selected for in its own right. Passage A infers from shared neurological processing that music and language evolved together, but concludes from the present primacy of language that selection operated on language alone and that music, having little adaptive value, developed on its coattails. Passage B answers Darwin's puzzle about music's apparent uselessness by locating its origins in mother-infant interaction, whose improvised exchanges are built from musical elements and whose emotional bonds would have been advantageous once narrowing birth canals and expanding brains left infants helpless. B thus grants music the independent adaptive value that A denies it.

passage_html:
The World Wide Web, a network of electronically produced and interconnected (or "linked") sites, called pages, that are accessible via personal computer, raises legal issues about the rights of owners of intellectual property, notably those who create documents for inclusion on Web pages. Some of these owners of intellectual property claim that unless copyright law is strengthened, intellectual property on the Web will not be protected from copyright infringement. Web users, however, claim that if their ability to access information on Web pages is reduced, the Web cannot live up to its potential as an open, interactive medium of communication.

The debate arises from the Web's ability to link one document to another. Links between sites are analogous to the inclusion in a printed text of references to other works, but with one difference: the cited document is instantly retrievable by a user who activates the link. This immediate accessibility creates a problem, since current copyright laws give owners of intellectual property the right to sue a distributor of unauthorized copies of their material even if that distributor did not personally make the copies. If person A, the author of a document, puts the document on a Web page, and person B, the creator of another Web page, creates a link to A's document, is B committing copyright infringement?

To answer this question, it must first be determined who controls distribution of a document on the Web. When A places a document on a Web page, this is comparable to recording an outgoing message on one's telephone answering machine for others to hear. When B creates a link to A's document, this is akin to B's giving out A's telephone number, thereby allowing third parties to hear the outgoing message for themselves. Anyone who calls can listen to the message; that is its purpose. While B's link may indeed facilitate access to A's document, the crucial point is that A, simply by placing that document on the Web, is thereby offering it for distribution. Therefore, even if B leads others to the document, it is A who actually controls access to it. Hence creating a link to a document is not the same as making or distributing a copy of that document. Moreover, techniques are already available by which A can restrict access to a document. For example, A may require a password to gain entry to A's Web page, just as a telephone owner can request an unlisted number and disclose it only to selected parties. Such a solution would compromise the openness of the Web somewhat, but not as much as the threat of copyright infringement litigation. Changing copyright law to benefit owners of intellectual property is thus ill-advised because it would impede the development of the Web as a public forum dedicated to the free exchange of ideas.
explanation_html:
The opening frames a conflict rather than a phenomenon. The Web is a network of linked pages, and because those pages carry documents somebody wrote, it raises questions about intellectual property. Two positions go on the board immediately. The Owners, the people who create documents for Web pages, warn that without stronger copyright law their material will not be protected from infringement. The Web Users counter that reducing access to pages defeats the whole point of an open, interactive medium of communication. Notice that the author has not taken a side yet; keep both positions available, because the final paragraph comes down firmly on one of them.

The second paragraph explains what actually generates the dispute: linking. A link works much like a footnote citing another work, with one decisive difference, since the cited document is retrievable the instant a user activates the link. That matters legally because copyright law lets an owner sue whoever distributes unauthorized copies, even a distributor who never personally made a copy. The paragraph closes on the precise question the passage exists to answer: if person A posts a document and person B links to it, has B committed infringement? Read this as setup rather than argument, with the problem defined carefully so the analogy that follows can dissolve it.

Now the author's own answer, and the reasoning turns on who controls distribution. Posting a document is like recording an outgoing message on an answering machine, and linking to it is like giving out the phone number. Anyone who calls hears the message, because that is what the message is for. B may make access easier, but A, simply by posting, is the one offering the document for distribution, so a link is not a copy. The author adds that A already has a remedy, password protection, much as a phone owner keeps an unlisted number and shares it selectively. That costs some openness, though less than the threat of litigation would. Hence the verdict: strengthening copyright law is ill-advised.
overall_html: The passage argues that creating a link to someone else's Web document is not copyright infringement, since the person who posts a document is the one offering it for distribution and can restrict access by other means, so changing copyright law to favor intellectual property owners would be ill-advised. The author's purpose is to resolve a dispute rather than merely report it, moving from the clash between The Owners, who want stronger protection, and The Web Users, who want open access, to the legal question raised by instant linking, and finally to an answering-machine analogy that supplies the answer. Only the author reaches a verdict; the two opening positions are reported, not endorsed.

passage_html:
In tracing the changing face of the Irish landscape, scholars have traditionally relied primarily on evidence from historical documents. However, such documentary sources provide a fragmentary record at best. Reliable accounts are very scarce for many parts of Ireland prior to the seventeenth century, and many of the relevant documents from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries focus selectively on matters relating to military or commercial interests.

Studies of fossilized pollen grains preserved in peats and lake muds provide an additional means of investigating vegetative landscape change. Details of changes in vegetation resulting from both human activities and natural events are reflected in the kinds and quantities of minute pollen grains that become trapped in sediments. Analysis of samples can identify which kinds of plants produced the preserved pollen grains and when they were deposited, and in many cases the findings can serve to supplement or correct the documentary record.

For example, analyses of samples from Long Lough in County Down have revealed significant patterns of cereal-grain pollen beginning by about 400 A.D. The substantial clay content of the soil in this part of Down makes cultivation by primitive tools difficult. Historians thought that such soils were not tilled to any significant extent until the introduction of the moldboard plough to Ireland in the seventh century A.D. Because cereal cultivation would have required tilling of the soil, the pollen evidence indicates that these soils must indeed have been successfully tilled before the introduction of the new plough.

Another example concerns flax cultivation in County Down, one of the great linen-producing areas of Ireland during the eighteenth century. Some aspects of linen production in Down are well documented, but the documentary record tells little about the cultivation of flax, the plant from which linen is made, in that area. The record of eighteenth-century linen production in Down, together with the knowledge that flax cultivation had been established in Ireland centuries before that time, led some historians to surmise that this plant was being cultivated in Down before the eighteenth century. But pollen analyses indicate that this is not the case; flax pollen was found only in deposits laid down since the eighteenth century.

It must be stressed, though, that there are limits to the ability of the pollen record to reflect the vegetative history of the landscape. For example, pollen analyses cannot identify the species, but only the genus or family, of some plants. Among these is madder, a cultivated dye plant of historical importance in Ireland. Madder belongs to a plant family that also comprises various native weeds, including goosegrass. If madder pollen were present in a deposit it would be indistinguishable from that of uncultivated native species.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a limitation. Scholars tracing changes in the Irish landscape have leaned mainly on historical documents, and The Historians who do so are working from a record the author calls fragmentary at best. Reliable accounts barely exist for much of Ireland before the seventeenth century, and the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century documents that survive tend to be written with military or commercial concerns in mind, so they notice selectively. Nothing here attacks any particular conclusion yet; the paragraph is clearing space for a second kind of evidence.

That second source arrives immediately: fossilized pollen grains preserved in peats and lake muds. The idea is simpler than the terminology suggests. Plants shed pollen, sediments trap it, and the kinds and quantities of grains lodged at a given depth record what was growing and when, whether the change came from human activity or a natural event. Analysis can name the plants and date the deposit. Note the author's careful claim about what this buys you, since pollen evidence can either supplement the documentary record or correct it. The two examples that follow give you one of each.

The first example does the correcting. Samples from Long Lough in County Down show cereal-grain pollen appearing by about 400 A.D. Growing cereals means tilling, and the soil there carries heavy clay that primitive tools struggle to break. The Historians had therefore assumed such land went largely untilled until the moldboard plough reached Ireland in the seventh century. The pollen puts grain in that ground centuries too early for the assumption to hold, so the inference is that these difficult soils were in fact being tilled successfully before the new plough arrived.

The flax case works in the opposite direction, deflating a guess rather than revising a technological assumption. County Down was one of the great linen regions of eighteenth-century Ireland, and linen comes from flax, yet the documents say little about growing the plant there. Knowing that flax cultivation was established in Ireland centuries earlier, The Historians surmised that Down must have grown it before the eighteenth century too. Pollen analysis says otherwise, since flax pollen appears only in deposits laid down from the eighteenth century onward. Same method, opposite service.

The closing paragraph is the author's own qualification, and it keeps the passage from reading as pure advocacy. Pollen cannot always be resolved to species; for some plants it identifies only the genus or family. Madder, a cultivated dye plant of real historical importance in Ireland, belongs to a family that also contains native weeds such as goosegrass, so madder pollen in a deposit would be indistinguishable from the pollen of plants nobody planted. Carry this forward as a limit on resolution rather than on reliability, since the author still treats the pollen record as a genuine supplement to documents.
overall_html: The passage puts forward pollen analysis as a corrective supplement to the documentary sources that scholars of the Irish landscape have traditionally relied on, illustrating with two County Down cases in which preserved pollen revised what historians believed about early tilling of clay soils and about when flax cultivation began there. The author's purpose is to recommend a method while marking its boundaries, and the structure follows that aim: the shortcomings of documents, an introduction to the pollen record, two supporting examples, then a closing qualification about pollen identifiable only to genus or family. The viewpoints to keep apart are The Historians, whose inferences get revised, and the author, who is measured rather than triumphant.

passage_html:
Asian American poetry from Hawaii, the Pacific island state of the United States, is generally characterizable in one of two ways: either as portraying a model multicultural paradise, or as exemplifying familiar Asian American literary themes such as generational conflict. In this light, the recent work of Wing Tek Lum in Expounding the Doubtful Points is striking for its demand to be understood on its own terms. Lum offers no romanticized notions of multicultural life in Hawaii, and while he does explore themes of family, identity, history, and literary tradition, he does not do so at the expense of attempting to discover and retain a local sensibility. For Lum such a sensibility is informed by the fact that Hawaii's population, unlike that of the continental U.S., has historically consisted predominantly of people of Asian and Pacific island descent, making the experience of its Asian Americans somewhat different than that of mainland Asian Americans.

In one poem, Lum meditates on the ways in which a traditional Chinese lunar celebration he is attending at a local beach both connects him to and separates him from the past. In the company of new Chinese immigrants, the speaker realizes that while ties to the homeland are comforting and necessary, it is equally important to have "a sense of new family" in this new land of Hawaii, and hence a new identity—one that is sensitive to its new environment. The role of immigrants in this poem is significant in that, through their presence, Lum is able to refer both to the traditional culture of his ancestral homeland as well as to the flux within Hawaiian society that has been integral to its heterogeneity. Even in a laudatory poem to famous Chinese poet Li Po (701–762 A.D.), which partly serves to place Lum's work within a distinguished literary tradition, Lum refuses to offer a stereotypical nostalgia for the past, instead pointing out the often elitist tendencies inherent in the work of some traditionally acclaimed Chinese poets.

Lum closes his volume with a poem that further points to the complex relationships between heritage and local culture in determining one's identity. Pulling together images and figures as vastly disparate as a famous Chinese American literary character and an old woman selling bread, Lum avoids an excessively romantic vision of U.S. culture, while simultaneously acknowledging the dream of this culture held by many newly arrived immigrants. The central image of a communal pot where each person chooses what she or he wishes to eat but shares with others the "sweet soup / spooned out at the end of the meal" is a hopeful one; however, it also appears to caution that the strong cultural emphasis in the U.S. on individual drive and success that makes retaining a sense of homeland tradition difficult should be identified and responded to in ways that allow for a healthy new sense of identity to be formed.
explanation_html:
Start by noticing that the passage opens with a category Lum is about to escape. Conventional Criticism reads Asian American poetry from Hawaii in one of two ways, either as a portrait of a model multicultural paradise or as a vehicle for familiar Asian American themes such as generational conflict. Against that backdrop The Author presents Wing Tek Lum's recent collection as striking, precisely because it demands to be understood on its own terms. Lum offers no romanticized multiculturalism, and although he does write about family, identity, history and literary tradition, he does not sacrifice a local sensibility to do it. That sensibility rests on a demographic fact the author spells out: Hawaii's population has historically been predominantly of Asian and Pacific island descent, so the Asian American experience there differs from the mainland one.

Evidence arrives next, two poems read for the same quality. In the first, the speaker attends a traditional Chinese lunar celebration at a local beach and finds that it both connects him to the past and separates him from it; among new Chinese immigrants he realizes that ties to the homeland are comforting and necessary, yet a sense of new family in Hawaii matters equally, yielding an identity sensitive to its new environment. The immigrants do double duty here, pointing back to the ancestral culture and forward to the flux that has made Hawaiian society heterogeneous. The second poem praises the classical poet Li Po and so places Lum within a distinguished tradition, but even there he declines stereotypical nostalgia, noting instead the elitist tendencies in some traditionally acclaimed Chinese poetry.

The volume's closing poem gets the last paragraph, and the author reads it as the fullest statement of the tension tracked throughout, between inherited heritage and local culture in shaping identity. Lum yokes together strikingly unlike figures, a famous Chinese American literary character and an old woman selling bread, refusing an excessively romantic vision of United States culture while still acknowledging the dream that many newly arrived immigrants attach to it. The image of a communal pot, where each person takes what she or he wishes but shares the sweet soup at the end, reads as hopeful. The author hears a warning inside the hope, though: the strong American emphasis on individual drive and success makes homeland tradition hard to retain, and that pressure must be identified and answered before a healthy new identity can form.
overall_html: The passage presents Wing Tek Lum's poetry as work that escapes the two standard readings of Asian American writing from Hawaii, neither idealizing multicultural life nor reducing itself to familiar generational themes, and instead holding ancestral heritage and a distinctly local sensibility in deliberate tension. The author's purpose is appreciative interpretation rather than plain description, opening with the conventional categories Lum refuses, then reading a lunar-celebration poem and a tribute to Li Po as evidence, and closing with the volume's final poem and its image of a shared pot. The only developed viewpoints are Conventional Criticism, invoked briefly as a foil, and the author's own admiring assessment of Lum.

passage_html:
In England the burden of history weighs heavily on common law, that unwritten code of time-honored laws derived largely from English judicial custom and precedent. Students of contemporary British law are frequently required to study medieval cases, to interpret archaic Latin maxims, or to confront doctrinal principles whose validity is based solely on their being part of the "timeless reason" of the English legal tradition. Centuries-old custom serves as the basis both for the divisions of law school subject matter and for much of the terminology of legal redress. Connected not only with legal history but also with the cultural history of the English people, common law cannot properly be understood without taking a long historical view.

Yet the academic study of jurisprudence has seldom treated common law as a constantly evolving phenomenon rooted in history; those interpretive theories that do acknowledge the antiquity of common law ignore the practical contemporary significance of its historical forms. The reasons for this omission are partly theoretical and partly political. In theoretical terms, modern jurisprudence has consistently treated law as a unified system of rules that can be studied at any given moment in time as a logical whole. The notion of jurisprudence as a system of norms or principles deemphasizes history in favor of the coherence of a system. In this view, the past of the system is conceived as no more than the continuous succession of its states of presence. In political terms, believing in the logic of law is a necessary part of believing in its fairness; even if history shows the legal tradition to be far from unitary and seldom logical, the prestige of the legal institution requires that jurisprudence treat the tradition as if it were, in essence, the application of known rules to objectively determined facts. To suggest otherwise would be dispiriting for the student and demoralizing for the public.

Legal historian Peter Goodrich has argued, however, that common law is most fruitfully studied as a continually developing tradition rather than as a set of rules. Taking his cue from the study of literature, Goodrich sees common law as a sort of literary text, with history and tradition serving as the text's narrative development. To study the common law historically, says Goodrich, is to study a text in which fiction is as influential as analysis, perception as significant as rule, and the play of memory as strong as the logic of argument. The concept of tradition, for Goodrich, implies not only the preservation and transmission of existing forms, but also the continuous rewriting of those forms to adapt them to contemporary legal circumstances.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph makes a claim about what common law is and how it has to be studied. Common law is the unwritten body of English law built out of judicial custom and precedent, and history sits heavily on it: British law students read medieval cases, parse archaic Latin maxims, and meet doctrines whose validity rests on nothing but their place in the timeless reason of the tradition. Even the way law school subjects are divided and the vocabulary of legal redress descend from centuries-old custom. The Author draws the conclusion plainly, that because common law is bound up with the cultural history of the English people as well as with legal history, it cannot properly be understood without taking a long historical view.

A pivot on 'Yet' identifies the gap the passage exists to expose. Academic jurisprudence has seldom treated common law as a phenomenon that evolves in history, and the interpretive theories that do concede its antiquity still ignore what its historical forms mean in practice today. Two explanations follow. Theoretically, Modern Jurisprudence treats law as a unified system of rules examinable at any moment as a logical whole, which shrinks the past into a mere succession of present states. Politically, believing in law's logic is part of believing in its fairness, so the prestige of the institution requires that the tradition be presented as known rules applied to objectively determined facts, since conceding otherwise would dispirit students and demoralize the public.

The alternative arrives last and belongs to Goodrich, a legal historian whose approach the author reports approvingly. Study common law as a continually developing tradition, he argues, not as a set of rules. Taking his cue from literary study, he treats it as a kind of text whose narrative development is its history and tradition, so that on this reading fiction weighs as much as analysis, perception as much as rule, and memory as much as the logic of argument. Notice how neatly this answers the theoretical objection raised just before it. Tradition in Goodrich's sense means not only preserving and transmitting inherited forms but continuously rewriting them to suit contemporary legal circumstances, which is exactly the evolving quality Modern Jurisprudence leaves out.
overall_html: The passage holds that common law is inseparable from its history yet has rarely been studied that way, and it presents Goodrich's proposal to treat common law as a continually developing tradition, read much as one reads a literary text, rather than as a fixed system of rules. The author's purpose is to diagnose an omission and point toward a remedy, moving from the weight of history on common law, to the theoretical and political reasons jurisprudence has set that history aside, to Goodrich's alternative. Three viewpoints are in play: The Author, who insists on the long historical view, Modern Jurisprudence, which treats law as a logical whole, and Goodrich, whose approach the author presents as more fruitful.

passage_html:
The passages discuss relationships between business interests and university research.

Passage A

As university researchers working in a "gift economy" dedicated to collegial sharing of ideas, we have long been insulated from market pressures. The recent tendency to treat research findings as commodities, tradable for cash, threatens this tradition and the role of research as a public good.

The nurseries for new ideas are traditionally universities, which provide an environment uniquely suited to the painstaking testing and revision of theories. Unfortunately, the market process and values governing commodity exchange are ill suited to the cultivation and management of new ideas. With their shareholders impatient for quick returns, businesses are averse to wide-ranging experimentation. And, what is even more important, few commercial enterprises contain the range of expertise needed to handle the replacement of shattered theoretical frameworks.

Further, since entrepreneurs usually have little affinity for adventure of the intellectual sort, they can buy research and bury its products, hiding knowledge useful to society or to their competitors. The growth of industrial biotechnology, for example, has been accompanied by a reduction in the free sharing of research methods and results—a high price to pay for the undoubted benefits of new drugs and therapies.

Important new experimental results once led university scientists to rush down the hall and share their excitement with colleagues. When instead the rush is to patent lawyers and venture capitalists, I worry about the long-term future of scientific discovery.

Passage B

The fruits of pure science were once considered primarily a public good, available for society as a whole. The argument for this view was that most of these benefits were produced through government support of universities, and thus no individual was entitled to restrict access to them.

Today, however, the critical role of science in the modern "information economy" means that what was previously seen as a public good is being transformed into a market commodity. For example, by exploiting the information that basic research has accumulated about the detailed structures of cells and genes, the biotechnology industry can derive profitable pharmaceuticals or medical screening technologies. In this context, assertion of legal claims to "intellectual property"—not just in commercial products but in the underlying scientific knowledge—becomes crucial.

Previously, the distinction between a scientific "discovery" (which could not be patented) and a technical "invention" (which could) defined the limits of industry's ability to patent something. Today, however, the speed with which scientific discoveries can be turned into products and the large profits resulting from this transformation have led to a blurring of both the legal distinction between discovery and invention and the moral distinction between what should and should not be patented.

Industry argues that if it has supported—either in its own laboratories or in a university—the makers of a scientific discovery, then it is entitled to seek a return on its investment, either by charging others for using the discovery or by keeping it for its own exclusive use.
explanation_html:
Passage A speaks in the first person, and you should register that voice immediately. The University Researcher describes academic science as a gift economy, a culture of collegial sharing that has long kept researchers insulated from market pressure. The recent habit of treating findings as commodities tradable for cash is framed as a threat both to that tradition and to research as a public good. This is a position statement rather than a neutral survey, so expect argument in what follows.

The case for universities comes next. They are the nurseries of new ideas because they supply conditions suited to slow, painstaking testing and revision of theories, and the values governing commodity exchange fit that work badly. Two reasons are offered: shareholders impatient for quick returns make firms averse to wide-ranging experimentation, and, the point The University Researcher calls more important still, few commercial enterprises hold the breadth of expertise needed when an entire theoretical framework shatters and must be replaced.

A second objection follows, this one about secrecy rather than capability. Entrepreneurs with little affinity for intellectual adventure can buy research and bury its products, withholding knowledge useful to society or to competitors. Industrial biotechnology supplies the illustration, since its growth has coincided with less free sharing of research methods and results. Notice the concession folded into the sentence, since the new drugs and therapies are called undoubted benefits; the complaint concerns the price paid for them.

Passage A closes by trading argument for image. Important results once sent university scientists rushing down the hall to share the excitement with colleagues, and now the rush is toward patent lawyers and venture capitalists. Nothing further is proved here; the register turns personal and ends on worry about the long-term future of scientific discovery. Read this as a value judgment about a change in culture, not as a claim that discovery itself has stopped.

Passage B opens on the same transformation in a detached, explanatory voice with no personal stake. The fruits of pure science, it notes, were once considered primarily a public good available to society as a whole. The justification for that older view turned on funding: most of those benefits were produced through government support of universities, so no individual was entitled to restrict access to them. Watch how carefully this is presented as a past consensus rather than as the writer's own commitment.

Now the shift. Because science is critical to the modern information economy, what was previously seen as a public good is being transformed into a market commodity. Biotechnology reappears as the example, though the use differs from Passage A's; here it shows how basic research on the detailed structures of cells and genes gets converted into profitable pharmaceuticals and medical screening technologies. In that context, legal claims to intellectual property become crucial, and the important detail is that such claims now reach the underlying scientific knowledge, not merely the commercial products.

The relevant legal history is spelled out next. Patents were once bounded by a distinction between a scientific discovery, which could not be patented, and a technical invention, which could. Speed and money have eroded that boundary: discoveries turn into products quickly and the resulting profits are large, so both the legal line between discovery and invention and the moral line about what should be patentable have blurred. Passage B records the blurring without pronouncing it regrettable.

The final paragraph hands the argument to Industry, and the reasoning is straightforward. Where a company has supported the makers of a scientific discovery, whether in its own laboratories or in a university, it claims entitlement to a return on that investment, either by charging others for use of the discovery or by keeping it for its exclusive use. The position is reported rather than assessed, which is precisely what separates this passage from the first.
overall_html: Both passages address the same development, the conversion of scientific knowledge from a shared public good into privately held property, but they handle it very differently. Passage A is an argument, in which The University Researcher defends the academic gift economy on the grounds that market values suit neither long-term theoretical work nor open sharing, closing on worry about the future of discovery. Passage B is an explanation, tracing how the role of science in the information economy has made intellectual property claims central and blurred the old legal and moral line between discovery and invention, and ending with Industry's own justification for seeking a return. In short, Passage A evaluates the shift that Passage B analyzes neutrally.

Sometimes there is no more effective means of controlling an agricultural pest than giving free rein to its natural predators. A case in point is the cyclamen mite, a pest whose population can be effectively controlled by a predatory mite of the genus Typhlodromus. Cyclamen mites infest strawberry plants; they typically establish themselves in a strawberry field shortly after planting, but their populations do not reach significantly damaging levels until the plants' second year. Typhlodromus mites usually invade the strawberry fields during the second year, rapidly subdue the cyclamen mite populations, and keep them from reaching significantly damaging levels.

Typhlodromus owes its effectiveness as a predator to several factors in addition to its voracious appetite. Its population can increase as rapidly as that of its prey. Both species reproduce by parthenogenesis—a mode of reproduction in which unfertilized eggs develop into fertile females. Cyclamen mites lay three eggs per day over the four or five days of their reproductive life span; Typhlodromus lay two or three eggs per day for eight to ten days. Seasonal synchrony of Typhlodromus reproduction with the growth of prey populations and ability to survive at low prey densities also contribute to the predatory efficiency of Typhlodromus. During winter, when cyclamen mite populations dwindle to a few individuals hidden in the crevices and folds of leaves in the crowns of the strawberry plants, the predatory mites subsist on the honeydew produced by aphids and white flies. They do not reproduce except when they are feeding on the cyclamen mites. These features, which make Typhlodromus well-suited for exploiting the seasonal rises and falls of its prey, are common among predators that control prey populations.

Greenhouse experiments have verified the importance of Typhlodromus predation for keeping cyclamen mites in check. One group of strawberry plants was stocked with both predator and prey mites; a second group was kept predator-free by regular application of parathion, an insecticide that kills the predatory species but does not affect the cyclamen mite. Throughout the study, populations of cyclamen mites remained low in plots shared with Typhlodromus, but their infestation attained significantly damaging proportions on predator-free plants.

Applying parathion in this instance is a clear case in which using a pesticide would do far more harm than good to an agricultural enterprise. The results were similar in field plantings of strawberries, where cyclamen mites also reached damaging levels when predators were eliminated by parathion, but they did not attain such levels in untreated plots. When cyclamen mite populations began to increase in an untreated planting, the predator populations quickly responded to reduce the outbreak. On average, cyclamen mites were about 25 times more abundant in the absence of predators than in their presence.
explanation_html:
A general claim opens the passage and a single case immediately narrows it: sometimes nothing controls an agricultural pest better than giving its natural predators free rein. The pest here is the cyclamen mite, which infests strawberry plants, and the predator is a mite of the genus Typhlodromus. Pay attention to the timing, because it does much of the work in the argument. Cyclamen mites establish themselves shortly after planting but only reach significantly damaging numbers in the plants' second year, and Typhlodromus tends to invade during that same second year, subduing them rapidly.

Why the predator works so well occupies the second paragraph, and appetite is only the beginning. Its population can increase as fast as its prey's, helped by parthenogenesis in both species, a mode of reproduction in which unfertilized eggs develop into fertile females; cyclamen mites lay three eggs a day across a four or five day reproductive life, Typhlodromus two or three a day for eight to ten days. Two further traits matter: its breeding is seasonally synchronized with the growth of prey populations, and it endures lean stretches, wintering on honeydew from aphids and white flies while cyclamen mites shelter in leaf crevices. It breeds only while feeding on its prey. Such traits, the author notes, are common among predators that keep prey in check.

Evidence follows the explanation. In greenhouse trials one group of strawberry plants was stocked with both predator and prey, while a second was kept predator-free through regular application of parathion, an insecticide that is conveniently selective in that it kills the predatory species but does not affect the cyclamen mite. That selectivity is what makes the comparison clean, since only one variable changes. Cyclamen mite numbers stayed low wherever Typhlodromus was present and climbed to significantly damaging proportions on the predator-free plants.

The closing paragraph carries the finding outdoors and draws the practical moral, opening with the judgment that spraying parathion here would do an agricultural enterprise far more harm than good. Field plantings repeated the greenhouse pattern: removing predators let cyclamen mites reach damaging levels, untreated plots never got there, and when numbers did start to climb in an untreated planting the predator population responded quickly enough to cut the outbreak short. The summary figure is the one to carry away, roughly twenty-five times more cyclamen mites on average in the absence of predators than in their presence.
overall_html: The passage argues that letting natural predators work can be the most effective way to control an agricultural pest, and it builds that case on one demonstration, the predatory mite Typhlodromus and its prey the strawberry-infesting cyclamen mite. The author's purpose is to establish the claim with evidence, moving from the two species and their seasonal timing, to the biological traits that make Typhlodromus an efficient controller, to greenhouse trials that removed the predator with a selective insecticide, and finally to field results in which cyclamen mites were about twenty-five times more abundant without predators. No competing viewpoints are developed; only the author's position appears, closing on the warning that spraying in this case would hurt the grower rather than help.

This passage was adapted from an article published in 1996.

The Internet is a system of computer networks that allows individuals and organizations to communicate freely with other Internet users throughout the world. As a result, an astonishing variety of information is able to flow unimpeded across national and other political borders, presenting serious difficulties for traditional approaches to legislation and law enforcement, to which such borders are crucial.

Control over physical space and the objects located in it is a defining attribute of sovereignty. Lawmaking presupposes some mechanism for enforcement, i.e., the ability to control violations. But jurisdictions cannot control the information and transactions flowing across their borders via the Internet. For example, a government might seek to intercept transmissions that propagate the kinds of consumer fraud that it regulates within its jurisdiction. But the volume of electronic communications crossing its territorial boundaries is too great to allow for effective control over individual transmissions. In order to deny its citizens access to specific materials, a government would thus have to prevent them from using the Internet altogether. Such a draconian measure would almost certainly be extremely unpopular, since most affected citizens would probably feel that the benefits of using the Internet decidedly outweigh the risks.

One legal domain that is especially sensitive to geographical considerations is that governing trademarks. There is no global registration of trademarks; international protection requires registration in each country. Moreover, within a country, the same name can sometimes be used proprietarily by businesses of different kinds in the same locality, or by businesses of the same kind in different localities, on the grounds that use of the trademark by one such business does not affect the others. But with the advent of the Internet, a business name can be displayed in such a way as to be accessible from any computer connected to the Internet anywhere in the world. Should such a display advertising a restaurant in Norway be deemed to infringe a trademark in Brazil just because it can be accessed freely from Brazil? It is not clear that any particular country's trademark authorities possess, or should possess, jurisdiction over such displays. Otherwise, any use of a trademark on the Internet could be subject to the jurisdiction of every country simultaneously.

The Internet also gives rise to situations in which regulation is needed but cannot be provided within the existing framework. For example, electronic communications, which may pass through many different territorial jurisdictions, pose perplexing new questions about the nature and adequacy of privacy protections. Should French officials have lawful access to messages traveling via the Internet from Canada to Japan? This is just one among many questions that collectively challenge the notion that the Internet can be effectively controlled by the existing system of territorial jurisdictions.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining its subject in the plainest possible terms: the Internet lets people and organizations anywhere talk to each other freely. The consequence is what matters. Information crosses national and political borders without being stopped, and that creates real trouble for conventional lawmaking and law enforcement, both of which are built on those borders. Keep this framing in view, because everything that follows is an elaboration of one tension between a borderless communication system and a legal order organized by territory. The voice here is the Author's own, and the author is not neutral about the difficulty being described.

Now the author explains why borders matter legally. Sovereignty is defined by control over physical space and the things in it, and lawmaking assumes you can actually enforce rules against violators. That assumption fails online, since governments cannot police the information and transactions streaming across their borders. The consumer fraud example does the work: a government might want to intercept fraudulent transmissions, but the sheer volume of traffic makes screening individual messages impossible. The only way left to block specific material would be cutting off Internet access entirely, which the author dismisses as politically impossible because citizens judge the benefits to outweigh the risks.

Having argued the general point, the author narrows to one legal area where geography is built into the rules. Trademark protection is national, not global, so a business must register country by country, and even inside a single country the same name can be used by different kinds of business in one place or by similar businesses in different places, on the theory that they do not interfere with one another. The Internet collapses that logic, since a name displayed online is visible everywhere at once. The Norwegian restaurant question is rhetorical: no single country plausibly has jurisdiction, because granting it to one grants it to all simultaneously.

The final paragraph widens the problem from conflicting rules to missing ones. Beyond areas where existing law fits badly, there are situations where regulation is genuinely needed and the current framework simply cannot supply it. Privacy is the illustration, since an electronic message may cross many jurisdictions on its way, raising the question of whether French officials may lawfully read traffic passing from Canada to Japan. Notice the author never answers these questions. They are posed to make a cumulative case, and the closing sentence states the thesis outright: territorial jurisdiction cannot effectively control the Internet.
overall_html: The passage argues that the Internet's indifference to national borders undermines a legal system whose authority rests on territorial control, so existing jurisdictional arrangements cannot effectively regulate online activity. The author's purpose is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, moving from a general account of why enforcement presupposes control over physical space, to trademark law as a domain where geography is written into the rules and the Internet breaks them, to privacy as an area where needed regulation cannot be provided at all. Only the author's viewpoint is developed; the illustrations and unanswered questions build a single cumulative case rather than staging a debate between competing positions.

Passage A

Drilling fluids, including the various mixtures known as drilling muds, play essential roles in oil-well drilling. As they are circulated down through the drill pipe and back up the well itself, they lubricate the drill bit, bearings, and drill pipe; clean and cool the drill bit as it cuts into the rock; lift rock chips (cuttings) to the surface; provide information about what is happening downhole, allowing the drillers to monitor the behavior, flow rate, pressure, and composition of the drilling fluid; and maintain well pressure to control cave-ins.

Drilling muds are made of bentonite and other clays and polymers, mixed with a fluid to the desired viscosity. By far the largest ingredient of drilling muds, by weight, is barite, a very heavy mineral of density 4.3 to 4.6. It is also used as an inert filler in some foods and is more familiar in its medical use as the "barium meal" administered before X-raying the digestive tract.

Over the years individual drilling companies and their expert drillers have devised proprietary formulations, or mud "recipes," to deal with specific types of drilling jobs. One problem in studying the effects of drilling waste discharges is that the drilling fluids are made from a range of over 1,000, sometimes toxic, ingredients—many of them known, confusingly, by different trade names, generic descriptions, chemical formulae, and regional or industry slang words, and many of them kept secret by companies or individual formulators.

Passage B

Drilling mud, cuttings, and associated chemicals are normally released only during the drilling phase of a well's existence. These discharges are the main environmental concern in offshore oil production, and their use is tightly regulated. The discharges are closely monitored by the offshore operator, and releases are controlled as a condition of the operating permit.

One type of mud—water-based mud (WBM)—is a mixture of water, bentonite clay, and chemical additives, and is used to drill shallow parts of wells. It is not particularly toxic to marine organisms and disperses readily. Under current regulations, it can be dumped directly overboard. Companies typically recycle WBMs until their properties are no longer suitable and then, over a period of hours, dump the entire batch into the sea.

For drilling deeper wells, oil-based mud (OBM) is normally used. The typical difference from WBM is the high content of mineral oil (typically 30 percent). OBMs also contain greater concentrations of barite, a powdered heavy mineral, and a number of additives. OBMs have a greater potential for negative environmental impact, partly because they do not disperse as readily. Barite may impact some organisms, particularly scallops, and the mineral oil may have toxic effects. Currently only the residues of OBMs adhering to cuttings that remain after the cuttings are sieved from the drilling fluids may be discharged overboard, and then only mixtures up to a specified maximum oil content.
explanation_html:
Passage A begins with function, and the list matters more than it first appears. Drilling fluids, including the mixtures known as drilling muds, are circulated down the drill pipe and back up the well, and along the way they lubricate the bit, bearings and pipe, cool the bit as it cuts into rock, lift rock chips called cuttings to the surface, let drillers monitor what is happening downhole through the fluid's behavior, flow rate, pressure and composition, and maintain well pressure to control cave-ins. Every one of those jobs is operational; no environmental question has been raised yet.

Composition follows function. Muds combine bentonite and other clays and polymers with a fluid mixed to whatever viscosity the job demands, and by weight the dominant ingredient is barite, an unusually heavy mineral. Passage A domesticates barite rather than alarming you about it, noting that the same mineral serves as an inert filler in some foods and is more familiar as the barium meal a patient swallows before an X-ray of the digestive tract. Hold that framing in mind, because the second passage introduces barite in a very different light.

A complication arrives in the third paragraph, though it is a research complication rather than an ecological one. Individual drilling companies and their expert drillers have devised proprietary recipes for particular kinds of job, and the ingredient pool runs beyond a thousand substances, some of them toxic. Studying the effects of drilling waste discharges is therefore hard for two reasons spelled out here: one substance may circulate under different trade names, generic descriptions, chemical formulae and regional or industry slang, and many formulations are kept secret by companies or individual formulators. Discharge effects appear at this point only as something difficult to investigate.

Passage B picks up exactly where that left off and treats the ground as settled. Drilling mud, cuttings and associated chemicals are normally released only during the drilling phase of a well's existence, these discharges are the main environmental concern in offshore oil production, and their use is tightly regulated. The offshore operator monitors releases closely, and control over them is written into the operating permit as a condition. The framing throughout is regulatory rather than investigative.

Two types of mud are then compared, water-based mud first. WBM mixes water, bentonite clay and chemical additives and is used to drill the shallow parts of wells. By the standards of this passage its profile is benign, since it is not particularly toxic to marine organisms and disperses readily, which is why current regulations allow it to be dumped directly overboard. Companies typically recycle a batch until its properties are no longer suitable, then release the entire batch into the sea over a period of hours.

Oil-based mud, used for deeper wells, is the contrast case and draws stricter treatment. What distinguishes OBM is a high mineral oil content, typically around thirty percent, together with greater concentrations of barite and a number of additives. Its potential for negative environmental impact is larger partly because it does not disperse as readily, and here the passage names specific risks where the first named none: barite may affect some organisms, scallops especially, and the mineral oil may be toxic. Regulation tracks that risk, so only OBM residues still adhering to cuttings after sieving may be discharged, and then only below a specified maximum oil content.
overall_html: The two passages approach drilling muds from different angles rather than disagreeing. Passage A is descriptive and technical, explaining what drilling fluids do in a well, what they are made of, and why the sheer number of ingredients, the inconsistent naming and the industry's proprietary secrecy make the effects of waste discharges hard to study. Passage B takes those discharges as its actual subject, calling them the main environmental concern in offshore production and setting out how regulation separates water-based mud, which may be dumped directly overboard, from oil-based mud, which disperses poorly and may be released only as residue on sieved cuttings. Passage B works on the environmental problem that Passage A only gestures toward.
