Aida Overton Walker (1880–1914), one of the most widely acclaimed African American performers of the early twentieth century, was known largely for popularizing a dance form known as the cakewalk through her choreographing, performance, and teaching of the dance. The cakewalk was originally developed prior to the United States Civil War by African Americans, for whom dance was a means of maintaining cultural links within a slave society. It was based on traditional West African ceremonial dances, and like many other African American dances, it retained features characteristic of African dance forms, such as gliding steps and an emphasis on improvisation.

To this African-derived foundation, the cakewalk added certain elements from European dances: where African dances feature flexible body postures, large groups and separate-sex dancing, the cakewalk developed into a high-kicking walk performed by a procession of couples. Ironically, while these modifications later enabled the cakewalk to appeal to European Americans and become one of the first cultural forms to cross the racial divide in North America, they were originally introduced with satiric intent. Slaves performed the grandiloquent walks in order to parody the processional dances performed at slave owners' balls and, in general, the self-important manners of slave owners. To add a further irony, by the end of the nineteenth century, the cakewalk was itself being parodied by European American stage performers, and these parodies in turn helped shape subsequent versions of the cakewalk.

While this complex evolution meant that the cakewalk was not a simple cultural phenomenon—one scholar has characterized this layering of parody upon parody with the phrase "mimetic vertigo"—it is in fact what enabled the dance to attract its wide audience. In the cultural and socioeconomic flux of the turn-of-the-century United States, where industrialization, urbanization, mass immigration, and rapid social mobility all reshaped the cultural landscape, an art form had to be capable of being many things to many people in order to appeal to a large audience.

Walker's remarkable success at popularizing the cakewalk across otherwise relatively rigid racial boundaries rested on her ability to address within her interpretation of it the varying and sometimes conflicting demands placed on the dance. Middle-class African Americans, for example, often denounced the cakewalk as disreputable, a complaint reinforced by the parodies circulating at the time. Walker won over this audience by refining the cakewalk and emphasizing its fundamental grace. Meanwhile, because middle- and upper-class European Americans often felt threatened by the tremendous cultural flux around them, they prized what they regarded as authentic art forms as bastions of stability; much of Walker's success with this audience derived from her distillation of what was widely acclaimed as the most authentic cakewalk. Finally, Walker was able to gain the admiration of many newly rich industrialists and financiers, who found in the grand flourishes of her version of the cakewalk a fitting vehicle for celebrating their newfound social rank.
explanation_html:
The passage names its subject and then reaches back well past her. Aida Overton Walker was among the most widely acclaimed African American performers of the early twentieth century, known chiefly for popularizing the cakewalk through her choreographing, performance and teaching of it. Before developing her story, the author establishes the dance's lineage: it was created by African Americans before the United States Civil War, when dance served to maintain cultural links inside a slave society, and it grew out of traditional West African ceremonial dances, keeping features such as gliding steps and an emphasis on improvisation. Track that layered origin, since layering turns out to be the passage's governing idea.

European elements join the African foundation next, and the author flags two ironies as they arrive. Where African dances feature flexible body postures, large groups and separate-sex dancing, the cakewalk developed into a high-kicking walk performed by a procession of couples. The first irony is that these very modifications later allowed the dance to appeal to European Americans and cross the racial divide, even though they were introduced satirically, since enslaved performers used the grandiloquent walk to parody the processional dances at slave owners' balls and the owners' self-important manners generally. The second irony compounds the first, because by the end of the nineteenth century European American stage performers were parodying the cakewalk, and those parodies then shaped later versions of it.

That tangled history becomes an explanation rather than a curiosity in the third paragraph. One scholar's term for parody piled on parody is mimetic vertigo, and the author's claim is that precisely this complexity is what won the dance so wide an audience. The reasoning depends on the moment: in a United States being remade by industrialization, urbanization, mass immigration and rapid social mobility, an art form could reach a large public only by being capable of being many things to many people. Complexity, in other words, worked as accessibility.

The principle is then applied to Walker herself, and the paragraph is built as three audiences making three different demands. Middle-Class African Americans often denounced the cakewalk as disreputable, a complaint the circulating parodies reinforced, so Walker won them over by refining the dance and emphasizing its fundamental grace. European American Elites, feeling threatened by the cultural flux around them, prized what they took to be authentic art forms as bastions of stability, and her version was widely acclaimed as the most authentic cakewalk. The Newly Rich industrialists and financiers found in her grand flourishes a fitting vehicle for celebrating their new social rank. One interpretation, three constituencies satisfied.
overall_html: The passage accounts for the extraordinary reach of Aida Overton Walker's cakewalk by arguing that the dance's layered history, African in foundation, European in its added elements, satiric in original intent and later parodied in turn, left it flexible enough to mean different things to different audiences during a period of rapid social change. The author's purpose is to explain a success rather than merely narrate it, moving from the dance's origins, to its ironic borrowings and reparodies, to the claim that such complexity is what drew a broad public, and finally to Walker's ability to satisfy Middle-Class African Americans, European American Elites and The Newly Rich at the same time. The only evaluative voice is the author's.

In principle, a cohesive group—one whose members generally agree with one another and support one another's judgments—can do a much better job at decision making than it could if it were noncohesive. When cohesiveness is low or lacking entirely, compliance out of fear of recrimination is likely to be strongest. To overcome this fear, participants in the group's deliberations need to be confident that they are members in good standing and that the others will continue to value their role in the group, whether or not they agree about a particular issue under discussion. As members of a group feel more accepted by the others, they acquire greater freedom to say what they really think, becoming less likely to use deceitful arguments or to play it safe by dancing around the issues with vapid or conventional comments. Typically, then, the more cohesive a group becomes, the less its members will deliberately censor what they say out of fear of being punished socially for antagonizing their fellow members.

But group cohesiveness can have pitfalls as well: while the members of a highly cohesive group can feel much freer to deviate from the majority, their desire for genuine concurrence on every important issue often inclines them not to use this freedom. In a highly cohesive group of decision makers, the danger is not that individuals will conceal objections they harbor regarding a proposal favored by the majority, but that they will think the proposal is a good one without attempting to carry out a critical scrutiny that could reveal grounds for strong objections. Members may then decide that any misgivings they feel are not worth pursuing—that the benefit of any doubt should be given to the group consensus. In this way, they may fall victim to a syndrome known as "groupthink," which one psychologist concerned with collective decision making has defined as "a deterioration of mental efficiency, reality testing, and moral judgment that results from in-group pressures."

Based on analyses of major fiascoes of international diplomacy and military decision making, researchers have identified groupthink behavior as a recurring pattern that involves several factors: overestimation of the group's power and morality, manifested, for example, in an illusion of invulnerability, which creates excessive optimism; closed-mindedness to warnings of problems and to alternative viewpoints; and unwarranted pressures toward uniformity, including self-censorship with respect to doubts about the group's reasoning and a concomitant shared illusion of unanimity concerning group decisions. Cohesiveness of the decision-making group is an essential antecedent condition for this syndrome but not a sufficient one, so it is important to work toward identifying the additional factors that determine whether group cohesiveness will deteriorate into groupthink or allow for effective decision making.
explanation_html:
The upside comes first, and the hedge in the opening words is worth noticing. In principle a cohesive group, meaning one whose members generally agree with and support one another's judgments, can make decisions far better than a noncohesive one could. The mechanism is fear. Where cohesiveness is low or missing, compliance driven by dread of recrimination is strongest, and escaping that pressure requires members to feel confident that they are in good standing and will still be valued whether or not they agree on the issue at hand. Feeling accepted, people say what they actually think rather than resorting to deceitful arguments or playing it safe with vapid, conventional comments. Hence the summary claim: the more cohesive a group grows, the less its members deliberately censor themselves.

A pivot on 'but' delivers the reversal, and it is subtler than a flat contradiction. Members of a highly cohesive group really are freer to depart from the majority; the trouble is that their desire for genuine concurrence on every important issue inclines them not to use that freedom. Read the distinction carefully, since so much depends on it. The danger is not that individuals conceal objections they privately harbor, but that they never develop objections at all, thinking a proposal good without attempting the critical scrutiny that might expose strong grounds against it. Misgivings get written off as not worth pursuing, and the group consensus receives the benefit of the doubt. The pattern has a name, groupthink, defined by one psychologist as a deterioration of mental efficiency, reality testing and moral judgment brought on by in-group pressures.

Empirical grounding arrives last. The Researchers, working from analyses of major fiascoes in international diplomacy and military decision making, describe groupthink as a recurring pattern with several components: the group overestimates its own power and morality, which shows up as an illusion of invulnerability and excessive optimism; it becomes closed-minded toward warnings of problems and toward alternative viewpoints; and it generates unwarranted pressure toward uniformity, including self-censorship of doubts about the group's reasoning and a shared illusion that everyone agrees. Hold onto the closing qualification, because it keeps the argument honest. Cohesiveness is an essential antecedent condition for the syndrome but not a sufficient one, which leaves the further factors that decide between groupthink and effective decision making still to be identified.
overall_html: The passage traces a double effect of cohesiveness on group decision making, arguing that cohesion first improves deliberation by removing the fear of recrimination that makes members censor themselves, and then endangers it by strengthening the appetite for agreement to the point where favored proposals escape critical scrutiny, the syndrome called groupthink. The author's purpose is explanatory rather than polemical, moving from benefit, to pitfall, to the cluster of symptoms The Researchers have identified in diplomatic and military fiascoes, and closing on the qualification that cohesiveness is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the syndrome. No opposing viewpoints are staged against each other; the analysis belongs to the author throughout.

Most of what has been written about Thurgood Marshall, a former United States Supreme Court justice who served from 1967 to 1991, has just focused on his judicial record and on the ideological content of his earlier achievements as a lawyer pursuing civil rights issues in the courts. But when Marshall's career is viewed from a technical perspective, his work with the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) reveals a strategic and methodological legacy to the field of public interest law. Though the NAACP, under Marshall's direction, was not the first legal organization in the U.S. to be driven by a political and social agenda, he and the NAACP developed innovations that forever changed the landscape of public interest law: during the 1940s and 1950s, in their campaign against state-sanctioned racial segregation, Marshall and the NAACP, instead of simply pursuing cases as the opportunity arose, set up a predetermined legal campaign that was meticulously crafted and carefully coordinated.

One aspect of this campaign, the test case strategy, involved sponsoring litigation of tactically chosen cases at the trial court level with careful evaluation of the precedential nuances and potential impact of each decision. This allowed Marshall to try out different approaches and discover which was the best to be used. An essential element in the success of this tactic was the explicit recognition that in a public interest legal campaign, choosing the right plaintiff can mean the difference between success and failure. Marshall carefully selected cases with sympathetic litigants, whose public appeal, credibility, and commitment to the NAACP's goals were unsurpassed.

In addition, Marshall used sociological and psychological statistics—presented in expert testimony, for example, about the psychological impact of enforced segregation—as a means of transforming constitutional law by persuading the courts that certain discriminatory laws produced public harms in violation of constitutional principles. This tactic, while often effective, has been criticized by some legal scholars as a pragmatic attempt to give judges nonlegal material with which to fill gaps in their justifications for decisions where the purely legal principles appear inconclusive.

Since the time of Marshall's work with the NAACP, the number of public interest law firms in the U.S. has grown substantially, and they have widely adopted his combination of strategies for litigation, devoting them to various public purposes. These strategies have been used, for example, in consumer advocacy campaigns and, more recently, by politically conservative public interest lawyers seeking to achieve, through litigation, changes in the law that they have not been able to accomplish in the legislature. If we focus on the particular content of Marshall's goals and successes, it might seem surprising that his work has influenced the quest for such divergent political objectives, but the techniques that he honed—originally considered to be a radical departure from accepted conventions—have become the norm for U.S. public interest litigation today.

Previous Commentators writing about Thurgood Marshall, a United States Supreme Court justice from 1967 to 1991, have concentrated on his judicial record and on the ideological content of his earlier civil rights work as a lawyer. The claim is carefully limited, since the NAACP was not the first legal organization in the country driven by a political and social agenda. What was new, in the campaign against state-sanctioned racial segregation during the 1940s and 1950s, was replacing opportunistic case-by-case litigation with a meticulously crafted and coordinated plan.

The first component of that plan gets a paragraph of its own. Under the test case strategy, the NAACP sponsored tactically chosen cases at the trial court level, evaluating in advance the precedential nuances and potential impact of each decision, which let Marshall try out different approaches and discover which worked best. One element of the tactic is singled out as essential, and it is more practical than doctrinal: in a public interest campaign the choice of plaintiff can decide success or failure, so Marshall selected litigants whose public appeal, credibility and commitment to the organization's goals were unsurpassed.

The second component shifts from who brings the case to what kind of evidence it carries. Marshall introduced sociological and psychological statistics, presented for example as expert testimony about the psychological impact of enforced segregation, in order to persuade courts that particular discriminatory laws produced public harms violating constitutional principles. The author calls the tactic often effective and then reports pushback, the only dissenting note in the passage. The legacy gets measured last, and the measure is deliberately uncomfortable. Focus on the particular content of Marshall's goals and that spread looks surprising; focus instead, as the author urges, on technique, and it follows naturally, since methods once seen as a radical departure from convention have become the norm.

The author's purpose is to reframe a familiar figure, moving from the neglected angle, through the two signature tactics, to the observation that these once-radical methods now count as standard and serve political ends as divergent as consumer advocacy and conservative law reform. Three voices appear: Previous Commentators, whose emphasis the author redirects, Some Legal Scholars, who question the use of nonlegal material, and The Author's own appraisal.

The painter Roy Lichtenstein helped to define pop art—the movement that incorporated commonplace objects and commercial-art techniques into paintings—by paraphrasing the style of comic books in his work. His merger of a popular genre with the forms and intentions of fine art generated a complex result: while poking fun at the pretensions of the art world, Lichtenstein's work also managed to convey a seriousness of theme that enabled it to transcend mere parody.

That Lichtenstein's images were fine art was at first difficult to see, because, with their word balloons and highly stylized figures, they looked like nothing more than the comic book panels from which they were copied. Standard art history holds that pop art emerged as an impersonal alternative to the histrionics of abstract expressionism, a movement in which painters conveyed their private attitudes and emotions using nonrepresentational techniques. The truth is that by the time pop art first appeared in the early 1960s, abstract expressionism had already lost much of its force. Pop art painters weren't quarreling with the powerful early abstract expressionist work of the late 1940s but with a second generation of abstract expressionists whose work seemed airy, high-minded, and overly lyrical. Pop art paintings were full of simple black lines and large areas of primary color. Lichtenstein's work was part of a general rebellion against the fading emotional power of abstract expressionism, rather than an aloof attempt to ignore it.

But if rebellion against previous art by means of the careful imitation of a popular genre were all that characterized Lichtenstein's work, it would possess only the reflective power that parodies have in relation to their subjects. Beneath its cartoonish methods, his work displayed an impulse toward realism, an urge to say that what was missing from contemporary painting was the depiction of contemporary life. The stilted romances and war stories portrayed in the comic books on which he based his canvases, the stylized automobiles, hot dogs, and table lamps that appeared in his pictures, were reflections of the culture Lichtenstein inhabited. But, in contrast to some pop art, Lichtenstein's work exuded not a jaded cynicism about consumer culture, but a kind of deliberate naivete, intended as a response to the excess of sophistication he observed not only in the later abstract expressionists but in some other pop artists. With the comics—typically the domain of youth and innocence—as his reference point, a nostalgia fills his paintings that gives them, for all their surface bravado, an inner sweetness. His persistent use of comic-art conventions demonstrates a faith in reconciliation, not only between cartoons and fine art, but between parody and true feeling.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining both a movement and a puzzle. Pop art brought commonplace objects and commercial-art techniques into painting, and Roy Lichtenstein helped define it by paraphrasing the style of comic books. The second sentence sets the agenda: the result was complex, because the work pokes fun at the pretensions of the art world and still conveys enough seriousness of theme to transcend mere parody. That two-sidedness is what the rest of the passage exists to explain, so keep both halves live as you read. The Author is committed to the second half in particular, and each later paragraph works to show that the comic-book surface is not the whole story.

A correction follows, aimed squarely at the received account. Lichtenstein's images were hard to recognize as fine art at first, since word balloons and highly stylized figures made them look like the panels they were copied from. Standard Art History explains pop art as an impersonal alternative to the histrionics of abstract expressionism, the movement whose painters conveyed private attitudes and emotions through nonrepresentational technique. The author disputes both the timing and the target. By the early 1960s abstract expressionism had already lost much of its force, and the pop painters were not quarreling with the powerful early work of the late 1940s but with a second generation whose canvases struck them as airy, high-minded and overly lyrical. The conclusion inverts the standard reading, making Lichtenstein part of a rebellion against a fading movement rather than an aloof attempt to ignore it.

The seriousness promised at the outset arrives last. If careful imitation of a popular genre were all Lichtenstein offered, his work would carry only the reflective power any parody has toward its subject. Beneath the cartoonish method, though, the author finds an impulse toward realism, an insistence that contemporary painting had stopped depicting contemporary life; the stilted romances and war stories, the automobiles, hot dogs and table lamps, reflected the culture he actually inhabited. Unlike some pop art, his work exudes no jaded cynicism about consumer culture but a deliberate naivete, a response to the excess of sophistication he saw in later abstract expressionists and in some fellow pop artists. Because comics belong to youth and innocence, nostalgia fills the paintings and lends them an inner sweetness beneath the surface bravado, evidence of a faith in reconciliation between cartoons and fine art, and between parody and true feeling.
overall_html: The passage argues that Lichtenstein's comic-derived paintings amount to far more than parody, joining a joke at the art world's expense to a genuine realism about contemporary life and an unfashionable sweetness of feeling. The author's purpose is interpretive and partly corrective, first stating the complexity of the work, then challenging Standard Art History's account of pop art as an impersonal alternative to abstract expressionism by placing Lichtenstein inside a rebellion against that movement's weakened second generation, and finally reading his deliberate naivete and nostalgia as faith in reconciliation between cartoon and fine art. Two viewpoints matter here: Standard Art History, which the author revises, and The Author's own admiring reading of the paintings.

Because the market system enables entrepreneurs and investors who develop new technology to reap financial rewards from their risk of capital, it may seem that the primary result of this activity is that some people who have spare capital accumulate more. But in spite of the fact that the profits derived from various technological developments have accrued to relatively few people, the developments themselves have served overall as a remarkable democratizing force. In fact, under the regime of the market, the gap in benefits accruing to different groups of people has been narrowed in the long term.

This tendency can be seen in various well-known technological developments. For example, before the printing press was introduced centuries ago, few people had access to written materials, much less to scribes and private secretaries to produce and transcribe documents. Since printed materials have become widely available, however, people without special position or resources—and in numbers once thought impossible—can take literacy and the use of printed texts for granted. With the distribution of books and periodicals in public libraries, this process has been extended to the point where people in general can have essentially equal access to a vast range of texts that would once have been available only to a very few. A more recent technological development extends this process beyond printed documents. A child in school with access to a personal computer and modem—which is becoming fairly common in technologically advanced societies—has computing power and database access equal to that of the best-connected scientists and engineers at top-level labs of just fifteen years ago, a time when relatively few people had personal access to any computing power. Or consider the uses of technology for leisure. In previous centuries only a few people with abundant resources had the ability and time to hire professional entertainment, and to have contact through travel and written communication—both of which were prohibitively expensive—with distant people. But now broadcast technology is widely available, and so almost anyone can have an entertainment cornucopia unimagined in earlier times. Similarly, the development of inexpensive mail distribution and telephone connections and, more recently, the establishment of the even more efficient medium of electronic mail have greatly extended the power of distant communication.

This kind of gradual diffusion of benefits across society is not an accident of these particular technological developments, but rather the result of a general tendency of the market system. Entrepreneurs and investors often are unable to maximize financial success without expanding their market, and this involves structuring their prices to the consumers so as to make their technologies genuinely accessible to an ever-larger share of the population. In other words, because market competition drives prices down, it tends to diffuse access to new technology across society as a result.
explanation_html:
Start with the concession, since the paragraph is built as one. Because the market system lets entrepreneurs and investors who develop new technology profit from risking capital, it can look as though the main result is that people with spare capital accumulate more of it. The Author grants the premise, that profits from various technological developments have gone to relatively few people, and rejects the conclusion drawn from it. Those developments have served overall as a remarkable democratizing force, and under the regime of the market the gap in benefits accruing to different groups has narrowed in the long term. Note the phrase carrying the weight, in the long term, and note also that the claim is about benefits rather than about who ends up rich.

Examples fill the entire middle, arranged so that each repeats the same movement, from a privileged few to nearly everyone. Before the printing press, written material was scarce and only those with position or resources had scribes and private secretaries; printed texts made literacy and the use of documents ordinary, and public libraries pushed the process further, giving people in general essentially equal access to a range of texts once available to very few. Computing repeats the pattern more recently, since a schoolchild with a personal computer and modem holds the computing power and database access that only the best-connected scientists at top laboratories commanded fifteen years earlier. Leisure follows the same arc, since hired entertainment, travel and correspondence with distant people were once prohibitively expensive, while broadcast technology now offers almost anyone an entertainment cornucopia, and cheap mail, telephones and electronic mail have extended distant communication broadly.

The mechanism comes last, and it is what converts a list of examples into an argument. This gradual diffusion is not an accident of these particular inventions but the result of a general tendency in the market system. The reasoning runs through incentives: entrepreneurs and investors usually cannot maximize financial success without expanding their market, and expanding it means structuring prices so that an ever-larger share of the population can genuinely afford the technology. Competition drives prices down, and falling prices spread access across society. That closes the loop on the objection raised at the start, since the same profit motive that concentrates the gains in few hands also disperses the technology itself.
overall_html: The passage maintains that although the profits from new technology accrue to relatively few people, the technologies themselves act as a powerful democratizing force, narrowing over the long term the gap in benefits available to different groups. The author's purpose is to defend that counterintuitive claim, opening with the appearance it must overcome, filling the middle with parallel examples running from printing and public libraries to personal computers, broadcasting and electronic mail, and closing with the mechanism that makes the pattern systematic, namely that profit-seeking firms must expand their markets and competition pushes prices down. The Author is the only viewpoint developed, and the opening impression is raised only in order to be corrected.

Neurobiologists once believed that the workings of the brain were guided exclusively by electrical signals; according to this theory, communication between neurons (brain cells) is possible because electrical impulses travel from one neuron to the next by literally leaping across the synapses (gaps between neurons). But many neurobiologists puzzled over how this leaping across synapses might be achieved, and as early as 1904 some speculated that electrical impulses are transmitted between neurons chemically rather than electrically. According to this alternative theory, the excited neuron secretes a chemical called a neurotransmitter that binds with its corresponding receptor molecule in the receiving neuron. This binding of the neurotransmitter renders the neuron permeable to ions, and as the ions move into the receiving neuron they generate an electrical impulse that runs through the cell; the electrical impulse is thereby transmitted to the receiving neuron.

This theory has gradually won acceptance in the scientific community, but for a long time little was known about the mechanism by which neurotransmitters manage to render the receiving neuron permeable to ions. In fact, some scientists remained skeptical of the theory because they had trouble imagining how the binding of a chemical to a receptor at the cell surface could influence the flow of ions through the cell membrane. Recently, however, researchers have gathered enough evidence for a convincing explanation: that the structure of receptors plays the pivotal role in mediating the conversion of chemical signals into electrical activity.

The new evidence shows that receptors for neurotransmitters contain both a neurotransmitter binding site and a separate region that functions as a channel for ions; attachment of the neurotransmitter to the binding site causes the receptor to change shape and so results in the opening of its channel component. Several types of receptors have been isolated that conform to this structure, among them the receptors for acetylcholine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glycine, and serotonin. These receptors display enough similarities to constitute a family, known collectively as neurotransmitter-gated ion channels.

It has also been discovered that each of the receptors in this family comes in several varieties so that, for example, a GABA receptor in one part of the brain has slightly different properties than a GABA receptor in another part of the brain. This discovery is medically significant because it raises the possibility of the highly selective treatment of certain brain disorders. As the precise effect on behavior of every variety of each neurotransmitter-gated ion channel is deciphered, pharmacologists may be able to design drugs targeted to specific receptors on defined categories of neurons that will selectively impede or enhance these effects. Such drugs could potentially help ameliorate any number of debilitating conditions, including mood disorders, tissue damage associated with stroke, or Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a theory that turned out to be wrong, and that is worth marking, because what follows is the history of a correction. Early Neurobiologists held that the brain works by electrical signals alone, with impulses literally leaping across the synapses, the gaps between neurons. Nobody could explain how such a leap would happen, and as early as 1904 some researchers proposed that the transfer is chemical instead. On that alternative account, an excited neuron secretes a chemical called a neurotransmitter, the chemical binds to its corresponding receptor molecule on the receiving neuron, the binding makes that neuron permeable to ions, and the ions moving in generate an electrical impulse that runs through the cell.

The theory's fortunes come next, along with the gap that stayed open. The chemical account gradually won acceptance in the scientific community, yet for a long time nobody knew by what mechanism a neurotransmitter renders the receiving neuron permeable to ions. That missing step kept The Skeptics in play, since they had trouble imagining how a chemical binding at the cell surface could influence the flow of ions through the membrane. Then comes the pivot the rest of the passage develops: researchers have recently gathered enough evidence for a convincing explanation, and it turns on the structure of the receptors themselves.

That explanation is structural and pleasingly simple. A receptor contains two parts, a site where the neurotransmitter binds and a separate region that functions as a channel for ions, and attachment of the neurotransmitter to the binding site changes the receptor's shape so that the channel opens. That is the entire mechanism, and it dissolves precisely the difficulty The Skeptics raised. Several receptors conforming to this design have been isolated, among them those for acetylcholine, gamma-aminobutyric acid, known as GABA, glycine and serotonin, and their similarities are close enough for the group to be treated as a family, the neurotransmitter-gated ion channels.

A refinement closes the passage, followed by what it might be good for. Each receptor in the family comes in several varieties, so a GABA receptor in one part of the brain has slightly different properties from a GABA receptor elsewhere. The medical significance rests on that variation. Once the precise effect on behavior of every variety is deciphered, pharmacologists may be able to design drugs aimed at specific receptors on defined categories of neurons, selectively impeding or enhancing those effects. Watch the hedged phrasing, since help for mood disorders, tissue damage from stroke and Alzheimer's disease is offered as a potential result rather than an accomplished one.
overall_html: The passage recounts how neurobiology moved from a purely electrical picture of communication between neurons to a chemical one, then explains the structural discovery that finally supplied the missing mechanism, receptors combining a neurotransmitter binding site with a separate ion channel that opens when the receptor changes shape. The author's purpose is expository, tracing a problem and its resolution in four steps, from the old electrical theory and its chemical rival, through the doubts that lingered while the mechanism was unknown, to the receptor family called neurotransmitter-gated ion channels, and finally to the prospect of drugs targeted at particular receptor varieties. No live dispute remains; Early Neurobiologists and The Skeptics figure as stages the evidence has moved past.

Often when a highly skilled and experienced employee leaves one company to work for another, there is the potential for a transfer of sensitive information between competitors. Two basic principles in such cases appear irreconcilable: the right of the company to its intellectual property—its proprietary data and trade secrets—and the right of individuals to seek gainful employment and to make free use of their abilities. Nevertheless, the courts have often tried to preserve both parties' legal rights by refusing to prohibit the employee from working for the competitor, but at the same time providing an injunction against disclosure of any of the former employer's secrets. It has been argued that because such measures help generate suspicions and similar psychological barriers to full and free utilization of abilities in the employee's new situation, they are hardly effective in upholding the individual's rights to free employment decisions. But it is also doubtful that they are effective in preserving trade secrets.

It is obviously impossible to divest oneself of that part of one's expertise that one has acquired from former employers and coworkers. Nor, in general, can one selectively refrain from its use, given that it has become an integral part of one's total intellectual capacity. Nevertheless, almost any such information that is not public knowledge may legitimately be claimed as corporate property: normal employment agreements provide for corporate ownership of all relevant data, including inventions, generated by the employee in connection with the company's business.

Once an employee takes a position with a competitor, the trade secrets that have been acquired by that employee may manifest themselves clearly and consciously. This is what court injunctions seek to prohibit. But they are far more likely to manifest themselves subconsciously and inconspicuously—for example, in one's daily decisions at the new post, or in the many small contributions one might make to a large team effort—often in the form of an intuitive sense of what to do or to avoid. Theoretically, an injunction also prohibits such inadvertent "leakage." However, the former employer faces the practical problem of securing evidence of such leakage, for little will usually be apparent from the public activities of the new employer. And even if the new employee's activities appear suspicious, there is the further problem of distinguishing trade secrets from what may be legitimately asserted as technological skills developed independently by the employee or already possessed by the new employer. This is a major stumbling block in the attempt to protect trade secrets, since the proprietor has no recourse against others who independently generate the same information. It is therefore unlikely that an injunction against disclosure of trade secrets to future employers actually prevents any transfer of information except for the passage of documents and other concrete embodiments of the secrets.
explanation_html:
The setup is a genuine conflict rather than a misunderstanding. When a highly skilled employee leaves for a competitor, sensitive information may travel along, and two principles collide: a company's right to its intellectual property, meaning proprietary data and trade secrets, and an individual's right to seek gainful employment and make free use of his or her abilities. The Courts have tried to honor both by refusing to bar the employee from working for the competitor while issuing an injunction against disclosing the former employer's secrets. Some Critics object that this compromise fails the employee, since the suspicions and psychological barriers it generates prevent abilities from being fully used at the new post. The final sentence is where The Author enters, doubting that the compromise preserves trade secrets either, and that doubt is the thesis of the passage.

Why the employee side of the problem is intractable comes next. Expertise picked up from former employers and coworkers cannot be divested, and in general it cannot be selectively withheld either, having become an integral part of one's total intellectual capacity. Set against that fact is the breadth of the employer's claim, since almost any information that is not public knowledge may legitimately be claimed as corporate property, normal employment agreements providing for company ownership of all relevant data, inventions included, generated by the employee in connection with the business. Two realities, badly matched.

The case for the author's thesis is then built in stages. Trade secrets may indeed manifest themselves clearly and consciously at the new post, which is what injunctions are written to prohibit. Far more often, though, they surface subconsciously and inconspicuously, in daily decisions or in small contributions to a large team effort, as an intuitive sense of what to do or avoid. Such inadvertent leakage is theoretically covered too, but the former employer then faces the practical problem of securing evidence, since little is apparent from the new employer's public activities. Even suspicious activity leaves a further obstacle, distinguishing trade secrets from skills the employee developed independently or knowledge the new employer already had, since a proprietor has no recourse against others who generate the same information on their own. Hence the verdict that injunctions are unlikely to prevent any transfer except of documents and other concrete embodiments.
overall_html: The passage argues that court injunctions forbidding a departing employee to disclose a former employer's trade secrets, while permitting that employee to work for a competitor, are unlikely to prevent much transfer of information beyond documents and other concrete embodiments of the secrets. The author's purpose is skeptical assessment, opening with the clash between corporate property rights and individual freedom to work along with the compromise The Courts devised, then observing that acquired expertise can neither be shed nor selectively suppressed, and finally showing that subconscious, inadvertent leakage is both the likelier form of transfer and nearly impossible to prove or to separate from independently developed skill. Some Critics doubt the compromise helps employees; The Author doubts it protects employers.

The following passages concern a plant called purple loosestrife. Passage A is excerpted from a report issued by a prairie research council; passage B from a journal of sociology.

Passage A

Purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria), an aggressive and invasive perennial of Eurasian origin, arrived with settlers in eastern North America in the early 1800s and has spread across the continent's midlatitude wetlands. The impact of purple loosestrife on native vegetation has been disastrous, with more than 50 percent of the biomass of some wetland communities displaced. Monospecific blocks of this weed have maintained themselves for at least 20 years. Impacts on wildlife have not been well studied, but serious reductions in waterfowl and aquatic furbearer productivity have been observed. In addition, several endangered species of vertebrates are threatened with further degradation of their breeding habitats. Although purple loosestrife can invade relatively undisturbed habitats, the spread and dominance of this weed have been greatly accelerated in disturbed habitats. While digging out the plants can temporarily halt their spread, there has been little research on long-term purple loosestrife control. Glyphosate has been used successfully, but no measure of the impact of this herbicide on native plant communities has been made.

 With the spread of purple loosestrife growing exponentially, some form of integrated control is needed. At present, coping with purple loosestrife hinges on early detection of the weed's arrival in areas, which allows local eradication to be carried out with minimum damage to the native plant community.

Passage B

 The war on purple loosestrife is apparently conducted on behalf of nature, an attempt to liberate the biotic community from the tyrannical influence of a life-destroying invasive weed. Indeed, purple loosestrife control is portrayed by its practitioners as an environmental initiative intended to save nature rather than control it. Accordingly, the purple loosestrife literature, scientific and otherwise, dutifully discusses the impacts of the weed on endangered species—and on threatened biodiversity more generally. Purple loosestrife is a pollution, according to the scientific community, and all of nature suffers under its pervasive influence.

Regardless of the perceived and actual ecological effects of the purple invader, it is apparent that popular pollution ideologies have been extended into the wetlands of North America. Consequently, the scientific effort to liberate nature from purple loosestrife has failed to decouple itself from its philosophical origin as an instrument to control nature to the satisfaction of human desires. Birds, particularly game birds and waterfowl, provide the bulk of the justification for loosestrife management. However, no bird species other than the canvasback has been identified in the literature as endangered by purple loosestrife. The impact of purple loosestrife on furbearing mammals is discussed at great length, though none of the species highlighted (muskrat, mink) can be considered threatened in North America. What is threatened by purple loosestrife is the economics of exploiting such preferred species and the millions of dollars that will be lost to the economies of the United States and Canada from reduced hunting, trapping, and recreation revenues due to a decline in the production of the wetland resource.
explanation_html:
Passage A writes from inside the control effort and frames the issue in ecological terms. Purple loosestrife is an aggressive Eurasian perennial that arrived with settlers in eastern North America in the early 1800s and has since spread across the continent's midlatitude wetlands, displacing more than half the biomass of some wetland communities and holding single-species stands for at least twenty years. Effects on wildlife are conceded to be poorly studied, though serious reductions in waterfowl and aquatic furbearer productivity have been observed and several endangered vertebrates face further degradation of their breeding habitats. Control options look thin: digging the plants out halts them only temporarily, long-term research is scarce, and glyphosate has worked without anyone measuring its effect on native plant communities.

That survey turns into a recommendation in a short second paragraph. With the spread growing exponentially, some form of integrated control is needed, and for now the workable approach depends on catching the invasion early. Detect the weed soon after it reaches an area and local eradication can be carried out with minimum damage to the surrounding native plant community. Notice that the goal of eradication is never itself put in question here.

Passage B questions precisely that, and it does so by examining how the campaign describes itself rather than by disputing how fast the plant spreads. The Critic observes that the war on purple loosestrife is portrayed as action taken on nature's behalf, an environmental initiative meant to save nature rather than control it, and that the literature, scientific and otherwise, dutifully rehearses the weed's impact on endangered species and on threatened biodiversity generally. The word to watch is pollution, since casting the plant as a pollutant makes all of nature its victim. Tone matters as much as content in this paragraph.

The critique then names what it takes to be the real motive. Whatever the plant's perceived and actual ecological effects, The Critic argues that popular pollution ideologies have been extended into North American wetlands, so the scientific effort to liberate nature has never decoupled itself from its philosophical origin as an instrument for controlling nature to satisfy human desires. The evidence offered is a mismatch between the justifications and the species involved: birds, particularly game birds and waterfowl, supply the bulk of the rationale, yet only the canvasback has been identified in the literature as endangered by the weed, and the furbearers discussed at length, muskrat and mink, are not threatened in North America. What is genuinely at risk, on this account, is revenue from hunting, trapping and recreation.
overall_html: The two passages take up the same invasive plant from incompatible angles. Passage A writes from within the management project, cataloguing purple loosestrife's spread and its damage to wetland biomass, waterfowl and furbearers, conceding how little is known about long-term control, and recommending early detection followed by local eradication. Passage B does not dispute those facts so much as examine the rhetoric around them, with The Critic arguing that the campaign borrows the language of pollution and claims to be rescuing nature even though the species invoked are largely not threatened, so that what the effort really protects is the hunting, trapping and recreation revenue attached to preferred species. Passage B is therefore a critique of assumptions Passage A takes for granted.

With their recognition of Maxine Hong Kingston as a major literary figure, some critics have suggested that her works have been produced almost ex nihilo, saying that they lack a large traceable body of direct literary antecedents especially within the Chinese American heritage in which her work is embedded. But these critics, who have examined only the development of written texts, the most visible signs of a culture's narrative production, have overlooked Kingston's connection to the long Chinese tradition of a highly developed genre of song and spoken narrative known as "talk-story" (gong gu tsai).

Traditionally performed in the dialects of various ethnic enclaves, talk-story has been maintained within the confines of the family and has rarely surfaced into print. The tradition dates back to Sung dynasty (A.D. 970–1279) storytellers in China, and in the United States it is continually revitalized by an overlapping sequence of immigration from China. Thus, Chinese immigrants to the U.S. had a fully established, sophisticated oral culture, already ancient and capable of producing masterpieces, by the time they began arriving in the early nineteenth century. This transplanted oral heritage simply embraced new subject matter or new forms of Western discourse, as in the case of Kingston's adaptations written in English.

Kingston herself believes that as a literary artist she is one in a long line of performers shaping a recalcitrant history into talk-story form. She distinguishes her "thematic" storytelling memory processes, which sift and reconstruct the essential elements of personally remembered stories, from the memory processes of a print-oriented culture that emphasizes the retention of precise sequences of words. Nor does the entry of print into the storytelling process substantially change her notion of the character of oral tradition. For Kingston, "writer" is synonymous with "singer" or "performer" in the ancient sense of privileged keeper, transmitter, and creator of stories whose current stage of development can be frozen in print, but which continue to grow both around and from that frozen text.

Kingston's participation in the tradition of talk-story is evidenced in her book China Men, which utilizes forms typical of that genre and common to most oral cultures including: a fixed "grammar" of repetitive themes; a spectrum of stock characters; symmetrical structures, including balanced oppositions (verbal or physical contests, antithetical characters, dialectical discourse such as question-answer forms and riddles); and repetition. In China Men, Kingston also succeeds in investing idiomatic English with the allusive texture and oral-aural qualities of the Chinese language, a language rich in aural and visual puns, making her work a written form of talk-story.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a claim the author intends to correct. The Critics, having elevated Maxine Hong Kingston to major status, describe her work as arriving out of nowhere, with no substantial body of literary ancestors behind it, least of all within Chinese American culture. The author's rebuttal identifies the blind spot precisely: these critics looked only at written texts, the most visible record a culture leaves, and so missed her debt to talk-story, a long-established Chinese genre of song and spoken narrative. Everything that follows exists to document that overlooked lineage.

Next comes the background needed to make the rebuttal stick. Talk-story is explained as a family-bound, dialect-based practice that almost never reached print, which is exactly why text-focused critics would fail to see it. The author then supplies its pedigree, tracing it to Sung dynasty storytellers roughly a thousand years ago and noting that waves of immigration kept refreshing it in the United States. The conclusion is pointed: Chinese immigrants of the early nineteenth century did not lack a literary culture, they carried a sophisticated one that simply absorbed new material and new Western forms, Kingston's English writing among them.

Attention shifts from the tradition to Kingston herself, now treated as a viewpoint in her own right. She places herself in a line of performers who shape difficult history into talk-story, and she draws a distinction worth holding onto: her memory works thematically, sifting and rebuilding the essentials of a remembered story, whereas print culture prizes getting the exact sequence of words right. Committing a story to print, she adds, does not alter the oral nature of the enterprise. For her, writer, singer and performer name the same role, and the printed text is a frozen stage that stories keep growing beyond.

The final paragraph supplies the concrete proof the argument has been building toward, turning a claim about heritage into observable features of a book. In China Men the author finds the standard equipment of oral genres: recurring themes functioning as a kind of grammar, a familiar cast of stock characters, symmetrical structures built on paired oppositions such as contests, opposed characters and question-and-answer exchanges, and outright repetition. Beyond structure, Kingston works the sound and suggestiveness of Chinese, a language dense with puns, into ordinary English, so that the finished book counts as talk-story in written form.
overall_html: The passage argues that Maxine Hong Kingston's writing, far from being without precedent, descends directly from talk-story, the centuries-old Chinese oral narrative tradition that immigrants carried to the United States and that critics missed because it rarely appeared in print. The author's purpose is corrective, moving from the critics' claim of an absent lineage, to a history of talk-story itself, to Kingston's own account of writing as performance, and finally to the formal features of China Men that demonstrate the inheritance. Two viewpoints matter: The Critics, whose text-only method produced the error, and Kingston, whose self-understanding the author endorses and then confirms with evidence.

In economics, the term "speculative bubble" refers to a large upward move in an asset's price driven not by the asset's fundamentals—that is, by the earnings derivable from the asset—but rather by mere speculation that someone else will be willing to pay a higher price for it. The price increase is then followed by a dramatic decline in price, due to a loss in confidence that the price will continue to rise, and the "bubble" is said to have burst. According to Charles Mackay's classic nineteenth-century account, the seventeenth-century Dutch tulip market provides an example of a speculative bubble. But the economist Peter Garber challenges Mackay's view, arguing that there is no evidence that the Dutch tulip market really involved a speculative bubble.

By the seventeenth century, the Netherlands had become a center of cultivation and development of new tulip varieties, and a market had developed in which rare varieties of bulbs sold at high prices. For example, a Semper Augustus bulb sold in 1625 for an amount of gold worth about U.S.$11,000 in 1999. Common bulb varieties, on the other hand, sold for very low prices. According to Mackay, by 1636 rapid price rises attracted speculators, and prices of many varieties surged upward from November 1636 through January 1637. Mackay further states that in February 1637 prices suddenly collapsed; bulbs could not be sold at 10 percent of their peak values. By 1739, the prices of all the most prized kinds of bulbs had fallen to no more than one two-hundredth of 1 percent of Semper Augustus's peak price.

Garber acknowledges that bulb prices increased dramatically from 1636 to 1637 and eventually reached very low levels. But he argues that this episode should not be described as a speculative bubble, for the increase and eventual decline in bulb prices can be explained in terms of the fundamentals. Garber argues that a standard pricing pattern occurs for new varieties of flowers. When a particularly prized variety is developed, its original bulb sells for a high price. Thus, the dramatic rise in the price of some original tulip bulbs could have resulted as tulips in general, and certain varieties in particular, became fashionable. However, as the prized bulbs become more readily available through reproduction from the original bulb, their price falls rapidly; after less than 30 years, bulbs sell at reproduction cost. But this does not mean that the high prices of original bulbs are irrational, for earnings derivable from the millions of bulbs descendent from the original bulbs can be very high, even if each individual descendent bulb commands a very low price. Given that an original bulb can generate a reasonable return on investment even if the price of descendent bulbs decreases dramatically, a rapid rise and eventual fall of tulip bulb prices need not indicate a speculative bubble.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph does two jobs: it defines the technical term the whole passage turns on, and it sets up a dispute about whether that term applies to a famous historical case. A speculative bubble is a price surge driven not by fundamentals, meaning the earnings the asset can actually produce, but purely by the expectation that someone else will pay more later, followed by a collapse once that confidence evaporates. Mackay, writing in the nineteenth century, treats the seventeenth-century Dutch tulip market as a textbook instance. Garber denies it, saying the evidence for a bubble is not there. Notice that the disagreement is about interpretation, not about the raw prices.

Here you get the factual record both sides work from, presented in the author's neutral voice. The Netherlands had become a hub for breeding new tulip varieties, and rare bulbs commanded enormous sums while ordinary ones stayed cheap. Mackay's narrative is then laid over those facts: speculators arrived as prices climbed, values surged through the winter of 1636 into 1637, and in February 1637 the market broke so badly that bulbs would not fetch a tenth of their peak. The long decline that followed left even the most prized varieties at a minute fraction of the old top price. Keep this data separate from the interpretation, because the next paragraph accepts the data and rejects the interpretation.

The final paragraph gives Garber's alternative explanation, and it is the heart of the passage. He grants the rise and the eventual collapse, then argues both follow from fundamentals rather than from speculative mania. His model is a normal pricing pattern for newly bred flowers: a prized new variety exists as a single original bulb, so it sells dear, and fashion can push that price higher still. As the variety is propagated it becomes common and the price falls toward the cost of reproduction. Crucially, that decline does not make the original price irrational, since the original bulb yields millions of descendants whose combined earnings can repay the investment even at low unit prices.
overall_html: The passage examines whether the seventeenth-century Dutch tulip market was a speculative bubble, setting Mackay's classic account of mania and crash against Garber's argument that the same price history is fully explained by fundamentals, since an original bulb of a prized new variety can earn a strong return through its many descendants even as their individual prices collapse. The author's purpose is expository rather than partisan, defining the key term, laying out the agreed factual record of prices from 1625 through the crash of 1637, and then presenting Garber's reinterpretation of that record. The two viewpoints to keep apart are Mackay's bubble reading and Garber's fundamentals-based challenge to it.

With his first published works in the 1950s, Amos Tutuola became the first Nigerian writer to receive wide international recognition. Written in a mix of standard English, idiomatic Nigerian English, and literal translation of his native language, Yoruba, Tutuola's works were quick to be praised by many literary critics as fresh, inventive approaches to the form of the novel. Others, however, dismissed his works as simple retellings of local tales, full of unwelcome liberties taken with the details of the well-known story lines. However, to estimate properly Tutuola's rightful position in world literature, it is essential to be clear about the genre in which he wrote; literary critics have assumed too facilely that he wrote novels.

No matter how flexible a definition of the novel one uses, establishing a set of criteria that enable Tutuola's works to be described as such applies to his works a body of assumptions the works are not designed to satisfy. Tutuola is not a novelist but a teller of folktales. Many of his critics are right to suggest that Tutuola's subjects are not strikingly original, but it is important to bear in mind that whereas realism and originality are expected of the novel, the teller of folktales is expected to derive subjects and frameworks from the corpus of traditional lore. The most useful approach to Tutuola's works, then, is one that regards him as working within the African oral tradition.

Within this tradition, a folktale is common property, an expression of a people's culture and social circumstances. The teller of folktales knows that the basic story is already known to most listeners and, equally, that the teller's reputation depends on the inventiveness with which the tale is modified and embellished, for what the audience anticipates is not an accurate retelling of the story but effective improvisation and delivery. Thus, within the framework of the basic story, the teller is allowed considerable room to maneuver—in fact, the most brilliant tellers of folktales transform them into unique works.

Tutuola's adherence to this tradition is clear: specific episodes, for example, are often repeated for emphasis, and he embellishes familiar tales with personal interpretations or by transferring them to modern settings. The blend of English with local idiom and Yoruba grammatical constructs, in which adjectives and verbs are often interchangeable, re-creates the folktales in singular ways. And, perhaps most revealingly, in the majority of Tutuola's works, the traditional accents and techniques of the teller of folktales are clearly discernible, for example in the adoption of an omniscient, summarizing voice at the end of his narratives, a device that is generally recognized as being employed to conclude most folktales.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up a reputation and then a dispute about how to read it. Amos Tutuola was the first Nigerian writer to win wide international attention, writing in a blend of standard English, Nigerian idiom and phrasing carried straight over from Yoruba. The Admiring Critics called this a fresh reworking of the novel form, while The Dismissive Critics saw only local tales retold with careless changes. The Author then states the thesis and it is not a compromise between the two camps: both sides went wrong earlier, by assuming without argument that what Tutuola wrote were novels.

The thesis gets its defense here, and the move is a reclassification rather than a defense of quality. Stretch the definition of the novel however you like, the author argues, and you still end up judging Tutuola by expectations his work was never built to meet. He is a teller of folktales, not a novelist. That reframing disarms The Dismissive Critics without denying their observation: they were right that his subjects are unoriginal, but originality and realism are demands the novel makes, whereas a folktale teller is supposed to take subjects and structures from inherited lore. The proper frame is the African oral tradition.

Before applying that frame, the author explains how it works. In the oral tradition a folktale belongs to everyone, carrying a community's culture and circumstances rather than an individual's invention. The teller assumes the audience already knows the plot, so reputation rests entirely on how inventively the tale is altered and decorated; listeners come for improvisation and delivery, not fidelity. Watch what this does to the earlier complaint about liberties taken with familiar story lines. Within the fixed outline the teller has wide latitude, and the finest tellers turn a shared story into something singular.

The closing paragraph tests Tutuola against the criteria just established, and he satisfies them point by point. Episodes recur for emphasis, familiar tales are reshaped by personal interpretation or moved into modern settings, and the mixture of English with local idiom and Yoruba structures, where adjectives and verbs can trade places, remakes the stories in a distinctive voice. The author saves the most telling evidence for last: the audible presence of the storyteller's own techniques, particularly the shift to an omniscient summarizing voice at the close, a signature ending of folktales rather than of novels.
overall_html: The passage argues that Tutuola has been misjudged because critics on both sides assumed he was writing novels, when his work belongs to the African oral tradition of folktale telling, where derived subjects and inventive embellishment are the expected virtues rather than failings. The author's purpose is to reclassify the work so it can be evaluated fairly, moving from the critical dispute, to the claim that novel criteria do not apply, to an account of how folktale telling operates, and finally to the specific features of Tutuola's writing that fit that account. Three viewpoints run through it: the critics who praised him as a novelist, those who dismissed him as a mere reteller, and the author's own reframing.

Mechanisms for recognizing kin are found throughout the plant and animal kingdoms, regardless of an organism's social or mental complexity. Improvements in the general understanding of these mechanisms have turned some biologists' attention to the question of why kin recognition occurs at all. One response to this question is offered by the inclusive fitness theory, which was developed in the 1960s. The theory is based on the realization that an organism transmits its genetic attributes to succeeding generations not solely through its offspring, but more generally through all of its close relatives. Whereas the traditional view of evolution held that natural selection favors the continued genetic representation of individuals within a species that produce the greatest number of offspring, the inclusive fitness theory posits that natural selection similarly favors organisms that help their relatives, because doing so also increases their own total genetic representation. The theory has helped to explain previously mysterious phenomena, including the evolution of social insect species like the honeybee, most of whose members do not produce offspring and exist only to nurture relatives.

Inclusive fitness theory has also been applied usefully to new findings concerning cannibalism within animal species. Based on the theory, cannibals should have evolved to avoid eating their own kin because of the obvious genetic costs of such a practice. Spadefoot toad tadpoles provide an illustration. Biologists have found that all tadpoles of that species begin life as omnivores, feeding mainly on organic debris in their soon-to-be-dry pool in the desert, but that occasionally one tadpole eats another or eats a freshwater shrimp. This event can trigger changes in the tadpole's physiology and dietary preference, causing the tadpole to become larger and exclusively carnivorous, feasting on other animals including members of its own species. Yet the cannibals have a procedure of discrimination whereby they nip at other tadpoles, eating nonsiblings but releasing siblings unharmed. This suggests that the inclusive fitness theory offers at least a partial answer to why kin recognition develops. Interestingly, a cannibal tadpole is less likely to avoid eating kin when it becomes very hungry, apparently putting its own unique genetic makeup ahead of its siblings'.

But there may be other reasons why organisms recognize kin. For example, it has recently been found that tiger salamander larvae, also either omnivorous or cannibalistic, are plagued in nature by a deadly bacterium. Furthermore, it was determined that cannibal larvae are especially likely to be infected by eating diseased species members. The fact that this bacterium is more deadly when it comes from a close relative with a similar immune system suggests that natural selection may favor cannibals that avoid such pathogens by not eating kin. For tiger salamanders then, kin recognition can be explained simply as a means by which an organism preserves its own life, not as a means to aid in relatives' survival.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a puzzle and the leading answer to it. Kin recognition turns up all over the plant and animal kingdoms, in organisms with no social or mental sophistication at all, which raises the question of why it should exist. The Inclusive Fitness Theory, from the 1960s, supplies one answer built on a shift in what counts as passing on your genes. Traditional evolutionary thinking rewarded whoever produced the most offspring; inclusive fitness notes that relatives carry your genetic material too, so helping them also boosts your own genetic representation. Its showpiece is the honeybee, whose sterile members exist to raise relatives.

Next the theory is put to work on cannibalism, and the prediction is straightforward: if eating a relative destroys copies of your own genes, selection should build in a way to avoid it. The spadefoot toad supplies the test case. Tadpoles start out omnivorous, scavenging debris in a drying desert pool, but one that happens to eat another tadpole or a shrimp transforms, growing larger and turning strictly carnivorous. The revealing detail is the sorting behavior: the cannibal nips at others, swallows nonsiblings and lets siblings go. Note the limit the author flags, since a starving cannibal stops discriminating, favoring its own survival over its siblings'.

The final paragraph opens a competing explanation rather than overturning the first, and the pivot word signals it. Tiger salamander larvae, likewise omnivorous or cannibalistic, face a lethal bacterium in the wild, and cannibals catch it by eating infected members of their own species. The crucial finding is that the pathogen does more damage when it comes from a close relative, whose immune system resembles the eater's. So selection could favor avoiding kin purely for self-protection. For these salamanders, kin recognition preserves the individual's own life rather than serving relatives' survival.
overall_html: The passage asks why organisms recognize their kin, presents inclusive fitness theory as the standard answer, illustrates it with spadefoot toad tadpoles that spare their siblings while eating unrelated tadpoles, and then offers tiger salamanders as a case where kin avoidance is better explained by self-preservation, since a deadly bacterium is most dangerous when caught from a close relative. The author's purpose is to show that a single behavior may have more than one evolutionary explanation, moving from theory, to a confirming example, to a case the theory does not cover. The only real viewpoint developed is inclusive fitness theory itself, which the author treats as useful but incomplete.
