The following passages are adapted from critical essays on the American writer Willa Cather (1873–1947).

Passage A

When Cather gave examples of high quality in fiction, she invariably cited Russian writers Ivan Turgenev or Leo Tolstoy or both. Indeed, Edmund Wilson noted in 1922 that Cather followed the manner of Turgenev, not depicting her characters' emotions directly but telling us how they behave and letting their "inner blaze of glory shine through the simple recital." Turgenev's method was to select details that described a character's appearance and actions without trying to explain them. A writer, he said, "must be a psychologist—but a secret one; he must know and feel the roots of phenomena, but only present the phenomena themselves." Similarly, he argued that a writer must have complete knowledge of a character so as to avoid overloading the work with unnecessary detail, concentrating instead on what is characteristic and typical.

Here we have an impressionistic aesthetic that anticipates Cather's: what Turgenev referred to as secret knowledge Cather called "the thing not named." In one essay she writes that "whatever is felt upon the page without being specifically named there—that, one might say, is created." For both writers, there is the absolute importance of selection and simplification; for both, art is the fusing of the physical world of setting and actions with the emotional reality of the characters. What synthesizes all the elements of narrative for these writers is the establishment of a prevailing mood.

Passage B

 In a famous 1927 letter, Cather writes of her novel Death Comes for the Archbishop, "Many [reviewers] assert vehemently that it is not a novel. Myself, I prefer to call it a narrative." Cather's preference anticipated an important reformulation of the criticism of fiction: the body of literary theory, called "narratology," articulated by French literary theorists in the 1960s. This approach broadens and simplifies the fundamental paradigms according to which we view fiction: they ask of narrative only that it be narrative, that it tell a story. Narratologists tend not to focus on the characteristics of narrative's dominant modern Western form, the "realistic novel": direct psychological characterization, realistic treatment of time, causal plotting, logical closure. Such a model of criticism, which takes as its object "narrative" rather than the "novel," seems exactly appropriate to Cather's work.

Indeed, her severest critics have always questioned precisely her capabilities as a novelist. Morton Zabel argued that "[Cather's] themes...could readily fail to find the structure and substance that might have given them life or redeemed them from the tenuity of a sketch"; Leon Edel called one of her novels "two inconclusive fragments." These critics and others like them treat as failures some of the central features of Cather's impressionistic technique: unusual treatment of narrative time, unexpected focus, ambiguous conclusions, a preference for the bold, simple, and stylized in character as well as in landscape. These "non-novelistic" structures indirectly articulate the essential and conflicting forces of desire at work throughout Cather's fiction.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by grounding Cather's practice in a literary lineage. Whenever Cather pointed to fiction she admired she named the Russians, Turgenev or Tolstoy, and Edmund Wilson had already noticed in 1922 that she wrote in Turgenev's manner: emotion is never stated outright, only allowed to show through what characters do. The method Turgenev described is deliberately restrained, choosing details of appearance and action, presenting the phenomena without explaining them, and keeping the psychology hidden. Knowing a character completely is what makes that restraint possible, since it lets a writer discard everything that is not characteristic. Notice that nothing is in dispute yet; A is establishing a shared technique.

The second paragraph names the aesthetic and makes the parallel explicit. Turgenev's secret knowledge and Cather's phrase about the thing not named are treated as one idea under two labels: what is felt on the page without being stated is what the writing actually creates. Impressionistic, in this context, simply means suggesting rather than reporting. Both writers depend on selection and simplification, both fuse the physical world of setting and action with the emotional reality of their characters, and for both the element that binds a narrative together is a prevailing mood rather than plot machinery. This completes A's case that Turgenev anticipated Cather.

Passage B starts from Cather's own vocabulary rather than her influences. Reviewers of Death Comes for the Archbishop insisted it was not a novel, and she answered that she would rather call it a narrative, a preference B reads as anticipating the narratologists, the French theorists of the 1960s who asked of narrative only that it tell a story. That move matters because it drops the checklist by which the realistic novel is normally judged: direct psychological characterization, realistic treatment of time, causal plotting, logical closure. B's claim is that a criticism organized around narrative rather than the novel is the frame Cather's work actually fits.

The closing paragraph shows what the wrong frame costs. Cather's critics have attacked her precisely as a novelist, Zabel doubting that her themes ever found structure and Edel dismissing one book as inconclusive fragments, and B's response is that the traits they log as failures are the defining features of her impressionistic method: unusual handling of narrative time, unexpected focus, endings left ambiguous, character and landscape rendered bold and simple. Read as technique rather than incompetence, these non-novelistic structures are the indirect means by which her fiction articulates its conflicting forces of desire.
overall_html: Both passages set out to explain what makes Cather's fiction distinctive, but they come at it from different directions: Passage A traces her impressionistic technique of suggestion, selection and prevailing mood back to Turgenev's example, while Passage B argues that the standards of the realistic novel misjudge her work and that narratology, which asks only that a narrative tell a story, supplies the appropriate critical frame. Their purposes are complementary rather than opposed, A providing the aesthetic genealogy and B the critical vocabulary, and the very features A praises as Turgenevian restraint are the ones B says her critics wrongly counted as failures.

Fractal geometry is a mathematical theory devoted to the study of complex shapes called fractals. Although an exact definition of fractals has not been established, fractals commonly exhibit the property of self-similarity: the reiteration of irregular details or patterns at progressively smaller scales so that each part, when magnified, looks basically like the object as a whole. The Koch curve is a significant fractal in mathematics and examining it provides some insight into fractal geometry. To generate the Koch curve, one begins with a straight line. The middle third of the line is removed and replaced with two line segments, each as long as the removed piece, which are positioned so as to meet and form the top of a triangle. At this stage, the curve consists of four connected segments of equal length that form a pointed protrusion in the middle. This process is repeated on the four segments so that all the protrusions are on the same side of the curve, and then the process is repeated indefinitely on the segments at each stage of the construction.

Self-similarity is built into the construction process by treating segments at each stage the same way as the original segment was treated. Since the rules for getting from one stage to another are fully explicit and always the same, images of successive stages of the process can be generated by computer. Theoretically, the Koch curve is the result of infinitely many steps in the construction process, but the finest image approximating the Koch curve will be limited by the fact that eventually the segments will get too short to be drawn or displayed. However, using computer graphics to produce images of successive stages of the construction process dramatically illustrates a major attraction of fractal geometry: simple processes can be responsible for incredibly complex patterns.

A worldwide public has become captivated by fractal geometry after viewing astonishing computer-generated images of fractals; enthusiastic practitioners in the field of fractal geometry consider it a new language for describing complex natural and mathematical forms. They anticipate that fractal geometry's significance will rival that of calculus and expect that proficiency in fractal geometry will allow mathematicians to describe the form of a cloud as easily and precisely as an architect can describe a house using the language of traditional geometry. Other mathematicians have reservations about the fractal geometers' preoccupation with computer-generated graphic images and their lack of interest in theory. These mathematicians point out that traditional mathematics consists of proving theorems, and while many theorems about fractals have already been proven using the notions of pre-fractal mathematics, fractal geometers have proven only a handful of theorems that could not have been proven with pre-fractal mathematics. According to these mathematicians, fractal geometry can attain a lasting role in mathematics only if it becomes a precise language supporting a system of theorems and proofs.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by defining its subject and then immediately grounding it in one worked example. Fractal geometry studies complex shapes whose defining habit is self-similarity: the same irregular pattern reappears at smaller and smaller scales, so magnifying a piece gives you something that looks like the whole. Notice the hedge that an exact definition has not been settled, which matters later. The Koch curve is then built step by step: take a line, cut out the middle third, replace it with two segments of that same length angled to form the peak of a triangle, and repeat the operation on every resulting segment, always bumping the peaks out the same side.

Having built the object, the author explains why it behaves as it does and what makes it useful. Self-similarity is not discovered in the Koch curve; it is designed in, because every stage applies the identical rule to every segment. That is also what makes the curve a natural fit for a computer, since fully explicit and unchanging instructions can simply be run again and again. Two limits are worth holding apart: the true Koch curve requires infinitely many steps, while any drawn image stops once the segments become too small to render. The payoff the author highlights is the appeal of the field, that very simple procedures can generate extraordinarily complicated patterns.

Only in the final paragraph does a disagreement appear, and it splits cleanly in two. The fractal geometers, along with a public captivated by the computer imagery, treat the field as a new language for describing natural and mathematical forms and expect it to rival calculus, so that a cloud could be specified as precisely as an architect specifies a house. Other mathematicians object that fascination with pictures has crowded out theory: traditional mathematics proves theorems, and fractal geometers have proved only a handful that older methods could not already handle. Their condition is explicit, that the field earns a lasting place only by becoming a precise language supporting theorems and proofs.
overall_html: The passage introduces fractal geometry through the self-similar Koch curve, showing how a simple repeated construction rule generates enormous complexity, and then reports a dispute over whether the field deserves the status its enthusiasts claim for it. The author's purpose is largely expository, moving from definition and worked example, to the role of computer generation and the simple-process insight, before turning in the last paragraph to evaluation. Two viewpoints appear only at that point: the fractal geometers, who see a new descriptive language rivalling calculus, and other mathematicians, who note the shortage of genuinely new theorems and insist the field must support proofs to endure.

Traditional sources of evidence about ancient history are archaeological remains and surviving texts. Those investigating the crafts practiced by women in ancient times, however, often derive little information from these sources, and the archaeological record is particularly unavailing for the study of ancient textile production, as researchers are thwarted by the perishable nature of cloth. What shreds persisted through millennia were, until recently, often discarded by excavators as useless, as were loom weights, which appeared to be nothing more than blobs of clay. Ancient texts, meanwhile, rarely mention the creation of textiles; moreover, those references that do exist use archaic, unrevealing terminology. Yet despite these obstacles, researchers have learned a great deal about ancient textiles and those who made them, and also about how to piece together a whole picture from many disparate sources of evidence.

Technological advances in the analysis of archaeological remains provide much more information than was previously available, especially about minute remains. Successful modern methods include radiocarbon dating, infrared photography for seeing through dirt without removing it, isotope "fingerprinting" for tracing sources of raw materials, and thin-layer chromatography for analyzing dyes. As if in preparation for such advances, the field of archaeology has also undergone an important philosophical revolution in the past century. Once little more than a self-serving quest for artifacts to stock museums and private collections, the field has transformed itself into a scientific pursuit of knowledge about past cultures. As part of this process, archaeologists adopted the fundamental precept of preserving all objects, even those that have no immediately discernible value. Thus in the 1970s two researchers found the oldest known complete garment, a 5,000-year-old linen shirt, among a tumbled heap of dirty linens that had been preserved as part of the well-known Petrie collection decades before anyone began to study the history of textiles.

The history of textiles and of the craftswomen who produced them has also advanced on a different front: recreating the actual production of cloth. Reconstructing and implementing ancient production methods provides a valuable way of generating and checking hypotheses. For example, these techniques made it possible to confirm that the excavated pieces of clay once considered useless in fact functioned as loom weights. Similarly, scholars have until recently been obliged to speculate as to which one of two statues of Athena, one large and one small, was adorned with a dress created by a group of Athenian women for a festival, as described in surviving texts. Because records show that it took nine months to produce the dress, scholars assumed it must have adorned the large statue. But by investigating the methods of production and the size of the looms used, researchers have ascertained that in fact a dress for the small statue would have taken nine months to produce.
explanation_html:
Start by registering the problem the passage exists to solve. Ancient history normally rests on two pillars, physical remains and surviving texts, and both fail badly for the crafts women practiced, textile production most of all. Cloth rots, so almost nothing survives; the scraps that did survive were routinely thrown away by excavators as worthless, and loom weights were discarded because they looked like shapeless lumps of clay. Texts barely mention textiles, and when they do the vocabulary is archaic and tells you little. The last sentence supplies the thesis and the structure to come: despite all that, researchers have learned a great deal, partly by learning to assemble a picture from scattered evidence.

The first line of progress is the archaeological record itself, improved on two fronts at once. Technically, new methods extract far more from tiny remains, including radiocarbon dating, infrared photography that sees through dirt without disturbing it, isotope fingerprinting that identifies where raw materials came from, and chromatography that identifies dyes. Just as important is an attitude shift: archaeology stopped being a hunt for display-worthy objects and became a science of past cultures, which brought with it the rule that everything is kept, even material with no obvious value. The payoff is concrete, since the oldest known complete garment turned up in a heap of dirty linens preserved decades earlier.

The closing paragraph opens a second and quite different front: instead of analyzing what survives, researchers rebuild ancient production and run it. Reconstruction is presented as a way both to generate hypotheses and to test them, and two examples show each use. Recreating the work confirmed that those unpromising lumps of clay really were loom weights. The Athena example is the stronger one, because it overturns a settled assumption: scholars had reasoned that a dress recorded as taking nine months to make must have clothed the large statue, but studying the actual looms and methods showed that nine months is what the small statue's dress would have required.
overall_html: The passage argues that although the standard evidence of ancient history serves the study of women's textile work poorly, researchers have nonetheless recovered a great deal by combining improved analysis of surviving remains with experimental reconstruction of ancient production. The author's purpose is to explain how that obstacle was overcome, and the structure follows directly from it: one paragraph laying out why cloth, loom weights and texts yield so little, then one paragraph on new techniques and archaeology's shift toward preserving everything, then one on recreating production, closing with the Athena dress example in which reconstruction corrected a long-standing scholarly assumption. Only the author's own explanatory voice is present.

This passage was adapted from articles published in the 1990s.

The success that Nigerian-born computer scientist Philip Emeagwali (b. 1954) has had in designing computers that solve real-world problems has been fueled by his willingness to reach beyond established paradigms and draw inspiration for his designs from nature. In the 1980s, Emeagwali achieved breakthroughs in the design of parallel computer systems. Whereas single computers work sequentially, making one calculation at a time, computers connected in parallel can process calculations simultaneously. In 1989, Emeagwali pioneered the use of massively parallel computers that used a network of thousands of smaller computers to solve what is considered one of the most computationally difficult problems: predicting the flow of oil through the subterranean geologic formations that make up oil fields. Until that time, supercomputers had been used for oil field calculations, but because these supercomputers worked sequentially, they were too slow and inefficient to accurately predict such extremely complex movements.

To model oil field flow using a computer requires the simulation of the distribution of the oil at tens of thousands of locations throughout the field. At each location, hundreds of simultaneous calculations must be made at regular time intervals relating to such variables as temperature, direction of oil flow, viscosity, and pressure, as well as geologic properties of the basin holding the oil. In order to solve this problem, Emeagwali designed a massively parallel computer by using the Internet to connect to more than 65,000 smaller computers. One of the great difficulties of parallel computing is dividing up the tasks among the separate smaller computers so that they do not interfere with each other, and it was here that Emeagwali turned to natural processes for ideas, noting that tree species that survive today are those that, over the course of hundreds of millions of years, have developed branching patterns that have maximized the amount of sunlight gathered and the quantity of water and sap delivered. Emeagwali demonstrated that, for modeling certain phenomena such as subterranean oil flow, a network design based on the mathematical principle that underlies the branching structures of trees will enable a massively parallel computer to gather and broadcast the largest quantity of messages to its processing points in the shortest time.

In 1996 Emeagwali had another breakthrough when he presented the design for a massively parallel computer that he claims will be powerful enough to predict global weather patterns a century in advance. The computer's design is based on the geometry of bees' honeycombs, which use an extremely efficient three-dimensional spacing. Emeagwali believes that computer scientists in the future will increasingly look to nature for elegant solutions to complex technical problems. This paradigm shift, he asserts, will enable us to better understand the systems evolved by nature and, thereby, to facilitate the evolution of human technology.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph frames Emeagwali's career around a single organizing idea: he solves practical computing problems by looking outside established design conventions and borrowing from nature. The technical background you need is simple. A single computer works sequentially, handling one calculation at a time, while computers linked in parallel handle many at once. Emeagwali's 1989 achievement was using massively parallel computing, thousands of small machines working together, on a notoriously hard problem: predicting how oil moves through underground rock formations. The point of contrast is that supercomputers had been doing this job sequentially and were too slow and inefficient to model such complex movement accurately.

The middle paragraph supplies the detail that makes the achievement intelligible. Simulating an oil field means tracking distribution at tens of thousands of locations, each demanding hundreds of simultaneous calculations at regular intervals for variables like temperature, flow direction, viscosity, pressure and the geology of the basin. Emeagwali linked more than 65,000 small computers over the Internet. The real obstacle in parallel computing is dividing work so the machines do not interfere with each other, and this is where the nature theme becomes concrete: surviving tree species evolved branching patterns that maximize sunlight, water and sap delivery, and a network built on that same mathematical principle moves the most messages in the least time.

The closing paragraph extends the pattern forward in time and then generalizes it. Emeagwali's 1996 design, which he claims could forecast global weather a century ahead, borrows the efficient three-dimensional spacing of bees' honeycombs, so the nature-as-model method is shown working twice rather than once. The last two sentences shift from reporting accomplishments to reporting a prediction and a claim, both attributed to Emeagwali rather than asserted by the author: computer scientists will increasingly turn to nature, and doing so will both deepen our understanding of natural systems and speed the evolution of human technology.
overall_html: The passage presents Philip Emeagwali as a computer scientist whose major advances in massively parallel computing came from modeling machine architecture on natural structures, first the branching geometry of trees for predicting subterranean oil flow and later the spacing of honeycombs for long-range weather prediction. The author's purpose is expository and admiring rather than argumentative, moving from the breakthrough and the sequential-versus-parallel contrast that makes it significant, through the technical problem of dividing tasks among linked computers, to a second application and Emeagwali's own forecast of a broader shift toward nature-inspired design. Emeagwali is the only viewpoint developed, and the closing predictions are carefully attributed to him.

Proponents of the tangible-object theory of copyright argue that copyright and similar intellectual-property rights can be explained as logical extensions of the right to own concrete, tangible objects. This view depends on the claim that every copyrightable work can be manifested in some physical form, such as a manuscript or a videotape. It also accepts the premise that ownership of an object confers a number of rights on the owner, who may essentially do whatever he or she pleases with the object to the extent that this does not violate other people's rights. One may, for example, hide or display the object, copy it, or destroy it. One may also transfer ownership of it to another.

In creating a new and original object from materials that one owns, one becomes the owner of that object and thereby acquires all of the rights that ownership entails. But if the owner transfers ownership of the object, the full complement of rights is not necessarily transferred to the new owner; instead, the original owner may retain one or more of these rights. This notion of retained rights is common in many areas of law; for example, the seller of a piece of land may retain certain rights to the land in the form of easements or building restrictions. Applying the notion of retained rights to the domain of intellectual property, theorists argue that copyrighting a work secures official recognition of one's intention to retain certain rights to that work. Among the rights typically retained by the original producer of an object such as a literary manuscript or a musical score would be the right to copy the object for profit and the right to use it as a guide for the production of similar or analogous things—for example, a public performance of a musical score.

According to proponents of the tangible-object theory, its chief advantage is that it justifies intellectual property rights without recourse to the widely accepted but problematic supposition that one can own abstract, intangible things such as ideas. But while this account seems plausible for copyrightable entities that do, in fact, have enduring tangible forms, it cannot accommodate the standard assumption that such evanescent things as live broadcasts of sporting events can be copyrighted. More importantly, it does not acknowledge that in many cases the work of conceiving ideas is more crucial and more valuable than that of putting them into tangible form. Suppose that a poet dictates a new poem to a friend, who writes it down on paper that the friend has supplied. The creator of the tangible object in this case is not the poet but the friend, and there would seem to be no ground for the poet's claiming copyright unless the poet can be said to already own the ideas expressed in the work.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out a theory the author will later test, so read it as reported position rather than settled truth. The tangible-object theorists hold that copyright and related intellectual-property rights are nothing exotic; they are extensions of the ordinary right to own physical things. Two commitments carry that claim. First, anything copyrightable can take some physical form, a manuscript or a videotape. Second, owning an object brings a bundle of rights, so that within the limits set by other people's rights the owner may hide the thing, display it, copy it, destroy it, or hand ownership to someone else.

The second paragraph supplies the machinery that turns ownership into copyright, and the key idea is retention. Make something new from materials you own and you own the result together with the whole bundle of rights. Transfer that object, though, and the bundle need not travel intact; the original owner can hold specific rights back. The author stresses that this is familiar law rather than a special pleading, pointing to a seller of land keeping easements or building restrictions. Copyrighting a work, on this account, is simply official recognition that the maker retains particular rights, notably copying for profit and using the work as a guide to produce analogous things, such as performing a score.

The final paragraph is where the author steps forward as a critic. The advantage is granted first: the theory explains intellectual property without the awkward idea that anyone can own something abstract like an idea. Then the objections land. Some copyrightable things, such as a live broadcast of a sporting event, have no enduring physical form, yet everyone assumes they can be copyrighted. More seriously, the theory ignores that conceiving ideas is often the harder and more valuable work. The dictation example makes it sharp: the friend who writes the poem down owns the tangible object, so the poet has no claim unless the ideas themselves were already owned.
overall_html: The passage explains the tangible-object theory of copyright, which derives intellectual-property rights from ordinary ownership of physical objects plus the familiar legal notion that a seller can retain certain rights, and then argues that the theory fails at two points. The author's purpose is first expository and finally critical, devoting the opening paragraphs to a fair statement of the position and the closing one to its limits: evanescent works such as live broadcasts have no lasting physical form, and the theory undervalues conceiving ideas relative to embodying them. Two viewpoints matter, the tangible-object theorists and the author who ultimately rejects their account.

Passage A

In music, a certain complexity of sounds can be expected to have a positive effect on the listener. A single, pure tone is not that interesting to explore; a measure of intricacy is required to excite human curiosity. Sounds that are too complex or disorganized, however, tend to be overwhelming. We prefer some sort of coherence, a principle that connects the various sounds and makes them comprehensible.

In this respect, music is like human language. Single sounds are in most cases not sufficient to convey meaning in speech, whereas when put together in a sequence they form words and sentences. Likewise, if the tones in music are not perceived to be tied together sequentially or rhythmically—for example, in what is commonly called melody—listeners are less likely to feel any emotional connection or to show appreciation.

Certain music can also have a relaxing effect. The fact that such music tends to be continuous and rhythmical suggests a possible explanation for this effect. In a natural environment, danger tends to be accompanied by sudden, unexpected sounds. Thus, a background of constant noise suggests peaceful conditions; discontinuous sounds demand more attention. Even soft discontinuous sounds that we consciously realize do not signal danger can be disturbing—for example, the erratic dripping of a leaky tap. A continuous sound, particularly one that is judged to be safe, relaxes the brain.

Passage B

There are certain elements within music, such as a change of melodic line or rhythm, that create expectations about the future development of the music. The expectation the listener has about the further course of musical events is a key determinant for the experience of "musical emotions." Music creates expectations that, if not immediately satisfied, create tension. Emotion is experienced in relation to the buildup and release of tension. The more elaborate the buildup of tension, the more intense the emotions that will be experienced. When resolution occurs, relaxation follows.

The interruption of the expected musical course, depending on one's personal involvement, causes the search for an explanation. This results from a "mismatch" between one's musical expectation and the actual course of the music. Negative emotions will be the result of an extreme mismatch between expectations and experience. Positive emotions result if the converse happens.

When we listen to music, we take into account factors such as the complexity and novelty of the music. The degree to which the music sounds familiar determines whether the music is experienced as pleasurable or uncomfortable. The pleasure experienced is minimal when the music is entirely new to the listener, increases with increasing familiarity, and decreases again when the music is totally known. Musical preference is based on one's desire to maintain a constant level of certain preferable emotions. As such, a trained listener will have a greater preference for complex melodies than will a naive listener, as the threshold for experiencing emotion is higher.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a claim about the level of complexity music needs. A single pure tone gives the listener nothing to explore, so some intricacy is required to hold interest, but sound that is too tangled or disordered simply overwhelms. What listeners want sits between those extremes, and the balancing term A introduces is coherence, some organizing principle that ties the sounds together and makes them intelligible. Keep this pairing of complexity with coherence in mind, since the rest of A elaborates it.

An analogy follows, and its job is to make that abstract pairing concrete. Language works the same way: isolated sounds rarely carry meaning, and it is the arrangement of them into words and sentences that does. Music behaves similarly, so when tones are not heard as linked in sequence or rhythm, which is roughly what we mean by melody, listeners tend not to feel an emotional connection or to appreciate what they hear. Notice that A is still describing structural features of the sound itself rather than anything happening in the listener's expectations.

A third effect gets its own explanation, and here A reaches for an evolutionary rationale. Music that relaxes us tends to be continuous and rhythmical, and the suggested reason is environmental: in nature, danger announces itself with sudden and unexpected noise, so steady background sound signals safety while broken sound demands attention. The example of a dripping tap shows how strong the reflex is, since even a soft, obviously harmless discontinuous sound can unsettle us. The conclusion is that continuous sound judged to be safe relaxes the brain.

Passage B shifts the explanation from the properties of the sound to what the listener anticipates. Changes in melodic line or rhythm set up expectations about where the music is going, and B treats those expectations as the decisive factor behind musical emotion. The mechanism is tension: an expectation that is not satisfied right away creates it, emotion is felt in the building and releasing of that tension, and a more elaborate buildup yields a more intense response. Resolution brings relaxation, which is B's version of the effect A explained environmentally.

The short middle paragraph refines that mechanism by grading the mismatch. When the music departs from its expected course, a listener who is personally involved starts looking for an explanation, and what drives this is the gap between expectation and what actually happens. The size of the gap determines the feeling: an extreme mismatch produces negative emotion, while the converse produces positive emotion. This gives B a way to explain why the same interruption can delight one listener and irritate another.

B closes by adding familiarity and individual difference to the account. Listeners weigh complexity and novelty, and pleasure tracks familiarity along a curve rather than a straight line, being minimal when the music is wholly new, rising as it becomes better known, then falling once it is completely known. Preference, on this view, is an attempt to hold a desired emotional level steady. That explains the final contrast: a trained listener, whose threshold for emotional response is higher, prefers more complex melodies than a naive one.
overall_html: Both passages explain why music produces emotional responses, but they locate the explanation in different places, so their relationship is complementary rather than contradictory. Passage A works from the properties of the sound itself, arguing that listeners need complexity balanced by coherence, comparing music to language, and grounding music's relaxing effect in an environment where sudden noise signals danger; Passage B works from the listener's psychology, treating expectation, the buildup and release of tension, the size of any mismatch, and the degree of familiarity as what determines whether the experience is pleasurable. Each author speaks in a single explanatory voice, and neither addresses the other directly.

Passage A

Recent studies have shown that sophisticated computer models of the oceans and atmosphere are capable of simulating large-scale climate trends with remarkable accuracy. But these models make use of large numbers of variables, many of which have wide ranges of possible values. Because even small differences in those values can have a significant impact on what the simulations predict, it is important to determine the impact when values differ even slightly.

Since the interactions between the many variables in climate simulations are highly complex, there is no alternative to a "brute force" exploration of all possible combinations of their values if predictions are to be reliable. This method requires very large numbers of calculations and simulation runs. For example, exhaustive examination of five values for each of only nine variables would require 2 million calculation-intensive simulation runs. Currently available individual computers are completely inadequate for such a task.

However, the continuing increase in computing capacity of the average desktop computer means that climate simulations can now be run on privately owned desktop machines connected to one another via the Internet. The calculations are divided among the individual desktop computers, which work simultaneously on their share of the overall problem. Some public resource computing projects of this kind have already been successful, although only when they captured the public's interest sufficiently to secure widespread participation.

Passage B

Researchers are now learning that many problems in nature, human society, science, and engineering are naturally "parallel"; that is, that they can be effectively solved by using methods that work simultaneously in parallel. These problems share the common characteristic of involving a large number of similar elements such as molecules, animals, even people, whose individual actions are governed by simple rules but, taken collectively, function as a highly complex system.

An example is the method used by ants to forage for food. As Lewis Thomas observed, a solitary ant is little more than a few neurons strung together by fibers. Its behavior follows a few simple rules. But when one sees a dense mass of thousands of ants, crowded together around their anthill retrieving food or repelling an intruder, a more complex picture emerges; it is as if the whole is thinking, planning, calculating. It is an intelligence, a kind of live computer, with crawling bits for wits.

We are now living through a great paradigm shift in the field of computing, a shift from sequential computing (performing one calculation at a time) to massive parallel computing, which employs thousands of computers working simultaneously to solve one computation-intensive problem. Since many computation-intensive problems are inherently parallel, it only makes sense to use a computing model that exploits that parallelism. A computing model that resembles the inherently parallel problem it is trying to solve will perform best. The old paradigm, in contrast, is subject to the speed limits imposed by purely sequential computing.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by granting a strength before naming a problem. Sophisticated computer models of ocean and atmosphere can now reproduce large-scale climate trends with impressive accuracy, but they run on many variables, each of which can take a wide range of values. Because tiny differences in those values can swing what a simulation predicts, the author concludes that the effect of small variations has to be worked out. That conclusion sets up the practical difficulty the next paragraph quantifies.

The difficulty turns out to be sheer volume. Since the variables interact in highly complex ways, A sees no alternative to brute force, meaning every possible combination of values must be tried if the predictions are to be trusted. The illustration makes the scale vivid: just nine variables at five values apiece already demands two million calculation-heavy runs. The paragraph closes on the bottleneck that the following paragraph will relieve, namely that no individual computer available today can handle work on that scale.

The solution arrives with a however. Ordinary desktop machines keep gaining capacity, so climate simulations can be spread across privately owned computers linked by the Internet, each taking a share of the problem and working on it at the same time as the others. Note the qualification A attaches at the end, which keeps the proposal realistic rather than triumphant: projects of this public resource kind have worked, but only where they caught the public's imagination strongly enough to attract enough participants.

Passage B steps back from any single application to state a general principle. Researchers are finding that many problems across nature, society, science and engineering are naturally parallel, meaning they are best attacked by methods that operate simultaneously rather than in sequence. The shared signature B identifies is worth holding onto: such problems involve large numbers of similar elements, whether molecules, animals or people, each following simple rules individually while the collection of them behaves as a highly complex system.

An example makes the abstraction tangible. Drawing on Lewis Thomas, B contrasts the single ant, barely more than a few neurons on fibers and following a handful of simple rules, with the thousands of ants massed around an anthill gathering food or driving off an intruder. At that scale the colony looks like it is thinking, planning and calculating, which B describes as a kind of living computer. The example illustrates precisely the structure named in the previous paragraph, simple local rules producing collective complexity.

The closing paragraph turns the principle into a claim about computing itself. B describes a paradigm shift underway from sequential computing, one calculation at a time, to massive parallel computing, in which thousands of machines attack a single demanding problem together. The reasoning is fit between tool and task: since so many computation-intensive problems are inherently parallel, the computing model that mirrors that structure will perform best, while the older sequential approach remains bound by its own speed limits.
overall_html: Both passages concern parallel computing, and their relationship is one of specific case to general principle: Passage A argues that reliable climate prediction requires brute-force exploration of variable combinations beyond any single machine and proposes distributing the work across Internet-linked desktop computers, while Passage B claims that many problems in nature and society are inherently parallel and that a computing model mirroring that structure will outperform sequential computing. B supplies the rationale that A's proposal exemplifies. Each passage carries only its own author's voice, and neither responds to the other, though the ant colony in B gives concrete shape to A's distributed approach.

A proficiency in understanding, applying, and even formulating statutes—the actual texts of laws enacted by legislative bodies—is a vital aspect of the practice of law, but statutory law is often given too little attention by law schools. Much of legal education, with its focus on judicial decisions and analysis of cases, can give a law student the impression that the practice of law consists mainly in analyzing past cases to determine their relevance to a client's situation and arriving at a speculative interpretation of the law relevant to the client's legal problem.

Lawyers discover fairly soon, however, that much of their practice does not depend on the kind of painstaking analysis of cases that is performed in law school. For example, a lawyer representing the owner of a business can often find an explicit answer as to what the client should do about a certain tax-related issue by consulting the relevant statutes. In such a case the facts are clear and the statutes' relation to them transparent, so that the client's question can be answered by direct reference to the wording of the statutes. But statutes' meanings and their applicability to relevant situations are not always so obvious, and that is one reason that the ability to interpret them accurately is an essential skill for law students to learn.

Another skill that teaching statutory law would improve is synthesis. Law professors work hard at developing their students' ability to analyze individual cases, but in so doing they favor the ability to apply the law in particular cases over the ability to understand the interrelations among laws. In contrast, the study of all the statutes of a legal system in a certain small area of the law would enable the student to see how these laws form a coherent whole. Students would then be able to apply this ability to synthesize in other areas of statutory law that they encounter in their study or practice. This is especially important because most students intend to specialize in a chosen area, or areas, of the law.

One possible argument against including training in statutory law as a standard part of law school curricula is that many statutes vary from region to region within a nation, so that the mastery of a set of statutes would usually not be generally applicable. There is some truth to this objection; law schools that currently provide some training in statutes generally intend it as a preparation for practice in their particular region, but for schools that are nationally oriented, this could seem to be an inappropriate investment of time and resources. But while the knowledge of a particular region's statutory law is not generally transferable to other regions, the skills acquired in mastering a particular set of statutes are, making the study of statutory law an important undertaking even for law schools with a national orientation.
explanation_html:
The thesis lands in the first sentence, so identify it early: handling statutes, the actual texts legislatures enact, is central to practising law, and law schools neglect it. The author is arguing for a curriculum change, not describing one. The rest of the paragraph diagnoses the cost of the neglect. Because legal education revolves around judicial decisions and case analysis, students come away thinking the job consists of sifting past cases for relevance to a client's situation and producing an interpretation of the law that is necessarily speculative. Watch that word, since the contrast with definite statutory answers drives the next paragraph.

The first supporting argument draws on what practice actually looks like. Much of a lawyer's work does not call for the painstaking case analysis law school drills, and the tax example shows why: a business owner's question can often be answered by reading the relevant statutes directly, because the facts are plain and the statutes apply to them transparently. Notice that the author does not overstate this. The concession that statutes are not always so clear is what converts the example into an argument, since interpreting them accurately is a skill precisely because their meaning and reach are sometimes obscure.

A second and more ambitious benefit follows, and it operates at a different level. Case-by-case teaching builds the ability to apply law to particular situations but does nothing for synthesis, the grasp of how laws relate to one another. Studying all the statutes in one narrow area would let a student see them fitting together as a coherent whole, and the author's claim is that this capacity then transfers to other statutory areas encountered in study or practice. The reason given for its importance is practical: most students plan to specialize, so the ability to see a body of law whole pays off directly.

The final paragraph anticipates the strongest objection and turns it. The objection is that statutes vary between regions, so mastering one set has limited general use, which looks damaging for nationally oriented schools that would be spending time and resources on locally applicable material. The author concedes real force here, granting that schools which do teach statutes usually aim at their own region. The reply rests on a distinction between content and skill: the particular region's statutory law does not transfer, but the skills built by mastering any set of statutes do, which is enough to justify the study even nationally.
overall_html: The passage argues that law schools should teach statutory law, on the grounds that practising lawyers frequently resolve matters by direct reference to statutes and that studying a body of statutes develops both accurate interpretation and the ability to synthesize how laws interrelate. The author's purpose is to advocate a curricular change, and the structure follows a standard argumentative shape: a diagnosis of what case-focused teaching leaves out, two positive benefits in turn, and then an anticipated objection about regional variation that is conceded in part and answered by distinguishing transferable skills from non-transferable content. The only developed viewpoint is the author's own.

The Japanese American sculptor Isamu Noguchi (1904–1988) was an artist who intuitively asked—and responded to—deeply original questions. He might well have become a scientist within a standard scientific discipline, but he instead became an artist who repeatedly veered off at wide angles from the well-known courses followed by conventionally talented artists of both the traditional and modern schools. The story behind one particular sculpture typifies this aspect of his creativeness.

By his early twenties, Noguchi's sculptures showed such exquisite comprehension of human anatomy and deft conceptual realization that he won a Guggenheim Fellowship for travel in Europe. After arriving in Paris in 1927, Noguchi asked the Romanian-born sculptor Constantin Brancusi if he might become his student. When Brancusi said no, that he never took students, Noguchi asked if he needed a stonecutter. Brancusi did. Noguchi cut and polished stone for Brancusi in his studio, frequently also polishing Brancusi's brass and bronze sculptures. Noguchi, with his scientist's mind, pondered the fact that sculptors through the ages had relied exclusively upon negative light—that is, shadows—for their conceptual communication, precisely because no metals, other than the expensive, nonoxidizing gold, could be relied upon to give off positive-light reflections.

Noguchi wanted to create a sculpture that was purely reflective. In 1929, after returning to the United States, he met the architect and philosopher R. Buckminster Fuller, offering to sculpt a portrait of him. When Fuller heard of Noguchi's ideas regarding positive-light sculpture, he suggested using chrome-nickel steel, which Henry Ford, through automotive research and development, had just made commercially available for the first time in history. Here, finally, was a permanently reflective surface, economically available in massive quantities.

In sculpting his portrait of Fuller, Noguchi did not think of it as merely a shiny alternate model of traditional, negative-light sculptures. What he saw was that completely reflective surfaces provided a fundamental invisibility of surface like that of utterly still waters, whose presence can be apprehended only when objects—a ship's mast, a tree, or sky—are reflected in them. Seaplane pilots making offshore landings in dead calm cannot tell where the water is and must glide in, waiting for the unpredictable touchdown. Noguchi conceived a similarly invisible sculpture, hidden in and communicating through the reflections of images surrounding it. Then only the distortion of familiar shapes in the surrounding environment could be seen by the viewer. The viewer's awareness of the "invisible" sculpture's presence and dimensional relationships would be derived only secondarily.

Even after this stunning discovery, Noguchi remained faithful to his inquisitive nature. At the moment when his explorations had won critical recognition of the genius of his original and fundamental conception, Noguchi proceeded to the next phase of his evolution.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph sets a thesis and then promises a case study, which tells you the shape of everything that follows. The author presents Noguchi as someone whose gift was for asking genuinely original questions, a temperament that could as easily have made him a scientist. Instead he became an artist who kept veering away from the paths that conventionally talented artists followed, traditional and modern alike. The last sentence narrows the scope deliberately: rather than surveying a career, the passage will trace the story behind one sculpture because it typifies that habit of mind.

The narrative starts with credentials and then plants the technical problem. By his early twenties Noguchi's grasp of anatomy and his conceptual skill had earned him a Guggenheim Fellowship, which took him to Paris in 1927, and when Brancusi refused to take students he offered himself as a stonecutter instead. Polishing stone, brass and bronze in that studio is what prompts the key observation, and it is described as the work of his scientist's mind. Sculptors had always communicated through negative light, meaning shadow, for a simple material reason: apart from costly gold, no metal could be counted on to keep giving off reflections rather than oxidizing.

The obstacle identified, the solution arrives through an unrelated encounter. Noguchi wanted a sculpture that was purely reflective, and back in the United States in 1929 he offered to sculpt a portrait of Fuller. Hearing about the positive-light idea, Fuller proposed chrome-nickel steel, newly commercially available thanks to Ford's automotive research. Note how precisely the material answers the problem stated in the previous paragraph: it stays reflective permanently, and unlike gold it could be had cheaply and in quantity. The chronology matters here, since the idea existed before the material that could realize it.

The heart of the passage is what Noguchi understood the new surface to mean. A fully reflective sculpture is not a shiny version of the old shadow-based kind; it becomes invisible in the way perfectly still water is, detectable only through the mast, tree or sky reflected in it. The seaplane image drives this home, since a pilot landing in dead calm cannot locate the surface and must glide down waiting for contact. What the viewer of such a sculpture sees is the surrounding world distorted, and awareness of the object's own presence and proportions arrives only indirectly, as a secondary inference.

The brief closing paragraph returns to the opening claim rather than adding new material. Having made a discovery the author calls stunning, and at the very point where critics were recognizing the originality of his conception, Noguchi did not settle in and exploit it but moved on to the next stage of his development. That timing is the whole point: it confirms the inquisitive nature announced at the start, showing that the questioning temperament, not any single achievement, is what the passage set out to illustrate.
overall_html: The passage uses the story of Noguchi's reflective portrait of Buckminster Fuller to illustrate a claim about the artist's character, that he worked like a scientist asking original questions and repeatedly left conventional artistic paths behind. The author's purpose is admiring and illustrative rather than evaluative, and the structure is chronological: a thesis paragraph, then the Brancusi studio where Noguchi recognized sculpture's reliance on shadow, then the chrome-nickel steel that made positive-light sculpture possible, then his insight that a fully reflective surface becomes invisible like still water, and finally his departure for a new phase just as recognition arrived. Only the author's viewpoint is developed.

passage_html:
In an experiment, two strangers are given the opportunity to share $100, subject to the following constraints: One person—the "proposer"—is to suggest how to divide the money and can make only one such proposal. The other person—the "responder"— must either accept or reject the offer without qualification. Both parties know that if the offer is accepted, the money will be split as agreed, but if the offer is rejected, neither will receive anything.

This scenario is called the Ultimatum Game. Researchers have conducted it numerous times with a wide variety of volunteers. Many participants in the role of the proposer seem instinctively to feel that they should offer 50 percent to the responder, because such a division is "fair" and therefore likely to be accepted. Two-thirds of proposers offer responders between 40 and 50 percent. Only 4 in 100 offer less than 20 percent. Offering such a small amount is quite risky; most responders reject such offers. This is a puzzle: Why would anyone reject an offer as too small? Responders who reject an offer receive nothing, so if one assumes—as theoretical economics traditionally has—that people make economic decisions primarily out of rational self-interest, one would expect that an individual would accept any offer.

Some theorists explain the insistence on fair divisions in the Ultimatum Game by citing our prehistoric ancestors' need for the support of a strong group. Small groups of hunter-gatherers depended for survival on their members' strengths. It is counterproductive to outcompete rivals within one's group to the point where one can no longer depend on them in contests with other groups. But this hypothesis at best explains why proposers offer large amounts, not why responders reject low offers.

A more compelling explanation is that our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups, where it is hard to keep secrets. Our emotions are therefore not finely tuned to one-time, strictly anonymous interactions. In real life we expect our friends and neighbors to notice our decisions. If people know that someone is content with a small share, they are likely to make that person low offers. But if someone is known to angrily reject low offers, others have an incentive to make that person high offers. Consequently, evolution should have favored angry responses to low offers; if one regularly receives fair offers when food is divided, one is more likely to survive. Because one-shot interactions were rare during human evolution, our emotions do not discriminate between one-shot and repeated interactions. Therefore, we respond emotionally to low offers in the Ultimatum Game because we instinctively feel the need to reject dismal offers in order to keep our self-esteem. This self-esteem helps us to acquire a reputation that is beneficial in future encounters.
explanation_html:
Read the opening paragraph as a rulebook, since every later argument depends on getting the setup exactly right. Two strangers can share one hundred dollars under tight constraints. One of them, the proposer, suggests a split and gets only that single attempt. The other, the responder, must take the offer as it stands or refuse it outright, with no bargaining permitted. Both know the stakes in advance: acceptance means the money is divided as proposed, refusal means neither person receives anything at all. Note that the anonymity and the one-shot structure become crucial once the explanations begin.

Naming the experiment as the Ultimatum Game, the author reports what actually happens and then extracts a puzzle from it. Proposers tend to feel that half is the fair share and therefore the likely one to be accepted, and the numbers bear that instinct out, with two-thirds offering between forty and fifty percent and only four in a hundred going below twenty. The genuinely surprising result is on the other side, since stingy offers are usually rejected. On the traditional economic assumption that people act from rational self-interest, any offer beats nothing, so refusing it should not happen.

The first attempted answer is evolutionary, and the author dispatches it quickly. Some theorists trace the insistence on fairness to prehistoric life in small hunter-gatherer bands, where survival depended on the strengths of the other members. On that account it is self-defeating to beat your own group's members so thoroughly that you can no longer rely on them when your group faces another. Notice how narrowly the objection is aimed rather than sweeping: the hypothesis may well explain why proposers hand over large shares, but it leaves the actual puzzle, the responder's refusal, untouched.

The explanation the author endorses keeps the evolutionary frame but relocates the mechanism in emotion and reputation. Feelings were shaped over millions of years in small groups where secrets were hard to keep, so they are not calibrated for anonymous one-off encounters. Where neighbors observe your decisions, being known to accept scraps invites low offers while being known to react angrily invites generous ones, so evolution favored anger at low offers and the better food shares that follow. Since one-shot situations were rare, our emotions do not distinguish them, and the rejection in the laboratory is that reputation-protecting instinct firing out of context.
overall_html: The passage sets out the Ultimatum Game and the puzzle it produces, that responders reject small offers even though refusing leaves them with nothing, and argues that the best explanation is an emotional apparatus shaped by small-group life in which rejecting insulting offers protected one's reputation and future share. The author's purpose is to weigh explanations and endorse one, moving from the rules, to the experimental results and their conflict with the assumption of rational self-interest, to a group-strength hypothesis rejected as explaining only proposers, and finally to the reputation account. The viewpoints to separate are traditional economics, some theorists, and the author.

passage_html:
To study centuries-old earthquakes and the geologic faults that caused them, seismologists usually dig trenches along visible fault lines, looking for sediments that show evidence of having shifted. Using radiocarbon dating, they measure the quantity of the radioactive isotope carbon 14 present in wood or other organic material trapped in the sediments when they shifted. Since carbon 14 occurs naturally in organic materials and decays at a constant rate, the age of organic materials can be reconstructed from the amount of the isotope remaining in them. These data can show the location and frequency of past earthquakes and provide hints about the likelihood and location of future earthquakes.

Geologists William Bull and Mark Brandon have recently developed a new method, called lichenometry, for detecting and dating past earthquakes. Bull and Brandon developed the method based on the fact that large earthquakes generate numerous simultaneous rockfalls in mountain ranges that are sensitive to seismic shaking. Instead of dating fault-line sediments, lichenometry involves measuring the size of lichens growing on the rocks exposed by these rockfalls. Lichens—symbiotic organisms consisting of a fungus and an alga—quickly colonize newly exposed rock surfaces in the wake of rockfalls, and once established they grow radially, flat against the rocks, at a slow but constant rate for as long as 1,000 years if left undisturbed. One species of North American lichen, for example, spreads outward by about 9.5 millimeters each century. Hence, the diameter of the largest lichen on a boulder provides direct evidence of when the boulder was dislodged and repositioned. If many rockfalls over a large geographic area occurred simultaneously, that pattern would imply that there had been a strong earthquake. The location of the earthquake's epicenter can then be determined by mapping these rockfalls, since they decrease in abundance as the distance from the epicenter increases.

Lichenometry has distinct advantages over radiocarbon dating. Radiocarbon dating is accurate only to within plus or minus 40 years, because the amount of the carbon 14 isotope varies naturally in the environment depending on the intensity of the radiation striking Earth's upper atmosphere. Additionally, this intensity has fluctuated greatly during the past 300 years, causing many radiocarbon datings of events during this period to be of little value. Lichenometry, Bull and Brandon claim, can accurately date an earthquake to within ten years. They note, however, that using lichenometry requires careful site selection and accurate calibration of lichen growth rates, adding that the method is best used for earthquakes that occurred within the last 500 years. Sites must be selected to minimize the influence of snow avalanches and other disturbances that would affect normal lichen growth, and conditions like shade and wind that promote faster lichen growth must be factored in.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the established technique, which functions as the baseline the new method will be measured against. To study earthquakes from centuries past, seismologists dig trenches along visible faults and look for sediments that shifted. Radiocarbon dating then supplies the timing: organic material such as wood caught in those sediments contains carbon 14, which occurs naturally and decays at a fixed rate, so the amount left indicates age. The purpose is forward-looking as well as historical, since knowing where past earthquakes struck and how often they recurred offers hints about future ones.

A new alternative is introduced, and its logic is worth following step by step. Bull and Brandon reasoned from the fact that large earthquakes trigger many rockfalls at once in mountains sensitive to shaking. Rather than dating sediments, their method measures lichens, the fungus-and-alga organisms that quickly colonize freshly exposed rock and then spread outward flat against it at a slow but steady rate for up to a thousand years, one North American species widening by about nine and a half millimeters a century. The largest lichen on a boulder therefore dates the fall. Widespread simultaneous rockfalls indicate a strong earthquake, and because rockfalls thin out with distance, mapping them locates the epicenter.

The final paragraph evaluates, and the balance of it matters more than the headline. Radiocarbon dating is accurate only to within forty years either way, because atmospheric radiation striking the Earth makes the natural quantity of carbon 14 vary, and that intensity has swung sharply over the last three hundred years, leaving many datings from that period nearly worthless. Against this, Bull and Brandon claim accuracy within ten years. Note that they supply the limits themselves: sites must be chosen to exclude avalanches and similar disturbances, growth rates must be calibrated for conditions like shade and wind, and the method suits earthquakes of the last five hundred years.
overall_html: The passage introduces lichenometry, a method of dating past earthquakes by measuring the lichens growing on rocks exposed by earthquake-triggered rockfalls, and presents it as a more precise alternative to the radiocarbon dating of fault-line sediments. The author's purpose is expository and comparative rather than argumentative, first describing the traditional trenching and radiocarbon technique, then explaining how Bull and Brandon's method works and how mapping rockfalls locates an epicenter, and finally weighing its tenfold gain in accuracy against the conditions it requires, including careful site selection, calibrated growth rates, and a limit of roughly five hundred years. The only viewpoint developed is that of Bull and Brandon.

While courts have long allowed custom-made medical illustrations depicting personal injury to be presented as evidence in legal cases, the issue of whether they have a legitimate place in the courtroom is surrounded by ongoing debate and misinformation. Some opponents of their general use argue that while illustrations are sometimes invaluable in presenting the physical details of a personal injury, in all cases except those involving the most unusual injuries, illustrations from medical textbooks can be adequate. Most injuries, such as fractures and whiplash, they say, are rather generic in nature—certain commonly encountered forces act on particular areas of the body in standard ways—so they can be represented by generic illustrations.

Another line of complaint stems from the belief that custom-made illustrations often misrepresent the facts in order to comply with the partisan interests of litigants. Even some lawyers appear to share a version of this view, believing that such illustrations can be used to bolster a weak case. Illustrators are sometimes approached by lawyers who, unable to find medical experts to support their clients' claims, think that they can replace expert testimony with such deceptive professional illustrations. But this is mistaken. Even if an unscrupulous illustrator could be found, such illustrations would be inadmissible as evidence in the courtroom unless a medical expert were present to testify to their accuracy.

It has also been maintained that custom-made illustrations may subtly distort the issues through the use of emphasis, coloration, and other means, even if they are technically accurate. But professional medical illustrators strive for objective accuracy and avoid devices that have inflammatory potential, sometimes even eschewing the use of color. Unlike illustrations in medical textbooks, which are designed to include the extensive detail required by medical students, custom-made medical illustrations are designed to include only the information that is relevant for those deciding a case. The end user is typically a jury or a judge, for whose benefit the depiction is reduced to the details that are crucial to determining the legally relevant facts. The more complex details often found in textbooks can be deleted so as not to confuse the issue. For example, illustrations of such things as veins and arteries would only get in the way when an illustration is supposed to be used to explain the nature of a bone fracture.

Custom-made medical illustrations, which are based on a plaintiff's X rays, computerized tomography scans, and medical records and reports, are especially valuable in that they provide visual representations of data whose verbal description would be very complex. Expert testimony by medical professionals often relies heavily on the use of technical terminology, which those who are not specially trained in the field find difficult to translate mentally into visual imagery. Since, for most people, adequate understanding of physical data depends on thinking at least partly in visual terms, the clearly presented visual stimulation provided by custom-made illustrations can be quite instructive.
explanation_html:
The passage frames a live dispute and immediately gives the other side the floor. Courts have long admitted custom-made medical illustrations of personal injury, yet debate and misinformation persist about whether they belong there. The first complaint from the opponents is that custom work is usually unnecessary: illustrations can be invaluable for showing physical detail, but except for genuinely unusual injuries, textbook illustrations would do. Their reasoning is that most injuries, fractures and whiplash among them, are generic, since familiar forces act on particular body parts in standard ways, so generic pictures can represent them. Notice this objection goes unanswered for now.

A second objection concerns honesty rather than necessity, and here the author answers directly. The worry is that custom illustrations bend the facts to serve whichever litigant paid for them, a belief some lawyers share, imagining that a picture can prop up a weak case. The passage confirms the temptation is real, since lawyers who cannot find supportive medical experts sometimes approach illustrators hoping deceptive images will substitute for testimony. The rebuttal is procedural rather than moral: even if a dishonest illustrator existed, such an illustration could not be admitted as evidence unless a medical expert testified to its accuracy.

The third objection is subtler, alleging that emphasis, coloration and similar choices can skew the issues even in a technically accurate image, and the author's answer is the longest in the passage. Professional illustrators aim at objective accuracy and steer clear of inflammatory devices, sometimes dropping color altogether. The stronger point turns the first objection on its head: textbook illustrations carry the exhaustive detail medical students need, while custom images are built for a judge or jury and pared down to what determines the legally relevant facts. Veins and arteries would merely obscure a picture meant to explain a fracture.

Having cleared the objections, the author closes with the affirmative case. Custom illustrations are constructed from the plaintiff's own X rays, scans, records and reports, and their value lies in turning data whose verbal description would be forbiddingly complex into something visible. Expert testimony leans on technical vocabulary that untrained listeners struggle to convert into mental pictures, which is the real obstacle in the courtroom. Since most people need at least some visual thinking to grasp physical data properly, the clear visual stimulation these illustrations supply is genuinely instructive rather than merely persuasive.
overall_html: The passage defends the use of custom-made medical illustrations as courtroom evidence, answering the charges that textbook images would suffice, that custom work misrepresents facts for partisan advantage, and that even accurate images distort through emphasis and color, before arguing positively that such illustrations make complex physical data comprehensible to judges and juries who cannot easily visualize technical testimony. The author's purpose is persuasive, and the structure is objection-and-response across three paragraphs followed by an affirmative case. Two viewpoints are in play, the opponents whose three lines of complaint organize the passage, and the author, who rebuts the second and third directly.
