Passage A

Because dental caries (decay) is strongly linked to consumption of the sticky, carbohydrate-rich staples of agricultural diets, prehistoric human teeth can provide clues about when a population made the transition from a hunter-gatherer diet to an agricultural one. Caries formation is influenced by several factors, including tooth structure, bacteria in the mouth, and diet. In particular, caries formation is affected by carbohydrates' texture and composition, since carbohydrates more readily stick to teeth.

Many researchers have demonstrated the link between carbohydrate consumption and caries. In North America, Leigh studied caries in archaeologically derived teeth, noting that caries rates differed between indigenous populations that primarily consumed meat (a Sioux sample showed almost no caries) and those heavily dependent on cultivated maize (a Zuni sample had 75 percent carious teeth). Leigh's findings have been frequently confirmed by other researchers, who have shown that, in general, the greater a population's dependence on agriculture is, the higher its rate of caries formation will be.

Under some circumstances, however, nonagricultural populations may exhibit relatively high caries rates. For example, early nonagricultural populations in western North America who consumed large amounts of highly processed stone-ground flour made from gathered acorns show relatively high caries frequencies. And wild plants collected by the Hopi included several species with high cariogenic potential, notably pinyon nuts and wild tubers.

Passage B

Archaeologists recovered human skeletal remains interred over a 2,000-year period in prehistoric Ban Chiang, Thailand. The site's early inhabitants appear to have had a hunter-gatherer-cultivator economy. Evidence indicates that, over time, the population became increasingly dependent on agriculture.

Research suggests that agricultural intensification results in declining human health, including dental health. Studies show that dental caries is uncommon in pre-agricultural populations. Increased caries frequency may result from increased consumption of starchy-sticky foodstuffs or from alterations in tooth wear. The wearing down of tooth crown surfaces reduces caries formation by removing fissures that can trap food particles. A reduction of fiber or grit in a diet may diminish tooth wear, thus increasing caries frequency. However, severe wear that exposes a tooth's pulp cavity may also result in caries.

The diet of Ban Chiang's inhabitants included some cultivated rice and yams from the beginning of the period represented by the recovered remains. These were part of a varied diet that also included wild plant and animal foods. Since both rice and yams are carbohydrates, increased reliance on either or both should theoretically result in increased caries frequency.

Yet comparisons of caries frequency in the Early and Late Ban Chiang Groups indicate that overall caries frequency is slightly greater in the Early Group. Tooth wear patterns do not indicate tooth wear changes between Early and Late Groups that would explain this unexpected finding. It is more likely that, although dependence on agriculture increased, the diet in the Late period remained varied enough that no single food dominated. Furthermore, there may have been a shift from sweeter carbohydrates (yams) toward rice, a less cariogenic carbohydrate.
explanation_html:
Passage A establishes the principle everything after it depends on. Dental caries, ordinary tooth decay, is tightly linked to the sticky, carbohydrate-heavy foods that agriculture supplies, so prehistoric teeth can indicate when a population shifted from hunting and gathering to farming. The author is careful not to make decay a simple function of diet, listing tooth structure and oral bacteria alongside it. Within diet, the detail that matters is texture and composition, because some carbohydrates cling to teeth more readily than others.

Evidence for the link comes next, moving from one striking case to a general rule. Leigh examined teeth recovered archaeologically in North America and found the rates diverging sharply by diet, with a largely meat-eating Sioux sample showing almost no caries and a maize-dependent Zuni sample showing three-quarters of teeth decayed. The paragraph then widens the claim: other researchers have repeatedly confirmed Leigh's result, so that in general the more a population depends on agriculture, the higher its caries rate. Hold onto the phrase in general, because the next paragraph qualifies it.

The qualification arrives right on schedule and keeps A from overstating its own rule. Some populations that never farmed still show relatively high caries rates, and two examples make the point. Early nonagricultural groups in western North America ate large quantities of finely stone-ground acorn flour, a highly processed carbohydrate, and their caries frequencies are correspondingly high. Wild plants gathered by the Hopi included several with strong decay-causing potential, notably pinyon nuts and wild tubers. The lesson is that processing and plant type, not farming as such, drive the effect.

Passage B narrows from principle to a single excavation. Human remains buried over a two-thousand-year span were recovered at prehistoric Ban Chiang in Thailand, and the earliest inhabitants appear to have combined hunting, gathering and cultivation. The one trend B establishes here is that the population grew steadily more dependent on agriculture over that span. Notice how neatly this site fits the framework A supplied, since an increasing reliance on farming is precisely the condition under which caries rates are expected to climb.

Before reporting results, B lays out the expectations and the mechanisms in play. Research generally indicates that intensifying agriculture worsens human health, dental health included, and that caries is uncommon before farming. Two possible causes are distinguished: more starchy, sticky food, or changes in how teeth wear down. The wear mechanism runs both ways and repays close reading. Wearing away the crown surface removes the fissures that trap food and so reduces decay, meaning less fiber or grit increases caries, yet wear severe enough to expose the pulp cavity causes caries too.

The Ban Chiang diet is then specified, sharpening the prediction. Cultivated rice and yams were present from the very start of the period covered by the remains, but they formed part of a mixed diet that also drew on wild plants and animals. Since both rice and yams are carbohydrates, the theory just outlined predicts that leaning more heavily on either or both should push caries frequency up. That prediction is stated explicitly so the finding in the last paragraph registers as a genuine surprise.

The results contradict the prediction, and the closing paragraph works through why. Caries frequency is slightly higher in the Early Group than the Late Group, the reverse of what increasing agriculture should produce, and the wear patterns show no change between the groups that could account for it. Two explanations are offered, both tentative. The Late diet may have stayed varied enough that no single food dominated, and there may have been a move away from sweeter yams toward rice, a carbohydrate less likely to cause decay.
overall_html: Both passages concern what dental caries reveals about ancient diets, and the relationship is one of general rule applied to a particular site, with the application producing an unexpected result. Passage A establishes that caries rates rise with dependence on agriculture while noting that heavily processed or naturally cariogenic wild plants can raise them too; Passage B examines two thousand years of remains from Ban Chiang, where reliance on farming increased yet caries frequency was slightly higher in the earlier group, and explains this by a persistently varied diet and a possible shift from yams to less cariogenic rice. Each passage reports researchers' findings in a single expository voice.

Recent criticism has sought to align Sarah Orne Jewett, a notable writer of regional fiction in the nineteenth-century United States, with the domestic novelists of the previous generation. Her work does resemble the domestic novels of the 1850s in its focus on women, their domestic occupations, and their social interactions, with men relegated to the periphery. But it also differs markedly from these antecedents. The world depicted in the latter revolves around children. Young children play prominent roles in the domestic novels and the work of child rearing—the struggle to instill a mother's values in a child's character—is their chief source of drama. By contrast, children and child rearing are almost entirely absent from the world of Jewett's fiction. Even more strikingly, while the literary world of the earlier domestic novelists is insistently religious, grounded in the structures of Protestant religious belief, to turn from these writers to Jewett is to encounter an almost wholly secular world.

To the extent that these differences do not merely reflect the personal preferences of the authors, we might attribute them to such historical transformations as the migration of the rural young to cities or the increasing secularization of society. But while such factors may help to explain the differences, it can be argued that these differences ultimately reflect different conceptions of the nature and purpose of fiction. The domestic novel of the mid-nineteenth century is based on a conception of fiction as part of a continuum that also included writings devoted to piety and domestic instruction, bound together by a common goal of promoting domestic morality and religious belief. It was not uncommon for the same multipurpose book to be indistinguishably a novel, a child-rearing manual, and a tract on Christian duty. The more didactic aims are absent from Jewett's writing, which rather embodies the late nineteenth-century "high-cultural" conception of fiction as an autonomous sphere with value in and of itself.

This high-cultural aesthetic was one among several conceptions of fiction operative in the United States in the 1850s and 1860s, but it became the dominant one later in the nineteenth century and remained so for most of the twentieth. On this conception, fiction came to be seen as pure art: a work was to be viewed in isolation and valued for the formal arrangement of its elements rather than for its larger social connections or the promotion of extraliterary goods. Thus, unlike the domestic novelists, Jewett intended her works not as a means to an end but as an end in themselves. This fundamental difference should be given more weight in assessing their affinities than any superficial similarity in subject matter.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a claim the author intends to complicate. Recent critics have grouped Sarah Orne Jewett with the domestic novelists of the previous generation, and the author grants the resemblance: her fiction centers on women, their household occupations and their social lives, with men pushed to the margins. Then comes the pivot on which everything turns, marked by a plain but. Two differences follow, and the second is flagged as the more striking. Domestic novels revolve around children, and their central drama is child rearing, a mother working to plant her values in a child's character, whereas children barely appear in Jewett. The earlier writers' world is insistently religious; Jewett's is almost entirely secular.

Having established the differences, the author asks what explains them, and the paragraph is structured as one answer displacing another. Personal preference aside, the obvious candidates are historical, such as young people leaving the countryside for cities and society growing more secular. Those factors may contribute, but the author argues the real source lies deeper, in rival conceptions of what fiction is for. Domestic novelists treated their books as part of a continuum with devotional writing and household instruction, all aimed at promoting domestic morality and religious belief, so a single book could function equally as novel, child-rearing manual and religious tract. Jewett's writing drops that instructional purpose and treats fiction as an autonomous sphere valuable in itself.

The closing paragraph situates Jewett's position historically and then draws the payoff. The high-cultural view of fiction was only one option in the eighteen fifties and sixties, but it became dominant later in the century and stayed dominant through most of the next. On that view a work is pure art, to be judged in isolation for how its formal elements are arranged rather than for its social ties or any good it promotes beyond literature. Hence the sharp formulation the author wants you to carry away: the domestic novelists wrote as a means to an end, Jewett wrote works that were ends in themselves, and this difference should outweigh surface similarities of subject matter.
overall_html: The passage concedes that Jewett's fiction resembles the earlier domestic novels in subject matter but argues that the two are fundamentally unlike, because the domestic novelists conceived fiction as an instrument of moral and religious instruction while Jewett worked from the later high-cultural conception of fiction as autonomous art valuable in itself. The author's purpose is corrective, resisting the recent critics who align her with that tradition, and the structure moves from shared features to two pointed differences, then past historical explanations to the difference in conceptions of fiction, and finally to the verdict that this outweighs any superficial affinity. The viewpoints to track are the recent critics and the author.

The work of South African writer Ezekiel Mphahlele has confounded literary critics, especially those who feel compelled to draw a sharp distinction between autobiography and fiction. These critics point to Mphahlele's best-known works—his 1959 autobiography Down Second Avenue and his 1971 novel The Wanderers—to illustrate the problem of categorizing his work. While his autobiography traces his life from age five until the beginning of his self-imposed 20-year exile at age thirty-eight, The Wanderers appears to pick up at the beginning of his exile and go on from there. Critics have variously decried the former as too fictionalized and the latter as too autobiographical, but those who focus on traditional labels inevitably miss the fact that Mphahlele manipulates different prose forms purely in the service of the social message he advances.

Even where critics give him a favorable reading, all too often their reviews carry a negative subtext. For example, one critic said of The Wanderers that if anger, firsthand experiences, compassion, and topicality were the sole requirements for great literature, the novel might well be one of the masterpieces of this declining part of the twentieth century. And although this critic may not have meant to question the literary contribution of the novel, there are those who are outright dismissive of The Wanderers because it contains an autobiographical framework and is populated with real-world characters. Mphahlele briefly defends against such charges by pointing out the importance of the fictional father-son relationship that opens and closes the novel. But his greater concern is the social vision that pervades his work, though it too is prone to misunderstandings and underappreciation. Mphahlele is a humanist and an integrationist, and his writings wonderfully articulate his vision of the future; but critics often balk at this vision because Mphahlele provides no road maps for bringing such a future about.

Mphahlele himself shows little interest in establishing guidelines to distinguish autobiography from fiction. Though he does refer to Down Second Avenue as an autobiography and The Wanderers as a novel, he asserts that no novelist can write complete fiction or absolute fact. It is the nature of writing, at least the writing he cares about, that the details must be drawn from the writer's experiences, and thus are in some sense fact, but conveyed in such a way as to maximize the effectiveness of the social message contained in the work, and thus inevitably fiction. As he claims, the whole point of the exercise of writing has nothing to do with classification; in all forms writing is the transmission of ideas, and important ideas at that: "Whenever you write prose or poetry or drama you are writing a social criticism of one kind or another. If you don't, you are completely irrelevant—you don't count."
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph sets up a conflict between a writer and the categories used to read him. The critics who insist on a firm line between autobiography and fiction have found Mphahlele's work hard to place, and the two books they cite show why: his 1959 autobiography covers his life from five to thirty-eight, when his self-imposed twenty-year exile began, and his 1971 novel seems to take up at that same point and continue. Their verdicts pull in opposite directions, the autobiography faulted as too fictionalized and the novel as too autobiographical. The author supplies the thesis in the final clause: preoccupation with labels misses that he uses prose forms in whatever way serves his social message.

The second paragraph shows the criticism operating even where it seems friendly. One reviewer allowed that if anger, firsthand experience, compassion and topicality were all great literature required, the novel might be a masterpiece of the century's decline, a compliment built around a withheld judgment. Others dismiss the novel outright for its autobiographical framework and real-world characters. Mphahlele answers only briefly, pointing to the invented father-son relationship that frames the book, because what he cares about is his social vision. Note where the resistance lies: he is a humanist and integrationist whose writing articulates a future, and critics balk because he offers no route to reaching it.

The last paragraph hands the argument to Mphahlele himself and resolves the categorization question by dissolving it. He will use the labels loosely, calling one book an autobiography and the other a novel, while denying that any novelist writes complete fiction or absolute fact. His reasoning is that the details of the writing he values must come from lived experience, which makes them factual, yet they are shaped to make the social message land, which makes them fictional. Classification is therefore beside the point, since writing exists to transmit ideas, and as he puts it, prose that is not social criticism does not count.
overall_html: The passage argues that critics who insist on classifying Ezekiel Mphahlele's books as either autobiography or fiction have misread him, because he treats prose forms as instruments for delivering a social message and denies that any writing is wholly factual or wholly invented. The author's purpose is corrective and defensive, moving from the critics' contradictory complaints about his autobiography and his novel, to the negative subtext running even through favorable reviews and their discomfort with a vision that offers no road map, and finally to Mphahlele's own position that writing exists to transmit ideas. The viewpoints to keep apart are the critics, Mphahlele, and the sympathetic author.

A vigorous debate in astronomy centers on an epoch in planetary history that was first identified by analysis of rock samples obtained in lunar missions. Scientists discovered that the major craters on the Moon were created by a vigorous bombardment of debris approximately four billion years ago—the so-called late heavy bombardment (LHB). Projectiles from this bombardment that affected the Moon should also have struck Earth, a likelihood with profound consequences for the history of Earth since, until the LHB ended, life could not have survived here.

Various theoretical approaches have been developed to account for both the evidence gleaned from samples of Moon rock collected during lunar explorations and the size and distribution of craters on the Moon. Since the sizes of LHB craters suggest they were formed by large bodies, some astronomers believe that the LHB was linked to the disintegration of an asteroid or comet orbiting the Sun. In this view, a large body broke apart and peppered the inner solar system with debris. Other scientists disagree and believe that the label "LHB" is in itself a misnomer. These researchers claim that a cataclysm is not necessary to explain the LHB evidence. They claim that the Moon's evidence merely provides a view of the period concluding billions of years of a continuous, declining heavy bombardment throughout the inner solar system. According to them, the impacts from the latter part of the bombardment were so intense that they obliterated evidence of earlier impacts. A third group contends that the Moon's evidence supports the view that the LHB was a sharply defined cataclysmic cratering period, but these scientists believe that because of its relatively brief duration, this cataclysm did not extend throughout the inner solar system. They hold that the LHB involved only the disintegration of a body within the Earth-Moon system, because the debris from such an event would have been swept up relatively quickly.

New support for the hypothesis that a late bombardment extended throughout the inner solar system has been found in evidence from the textural features and chemical makeup of a meteorite that has been found on Earth. It seems to be a rare example of a Mars rock that made its way to Earth after being knocked from the surface of Mars. The rock has recently been experimentally dated at about four billion years old, which means that, if the rock is indeed from Mars, it was knocked from the planet at about the same time that the Moon was experiencing the LHB. This tiny piece of evidence suggests that at least two planetary systems in the inner solar system experienced bombardment at the same time. However, to determine the pervasiveness of the LHB, scientists will need to locate many more such rocks and perhaps obtain surface samples from other planets in the inner solar system.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by establishing the phenomenon that the rest of it will argue about. Analysis of rocks brought back from the Moon showed that its major craters were produced by an intense bombardment of debris roughly four billion years ago, an episode named the late heavy bombardment. The step that makes this more than lunar geology comes next: whatever struck the Moon should have struck Earth as well. Note the consequence the author draws, since it explains why the debate matters at all. If the bombardment reached Earth, life here could not have survived until it stopped.

Three positions are then set out, and the efficient way to hold them apart is to ask what each says about the event's cause and its reach. The solar system cataclysm group reads the large crater sizes as the work of big bodies and links the bombardment to an asteroid or comet that broke up in orbit and scattered debris through the inner solar system. The gradual decline group calls the label itself a misnomer, arguing that no catastrophe is needed: the Moon simply records the tail end of billions of years of steadily diminishing bombardment, with the late impacts so fierce that they erased the traces of earlier ones. The local cataclysm group accepts a sharply defined cratering episode but confines it to the Earth-Moon system, reasoning that its brief duration fits debris from a body that broke up nearby and was swept up quickly.

New evidence arrives in the final paragraph, and it supports one of those three positions rather than settling the dispute. A meteorite found on Earth, identified by its texture and chemistry as a rare piece of Mars knocked loose from that planet's surface, has been dated experimentally to about four billion years. If the identification holds, Mars was being struck at the same time the Moon was, which points to at least two planetary systems bombarded simultaneously and thus to the solar-system-wide view. Notice how heavily the author qualifies the finding, calling it tiny and requiring more such rocks and surface samples from other planets.
overall_html: The passage explains the astronomical debate over the late heavy bombardment, the episode of intense cratering about four billion years ago recorded in lunar rock, and reports new meteorite evidence that a similar bombardment reached Mars. The author's purpose is expository rather than partisan, first establishing the phenomenon and its implication that life on Earth could not have survived until it ended, then laying out three competing accounts, and finally presenting evidence that tips toward one of them while stressing how much more is needed. Keep the three groups distinct: those positing a solar-system-wide cataclysm, those denying any cataclysm, and those confining it to the Earth-Moon system.

Specialists in international communications almost unanimously assert that the broadcasting in developing nations of television programs produced by industrialized countries amounts to cultural imperialism: the phenomenon of one culture's productions overwhelming another's, to the detriment of the flourishing of the latter. This assertion assumes the automatic dominance of the imported productions and their negative effect on the domestic culture. But the assertion is polemical and abstract, based on little or no research into the place held by imported programs in the economies of importing countries or in the lives of viewers. This is not to deny that dominance is sometimes a risk in relationships between cultures, but rather to say that the assertion lacks empirical foundation and in some cases goes against fact. For one example, imported programs rarely threaten the economic viability of the importing country's own television industry. For another, imported programs do not uniformly attract larger audiences than domestically produced programs; viewers are not part of a passive, undifferentiated mass but are individuals with personal tastes, and most of them tend to prefer domestically produced television over imported television.

The role of television in developing nations is far removed from what the specialists assert. An anthropological study of one community that deals in part with residents' viewing habits where imported programs are available cites the popularity of domestically produced serial dramas and points out that, because viewers enjoy following the dramas from day to day, television in the community can serve an analogous function to that of oral poetry, which the residents often use at public gatherings as a daily journal of events of interest.

An empirical approach not unlike that of anthropologists is needed if communications specialists are to understand the impact of external cultural influences on the lives of people in a society. The first question they must investigate is: Given the evidence suggesting that the primary relationship of imported cultural productions to domestic ones is not dominance, then what model best represents the true relationship? One possibility is that, rather than one culture's productions dominating another's, the domestic culture absorbs the imported productions and becomes enriched. Another is that the imported productions fuse with domestic culture only where the two share common aspects, such as the use of themes, situations, or character types that are relevant and interesting to both cultures.

Communications researchers will also need to consider how to assess the position of the individual viewer in their model of cultural relationships. This model must emphasize the diversity of human responses, and will require engaging with the actual experiences of viewers, taking into account the variable contexts in which productions are experienced, and the complex manner in which individuals ascribe meanings to those productions.
explanation_html:

Computers have long been utilized in the sphere of law in the form of word processors, spreadsheets, legal research systems, and practice management systems. Most exciting, however, has been the prospect of using artificial intelligence techniques to create so-called legal reasoning systems—computer programs that can help to resolve legal disputes by reasoning from and applying the law. But the practical benefits of such automated reasoning systems have fallen short of optimistic early predictions and have not resulted in computer systems that can independently provide expert advice about substantive law. This is not surprising in light of the difficulty in resolving problems involving the meaning and applicability of rules set out in a legal text.

Early attempts at automated legal reasoning focused on the doctrinal nature of law. They viewed law as a set of rules, and the resulting computer systems were engineered to make legal decisions by determining the consequences that followed when its stored set of legal rules was applied to a collection of evidentiary data. Such systems underestimated the problems of interpretation that can arise at every stage of a legal argument. Examples abound of situations that are open to differing interpretations: whether a mobile home in a trailer park is a house or a motor vehicle, whether a couple can be regarded as married in the absence of a formal legal ceremony, and so on. Indeed, many notions invoked in the text of a statute may be deliberately left undefined so as to allow the law to be adapted to unforeseen circumstances. But in order to be able to apply legal rules to novel situations, systems have to be equipped with a kind of comprehensive knowledge of the world that is far beyond their capabilities at present or in the foreseeable future.

Proponents of legal reasoning systems now argue that accommodating reference to, and reasoning from, cases improves the chances of producing a successful system. By focusing on the practice of reasoning from precedents, researchers have designed systems called case-based reasoners, which store individual example cases in their knowledge bases. In contrast to a system that models legal knowledge based on a set of rules, a case-based reasoner, when given a concrete problem, manipulates the cases in its knowledge base to reach a conclusion based on a similar case. Unfortunately, in the case-based systems currently in development, the criteria for similarity among cases are system dependent and fixed by the designer, so that similarity is found only by testing for the presence or absence of predefined factors. This simply postpones the apparently intractable problem of developing a system that can discover for itself the factors that make cases similar in relevant ways.

The explanation offered is the difficulty of settling what rules in a legal text mean and when they apply. Treat that interpretive problem as the passage's organizing theme, because both remaining paragraphs are versions of it.

Attention turns to the first generation of attempts, which treated law as doctrine, a set of rules. Those systems were engineered to reach decisions by applying their stored rules to a body of evidentiary data, and their weakness, in the author's account, is that they underestimated how much interpretation every stage of a legal argument demands. The examples are deliberately homely: whether a mobile home in a trailer park counts as a house or a motor vehicle, whether a couple can be regarded as married without a formal ceremony. Worse, statutes often leave notions undefined on purpose so the law can stretch to unforeseen circumstances. Applying rules to novel situations would therefore require something like comprehensive knowledge of the world, which the author says is far beyond these systems now and for the foreseeable future.

In Alaska, tradition is a powerful legal concept, appearing in a wide variety of legal contexts relating to natural-resource and public-lands activities. Both state and federal laws in the United States assign privileges and exemptions to individuals engaged in "traditional" activities using otherwise off-limits land and resources. But in spite of its prevalence in statutory law, the term "tradition" is rarely defined. Instead, there seems to be a presumption that its meaning is obvious. Failure to define "tradition" clearly in written law has given rise to problematic and inconsistent legal results.

One of the most prevalent ideas associated with the term "tradition" in the law is that tradition is based on long-standing practice, where "long-standing" refers not only to the passage of time but also to the continuity and regularity of a practice. But two recent court cases involving indigenous use of sea otter pelts illustrate the problems that can arise in the application of this sense of "traditional."

The hunting of sea otters was initially prohibited by the Fur Seal Treaty of 1910. The Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) of 1972 continued the prohibition, but it also included an Alaska Native exemption, which allowed takings of protected animals for use in creating authentic native articles by means of "traditional native handicrafts." The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) subsequently issued regulations defining authentic native articles as those "commonly produced" before 1972, when the MMPA took effect. Not covered by the exemption, according to the FWS, were items produced from sea otter pelts, because Alaska Natives had not produced such handicrafts "within living memory."

In 1986, FWS agents seized articles of clothing made from sea otter pelts from Marina Katelnikoff, an Aleut. She sued, but the district court upheld the FWS regulations. Then in 1991 Katelnikoff joined a similar suit brought by Boyd Dickinson, a Tlingit from whom articles of clothing made from sea otter pelts had also been seized. After hearing testimony establishing that Alaska Natives had made many uses of sea otters before the occupation of the territory by Russia in the late 1700s, the court reconsidered what constituted a traditional item under the statute. The court now held that the FWS's regulations were based on a "strained interpretation" of the word "traditional," and that the reference to "living memory" imposed an excessively restrictive time frame. The court stated, "The fact that Alaskan natives were prevented, by circumstances beyond their control, from exercising a tradition for a given period of time does not mean that it has been lost forever or that it has become any less a 'tradition.' It defies common sense to define 'traditional' in such a way that only those traditions that were exercised during a comparatively short period in history could qualify as 'traditional.'"
explanation_html:
The opening establishes the topic and the trouble with it in the same breath. In Alaska, tradition does real legal work, turning up throughout the law governing natural resources and public lands, where both state and federal statutes grant privileges and exemptions to people engaged in traditional activities using land and resources that are otherwise off-limits. Yet for all its prevalence in statutory law, the term is rarely defined, as though its meaning were self-evident. The author's thesis lands flatly at the end of the paragraph: that failure to define it has produced legal outcomes that are both problematic and inconsistent.

Next comes the working definition the law tends to assume. The most common legal idea of tradition ties it to long-standing practice, and notice the two components packed into that phrase, since long-standing refers not only to elapsed time but also to the continuity and regularity of the practice. The second component is what will cause the difficulty. Two recent court cases involving indigenous use of sea otter pelts are introduced here as the illustration, so read the rest of the passage as a test of whether this sense of traditional can survive contact with actual facts.

The statutory history is laid out carefully, so track the sequence. Hunting sea otters was first prohibited by the Fur Seal Treaty of 1910, and the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 continued the prohibition while carving out an Alaska Native exemption for takings used to create authentic native articles through traditional native handicrafts. The FWS then supplied the definition Congress had not, declaring authentic articles to be those commonly produced before 1972, and further excluding items made from sea otter pelts on the ground that Alaska Natives had not produced such handicrafts within living memory. Watch what the agency has quietly done, converting traditional into recent and uninterrupted practice.

Litigation shows the consequence and then the correction. When agents seized clothing made from sea otter pelts from Marina Katelnikoff, an Aleut, in 1986, the district court upheld the regulations; in 1991 she joined a similar suit brought by Boyd Dickinson, a Tlingit whose garments had also been seized. This time testimony established that Alaska Natives had made many uses of sea otters before Russian occupation of the territory in the late 1700s, and the 1991 court reconsidered. It called the agency's reading strained and its living memory standard excessively restrictive, reasoning that a tradition interrupted by circumstances beyond a people's control is not lost forever. The continuity requirement, in short, penalizes precisely those whose practice was suppressed.
overall_html: The passage argues that law leans heavily on the word tradition while almost never defining it, and that the prevailing working sense of the term, long-standing practice understood to require continuity and regularity, generates inconsistent and unfair results. The author's purpose is to expose that definitional gap and demonstrate its consequences concretely, moving from the general problem to the dominant legal idea of tradition and then to a detailed history in which the FWS excluded sea otter handicrafts because Alaska Natives had not made them within living memory, until a court rejected that reading as strained. The competing positions to keep apart are the FWS's restrictive definition and the 1991 court's broader one.

The literary development of Kate Chopin, author of The Awakening (1899), took her through several phases of nineteenth-century women's fiction. Born in 1850, Chopin grew up with the sentimental novels that formed the bulk of the fiction of the mid–nineteenth century. In these works, authors employed elevated, romantic language to portray female characters whose sole concern was to establish their social positions through courtship and marriage. Later, when she started writing her own fiction, Chopin took as her models the works of a group of women writers known as the local colorists.

After 1865, what had traditionally been regarded as "women's culture" began to dissolve as women entered higher education, the professions, and the political world in greater numbers. The local colorists, who published stories about regional life in the 1870s and 1880s, were attracted to the new worlds opening up to women, and felt free to move within these worlds as artists. Like anthropologists, the local colorists observed culture and character with almost scientific detachment. However, as "women's culture" continued to disappear, the local colorists began to mourn its demise by investing its images with mythic significance. In their stories, the garden became a paradisal sanctuary; the house became an emblem of female nurturing; and the artifacts of domesticity became virtual totemic objects.

Unlike the local colorists, Chopin devoted herself to telling stories of loneliness, isolation, and frustration. But she used the conventions of the local colorists to solve a specific narrative problem: how to deal with extreme psychological states without resorting to the excesses of the sentimental novels she read as a youth. By reporting narrative events as if they were part of a region's "local color," Chopin could tell rather shocking or even melodramatic tales in an uninflected manner.

Chopin did not share the local colorists' growing nostalgia for the past, however, and by the 1890s she was looking beyond them to the more ambitious models offered by a movement known as the New Women. In the form as well as the content of their work, the New Women writers pursued freedom and innovation. They modified the form of the sentimental novel to make room for interludes of fantasy and parable, especially episodes in which women dream of an entirely different world than the one they inhabit. Instead of the crisply plotted short stories that had been the primary genre of the local colorists, the New Women writers experimented with impressionistic methods in an effort to explore hitherto unrecorded aspects of female consciousness. In The Awakening, Chopin embraced this impressionistic approach more fully to produce 39 numbered sections of uneven length unified less by their style or content than by their sustained focus on faithfully rendering the workings of the protagonist's mind.
explanation_html:
Chopin's career is framed at the outset as a passage through successive phases of nineteenth-century women's fiction, so expect the passage to be organized chronologically by influence. Born in 1850, Kate Chopin grew up reading the sentimental novels that made up the bulk of mid-century fiction, works whose elevated, romantic language depicted women wholly occupied with securing a social position through courtship and marriage. When she began writing herself she looked instead to the Local Colorists, a group of women writers who supplied her first models. Those influences, and a third still to come, structure everything that follows.

Historical context arrives next to explain why the local colorists mattered. After 1865 what had traditionally been thought of as women's culture began dissolving as women entered higher education, the professions and political life in greater numbers. The local colorists, publishing regional stories through the 1870s and 1880s, were drawn to these opening worlds and felt free to move within them as artists, observing culture and character with an almost scientific detachment. But as women's culture kept receding they began to mourn it, loading its images with mythic weight, so that the garden became a paradisal sanctuary, the house an emblem of female nurturing, and household objects virtual totems.

Chopin is now separated from her models, though the paragraph also explains what she took from them. Her subjects were loneliness, isolation and frustration rather than regional life, yet the local colorists' conventions solved a technical difficulty for her: how to handle extreme psychological states without falling into the excesses of the sentimental novels she had read as a girl. Reporting events as though they were simply a region's local color let her narrate shocking, even melodramatic material in a flat, uninflected voice. Notice that the emphasis here is on craft, on borrowed technique put to unfamiliar use.

The final phase completes the sequence. Chopin did not share the local colorists' growing nostalgia for the past, and by the 1890s she was looking past them to the more ambitious models of the New Women writers, who pursued freedom and innovation in form as much as in content. They reworked the sentimental novel to admit interludes of fantasy and parable, especially episodes in which women dream of a world wholly unlike their own, and they abandoned the crisply plotted short story for impressionistic methods aimed at aspects of female consciousness no one had recorded. The Awakening takes that approach furthest, in thirty-nine numbered sections of uneven length held together chiefly by their sustained attention to the protagonist's mind.
overall_html: The passage traces Kate Chopin's literary development through three successive influences in nineteenth-century women's fiction: the sentimental novels of her childhood, the local colorists whose detached regional manner gave her a way to narrate extreme psychological states without melodrama, and the New Women writers whose formal experiments she carried furthest in The Awakening. The author's purpose is expository and chronological rather than evaluative, showing at each stage what Chopin borrowed and what she declined to take, notably the local colorists' nostalgia for a vanishing women's culture. The profiles to keep distinct are the sentimental novelists, the local colorists, the New Women, and Chopin herself as a selective borrower from each.

Until the 1950s, most scientists believed that the geology of the ocean floor had remained essentially unchanged for many millions of years. But this idea became insupportable as new discoveries were made. First, scientists noticed that the ocean floor exhibited odd magnetic variations. Though unexpected, this was not entirely surprising, because it was known that basalt—the volcanic rock making up much of the ocean floor—contains magnetite, a strongly magnetic mineral that was already known to locally distort compass readings on land. This distortion is due to the fact that although some basalt has so-called "normal" polarity—that is, the magnetite in it has the same polarity as the earth's present magnetic field—other basalt has reversed polarity, an alignment opposite that of the present field. This occurs because in magma (molten rock), grains of magnetite—behaving like little compass needles—align themselves with the earth's magnetic field, which has reversed at various times throughout history. When magma cools to form solid basalt, the alignment of the magnetite grains is "locked in," recording the earth's polarity at the time of cooling.

As more of the ocean floor was mapped, the magnetic variations revealed recognizable patterns, particularly in the area around the other great oceanic discovery of the 1950s: the global mid-ocean ridge, an immense submarine mountain range that winds its way around the earth much like the seams of a baseball. Alternating stripes of rock with differing polarities are laid out in rows on either side of the mid-ocean ridge: one stripe with normal polarity and the next with reversed polarity. Scientists theorized that mid-ocean ridges mark structurally weak zones where the ocean floor is being pulled apart along the ridge crest. New magma from deep within the earth rises easily through these weak zones and eventually erupts along the crest of the ridges to create new oceanic crust. Over millions of years, this process, called ocean floor spreading, built the mid-ocean ridge.

This theory was supported by several lines of evidence. First, at or near the ridge crest, the rocks are very young, and they become progressively older away from the crest. Further, the youngest rocks all have normal polarity. Finally, because geophysicists had already determined the ages of continental volcanic rocks and, by measuring the magnetic orientation of these same rocks, had assigned ages to the earth's recent magnetic reversals, they were able to compare these known ages of magnetic reversals with the ocean floor's magnetic striping pattern, enabling scientists to show that, if we assume that the ocean floor moved away from the spreading center at a rate of several centimeters per year, there is a remarkable correlation between the ages of the earth's magnetic reversals and the striping pattern.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by dating a change of mind and then explaining the discovery that forced it. Until the 1950s most scientists took the geology of the ocean floor to have been essentially unchanged for many millions of years, a view new findings made insupportable. The first was odd magnetic variation across the ocean floor, not wholly surprising because basalt, the volcanic rock forming much of that floor, contains magnetite, a strongly magnetic mineral already known to distort compass readings on land. Some basalt matches the earth's present field, called normal polarity, while other basalt is aligned opposite to it. The reason is that magnetite grains in magma swing like tiny compass needles toward whatever field exists at the time, and cooling locks that alignment in, so each rock records the earth's polarity when it hardened.

The second great discovery of the decade joins the first, and together they generate the theory. As more of the floor was mapped, the magnetic variations resolved into recognizable patterns, clearest around the global mid-ocean ridge, an immense submarine mountain range winding around the planet like the seams of a baseball. Flanking that ridge are alternating stripes of rock, one normal in polarity and the next reversed. Scientists proposed that ridges sit over structurally weak zones where the ocean floor is being pulled apart along the crest, so magma from deep in the earth rises easily through the weakness, erupts at the crest and forms new oceanic crust. That process, ocean floor spreading, built the ridge over millions of years.

Corroboration fills the closing paragraph, and it comes in three steps worth keeping separate. Rocks at or near the ridge crest are very young and grow progressively older with distance from it, exactly as spreading predicts. The youngest rocks all show normal polarity. The third piece is the most intricate: geophysicists had already dated continental volcanic rocks and, by measuring the magnetic orientation of those same rocks, had assigned ages to the earth's recent magnetic reversals, which meant those ages could be set against the ocean floor's striping. Assuming the floor moves away from the spreading center at several centimeters a year, the correlation between the two records turns out to be remarkable.
overall_html: The passage explains how the older belief in a geologically static ocean floor gave way to the theory of ocean floor spreading, in which new crust forms as magma rises through weak zones along the mid-ocean ridge and then moves outward. The author's purpose is expository, building the account in stages: first the magnetic behavior of basalt, whose magnetite grains lock in the earth's polarity as magma cools, then the striped pattern of normal and reversed polarity flanking the newly mapped ridge, and finally three lines of supporting evidence, culminating in the match between independently dated magnetic reversals and the striping itself. No competing viewpoints are developed beyond the superseded older belief.

Passage A

Central to the historian's profession and scholarship has been the ideal of objectivity. The assumptions upon which this ideal rests include a commitment to the reality of the past, a sharp separation between fact and value, and above all, a distinction between history and fiction.

According to this ideal, historical facts are prior to and independent of interpretation: the value of an interpretation should be judged by how well it accounts for the facts; if an interpretation is contradicted by facts, it should be abandoned. The fact that successive generations of historians have ascribed different meanings to past events does not mean, as relativist historians claim, that the events themselves lack fixed or absolute meanings.

Objective historians see their role as that of a neutral judge, one who must never become an advocate or, worse, propagandist. Their conclusions should display the judicial qualities of balance and evenhandedness. As with the judiciary, these qualities require insulation from political considerations, and avoidance of partisanship or bias. Thus objective historians must purge themselves of external loyalties; their primary allegiance is to objective historical truth and to colleagues who share a commitment to its discovery.

Passage B

The very possibility of historical scholarship as an enterprise distinct from propaganda requires of its practitioners that self-discipline that enables them to do such things as abandon wishful thinking, assimilate bad news, and discard pleasing interpretations that fail elementary tests of evidence and logic.

Yet objectivity, for the historian, should not be confused with neutrality. Objectivity is perfectly compatible with strong political commitment. The objective thinker does not value detachment as an end in itself but only as an indispensable means of achieving deeper understanding. In historical scholarship, the ideal of objectivity is most compellingly embodied in the powerful argument—one that reveals by its every twist and turn its respectful appreciation of the alternative arguments it rejects. Such a text attains power precisely because its author has managed to suspend momentarily his or her own perceptions so as to anticipate and take into account objections and alternative constructions—not those of straw men, but those that truly issue from the rival's position, understood as sensitively and stated as eloquently as the rival could desire. To mount a telling attack on a position, one must first inhabit it. Those so habituated to their customary intellectual abode that they cannot even explore others can never be persuasive to anyone but fellow habitués.

Such arguments are often more faithful to the complexity of historical interpretation—more faithful even to the irreducible plurality of human perspectives—than texts that abjure position-taking altogether. The powerful argument is the highest fruit of the kind of thinking I would call objective, and in it neutrality plays no part. Authentic objectivity bears no resemblance to the television newscaster's mechanical gesture of allocating the same number of seconds to both sides of a question, editorially splitting the difference between them, irrespective of their perceived merits.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by naming the ideal it will lay out: objectivity, presented as central to the historian's profession and scholarship. Three assumptions are said to underpin it, and all three are worth holding onto, since the rest of the passage unpacks them. There is a commitment to the reality of the past, a sharp separation between fact and value, and above all a distinction between history and fiction. Nothing is argued for yet; this paragraph simply states the foundations on which the position will be built.

The relationship between facts and interpretation comes next. On this ideal, historical facts are prior to and independent of any reading of them, so an interpretation earns its keep by accounting for the facts and must be abandoned when the facts contradict it. The paragraph then blocks an objection. The Relativist Historians take the fact that successive generations have ascribed different meanings to past events as evidence that events lack fixed meanings; Passage A denies the inference, treating shifting interpretations as a fact about historians rather than about the past itself.

The ideal is now converted into a professional role, and the governing image is judicial. The Objective Historians see themselves as neutral judges, never advocates and still less propagandists, and their conclusions are expected to display balance and evenhandedness. As with the judiciary, those qualities demand insulation from political considerations and the avoidance of partisanship or bias. The demand is strong: such historians must purge themselves of external loyalties, owing primary allegiance only to objective historical truth and to colleagues committed to finding it. Notice how tightly objectivity and neutrality are bound together here, because that link is what the second passage will cut.

Passage B opens on ground the two passages share. Historical scholarship can only count as something other than propaganda if its practitioners exercise self-discipline, which means abandoning wishful thinking, assimilating bad news, and discarding pleasing interpretations that fail elementary tests of evidence and logic. Read this as a concession offered before the disagreement arrives, since nothing in it would trouble Passage A at all. The single paragraph establishes that the argument to come is not a rejection of objectivity but a quarrel about what objectivity consists in.

The disagreement lands squarely on the word neutrality. Objectivity must not be confused with it, Passage B insists, and is perfectly compatible with strong political commitment; detachment is valued not as an end but as the indispensable means to deeper understanding. What embodies objectivity is the powerful argument, a text whose every turn shows respectful appreciation of the positions it rejects. Its author suspends his or her own perceptions long enough to state a rival's case as sensitively and eloquently as the rival could desire, because to attack a position tellingly you must first inhabit it. Anyone too settled in a single intellectual home, the argument runs, persuades only those already living there.

The closing paragraph presses the claim further. Arguments of that kind are often more faithful to the complexity of historical interpretation, and to the irreducible plurality of human perspectives, than texts that refuse to take any position at all. Passage B calls the powerful argument the highest fruit of objective thinking and says plainly that neutrality plays no part in it. A final image sharpens the contrast: authentic objectivity looks nothing like a newscaster mechanically allotting equal seconds to both sides and splitting the difference regardless of their merits.
overall_html: Both passages defend historical objectivity but divide over what it requires. Passage A sets out the traditional ideal, grounded in the reality of the past and a sharp separation of fact from value, and casts the objective historian as a neutral judge who must purge external loyalties and stay insulated from politics. Passage B accepts the same evidentiary self-discipline but denies that objectivity means neutrality, holding that it is compatible with strong political commitment and is best realized in the powerful argument, which states a rival's case as forcefully as the rival would. The relationship is agreement on foundations combined with direct disagreement over whether neutrality belongs to objectivity at all.

Determining the most effective way to deter deliberate crimes, such as fraud, as opposed to impulsive crimes, such as crimes of passion, is a problem currently being debated in the legal community. On one side of the debate are those scholars who believe that deliberate crimes are a product of the influence of societal norms and institutions on individuals. These scholars suggest that changing people's beliefs about crime, increasing the access of the most economically alienated individuals to economic institutions, and rehabilitating those convicted of this type of crime will reduce the crime rate. On the other side are those legal scholars who believe that the decision to commit a deliberate crime is primarily the result of individual choice. They suggest that increasing the fines and penalties associated with criminal activity, along with efficacious law enforcement, is the best deterrence method. However, some recent legal scholarship has changed the nature of this debate by introducing an economic principle that shows that these two positions, far from being antithetical, are surprisingly complementary.

The economic principle that reconciles the two positions is that of utility maximization, which holds that, given a choice of actions, rational individuals will choose the action that maximizes their anticipated overall satisfaction, or expected utility. The expected utility of an action is ascertained by determining the utilities of the possible outcomes of that action, weighing them according to the likelihood of each outcome's coming to pass, and then adding up those weighted utilities. Using this economic framework, an individual's decision to commit a crime can be analyzed as a rational economic choice.

According to the utility maximization principle a person who responds rationally to economic incentives or disincentives will commit a crime if the expected utility from doing so, given the chance of getting caught, exceeds the expected utility from activity that is lawful. Within this framework the two crime-deterrence methods have the same overall effect. For instance, the recommendations on one side of the crime deterrence debate to increase penalties for crimes and strengthen law enforcement result in an increased likelihood of detection and punishment and impose an increased cost to the individual if detected and punished. This lowers the expected utility from criminal activity, thereby making a person less likely to choose to commit a deliberate crime. The recommendations on the other side of the debate, such as increasing the economic opportunities of individuals most alienated from economic institutions, also affect the utility equation. All else being equal, enacting these types of policies will effectively increase the expected utility from lawful activity. This economic analysis demonstrates that the two positions are not fundamentally in conflict, and that the optimal approach to crime deterrence would include elements of both deterrence strategies.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by staking out a live debate in the legal community over how best to deter deliberate crimes such as fraud, as opposed to impulsive ones such as crimes of passion. The Social-Influence Scholars hold that deliberate crime grows out of the influence of societal norms and institutions on individuals, so they recommend changing people's beliefs about crime, giving the most economically alienated individuals better access to economic institutions, and rehabilitating offenders. The Individual-Choice Scholars treat the decision to offend as primarily a matter of individual choice and prescribe heavier fines and penalties backed by efficacious law enforcement. The final sentence signals where the passage is going: recent scholarship claims the two camps are complementary rather than antithetical.

The reconciling tool is defined next, and it pays to get the definition straight before the argument puts it to work. Utility maximization holds that a rational individual facing a choice of actions will take the one that maximizes anticipated overall satisfaction, known as expected utility. Calculating an action's expected utility means identifying the utilities of its possible outcomes, weighting each by how likely that outcome is, and adding the weighted results together. Applied to crime, this recasts the decision to offend as a rational economic choice rather than a moral or sociological mystery. Nothing is argued here; the paragraph simply supplies machinery.

That machinery is now run, and the payoff is that both sets of recommendations move the same equation. Someone responding rationally to economic incentives commits a crime when its expected utility, discounted by the chance of getting caught, exceeds the expected utility of lawful activity. Stiffer penalties and stronger enforcement raise both the likelihood of detection and the cost of being punished, which drives the expected utility of crime down. Increasing the economic opportunities of the most alienated individuals works on the other term, raising the expected utility of lawful activity. Same equation, opposite sides. Hence the conclusion the author draws, that the positions are not fundamentally in conflict and the optimal approach would combine elements of both.
overall_html: The passage argues that two apparently opposed approaches to deterring deliberate crime, one attributing such crime to societal norms and institutions and the other to individual choice, turn out to be complementary once the economic principle of utility maximization is applied. The author's purpose is reconciliatory: after setting out the debate, the passage defines expected utility as the probability-weighted sum of an action's possible outcomes, then shows that harsher penalties and better enforcement lower the expected utility of crime while expanded economic opportunity raises the expected utility of lawful activity. The viewpoints to track are the two scholarly camps and the recent economic analysis the author endorses, which concludes that optimal deterrence draws on both strategies.

Mexican Americans share with speakers of Spanish throughout the world a rich and varied repertoire of proverbs as well as a vital tradition of proverb use. The term "proverb" refers to a self-contained saying that can be understood independent of a specific verbal context and that has as its main purpose the carrying of a message or piece of wisdom. The great majority of Spanish-language proverbs reached Mexico from peninsular Spain, though they did not all originate there. Many belong, in fact, to the common proverb tradition of Europe and have exact equivalents in English-language proverbial speech.

Each use of a proverb is an individual act whose meaning varies depending on the individual speaker and the particular social context in which the use occurs. Nonetheless, it is important to recognize that proverb use is also shaped by the larger community with which the individual interacts. The fact that proverbs often serve a didactic purpose points us to one important function that proverbs serve in Mexican American communities: the instruction of the young. In fact, this function seems to be much more prominent in Mexican tradition in general than in English-speaking traditions. Adolescents of Mexican descent in the United States consistently report the frequent use of proverbs by their parents as a teaching tool, in areas ranging from the inculcation of table manners to the regulation of peer-group relationships. The latter area is a particularly frequent focus of proverb use within Mexican American communities: one of the most frequently used proverbs, for example, translates roughly as, "Tell me who you run with and I'll tell you who you are." Perhaps this emphasis on peer-group relations derives from a sense that traditional, community-approved norms are threatened by those prevalent in the surrounding society, or from a sense that, in dealing with older children especially, parents need to appeal to traditional wisdom to bolster their authority.

Another dimension of proverb use within Mexican American communities is that proverbs often serve to foster a consciousness of ethnicity, that is, of membership in a particular ethnic group possessing features that distinguish it from other groups within a multiethnic environment. Even those Mexican American proverbs that do not have an explicitly didactic purpose nevertheless serve as a vehicle for the transmission of both the Spanish language and Mexican culture. It is in these sayings that links to folklore and other aspects of Mexican culture are established and maintained. Proverbs thus provide a means of enhancing Mexican American young people's familiarity with their heritage, thereby strengthening their ties to Mexican tradition.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by locating its subject and pinning down its key term. Mexican Americans share with Spanish speakers throughout the world a rich stock of proverbs and an active tradition of using them. A proverb, as defined here, is a self-contained saying that can be understood apart from any particular verbal context and whose main purpose is to carry a message or piece of wisdom. Origins are then traced with some care: most Spanish-language proverbs reached Mexico from peninsular Spain without necessarily originating there, since many belong to a common European proverb tradition and have exact equivalents in English.

A tension is raised and then absorbed before the main claim arrives. Each use of a proverb is an individual act whose meaning varies with the speaker and the social context, yet proverb use is also shaped by the larger community the individual moves in. That community dimension leads to the first function the author identifies, the instruction of the young, which is said to be considerably more prominent in Mexican tradition than in English-speaking ones. Adolescents of Mexican descent consistently report parents using proverbs to teach everything from table manners to the handling of peer-group relationships, the latter an especially frequent focus. Notice that the two explanations offered for that emphasis, community norms feeling threatened and parents borrowing authority from traditional wisdom, are floated as possibilities rather than asserted.

A second function closes the passage and widens the claim beyond teaching. Proverbs also foster a consciousness of ethnicity, meaning an awareness of belonging to a group with features that mark it off from others in a multiethnic environment. The crucial move is that even proverbs carrying no explicitly didactic purpose still perform this work, because using them transmits the Spanish language and Mexican culture and keeps links to folklore alive. The conclusion follows directly from that: proverbs deepen young Mexican Americans' familiarity with their heritage and in doing so strengthen their ties to Mexican tradition.
overall_html: The passage describes the place of proverbs in Mexican American communities, defining a proverb as a self-contained saying whose purpose is to carry wisdom and tracing the Spanish-language repertoire back through peninsular Spain to a common European tradition. The author's purpose is expository and analytical, identifying two functions in turn: the didactic instruction of the young, more prominent here than in English-speaking traditions and focused heavily on peer-group relationships, and the fostering of ethnic consciousness, which even non-didactic proverbs accomplish by transmitting language, folklore and culture. No competing viewpoints are developed, since the passage carries the author's descriptive voice throughout, with two tentative explanations offered for the emphasis on peers.

Passage A

 Evolutionary psychology has taught us to examine human behavior from the standpoint of the theory of evolution—to explain a given type of human behavior by examining how it contributes to the reproductive success of individuals exhibiting the behavior, and thereby to the proliferation of the genetic material responsible for causing that behavior. From an evolutionary standpoint, the problem of altruism is a thorny one: what accounts for the evolution of behavior in which an individual expends energy or other valuable resources promoting the welfare of another individual?

The answer probably lies in the psychological experiences of identification and empathy. Such experiences could have initially arisen in response to cues (like physical resemblance) that indicated the presence of shared genetic material in human ancestors. The psychological states provoked by these cues could have increased the chances of related individuals' receiving assistance, thereby enhancing the survival and replication of genes influencing the capacity for identification and empathy. This would account, for example, for a mother's rushing to help her injured child; genes promoting their own self-propagation may thus operate through instinctive actions that appear unselfish.

Since human ancestors lived in small, kin-based groups, the application of altruistic mechanisms to the entire group would have promoted the propagation of the genes responsible for those mechanisms. Later, these mechanisms may have come to apply to humans who are not kin when communities grew larger. In this way, apparently altruistic mechanisms may have arisen within a genetically "selfish" system.

Passage B

Evolutionary psychology is a kind of conspiracy theory; that is, it explains behavior by imputing an interest (the proliferation of genes) that the agent of the behavior does not openly acknowledge, or indeed, is not even aware of. Thus, what seemed to be your unsurprising interest in your child's well-being turns out to be your genes' conspiracy to propagate themselves.

Such arguments can appear persuasive on the face of it. According to some evolutionary psychologists, an interest in the proliferation of genes explains monogamous families in animals whose offspring mature slowly. Human offspring mature slowly; and, at least in numerical terms, our species favors monogamous families. Evolutionary psychologists take this as evidence that humans form monogamous families because of our interest in propagating our genes. Are they right?

Maybe yes, maybe no; this kind of inference needs to be handled with great care. There are, most often, all sorts of interests that would explain any given behavior. What is needed to make it decisive that a particular interest explains a particular behavior is that the behavior would be reasonable only if one had that interest. But such cases are vanishingly rare: an interest in Y might explain doing X, but so too would an interest in doing X. A concern to propagate one's genes would explain promoting the welfare of one's children; but so too would an interest in the welfare of one's children. Not all of one's motives can be instrumental, after all; there must be some things that one cares for just for their own sakes.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by stating the method it will apply. Evolutionary psychology explains a type of human behavior by asking how it contributes to the reproductive success of the individuals who display it, and so to the spread of the genetic material responsible for causing it. The paragraph then names the difficulty that will occupy the rest of the passage: altruism is a thorny case for this approach, because it is hard to see how behavior could evolve in which an individual spends energy or other valuable resources promoting someone else's welfare.

A solution follows, and notice how tentatively it is offered, as what probably lies behind the puzzle. Identification and empathy are the psychological experiences at issue, and they could have arisen originally in response to cues such as physical resemblance, which in human ancestors indicated shared genetic material. Feeling those states toward such people made it likelier that relatives received assistance, which in turn helped the genes underlying identification and empathy survive and replicate. A mother rushing to her injured child is the illustration given. The striking formulation is that genes promoting their own self-propagation may operate through instinctive actions that look entirely unselfish.

Scale is what the third paragraph adds, completing the argument. Because human ancestors lived in small, kin-based groups, extending altruistic mechanisms to the whole group would still have propagated the genes responsible for them, and later, as communities grew larger, those same mechanisms may have come to cover people who are not kin at all. The closing phrase captures Passage A's whole position neatly: apparently altruistic mechanisms arising within a genetically selfish system, which resolves the tension the first paragraph raised.

Passage B opens with a characterization rather than a direct rebuttal, and a pointed one. Evolutionary psychology is called a kind of conspiracy theory, since it explains behavior by imputing to the agent an interest, the proliferation of genes, that the agent never openly acknowledges and may not even be aware of. The example lands squarely on the territory Passage A occupied, since what looked like your unsurprising interest in your child's well-being is recast as your genes conspiring to propagate themselves.

Fairness comes next, because Passage B concedes that such arguments can appear persuasive at first glance. The illustration is monogamy. Some evolutionary psychologists explain monogamous families in animals whose offspring mature slowly by an interest in gene proliferation; human offspring also mature slowly, and in numerical terms our species favors monogamous families, so the same interest is taken to explain the human arrangement. The paragraph ends on a question rather than a verdict, which sets up the examination of the reasoning itself in the final paragraph.

The objection, when it arrives, is logical rather than empirical. Passage B answers its own question with maybe yes, maybe no, then explains why this kind of inference needs care: all sorts of interests would explain any given behavior, and an interest only decisively explains a behavior if the behavior would be reasonable only for someone holding that interest. Such cases are said to be vanishingly rare, because an interest in Y might explain doing X, but so would an interest in doing X. Wanting to propagate one's genes would explain promoting a child's welfare, but so would caring about the child's welfare. Not all motives can be instrumental; some things must be cared for simply for their own sakes.
overall_html: Both passages take up evolutionary psychology's account of altruism, and they disagree about whether that account is warranted. Passage A argues from inside the framework, presenting identification and empathy as mechanisms that arose because cues like physical resemblance marked shared genes, so that helping kin, and later non-kin once communities grew, propagated the very genes behind the helping. Passage B stands outside it, calling evolutionary psychology a conspiracy theory and objecting on logical grounds that many competing interests could explain any behavior, so an interest in propagating one's genes explains parental care no better than simply caring about one's child does. B is a methodological critique of exactly the reasoning A exemplifies.
