During Dostoyevsky's time there were two significant and opposing directions in Russian literary criticism. One position maintained that art stood high above the present and the everyday, while the radical view maintained that art had a right to exist only if it found its sources in concrete reality, and, through the exposure of want and injustice, it contributed to the creation of a new society; literature, in other words, should be useful. Dostoyevsky took a third position. As a realist, he never doubted that reality was literature's crucial source. But his understanding of reality went deeper than the one prevailing among radical critics, since for Dostoyevsky there was no distinction in principle between fantasy and reality, and reality was far more than the merely tangible.

The radical critics' demand that reality be depicted "as it is" was meaningless for Dostoyevsky; reality was necessarily shaped by the person who experienced it: what may not be reality for you may be reality for me. The task of the writer was to explode the boundaries of the so-called real world. Within perceptible "reality" exists another sphere, the fantastic, which is not in any way superfluous to a writer's concerns: "The fantastic must be so intimately bound up with the real that one almost believes in it."

The radical critics' insistence that art must serve a particular political view was for Dostoyevsky the equivalent of assigning to art "a shameful destiny." A literary work must stand or fall on its "artistic merit," he explained. The utilitarian claim that the formal aspects of a work were of secondary importance so long as its goal was good and its purpose clear struck Dostoyevsky as a contradiction in terms. Only fully realized artistic works could fulfill their goals. But what does it mean to say that a work is "artistic"? Dostoyevsky defined it thus: "To say that a novelist is `artistic' means that he possesses a talent to express his thoughts in characters and images so that when the reader has finished the novel, he has fully understood the author's thoughts. Therefore, artistry is quite simply the ability to write well."

The radical critics' requirement that art must at all costs be "useful" to people and society seemed to Dostoyevsky unsatisfactory. How can we know what will show itself to be useful? Can we say with assurance how useful the Iliad has been to humankind? No, Dostoyevsky believed, when it comes to this we encounter breadths that cannot be measured with any precision; sometimes a work of art may appear to deviate from reality and serve no useful purpose because we cannot see clearly what paths it may take to become useful.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by mapping the critical landscape Dostoyevsky worked in, so keep the three positions distinct from the start. The Idealist Critics held that art stood high above the present and the everyday. The Radical Critics insisted that art had a right to exist only if it drew on concrete reality and, by exposing want and injustice, helped bring a new society into being; literature, in short, should be useful. Dostoyevsky took a third position rather than joining either camp. As a realist he never doubted that reality was literature's crucial source, but his sense of reality ran deeper, admitting no distinction in principle between fantasy and reality and refusing to confine reality to the tangible.

Each remaining paragraph takes one radical demand and shows why Dostoyevsky rejected it, beginning with the demand that reality be depicted as it is. That phrase was meaningless to him, since reality is necessarily shaped by whoever experiences it, so what is not reality for you may be reality for me. The writer's task, on this view, is to explode the boundaries of the so-called real world, because within perceptible reality lies another sphere, the fantastic, which is no distraction from a writer's proper concerns but must be bound so intimately to the real that one almost believes in it.

The second demand concerns politics, and Dostoyevsky's language here is harsh: requiring art to serve a particular political view assigns it a shameful destiny. A literary work must stand or fall on its artistic merit instead. He regarded the utilitarian claim that a work's formal aspects matter less so long as its goal is good and its purpose clear as a contradiction in terms, since only fully realized artistic works can accomplish their goals at all. His definition of artistic follows, and it is worth holding onto because it is deliberately plain: a novelist is artistic when he can express his thoughts in characters and images so that the reader finishes having fully understood them, which makes artistry simply the ability to write well.

Usefulness is the last demand, and the objection this time is about knowledge rather than aesthetics. Dostoyevsky answers with a question: how can anyone know in advance what will show itself to be useful? Nobody can say with assurance how useful the Iliad has been to humankind. What we run into, on his account, are breadths that cannot be measured with any precision, so a work may appear to deviate from reality and serve no useful purpose merely because the paths by which it might become useful are not yet visible to us.
overall_html: The passage sets out Dostoyevsky's view of literature as a third position between the idealist critics who placed art above everyday life and the radical critics who demanded that art draw on concrete reality and serve social reform. The author's purpose is expository, and the structure is systematic: after establishing that Dostoyevsky was a realist with an unusually capacious idea of reality, the passage takes each radical demand in turn and supplies his answer, rejecting depiction of reality as it is, rejecting art placed in the service of politics in favor of artistic merit plainly defined, and rejecting usefulness on the ground that no one can foresee what will eventually prove useful.

In the 1980s there was a proliferation of poetry collections, short stories, and novels published by women of Latin American descent in the United States. By the end of the decade, another genre of U.S. Latina writing, the autobiography, also came into prominence with the publication of three notable autobiographical collections: Loving in the War Years: Lo Que Nunca Pasó Por Sus Labios, by Cherríe Moraga; Getting Home Alive, by Aurora Levins Morales and Rosario Morales; and Borderlands/La Frontera, by Gloria Anzaldúa.

These collections are innovative at many levels. They confront traditional linguistic boundaries by using a mix of English and Spanish, and they each address the politics of multiple cultural identities by exploring the interrelationships among such factors as ethnicity, gender, and language. This effort manifests itself in the generically mixed structure of these works, which combine essays, sketches, short stories, poems, and journal entries without, for the most part, giving preference to any of these modes of presentation.

In Borderlands/La Frontera, Anzaldúa presents her personal history and the history of the Mexican American community to which she belongs by juxtaposing narrative sequences and poetry. Moraga's Loving in the War Years is likewise characterized by a mixture of genres, and, as she states in her introduction, the events in her life story are not arranged chronologically, but rather in terms of her political development. According to one literary critic who specializes in the genre of autobiography, this departure from chronological ordering represents an important difference between autobiographies written by women and those traditionally written by men. Getting Home Alive departs even further from the conventions typical of autobiography by bringing together the voices of two people, a mother and her daughter, each of whom authors a portion of the text. The narratives and poems of each author are not assigned to separate sections of the text, but rather are woven together, with a piece by one sometimes commenting on a piece by the other. While this ordering may seem fragmentary and confusing, it is in fact a fully intentional and carefully designed experiment with literary structure. In a sense, this mixing of structures parallels the content of these autobiographies: the writers employ multigeneric and multivocal forms to express the complexities inherent in the formation of their identities.

Rather than forcing their personal histories to conform to existing generic parameters, these writers have revolutionized the genre of autobiography, redrawing the boundaries of this literary form to make it more amenable to the expression of their own experiences. In doing so, they have shown a strong determination to speak for themselves in a world that they feel has for too long taken their silence for granted.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with literary history rather than argument. Through the 1980s, women of Latin American descent in the United States published a growing body of poetry collections, short stories and novels, and by the end of the decade a further genre of U.S. Latina writing, the autobiography, had come to prominence as well. Three collections are named as the notable instances, by Cherríe Moraga, by Aurora Levins Morales together with Rosario Morales, and by Gloria Anzaldúa. Expect these three to serve as the passage's running examples, since everything that follows works through them.

A general claim about what makes the collections innovative comes next, and it operates on several levels at once. They confront traditional linguistic boundaries by mixing English and Spanish rather than choosing between them, and each addresses the politics of multiple cultural identities by exploring how factors such as ethnicity, gender and language bear on one another. The formal consequence matters most for what follows: that concern shows up in the generically mixed structure of the works, which combine essays, sketches, short stories, poems and journal entries while mostly declining to give preference to any one mode.

The general claim is now cashed out work by work, in ascending order of departure from convention. Anzaldúa juxtaposes narrative sequences with poetry to present her own history alongside that of the Mexican American community she belongs to. Moraga likewise mixes genres and arranges the events of her life by her political development rather than chronologically, which one critic specializing in autobiography treats as an important difference between women's autobiographies and those traditionally written by men. Getting Home Alive goes furthest, since a mother and daughter each author part of the text and their pieces are woven together rather than kept in separate sections, one sometimes commenting on another. What can look fragmentary is a deliberate structural experiment, and the mixed form mirrors the mixed identities being described.

A brief conclusion states the significance directly. Rather than forcing their personal histories into the shapes autobiography already offered, these writers revolutionized the genre, redrawing its boundaries so that the form could carry their own experience. The closing sentence supplies the motive behind the formal experimentation, which is a strong determination to speak for themselves in a world they feel has for too long taken their silence for granted.
overall_html: The passage argues that the U.S. Latina autobiographical collections appearing at the end of the 1980s did not simply add to the genre but transformed it, mixing English and Spanish and combining essays, poems, stories and journal entries so that the form itself expresses the complexity of multiple cultural identities. The author's purpose is expository and appreciative, moving from the innovations these works share to a work-by-work demonstration in Anzaldúa, Moraga, and the jointly authored Getting Home Alive, each departing further from convention than the last, before concluding that the writers redrew the genre's boundaries in order to speak for themselves. The author's is the only viewpoint developed.

While recent decades have seen more information recorded than any other era, the potential for losing this information is now greater than ever. This prospect is of great concern to archivists, who are charged with preserving vital records and documents indefinitely. One archivist notes that while the quantity of material being saved has increased exponentially, the durability of recording media has decreased almost as rapidly. The clay tablets that contain the laws of ancient Mesopotamia, for example, are still displayed in museums around the world, and many medieval manuscripts written on animal parchment still look as though they were copied yesterday, whereas books printed on acidic paper as recently as the 1980s are already unreadable. Black-and-white photographs will last for a couple of centuries, but most color photographs become unstable within 40 years, and videotapes last only about 20 years.

Computer technology would seem to offer archivists an answer, as maps, photographs, films, videotapes, and all forms of printed material may now be transferred to and stored electronically on computer disks or tape, occupying very little space. But as the pace of technological change increases, so too does the speed with which each new generation of technology supplants the last. For example, many documents and images transferred in the 1980s to optical computer disks—then the cutting edge of technology—may not now be retrievable because they depend on computer software and hardware that are no longer available. And recent generations of digital storage tape are considered safe from deterioration for only ten years. Yet, even as some archivists are reluctant to become dependent on ever-changing computer technology, they are also quickly running out of time.

Even if viable storage systems are developed—new computer technologies are emerging that may soon provide archivists with the information storage durability they require—decisions about what to keep and what to discard will have to be made quickly, as materials recorded on conventional media continue to deteriorate. Ideally, these decisions should be informed by an assessment of the value of each document. Printed versions of ancient works by Homer and Virgil, for example, survived intact because their enduring popularity resulted in multiple copies of the works being made at different historical moments. But many great works, including those of Plato, were lost for several centuries and are known today only because random copies turned up in the archives of medieval monasteries or in other scholarly collections. Undoubtedly, many important works have not survived at all. The danger now is not so much that some recent masterpiece will be lost for an extended period of time, but rather that the sheer volume of accumulated records stored on nondurable media will make it virtually impossible for archivists to sort the essential from the dispensable in time to save it.
explanation_html:
The passage opens on a paradox and then documents it. More information has been recorded in recent decades than in any earlier era, yet the potential for losing it has never been greater, which alarms archivists, whose charge is to preserve vital records and documents indefinitely. One archivist frames it as two curves moving in opposite directions: the quantity of material saved has grown exponentially while the durability of recording media has fallen almost as fast. The examples run forward through time to make the point vivid. Mesopotamian clay tablets are still displayed in museums and medieval animal parchment can look freshly copied, while books printed on acidic paper as recently as the 1980s are already unreadable, most color photographs destabilize within forty years, and videotape lasts about twenty.

An apparent solution is raised and then dismantled, which is this paragraph's whole function. Computers seem to answer the problem, since maps, photographs, films, videotapes and every kind of printed material can be transferred to disk or tape and stored in almost no space. The difficulty is that technology now changes fast enough that each generation supplants the last before the records outlive their format. Documents moved to optical disks in the 1980s, then the cutting edge, may be unretrievable because the software and hardware they depend on no longer exist, and recent digital storage tape is considered safe for only ten years. The bind is stated plainly: archivists are reluctant to depend on shifting technology, yet they are also running out of time.

The closing paragraph shifts from storage to selection, which the author treats as the deeper problem. Even granting that durable new systems arrive soon, material on conventional media keeps deteriorating, so decisions about what to keep and what to discard must be made quickly, ideally informed by an assessment of each document's value. History supplies one encouraging case and one discouraging one. Homer and Virgil survived intact because enduring popularity meant fresh copies were made at different historical moments, whereas Plato was lost for centuries and reaches us only because random copies surfaced in medieval monastic archives and scholarly collections, and many important works vanished altogether. The danger now is not a masterpiece disappearing for a while but the sheer volume of fragile records making timely triage impossible.
overall_html: The passage warns that the era recording more information than any other is also the one most likely to lose it, because the durability of recording media has declined about as fast as the volume of material has grown. The author's purpose is to define that problem and show why the obvious remedy falls short, moving from the decay of physical media, through the trap of electronic storage, whose formats become unreadable faster than the records themselves deteriorate, to the selection problem that persists even if durable systems arrive. Drawing on the survival of Homer and Virgil against the near-loss of Plato, the author concludes that the real threat is volume outpacing archivists' ability to sort the essential from the dispensable in time.

The following passages are adapted from articles recently published in North American law review journals.

Passage A

In Canadian and United States common law, blackmail is unique among major crimes: no one has yet adequately explained why it ought to be illegal. The heart of the problem—known as the blackmail paradox—is that two acts, each of which is legally permissible separately, become illegal when combined. If I threaten to expose a criminal act or embarrassing private information unless I am paid money, I have committed blackmail. But the right to free speech protects my right to make such a disclosure, and, in many circumstances, I have a legal right to seek money. So why is it illegal to combine them?

The lack of a successful theory of blackmail has damaging consequences: drawing a clear line between legal and illegal acts has proved impossible without one. Consequently, most blackmail statutes broadly prohibit behavior that no one really believes is criminal and rely on the good judgment of prosecutors not to enforce relevant statutes precisely as written.

It is possible, however, to articulate a coherent theory of blackmail. The key to the wrongness of the blackmail transaction is its triangular structure. The blackmailer obtains what he wants by using a supplementary leverage, leverage that depends upon a third party. The blackmail victim pays to avoid being harmed by persons other than the blackmailer. For example, when a blackmailer threatens to turn in a criminal unless paid money, the blackmailer is bargaining with the state's chip. Thus, blackmail is criminal because it involves the misuse of a third party for the blackmailer's own benefit.

Passage B

Classical Roman law had no special category for blackmail; it was not necessary. Roman jurists began their evaluation of specific categories of actions by considering whether the action caused harm, not by considering the legality or illegality of the action itself.

Their assumption—true enough, it seems—was that a victim of blackmail would be harmed if shameful but private information were revealed to the world. And if the shame would cause harm to the person's status or reputation, then prima facie the threatened act of revelation was unlawful. The burden of proof shifted to the possessor of the information: the party who had or threatened to reveal shameful facts had to show positive cause for the privilege of revealing the information.

In short, assertion of the truth of the shameful fact being revealed was not, in itself, sufficient to constitute a legal privilege. Granted, truth was not wholly irrelevant; false disclosures were granted even less protection than true ones. But even if it were true, the revelation of shameful information was protected only if the revelation had been made for a legitimate purpose and dealt with a matter that the public authorities had an interest in having revealed. Just because something shameful happened to be true did not mean it was lawful to reveal it.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by naming a genuine oddity in Canadian and United States common law: blackmail is the one major crime whose illegality nobody has adequately explained. The blackmail paradox is that two acts, each permissible on its own, become criminal in combination. Threatening to expose a criminal act or embarrassing private information unless paid is blackmail, yet free speech protects the right to make such a disclosure and in many circumstances one has a legal right to seek money. Hold that structure in mind, since Passage A will resolve the paradox by locating something in the combination that neither part contains.

The consequences of having no theory come next, and they are practical rather than merely academic. Without a successful account, drawing a clear line between legal and illegal acts has proved impossible. What follows is a compromise Passage A plainly finds unsatisfactory: most blackmail statutes prohibit behavior so broadly that they sweep in conduct nobody really believes is criminal, and then rely on the good judgment of prosecutors to decline to enforce those statutes precisely as written.

Passage A's own theory arrives here, and the key word is triangular. What makes the transaction wrong is that it involves three parties rather than two: the blackmailer gets what he wants through supplementary leverage that depends on somebody else, and the victim pays to avoid harm that would come from persons other than the blackmailer. The example is exact. A blackmailer threatening to turn in a criminal is bargaining with the state's chip rather than his own. Blackmail is therefore criminal because it misuses a third party for the blackmailer's own benefit, which is the element neither component act supplies alone.

Passage B begins somewhere else entirely, in classical Roman law, which had no special category for blackmail and, on this account, needed none. The reason lies in method: Roman jurists evaluated a category of action by first asking whether the action caused harm, not by asking whether the action was in itself legal or illegal. Notice that this reframing dissolves the paradox rather than solving it, since the question that generates the puzzle is never asked in that form.

The Roman analysis is then applied to the case at hand. The jurists assumed, and Passage B endorses the assumption as true enough, that a blackmail victim is harmed when shameful but private information is revealed to the world. If the resulting shame would damage the person's status or reputation, the threatened revelation was on its face unlawful. That verdict was provisional, and its consequence was procedural: the burden of proof shifted to whoever held or threatened to reveal the information, who then had to show positive cause for the privilege of revealing it.

What that burden actually required is drawn out at the close, and modern readers may find it counterintuitive. Merely asserting that the shameful fact was true did not by itself constitute a legal privilege. Truth was not wholly irrelevant, since false disclosures got even less protection than true ones, but a true revelation of shameful information was protected only where it served a legitimate purpose and concerned a matter the public authorities had an interest in having revealed. The closing line states it flatly: something being true did not make revealing it lawful.
overall_html: Both passages address why blackmail should be illegal, and they come at the question from opposite directions. Passage A frames the blackmail paradox, that two individually lawful acts become criminal when combined, notes the overbroad statutes that result from having no theory, and resolves it by arguing that blackmail is wrong because of its triangular structure, since the blackmailer exploits leverage that belongs to a third party. Passage B turns instead to classical Roman law, which needed no special category because its jurists began from harm rather than from the legality of an act, treating a damaging revelation as unlawful unless the discloser showed a legitimate purpose. B dissolves the paradox that A sets out to solve.

As part of an international effort to address environmental problems resulting from agricultural overproduction, hundreds of thousands of acres of surplus farmland throughout Europe will be taken out of production in coming years. Restoring a natural balance of flora to this land will be difficult, however, because the nutrients in soil that has been in constant agricultural use are depleted. Moreover, much of this land has been heavily fertilized, and when such land is left unplanted, problem weeds like thistles often proliferate, preventing many native plants from establishing themselves. While the quickest way to restore heavily fertilized land is to remove and replace the topsoil, this is impractical on a large scale such as that of the European effort. And while it is generally believed that damaged ecological systems will restore themselves very gradually over time, a study underway in the Netherlands is investigating the possibility of artificially accelerating the processes through which nature slowly reestablishes plant diversity on previously farmed land.

In the study, a former cornfield was raked to get rid of cornstalks and weeds, then divided into 20 plots of roughly equal size. Control plots were replanted with corn or sown with nothing at all. The remaining plots were divided into two groups: plots in one group were sown with a mixture of native grasses and herbs; those in the other group received the same mixture of grasses and herbs together with clover and toadflax. After three years, thistles have been forced out of the plots where the broadest variety of species was sown and have also disappeared from mats of grass in the plots sown with fewer seed varieties. On the control plots that were left untouched, thistles have become dominant.

On some of the plots sown with seeds of native plant species, soil from nearby land that had been taken out of production 20 years earlier was scattered to see what effect introducing nematodes, fungi, and other beneficial microorganisms associated with later stages of natural soil development might have on the process of native plant repopulation. The seeds sown on these enriched plots have fared better than seeds sown on the unenriched plots, but still not as well as those growing naturally on the nearby land. Researchers have concluded that this is because fields farmed for many years are overrun with aggressive disease organisms, while, for example, beneficial mycorrhiza—fungi that live symbiotically on plant roots and strengthen them against the effects of disease organisms—are lacking. These preliminary results suggest that restoring natural plant diversity to overfarmed land hinges on restoring a natural balance of microorganisms in the soil. In other words, diversity underground fosters diversity aboveground. Researchers now believe that both kinds of diversity can be restored more quickly to damaged land if beneficial microorganisms are "sown" systematically into the soil along with a wide variety of native plant seeds.
explanation_html:
A practical problem is set up before the research that addresses it. Hundreds of thousands of acres of surplus European farmland are being retired to deal with the environmental costs of agricultural overproduction, but restoring a natural balance of flora is difficult, because constant farming has depleted the soil's nutrients. Heavy fertilizing makes it worse, since land treated that way and then left unplanted tends to be taken over by problem weeds such as thistles, which prevent native plants from establishing themselves. Removing and replacing the topsoil would be quickest but is impractical at this scale, and the general belief is that damaged systems recover only very gradually. A Dutch study is testing whether that natural process can be artificially accelerated.

The design comes next, and it repays reading as a comparison of treatments. A former cornfield was raked clear of cornstalks and weeds, then divided into twenty roughly equal plots. Control plots were either replanted with corn or sown with nothing. The remainder were split into two groups, one sown with a mixture of native grasses and herbs and the other with that same mixture plus clover and toadflax. Three years on, thistles have been forced out of the plots carrying the broadest variety of species and have also disappeared from mats of grass in the less varied plots, while on the untouched controls thistles have become dominant.

A second variable takes the explanation underground. On some of the sown plots, researchers scattered soil from nearby land retired twenty years earlier, to see whether the nematodes, fungi and other beneficial microorganisms of more developed soil would help native plants repopulate. Seeds on those enriched plots fared better than seeds on unenriched ones, though still not as well as the plants growing naturally on the neighboring land. The proposed reason is that long-farmed fields are overrun with aggressive disease organisms and short of helpful ones such as mycorrhiza, fungi living symbiotically on roots that strengthen plants against disease. Hence the conclusion, neatly phrased: diversity underground fosters diversity aboveground, so microorganisms should be sown systematically alongside native seed.
overall_html: The passage reports a Dutch study testing whether the slow natural return of plant diversity to retired farmland can be accelerated, a question made urgent by the hundreds of thousands of European acres coming out of production with depleted, heavily fertilized soil prone to thistle takeover. The author's purpose is expository, moving from that problem through an experiment comparing plots sown with different mixtures of native species against replanted and untouched controls, and then to a further trial in which mature soil was scattered to supply beneficial microorganisms. The preliminary finding is that restoring plant diversity depends on restoring the soil's microbial balance, so seeds and microorganisms should be sown together.

The Internet makes possible the instantaneous transmission and retrieval of digital text. It is widely assumed that this capacity will lead to the displacement of printed books by digitized books that are read mainly on computer screens or handheld electronic devices. But it is more likely, I believe, that most digital files of books will be printed and bound on demand at point of sale by machines that can quickly and inexpensively make single copies that are indistinguishable from books made in factories. Once most books have been digitized, anyone with access to the Internet will be able to purchase printed books from a practically limitless digital catalog that includes even those books that, under traditional publishing assumptions, would have been designated "out of print."

Also, the digital publication of a book online involves no physical inventory, thereby eliminating the costs of warehousing, shipping books to wholesalers and to retail stores, displaying physical books in retail stores, and returning unsold books to publishers. This would make digital publishing much less expensive than traditional publishing. Given the economic efficiency and convenience for customers of this new digital model of publishing, it is likely to eventually supplant or at least rival traditional publishing—although it will be some time before a catalog of printable digitized books becomes large enough to justify investment in book printing machines at numerous regional sites.

Moreover, the elimination of whole categories of expense means that under the digital publishing model, authors would be responsible for a greater proportion of the value of the final product and would therefore, according to literary agents, be entitled to a larger share of the proceeds. Currently a large percentage of publishers' revenue is absorbed by the costs of printing, selling, and distributing physical books, costs that are irrelevant to digital publication. Literary agents marketing new manuscripts could thus be expected to demand a significantly bigger slice of revenue for their authors than has been traditional. But large, established publishing houses, which are heavily invested in the infrastructure of traditional publishing, initially will be reluctant to accede. So the opportunity to bid for new manuscripts will go first to upstart digital-publishing firms unfettered by traditional practices or infrastructure. Under this competitive pressure, traditional publishers will have to reduce their redundant functions in order to accommodate higher royalty payments to authors or else they will lose their authors. Such adjustments are typical of the interval between a departing economic model and its successor and may help explain the caution with which today's publishing conglomerates are approaching the digital future.
explanation_html:
A common prediction is rejected at the outset and the author's own substituted for it. Everyone accepts that the Internet allows digital text to be transmitted and retrieved instantly, and the widespread assumption is that printed books will therefore give way to digitized ones read on screens or handheld devices. The Author disagrees, and says so in the first person: what is more likely is that digital files will be printed and bound on demand at the point of sale, by machines turning out single copies indistinguishable from factory-made books. The payoff is a practically limitless catalog open to anyone online, including titles that traditional publishing would have declared out of print. Notice the prediction concerns how books get made and sold, not whether they stay physical.

Economics supplies the argument behind that forecast. Publishing a book digitally involves no physical inventory, which removes at a stroke the costs of warehousing, shipping to wholesalers and retail stores, displaying stock in shops, and returning unsold copies to the publisher. Digital publishing therefore comes out much cheaper than the traditional kind, and between that efficiency and the convenience for customers the author expects the new model to supplant traditional publishing or at least rival it. The hedge is about timing rather than direction, since the catalog of printable digitized books must grow considerably before anyone invests in printing machines at numerous regional sites.

Consequences are traced through the industry in the final paragraph, and the chain of reasoning is worth following link by link. With whole categories of expense gone, authors account for more of the final product's value, so the Literary Agents hold that authors are entitled to a larger share of the proceeds and can be expected to demand one. Printing, selling and distributing physical books currently absorbs much of publishers' revenue and is simply irrelevant to digital publication. The Established Publishers, heavily invested in traditional infrastructure, will initially refuse, so new manuscripts will go first to upstart digital firms, and competitive pressure will force the old houses to cut redundant functions or lose their authors. The author reads today's conglomerate caution as typical of such a transition.
overall_html: The passage predicts that the Internet will transform publishing not by replacing printed books with screens, as is widely assumed, but by shifting to digital files printed and bound on demand at the point of sale from a practically limitless catalog. The author's purpose is to argue for that forecast and trace its consequences, moving from the prediction itself, to the economics that make it likely once inventory, shipping, display and returns costs disappear, to the industry realignment that follows, in which literary agents demand larger shares for authors, established publishers resist, and upstart digital firms take the new manuscripts. The author's own first-person voice is the controlling viewpoint throughout.

In this appeal of his criminal conviction, the defendant challenges the fingerprint evidence used against him at trial, claiming that fingerprint identification theory has not been adequately tested. He cites the inability of the fingerprint examiner who incriminated him at trial to name any studies establishing that no two persons have identical fingerprints.

The defendant claims that there are no established error rates revealing how often fingerprint examiners incorrectly identify a fingerprint as a particular person's, and asserts that fingerprint examiners lack uniform, objective standards. He cites testimony given by the fingerprint examiner at trial that there is no generally accepted standard regarding the number of "points of identification" required for a positive identification.

Although fingerprint identification has not attained the status of scientific law, it has been used in criminal trials for 100 years, and experts have long concurred about its reliability. While further testing and the development of even more consistent standards may be desirable, this court sees no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time.

While it may be true that different agencies require different degrees of correlation before permitting a positive identification, fingerprint examiners are held to a consistent "points and characteristics" approach to identification. As the fingerprint expert testified at the defendant's trial, examiners are regularly subjected to testing and proficiency requirements, and uniform standards have been established through professional training and peer review. The trial court below was therefore within its discretion in crediting testimony that fingerprint identification has an exceedingly low error rate.

Passage B

Fingerprint examiners lack objective standards for evaluating whether two prints "match." There is simply no consensus about what constitutes a sufficient basis for identification. Some examiners use a "point-counting" method that entails counting the number of similar "ridge" characteristics on prints, but there is no fixed requirement about how many points of similarity are needed, and local practices vary. Others reject point counting for a more holistic approach. Either way, there is no generally agreed-on standard for determining precisely when to declare a match.

Although we know that different individuals can share certain ridge characteristics, the chance of two individuals sharing any given number of identifying characteristics is unknown. How likely is it that two people could have four points of resemblance, or five, or eight? Moreover, fingerprints used in forensic identification are typically partial and smudged. Are the odds that two partial prints from different people will match one in a thousand, one in a million, or one in a billion? No fingerprint examiner can answer such questions decisively, yet the answers are critical to evaluating the value of fingerprint evidence.

The error rate for fingerprint identification in actual practice has received little systematic study. How often do fingerprint examiners mistakenly declare a match? Although some proficiency tests show examiners making few or no errors, these tests have been criticized as lax; a more rigorous test showed a 34 percent rate of erroneous identification.
explanation_html:
Passage A is a court's opinion, and it opens by reporting the challenge it must answer rather than any view of its own. The Defendant, appealing a criminal conviction, attacks the fingerprint evidence used against him on the ground that fingerprint identification theory has not been adequately tested. His support is specific: the examiner who incriminated him at trial could not name any study establishing that no two persons have identical fingerprints. Keep the defendant's voice separate from the court's, because the passage does not endorse him yet.

Two further complaints complete the challenge. The defendant argues that no established error rates show how often examiners wrongly identify a fingerprint as a particular person's, and that examiners lack uniform, objective standards. He again draws on trial testimony, this time the examiner's admission that no generally accepted standard governs how many points of identification a positive identification requires. Notice that these are precisely the two issues, objective standards and measured error rates, that the second passage will develop at length and press much harder.

The court's own voice takes over here, and it begins with a concession. The Court grants that fingerprint identification has not attained the status of scientific law, then sets against that a hundred years of use in criminal trials and long-standing expert agreement about its reliability. Further testing and more consistent standards may be desirable, it allows, but that is no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time. The reasoning is institutional and pragmatic rather than scientific, resting on longevity and consensus.

The standards objection is answered directly next. The court concedes that different agencies may require different degrees of correlation before permitting a positive identification, yet insists examiners are held to a consistent points and characteristics approach. Relying once more on the expert's testimony, it notes that examiners are regularly subjected to testing and proficiency requirements and that uniform standards have been established through professional training and peer review. The conclusion is deferential in form: the trial court was within its discretion in crediting testimony that the error rate is exceedingly low.

Passage B opens on exactly the point Passage A had brushed aside, and takes the opposite view of it. Examiners lack objective standards for evaluating whether two prints match, and no consensus exists about what constitutes a sufficient basis for identification. Some count similar ridge characteristics, but no fixed number of points is required and local practices vary; others reject point counting altogether for a more holistic approach. Either way, nothing generally agreed determines precisely when a match may be declared.

The second gap is statistical and cuts deeper than standards do. Different individuals are known to share certain ridge characteristics, yet the chance of two people sharing any given number of identifying characteristics is unknown, so questions about four, five or eight points of resemblance have no answers. Compounding that, prints used in forensic identification are typically partial and smudged, which means nobody can say whether the odds of two partial prints from different people matching are one in a thousand, one in a million, or one in a billion. Those unanswerable questions are what evaluating the evidence actually requires.

The closing paragraph goes after the low error rate the court had accepted. How often examiners mistakenly declare a match has received little systematic study. Passage B acknowledges that some proficiency tests show examiners making few or no errors, then undercuts them with the criticism that such tests are lax, and ends on the single most damaging figure in either passage: a more rigorous test produced a thirty-four percent rate of erroneous identification.
overall_html: Both passages assess the reliability of fingerprint identification and reach opposite conclusions. Passage A is a court opinion that recites a defendant's challenge, namely that the theory is untested, error rates unestablished and standards not uniform, and then rejects it, conceding that fingerprinting is not scientific law but relying on a century of courtroom use, expert consensus, and testimony that examiners undergo proficiency testing and peer review. Passage B presses those same objections in detail, arguing that no agreed standard defines a match, that the probability of two people sharing a given number of ridge characteristics is unknown, especially for partial smudged prints, and that a rigorous test found a thirty-four percent error rate.

Music and literature, rivals among the arts, have not coexisted without intruding on each other's terrain. Ever since what we think of as "literature" developed out of the sounds of spoken, sung, and chanted art, writing has aspired to the condition of music, in which form contributes significantly to content. Nowhere is this truer than in the African American tradition, whose music is often considered its greatest artistic achievement and one of the greatest contributions to North American art. But while many African American writers have used musicians and music as theme and metaphor in their writing, none had attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for an entire novel until Toni Morrison did so in her 1992 novel Jazz, a novel set in the Harlem section of New York City in 1926.

In Jazz, the connection to music is found not only in the novel's plot but, more strikingly, in the way in which the story is told. The narration slips easily from the third-person omniscience of the narrator's disembodied voice—which, though sensitive and sympathetic, claims no particular identity, gender, or immersion in specific social circumstances—to the first-person lyricism of key characters. But throughout these shifts, the narrator is both generous with the characters' voices and protective of his or her mastery over the narrative as a whole. On the one hand, the central characters are given the responsibility of relating their parts of the overarching story, but on the other hand, their sections are set off by quotation marks, reminders that the narrator is allowing them to speak. In this way, the narrative is analogous in structure to the playing of a jazz band which intertwines its ensemble sound with the individuality of embedded solo performances.

In jazz, composer and conductor Duke Ellington was the first to construct his compositions with his individual musicians and their unique "voices" in mind. Yet no matter how lengthy his musicians' improvisations, no matter how bold or inventive their solos might be, they always performed within the undeniable logic of the composer's frame—they always, in other words, performed as if with quotation marks around their improvisations and solos. It is this same effect that Toni Morrison has achieved in Jazz, a literary rendering of an art of composition that Duke Ellington perfected around the time in which Jazz is set.

In this novel, Morrison has found a way, paradoxically, to create the sense of an ensemble of characters improvising within the fixed scope of a carefully constructed collective narration. By simulating the style of a genius of music while exhibiting Morrison's own linguistic virtuosity, Jazz serves to redefine the very possibilities of narrative point of view.
explanation_html:
Music and literature are set up as rivals that keep trespassing on each other's ground. The claim to hold onto is that writing has long aspired to the condition of music, where form itself carries meaning rather than just delivering content, and that this is truest in the African American tradition, whose music is often treated as its greatest artistic achievement. Plenty of African American writers have used musicians and music as theme and metaphor; what the author says none had done is build an entire novel on the structural logic of a musical genre. Morrison's Jazz, set in 1926 Harlem, is offered as the first.

The focus now shifts from what the novel is about to how it is told, which is where the author locates the real musical connection. The narration slides between a third-person voice that knows everything while claiming no identity, gender, or social position, and the first-person lyricism of individual characters. Notice the balance being stressed: characters take responsibility for relating their own portions of the story, yet those portions sit inside quotation marks, a reminder that the narrator is granting them the floor rather than surrendering control. The analogy that closes the paragraph is the payoff — an ensemble sound with individual solos embedded inside it.

Duke Ellington enters as the musical precedent that makes the analogy concrete rather than decorative. He was the first to compose with the particular sound of each of his players in mind, so their improvisations were genuinely their own; but however long or inventive a solo, it stayed inside the logic of the composer's frame, performed as if in quotation marks. That phrase deliberately repeats the description of Morrison's characters, and the paragraph closes the loop by dating Ellington's perfection of this method to roughly the period in which Jazz is set.

The close states the verdict, and the word to notice is paradoxically. Morrison produces the impression of characters improvising freely inside a collective narration that is in fact tightly constructed, which is exactly the tension the Ellington comparison prepared. Watch the evaluative language, since it is the clearest signal of where the author stands: a genius of music simulated, Morrison's own virtuosity on display, and narrative point of view redefined. No rival reading is entertained anywhere in the passage, so treat the whole thing as one continuous appreciative argument that this paragraph brings to its conclusion.
overall_html: The passage argues that Toni Morrison's Jazz is the first novel to use a musical genre not merely as subject or metaphor but as the organizing principle of its narration, and that its shifts between a disembodied omniscient narrator and quoted first-person voices reproduce the way a jazz band embeds solos within an ensemble sound. The author's purpose is appreciative and explanatory rather than contentious: a broad opening claim about literature's aspiration to music narrows to Morrison, the second paragraph analyzes her narrative technique, Duke Ellington's compositional method supplies the historical precedent, and a brief close credits Morrison with redefining the possibilities of point of view. The only viewpoint developed is the author's own.

Advances in scientific understanding often do not build directly or smoothly in response to the data that are amassed, and in retrospect, after a major revision of theory, it may seem strange that a crucial hypothesis was long overlooked. A case in point is the discovery of a means by which the nuclei of atoms can be split. Between 1934, when a group of Italian physicists including Enrico Fermi first bombarded uranium with neutrons, and 1939, when exiled Austrian physicist Lise Meitner provided the crucial theoretical connection, scientists compiled increasing evidence that nuclear fission had been achieved, without, however, recognizing what they were witnessing.

Earlier, even before the neutron and proton composition of atomic nuclei had been experimentally demonstrated, some theoretical physicists had produced calculations indicating that in principle it should be possible to break atoms apart. But the neutron-bombardment experiments were not aimed at achieving such a result, and researchers were not even receptive to the possibility that it might happen in that context. A common view was that a neutron's breaking apart a uranium nucleus would be analogous to a pebble, thrown through a window, causing a house to collapse.

In Berlin, Meitner pursued research related to that of the Italians, discovering a puzzling group of radioactive substances produced by neutron bombardment of uranium. Fermi and others achieved numerous similar results. These products remained unidentified partly because precise chemical analyses were hampered by the minute quantities of the substances produced and the dangers of working with highly radioactive materials, but more significantly because of the expectation that they would all be elements close to uranium in nuclear composition. In 1938 Meitner escaped from Nazi Germany and undertook related research in Sweden, but her research partner Otto Hahn kept her informed of his continuing experimentation. Late in that year he wrote to her of a surprising result: one of the substances resulting from the neutron bombardment of uranium had been conclusively identified as barium, an element whose structure would have made it impossible to produce through any mechanism he envisaged as being involved in the experiments. Hahn even remarked that, despite the clear chemical evidence of what had occurred, it went "against all previous experiences of nuclear physics," but he also noted that together the number of protons and neutrons in the nuclei of barium and technetium, the accompanying product of the experiment, added up to the number of such particles that compose a uranium nucleus.

It was Meitner who finally recognized the significance of the data in relation to underlying theoretical considerations: the researchers had actually been splitting uranium atoms. Coining the term "nuclear fission," she quickly submitted her conclusion for publication in a paper coauthored with physicist Otto Frisch. When scientists in Europe and North America rushed to corroborate the findings, it became clear that the relevant evidence had been present for some time, lacking mainly the right conceptual link.
explanation_html:
A general claim arrives first, and the case study that supports it second. The claim is that scientific understanding does not accumulate smoothly out of the data, so in hindsight it can look strange that a crucial hypothesis went unconsidered for years. The illustration is the splitting of the atom. Fix the two dates, because the whole passage is organized around the gap between them: Italian physicists including Fermi began bombarding uranium with neutrons in 1934, and only in 1939 did the exiled Lise Meitner supply the theoretical connection. In between, evidence that fission had occurred kept accumulating while nobody recognized what they were seeing.

Before resuming the story, the author establishes that the idea itself was not unthinkable. Theorists had calculated that atoms should in principle be breakable apart, and had done so even before nuclei were experimentally shown to contain neutrons and protons. What blocked recognition was framing rather than missing theory: the bombardment experiments were aimed at other results, and the researchers were not receptive to fission as a possibility in that setting. The pebble-through-a-window image captures their reasoning, since a small projectile obviously cannot bring down a house. Treat this paragraph as the author's diagnosis of the obstacle; the next one shows it at work.

The long third paragraph puts that obstacle into motion. Meitner in Berlin, and Fermi and others elsewhere, kept producing radioactive substances nobody could identify. Two reasons were practical, minute quantities and dangerous radioactivity, but the author marks a third as more significant: everyone expected the products to be elements close to uranium, so nothing else was entertained. Then the anomaly. After Meitner escaped to Sweden in 1938, her partner Otto Hahn wrote that one product was conclusively barium, which no mechanism he envisaged could produce. Notice that Hahn held both halves of the answer: he admitted the result defied established nuclear physics, and he saw that barium and technetium together match uranium's particle count. Only the interpretation was missing.

Meitner supplies that interpretation, and the closing paragraph is short because the intellectual move is a single step: she connected the data to the underlying theory and saw that uranium atoms had been split. She coined the term nuclear fission and published the conclusion with Otto Frisch. The final sentence loops back to the opening claim and completes the argument. Once laboratories across Europe and North America confirmed the finding, it was plain that the relevant evidence had been available for years, and that what had been missing was a conceptual link rather than any new experiment.
overall_html: The passage uses the discovery of nuclear fission to support a general claim about how science advances: data can accumulate for years without being understood, because researchers read results through the expectations they already hold. The author's purpose is explanatory, developing that thesis through one sustained historical case, and the structure moves from the claim and its 1934 to 1939 timeline, to the reasons fission seemed implausible, to the mounting anomalous results culminating in Hahn's identification of barium, and finally to Meitner's recognition of what those results meant. The viewpoints worth separating are the shared assumption of the researchers and the author's diagnosis of why it held them back.

Many critics agree that the primary characteristic of Senegalese filmmaker Ousmane Sembène's work is its sociopolitical commitment. Sembène was trained in Moscow in the cinematic methods of socialist realism, and he asserts that his films are not meant to entertain his compatriots, but rather to raise their awareness of the past and present realities of their society. But his originality as a filmmaker lies most strikingly in his having successfully adapted film, originally a Western cultural medium, to the needs, pace, and structures of West African culture. In particular, Sembène has found within African oral culture techniques and strategies that enable him to express his views and to reach both literate and nonliterate Senegalese viewers.

A number of Sembène's characters and motifs can be traced to those found in traditional West African storytelling. The tree, for instance, which in countless West African tales symbolizes knowledge, life, death, and rebirth, is a salient motif in Emitaï. The trickster, usually a dishonest individual who personifies antisocial traits, appears in Borom Sarret, Mandabi, and Xala as a thief, a corrupted civil servant, and a member of the elite, respectively. In fact, most of Sembène's characters, like those of many oral West African narratives, are types embodying collective ideas or attitudes. And in the oral tradition, these types face archetypal predicaments, as is true, for example, of the protagonist of Borom Sarret, who has no name and is recognizable instead by his trade—he is a street merchant—and by the difficulties he encounters but is unable to overcome.

Moreover, many of Sembène's films derive their structure from West African dilemma tales, the outcomes of which are debated and decided by their audiences. The open-endedness of most of his plots reveals that Sembène similarly leaves it to his viewers to complete his narratives: in such films as Borom Sarret, Mandabi, and Ceddo, for example, he provides his spectators with several alternatives as the films end. The openness of his narratives is also evidenced by his frequent use of freeze-frames, which carry the suggestion of continued action.

Finally, like many West African oral tales, Sembène's narratives take the form of initiatory journeys that bring about a basic change in the worldview of the protagonist and ultimately, Sembène hopes, in that of the viewer. His films denounce social and political injustice, and his protagonists' social consciousness emerges from an acute self-consciousness brought about by the juxtaposition of opposites within the films' social context: good versus evil, powerlessness versus power, or poverty versus wealth. Such binary oppositions are used analogously in West African tales, and it seems likely that these dialectical elements are related to African oral storytelling more than, as many critics have supposed, to the Marxist components of his ideology.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up a contrast worth marking immediately. The critics largely agree that sociopolitical commitment is the defining feature of Sembène's work, and there is support for that in his Moscow training in socialist realism and in his own statement that his films exist to raise his compatriots' awareness rather than to entertain them. Then comes the turn that carries the author's thesis: what is most original about him is not the politics but the adaptation of film, a Western medium, to West African needs, pace, and structures. The mechanism named is oral culture, which lets him reach literate and nonliterate viewers alike.

Evidence begins with the smallest units, character and motif. The tree, a stock symbol of knowledge, life, death, and rebirth across West African tales, is prominent in one film; the trickster, the figure who personifies antisocial traits, turns up in three others as a thief, a corrupt civil servant, and a member of the elite. The larger claim is that his characters work the way oral-narrative characters do, functioning as types that embody collective ideas rather than as individuals, and facing archetypal predicaments. The unnamed street merchant, identified only by his trade and by difficulties he cannot overcome, is the clean example.

Structure supplies the second parallel, and the word moreover tells you the argument is accumulating rather than shifting ground. West African dilemma tales hand their outcomes to the audience to debate and decide, and Sembène's plots are said to do the same, since several of his films close by laying out alternatives instead of settling on one. His frequent freeze-frames get read the same way, as images that imply the action continues beyond the ending. Keep the division clear: the previous paragraph was about what his narratives contain, this one about the shape they take.

The third parallel arrives with the argumentative payoff attached. Sembène's films are built as initiatory journeys that transform the protagonist's worldview and, he hopes, the viewer's, and that transformation runs on stark oppositions between good and evil, powerlessness and power, poverty and wealth, which push the protagonist from self-consciousness into social consciousness. Because West African tales use the same device, the author concludes that these dialectical elements derive from oral storytelling rather than from the Marxist strand in his ideology. That is a direct reply to the critics, whose reading the first paragraph had set up precisely so it could be corrected here.
overall_html: Against the critical consensus that Ousmane Sembène's work is defined above all by its sociopolitical commitment, the passage argues that his real originality lies in adapting film, a Western medium, to the techniques of West African oral storytelling. The author's purpose is to establish and defend that thesis, and the macro-structure is a single claim followed by three cumulative parallels: characters and motifs drawn from traditional tales, plots that leave resolution to the audience as dilemma tales do, and initiatory journeys built on binary oppositions. The last parallel answers the critics directly by tracing Sembène's dialectical elements to oral tradition rather than to the Marxist component of his thinking.

Readers, like writers, need to search for answers. Part of the joy of reading is in being surprised, but academic historians leave little to the imagination. The perniciousness of the historiographic approach became fully evident to me when I started teaching. Historians require undergraduates to read scholarly monographs that sap the vitality of history; they visit on students what was visited on them in graduate school. They assign books with formulaic arguments that transform history into an abstract debate that would have been unfathomable to those who lived in the past. Aimed so squarely at the head, such books cannot stimulate students who yearn to connect to history emotionally as well as intellectually.

In an effort to address this problem, some historians have begun to rediscover stories. It has even become something of a fad within the profession. This year, the American Historical Association chose as the theme for its annual conference some putative connection to storytelling: "Practices of Historical Narrative." Predictably, historians responded by adding the word "narrative" to their titles and presenting papers at sessions on "Oral History and the Narrative of Class Identity," and "Meaning and Time: The Problem of Historical Narrative." But it was still historiography, intended only for other academics. At meetings of historians, we still encounter very few historians telling stories or moving audiences to smiles, chills, or tears.

Passage B

Writing is at the heart of the lawyer's craft, and so, like it or not, we who teach the law inevitably teach aspiring lawyers how lawyers write. We do this in a few stand-alone courses and, to a greater extent, through the constraints that we impose on their writing throughout the curriculum. Legal writing, because of the purposes it serves, is necessarily ruled by linear logic, creating a path without diversions, surprises, or reversals. Conformity is a virtue, creativity suspect, humor forbidden, and voice mute.

Lawyers write as they see other lawyers write, and, influenced by education, profession, economic constraints, and perceived self-interest, they too often write badly. Perhaps the currently fashionable call for attention to narrative in legal education could have an effect on this. It is not yet exactly clear what role narrative should play in the law, but it is nonetheless true that every case has at its heart a story—of real events and people, of concerns, misfortunes, conflicts, feelings. But because legal analysis strips the human narrative content from the abstract, canonical legal form of the case, law students learn to act as if there is no such story.

It may well turn out that some of the terminology and public rhetoric of this potentially subversive movement toward attention to narrative will find its way into the law curriculum, but without producing corresponding changes in how legal writing is actually taught or in how our future colleagues will write. Still, even mere awareness of the value of narrative could perhaps serve as an important corrective.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens in the voice of the historian, who treats a professional habit as harmful rather than merely dull. Reading, the claim goes, depends on surprise and on searching for answers, and academic history leaves no room for either. Teaching is what made the problem vivid: undergraduates are assigned monographs that drain the vitality out of the subject, because instructors simply inflict on students what graduate school inflicted on them. Note the charge, since it returns later — formulaic argument converts the past into an abstract debate that the people who lived it would find unintelligible. Such books reach only the intellect, and students want an emotional connection too.

A concession appears and is then withdrawn. Some historians have begun rediscovering stories, enough for the historian to call it a fad, and the profession's main association even built its annual conference around historical narrative. The response was cosmetic: the word narrative added to titles, papers delivered in sessions that were still historiography and still aimed at other academics. The closing sentence gives you the test being applied throughout, which is effect rather than vocabulary — at these meetings almost nobody actually tells a story or moves an audience to smiles, chills, or tears.

Passage B moves to legal education and a second speaker, the law teacher, but the shape of the complaint is recognizably the same. Law schools teach students to write like lawyers whether they mean to or not, partly through a few dedicated courses and far more through constraints imposed across the entire curriculum. The description of legal writing is the heart of the paragraph: linear logic, a path free of diversions, surprises, or reversals, and a value system in which conformity counts as a virtue, creativity draws suspicion, humor is forbidden, and personal voice vanishes. Set that beside the historian's objection about imagination.

Cause and possible cure occupy this paragraph. Lawyers write badly, the argument runs, because they imitate the bad writing around them, with education, professional norms, economic pressure, and self-interest reinforcing the habit. The law teacher then raises the same fashionable remedy Passage A examined, the current call for attention to narrative, while treating its proper role in law as genuinely unsettled. The reason it might matter is stated plainly: every case starts as a story of real people, events, conflicts, and feelings, but legal analysis strips that human content away to leave an abstract canonical form, training students to act as though no story existed.

The close is a prediction with a small hedge attached. The law teacher expects the terminology and public rhetoric of the narrative movement to seep into the curriculum while the actual teaching of legal writing, and the writing future lawyers produce, stay exactly as they are. That is the same hollow adoption the historian described in the history profession, which is why the two passages feel like one argument told twice. The final sentence is where the tone diverges slightly, since awareness of narrative's value is allowed to count, on its own, as an important corrective.
overall_html: Both passages are insider critiques of how a profession trains its members to write, and both weigh the same fashionable remedy. The historian of Passage A argues that academic historiography drains history of surprise and emotion and that the discipline's new interest in narrative has produced little beyond relabeled conference papers; the law teacher of Passage B argues that legal writing enforces linear logic and suppresses creativity, humor, and voice, and that legal analysis strips the human story out of every case. The relationship is close agreement across different fields, with each writer doubting that the turn to narrative will change practice, though the law teacher ends by granting that mere awareness of narrative's value could still serve as a corrective.

Traditional theories of animal behavior assert that animal conflict within a species is highly ritualized and does not vary from contest to contest. This species-specific model assumes that repetitive use of the same visual and vocal displays and an absence of escalated fighting evolved to prevent injury. The contestant that exhibits the "best" display wins the contested resource. Galápagos tortoises, for instance, settle contests on the basis of height: the ritualized display consists of two tortoises facing one another and stretching their necks skyward; the tortoise perceived as being "taller" wins.

In populations of the spider Agelenopsis aperta, however, fighting behavior varies greatly from contest to contest. In addition, fighting is not limited to displays: biting and shoving are common. Susan Riechert argues that a recently developed model, evolutionary game theory, provides a closer fit to A. aperta territorial disputes than does the species-specific model, because it explains variations in conflict behavior that may result from varying conditions, such as differences in size, age, and experience of combatants. Evolutionary game theory was adapted from the classical game theory that was developed by von Neumann and Morgenstern to explain human behavior in conflict situations. In both classical and evolutionary game theory, strategies are weighed in terms of maximizing the average payoff against contestants employing both the same and different strategies. For example, a spider may engage in escalated fighting during a dispute only if the disputed resource is valuable enough to warrant the risk of physical injury. There are, however, two major differences between the classical and evolutionary theories. First, whereas in classical game theory it is assumed that rational thought is used to determine which action to take, evolutionary game theory assumes that instinct and long-term species advantage ultimately determine the strategies that are exhibited. The other difference is in the payoffs: in classical game theory, the payoffs are determined by an individual's personal judgment of what constitutes winning; in evolutionary game theory, the payoffs are defined in terms of reproductive success.

In studying populations of A. aperta in a grassland habitat and a riparian habitat, Riechert predicts that such factors as the size of the opponents, the potential rate of predation in a habitat, and the probability of winning a subsequent site if the dispute is lost will all affect the behavior of spiders in territorial disputes. In addition, she predicts that the markedly different levels of competition for web sites in the two habitats will affect the spiders' willingness to engage in escalated fighting. In the grassland, where 12 percent of the habitat is available for occupation by A. aperta, Riechert predicts that spiders will be more willing to engage in escalated fighting than in the riparian habitat, where 90 percent of the habitat is suitable for occupation.
explanation_html:
Begin with the model the passage exists to complicate. Traditional theories hold that conflict between members of the same species is ritualized and essentially identical from one contest to the next, on the reasoning that repeating fixed visual and vocal displays, and never escalating into real fighting, evolved to keep animals from getting hurt. Whichever contestant produces the best display takes the resource. The tortoise case makes that abstraction concrete: two animals face each other, stretch their necks upward, and the one perceived as taller wins without any contact. This is the species-specific model, and the passage keeps that label, so hold onto it.

A counterexample arrives and brings a rival framework with it. In one spider species, fighting differs sharply from contest to contest and includes biting and shoving, not just display. Susan Riechert argues that evolutionary game theory fits these territorial disputes better than the species-specific model does, because it accounts for variation produced by conditions such as a combatant's size, age, and experience. The rest of the paragraph explains the theory through its parent. Classical game theory, built to model human conflict, and its offshoot both judge a strategy by the average payoff it earns against opponents using the same and different strategies, so a spider escalates only when the resource justifies the risk. Two differences separate them: classical theory assumes rational deliberation while the newer version substitutes instinct and long-term species advantage, and classical payoffs reflect an individual's own judgment of winning while evolutionary payoffs are measured as reproductive success.

Prediction is what the closing paragraph adds, converting the framework into expectations that could be checked in the field. Riechert expects an opponent's size, the rate of predation in a habitat, and the chance of securing another web site after a loss all to shape how a spider handles a dispute. The sharper prediction concerns scarcity. Only about a tenth of the grassland is available for occupation, against nearly all of the riparian habitat, so competition for sites is far more intense in the grassland and spiders there should be readier to escalate. Notice that this is exactly the context-driven variation the species-specific model has no room for.
overall_html: The passage sets two accounts of animal conflict against each other: the traditional species-specific model, on which contests within a species are invariant rituals of display that evolved to prevent injury, and evolutionary game theory, which Susan Riechert argues better explains the highly variable and often physically rough territorial disputes of one spider species. The author's purpose is expository rather than argumentative, first laying out the older model with the tortoise example, then introducing Riechert's alternative and distinguishing it from the classical game theory it was adapted from, and finally reporting her predictions about how habitat scarcity and other local conditions should govern a spider's willingness to escalate. The positions to keep apart are the traditional theories and Riechert's.
