Most people acknowledge that not all governments have a moral right to govern and that there are sometimes morally legitimate reasons for disobeying the law, as when a particular law prescribes behavior that is clearly immoral. It is also commonly supposed that such cases are special exceptions and that, in general, the fact that something is against the law counts as a moral, as well as legal, ground for not doing it; i.e., we generally have a moral duty to obey a law simply because it is the law. But the theory known as philosophical anarchism denies this view, arguing instead that people who live under the jurisdiction of governments have no moral duty to those governments to obey their laws. Some commentators have rejected this position because of what they take to be its highly counterintuitive implications: (1) that no existing government is morally better than any other (since all are, in a sense, equally illegitimate), and (2) that, lacking any moral obligation to obey any laws, people may do as they please without scruple. In fact, however, philosophical anarchism does not entail these claims.

First, the conclusion that no government is morally better than any other does not follow from the claim that nobody owes moral obedience to any government. Even if one denies that there is a moral obligation to follow the laws of any government, one can still evaluate the morality of the policies and actions of various governments. Some governments do more good than harm, and others more harm than good, to their subjects. Some violate the moral rights of individuals more regularly, systematically, and seriously than others. In short, it is perfectly consistent with philosophical anarchism to hold that governments vary widely in their moral stature.

Second, philosophical anarchists maintain that all individuals have basic, nonlegal moral duties to one another—duties not to harm others in their lives, liberty, health, or goods. Even if governmental laws have no moral force, individuals still have duties to refrain from those actions that constitute crimes in the majority of legal systems (such as murder, assault, theft, and fraud). Moreover, philosophical anarchists hold that people have a positive moral obligation to care for one another, a moral obligation that they might even choose to discharge by supporting cooperative efforts by governments to help those in need. And where others are abiding by established laws, even those laws derived from mere conventions, individuals are morally bound not to violate those laws when doing so would endanger others. Thus, if others obey the law and drive their vehicles on the right, one must not endanger them by driving on the left, for, even though driving on the left is not inherently immoral, it is morally wrong to deliberately harm the innocent.
explanation_html:
The setup arrives in stages, so track them separately. Most people accept that some governments lack the moral right to govern and that a clearly immoral law may be disobeyed, but treat those as special exceptions to a general moral duty to obey a law simply because it is the law. Philosophical anarchism denies that general duty outright: living under a government's jurisdiction creates no moral obligation to obey its laws. Some commentators reject the theory for two implications they find impossible to swallow, that no government could be morally better than any other since all are equally illegitimate, and that with no duty to obey, people may do as they please. The last sentence states the author's thesis, and it is narrow — the theory entails neither implication.

The first rebuttal pulls apart two questions the commentators had run together. Denying that anyone owes a government obedience says nothing about whether governments can be compared morally, since their policies and actions remain open to evaluation on independent grounds. Some do more good than harm to their subjects and some the reverse; some violate individual rights more regularly, more systematically, and more seriously than others. Philosophical anarchism is therefore perfectly consistent with holding that governments differ widely in moral stature, which is all the author needs to defeat the first objection.

The second rebuttal does the heavier work, and it operates by relocating morality outside the law. Individuals owe one another basic nonlegal duties not to damage another person's life, liberty, health, or goods, and those duties already rule out murder, assault, theft, and fraud whether or not statutes carry moral force. Added to them is a positive obligation of mutual care, which someone might even discharge by backing government efforts to help the needy. The last move covers merely conventional rules: where others are already following an established law, breaking it puts them in danger, so you are morally bound to comply. Driving on the left is not wrong in itself, but doing it among right-hand drivers harms the innocent, and that is what makes it wrong.
overall_html: The passage defends philosophical anarchism, the view that people living under a government have no moral duty to obey its laws, against critics who dismiss it for two supposedly unacceptable implications. The author's purpose is to rebut those objections rather than to prove the theory correct, and the structure is a single thesis followed by the two answers in order: governments can still be ranked morally by the good and harm their policies do, and individuals still owe each other nonlegal duties, including a duty not to endanger people by flouting conventional laws everyone else observes. Keep three positions apart as you read: the common view of legal obligation, the commentators' objections, and the anarchist position the author is clearing.

Until my present study, African American entertainer Lorenzo Tucker had not been extensively discussed in histories of United States theater and film. Yet during a span of 60 years, from 1926 to 1986, he acted in 20 films and performed hundreds of times on stage as a dancer, vaudeville straight man, singer, actor, and master of ceremonies. Behind the scenes he worked as a producer, company manager, publicity person, lighting designer, photographer, and actors' union administrator. In addition, Tucker was a firsthand witness to the history of African American theater and film from the late 1920s until his death in 1986. During his later years, he amassed a large collection of African American theater and film memorabilia, and these artifacts, along with his personal memories, help shed new light on a part of U.S. entertainment history about which, so far, there has been insufficient scholarship.

I gathered much of the background material for my study of Tucker's life through research in special collections of the New York and Los Angeles public libraries, including microfilmed correspondence, photographs, programs, and newspapers. Also examined—as primary source material for an analysis of Tucker's acting technique—were the ten still available films in which Tucker appeared. Additional information was acquired through interviews with some of Tucker's contemporaries and fellow performers. The primary source of information for this study, however, was a group of personal, in-depth interviews I conducted with Tucker himself in 1985 and 1986.

There are both advantages and disadvantages in undertaking a biographical study of a living person. The greatest advantage is that the contemporary biographer has access to that person's oral testimony. Yet this testimony must be approached with caution, since each person recounting his or her version of events for the historical record has a vested interest in the project, and no matter how fair-minded and objective one intends to be, the fact is that people often remember the events they want to remember in the version they prefer. It is the duty of the biographer, therefore, to verify as much of the oral narrative as possible.

Information from Tucker has undergone careful scrutiny and has been placed up against the known facts for verification, and for the most part, information that could not be verified was not included in this study. But Tucker's recollections of his personal life could not always be independently verified, of course, since most of the daily events in the life of any individual go unrecorded. So only those elements of Tucker's personal life that had a bearing on his career have been recorded here. At the same time, however, it is important to note that the majority of these recollections tend to corroborate, while illuminating and providing a valuable perspective on, other relevant historical evidence that is available. This study, therefore, will weave together oral and other evidence to create the career biography of Lorenzo Tucker.
explanation_html:
The opening justifies the project. Lorenzo Tucker has gone largely unexamined in histories of United States theater and film, yet his working life ran sixty years and covered nearly every job in the business, onstage as dancer, vaudeville straight man, singer, actor, and master of ceremonies, and offstage as producer, company manager, publicist, lighting designer, photographer, and union administrator. Two further facts do the real persuading: he watched the history of African American theater and film unfold at first hand from the late 1920s onward, and he built a large memorabilia collection late in life. Those artifacts and memories, the author claims, can illuminate an underserved corner of entertainment history.

Method follows, and the sources are listed in an order that builds toward the most important one. Background came from special collections at the New York and Los Angeles public libraries, including microfilmed correspondence, photographs, programs, and newspapers, while the ten surviving films Tucker appeared in served as primary evidence for analyzing his acting technique. Interviews with contemporaries and fellow performers added more. Then the sentence that governs the rest of the passage: the study rests chiefly on a set of in-depth personal interviews the author conducted with Tucker himself in his final two years.

Having identified oral testimony as the main source, the author immediately raises the problem that creates. Writing about a living subject gives you their own account, which is the great advantage; the cost is that anyone narrating his life for the historical record has a stake in the result, and even a person trying to be fair tends to remember the events he wants in the version he prefers. Notice that this is a concession the author volunteers rather than a charge someone else has made. The paragraph closes by turning the worry into a professional duty, namely to verify as much of the oral narrative as possible.

The last paragraph reports how that duty was discharged, and it functions as a defense of the study's reliability. Tucker's information was scrutinized and measured against known facts, and material that could not be verified was generally excluded. One limit is admitted openly: most of the daily detail of anyone's private life goes unrecorded and so cannot be checked, and the author's response was to include only those personal elements bearing on the career. The reassurance at the end is that Tucker's recollections mostly corroborate other available evidence while adding perspective to it, which is what licenses weaving oral and documentary material into a single career biography.
overall_html: The passage is a biographer's account of why Lorenzo Tucker, a versatile African American entertainer overlooked by theater and film history, deserves a study and of how that study was conducted. The author's purpose is to establish both the subject's significance and the work's credibility, and the structure moves from Tucker's range of onstage and behind-the-scenes work, through an inventory of archival, filmic, and interview sources that culminates in the author's own interviews with Tucker, to a frank discussion of the hazards of relying on a living subject's memory and the verification procedures used to contain them. The only viewpoint developed is the author's, offered as a self-aware methodological defense rather than as an argument against other scholars.

Taking the explication of experience as its object as well as its method, Marjorie Shostak's Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman weaves together three narrative strands, and in doing so challenges the ethnographer's penchant for the general and the anonymous. The first strand, the autobiographical details of a 50-year-old woman's life among the seminomadic !Kung hunter-gatherers of Botswana, adds to the ethnographical literature on the !Kung. The second presents Nisa's story as a metaphor for woman's experience, a story that reflects many of the experiences and dilemmas addressed in recent feminist writing. The third tells the story of an intercultural encounter in which the distinction between ethnographer and subject becomes blurred.

Nisa explains Nisa's personality in terms of !Kung ways and, for the general reader, corrects and qualifies a number of received attitudes about "simple" societies. Michel Leiris' warning that "We are all too inclined to consider a people happy if considering them makes us happy" applies particularly to the !Kung, whose seemingly uncomplicated way of life, enlightened attitudes toward child rearing, and undeniable charm make them prime candidates for Western appreciation. But Nisa's answer to Shostak's question, "What is it to be a !Kung woman?" makes us feel the force of ugly facts we might otherwise skim over. Only 54 percent of !Kung children live to marry; Nisa loses all four of her children and a cherished husband. Nisa's memories of sibling rivalries, of her terrible rages when denied her mother, of nasty fights over food undermine the idyllic vision Westerners cherish of childhoods lived in such "simple" circumstances.

Woven into Nisa's autobiography are allusions to Shostak's personal engagement with issues of gender. Nisa's response to "What is it to be a !Kung woman?" also seems to answer another question, "What is it to be a woman?" In fact, Nisa's answers illuminate not just one woman's experience, but women's experience in general. It is a salutary shock to realize how much ethnographic literature omits the perspective of women about women.

Nisa's story is interwoven with Shostak's presentation of their encounter; at times each seems to exist primarily in response to the other. Nisa's autobiography is a distinct narrative in a particular voice, but it is manifestly the product of a collaboration. Indeed, by casting Nisa in the shape of a "life," Shostak employs a potent Western literary convention. Real lives, in fact, do not easily arrange themselves as stories that have recognizable shapes: Nisa, for example, often says "We lived in that place, eating things. Then we left and went somewhere else." It is in the process of the dialogue between Nisa and Shostak that a shaped story emerges from this seemingly featureless background.
explanation_html:
The opening does the organizational work for everything that follows: Shostak's book is presented as three interwoven strands, and the next three paragraphs take them in that order. The first is ordinary ethnography, the autobiography of Nisa, a fifty-year-old woman living among the seminomadic !Kung hunter-gatherers of Botswana. The second reads her story as a metaphor for women's experience, echoing concerns in recent feminist writing. The third is the intercultural encounter itself, where the boundary between ethnographer and subject dissolves. Attached to all this is an evaluative claim worth marking, that focusing on one named person pushes back against ethnography's habitual taste for the general and the anonymous.

The first strand is developed as a corrective. Explaining Nisa's personality through !Kung ways revises what a general reader assumes about so-called simple societies, and Michel Leiris' warning supplies the reason such revision is needed: we are quick to call a people happy when believing so makes us happy. The !Kung, with their apparently uncomplicated life, enlightened child rearing, and charm, invite exactly that sentimentality. Nisa's testimony blocks it. Only about half of !Kung children survive to marry, Nisa lost four children and a husband she loved, and her memories of sibling rivalry, of fury at being denied her mother, and of fights over food dismantle the idyllic picture Westerners hold.

The second strand gets brief treatment. Shostak's own engagement with questions of gender runs through the book, so the question she puts to Nisa about !Kung womanhood turns out to answer a broader one about womanhood itself, and the author accepts that Nisa's answers illuminate women's experience generally rather than one life alone. The closing sentence is the author's own judgment rather than a report of Shostak's: recognizing how much ethnographic literature leaves out what women say about women is described as a salutary shock.

The third strand raises the hardest problem, which is the book's own construction. Nisa and Shostak are so entangled that each at moments seems to exist chiefly in response to the other, and while Nisa's narrative keeps a distinct voice, it is openly a collaboration. The author then presses further: shaping the material into a life imports a powerful Western literary convention, and real lives do not fall into recognizable story shapes by themselves. The evidence is the flatness of Nisa's own phrasing about living in a place, eating, and moving on. What turns that featureless material into a shaped story is the dialogue between the two women.
overall_html: The passage assesses Marjorie Shostak's Nisa as a book operating on three levels at once, an ethnographic record of one !Kung woman's life, a portrait of women's experience in general, and an account of the encounter between ethnographer and subject, and treats that concentration on a single named person as a challenge to ethnography's preference for the general and the anonymous. The author's purpose is appreciative analysis, and the macro-structure is unusually clean, since the three strands are announced in the first paragraph and then examined one per paragraph, ending with the collaborative shaping of Nisa's story. The perspectives to track are Shostak's aims, Nisa's own testimony, and the author's evaluation of what the book achieves.

Passage A

Until recently, conservationists were often complacent about the effect of nonindigenous plant and animal species on the ecosystems they invade. Many shared Charles Elton's view, introduced in his 1958 book on invasive species, that disturbed habitats are most vulnerable to new arrivals because they contain fewer or less vigorous native species. Now, however, ecologists realize that when humans introduce new species into existing ecosystems, even pristine, species-rich habitats are threatened. The rapidly increasing conservation problems and high damage and control costs generated by these invasions merit serious concern.

Invasive plants profoundly affect ecosystems and threaten biodiversity throughout the world. For example, to the untrained eye, the Everglades National Park in Florida appears wild and natural. Yet this and other unique ecosystems are being degraded as surely as if by chemical pollution. In Florida, forests are growing where none existed before. Traditionally, saw grass dominated large regions of Florida's marshes, providing habitat for unique Everglades wildlife. Although saw grass grows over 9 feet tall, introduced Australian melaleuca trees, typically 70 feet tall, now outcompete marsh plants for sunlight. As melaleuca trees grow and form dense stands, their leaf litter increases soil elevations, inhibiting normal water flow. Wildlife associated with saw grass marshes declines. Similarly, in Australia, the introduction of Scotch broom plants led to the disappearance of a diverse set of native reptiles.

Passage B

The real threat posed by so-called invasive species isn't against nature but against humans' ideas of what nature is supposed to be. Species invasion is not a zero-sum game, with new species replacing old ones at a one-to-one ratio. Rather, and with critical exceptions, it is a positive-sum game, in which ecosystems can accept more and more species. Indeed, in both marine and terrestrial ecosystems, ecologists have found that invasions often increase biodiversity at the local level: if you add many new species and lose few or no native species, the overall species count goes up.

Invasions don't cause ecosystems to collapse. Invasions may radically alter the components of an ecosystem, perhaps to a point at which the ecosystem becomes less valuable or engaging to humans. But 50 years of study has failed to identify a clear ecological difference between an ecosystem rich in native species and one chock-full of introduced species. Unlike ecosystem destruction—clear cutting of forests, for example—invasions don't make ecosystems shrink or disappear. They simply transform them into different ecosystems.

When the issue is phrased as one of ecosystem destruction, the stakes are stark: we choose between nature's life and nature's death. In actuality, introduced species present a continuum. A few species do cause costly damage and tragic extinctions. But most plant and animal species simply blend in harmlessly. The issue they present for humans is not whether we will be surrounded by nature but rather what kind of nature we will have around us.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by charting a change in expert opinion. Conservationists used to be complacent about non-native species, largely because many followed Charles Elton, whose 1958 account held that disturbed habitats, with their fewer or weaker native species, were the vulnerable ones. The correction is stated as settled fact rather than as one side of a debate: ecologists now recognize that species introduced by humans threaten even pristine, species-rich habitats. The paragraph ends on stakes, naming the growing conservation problems and the high cost of the damage and of control, which is how this author signals that action is warranted.

Examples carry the argument here. The Everglades looks wild to an untrained eye, yet the author insists it is being degraded as surely as if by chemical pollution, and that comparison matters because it treats invasion as damage rather than mere change. The mechanism is laid out step by step: saw grass, which long dominated Florida's marshes and supported their distinctive wildlife, grows about nine feet, while introduced Australian melaleuca trees reach seventy and take the sunlight. Dense melaleuca stands drop litter, raise the soil, and block normal water flow, so saw-grass wildlife declines. Scotch broom eliminating native reptiles in Australia shows the pattern is not peculiar to Florida.

Passage B opens by relocating the threat, and that reframing is the move to grasp. What invasions endanger, this author argues, is not nature but human ideas about what nature is supposed to be. The supporting claim is essentially arithmetic: invasion is not a one-for-one swap of newcomers for natives but usually a positive-sum process in which an ecosystem takes on more and more species. Ecologists working in marine and terrestrial systems have often found local biodiversity rising, since adding many species while losing few or none raises the total. Note the hedge about critical exceptions, which returns at the end.

The strongest word in the debate now gets confronted directly, which is collapse. Invasions can radically change an ecosystem's components, possibly leaving it less valuable or engaging to people, but fifty years of study has not produced a clear ecological difference between a system rich in natives and one full of introduced species. The comparison with clear cutting does the real work: destruction makes an ecosystem shrink or disappear, whereas invasion simply yields a different ecosystem. Read this as the direct answer to Passage A's equation of invasion with chemical pollution.

The close turns the dispute into a question of framing. Describing the issue as ecosystem destruction forces a choice between nature's life and nature's death, and this author rejects that binary in favor of a continuum. The concession is genuine and worth marking, since a few species are admitted to cause costly damage and tragic extinctions, which is precisely the territory Passage A's examples occupy. Most introduced species, though, blend in harmlessly. What remains at issue is therefore not whether nature will surround us but what kind of nature that will be.
overall_html: The two passages disagree about how serious an ecological problem invasive species are. Passage A reports that experts have abandoned Charles Elton's older view that only disturbed habitats are vulnerable and argues, through the melaleuca invasion of the Everglades and Scotch broom in Australia, that introduced species degrade even pristine ecosystems as surely as pollution does. Passage B argues that invasion is usually positive-sum and often raises local biodiversity, that no clear ecological difference separates native-rich from introduction-rich systems, and that what is really threatened is the human idea of nature. The relationship is direct disagreement over how to interpret shared facts, softened only by Passage B's concession that a few invaders do cause real damage and extinctions.

Can a sovereign have unlimited legal power? If a sovereign does have unlimited legal power, then the sovereign presumably has the legal power to limit or even completely abdicate its own legal power. But doing so would mean that the sovereign no longer has unlimited legal power, thereby contradicting the initial supposition. This theoretical conundrum is traditionally known as the paradox of omnipotence.

Social scientists have recognized that sovereign omnipotence can be a source of considerable practical difficulty for sovereigns themselves. Douglass North and Barry Weingast show that English and French monarchies in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries confronted a practical challenge created by the paradox of their own omnipotence.

North and Weingast point out that it is often in a sovereign's best interest to make a credible commitment not to perform certain acts. For example, a sovereign with absolute power can refuse to honor its financial commitments. Yet creditors will not voluntarily lend generous amounts at favorable terms to an absolute monarch who can renege upon debts at will.

In the struggle to expand their empires, the English and French monarchies required vast amounts of capital. At the outset of the seventeenth century, however, neither regime could credibly commit itself to repay debts or to honor property rights. The absence of limitations upon the legal power of monarchs meant that there was no law or commitment monarchs could make that they could not also unmake or disregard. Consequently, these monarchs earned a reputation for expropriating wealth, repudiating debts, and reneging upon commitments. Not surprisingly, creditors took such behavior into account and demanded higher interest rates from monarchs than from the monarchs' wealthy subjects.

North and Weingast argue that the constitutional settlement imposed in England by the Glorious Revolution of 1688 halted such faithless conduct. Henceforth, Parliament controlled the Crown's purse strings. Parliament, in turn, represented commercial interests that would not tolerate governmental disregard for property rights. The Crown's newfound inability to dishonor its commitments translated into a newfound ability to borrow: the Crown's borrowing increased and interest rates fell, because lenders concluded that the Crown would honor its debts.

Thanks to North, Weingast, and others writing in the same vein, it is now conventional to hold that constitutional arrangements benefit sovereigns by limiting their power. But such scholars neglect the extent to which constitutions can fail in this regard. For example, the constitutional settlement imposed by the Glorious Revolution did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another: whereas it was once the Crown that lacked the power to bind itself, it is now Parliament that lacks this power. The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty is a pillar of England's unwritten constitution, and it provides that Parliament lacks legal power over the extent of its own legal power.
explanation_html:
A logical puzzle opens the passage, and you need it precisely before anything else lands. If a sovereign's legal power is truly unlimited, that power must include the power to restrict or even give up its own authority; but using it would leave the sovereign without unlimited power, contradicting the premise. Either branch defeats the supposition. That is the paradox of omnipotence, and the paragraphs that follow move it out of pure theory and into economic history.

The bridge from theory to practice is deliberately short, since it only has to introduce the study the passage will lean on. Social scientists have observed that being all-powerful causes genuine practical trouble for the powerful themselves. North and Weingast are named as the source for that observation, and their subject is the bind the English and French monarchies found themselves in during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Their organizing concept is the credible commitment. A sovereign frequently benefits from being able to promise convincingly that it will not do something, and borrowing supplies the clean illustration: a monarch with absolute power can simply refuse to honor a debt, so lenders will not hand over generous sums on favorable terms to someone free to renege at will. Notice what this accomplishes for the argument, turning an abstract contradiction into a concrete cost the sovereign pays.

History now supplies the evidence. Both monarchies needed vast capital for imperial expansion, and at the start of the seventeenth century neither could promise believably to repay debts or respect property rights, because unlimited legal power meant every law and commitment could be unmade or ignored. The consequence was predictable: a reputation for expropriating wealth, repudiating debts, and breaking promises, and creditors who priced that risk in by demanding higher interest from monarchs than from the monarchs' own wealthy subjects.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688 arrives, on North and Weingast's account, as the remedy. Its constitutional settlement put the Crown's finances under Parliament, and Parliament answered to commercial interests unwilling to tolerate official disregard for property rights. Watch the reversal, because it is the payoff of the whole argument: losing the ability to break its promises gave the Crown a new ability to borrow, so its borrowing rose and its interest rates fell once lenders believed the debts would be paid.

Only in the final paragraph does the author's own position surface, and it qualifies the account rather than rejecting it. Thanks to these scholars it has become conventional to say that constitutional arrangements benefit sovereigns by limiting them; what that consensus neglects is the extent to which constitutions can fail at the job. The 1688 settlement did not dissolve the paradox of omnipotence but moved it, since the body that now cannot bind itself is Parliament rather than the Crown. Parliamentary sovereignty, a pillar of England's unwritten constitution, means exactly that Parliament holds no legal power over the extent of its own legal power.
overall_html: The passage takes the paradox of omnipotence, the puzzle that an unlimited sovereign power must include the power to limit itself and so cannot remain unlimited, and traces its practical consequences through North and Weingast's account of early modern monarchy, where the inability to make credible commitments made royal borrowing expensive until the settlement of 1688 subordinated the Crown's finances to Parliament. The author's purpose is to accept that historical account and then qualify the consensus built on it, arguing at the close that constitutional limits merely relocated the paradox, because parliamentary sovereignty leaves Parliament unable to bind itself. The two viewpoints to track are North and Weingast's thesis and the author's partial dissent from it.

The corrido, a type of narrative folk song, comes from a region half in Mexico and half in the United States known as the Lower Rio Grande Border. Corridos, which flourished from about 1836 to the late 1930s, are part of a long-standing ballad tradition that has roots in eighteenth-century Spain. Sung in Spanish, corridos combine formal features of several different types of folk songs, but their narratives consistently deal with subject matter specific to the Border region. For example, "El Corrido de Kiansis" (c. 1870), the oldest corrido surviving in complete form, records the first cattle drives to Kansas in the late 1860s. A single important event is likely to have inspired several corrido variants, yet the different versions of any given story all partake of standard generic elements. When sung at social gatherings, corridos served to commemorate significant local happenings, but more importantly, their heavy reliance on familiar linguistic and thematic conventions served to affirm the cohesiveness of Border communities.

Corridos take their name from the Spanish verb correr, meaning to run or to flow, for corridos tell their stories simply and swiftly, without embellishments. Figures of speech such as metaphors are generally rare in corridos, and when metaphors are used, they usually incorporate everyday images that are familiar to the songs' listeners. In the popular "El Corrido de Gregorio Cortez," for example, the hero Cortez, fighting off pursuers, uses the metaphor of a thunderstorm to boast that he has had harder fights than the one they gave him: "I have weathered thunderstorms; / This little mist doesn't bother me." Similar storm imagery is found in other corridos including "Kiansis," which tells of stampedes caused by thunderstorms during the Kansas cattle drives. Such imagery, highly conventional and readily recognizable to corrido listeners, reflects and strengthens the continuity of the corrido tradition.

The corrido is composed not only of familiar images but also of certain ready-made lines that travel easily from one ballad to another. This is most evident in the corrido's formal closing verse, or despedida. The despedida of one variant of "Gregorio Cortez" is translated as follows: "Now with this I say farewell / In the shade of a cypress tree; / This is the end of the ballad / Of Don Gregorio Cortez." The first and third lines are a set convention. The second and fourth lines are variable, the fourth carrying the name of the corrido or expressing its subject, and the second varying according to exigencies of rhyme. In the despedida, perhaps the clearest marker of both the corrido's uniqueness and its generic continuity, the corrido's maker asserts that the task of relating an authentic Border tale has been accomplished.
explanation_html:
Definition and context come first, and the details reward organizing rather than absorbing as a blur. The corrido is a narrative folk song from the Lower Rio Grande Border, a region split between Mexico and the United States, sung in Spanish and flourishing from about 1836 to the late 1930s within a ballad tradition reaching back to eighteenth-century Spain. Two features are set against each other from the start: the form borrows conventions from several kinds of folk song, while the content stays strictly local, as with the oldest complete surviving corrido, which records the first cattle drives to Kansas. One event might generate several variants, all built from the same generic elements. Notice the ranking in the final sentence, since commemorating local happenings mattered less than the way familiar language and themes held Border communities together.

The name is used to introduce the style. Corrido derives from a verb meaning to run or flow, and the songs narrate the same way, quickly and plainly and without ornament. That leads to the paragraph's real subject, which is how sparingly and how conventionally these ballads use metaphor. When a figure of speech does appear, it draws on imagery the audience already knows, as when a hero fighting off pursuers boasts that he has weathered thunderstorms and this little mist is nothing. Storm imagery recurs elsewhere, including in the Kansas cattle-drive ballad, where thunderstorms set off stampedes. Draw the conclusion the author draws: because such images are conventional and instantly recognizable, they both reflect the tradition's continuity and reinforce it.

Beyond recurring images, whole lines travel from one ballad to another, and the closing verse known as the despedida is where that is clearest. The structure is precise. In the farewell verse of one Cortez variant, the first and third lines are fixed convention while the second and fourth vary, the fourth naming the corrido or stating its subject and the second bending to whatever the rhyme demands. A single stanza therefore carries both what every corrido shares and what belongs to this one song, which is why the author treats the despedida as the clearest marker of the corrido's uniqueness and its generic continuity at once. It ends with the maker claiming to have delivered an authentic Border tale.
overall_html: The passage explains what a corrido is and how its conventions operate: a Spanish-language narrative ballad from the Lower Rio Grande Border, flourishing between 1836 and the late 1930s, whose stories are strictly local while its form is highly standardized. The author's purpose is expository rather than evaluative, moving from the genre's origins, subject matter, and social function, to its swift unornamented style and stock imagery such as the recurring thunderstorm, to the ready-made lines of the closing despedida with its mix of fixed and variable elements. The claim tying the three paragraphs together is that these shared conventions both express and strengthen the continuity of the tradition and the cohesiveness of the communities that sang it. No competing viewpoints appear.

The characteristic smell or taste of a plant, to insects as well as to humans, depends on its chemical composition. Broadly speaking, plants contain two categories of chemical substances: primary and secondary. The primary substances, such as proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins, and hormones, are required for growth and proper functioning and are found in all plants. The secondary substances are a diverse and multitudinous array of chemicals that have no known role in the internal chemical processes of plants' growth or metabolism. Only a few of these substances occur in any one species of plant, but the same or similar ones tend to occur in related plants such as the various species that constitute a single family. It is these secondary substances that give plants their distinctive tastes and smells.

Insects appear to have played a major role in many plants' having the secondary substances they have today. Such substances undoubtedly first appeared, and new ones continue to appear, as the result of genetic mutations in individual plants. But if a mutation is to survive and be passed on to subsequent generations, it must pass the muster of natural selection—that is, it must increase the likelihood of the organism's surviving and reproducing. Some secondary substances are favored by natural selection because they are scents that attract pollinating insects to blossoms. Such scents signal the presence of nectar, which nourishes the insects without damage to the plants. Other secondary substances that arose by mutation were conserved by natural selection because they proved to be biochemical defenses against the enemies of plants, the majority of which are insects. Some of these defensive substances cause insects to suffer unpleasant symptoms or even to die. Still other secondary substances are not in themselves harmful to insects, but are characteristic smells or tastes that dissuade the insect from feeding by warning it of the presence of some other substance that is harmful.

For hundreds of millions of years there has been an evolutionary competition for advantage between plants and plant-eating insects. If insects are to survive as the plants they eat develop defenses against them, they must switch to other foods or evolve ways to circumvent the plants' defenses. They may evolve a way to detoxify a harmful substance, to store it in their bodies out of harm's way, or to avoid its effects in some other manner. Insects quickly come to prefer the plants whose defenses they can circumvent, and they eventually evolve the ability to identify them by their characteristic flavors or odors, or both. As the competition has progressed, fewer and fewer plants have remained as suitable food sources for any one species of insect; species of insects have thus tended to become associated with narrowly defined and often botanically restricted groups of plants.
explanation_html:
Chemistry sets up everything that follows, so keep the two categories clean. Primary substances, among them proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins, and hormones, are what a plant needs to grow and function properly, and every plant has them. Secondary substances are the opposite in nearly every respect: an enormous and varied collection of chemicals with no known role in growth or metabolism, present only a few at a time in any one species, and shared among botanical relatives, so plants within a single family tend to carry the same or similar ones. The closing sentence explains why any of this matters for the rest of the passage, since the secondary substances are what give a plant its distinctive taste and smell, to insects as much as to people.

Origin is the question here, and the answer runs through natural selection. New secondary substances arise by genetic mutation in individual plants, but a mutation survives into later generations only if it improves the plant's odds of surviving and reproducing. Insects supply that advantage in three ways worth holding apart. Some substances are scents that pull pollinators toward blossoms by signaling nectar, a bargain that feeds the insect and costs the plant nothing. Others were preserved because they function as biochemical defenses against the insects that make up most of a plant's enemies, sickening or killing them. A third group does no harm at all but works as a warning label, a taste or smell announcing that something genuinely damaging is present.

The closing paragraph turns all of this into an arms race running hundreds of millions of years. As plants develop defenses, insects must either move to other foods or evolve ways around them, whether by detoxifying a harmful chemical, storing it somewhere it cannot do damage, or evading its effects some other way. Here the earlier point about smell and taste pays off: insects come to favor the plants whose defenses they can beat and evolve the ability to recognize those plants by their characteristic flavors or odors, the very substances meant to repel them. The long-run result is narrowing, since fewer and fewer plants stay edible for any one insect species, and each species ends up tied to a small, botanically restricted group of plants.
overall_html: The passage explains why plants taste and smell as they do and how insects shaped that chemistry. The central claim is that secondary substances, which play no role in a plant's own growth or metabolism, persist because natural selection favored those that attract pollinating insects or deter plant-eating ones, either by poisoning them or by signaling that something harmful is present. The author's purpose is explanatory, and the structure builds in three steps: a distinction between primary and secondary substances, an account of how insects drove the selection of the secondary ones, and a closing look at the long evolutionary contest that has left each insect species confined to a narrow range of plants. No competing viewpoints are developed.

David Warsh's book describes a great contradiction inherent in economic theory since 1776, when Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations. Warsh calls it the struggle between the Pin Factory and the Invisible Hand.

Using the example of a pin factory, Smith emphasized the huge increases in efficiency that could be achieved through increased size. The pin factory's employees, by specializing on narrow tasks, produce far more than they could if each worked independently. Also, Smith was the first to recognize how a market economy can harness self-interest to the common good, leading each individual as though "by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention." For example, businesses sell products that people want, at reasonable prices, not because the business owners inherently want to please people but because doing so enables them to make money in a competitive marketplace.

These two concepts, however, are opposed to each other. The parable of the pin factory says that there are increasing returns to scale—the bigger the pin factory, the more specialized its workers can be, and therefore the more pins the factory can produce per worker. But increasing returns create a natural tendency toward monopoly, because a large business can achieve larger scale and hence lower costs than a small business. So given increasing returns, bigger firms tend to drive smaller firms out of business, until each industry is dominated by just a few players. But for the invisible hand to work properly, there must be many competitors in each industry, so that nobody can exert monopoly power. Therefore, the idea that free markets always get it right depends on the assumption that returns to scale are diminishing, not increasing.

For almost two centuries, the assumption of diminishing returns dominated economic theory, with the Pin Factory de-emphasized. Why? As Warsh explains, it wasn't about ideology; it was about following the line of least mathematical resistance. Economics has always had scientific aspirations; economists have always sought the rigor and clarity that comes from representing their ideas using numbers and equations. And the economics of diminishing returns lend themselves readily to elegant formalism, while those of increasing returns—the Pin Factory—are notoriously hard to represent mathematically.

Many economists tried repeatedly to bring the Pin Factory into the mainstream of economic thought to reflect the fact that increasing returns obviously characterized many enterprises, such as railroads. Yet they repeatedly failed because they could not state their ideas rigorously enough. Only since the late 1970s has this "underground river"—a term used to describe the role of increasing returns in economic thought—surfaced into the mainstream of economic thought. By then, economists had finally found ways to describe the Pin Factory with the rigor needed to make it respectable.
explanation_html:
The passage opens as a report on someone else's book, and the framing sentence is all you need for now. David Warsh identifies a contradiction that has run through economic theory ever since Adam Smith published in 1776, and he gives its two sides memorable labels, the Pin Factory and the Invisible Hand. Expect what follows to define each side, show why the two collide, and explain how the profession dealt with the collision.

Both halves of Smith arrive next, in order. The pin factory illustrates the gains that come from size, since employees who each specialize in one narrow task turn out far more than the same people working independently. The invisible hand is the second insight, that a market economy can turn self-interest toward the common good, leading a person to promote an end he never intended. The example is deliberately ordinary: sellers offer wanted goods at reasonable prices not out of goodwill but because competition makes that the way to make money. Notice that nothing has been called contradictory yet.

Now the collision. The pin factory implies increasing returns to scale, because a bigger factory allows finer specialization and so more output per worker. Follow the consequence closely, since the whole passage turns on it: increasing returns push naturally toward monopoly, as large firms reach lower costs than small ones and drive them out until an industry holds only a few players. The invisible hand, however, requires many competitors, so that nobody can wield monopoly power. Confidence that free markets always get it right therefore depends on returns being diminishing rather than increasing, which is exactly what the pin factory denies.

Why the profession sided with diminishing returns for nearly two centuries is the question, and Warsh's answer is deliberately deflationary. Ideology had nothing to do with it; mathematics did. Economics has always wanted scientific standing, which meant expressing ideas in numbers and equations, so the branch that formalizes elegantly won by default. Diminishing returns cooperate with that ambition, while increasing returns are notoriously hard to represent mathematically. The Pin Factory was set aside not because anyone thought it false but because it was difficult to write down.

The closing paragraph finishes the history and confirms the diagnosis. Economists kept trying to bring increasing returns into the mainstream, and they had good reason, since enterprises such as railroads obviously display them, but attempt after attempt failed on the same point, an inability to state the ideas rigorously enough. The underground river metaphor captures the result nicely, an idea flowing out of sight beneath the visible discipline. Only from the late 1970s did the mathematics catch up, and only then did the Pin Factory become respectable.
overall_html: Reviewing David Warsh's book, the passage lays out a contradiction Warsh traces through economics since Adam Smith: the Pin Factory, with its increasing returns to scale, tends toward monopoly, while the Invisible Hand requires many competing firms, so confidence in free markets depends on assuming that returns diminish. The author's purpose is expository, relaying Warsh's argument along with his explanation of why the profession behaved as it did, and the structure moves from the two Smithian ideas, to the conflict between them, to the claim that mathematical tractability rather than ideology kept increasing returns underground until the late 1970s. The perspectives in play are Smith's original insights and Warsh's account of what later economists made of them.

Passage A

Law enforcement agencies can effectively nullify particular laws, or particular applications of law, simply by declining to prosecute violators. This power appears to be exercised frequently and I attempt here to explain why.

Rules of law are almost always overinclusive: read literally, they forbid some conduct that the legislature that formulated the rule did not want to forbid. The costs of precisely tailoring a rule to the conduct intended to be forbidden would be prohibitive given the limitations of human foresight and the inherent ambiguities of language. The more particularly the legislature tries to describe the forbidden conduct, the more loopholes it will create. Enforcing an overinclusive rule to the letter could impose very heavy social costs. The effect would be like punishing an innocent person in order to reduce the probability of acquitting a guilty one. Of course, the danger of punishing the innocent is not a decisive blow against the use of a particular method of law enforcement; the danger must be traded off against the costs of alternative methods that would reduce it. But there is a technique—discretionary nonenforcement—by which the costs of overinclusion can be reduced without a corresponding increase in underinclusion (loopholes).

Of course, allowing discretionary nonenforcement does not determine the principle by which the law enforcement agency will select its cases. Conceivably the agency could concentrate its resources on those areas of conduct that had been brought inadvertently within the scope of the rule. But this seems unlikely. Capricious enforcement is not unknown (or even rare) but it does not appear to be the central tendency since legislative oversight assures that the agency does not stray too far from the intended, as distinct from the enacted, regulation being enforced.

Passage B

The newspaper reported that 231,000 water customers in the city are late paying their bills—some by months, others by decades. In all, these water delinquents owe the city more than $625 million in overdue bills and penalties. So officials are planning to selectively cut the water to a few residences with outstanding bills to show that they are serious about collecting those debts. Officials plan to target only high-income neighborhoods, to make examples of a few privileged residents who will be in no position to complain since they were caught stiffing the system.

But property owners are responsible for water bills. So why not just do what every other property-related creditor or tax authority does—attach a lien to the property? The money owed would automatically be available whenever a property was sold, and the threat of negative credit implications would be a powerful incentive to keep current with one's water obligations.

Well, here's an answer: a loophole prohibits debts other than taxes from being subject to liens by the city, and, technically, water charges are not taxes. But if the problem is with the law, then why not change the law? Wouldn't that be easier, and politically smarter, than shutting off people's water?
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a claim and a promise. The legal theorist writing it observes that enforcement agencies can effectively nullify a law, or particular applications of one, simply by declining to prosecute, and that the power gets used often. What follows is offered as an explanation of why, so read the rest of this passage as justification rather than complaint.

The explanation rests on a structural fact about rules: they are nearly always overinclusive, forbidding on their face conduct the legislature never meant to reach. Drafting precisely enough to avoid that would cost too much, given the limits of human foresight and the ambiguity of language, and each added specification opens another loophole. Enforcing an overinclusive rule to the letter would carry heavy social costs, which the theorist likens to punishing an innocent person to reduce the chance of acquitting a guilty one. The payoff comes last: discretionary nonenforcement cuts the costs of overinclusion without widening the loopholes that finer drafting would create.

A gap in that argument gets acknowledged before anyone else can press it. Permitting discretion says nothing about which cases an agency will actually drop; in principle it could focus on conduct the rule captured inadvertently, but the theorist doubts agencies are that careful. The concession is real, since capricious enforcement is described as neither unknown nor even rare. What keeps caprice from being the central tendency is legislative oversight, which holds agencies reasonably close to the regulation the legislature intended as distinct from the one it actually enacted.

Passage B abandons theory and reports a case. A newspaper found that 231,000 water customers in one city are behind on their bills, some by decades, owing the city more than $625 million in charges and penalties. Officials plan to cut service at a few homes to demonstrate seriousness, and to pick those homes in high-income neighborhoods, on the theory that wealthy residents caught stiffing the system will be in no position to object. That is selective enforcement of exactly the kind Passage A described, now attached to real consequences.

An alternative follows, framed as an obvious question rather than a legal argument. Since property owners are the ones responsible for water bills, the city could simply do what other property-related creditors and tax authorities do and attach a lien to the property. The debt would then be collected automatically whenever the property was sold, and the prospect of damaged credit would give owners a strong reason to stay current, all without anyone's water being shut off.

The answer turns out to be a technicality, and the commentator declines to accept it as a reason. City liens may cover taxes only, and water charges do not technically qualify as taxes, so the lien route is closed by a loophole. The closing questions carry the argument: if the law is the problem, change the law, which would be easier and politically smarter than shutting off people's water. Where Passage A treats enforcement discretion as a sensible accommodation to imperfect rules, this ending insists that the rule itself be repaired.
overall_html: Passage A argues that selective nonenforcement is a rational response to the fact that legal rules are inevitably overinclusive, since drafting them precisely would be prohibitively costly and would only create more loopholes, with legislative oversight keeping agencies roughly aligned with what the legislature intended. Passage B reports a city preparing to cut water service to a few wealthy delinquents as an example to 231,000 debtors, notes that liens would collect the money automatically, and objects that a technicality blocking liens ought to be fixed by amending the law. The relationship is theory met with a troubling case: B supplies a concrete instance of the discretion A defends and treats changing the rule, rather than enforcing it selectively, as the right remedy.

Over the past 50 years, expansive, low-density communities have proliferated at the edges of many cities in the United States and Canada, creating a phenomenon known as suburban sprawl. Andres Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, and Jeff Speck, a group of prominent town planners belonging to a movement called New Urbanism, contend that suburban sprawl contributes to the decline of civic life and civility. For reasons involving the flow of automobile traffic, they note, zoning laws usually dictate that suburban homes, stores, businesses, and schools be built in separate areas, and this separation robs people of communal space where they can interact and get to know one another. It is as difficult to imagine the concept of community without a town square or local pub, these town planners contend, as it is to imagine the concept of family independent of the home.

Suburban housing subdivisions, Duany and his colleagues add, usually contain homes identical not only in appearance but also in price, resulting in a de facto economic segregation of residential neighborhoods. Children growing up in these neighborhoods, whatever their economic circumstances, are certain to be ill prepared for life in a diverse society. Moreover, because the widely separated suburban homes and businesses are connected only by "collector roads," residents are forced to drive, often in heavy traffic, in order to perform many daily tasks. Time that would in a town center involve social interaction within a physical public realm is now spent inside the automobile, where people cease to be community members and instead become motorists, competing for road space, often acting antisocially. Pedestrians rarely act in this manner toward each other. Duany and his colleagues advocate development based on early-twentieth-century urban neighborhoods that mix housing of different prices and offer residents a "gratifying public realm" that includes narrow, tree-lined streets, parks, corner grocery stores, cafes, small neighborhood schools, all within walking distance. This, they believe, would give people of diverse backgrounds and lifestyles an opportunity to interact and thus develop mutual respect.

Opponents of New Urbanism claim that migration to sprawling suburbs is an expression of people's legitimate desire to secure the enjoyment and personal mobility provided by the automobile and the lifestyle that it makes possible. However, the New Urbanists do not question people's right to their own values; instead, they suggest that we should take a more critical view of these values and of the sprawl-conducive zoning and subdivision policies that reflect them. New Urbanists are fundamentally concerned with the long-term social costs of the now-prevailing attitude that individual mobility, consumption, and wealth should be valued absolutely, regardless of their impact on community life.
explanation_html:
The main viewpoint arrives right after the phenomenon is defined. Suburban sprawl names the expansive, low-density communities that have spread at the edges of North American cities over the past fifty years. The New Urbanists, a movement represented here by three prominent town planners, contend that sprawl erodes civic life and civility. Their reasoning begins with zoning: because rules written around the flow of automobile traffic place homes, stores, businesses, and schools in separate areas, residents lose the communal spaces where they would otherwise meet and come to know one another. The analogy they offer makes the claim vivid, since a community without a town square or local pub is said to be as hard to imagine as a family without a home.

The case expands here, and it helps to track it as three linked harms. Subdivision houses tend to be identical in price as well as appearance, so neighborhoods become economically segregated in practice and the children raised in them, at any income level, grow up unready for a diverse society. Because homes and businesses are joined only by collector roads, ordinary daily tasks require driving, and hours that a town center would fill with contact in a public realm are instead spent in traffic, where people stop acting as community members and start acting as motorists competing for road space, often antisocially, in a way pedestrians rarely do to one another. The remedy follows directly: neighborhoods modeled on early-twentieth-century ones, mixing price levels and putting narrow tree-lined streets, parks, corner groceries, cafes, and small schools within walking distance, so that different sorts of people meet and develop mutual respect.

A counterargument finally appears, and it is answered rather than dismissed. Opponents of New Urbanism hold that moving to sprawling suburbs expresses a legitimate desire for the enjoyment and personal mobility a car provides and for the life it makes possible. Watch precisely what is conceded and what is refused. The New Urbanists do not challenge anyone's right to hold those values; they ask that the values, and the zoning and subdivision policies built to serve them, be viewed more critically. The closing sentence states their underlying worry, which is the long-term social cost of treating individual mobility, consumption, and wealth as absolute goods whatever happens to community life.
overall_html: The passage lays out the New Urbanist critique of suburban sprawl, on which zoning that separates homes from stores, workplaces, and schools strips away the shared public space communities need, segregates neighborhoods by income, and replaces face-to-face contact with time spent driving. The author's purpose is to present that position together with its proposed alternative, walkable mixed-price neighborhoods modeled on early-twentieth-century urban ones, and then to report how its proponents answer their critics. The two viewpoints to keep apart are the New Urbanists, represented by Duany and his colleagues, and the opponents who defend suburban life as a legitimate choice about personal mobility, a right the New Urbanists grant while still questioning the values behind it.

Passage A

In ancient Greece, Aristotle documented the ability of foraging honeybees to recruit nestmates to a good food source. He did not speculate on how the communication occurred, but he and naturalists since then have observed that a bee that finds a new food source returns to the nest and "dances" for its nestmates. In the 1940s, von Frisch and colleagues discovered a pattern in the dance. They observed a foraging honeybee's dance, deciphered it, and thereby deduced the location of the food source the bee had discovered. Yet questions still remained regarding the precise mechanism used to transmit that information.

In the 1960s, Wenner and Esch each discovered independently that dancing honeybees emit low-frequency sounds, which we now know to come from wing vibrations. Both researchers reasoned that this might explain the bees' ability to communicate effectively even in completely dark nests. But at that time many scientists mistakenly believed that honeybees lack hearing, so the issue remained unresolved. Wenner subsequently proposed that smell rather than hearing was the key to honeybee communication. He hypothesized that honeybees derive information not from sound, but from odors the forager conveys from the food source.

Yet Gould has shown that foragers can dispatch bees to sites they had not actually visited, something that would not be possible if odor were in fact necessary to bees' communication. Finally, using a honeybee robot to simulate the forager's dance, Kirchner and Michelsen showed that sounds emitted during the forager's dance do indeed play an essential role in conveying information about the food's location.

Passage B

All animals communicate in some sense. Bees dance, ants leave trails, some fish emit high-voltage signals. But some species—bees, birds, and primates, for example—communicate symbolically. In an experiment with vervet monkeys in the wild, Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler found that prerecorded vervet alarm calls from a loudspeaker elicited the same response as did naturally produced vervet calls alerting the group to the presence of a predator of a particular type. Vervets looked upward upon hearing an eagle alarm call, and they scanned the ground below in response to a snake alarm call. These responses suggest that each alarm call represents, for vervets, a specific type of predator.

Karl von Frisch was first to crack the code of the honeybee's dance, which he described as "language." The dance symbolically represents the distance, direction, and quality of newly discovered food. Adrian Wenner and others believed that bees rely on olfactory cues, as well as the dance, to find a food source, but this has turned out not to be so.

While it is true that bees have a simple nervous system, they do not automatically follow just any information. Biologist James Gould trained foraging bees to find food in a boat placed in the middle of a lake and then allowed them to return to the hive to indicate this new location. He found that hive members ignored the foragers' instructions, presumably because no pollinating flowers grow in such a place.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with the long history of a single question. Aristotle recorded that a foraging honeybee finding food can recruit nestmates, and naturalists ever since have watched the returning bee dance without knowing how the dance works. Von Frisch and his colleagues supplied the breakthrough in the 1940s, detecting a pattern in the dance and reading it well enough to deduce where the food lay. Note the loose end the paragraph deliberately leaves, because it drives everything after: knowing that the dance encodes a location did not reveal the mechanism by which the information gets transmitted.

Two candidate mechanisms enter, and the paragraph is really about why the question stalled. Wenner and Esch found independently in the 1960s that dancing bees emit low-frequency sounds, now known to come from wing vibrations, and both took this to explain how bees manage to communicate in a completely dark nest. The obstacle was a mistaken belief, common at the time, that honeybees cannot hear, which left the sound explanation unresolved. Wenner then changed position and proposed odor instead, arguing that nestmates take their information from smells the forager carries back from the food.

Resolution arrives in two strokes. Gould showed that foragers can dispatch bees to sites the foragers themselves had never visited, which odor alone could not accomplish, so smell cannot be necessary to the communication. Kirchner and Michelsen then built a robot bee to simulate the dance and demonstrated that the sounds produced during it really do carry essential information about the food's location. Wenner's odor hypothesis is set aside and the sound account confirmed, completing the arc the first paragraph promised.

Passage B begins somewhere else entirely, with a general claim about animal communication. Every animal communicates in some fashion, but a few species communicate symbolically, meaning a signal stands for something in particular. The vervet monkey study supplies the evidence: recorded alarm calls played through a loudspeaker drew the same reactions as genuine ones, with the monkeys looking upward at an eagle call and scanning the ground at a snake call. Because each response matches a specific predator, each call appears to represent that predator to the animals.

Bees now appear as a second instance of the same phenomenon, and notice how differently the shared research gets used. Von Frisch is credited with cracking the code of the dance and with calling it language, and what this author emphasizes is symbolic content, since the dance stands for the distance, direction, and quality of the food. Wenner's olfactory proposal receives a single dismissive clause saying it turned out not to be so. Passage A devoted two paragraphs to that dispute; here it is a detail inside an argument about symbols.

The closing paragraph adds a claim Passage A never makes, that bees assess what they are told. Their nervous system is simple, but they do not automatically act on just any information. Gould trained foragers to feed from a boat anchored in the middle of a lake and let them return to report the location, and the hive ignored the instructions, presumably because no pollinating flowers grow in open water. The dance is therefore treated not as an automatic trigger but as a message its recipients weigh against what they already know.
overall_html: Both passages draw on the same honeybee research but put it to different uses. Passage A traces a scientific question about mechanism, running from Aristotle through von Frisch's decoding of the dance to the contest between Wenner's odor hypothesis and the sound hypothesis, which Gould and then Kirchner and Michelsen's robot bee settled in favor of sound. Passage B is not concerned with mechanism at all: it argues that certain species communicate symbolically, offering vervet alarm calls and the bee dance as examples, and closes with Gould's lake experiment to show that bees evaluate the messages they receive. The relationship is one of different scope over shared evidence, with the two agreeing only that Wenner's odor explanation was wrong.

Most scholars of Mexican American history mark César Chávez's unionizing efforts among Mexican and Mexican American farm laborers in California as the beginning of Chicano political activism in the 1960s. By 1965, Chávez's United Farm Workers Union gained international recognition by initiating a worldwide boycott of grapes in an effort to get growers in California to sign union contracts. The year 1965 also marks the birth of contemporary Chicano theater, for that is the year Luis Valdez approached Chávez about using theater to organize farm workers. Valdez and the members of the resulting Teatro Campesino are generally credited by scholars as having initiated the Chicano theater movement, a movement that would reach its apex in the 1970s.

In the fall of 1965, Valdez gathered a group of striking farm workers and asked them to talk about their working conditions. A former farm worker himself, Valdez was no stranger to the players in the daily drama that was fieldwork. He asked people to illustrate what happened on the picket lines, and the less timid in the audience delighted in acting out their ridicule of the strikebreakers. Using the farm workers' basic improvisations, Valdez guided the group toward the creation of what he termed "actos," skits or sketches whose roots scholars have traced to various sources that had influenced Valdez as a student and as a member of the San Francisco Mime Troupe. Expanding beyond the initial setting of flatbed-truck stages at the fields' edges, the acto became the quintessential form of Chicano theater in the 1960s. According to Valdez, the acto should suggest a solution to the problems exposed in the brief comic statement, and, as with any good political theater, it should satirize the opposition and inspire the audience to social action. Because actos were based on participants' personal experiences, they had palpable immediacy.

In her book El Teatro Campesino, Yolanda Broyles-González rightly criticizes theater historians for having tended to credit Valdez individually with inventing actos as a genre, as if the striking farm workers' improvisational talent had depended entirely on his vision and expertise for the form it took. She traces especially the actos' connections to a similar genre of informal, often satirical shows known as carpas that were performed in tents to mainly working-class audiences. Carpas had flourished earlier in the twentieth century in the border area of Mexico and the United States. Many participants in the formation of the Teatro no doubt had substantial cultural links to this tradition and likely adapted it to their improvisations. The early development of the Teatro Campesino was, in fact, a collective accomplishment; still, Valdez's artistic contribution was a crucial one, for the resulting actos were neither carpas nor theater in the European tradition of Valdez's academic training, but a distinctive genre with connections to both.
explanation_html:
The opening does historical scene-setting, anchoring two movements to the same year. Most scholars of Mexican American history treat Cesar Chavez's unionizing of farm laborers in California as the start of Chicano political activism in the 1960s, and by 1965 his union had drawn international attention with a worldwide grape boycott aimed at forcing growers to sign contracts. That same year Luis Valdez approached Chavez about using theater to organize workers, and the group that followed, Teatro Campesino, is generally credited with launching the Chicano theater movement. Nothing is contested yet; the author is laying out the standard account, and the credit given to Valdez is exactly what the last paragraph will complicate.

The middle paragraph reconstructs how the form was actually built. Valdez, a former farm worker himself, gathered striking laborers and asked them to describe their conditions and then act out what happened on the picket lines, with the bolder ones relishing the chance to ridicule strikebreakers. Out of those rough improvisations he shaped what he called actos, short comic skits whose sources scholars trace to influences he absorbed as a student and as a member of a mime troupe. Two ingredients are already in play here: the workers' raw material and Valdez's shaping. By his own standard, an acto should expose a problem and suggest a solution, satirize the opposition, and move the audience to act, drawing its force from lived experience.

The closing paragraph adds a corrective and then the author's own balance. Yolanda Broyles-Gonzalez faults theater historians for treating actos as Valdez's individual invention, as though the workers' improvisational talent depended entirely on his vision, and she connects the form instead to carpas, informal and often satirical tent shows played to working-class audiences in the Mexico-United States border region earlier in the century. The author calls that criticism right and grants that many participants likely carried the carpa tradition into their improvising. Then comes the qualification: the Teatro's early development was genuinely collective, yet Valdez's artistic contribution was crucial, since the actos were neither carpas nor European-style theater but a distinct genre tied to both.
overall_html: The passage recounts the birth of Chicano theater in 1965, when Luis Valdez turned striking farm workers' improvisations into actos, and then weighs how much credit for that form belongs to Valdez alone. The author's purpose is partly narrative and partly evaluative: two paragraphs of history and description set up a final paragraph that endorses Broyles-Gonzalez's objection to the individual-genius account while insisting that Valdez's shaping still mattered. Keep three viewpoints apart, namely the scholars and theater historians who credit Valdez individually, Broyles-Gonzalez, who traces the actos to the carpa tradition, and the author, who calls the achievement collective yet defends Valdez's distinctive role.
