Some critics of advertising have assumed that the creation of false needs in consumers is the principal mechanism underlying what these critics regard as its manipulative and hegemonic power. Central to this type of critique are the writings of political theorist Herbert Marcuse, who maintained that modern people succumb to oppression by believing themselves satisfied in spite of their living in an objectively unsatisfying world. This process occurs because in mass market culture the powerful psychological techniques of advertising create "needs" that are false and whose satisfaction thus contributes, not to the genuine well-being of consumers, but rather to the profit—and thereby the disproportionate power—of corporations.

Marcuse supposed that we all have certain real needs, both physical and psychological. Advertising appropriates these needs for its own purposes, forging psychological associations between them and consumer items, e.g., between sex and perfume, thereby creating a false "need" for these items. Since the quest for fulfillment is thus displaced from its true objects to consumer items, the implicit promises of advertisements are never really fulfilled and the consumer remains at some level unsatisfied.

Unfortunately, the distinction between real and false needs upon which this critique depends is extremely problematic. If Marcusians are right, we cannot, with any assurance, separate our real needs from the alleged false needs we feel as a result of the manipulation of advertisers. For, in order to do so, it would be necessary to eliminate forces of persuasion that are so prevalent in society that they have come to inform our instinctive judgments about things.

But, in fact, Marcusians make a major mistake in assuming that the majority of consumers who respond to advertising do not do so autonomously. Advertising techniques are unable to induce unwilling behavior in rational, informed adults, and regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising claims. Moreover, evidence suggests that most adults understand and recognize the techniques used and are not merely passive instruments. If there is a real need for emotional fulfillment, and if we can freely and authentically choose our means of obtaining it, then free, informed individuals may choose to obtain it through the purchase of commodities or even through the enjoyment occasionally provided by advertisements themselves. It is no doubt true that in many—perhaps even most—cases the use of an advertised product does not yield the precise sort of emotional dividend that advertisements seem to promise. This does not mean, however, that consumers do not freely and intentionally use the product as a means to another sort of fulfillment, or even that its genuine fulfillment of needs must be less than the advertisement suggests.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by laying out the position it intends to dismantle. Some critics of advertising assume that advertising's manipulative and hegemonic power works chiefly by manufacturing false needs, and the theorist at the center of that view is Herbert Marcuse, who held that modern people succumb to oppression precisely by believing themselves satisfied while living in an objectively unsatisfying world. The proposed mechanism is worth stating plainly: in mass market culture, the psychological techniques of advertising create needs that are not real, and satisfying them serves corporate profit and the disproportionate power that comes with it rather than any genuine well-being.

Marcuse's account is spelled out in more detail here so that it can be tested later. He supposed that people have certain real needs, physical and psychological alike, which advertising then appropriates by forging associations between those needs and particular consumer items, the standard illustration being the link built between sex and perfume. Because the quest for fulfillment is displaced from its true objects onto purchasable goods, the promise implicit in an advertisement is never really kept, so the consumer remains unsatisfied at some level. Note that permanent dissatisfaction is a prediction of the theory, which matters once the author starts pushing back.

'Unfortunately' introduces the first objection, and it strikes at the foundation of the critique rather than its conclusions. The whole argument depends on separating real needs from false ones, and the author contends that this distinction is extremely problematic. If the Marcusians are right about how pervasive advertising's persuasion has become, then that persuasion has already shaped our instinctive judgments about things, and telling the authentic apart from the manufactured would require eliminating forces that saturate the society we do our judging in.

The second objection is stronger, and it targets the theory's picture of consumers. Marcusians make a major mistake, the author argues, in assuming that people who respond to advertising are not acting autonomously. Advertising cannot induce unwilling behavior in rational, informed adults, regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising, and evidence suggests most adults recognize the techniques used on them rather than absorbing them passively. From there the argument turns constructive. If the need for emotional fulfillment is real and people can freely choose how to pursue it, then buying an advertised product, or even enjoying the advertisement itself, can be a genuine choice. The author grants that products often fail to deliver the precise emotional dividend implied, but denies that this makes consumers dupes rather than people deliberately using a product toward some other satisfaction.
overall_html: The passage attacks the Marcusian claim that advertising dominates consumers by manufacturing false needs whose satisfaction feeds corporate profit rather than genuine well-being. The author's purpose is refutation, and the structure falls into two halves: the first two paragraphs present Marcuse's theory sympathetically and in enough detail to be tested, while the last two dismantle it, first by arguing that the distinction between real and false needs cannot be drawn in a society already saturated with persuasion, then by arguing that informed adults recognize advertising techniques and may freely choose commodities as a route to real emotional fulfillment. Keep the Marcusians and the author's own position firmly apart.

Passage A

There are two principles that are fundamental to a theory of justice regarding property. The principle of justice in acquisition specifies the conditions under which someone can legitimately come to own something that was previously not owned by anyone. The principle of justice in transfer specifies the conditions under which the transfer of property from one person to another is justified.

Given such principles, if the world were wholly just, the following definition would exhaustively cover the subject of justice regarding property:

1. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in acquisition is entitled to that property.

2. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in transfer, from someone else who is entitled to the property, is entitled to the property.

3. No one is entitled to any property except by (repeated) applications of 1 and 2.

However, not all actual situations are generated in accordance with the principles of justice in acquisition and justice in transfer. Some people steal from others or defraud them, for example. The existence of past injustice raises the issue of the rectification of injustice. If past injustice has shaped present ownership in various ways, what, if anything, ought to be done to rectify that injustice? A principle of rectification would use historical information about previous situations and injustices done in them, and information about the actual course of events that flowed from these injustices, to produce a description of the property ownership that should have resulted. Actual ownership of property must then be brought into conformity with this description.

Passage B

In 1790, the United States Congress passed the Indian Nonintercourse Act, which requires that all transfers of lands from Native Americans to others be approved by the federal government. The law has not been changed in any relevant respect, and it remains in effect today. Its purpose is clear. It was meant to guarantee security to Native Americans against fraudulent acquisition by others of the Native Americans' land holdings. Several suits have been initiated by Native American tribes for recovery of lands held by them when the Nonintercourse Act took effect.

One natural (one might almost say obvious) way of reasoning about Native American claims to land in North America is this: Native Americans were the first human occupants of this land. Before the European invasion of North America, the land belonged to them. In the course of that invasion and its aftermath, the land was illicitly taken from them. The current owners lack a well-founded right to the land, which now lies illicitly in their hands. Ideally, the land should be restored to its rightful owners. This may be impractical; compromises might have to be made. But the original wrong can most easily be righted by returning the land to them—or by returning it wherever that is feasible.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by naming the two building blocks of its theory of justice regarding property. The principle of justice in acquisition specifies how someone may legitimately come to own something that nobody owned before, and the principle of justice in transfer specifies when passing property from one person to another is justified. Everything that follows is assembled out of these two ideas, so fix them now: one governs original ownership, the other governs the movement of what is already owned.

A conditional frames the list that follows, and it is doing real work rather than serving as filler. Given those two principles, the claim is that if the world were wholly just, the definition about to be offered would exhaustively cover the subject of justice regarding property. Register that qualifier immediately, because the assumption of a wholly just world is exactly what the last paragraph of Passage A takes back.

The first clause of the definition simply converts the acquisition principle into an entitlement: a person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in acquisition is entitled to that property. Think of this as the ground floor of the system, since it covers the original taking of something previously unowned, and every later holding will have to trace back eventually to a step of this kind.

The second clause does the same work for transfers, with one condition attached that is easy to skim past. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in transfer is entitled to it, but only when the property came from someone who was already entitled to it. That requirement is what makes the whole chain of ownership matter, since a properly conducted transfer still fails to confer entitlement if the person handing the property over had no legitimate claim to it.

The third clause closes the system rather than adding anything new to it. No one is entitled to any property except through repeated applications of the first two clauses, which means every legitimate holding must be traceable back through a series of just transfers to a just original acquisition. Nothing outside that chain can generate an entitlement, and this exclusivity is what gives the theory its bite when real cases are examined.

Reality now intrudes on the ideal, and the earlier qualifier is cashed in. Actual situations are not all generated in accordance with the two principles, since some people steal from others or defraud them, which raises the further issue of rectifying injustice. If past injustice has shaped present ownership, the question is what ought to be done about it. The remedy proposed is historical in method, drawing on information about previous situations, the injustices done in them, and the actual course of events that followed, in order to describe the ownership that should have resulted, after which real ownership must be brought into conformity with that description.

Passage B moves from theory to a concrete legal case. In 1790 the United States Congress passed the Indian Nonintercourse Act, which requires that all transfers of land from Native Americans to others be approved by the federal government, and the law remains in effect today without relevant change. Its purpose was protective, meant to guarantee Native Americans security against fraudulent acquisition of their land holdings by others. The final sentence supplies the live consequence, since several tribes have initiated suits for recovery of lands they held when the Act took effect.

The closing paragraph sets out the line of reasoning it calls natural, almost obvious, and its shape should look familiar after Passage A. Native Americans were the first human occupants of the land, so before the European invasion it belonged to them; in the course of that invasion and its aftermath the land was illicitly taken; the current owners therefore lack a well-founded right to what now lies in their hands. The conclusion is that ideally the land should be restored to its rightful owners. Notice the concession attached, since the argument allows that this may be impractical and that compromises might be needed, while insisting the original wrong is most easily righted by returning land wherever doing so is feasible.
overall_html: Passage A sets out an entitlement theory of property built from principles of just acquisition and just transfer, observes that those alone would settle the subject only in a wholly just world, and therefore adds a principle of rectification that uses historical information to describe the ownership that should have resulted had past injustices not occurred. Passage B applies exactly that kind of reasoning to a real case, describing the Indian Nonintercourse Act and the tribal suits brought under it before sketching the natural argument that land illicitly taken from its first occupants should be given back. The relationship is theory and application, with B supplying a concrete historical injustice of the sort A's rectification principle is designed to address.

An organism is considered to have an infection when a disease-causing agent, called a pathogen, establishes a viable presence in the organism. This can occur only if the pathogenic agent is able to reproduce itself in the host organism. The only agents believed until recently to be responsible for infections—viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites—reproduce and regulate their other life processes by means of genetic material, composed of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA). It was thus widely assumed that all pathogens contain such genetic material in their cellular structure.

This assumption has been challenged, however, by scientists seeking to identify the pathogen that causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a degenerative form of dementia in humans. CJD causes the brain to become riddled with tiny holes, like a sponge (evidence of extensive nerve cell death). Its symptoms include impaired muscle control, loss of mental acuity, memory loss, and chronic insomnia. Extensive experiments aimed at identifying the pathogen responsible for CJD have led surprisingly to the isolation of a disease agent lacking nucleic acid and consisting mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. Researchers coined the term "prion" for this new type of protein pathogen.

Upon further study, scientists discovered that prions normally exist as harmless cellular proteins in many of the body's tissues, including white blood cells and nerve cells in the brain; however, they possess the capability of converting their structures into a dangerous abnormal shape. Prions exhibiting this abnormal conformation were found to have infectious properties and the ability to reproduce themselves in an unexpected way, by initiating a chain reaction that induces normally shaped prions to transform themselves on contact, one after another, into the abnormal, pathogenic conformation. This cascade of transformations produces a plaque, consisting of thread-like structures, that collects in the brain and ultimately destroys nerve cells. Because prions, unlike other pathogens, occur naturally in the body as proteins, the body does not produce an immune response when they are present. And in the absence of any effective therapy for preventing the cascade process by which affected prions reproduce themselves, CJD is inevitably fatal, though there are wide variations in pre-symptomatic incubation times and in how aggressively the disease progresses.

Although the discovery of the link between prions and CJD was initially received with great skepticism in the scientific community, subsequent research has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogens. Furthermore, it is now believed that a similar process of protein malformation may be involved in other, more common degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. This possibility has yet to be fully explored, however, and the exact mechanisms by which prions reproduce themselves and cause cellular destruction have yet to be completely understood.
explanation_html:
Definitions come first, and they set up the assumption the rest of the passage overturns. An organism counts as infected when a pathogen, meaning a disease-causing agent, establishes a viable presence in it, which can happen only if the agent is able to reproduce inside the host. Until recently the only agents believed capable of this were viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, all of which reproduce and regulate their life processes using genetic material made of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. From that shared feature came a widely held inference: every pathogen must contain such genetic material in its cellular structure.

The challenge arrives through research on one specific disease. Scientists hunting the pathogen behind Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a degenerative dementia that leaves the brain riddled with tiny holes where nerve cells have died and that brings impaired muscle control, loss of mental acuity, memory loss and chronic insomnia, found something the standing assumption did not allow for. Extensive experiments isolated a disease agent that lacks nucleic acid entirely and consists mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. Researchers coined the term prion for this new kind of protein pathogen, and the coinage itself signals that an existing category could not accommodate the find.

How something without genetic material reproduces is the puzzle solved here. Prions normally exist as harmless cellular proteins in many tissues, including white blood cells and nerve cells in the brain, but they can convert their structure into a dangerous abnormal shape, and prions in that conformation prove to be infectious. Reproduction works by contact rather than by copying instructions: an abnormal prion induces a normally shaped one it touches to transform, which then does the same to the next, in a chain reaction. The cascade produces a plaque of thread-like structures that collects in the brain and destroys nerve cells. Two consequences follow, both grim, since the body mounts no immune response against proteins that occur in it naturally, and with no therapy able to interrupt the cascade the disease is inevitably fatal.

The closing paragraph reports how the finding was received and how far its implications now stretch. Great skepticism greeted the link between prions and the disease at first, but subsequent research has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogen. Beyond that, a similar process of protein malformation is now thought to be involved in more common degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Watch the hedging in the final sentence, because the author is careful to note that this possibility is not yet fully explored and the exact mechanisms of prion reproduction and cell destruction remain incompletely understood.
overall_html: The passage traces how the search for the cause of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease overturned the long-standing assumption that every pathogen must contain nucleic acid, since the agent isolated proved to be a protein, the prion, that reproduces by inducing normally shaped proteins to refold into an abnormal, plaque-forming conformation. The author's purpose is expository, moving from the standard definition of infection, to the anomalous discovery, to the mechanism that explains how a pathogen without genetic material propagates and why the resulting disease resists immune response and treatment, and finally to broader implications for conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The voice is neutral scientific reporting, with no competing viewpoints beyond the early skepticism later research overcame.

One of the more striking developments in modern North American dance was African American choreographer Katherine Dunham's introduction of a technique known as dance-isolation, in which one part of the body moves in one rhythm while other parts are kept stationary or are moved in different rhythms. The incorporation of this technique into North American and European choreography is relatively recent, although various forms of the technique have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures. Dunham's success in bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques from those cultures into the mainstream of modern North American dance is due in no small part to her training in both anthropological research and choreography.

As an anthropologist in the 1930s, Dunham was one of the pioneers in the field of dance ethnology. Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry. Moreover, no other social scientist at that time was sufficiently trained in dance to be able to understand dance techniques, while experts in dance were not trained in the methods of social research.

Starting in 1935, Dunham conducted a series of research projects into traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture. Especially critical to her success was her approach to research, which diverged radically from the methodology that prevailed at the time. Colleagues in anthropology advised her not to become too closely involved in the dances she was observing, both because of the extreme physical demands of the dances, and because they subscribed to the long-standing view, now fortunately recognized as unrealistic, that effective data gathering can and must be conducted from a position of complete detachment. But because of her interest and her skill as a performer, she generally eschewed such caution and participated in the dances herself. Through prolonged immersion of this kind, Dunham was able not only to comprehend various dances as complex cultural practices, but also to learn the techniques well enough to teach them to others and incorporate them into new forms of ballet.

Between 1937 and 1945, Dunham developed a research-to-performance method that she used to adapt Caribbean dance forms for use in theatrical performance, combining them with modern dance styles she learned in Chicago. The ballets she created in this fashion were among the first North American dances to rectify the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance. Her work was thus crucial in establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right, making possible future companies such as Arthur Mitchell's Dance Theater of Harlem.
explanation_html:
The opening defines the technique and then explains why one particular person was able to import it. Dance-isolation means moving one part of the body in one rhythm while other parts stay stationary or move in rhythms of their own, and although its incorporation into North American and European choreography is relatively recent, forms of it have long been essential to traditional dances in certain African, Caribbean and Pacific-island cultures. Katherine Dunham is credited with carrying it into the mainstream, and the explanation offered is the one the whole passage develops: she was trained both in anthropological research and in choreography.

Background follows on why the field she entered was so empty. Working as an anthropologist in the 1930s, Dunham was a pioneer of dance ethnology, an area that barely existed because dance had been neglected as a subject of social research. Two causes are given for that neglect. Most social scientists gravitated toward topics their peers would recognize as scientifically rigorous and therefore legitimate, which left dance looking unserious, and there was a plain skills gap as well, since no social scientist of the period was trained enough in dance to understand its techniques, while experts in dance knew nothing of research methods.

Her method is the heart of the passage, and it is presented as a deliberate break with orthodoxy. From 1935 Dunham conducted research into traditional Caribbean dance forms and their origins in African culture, and what proved critical was her refusal of the prevailing methodology. Colleagues in anthropology advised her against becoming too closely involved, partly because the dances were physically demanding and partly because they held the long-standing view, which the author calls unrealistic, that effective data gathering must be conducted from complete detachment. Her own interest and her skill as a performer led her to dance the dances herself instead. That prolonged immersion paid off twice over, letting her grasp the dances as complex cultural practices and letting her learn them well enough to teach them and build them into new ballets.

The closing paragraph converts research into legacy. Between 1937 and 1945 Dunham developed a research-to-performance method for adapting Caribbean dance forms to theatrical use, combining them with the modern dance styles she had learned in Chicago. The ballets she made this way were among the first North American dances to correct the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance. The author's final claim concerns lasting consequence rather than personal achievement, since this work was crucial in establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right and made later companies such as Arthur Mitchell's Dance Theater of Harlem possible.
overall_html: The passage credits Katherine Dunham with bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques into mainstream North American dance, arguing that her dual training as anthropologist and choreographer, and above all her willingness to participate in the dances she studied, made that transfer possible. The author's purpose is appreciative and explanatory, moving from the technique and its cultural sources, to the neglected state of dance ethnology when she began, to the immersive method that broke with her colleagues' insistence on detachment, and finally to the ballets and the legacy they left. The one real clash of viewpoints is between Dunham's approach and the anthropological orthodoxy urging distance, a norm the author treats as discredited.

Passage A

Research concerning happiness and wealth reveals a paradox: at any one time richer people report higher levels of happiness than poorer people in the same society report, and yet over time advanced societies have not grown happier as they have grown richer. Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income. Two phenomena—habituation and rivalry—push up the norm.

When our living standards increase, we love it initially but then we adjust and it makes little difference. For example, if we ask people with different incomes what income they consider sufficient, the "required income" correlates strongly with their actual income: a rise in actual income causes a roughly equivalent rise in required income. We can also look at reported happiness over time. Job satisfaction depends little on the absolute level of wages but rises if wages rapidly increase.

We do not have the same experience with other aspects of our lives. We do not foresee how we adjust to material possessions, so we overinvest in acquiring them, at the expense of leisure.

Now consider the phenomenon of rivalry. In a study conducted by Solnick and Hemenway, people were asked to choose between two options, with all prices held constant:

A. You earn $50,000 a year while everyone else earns $25,000;

B. You earn $100,000 a year while others make $200,000.

The majority chose the first. They were happy to be poorer, provided their relative position improved.

And indeed, how people compare to their "reference group"—those most like them—is crucial for happiness. In East Germany, for example, living standards have soared since 1990, but the level of happiness has plummeted because people now compare themselves with West Germans, rather than with people in other Soviet bloc countries.

Passage B

Does the Solnick and Hemenway study mean that we care most about one-upmanship? Perhaps out of our primeval past comes the urge to demonstrate our superiority in order to help ensure mating prospects, keeping our genetic lines going. Still programmed like this, we get unexplainable pleasure from having a bigger house than our neighbors.

This theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not the explanation best supported by the evidence. Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.

If two people feel equally successful, they will be equally happy even if their incomes differ greatly. Of course, people who earn more generally view themselves as successful. But it is the success—not the money per se—that provides the happiness. We use material wealth to show not just that we are prosperous, but that we are prosperous because we create value.

What scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society. It is a bonus that it also brings happiness.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a paradox worth committing to memory: within one society at one moment, richer people report more happiness than poorer people, yet as whole advanced societies grow richer over decades, average happiness does not climb. The resolution offered is that people judge their income against a norm rather than against an absolute figure, and that norm rises along with actual income. Two forces are named as the drivers of the rising norm, habituation and rivalry, and the rest of the passage takes them up in exactly that order.

Habituation gets the first treatment. The claim is that a higher living standard thrills you briefly and then becomes the new baseline, so it stops registering. Two pieces of support follow. Ask people what income they would consider sufficient and the answer tracks whatever they currently earn, rising almost one-for-one when actual income rises. Job satisfaction shows the same signature: the absolute level of wages barely matters, but a rapid increase does lift satisfaction, which is what you would expect if only change, rather than level, is actually felt.

A brief but consequential extension follows. Adjustment of this kind does not govern every part of life, and, more importantly, we fail to anticipate it. Because people do not foresee how quickly a new possession stops feeling new, they overinvest in acquiring things and underinvest in leisure. Notice that this is the point where the author stops merely describing a mechanism and starts drawing a critical conclusion about how people misallocate their own lives, which is the first evaluative move in the passage.

With habituation covered, the author pivots to the second force, rivalry, and hands the argument over to evidence rather than assertion. The framing of the Solnick and Hemenway study is what matters here, so read it carefully: respondents choose between two income scenarios with all prices held constant. That last condition is the whole design, since fixing prices strips purchasing power out of the comparison and leaves relative standing as the only thing that varies between the two options.

The first option describes a low-absolute, high-relative world: you take home fifty thousand a year while everyone around you takes home half that. Hold on to the structure rather than the figures. Your own purchasing power here is modest, but you sit comfortably at the top of your comparison group. Because prices are held constant across both options, choosing this scenario can express only one thing, a preference about where you stand relative to other people rather than about what your money can buy.

The second option reverses both variables: your income doubles to a hundred thousand, but everyone else is earning twice what you do. In straightforward material terms you are far better off here than in the first scenario, so anyone who cared only about absolute living standards would take this one without hesitating. The pair is constructed so that absolute wealth and relative rank point in opposite directions, which forces respondents to reveal which of the two they actually weigh more heavily when made to choose.

The result arrives in a single sentence, and it is the payoff the setup was built for. Most respondents took the first option, accepting genuinely lower purchasing power in exchange for outranking the people around them. The author's gloss is precise and worth borrowing: they were happy to be poorer as long as their relative position improved. That is rivalry demonstrated rather than merely asserted, and it delivers the second half of the explanation promised at the end of the opening paragraph.

Rivalry is then sharpened into something more specific than generalized competition. What matters is not humanity at large but one's reference group, the people most like oneself, and that group can shift. East Germany supplies the case: living standards soared after 1990 while reported happiness dropped, because the comparison moved from other Soviet bloc populations to West Germans. The example closes the passage by showing that a rising norm can outrun a rising income and leave people materially better off but subjectively worse off.

Passage B opens by taking the same Solnick and Hemenway result and asking what it actually demonstrates. The author of B first lays out the popular reading, an evolutionary drive toward one-upmanship: ancestors who displayed superiority secured better mating prospects and kept their genetic lines going, and we are still running that program, which is why a house bigger than the neighbor's produces pleasure we cannot quite explain. Read this paragraph as a position being set up for evaluation, not as one the author endorses.

The turn comes immediately. The theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not what the evidence best supports. In its place the author offers a different reading of the same data: earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel successful, that they have created value. Notice exactly what kind of move this is. It does not deny that comparison drives the result; it reinterprets what the comparison is measuring, substituting a judgment about achievement for a competitive instinct.

The success interpretation is then tested against the cases that would separate it from a simple money explanation. Two people who feel equally successful end up equally happy even when their incomes differ greatly, which is the crucial dissociation, and income tracks happiness only because high earners generally do regard themselves as successful. On this account wealth functions as evidence rather than as cause, and what people display with material goods is not merely that they are prosperous but that their prosperity came from creating value.

The closing paragraph flips the moral verdict. Scholars routinely treat wanting more than others as an ignoble tendency, but on this reading it is the visible surface of a desire to create value, and creating value benefits society at large. Happiness, the author adds almost dismissively, is a bonus rather than the point. Set this against Passage A, which treats comparison as a trap that prevents rising societies from becoming happier; the same comparative instinct is recast here as socially productive rather than self-defeating.
overall_html: Both passages ask why relative rather than absolute income drives happiness, and they read the same evidence to opposite ends. Passage A explains the paradox that richer individuals are happier while richer societies are not, arguing that habituation and rivalry with a shifting reference group push up the norm against which income is judged, so real gains cancel out; its purpose is diagnostic, identifying a trap. Passage B accepts the Solnick and Hemenway finding but rejects the evolutionary one-upmanship interpretation of it, arguing that relative prosperity pleases people because it signals successful value creation, a tendency it defends as socially beneficial. The two agree on the data and disagree about what it means.

It is generally believed that while in some cases government should intervene to protect people from risk—by imposing air safety standards, for example—in other cases, such as mountain climbing, the onus should be on the individual to protect himself or herself. In the eyes of the public at large, the demarcation between the two kinds of cases has mainly to do with whether the risk in question is incurred voluntarily. This distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk may in fact be the chief difference between lay and expert judgments about risk. Policy experts tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake; laypeople care a great deal whether a risk is undertaken voluntarily. However, judgments about whether a risk is "involuntary" often stem from confusion and selective attention, and the real reason for such judgments frequently lies in an antecedent judgment of some other kind. They are thus of little utility in guiding policy decisions.

First, it is not easy to determine when a risk is voluntarily incurred. Although voluntariness may be entirely absent in the case of an unforeseeable collision with an asteroid, with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, it is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree. Risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash. But they can choose airlines on the basis of safety records or choose not to fly. In characterizing the risks as involuntary, people focus on a small part of a complex interaction, not the decision to fly, but the accident when it occurs.

Second, people often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. It is unlikely that people would want to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, even if the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved were quite good. By contrast, people would probably not object to spending enormous resources on improving the safety of firefighters, even though the decision to become a firefighter is voluntary. In short, there is no special magic in notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary." Therefore, regulatory policy should be guided by a better understanding of the factors that underlie judgments about voluntariness.

In general, the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction. Departures from this principle should be justified not by invoking the allegedly voluntary or involuntary nature of a particular risk, but rather by identifying the more specific considerations for which notions of voluntariness serve as proxies.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by laying out a distinction it intends to dismantle. Government sometimes intervenes to protect people from risk, as with air safety standards, and sometimes leaves protection to the individual, as with mountain climbing, and the public sorts cases by asking whether the risk was incurred voluntarily. The Author identifies this as the main split between policy experts, who focus on aggregate lives at stake, and laypeople, who care enormously about voluntariness. The thesis lands at the end of the paragraph and is blunt: such judgments stem from confusion and selective attention, usually stand in for some other judgment, and are therefore of little use in guiding policy.

The first of two supporting arguments attacks the coherence of the category itself. Voluntariness is rarely all or nothing; for most environmental, occupational and social risks it comes in degrees, with an unforeseeable asteroid collision as the rare pure case. Air travel makes the point concrete. Passengers are said to face involuntary risk because they cannot control whether the plane crashes, yet they can choose airlines by safety record or decline to fly at all. The author's diagnosis is that people fix on one narrow slice of a complex interaction, the accident itself, while ignoring the decision that led to it.

The second argument is sharper, because it exposes what the label is actually doing. People call a risk voluntary when they disapprove of the purpose for which it is run. Taxpayers would not pour resources into making skydiving safer even at a favorable ratio of dollars to lives saved, yet they would not object to large sums spent protecting firefighters, though becoming a firefighter is just as much a choice. The pair is matched so that approval of the activity is the only difference left. Hence the flat verdict that there is no special magic in these notions, and the call to understand what really underlies them.

Having cleared the ground, the author states the positive rule. Government should save as many lives as it can within the limited resources devoted to risk reduction, and departures from that principle need genuine justification rather than an appeal to how voluntary a risk was. Read the final phrase carefully, because it softens the attack in a useful way: voluntariness serves as a proxy for more specific considerations. The concept is not empty, then, but a crude substitute that should be replaced by the particular factors hiding behind it.
overall_html: The passage argues that the public's distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk, though it is the chief difference between lay judgments and those of policy experts who count aggregate lives, is too confused to guide regulation. The author's purpose is first critical and then prescriptive: one argument shows that voluntariness is a matter of degree that people assess by attending to a single slice of a longer interaction, a second shows that the label really tracks approval of the activity's purpose, and the closing paragraph substitutes a straightforward lives-saved standard while conceding that voluntariness functions as a proxy for more specific considerations worth identifying directly.

Given the amount of time and effort that curators, collectors, dealers, scholars, and critics spend on formulating judgments of taste in relation to oil paintings, it seems odd that so few are prepared to apply some of the same skills in exploring works of art that stimulate another sense altogether: that of smell. Why is great perfume not taken more seriously? While art professionals are very serious about many branches of literature, architecture, and music, I have yet to find a curatorial colleague who regularly beats a path to the fragrance counter in search of, say, Joy Parfum, the 1930 masterpiece by Henri Alméras.

And yet, the parallels between what ought to be regarded as sister arts are undeniable. Painters combine natural and, these days, synthetic pigments with media such as oils and resins, much as the perfumer carefully formulates natural and synthetic chemical compounds. The Old Masters deployed oil paint across the color spectrum, and applied layers on a determining ground and various kinds of underpainting, slowly building up to the surface, completing their work with thin glazes on top. Thus various types of mashed-up earth and vegetable suspended in linseed or poppy oil are brushed over a stretch of woven fabric. They begin to dry, and a picture is born. Its appearance changes over time, because the tendency of oil paint is to become gradually more transparent.

So, too, talented "noses" experiment with complex configurations of olfactory elements and produce in symphonic combination many small sensations, at times discordant, sweet, bitter, melancholy, or happy, as the case may be. These combinations change and develop in sequence or in unison as the substance and its constituents evaporate at different rates, some quickly, others slowly, thanks to the warmth of our skin. A brilliant perfumer may thus devise an imaginary world no less powerful, or intimate, than that of a great composer or painter, and in calling on our capacity to discover there some memory of childhood or of a long-forgotten experience, perfumers are in the same business as the artist who creates the illusion of life on canvas.

Perhaps one reason that truly great smells are so often undervalued is that perfumes are today made and distributed under the not particularly watchful gaze of a few large corporations. The cynical bean counters in Paris and Zurich do not hesitate to tamper with old formulas, insisting on the substitution of cheap chemical compounds that approximately resemble rarer, better ingredients in an effort to increase profits. They do not tell their customers when or how they do this; indeed, they presume their customers won't notice the difference. Consequently, fine perfume is now hopelessly entangled with the international cosmetic dollar, and ill-served by marketing and public relations.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a complaint dressed up as a puzzle. Enormous effort goes into formulating judgments of taste about oil painting, yet almost no one applies those same skills to an art addressed to smell. The Author is writing from inside the art world about his own colleagues, and the tone is pointed rather than neutral: professionals take branches of literature, architecture and music seriously, but no curatorial colleague regularly visits the fragrance counter. Calling a 1930 perfume a masterpiece and naming its creator is doing argumentative work, since masterpiece and named author are precisely the vocabulary reserved for recognized art.

Having posed the question, the author starts building the case that these are sister arts, and the method is a sustained technical parallel. Painters combine natural and now synthetic pigments with media such as oils and resins, much as a perfumer formulates natural and synthetic chemical compounds. The account of Old Master practice is deliberately concrete and unglamorous, layers built over a determining ground and various underpainting, finished with thin glazes, so that a painting turns out to be mashed earth and vegetable matter suspended in oil and brushed across woven fabric. The closing detail carries the most weight: because oil paint grows gradually more transparent, the work keeps changing after it is finished.

The comparison now runs in the other direction, and the shared feature turns out to be change over time. Talented noses experiment with complex configurations that yield many small sensations in symphonic combination, at times discordant, sweet, bitter or melancholy, and those combinations develop in sequence or together as different constituents evaporate at different rates on warm skin. That is the olfactory counterpart of a painting's shifting surface. The paragraph then makes the boldest claim in the passage: a perfumer can devise an imaginary world no less powerful than a composer's or a painter's, and in summoning a long-forgotten memory does the same work as an artist creating the illusion of life on canvas.

The closing paragraph offers an explanation for the neglect described at the start, and it shifts the blame away from the audience. A new profile appears, the corporations that now make and distribute perfume, whose accountants tamper with old formulas without hesitation, substituting cheap chemical compounds that only approximate rarer and better ingredients, and who assume customers will never notice the difference. The causal claim matters more than the contempt: because fine perfume is now hopelessly entangled with the international cosmetics trade and handled by marketing and public relations, it has become difficult to see as art at all.
overall_html: The passage argues that great perfume deserves the same serious critical attention given to painting, music and literature, and that its neglect reflects a failure of the art world rather than any limitation of the medium. The author's purpose is persuasive: after opening on the oddity that curators who scrutinize oil paintings ignore fragrance entirely, the two middle paragraphs construct a detailed parallel between the painter's layered materials and the perfumer's evaporating compounds, both of which change over time and both of which conjure an imaginary world out of memory, before the final paragraph attributes the undervaluation to corporations that quietly debase formulas and to the marketing that now surrounds them.

"Stealing thunder" is a courtroom strategy that consists in a lawyer's revealing negative information about a client before that information is revealed or elicited by an opposing lawyer. While there is no point in revealing a weakness that is unknown to one's opponents or that would not be exploited by them, many lawyers believe that if the weakness is likely to be revealed in opposing testimony, it should be volunteered; otherwise, the hostile revelation would be more damaging.

Although no empirical research has directly tested the effectiveness of stealing thunder in actual trials, studies involving simulated trial situations have suggested that the technique is, in fact, effective, at least within a reasonably broad range of applications. Lawyers' commonly held belief in the value of stealing thunder is not only corroborated by those experimental findings; it is also supported by several psychological explanations of why the technique should work. For one thing, volunteering damaging information early may create an image of credibility. Psychological research suggests that people who reveal information that appears to be against their own best interest are likely to be perceived as more credible and thus may be more persuasive. Stealing thunder may also provide juries with an impetus for critical assessment by previewing, and thus alerting them to, testimony that the opposition plans to present. In psychological experiments, audiences that were previously warned of an upcoming attempt at persuasion became more resistant to the persuasive attempt, forming counterarguments based on the warning. Also, the value placed on a persuasive message is probably much like the value placed on any commodity; the scarcer the commodity, the more valuable it is. A persuasive message will thus increase in value and effectiveness to the extent that it is seen as scarce. In the courtroom, a piece of evidence brought by both the prosecution and the defense, as when thunder is stolen, may be seen as less scarce—becoming "old news." Thus, unless that evidence is of overriding consequence, it should carry less weight than if it had been included only in hostile testimony.

Finally, stealing thunder may work because the lawyer can frame the evidence in his or her own terms and downplay its significance, just as politicians sometimes seek to put their "spin" on potentially damaging information. However, it may therefore be effective only when the negative information can be framed positively. Jurors, who often initially have little information about a case, are usually eager to solidify their position regarding the case. They can therefore be expected to use the early positive framing to guide their subsequent analysis of the trial information. But this also suggests limitations on the use of the technique: when information is very damaging, stealing thunder may create an early negative impression that forms a cognitive framework for jurors, who then filter subsequent information through this schema.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by defining its subject precisely, and the definition carries a built-in condition. Stealing thunder is a lawyer's disclosure of damaging information about a client before the opposing lawyer can reveal or elicit it. Notice the qualification attached immediately: there is no point volunteering a weakness the other side does not know about or would not exploit. The strategy applies only where the damaging fact is likely to surface in opposing testimony anyway, and the belief held by many lawyers is that in exactly that situation a hostile revelation would do more damage than a voluntary one.

The second paragraph establishes that the tactic works and then explains why, and its structure is a list of separate causes worth keeping apart. No empirical research has tested actual trials, but simulated trial studies suggest the technique is effective within a reasonably broad range of applications, and psychological theory supports what lawyers already believe. Three mechanisms follow. Volunteering harmful information builds credibility, since people who say things apparently against their own interest are perceived as more believable and so persuade more effectively. Previewing the opposition's evidence also functions as a warning, and warned audiences in experiments resist persuasion better because they begin forming counterarguments in advance. The third mechanism treats a persuasive message as a commodity subject to scarcity: evidence brought by both sides becomes old news rather than a scarce revelation, so unless it is of overriding consequence it should carry less weight than it would have in hostile testimony alone.

A fourth mechanism arrives, and with it the passage's turn toward limits. Going first lets the lawyer frame the evidence in his or her own terms and downplay its significance, much as politicians put a spin on damaging news. That advantage is conditional in a way the earlier three were not, since it works only when the negative information can be framed positively at all. The reasoning about jurors then cuts both ways. Because they usually start with little information and are eager to solidify a position, they take the early positive framing as a guide to everything that follows. That same eagerness is the danger: when the information is very damaging, the early disclosure hardens into a negative cognitive framework through which jurors filter the rest of the trial.
overall_html: The passage explains and largely supports stealing thunder, the courtroom practice of disclosing a client's damaging information before an opponent can, holding that simulated-trial research and four psychological mechanisms corroborate the belief lawyers already hold, while a final limitation constrains its use. The author's purpose is explanatory rather than adversarial, moving from a careful definition with its own built-in condition, through the credibility, forewarning and scarcity effects, to the framing advantage, whose dependence on jurors' eagerness to settle on a position also explains why very damaging information can backfire by fixing an early negative schema. The only viewpoints in play are the author's analysis and the common lawyerly belief it vindicates.

Passage A

 To a neuroscientist, you are your brain; nothing causes your behavior other than the operations of your brain. This viewpoint, together with recent findings in neuroscience, radically changes the way we think about the law. The official line in the law is that all that matters is whether you are rational, but you can have someone who is totally rational even though their strings are being pulled by something beyond their control. Indeed, people who believe themselves to be making a free and rational moral choice may really be deluding themselves—a brain scan might show that such a choice correlates with activity in emotional centers in the brain rather than in the region of the brain associated with deliberative problem solving. This insight suggests that the criminal-justice system should abandon the idea of retribution—the idea that bad people should be punished because of their freely chosen immoral acts—which is now dominant as a justification of punishment. Instead, the law should focus on deterring future harms. In some cases, this might mean lighter punishments. If it is really true that we do not get any prevention bang from our punishment buck when we punish some person, then it is not worth punishing that person.

Passage B

 Neuroscience constantly produces new mechanistic descriptions of how the physical brain causes behavior, adding fuel to the deterministic view that all human action is causally necessitated by events that are independent of the will. It has long been argued, however, that the concept of free will can coexist with determinism.

In 1954 English philosopher Alfred J. Ayer put forth a theory of "soft determinism." He argued, as the philosopher David Hume had two centuries earlier, that even in a deterministic world, a person can still act freely. Ayer distinguished between free actions and constrained actions. Free actions are those that are caused by internal sources, by one's own will (unless one is suffering from a disorder). Constrained actions are those that are caused by external sources, for example, by someone or something forcing you physically or mentally to perform an action, as in hypnosis or in mental disorders such as kleptomania. When someone performs a free action to do A, he or she could have done B instead, since no external source precluded doing so. When someone performs a constrained action to do A, he or she could have done only A.

Ayer argued that actions are free as long as they are not constrained. It is not the existence of a cause but the source of the cause that determines whether an action is free. Although Ayer did not explicitly discuss the brain's role, one could make the analogy that those actions—and indeed those wills—that originate from a disease-free brain are not constrained, and are therefore free, even though they may be determined.
explanation_html:
Passage A is one dense paragraph, so take it in steps. The Neuroscientist begins from an identity claim: you are your brain, and nothing causes your behavior except its operations. The law's official test is whether you are rational, but a person can be entirely rational while their strings are pulled by something beyond their control, and someone who believes they are making a free moral choice may be deluding themselves, since a scan might show that choice correlating with emotional centers rather than with the region tied to deliberative problem solving. The practical payoff is the part to hold on to: abandon retribution, currently dominant as a justification of punishment, in favor of deterring future harms, which sometimes means lighter penalties, because punishment that buys no prevention is not worth imposing.

Passage B opens on the same scientific trend but immediately marks out a different response to it. Mechanistic descriptions of how the physical brain causes behavior keep accumulating, feeding determinism, the view that all human action is causally necessitated by events independent of the will. Rather than treat that as the end of responsibility, this author observes that it has long been argued that free will and determinism can coexist. Notice how the projects diverge: Passage A runs straight from neuroscience to a proposal about punishment, while Passage B stops at the prior conceptual question of whether freedom survives determinism at all.

Soft determinism supplies the machinery, and the distinction it rests on is what to master. Ayer, arguing in 1954 as Hume had two centuries earlier, held that a person can still act freely in a deterministic world, because what matters is the kind of cause at work. Free actions are caused by internal sources, by one's own will, barring a disorder; constrained actions are caused by external sources, such as someone forcing you physically or mentally, hypnosis, or a condition like kleptomania. The test is counterfactual. Someone performing a free action to do A could have done B instead, since nothing external precluded it, while someone performing a constrained action could have done only A.

The closing paragraph states the conclusion and then stretches it toward the brain. Actions are free so long as they are not constrained, so it is not the existence of a cause but the source of the cause that settles the matter. The passage is careful to flag that Ayer said nothing explicit about the brain and that what follows is an analogy rather than his claim. On that analogy, actions and wills originating in a disease-free brain are unconstrained and therefore free, even though they are determined. That leaves responsibility intact at precisely the point where Passage A proposed to give it up.
overall_html: Both passages begin from the neuroscientific claim that the brain causes behavior, and they take it in opposite directions. Passage A treats that claim as grounds for legal reform, arguing that because apparently free moral choices may originate in emotional brain activity outside a person's control, the criminal-justice system should abandon retribution and punish only where punishment deters future harm. Passage B, drawing on Ayer's soft determinism and its distinction between internally caused free actions and externally constrained ones, argues that freedom is compatible with determinism, then extends the point by analogy to actions arising from a disease-free brain. B thus supplies a philosophical answer that undermines the premise on which A builds its reform.

This passage is adapted from a review of a 1991 book.

In a recent study, Mario García argues that in the United States between 1930 and 1960 the group of political activists he calls the "Mexican American Generation" was more radical and politically diverse than earlier historians have recognized. Through analysis of the work of some of the era's most important scholars, García does provide persuasive evidence that in the 1930s and 1940s these activists anticipated many of the reforms proposed by the more militant Chicanos of the 1960s and 1970s. His study, however, suffers from two flaws.

First, García's analysis of the evidence he provides to demonstrate the Mexican American Generation's political diversity is not entirely consistent. Indeed, he undermines his primary thesis by emphasizing an underlying consensus among various groups that tends to conceal the full significance of their differences. Groups such as the League of United Latin American Citizens, an organization that encouraged Mexican Americans to pursue a civil rights strategy of assimilation into the United States political and cultural mainstream, were often diametrically opposed to organizations such as the Congress of Spanish-Speaking People, a coalition group that advocated bilingual education and equal rights for resident aliens in the United States. García acknowledges these differences but dismisses them as insignificant, given that the goals of groups as disparate as these centered on liberal reform, not revolution. But one need only note the fierce controversies that occurred during the period over United States immigration policies and the question of assimilation versus cultural maintenance to recognize that Mexican American political history since 1930 has been characterized not by consensus but by intense and lively debate.

Second, García may be exaggerating the degree to which the views of these activists were representative of the ethnic Mexican population residing in the United States during this period. Noting that by 1930 the proportion of the Mexican American population that had been born in the United States had significantly increased, García argues that between 1930 and 1960 a new generation of Mexican American leaders appeared, one that was more acculturated and hence more politically active than its predecessor. Influenced by their experience of discrimination and by the inclusive rhetoric of World War II slogans, these leaders, according to García, were determined to achieve full civil rights for all United States residents of Mexican descent. However, it is not clear how far this outlook extended beyond these activists. Without a better understanding of the political implications of important variables such as patterns of bilingualism and rates of Mexican immigration and naturalization, and the variations in ethnic consciousness these variables help to create, one cannot assume that an increase in the proportion of Mexican Americans born in the United States necessarily resulted in an increase in the ethnic Mexican population's political activism.
explanation_html:
This is a book-review structure, so sort out the positions immediately. García claims that the political activists he labels the Mexican American Generation, active between 1930 and 1960, were more radical and more internally varied than earlier historians had allowed. The Author grants him real ground here, calling the evidence persuasive that these activists foreshadowed reforms later pushed by militant Chicanos in the 1960s and 1970s. Then comes the pivot the whole passage runs on: the study suffers from two flaws. Expect the remaining paragraphs to deliver those two objections in order, and note that the author's stance is critical but not dismissive.

The first objection is that García argues against himself. He wants to show diversity, yet he keeps stressing an underlying consensus, which the author says hides how much the groups actually differed. The example makes the gap concrete. The League of United Latin American Citizens urged assimilation into mainstream United States political and cultural life as a civil rights strategy, while the Congress of Spanish-Speaking People pushed bilingual education and equal rights for resident aliens, positions the author calls diametrically opposed. García notices the difference but waves it off because both sought liberal reform rather than revolution. The author's counter is the record itself: fierce disputes over immigration policy and over assimilation versus cultural maintenance show lively debate, not agreement.

The second objection targets scope rather than internal consistency. García reasons that because more Mexican Americans were United States-born by 1930, a more acculturated and therefore more politically active generation of leaders emerged, driven by experiences of discrimination and by the inclusive language of World War II slogans toward full civil rights for all United States residents of Mexican descent. The author does not dispute that the leaders held these views; the doubt is whether the wider ethnic Mexican population shared them. Without knowing how bilingualism, immigration rates and naturalization shaped ethnic consciousness, you cannot treat a rise in native-born share as automatically producing a rise in political activism.
overall_html: The passage is a measured critique of García's study of Mexican American political activists between 1930 and 1960, conceding that he persuasively shows these activists anticipated later Chicano reforms while arguing that his work has two defects: his emphasis on underlying consensus undercuts his own thesis of political diversity, and he overstates how far the activists' outlook represented the broader ethnic Mexican population. The author's purpose is evaluative, opening with credit and a preview of two flaws and then devoting one paragraph to each in turn. Keep three positions apart: García's claims, the earlier historians he is revising, and the author's own qualified objections.

Having spent several decades trying to eliminate the unself-conscious "colonial gaze" characteristic of so many early ethnographic films, visual anthropologists from the industrialized West who study indigenous cultures are presently struggling with an even more profound transformation of their discipline. Because inexpensive video equipment is now available throughout the world, many indigenous peoples who were once examined by the Western ethnographer's camera have begun to document their own cultures. Reaction to this phenomenon within Western anthropological circles is sharply divided.

One faction, led by anthropologist James Weiner, sees the proliferation of video and television as the final assault of Western values on indigenous cultures. Weiner argues that the spread of video represents "a devaluation of the different," culminating in the replacement of genuine historical, linguistic, social, and cultural difference with superficial difference among electronic images. He believes that video technologies inevitably purvey a Western ontology, one based on realism, immediacy, and self-expression. Thus, Weiner concludes, using video technology costs indigenous peoples the very cultural identity they seek to record. Moreover, he maintains that anthropologists who attribute a paramount truth value to these films simply because they are made by indigenous peoples are theoretically naive.

But Weiner's opponents contend that his views betray a certain nostalgia for the idea of the "noble savage." One such opponent, anthropologist Faye Ginsburg, concedes that no Western object that has entered cultural circulation since the fifteenth century has been neutral, but she considers it little more than boilerplate technological determinism to argue that using a video camera makes one unwittingly Western. Unlike Weiner, Ginsburg maintains that non-Western indigenous peoples can use Western media without adopting the conventions of Western culture. In fact, Ginsburg and many other anthropologists believe that video affords societies—especially oral ones—an invaluable opportunity to strengthen native languages and traditions threatened by Western exposure.

The Brazilian fieldwork of anthropologist Terence Turner, who studies the relationship between traditional Kayapo culture and Kayapo videotapes, lends credence to Ginsburg's position. Primarily an oral society, the Kayapo use video to document both ceremonial performances and transactions with representatives of the Brazilian government (this latter use is intended to provide legally binding records of the transactions). In contrast to Weiner's argument that video foists a Western ontology onto its users, Turner has found that the representations of Kayapo ceremonies, including everything from the camerawork to the editing, conform to the same principle of beauty embodied in the ceremonies themselves, one rooted in a complex pattern of repetition and sequential organization. The videos aesthetically mirror the ceremonies. The camera is not so at odds with Kayapo culture, it seems, that it transforms any Kayapo who uses it into a Westerner.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting up a disciplinary crisis in two stages. Visual anthropologists from the industrialized West have spent decades trying to strip the unself-conscious colonial gaze out of ethnographic film, and now face something larger. Because cheap video equipment is available everywhere, the peoples once examined by the Western camera have begun documenting their own cultures. The last sentence is your structural signpost, announcing that reaction within Western anthropological circles is sharply divided, which tells you the rest of the passage will be organized around opposing positions rather than a single line of argument.

The first camp gets a full hearing. Weiner reads the spread of video and television as the final assault of Western values on indigenous cultures, a devaluation of the different in which real historical, linguistic, social and cultural difference gives way to superficial difference among electronic images. His stronger claim is that the technology carries an ontology with it, one committed to realism, immediacy and self-expression, so that picking up a camera costs a people the very identity they set out to record. He adds a swipe at colleagues who treat such films as automatically truthful because indigenous people made them, calling that position theoretically naive.

The opposition answers on two levels. Weiner's critics first charge him with nostalgia for the noble savage, an accusation about motive rather than logic. Ginsburg then makes the substantive reply, and notice how much she concedes before disagreeing: no Western object in cultural circulation since the fifteenth century has been neutral. What she rejects is the leap from that to the claim that using a video camera makes one unwittingly Western, which she dismisses as boilerplate technological determinism. Her positive position is that indigenous peoples can use Western media without adopting Western conventions, and that video gives oral societies in particular a way to strengthen threatened languages and traditions.

Evidence arrives last, and the author's own hand shows in the phrase lends credence, which quietly takes a side. Turner's Brazilian fieldwork examines how the Kayapo, a largely oral society, use video both to record ceremonial performances and to produce legally binding records of dealings with the Brazilian government. The finding aims directly at Weiner's ontology claim. Everything in the Kayapo recordings, camerawork and editing alike, conforms to the same principle of beauty that governs the ceremonies themselves, rooted in repetition and sequential organization, so the videos mirror the ceremonies aesthetically. The closing line stays measured rather than triumphant: the camera does not turn its Kayapo users into Westerners.
overall_html: The passage lays out a dispute within Western visual anthropology over what happens when indigenous peoples use inexpensive video to document their own cultures, and it leans, gently, against the pessimistic side. Weiner holds that video inevitably carries a Western ontology and costs indigenous peoples the cultural identity they mean to preserve, while Ginsburg grants that no Western technology is neutral but denies that using a camera makes one Western, seeing instead a tool for sustaining threatened oral traditions. The author's purpose is to present the debate and then tilt it, closing with Turner's Kayapo fieldwork, where the aesthetics of the videos mirror the ceremonies recorded, as evidence supporting Ginsburg.
