It is commonly assumed that even if some forgeries have aesthetic merit, no forgery has as much as an original by the imitated artist would. Yet even the most prominent art specialists can be duped by a talented artist turned forger into mistaking an almost perfect forgery for an original. For instance, artist Han van Meegeren's The Disciples at Emmaus (1937)—painted under the forged signature of the acclaimed Dutch master Jan Vermeer (1632–1675)—attracted lavish praise from experts as one of Vermeer's finest works. The painting hung in a Rotterdam museum until 1945, when, to the great embarrassment of the critics, van Meegeren revealed its origin. Astonishingly, there was at least one highly reputed critic who persisted in believing it to be a Vermeer even after van Meegeren's confession.

Given the experts' initial enthusiasm, some philosophers argue that van Meegeren's painting must have possessed aesthetic characteristics that, in a Vermeer original, would have justified the critics' plaudits. Van Meegeren's Emmaus thus raises difficult questions regarding the status of superbly executed forgeries. Is a forgery inherently inferior as art? How are we justified, if indeed we are, in revising downwards our critical assessment of a work unmasked as a forgery? Philosopher of art Alfred Lessing proposes convincing answers to these questions.

A forged work is indeed inferior as art, Lessing argues, but not because of a shortfall in aesthetic qualities strictly defined, that is to say, in the qualities perceptible on the picture's surface. For example, in its composition, its technique, and its brilliant use of color, van Meegeren's work is flawless, even beautiful. Lessing argues instead that the deficiency lies in what might be called the painting's intangible qualities. All art, explains Lessing, involves technique, but not all art involves origination of a new vision, and originality of vision is one of the fundamental qualities by which artistic, as opposed to purely aesthetic, accomplishment is measured. Thus Vermeer is acclaimed for having inaugurated, in the seventeenth century, a new way of seeing, and for pioneering techniques for embodying this new way of seeing through distinctive treatment of light, color, and form.

Even if we grant that van Meegeren, with his undoubted mastery of Vermeer's innovative techniques, produced an aesthetically superior painting, he did so about three centuries after Vermeer developed the techniques in question. Whereas Vermeer's origination of these techniques in the seventeenth century represents a truly impressive and historic achievement, van Meegeren's production of The Disciples at Emmaus in the twentieth century presents nothing new or creative to the history of art. Van Meegeren's forgery therefore, for all its aesthetic merits, lacks the historical significance that makes Vermeer's work artistically great.
explanation_html:
A widely held assumption opens the passage, namely that a forgery can never match an original by the imitated artist in aesthetic merit, and the van Meegeren episode is produced immediately to strain it. Passed off under Vermeer's signature, The Disciples at Emmaus drew lavish praise from the experts as one of the Dutch master's finest works and hung in a Rotterdam museum until van Meegeren admitted authorship in 1945. Pay attention to the last detail, since it sharpens the puzzle: one highly reputed critic went on believing the picture was a Vermeer even after the confession.

The second paragraph turns the anecdote into a philosophical problem. Because the experts were genuinely enthusiastic, some philosophers conclude the painting must have had qualities that would have justified such praise had Vermeer produced it, which forces three questions: what status superb forgeries hold, whether forgery is inherently inferior as art, and how a downward revision of a work's rating can ever be justified once it is unmasked. Watch the last sentence closely, because in calling Lessing's answers convincing the author quietly takes a side before the argument has even been presented.

Lessing's answer is a distinction, and getting it straight is the whole passage. He agrees the forgery is inferior as art, but denies the shortfall lies in aesthetic qualities strictly defined, meaning what is perceptible on the picture's surface; van Meegeren's composition, technique and color are flawless, even beautiful. The deficiency sits instead in intangible qualities. Every work of art involves technique, but only some involve originating a new vision, and that originality is a fundamental measure of artistic as opposed to merely aesthetic accomplishment, which is why Vermeer is credited with inaugurating a new way of seeing.

The closing paragraph applies the distinction to the case and lands the conclusion. Grant van Meegeren everything, including mastery of Vermeer's innovative techniques and even an aesthetically superior painting, and one fact remains: he worked roughly three centuries after those techniques were invented. Vermeer's origination of them was an impressive and historic achievement, while a twentieth-century imitation contributes nothing new or creative to the history of art. The forgery therefore lacks historical significance, and that absence, not any flaw you could see on the canvas, is what keeps it from artistic greatness.
overall_html: The passage argues, following Lessing, that a forgery is inferior as art not because it looks worse but because artistic greatness depends on originality of vision and historical significance, qualities a copy cannot possess however aesthetically accomplished it is. The author's purpose is to explain and endorse a solution to a puzzle, moving from the van Meegeren case that fooled the experts, to the philosophical questions it raises, to Lessing's distinction between aesthetic and artistic merit, and finally to that distinction applied back to the forgery. The positions to track are the experts who praised the fake, the philosophers who infer real aesthetic quality from that praise, and Lessing, whose answers the author explicitly accepts.

Passage A

One function of language is to influence others' behavior by changing what they know, believe, or desire. For humans engaged in conversation, the perception of another's mental state is perhaps the most common vocalization stimulus.

While animal vocalizations may have evolved because they can potentially alter listeners' behavior to the signaler's benefit, such communication is—in contrast to human language—inadvertent, because most animals, with the possible exception of chimpanzees, cannot attribute mental states to others. The male Physalaemus frog calls because calling causes females to approach and other males to retreat, but there is no evidence that he does so because he attributes knowledge or desire to other frogs, or because he knows his calls will affect their knowledge and that this knowledge will, in turn, affect their behavior. Research also suggests that, in marked contrast to humans, nonhuman primates do not produce vocalizations in response to perception of another's need for information. Macaques, for example, give alarm calls when predators approach and coo calls upon finding food, yet experiments reveal no evidence that individuals were more likely to call about these events when they were aware of them but their offspring were clearly ignorant; similarly, chimpanzees do not appear to adjust their calling to inform ignorant individuals of their own location or that of food. Many animal vocalizations whose production initially seems goal-directed are not as purposeful as they first appear.

Passage B

Many scientists distinguish animal communication systems from human language on the grounds that the former are rigid responses to stimuli, whereas human language is spontaneous and creative.

In this connection, it is commonly stated that no animal can use its communication system to lie. Obviously, a lie requires intention to deceive: to judge whether a particular instance of animal communication is truly prevarication requires knowledge of the animal's intentions. Language philosopher H. P. Grice explains that for an individual to mean something by uttering x, the individual must intend, in expressing x, to induce an audience to believe something and must also intend the utterance to be recognized as so intended. But conscious intention is a category of mental experience widely believed to be uniquely human. Philosopher Jacques Maritain's discussion of the honeybee's elaborate "waggle-dance" exemplifies this view. Although bees returning to the hive communicate to other bees the distance and direction of food sources, such communication is, Maritain asserts, merely a conditioned reflex: animals may use communicative signs but lack conscious intention regarding their use.

But these arguments are circular: conscious intention is ruled out a priori and then its absence taken as evidence that animal communication is fundamentally different from human language. In fact, the narrowing of the perceived gap between animal communication and human language revealed by recent research with chimpanzees and other animals calls into question not only the assumption that the difference between animal and human communication is qualitative rather than merely quantitative, but also the accompanying assumption that animals respond mechanically to stimuli, whereas humans speak with conscious understanding and intent.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a functional account of language: one of its jobs is to change what other people know, believe or desire, and thereby their behavior. Add the second sentence and you get the benchmark the rest of the passage will apply, since for humans in conversation the usual prompt for speaking is reading someone else's mental state. Short as it is, this paragraph is doing setup work, defining the standard against which animal calls are about to be measured.

The comparison follows, and the key word is inadvertent. Animal vocalizations may well have evolved because they shift a listener's behavior to the signaler's advantage, but on the Author of Passage A's account most animals cannot attribute mental states at all, chimpanzees possibly excepted, so no intention to inform is involved. The male Physalaemus frog calls because calling draws females and repels rival males, with no evidence he credits other frogs with knowledge or desire. Experiments make the same point with primates: macaques do not call more readily when they know of a predator or food and their offspring plainly do not, and chimpanzees do not adjust calls to inform the ignorant.

Passage B begins by reporting the received distinction rather than asserting it. Many scientists, it says, separate animal communication from human language by treating the first as rigid response to stimuli and the second as spontaneous and creative. Keep the attribution firmly in mind, because everything through the next paragraph is a summary of the view B intends to dismantle, and mistaking summary for endorsement will scramble your reading of the passage.

The lying test is offered as the standard test case: no animal, it is said, can use its system to deceive. That claim depends on intention, since a lie requires an intent to deceive, so settling it means knowing an animal's intentions. Grice supplies the demanding standard, that meaning something by an utterance requires intending to induce a belief and intending the utterance to be recognized as so intended, and conscious intention is widely believed to be uniquely human. Maritain illustrates the resulting verdict, calling the honeybee's waggle-dance, which conveys distance and direction of food, a mere conditioned reflex.

Now the objection arrives, and it targets the reasoning rather than the facts. The Author of Passage B charges the arguments with circularity: conscious intention is excluded from animals in advance, and then its absence is treated as proof that their communication differs fundamentally from human language. Recent work with chimpanzees and other animals has narrowed the perceived gap, which puts pressure on two assumptions at once, that the difference is qualitative rather than merely one of degree, and that animals react mechanically while humans speak with understanding and intent.
overall_html: Both passages examine whether animal communication differs in kind from human language, and they come down on opposite sides: Passage A holds that animal vocalizations are inadvertent because most animals cannot attribute mental states, citing frog calls and primate experiments in which callers ignore what listeners need to know, while Passage B argues that the standard case for such a divide is circular, assuming animals lack conscious intention and then treating that assumption as evidence. The purposes differ accordingly, A presenting empirical findings to support the qualitative distinction and B critiquing the logic behind it. Track the Author of Passage A, the many scientists whose view Passage B reports through Grice and Maritain, and the Author of Passage B, who rejects it.

In contrast to the mainstream of U.S. historiography during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, African American historians of the period, such as George Washington Williams and W. E. B. DuBois, adopted a transnational perspective. This was true for several reasons, not the least of which was the necessity of doing so if certain aspects of the history of African Americans in the United States were to be treated honestly.

First, there was the problem of citizenship. Even after the adoption in 1868 of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which defined citizenship, the question of citizenship for African Americans had not been genuinely resolved. Because of this, emigrationist sentiment was a central issue in black political discourse, and both issues were critical topics for investigation. The implications for historical scholarship and national identity were enormous. While some black leaders insisted on their right to U.S. citizenship, others called on black people to emigrate and find a homeland of their own. Most African Americans were certainly not willing to relinquish their claims to the benefits of U.S. citizenship, but many had reached a point of profound pessimism and had begun to question their allegiance to the United States.

Mainstream U.S. historiography was firmly rooted in a nationalist approach during this period; the glorification of the nation and a focus on the nation-state as a historical force were dominant. The expanding spheres of influence of Europe and the United States prompted the creation of new genealogies of nations, new myths about the inevitability of nations, their "temperaments," their destinies. African American intellectuals who confronted the nationalist approach to historiography were troubled by its implications. Some argued that imperialism was a natural outgrowth of nationalism and its view that a state's strength is measured by the extension of its political power over colonial territory; the scramble for colonial empires was a distinct aspect of nationalism in the latter part of the nineteenth century.

Yet, for all their distrust of U.S. nationalism, most early black historians were themselves engaged in a sort of nation building. Deliberately or not, they contributed to the formation of a collective identity, reconstructing a glorious African past for the purposes of overturning degrading representations of blackness and establishing a firm cultural basis for a shared identity. Thus, one might argue that black historians' internationalism was a manifestation of a kind of nationalism that posits a diasporic community, which, while lacking a sovereign territory or official language, possesses a single culture, however mythical, with singular historical roots. Many members of this diaspora saw themselves as an oppressed "nation" without a homeland, or they imagined Africa as home. Hence, these historians understood their task to be the writing of the history of a people scattered by force and circumstance, a history that began in Africa.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by staking a contrast. While mainstream U.S. historiography of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries looked inward, early African American historians such as Williams and DuBois worked transnationally, looking beyond the borders of the United States. Several reasons lay behind this, and the one flagged as most important is necessity: certain parts of African American history simply could not be treated honestly within a national frame. Read this as a thesis paragraph promising an explanation, and expect the reasons to arrive in order.

The first reason is the unsettled status of citizenship. Although the Fourteenth Amendment had defined citizenship in 1868, the question remained genuinely unresolved for African Americans, which pushed emigration to the center of black political discourse and made both citizenship and emigration urgent subjects of research with large consequences for scholarship and national identity. Notice the split the paragraph records: some leaders pressed their claim to U.S. citizenship while others urged departure and a homeland elsewhere, and even those unwilling to surrender the benefits of citizenship had grown deeply pessimistic and were questioning their allegiance.

Attention shifts to what the mainstream was doing, supplying the second reason. Historiography of the era was nationalist through and through, glorifying the nation and treating the nation-state as the engine of history, and the expanding reach of Europe and the United States generated fresh genealogies of nations along with myths about their inevitability, temperaments and destinies. African American intellectuals found the implications disturbing, and some drew a direct line from nationalism to imperialism, since a doctrine that measures a state's strength by political power extended over colonies makes the scramble for empire a natural outgrowth rather than an aberration.

A complication closes the passage, signaled by that opening yet. For all their distrust of U.S. nationalism, these historians were engaged in nation building of their own, reconstructing a glorious African past in order to overturn degrading images of blackness and ground a shared identity. So their internationalism can be read as its own nationalism, one that posits a diasporic community holding a single culture, however mythical, with common roots but no sovereign territory or official language. Members of that diaspora saw themselves as an oppressed nation without a homeland, or imagined Africa as home, which made their task a history of a scattered people that begins in Africa.
overall_html: The passage explains why early African American historians departed from the nationalist mainstream of their era and wrote transnationally, pointing to the unresolved citizenship of African Americans and the emigration debate it fueled, and to their objection that nationalist historiography carried imperialism within it. Its purpose is analytic rather than evaluative: the author sets up the contrast, supplies the reasons behind it, and then closes with a paradox, arguing that these historians practiced a nationalism of their own by constructing a diasporic people with a glorious African past and a shared culture. The viewpoints to keep straight are the early African American historians, the nationalist mainstream they resisted, and the author's own qualified reading of their internationalism.

Passage A

Jury nullification occurs when the jury acquits the defendant in a criminal case in disregard of the judge's instructions and contrary to the jury's findings of fact. Sometimes a jury's nullification decision is based on mercy for the defendant, sometimes on dislike for the victim. Juries have also sometimes nullified when the defendant engaged in civil disobedience and the jurors agreed with the actions. While instances of jury nullification are probably few, the problems created by the jury's power to nullify are great.

First, we do not know how the power is used. Because juries are not required to and typically do not explain their verdicts, it is impossible to say how often nullification occurs. This means that we also do not know how often juries use this power for evil ends rather than for good ones.

Second, juries often have insufficient evidence to make a reasoned nullification decision. Evidence that might inform such a decision, such as a defendant’s past brushes with the law, usually is not admitted at trial because it is irrelevant to the technical question of guilt or innocence.

Third, jurors are not legislators. We have an elected legislature to pass laws and elected or appointed judges to interpret them. The jury is unelected, is unaccountable, and has no obligation to think through the effect an acquittal will have on others.

Reasonable people can disagree on the proper reach of the criminal laws. Nevertheless, the place for them to disagree is in public, where the reasons for revisions of the laws can be scrutinized and debated.

Passage B

Police and prosecutors have discretion to decide which violations of the law to pursue and which to overlook. Even with such discretion, however, these officials can sometimes be overzealous. In such cases, the jury can act as a safety valve and use its own discretion to decide, for example, that a case is too trivial or the circumstances too extenuating for the case to result in a conviction.

When a jury nullifies because it does not believe a law should be applied to a particular defendant, the jury can also be viewed as assisting the legislature. Legislatures create general laws both because they cannot foresee every variation that may arise, and because legislators often have competing views about what should be included in legislation and so must settle for broad language if any laws are to be passed.

Similarly, when a jury nullifies because it believes a law is unjust, it also performs a useful function vis-à-vis the legislature, namely indicating to the legislature that there may be a problem with the law in question.

It may happen that a jury will be persuaded to nullify by factors they should ignore, but such instances of nullification are likely to be uncommon. For a jury to agree to nullify means that the case for nullification must be so compelling that all twelve of the jurors, despite their different backgrounds and perspectives, nevertheless agree that nullification is the appropriate course of action.
explanation_html:
Passage A begins with a definition worth getting exactly right: nullification is an acquittal that defies the judge's instructions and runs contrary to the jury's own findings of fact. The motives listed are mixed, ranging from mercy for the defendant to dislike of the victim to sympathy with an act of civil disobedience. Then comes the thesis, and notice the concession built into it, since the Author of Passage A grants that nullification is probably rare and objects to the power itself rather than to its frequency.

The first objection is about what cannot be known. Juries are neither required to explain their verdicts nor inclined to, so there is no way to measure how often nullification happens. The consequence is the point: if the frequency is invisible, so is the balance between uses of the power that serve good ends and uses that serve bad ones. Read this as an epistemic complaint rather than an accusation of abuse.

The second objection concerns information. A nullification decision made responsibly would need material such as the defendant's earlier run-ins with the law, and that is precisely the sort of evidence normally excluded from trial because it has no bearing on the technical question of guilt. The trap is structural: the jury is being trusted with a judgment that depends on facts the trial deliberately keeps from it.

Third comes an argument about institutional roles rather than practicalities. Laws are made by an elected legislature and interpreted by judges who are elected or appointed, which places both under some form of public accountability. Jurors occupy neither position; they are unelected, answerable to no one, and carry no obligation to consider how an acquittal will affect anyone beyond the case in front of them.

The closing paragraph makes a concession and then converts it into the argument's finish. Reasonable disagreement about how far the criminal law should extend is granted freely, so the dispute is not about whether people may object to a law. What matters is venue. Such disagreement belongs in public, where the reasons for revising a law can be examined and argued over, rather than settled invisibly inside a jury room.

Passage B starts from a fact that reframes the whole issue: discretion is already built into criminal justice, since police and prosecutors choose which violations to pursue and which to let go. Because those officials can be overzealous, the Author of Passage B casts the jury as a safety valve exercising discretion of its own, free to decide that a case is too trivial or the circumstances too extenuating to end in conviction. The system, on this view, is not being invaded by discretion but corrected by it.

A second function follows, and it recasts the jury's relationship to the legislature as help rather than defiance. When a jury nullifies because it thinks a law should not reach this particular defendant, it is closing a gap lawmakers could not avoid leaving. Legislatures write in general terms both because no one can foresee every variation a law will meet and because legislators disagree among themselves, so broad language is often the price of passing anything at all.

The parallel case is handled briefly. Where the previous function concerned a law misapplied to one defendant, this one concerns a law the jury believes is unjust in itself, and here nullification works as a signal, telling the legislature that something about the law may need attention. The word similarly is your cue that the same relationship is being extended rather than a new argument begun.

The final paragraph answers the worry about misuse directly. Juries may indeed be swayed by considerations they ought to disregard, which Passage B concedes without dispute, but such cases should be rare. The reason offered is structural, and it rests on unanimity: nullification requires all twelve jurors, with their differing backgrounds and perspectives, to conclude that acquittal is the right course, which sets a high bar for a merely frivolous acquittal.
overall_html: The two passages assess jury nullification and reach opposing verdicts about the same practice. Passage A argues that the power is troubling regardless of how seldom it is used, because its frequency is unmeasurable, juries lack the evidence a reasoned decision would require, and unelected jurors are not entitled to do the legislature's work, concluding that disagreement about the law belongs in public debate. Passage B treats nullification as a useful safety valve within a system already governed by prosecutorial discretion, one that fills gaps in deliberately broad statutes and signals defective laws to lawmakers, and it answers the abuse objection by noting that unanimity among twelve jurors makes frivolous nullification unlikely.

Most sociohistorical interpretations of art view a body of work as the production of a class, generally a dominant or governing class, imposing its ideals. For example, Richard Taruskin writes in his Oxford History of Western Music that one of the defining characteristics of "high art" is that "it is produced by and for political and social elites." What Taruskin and others fail to clarify, however, is that there are two different ways that art, historically, was "produced by and for political and social elites."

The first way was for a member of the elite to engage a well-known artist to produce something for display. For instance, if one commissions a famous architect to design one's house, that may reflect great credit on one's taste, even if one finds the house impossible to live in. The second way was to create, or to have created, a work that expressed and mirrored one's ideals and way of life, like Raphael's frescoes in the Vatican apartments commissioned by Pope Julius II.

Sociohistorical critics like Taruskin prefer to deal with art produced the second way, because it enables them to construct a subtle analysis of the way such art embodied the ideology of the elite, whatever the identity of the artist. For this kind of analysis to work, however, it must be the case that the elite had a recognizable identity and displayed some kind of consensus about the world and the way life was to be lived, and it must also be the case that we can eliminate the possibility that artists subverted the ideals of the patron for their own reasons.

Historically, the two social classes able to commission art were the aristocratic, or governing class, and the well-to-do middle class, what used to be called the bourgeoisie. The taste of the aristocracy and the upper middle class has not always been apt to produce an art that endures. In his characterization of nineteenth-century English culture, cultural critic Matthew Arnold identified the aristocracy as Barbarians, interested largely in fox hunting and gaming, and the middle class as Philistines, obsessed with respectability. As a result, the more talented artists sometimes had to find a place in the margins of the establishment—engaged by a rich patron with eccentric tastes, for example.

Moreover, a great deal of art that went against the grain of elite values was paid for by the establishment unwillingly and with misgivings. Because some of this art endured, the sociohistorical critic, like Taruskin, must engage in an analogue of Freudian analysis, and claim that in hidden ways such art embodied the ideals of the elite, who were unaware that those ideals are revealed by work of which they overtly disapproved.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by naming the position it intends to complicate. Sociohistorical interpretation treats a body of art as the product of a class, usually the ruling one, imposing its ideals, and Taruskin supplies the representative formulation in defining high art as produced by and for political and social elites. The author does not deny that formulation but says it is underspecified, since art was produced by and for elites in two historically distinct ways. Expect the rest of the passage to run on that distinction, so fix it firmly before moving on.

The two ways arrive immediately. In the first, a member of the elite hires a celebrated artist and puts the result on display, where the payoff is the credit reflected on the patron's taste, which is why commissioning a famous architect flatters you even if the house turns out impossible to live in. In the second, the work is made to express and mirror the patron's own ideals and way of life, as Raphael's frescoes did for Julius II. Only the second sort actually carries an ideology; the first advertises status.

Here the distinction acquires teeth. Sociohistorical critics like Taruskin naturally prefer the second kind of art, because it supports subtle readings of how a work embodies elite ideology whatever the artist's identity. But such readings, the author points out, depend on two conditions that are rarely stated: the elite must have had a recognizable identity and some genuine consensus about the world and how life should be lived, and the possibility that artists quietly subverted a patron's ideals for reasons of their own must be ruled out. Watch how the next two paragraphs go after exactly these conditions.

Evidence against the consensus condition comes from the history of patronage. Only two classes could afford to commission art, the aristocracy and the prosperous middle class, and their taste has not reliably produced work that lasts. Matthew Arnold's account of nineteenth-century England is the illustration, casting the aristocracy as Barbarians absorbed in fox hunting and gaming and the middle class as Philistines fixated on respectability. The consequence matters more than the labels: gifted artists were sometimes pushed to the margins of the establishment, dependent on a wealthy patron with eccentric tastes rather than seated at the ideological center.

The last paragraph presses harder. A considerable amount of art that cut against elite values was financed by the establishment reluctantly and with misgivings, and some of it endured. To keep the sociohistorical reading intact in those cases, a critic must resort to something like Freudian analysis, arguing that such work secretly embodied ideals of an elite who failed to recognize themselves in art they openly disliked. The comparison is the author's judgment rather than a neutral description, since an interpretation that can absorb even open disapproval is one nothing could refute.
overall_html: The passage challenges the sociohistorical claim, exemplified by Taruskin, that high art expresses the ideology of the elite who paid for it, arguing that the formula conceals two very different kinds of patronage and that the analysis it supports rests on conditions history does not meet. The author's purpose is critical, proceeding by drawing the distinction between art commissioned for display and art made to mirror a patron's ideals, then naming the assumptions sociohistorical criticism needs, then undercutting them with Arnold's picture of philistine patrons and with the enduring art the establishment funded unwillingly. The positions to track are Taruskin and fellow sociohistorical critics, Arnold as supporting witness, and the author.

Hundreds of clay tablets marked in cuneiform have been found in excavations of the Sumerian city of Uruk (in present-day Iraq). Though the tablets date from roughly 3000 B.C., the writing on them uses relatively few pictographs; instead, numerous abstract symbols are used. The sign for "sheep," for example, is not an image of a sheep, but rather a circled cross, while the sign for "metal" is a crescent with five lines. Because of its early date, this seemingly sudden appearance of such abstract writing has long puzzled researchers. At the same time, among prepottery clay artifacts found at archaeological sites along the Jordan and nearby rivers are thousands of small, hand-modeled tokens of fired clay, some dating to before 4000 B.C. Often ignored by archaeologists—some concluded without evidence that they were amulets or game pieces—the tokens are identified by Denise Schmandt-Besserat in her book Before Writing (1992) as overlooked predecessors to the written word.

The earliest of the tokens were simple in form—small cones, spheres, and pyramids—and they were often inscribed. In 1966, a hollow tablet containing several of these tokens was discovered, and more than 100 additional tablets, which are now recognized as sealed envelopes of clay, have since been found. Later envelopes are also inscribed with impressions of tokens in the outer clay, signaling exactly what each envelope contained. Noting that these inscriptions are clearly traceable to later, known inscriptions of farm products, Schmandt-Besserat theorizes that the envelopes contained official records of villagers' contributions to temple-based grain and livestock pools. After 4000 B.C., hundreds of new token forms developed, as a rise in industry boosted the token system. Many forms are figurative, such as bowls or jars with handles, suggesting that villagers' crafts were becoming more diversified and sophisticated.

The token system, essentially a system of three-dimensional nouns, was replaced in about 3100 B.C. by a system of marks on clay tablets. A few centuries later, this latter system was to display the first use of numerals, where simple marks coded the concepts of one, two, and so forth. The eventual evolution of this system into mature writing, Schmandt-Besserat suggests, can be seen in the following example: At first it took two ovoid tokens to record two jars of oil. A little later, it took two markings on a clay tablet to achieve this—one mark, using the outline of the old token, to record the customary unit measure for oil, the jarful, and a second mark to convey the numeral: two oil jars. Eventually, it took three signs on the tablet, one for the numeral 2, one for the standard jarful, and a new symbol that denoted oil itself. With three such signs, an abstract and flexible written form had arrived.
explanation_html:
Two separate puzzles are laid side by side before anything is explained. At Uruk, hundreds of clay tablets from about 3000 B.C. carry cuneiform that relies not on pictures but on abstract signs, so that sheep is a circled cross and metal a crescent with five lines, and researchers have long found the early and apparently sudden arrival of such abstraction hard to account for. Separately, prepottery sites along the Jordan and nearby rivers have yielded thousands of small hand-modeled clay tokens, some older than 4000 B.C., which archaeologists largely ignored or wrote off, without evidence, as amulets or game pieces. Schmandt-Besserat joins the two, identifying the tokens as forgotten ancestors of writing.

The evidence for that claim is presented in sequence. Early tokens were simple cones, spheres and pyramids, frequently inscribed, and a hollow tablet found in 1966 turned out to contain some; more than a hundred comparable objects are now understood as sealed clay envelopes, with later examples bearing impressions of their contents pressed into the outer surface. Because those impressions can be traced forward to later inscriptions known to denote farm products, Schmandt-Besserat concludes that the envelopes held official records of villagers' contributions to temple grain and livestock pools. Note the further inference drawn from the hundreds of figurative forms appearing after 4000 B.C., such as handled bowls and jars, which suggest increasingly diversified crafts.

The closing paragraph traces the crossing from tokens to writing and thereby answers the puzzle raised at the start. Around 3100 B.C. the tokens, which amounted to a set of three-dimensional nouns, gave way to marks on clay tablets, and a few centuries later those tablets show the first numerals, simple marks standing for one, two and so on. Follow the worked example carefully, since it carries the argument: two ovoid tokens for two jars of oil become two marks on a tablet, one preserving the old token's outline as the customary jarful measure and one giving the number, and finally three signs, a numeral, the unit, and a new symbol for oil itself. Abstraction, on this account, was gradual rather than abrupt.
overall_html: The passage presents Schmandt-Besserat's argument that the abstract cuneiform signs appearing at Uruk around 3000 B.C. were not an abrupt invention but the endpoint of a long development from clay tokens used centuries earlier to record contributions of farm goods. The author's purpose is expository, setting up the puzzle of sudden abstraction alongside the neglected tokens, laying out the evidence from inscribed tokens and sealed clay envelopes, and then following the step-by-step transition through which one object standing for one jar of oil became separate signs for number, unit and commodity. Schmandt-Besserat is the only real viewpoint, with earlier archaeologists who dismissed the tokens noted briefly as the position she displaces.

By 1970 it was well established that ultraviolet light from the sun contributes to skin cancer. Fortunately, much of the sun's most damaging ultraviolet radiation is screened out by a thin, diffuse layer of ozone—a toxic form of oxygen—in the stratosphere, 10 to 25 miles above the earth's surface.

During the 1970s, however, public policy makers worldwide were alerted to the fragility of the ozone layer through the pioneering research and advocacy of two Nobel Prize-winning scientists, Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland. In the absence of pollutants, stratospheric ozone concentrations should remain stable over time, with natural production and destruction of the gas in rough equilibrium. Molina and Rowland showed how manufactured chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)—highly volatile chemicals, millions of tons of which had been used each year in products such as aerosol sprays and refrigerants—chemically attack and deplete the ozone layer, diminishing its effectiveness as a shield against ultraviolet radiation. Studying two freon gases—types of CFCs—they observed that, when released into the lower atmosphere (troposphere), these gases slowly diffuse upward into the stratosphere. There, subjected to massive ultraviolet radiation, they break down into their constituent elements, including chlorine. The resulting increase in the concentration of chlorine in the stratosphere is devastating to the ozone layer. Chlorine and ozone chemically react in a way that both destroys the ozone and regenerates the chlorine atoms. As a result of this chemical reaction, each chlorine atom could destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules before becoming inactive.

In 1974 the two scientists estimated that the atmosphere contained the accumulation of five years of global CFC production. This meant that, given the rate of diffusion and breakdown of CFCs in the atmosphere, the depletion of the ozone layer would continue for years, if not decades, even if the production and use of CFCs were to cease immediately. Recognizing this as a pressing environmental threat, Molina and Rowland became public advocates for a prompt and proportionate public policy response. As a result, Molina was invited to testify before the U.S. Congress and was later appointed to the U.S. National Science Foundation Committee on Fluorocarbon Technology Assessment.

Predictably, the work of Molina and Rowland and their advocacy of dramatic policy changes were subjected to attacks by critics, especially scientists with ties to the CFC industry. However, over time their views were corroborated, especially by the discovery of a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica, and this led to the development of an international agreement (the Montreal Protocol of 1987) to ban the production of ozone-depleting gases. In North America, CFCs were banned in the late 1970s, leading to a transformation in packaging for consumer spray products and the development of more environmentally friendly refrigerant chemicals.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph lays down the stakes before any controversy begins. By 1970 the link between the sun's ultraviolet light and skin cancer was settled, and the protective factor is introduced immediately: a thin, diffuse layer of ozone sitting ten to twenty-five miles up in the stratosphere screens out much of the most damaging radiation. Register the description of ozone as a toxic form of oxygen, since the same gas that harms at ground level shields us from above. Nothing here is disputed; the paragraph exists so the threat that follows has weight.

However signals the threat, and the paragraph is essentially a mechanism to follow step by step. Molina and Rowland alerted policy makers worldwide through research and advocacy, starting from the baseline that without pollutants stratospheric ozone should hold steady, its natural production and destruction roughly in balance. Chlorofluorocarbons, volatile manufactured chemicals used by the millions of tons in aerosols and refrigerants, break that balance. Released into the lower atmosphere, they drift slowly upward, where intense ultraviolet light splits them apart and frees chlorine. The crucial detail is that the reaction destroying ozone regenerates the chlorine atom, letting one atom destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules.

The third paragraph explains why the finding demanded speed. Their 1974 estimate put five years of accumulated global CFC production already in the atmosphere, and because diffusion and breakdown are slow, depletion would continue for years or decades even if all production stopped that day. Notice how the science converts into a policy claim: judging this a pressing environmental threat, Molina and Rowland took on public roles as advocates for a prompt and proportionate response, with Molina testifying before Congress and later serving on a national committee assessing fluorocarbon technology.

Resistance and vindication close the passage. The research and the call for dramatic policy change drew attacks, especially from scientists with CFC industry ties, and the author's word predictably is the one clear editorial touch in an otherwise neutral account. Corroboration came in time, most strikingly with the discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole, which paved the way for the Montreal Protocol of 1987 banning production of ozone-depleting gases. Concrete consequences follow: North America had banned CFCs by the late 1970s, reshaping consumer spray packaging and prompting friendlier refrigerant chemicals.
overall_html: The passage recounts how Molina and Rowland established that chlorofluorocarbons destroy stratospheric ozone, and how their findings, pressed through public advocacy and eventually confirmed by the Antarctic ozone hole, produced the ban embodied in the Montreal Protocol. The author's purpose is largely expository, moving from the protective function of the ozone layer, to the chemical mechanism by which chlorine released from CFCs destroys ozone while regenerating itself, to the urgency created by chemicals already accumulated in the atmosphere, and finally to opposition and vindication. Molina and Rowland are the central figures, with industry-linked scientists appearing as critics whose objections the record overtook.

Passage A

Muscle memory is a puzzling phenomenon. Most bodybuilders have experienced this phenomenon, yet virtually no discussions of it have appeared in scientific publications. Bodybuilders who start training again after a period of inactivity find that gaining muscle size seems easier the second time around—even if starting from the same place. With so many athletes observing muscle memory, some plausible explanation must exist.

One potential explanation of muscle memory involves the neurons (nerve cells) that stimulate your muscles, telling the muscle fibers to contract. It is well established that during weight lifting, only a small percentage of neurons for the working muscles are recruited. The more weight you lift, the more neurons are involved and the more muscle fibers are stimulated. But even when attempting your maximum weight, you don't recruit all the fibers in your working muscles. Now it could be that one way your body adapts to the demands of consistent training is by gradually increasing the percentage of muscle fibers that are stimulated by neurons during maximal lifts. When you're making a comeback, this ability to recruit more muscle fibers may remain intact. If so, your muscles would start with a greater capacity to develop force. Although you may think you're starting from the same place, this greater strength would enable faster progress.

Then again, it's also possible that the ease of retraining has nothing to do with your muscles: it could all be in your head. The first time you trained, you didn't know how much you could lift. So you increased weight cautiously. When retraining, you already know you can handle increasing weight because you've done it before. So you are likely to add weight more rapidly. These more rapid weight increases produce quicker gains in strength and size.

Passage B

Pumping up is easier for people who have been buff before, and now scientists think they know why—muscles retain one aspect of their former fitness even as they wither from lack of use.

Because muscle cells are huge, more than one nucleus is needed for making the large amounts of the proteins that give muscles their strength. Previous research has demonstrated that with exercise, muscle cells get even bigger by merging with stem cells that are nested between them. The muscle cells incorporate the nuclei that previously belonged to the stem cells. Researchers had thought that when muscles atrophy, the extra cell nuclei are killed by a cell death program called apoptosis.

In a recent study, researchers regularly stimulated the leg muscles of mice over a two-week period, during which time the muscle cells gained nuclei and increased in size. The researchers then let the muscles rest. As the muscles atrophied, the cells deflated to about 40 percent of their bulked-up size, but the number of nuclei in the cells did not change. Since the extra nuclei don't die, they could be poised to make muscle proteins again, providing a type of muscle memory at the cellular level.
explanation_html:
Passage A frames muscle memory as a puzzle with an evidence gap. Bodybuilders returning after a layoff commonly report that regaining size comes more easily than building it did the first time, even starting from the same point, yet scientific publications have barely addressed the phenomenon. Pay attention to the reasoning in the last sentence, since it drives everything that follows: because so many athletes observe the effect, some plausible explanation must exist. What comes next is therefore speculation working from anecdote rather than from experimental results.

The first candidate explanation is neural. Muscle fibers contract when neurons tell them to, and only a small share of the available neurons fire during a lift; heavier loads recruit more, but even a maximum effort leaves fibers untouched. The suggestion is that consistent training gradually raises the percentage of fibers recruited, and that this recruitment capacity survives the break. A returning lifter would then begin with greater force-producing capacity and progress faster while believing the starting point is unchanged. Notice the hedging throughout, since this is offered as a possibility rather than an established finding.

An entirely different explanation follows, and it relocates the cause from the body to the mind. A first-time trainee has no idea what he or she can handle and so adds weight cautiously. Someone retraining already knows from experience that increases are manageable and therefore loads the bar more aggressively, and faster weight increases produce quicker gains in strength and size. Note that Passage A leaves both accounts standing without choosing between them, which is consistent with its opening complaint that the phenomenon has gone unstudied.

Passage B opens where Passage A stops, announcing an answer instead of a puzzle. The observation is the same, that regaining fitness comes more easily to those who were fit before, but the framing is different, since scientists now think they know the reason. The proposed cause is physiological and stated compactly: muscles hold on to one aspect of their former fitness even as they waste away from disuse. Compare the confidence of this register with the guarded speculation of the previous passage.

Cell biology supplies the background. Muscle cells are unusually large, so a single nucleus cannot direct production of all the protein that gives muscle its strength, and multiple nuclei are required. Earlier work showed that exercise enlarges muscle cells further by merging them with stem cells nested between them, with the muscle cell absorbing nuclei that used to belong to those stem cells. The assumption to mark is the one now in question, namely that when muscles atrophy the extra nuclei are eliminated by apoptosis, a programmed cell death.

The study overturns that assumption. Researchers stimulated the leg muscles of mice regularly for two weeks, during which the cells gained nuclei and grew, then let the muscles rest. As atrophy set in, the cells shrank to roughly 40 percent of their enlarged size while the number of nuclei stayed put. The conclusion is stated carefully rather than triumphantly: since the extra nuclei survive, they may be ready to resume producing muscle proteins, which would furnish a cellular basis for muscle memory.
overall_html: Both passages address the same observation, that rebuilding muscle after a layoff is easier than building it the first time, but they differ in evidence and confidence rather than in conclusion. Passage A treats the effect as a puzzle scientists have neglected and offers two untested explanations, one holding that trained muscles retain the ability to recruit more fibers and the other holding that returning lifters simply add weight faster because they know what they can handle. Passage B answers the very gap Passage A complains of, reporting a mouse study in which extra cell nuclei gained through exercise survived atrophy, supplying a concrete cellular mechanism neither of Passage A's hypotheses proposes.

Best known for her work with lacquer, Eileen Gray (1878–1976) had a fascinating and multifaceted artistic career: she became a designer of ornaments, furniture, interiors, and eventually homes. Though her attention shifted from smaller objects to the very large, she always focused on details, even details that were forever hidden. In Paris she studied the Japanese tradition of lacquer, employing wood surfaces—e.g., bowls, screens, furniture—for the application of the clear, hard-drying liquid. It is a time-consuming craft, then little known in Europe, that superimposes layer upon layer, sometimes involving twenty layers or more. The tradition of lacquer fit well with her artistic sensibilities, as Gray eschewed the flowing, leafy lines of the Art Nouveau movement that had flourished in Paris, preferring the austere beauty of straight lines and simple forms juxtaposed.

In addition to requiring painstaking layering, the wood used in lacquer work must be lacquered on both sides to prevent warping. This tension between aesthetic demands and structural requirements, which invests Gray's work in lacquer with an architectural quality, is critical but not always apparent: a folding screen or door panel reveals more of the artist's work than does a flat panel, which hides one side. In Gray's early work she produced flat panels; later she made door panels and even unfolded the panels into screens. In a screen she made for the lobby of an apartment, she fully realizes the implications of this expansion from two to three dimensions: the screen juts out from a wall, and that wall visually disintegrates into panels of lacquered bricks on the screen. The screen thus becomes a painting, a piece of furniture, and an architectural element all at once. She subsequently became heavily invested in the design of furniture, often tailoring pieces to fit a particular interior environment. She often used modern materials, such as tubular steel, to create furniture and environments that, though visually austere, meet their occupants' needs.

Gray's work in both lacquer and interior design prefigures her work as an architect. She did not believe that one should divorce the structural design of the exterior from the design of the interior. She designed the interior elements of a house together with the more permanent structures, as an integrated whole. Architecture for her was like work in lacquer: it could only be achieved from the inside out. But in architecture we discover the hidden layers; in fact we inhabit them. We find storage cabinets in the recesses of a staircase, desks that are also cabinets, and tables that are set on pivots to serve different functions in different contexts. One such table can be positioned either outside, on a balcony, or inside the house. Gray placed a carpet underneath it in each location, as though to underscore that there is no important distinction between exterior and interior.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph introduces Eileen Gray and, more importantly, the through-line the passage will follow. Her career moved outward in scale, from ornaments and furniture to interiors and finally houses, yet her attention to detail never loosened, extending even to details that stay permanently hidden. Hold on to that idea, because hidden layers organize everything that comes after. Her study of the Japanese lacquer tradition matters in two ways: technically, since lacquer is built on wood surfaces through layer upon layer, sometimes twenty or more, in a slow craft then little known in Europe, and temperamentally, since she rejected the leafy curves of Art Nouveau in favor of straight lines and simple forms set beside one another.

A technical requirement becomes an aesthetic principle here. Lacquered wood must be treated on both sides or it warps, and this pull between what the design wants and what the structure demands is what gives Gray's lacquer an architectural character, though a flat panel conceals one side while a folding screen or door panel exposes more of the work. Her development follows that logic exactly, moving from flat panels to door panels to panels unfolded into screens. The lobby screen realizes the shift from two dimensions to three, jutting from the wall as the wall dissolves into lacquered brick panels, so that one object is painting, furniture and architecture at once. Furniture work followed, tailored to particular interiors and often built from modern materials such as tubular steel.

Everything preceding is now revealed as preparation for the architecture. Gray refused to separate the structural design of a building's exterior from the design of its interior, planning interior elements and permanent structures together as one integrated whole, and the analogy is hers: architecture, like lacquer, could only be worked from the inside out. Then comes the turn on the hidden-layer motif, since in a building we do not merely discover the concealed layers, we live inside them. The examples are practical, with cabinets set into the recesses of a staircase, desks doubling as cabinets, and pivoting tables that change function with their setting. One such table works on a balcony or indoors, with a carpet laid beneath it in both places, as if to deny any real boundary between outside and inside.
overall_html: The passage traces Eileen Gray's development from lacquer work through furniture and interiors to architecture, arguing that a single sensibility runs through all of it: an insistence on straight lines and simple forms, a preoccupation with layers and details that remain hidden, and a refusal to treat inside and outside as separate design problems. The author's purpose is appreciative and explanatory, using the technical demands of lacquer, the folding screen that becomes painting, furniture and architecture at once, and finally the built interiors we inhabit to show how each phase prepared the next. Only the author's own admiring assessment is at work, with no competing views to sort out.

It is generally accepted that woodland clearings were utilized by Mesolithic human populations (populations in Europe roughly 7,000 to 12,000 years ago) for food procurement. Whether there was deliberate removal of tree cover to attract grazing animals or whether naturally created clearings just afforded opportunistic hunting, the common view is that clearings had an economic use. The archaeological evidence for this, however, is at best circumstantial. Some locales where the presence of clearings has been demonstrated in the paleoecological record of vegetation have also yielded human artifacts from around the same time, but the two kinds of evidence are never securely linked. Furthermore, artifactual evidence that preparation of animals for human consumption took place within or near such clearings is generally lacking.

Most of the evidence invoked in favor of the resource-procurement model for clearings comes from ethnography rather than archaeology, and principally from the recognition that some recent premodern populations used fire to increase grazing areas. But while some ethnographic evidence has been used to bolster the resource-procurement model, other ethnographic evidence may suggest a different vision, a noneconomic one, of why clearings may have been deliberately created and/or used.

Geographer Yi-Fu Tuan argues that right up through the modern era, human behavior has been driven by fear of the wilderness. While we might be tempted to see this kind of anxiety as a product of modern urban life, it is clear that such fears are also manifest in preliterate and nonurban societies. If we apply this insight to the Mesolithic era, our view of the purpose and use of woodland clearings may change.

We have recently become aware of the importance of woodland paths in prehistory. The fact that Mesolithic human populations moved around the landscape is not a new idea. However, the fact that they may have done so along prescribed pathways has only recently come to the fore. I propose that one of the primary motivators in establishing paths may have been fear of the wooded surroundings—whether fear of harm from wildlife or spirits, or of simply getting lost.

From this view an alternative hypothesis may be developed. First, paths become established and acquire a measure of long-term permanence. Then this permanence leads to concentration of activity in some areas (near the paths) rather than others (away from the paths). This allows us to legitimately consider wilderness as a motivating concept in the Mesolithic, and may force us to consider environment as more than "backdrop." And finally, it may lead us to explain some clearings as purely social phenomena, since where paths meet, wider clearings emerge as corners are cut and intersections become convenient spots for resting.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the consensus it intends to unsettle. Mesolithic populations in Europe, roughly 7,000 to 12,000 years ago, are generally thought to have used woodland clearings to obtain food, whether by deliberately removing tree cover to attract grazing animals or by hunting opportunistically in clearings that formed naturally. Either way, on the common view a clearing served an economic purpose. The rest of the paragraph is a complaint about evidence: clearings documented in the paleoecological record and human artifacts of similar date turn up in the same locales but are never securely linked, and traces of animals being prepared for eating in or near clearings are generally missing.

Attention shifts to where the support actually comes from, and that is the weak point being exposed. Most of the case for the resource-procurement model rests on ethnography rather than archaeology, chiefly on observations that some recent premodern populations burned land to enlarge grazing areas. Watch the pivot that follows, because it does not dispute the data but denies that the data settles anything: other ethnographic evidence may point toward a noneconomic account of why clearings were created or used. That opening is what the remainder of the passage moves into.

A borrowed idea supplies the first building block of the alternative. Yi-Fu Tuan argues that fear of the wilderness has shaped human behavior right through the modern era, and the likely objection is blocked immediately, since such anxiety appears in preliterate and nonurban societies too rather than being a symptom of modern city life. Applied to the Mesolithic, that claim would change how the purpose and use of clearings look. Note that no conclusion is drawn yet; the paragraph is installing a premise the argument will need.

The second building block is paths. That Mesolithic populations moved around the landscape is long-established, but the recognition that they may have followed prescribed routes is recent, and the author takes that recent finding and joins it to Tuan's insight. The proposal is stated in the first person and carefully hedged: a primary motivator for establishing paths may have been fear of the wooded surroundings, whether fear of wildlife, of spirits, or simply of getting lost. Treat this as a suggestion offered for consideration, not a claim presented as demonstrated.

Everything now assembles into the alternative hypothesis, presented as a sequence you should be able to reproduce. Paths get established and acquire long-term permanence; that permanence concentrates activity near them and away from other areas; and that pattern makes wilderness a legitimate motivating concept for the period while pushing environment beyond the status of backdrop. The final step is the payoff for the opening dispute, since some clearings may then be purely social in origin, emerging where paths meet as corners are cut and intersections become convenient places to rest.
overall_html: The passage challenges the standard assumption that Mesolithic woodland clearings existed for food procurement, arguing that the archaeological evidence is circumstantial and that the ethnographic evidence supporting the economic reading can equally support a noneconomic one. The author's purpose is to propose an alternative, building it in stages from Tuan's claim that fear of wilderness drives human behavior, through the recent recognition that Mesolithic movement followed prescribed paths, to the suggestion that fear motivated those paths and that some clearings formed socially at the intersections. The positions to keep apart are the common view of clearings as economic, Tuan's thesis about wilderness, and the author's own hedged hypothesis.

A remedy that courts sometimes use in disputes involving a breach of contract is simply to compel the participants in the contract to do precisely what they have agreed to do. Specific performance, as this approach is called, can be used as an alternative to monetary damages—that is, to requiring the one who has violated the agreement to pay a specified amount of money in compensation for the loss that is incurred or the wrong that is suffered. But while there are some cases for which specific performance can be a better alternative than monetary damages, there are many instances in which it is clearly not a suitable remedy.

Whether or not specific performance is an appropriate remedy in a case depends on the particular characteristics of that case. It is often the only reasonable remedy when monetary damages could not adequately compensate the one who has been harmed by the breach of contract. For example, a contract may provide for one party to sell some item of personal property that is unique or of such subjective importance to the buyer that there is no way to assign an accurate financial measure of the buyer's loss in not possessing the item. When the promised seller in such a case refuses to complete the sale, the best remedy would be to order that the contract be fulfilled exactly according to its terms.

Nevertheless, in many cases monetary payment can adequately compensate for the refusal to fulfill the terms of a contract, and thus the court commonly need not consider ordering specific performance. In fact, in some types of cases, court-enforced performance of the contract would actually be detrimental to those involved in the dispute and thus should be avoided. This most often occurs when a contract calls for a service to be performed and the one who has previously agreed to perform the service now refuses to do so—especially if a contract has been broken through someone's refusal to undertake employment as promised. The most compelling reasons against enforcement of contracts in such cases have to do with the kind of coercion that enforcement would necessitate. Forcing someone to perform a service in association with, and especially under the direction of, another who has become an antagonist can, at the very least, heighten dissatisfaction and intensify psychological friction. Even if a court had the resources necessary to ensure that such a contract would be enforced according to its terms, it would often do better to avoid imposing such uncomfortable conditions. Awarding monetary compensation where possible in such cases permits the court to steer clear of entanglement in troublesome aspects of the disputed relationship while still providing relief to the wronged party.
explanation_html:
Definitions come first and they matter. Specific performance is a remedy in which a court orders the parties to do exactly what their contract said, standing as an alternative to monetary damages, which instead require the party in breach to pay a set sum for the loss incurred or the wrong suffered. The last sentence carries the thesis and is deliberately two-sided: in some cases specific performance is the better option, but in many it is clearly unsuitable. The author is the only voice in the passage, and the task ahead is a sorting exercise, so read for the features that put a case on one side or the other.

The favorable half arrives with a criterion attached. Suitability depends on the particular characteristics of the case, and specific performance is often the only reasonable remedy where money could not adequately compensate the party harmed by the breach. The example makes that abstract test concrete: a contract to sell an item of personal property so unique, or of such subjective importance to the buyer, that no accurate financial measure can be put on the loss of not having it. Where the seller then refuses to complete, ordering the contract carried out on its exact terms is the best available response.

The unfavorable half gets the most space, which signals where the author's emphasis lies. Where money compensates adequately, a court commonly need not consider ordering performance at all, and in some situations enforcement would actively harm the people involved. The recurring case is a contract for a service the promised performer now refuses to render, above all a refusal to take up agreed employment, and the objection is about coercion: compelling someone to work alongside, and especially under the direction of, a person who has become an antagonist can deepen dissatisfaction and intensify psychological friction. Even a court able to enforce such an order does better to award money, relieving the wronged party without entangling itself in the relationship.
overall_html: The passage explains specific performance, the remedy of ordering contracting parties to do exactly what they promised, and argues that although it suits some breaches it is unsuitable for many others. The author's purpose is to set out the criterion that distinguishes the two, namely whether monetary damages can adequately compensate the injured party, and the structure follows directly from that: a definition and a balanced thesis, then the case for the remedy where a unique item defies financial valuation, then the larger case against it where money will do and, in particular, where enforcing a personal service contract would coerce someone into working under an antagonist. Only the author's own evaluative voice is present.

In the last half-century, firefighters in North America have developed a powerful system for fighting wildfires using modern technology. But at the same time, foresters and ecologists are increasingly aware that too much firefighting can be worse than none at all. Over the millennia, many forest ecosystems have evolved in such a way that they are dependent on periodic fires for renewal and for limiting damage when fires do occur. Ancient ponderosa forests, for example, were stable in part because low-intensity fires maintained open forests with low levels of fuel for future fires. These fires burned lightly around the bases of mature trees, leaving these trees alive and clearing the understory of brush and young trees. Scientists can easily count the regular recurrence of fires in these forests over the centuries by examining the scars left on trunks; the typical interval between fires could be as short as 5 years and rarely extended beyond 25 years.

If fires are kept out of forests, however, deadwood and other fuels build up; then, when fire is sparked by lightning or some other cause, what results is a fire so large that it leaves total devastation. Such fires often kill off wildlife that might escape low-intensity fires, and they also reach the crowns of centuries-old trees, destroying them and ultimately enabling rains to erode the unprotected topsoil. Because of the relative success of fire-suppression efforts, many forests, including ponderosa forests, have now been free of fire for 50 years or longer, leaving them vulnerable to these devastating crown fires. It is therefore increasingly necessary for land managers in North America to strive to manage rather than eliminate fires; land management policies should recognize the essential role that fire plays in many ecosystems.

Fire behavior depends on the complex interaction of three factors—topography, weather, and fuel—and since topography is fixed and weather is unpredictable, fuel is the only element that land managers can control. Land managers should therefore focus their efforts on fuel. A new kind of wildfire management that is designed to simulate the natural role of fire through a combination of selective harvesting and prescribed fires is the most promising method for controlling fuel. Selective timber harvesting focuses on smaller trees—markets for this smaller material do exist—leaving the larger, fire-tolerant trees on the land and thinning the forest, thereby re-creating the conditions that allow for low-intensity burns. Prescribed fire management includes both the intentional lighting of controlled burns and the policy of allowing fires set by lightning to burn when the weather is damp enough to reduce the risk of extensive damage. Once fuels are reduced by these fires, maintenance burns at 15- to 20-year intervals will be needed. When wildfires inevitably occur, they will be more easily controlled and do much less damage.
explanation_html:
A technological success and an ecological complication are set against each other from the start. North American firefighters have built a powerful modern suppression system, yet foresters and ecologists increasingly recognize that too much firefighting can be worse than none, because many forest ecosystems evolved to depend on periodic fire for renewal and for limiting the damage fires do. Ancient ponderosa forests are the illustration to hold on to: frequent low-intensity fires kept them open and low in fuel, burning lightly around the bases of mature trees, leaving those trees alive and clearing brush and young growth from the understory. Scars on the trunks let scientists count the intervals, which could be as short as five years and rarely ran beyond twenty-five.

The consequences of removing that cycle occupy the second paragraph. Keep fire out and deadwood and other fuels accumulate, so that when lightning or some other source finally ignites them the resulting fire is large enough to leave total devastation. Follow the chain of damage: wildlife that would survive a light burn is killed, flames climb into the crowns of centuries-old trees and destroy them, and rain then erodes topsoil left without protection. Because suppression has largely succeeded, many forests including ponderosa have gone fifty years or more without fire, which is precisely what leaves them open to crown fires. The recommendation follows, that managers manage fire rather than eliminate it.

Having established the principle, the closing paragraph supplies the method. Fire behavior depends on topography, weather and fuel, and since the first is fixed and the second unpredictable, fuel is the only element managers can control, so that is where effort belongs. The proposed approach imitates the natural fire regime with two complementary tools. Selective harvesting removes smaller trees, for which markets exist, thinning the stand while leaving the larger fire-tolerant trees and restoring conditions suited to low-intensity burning. Prescribed fire management covers deliberately lit burns and letting lightning fires run in damp weather, after which maintenance burns every fifteen to twenty years keep fuel loads down.
overall_html: The passage argues that aggressive fire suppression has made North American forests more dangerous rather than safer, because ecosystems such as ponderosa pine evolved with frequent low-intensity fires that kept fuel loads low, and decades without burning have set up catastrophic crown fires. The author's purpose is to recommend a policy shift from eliminating fire to managing it, and the structure moves from the ecological role of natural fire, through the destruction that follows its removal, to a concrete program of selective harvesting of smaller trees and prescribed burns with maintenance burns every fifteen to twenty years. The only viewpoint developed is the author's, aligned with the foresters and ecologists cited at the outset.
