Passage A

In 1994, Estonia became the first country to introduce a "flat tax" on personal and corporate income. Income is taxed at a single uniform rate of 26 percent: no schedule of rates, no deductions. So far eight countries have followed Estonia's example. An old idea that for decades elicited the response, "Fine in theory, just not practical in the real world," seems to be working as well in practice as it does on the blackboard.

Practical types who said that flat taxes cannot work offer a further instant objection, once they are shown such taxes working, namely, that they are unfair. Enlightened countries, it is argued, have "progressive" tax systems, requiring high-income earners to forfeit a bigger share of their incomes in tax than low-income earners have to pay. A flat tax seems to rule this out in principle.

Not so. A flat tax on personal incomes combines a threshold (that is, an exempt amount) with a single rate of tax on all income above it. The extent to which such a system is progressive can be varied within wide limits using just these two variables. Under the systems operating in most developed countries, the incentives for high-income earners to avoid tax (legally or otherwise) are enormous; and the opportunities to do so, which arise from the very complexity of the codes, are commensurately large. So it is unsurprising that high-income earners usually pay about as much tax under new flat-tax regimes as they would have paid under the previous codes.

Passage B

A lot of people don't understand graduated, as opposed to "flat," taxes. They think that if you make more money you pay a higher rate on your entire earnings, which seems unfair. Actually, graduated progressive taxes treat all taxpayers equally. Every taxpayer pays the same rate on equivalent layers of income. People in higher brackets don't pay the higher rate on their entire income, only on the portion of income over a specified amount. People, not dollars, are treated equally.

All people are created equal, but not all dollars are created equal. Earnings of the working poor go almost entirely for survival expenses such as food, shelter, and clothing. At that level, every dollar is critical; even a small difference causes tremendous changes in quality of life. Middle-income earners are still very conscious of expenses, but have much greater flexibility in absorbing small fluctuations in income.

Even some of the flat tax proposals recognize this, and want to exempt a primary layer from the tax system. So, since they recognize that survival dollars are different from discretionary dollars, why go suddenly from one extreme (paying no taxes) to the other (paying the top rate)? Since flat tax proposals are supposed to bring in the same total amount of tax revenue, if the working poor are going to pay less and the high-income earners are going to pay less, it is naturally going to fall on the middle class to make up the difference.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a fact meant to settle an old argument. Estonia adopted a flat tax in 1994, meaning one uniform rate on personal and corporate income with no rate schedule and no deductions, and eight countries have since copied it. The rhetorical work is in the last sentence: a proposal long dismissed as fine on paper but unworkable in reality now appears to work in reality too. The Author of A is writing as an advocate, and the opening is designed to clear away the practicality objection before the fairness objection is taken up.

The second paragraph stages the objection The Author of A wants to answer. The Practical Types, having lost the argument that flat taxes cannot function, fall back on the claim that they are unfair. Their reasoning rests on progressivity: an enlightened system makes high earners surrender a larger share of income than low earners do, and a single rate seems to make that impossible by definition. Notice this paragraph states the opposing case rather than endorsing it, and the phrase 'seems to rule this out' is already flagging where the rebuttal will land.

'Not so' delivers the rebuttal. A flat tax pairs a single rate with a threshold of exempt income, and adjusting those two numbers can produce a wide range of progressivity, so the objection confuses one rate with no progressivity. The Author of A then adds a practical argument: existing codes are so complex that high earners have both strong incentives and abundant opportunities to avoid tax, which is why high earners in flat-tax countries end up paying roughly what they paid before. The defense is thus both theoretical and empirical.

Passage B opens by correcting a misunderstanding running the other direction. The Author of B says many people wrongly imagine that moving into a higher bracket means paying the higher rate on everything they earn, which would indeed look unfair. In fact a graduated system applies the same rate to the same layer of income for everyone, and the higher rate touches only the portion above a set amount. The formulation to hold onto is the closing one: people are treated equally, dollars are not. That distinction is the hinge of the entire passage.

The next paragraph supplies the moral reasoning behind that distinction. For the working poor, nearly every dollar goes to food, shelter and clothing, so each one is essential and a small loss produces a large drop in quality of life. Middle-income earners still watch expenses but can absorb minor swings. The argument is about the differing real value of a dollar at different income levels, and it explains why The Author of B thinks equal rates on unequal dollars would not in fact be equal treatment.

The close turns that principle against flat-tax proposals on their own terms. The Author of B points out that some such proposals already exempt a base layer of income, which concedes that survival dollars differ from discretionary dollars; if so, jumping straight from a zero rate to the top rate makes no sense. Then comes the arithmetic objection: since flat taxes are meant to raise the same total revenue, cutting what the working poor and high earners pay leaves the middle class to cover the shortfall. Note this directly contests the reassurance offered at the end of Passage A.
overall_html: Passage A defends the flat tax against the charge of unfairness, arguing that a threshold plus a single rate can deliver as much progressivity as desired and that high earners already pay about the same under flat regimes as under complex ones, while Passage B defends graduated taxation on the grounds that equal treatment of people requires unequal treatment of dollars, since income spent on survival differs in kind from discretionary income. The two disagree directly on fairness and on who bears the burden, with The Author of B closing on the claim that a revenue-neutral flat tax shifts cost onto the middle class. A's purpose is to rebut The Practical Types; B's is to explain and justify progressivity.

passage_html:
The following passage is adapted from a journal article. 

To understand John Rawls's theory of justice, one first needs to grasp what he was reacting against. The dominant approach in pre-Rawls political philosophy was utilitarianism, which emphasized maximizing the fulfillment of people's preferences. At first sight, utilitarianism seems plausible—what else should we do but try to achieve the most satisfaction possible for the greatest number of people?—but the theory has some odd consequences. Suppose executing an innocent person will appease a mob, and that doing so will therefore increase total satisfaction. Incredibly, a utilitarian would have to endorse the execution. Rawls accordingly complains that, in the utilitarian view, there is no reason "why the violation of the liberty of a few might not be made right by the greater good shared by many."

If we reject utilitarianism and its view about the aim of the good life, how can we know what justice requires? Rawls offers an ingenious answer. He asserts that even if people do not agree on the aim of the good life, they can accept a fair procedure for settling what the principles of justice should be. This is key to Rawls's theory: Whatever arises from a fair procedure is just.

But what is a fair procedure? Rawls again has a clever approach, beginning with his famous veil of ignorance. Suppose five children have to divide a cake among themselves. One child cuts the cake but does not know who will get which shares. The child is likely to divide the cake into equal shares to avoid the possibility of receiving the smallest share, an arrangement that the others will also admit to be fair. By denying the child information that would bias the result, a fair outcome can be achieved.

Rawls generalizes the point of this example of the veil of ignorance. His thought experiment features a situation, which he calls the original position, in which people are self-interested but do not know their own station in life, abilities, tastes, or even gender. Under the limits of this ignorance, individuals motivated by self-interest endeavor to arrive at a solution in which they will not lose, because nobody loses. The result will be a just arrangement.

Rawls thinks that people, regardless of their plan of life, want certain "primary goods." These include rights and liberties, powers and opportunities, and income and wealth. Without these primary goods, people cannot accomplish their goals, whatever they may be. Hence, any individual in the original position will agree that everyone should get at least a minimum amount of these primary goods. Unfortunately, this is an inherently redistributionist idea, since the primary goods are not natural properties of human beings. If someone lacks a primary good, it must be provided, at the expense of others if necessary.
explanation_html:
The passage begins by defining the target before the theory, since Rawls is best understood as a reaction. The Utilitarians dominated political philosophy before him, holding that we should maximize the satisfaction of people's preferences for the greatest number. That sounds reasonable until you press it, and the passage presses it with a hard case: if executing an innocent person would calm a mob and raise total satisfaction, utilitarianism must approve. Rawls objects that the view supplies no reason why trampling the liberty of a few cannot be offset by benefits to many.

With utilitarianism set aside, a problem opens up, and the paragraph poses it directly: without agreement on what makes a life good, how can we determine what justice demands? Rawls's move is to sidestep the disagreement rather than settle it. People who disagree about the aim of life can still agree on a fair way of deciding the rules. The sentence to fix in memory is the one the passage flags as key, that whatever comes out of a fair procedure counts as just. Everything after this develops what fairness in a procedure means.

Having promised a fair procedure, Rawls must specify one, and the veil of ignorance is introduced through a homely illustration. Five children divide a cake; the one who cuts it does not know which slice will be theirs, so self-interest itself pushes toward equal shares, and the others accept the result as fair. The lesson the passage draws is about information rather than generosity: withhold the knowledge that would let someone bias the outcome in their own favor, and a fair outcome follows automatically.

Here the cake example is scaled up into the argument proper. Rawls's thought experiment, the original position, places people who remain self-interested but who do not know their social station, abilities, tastes, or gender. Deprived of that knowledge, self-interest cannot be aimed anywhere in particular, so each person reasons toward an arrangement in which they cannot lose, which means one in which nobody loses. Notice that the mechanism is identical to the cake case, only generalized, and the output is a just arrangement rather than merely an agreeable one.

The final paragraph draws out what the original position actually produces, and ends on a complication. Rawls holds that whatever plan of life people have, they all want primary goods such as rights and liberties, powers and opportunities, income and wealth, because without them no goals can be pursued. Anyone reasoning behind the veil will therefore insist everyone receive at least a minimum of them. The closing turn matters: since primary goods are not natural human properties, guaranteeing that minimum means supplying them, at others' expense if need be, making the theory inherently redistributionist.
overall_html: The passage explains John Rawls's theory of justice as a response to utilitarianism, tracing how his rejection of preference-maximizing leads to a procedural standard of justice, then to the veil of ignorance and the original position as the device that makes a procedure fair, and finally to the guaranteed minimum of primary goods that follows from it. The purpose is expository rather than argumentative, walking the reader through the theory's steps in the order Rawls builds them, with a concrete cake-cutting illustration in the middle. The two positions in view are The Utilitarians, whose willingness to sacrifice a few for the many Rawls rejects, and Rawls himself.

passage_html:
This passage was adapted from an article written by three economists.

Roughly 40 percent of the African American population of the Southern United States left the South between 1915 and 1960, primarily for the industrial cities of the North. While there was some African American migration to the North during the nineteenth century, most accounts point to 1915 as the start of what historians call the Great Migration. There were at least three catalysts of the Great Migration. First, World War I increased labor demand in the industrial North. Second, the war in Europe cut off immigration, which led many Northern employers to send labor agents to recruit African American labor in the South. Finally, a boll weevil infestation ruined cotton crops and reduced labor demand in much of the South in the 1910s and 1920s.

In short, the Great Migration began in 1915 and not earlier, because it was only then that the North–South income gap became large enough to start such a large-scale migration. Less clear, however, is why migration continued, and even accelerated, in subsequent decades, at the same time that North–South income differences were narrowing.

We propose that once started, migration develops momentum over time as current migration reduces the difficulty and cost of future migration. Economists have typically assumed that people migrate if their expected earnings in the destination exceed those of the origin enough to outweigh the difficulties and one-time costs of migration. Previous research suggests that the difficulties and costs arise from several sources. First, the uncertainty that potential migrants face concerning housing and labor-market conditions in the destination presents a significant hindrance. Second, there is the simple cost in terms of time and money of physically moving from the origin to the destination. Third, new migrants must familiarize themselves with local labor- and housing-market institutions once they arrive; they must find housing and work, and they must often adapt to a new culture or language.

Empirical studies show that during the Great Migration, information was passed through letters that were often read by dozens of people and through conversation when migrants made trips back to their home communities. Thus early migrants provided information about labor- and housing-market conditions to friends and relatives who had not yet made the trip. First-time African American migrants often traveled with earlier migrants returning to the North after a visit to the South, which reduced physical costs. Additionally, previous migrants reduced new migrants' cost of adapting to a new locale and culture by providing them with temporary housing, food, and even credit. Previous migrants also provided a cultural cushion for later migrants, so that they did not have to struggle as hard with their new surroundings.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the phenomenon to be explained, stated as a fact rather than a claim: about 40 percent of African Americans in the Southern United States left between 1915 and 1960, mostly for Northern industrial cities. Some movement north happened in the nineteenth century, but historians date the Great Migration from 1915, and three causes are offered for that timing. World War I raised labor demand in Northern industry; the war also halted European immigration, prompting Northern employers to send agents south to recruit; and a boll weevil infestation destroyed cotton crops, cutting Southern labor demand through the 1910s and 1920s.

This short paragraph is the hinge of the entire passage, so read it carefully. The three catalysts are compressed into a single economic explanation: migration started in 1915 because that is when the income gap between North and South grew wide enough to move large numbers of people. Then the puzzle is set. Migration did not merely continue but sped up in later decades, even as the very income difference credited with starting it was shrinking. Whatever explains the beginning cannot explain the continuation, and supplying that missing explanation is the job of the rest of the passage.

Here the Authors state their own hypothesis: migration builds momentum, because each wave of migrants makes the next wave easier and cheaper. To see why that matters, notice the model they are amending. Economists have generally assumed people move when expected earnings at the destination exceed those at home by enough to cover the difficulties and one-time costs of moving. Earlier research breaks those costs into three kinds: uncertainty about housing and jobs at the destination, the money and time of physically relocating, and the work of learning local labor and housing institutions while adapting to a new culture or language.

The closing paragraph shows the mechanism working, matching evidence to each cost named just before. Letters circulated among dozens of readers and migrants talked with people back home during return visits, so early migrants supplied friends and relatives with information about jobs and housing, which attacks the uncertainty problem. First-time migrants often traveled alongside experienced ones heading back north, lowering the physical cost. Established migrants also offered temporary housing, food and even credit, and cushioned newcomers culturally so the adjustment was less of a struggle. Every element of the momentum claim is thereby grounded in empirical findings.
overall_html: The passage argues that while the Great Migration began in 1915 because the North-South income gap had grown large enough to justify moving, its continuation and acceleration in later decades, as that gap narrowed, is better explained by momentum: earlier migrants lowered the uncertainty, the physical cost and the difficulty of adapting that faced those who followed. The authors' purpose is explanatory, moving from the phenomenon and its three catalysts, to a compressed statement of the puzzle, to their own hypothesis set against the standard economic model of migration costs, and finally to empirical evidence matching each cost. The viewpoints in play are the authors' own and the economists whose assumption they extend.

passage_html:
Passage A

Insider-trading law makes it a crime to make stock transactions, or help others make stock transactions, based on information you have ahead of the general public because of your special position within a company.

However, trading based on information you have that everyone else doesn't—isn't this part of the very definition of a functioning stock market? The entire field of stock brokering is based on people gaining knowledge that others don't have and then using it to profit themselves or their clients. If you analyze a stock, decide that it is overvalued, and sell it, you are taking advantage of knowledge that many others don't have. That doesn't make you a criminal; it means you've done your homework.

Stock markets work best when all the relevant information about a company is spread as widely as possible, as quickly as possible. Stock prices represent a constantly shifting amalgamation of everyone's information about and evaluations of a company's value. It helps when those who have accurate information about changing circumstances are permitted to act so that stock prices reflect them.

Someone selling a stock because they know something will happen soon that will lower the stock's value helps spread the knowledge that the price ought to be dropping. Such actions help ensure that stock prices do reflect a more accurate assessment of all the relevant facts. That's good for everyone in the stock market.

When contemplating insider-trading law, it helps to consider a far more widespread practice: "insider nontrading"—stock sales or purchases that would have been made, but aren't because of inside knowledge. This is certainly happening every day, and rightfully so. No one would think to lock someone up for it.

Passage B

One of the basic principles of the stock market is transparency. In a transparent market, information that influences trading decisions is available to all participants at the same time. Success in the market can then be gained only by skill in analyzing the information and making good investing decisions. In a transparent stock market, everyone has the same chance of making a good investment, and success is based on individual merit and skill.

In insider-trading situations, some people make investment decisions based on information that other people don't have. People who don't have access to the inside information can't make similarly informed investment decisions. That unfairly compromises the market: people with inside information can make informed trade decisions far before everyone else, making it difficult or impossible for other people to earn money in the stock market.

This, in turn, causes a loss of investor confidence and could ultimately destroy the market. People invest in the stock market because they believe they can make money. The whole point of capital investments is to make good investing decisions and make money over time. If investors believe they can't make money, they won't invest. Undermining investor confidence would thus deny companies access to the funds they need to grow and be successful, and it could ultimately lead to widespread financial repercussions.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens flatly with the legal definition it intends to challenge. Insider-trading law criminalizes making stock trades, or helping others make them, on the strength of information you hold before the public does because of your special position inside a company. No evaluation appears yet, but the neutrality is temporary. Read this as the setup: The Author of A states the rule cleanly so that the objections can be aimed at it precisely in the paragraphs that follow.

The challenge begins with a rhetorical question that reframes inside information as ordinary market activity. Trading on knowledge others lack, The Author of A argues, is what a stock market is. Brokering as a whole consists of acquiring knowledge others do not have and profiting from it. Analyze a stock, conclude it is overvalued, sell it, and you have not committed a crime; you have done your homework. Notice the strategy here is to show that the feature the law targets cannot be what distinguishes wrongdoing, since honest analysts share it.

Next comes the positive case, shifting from what is permitted to what is beneficial. Markets work best when information about a company spreads as widely and quickly as possible, because a stock price is a constantly updating composite of everyone's information and judgments about value. It therefore helps, on this account, when people who know about changing circumstances are free to act on that knowledge, since their trades feed it into the price. The argument has moved from insider trading being no worse than analysis to it being socially useful.

The point is then applied to the specific case the law forbids. Someone who sells because they know of a coming event that will lower a stock's value is, in effect, broadcasting that the price should fall. Such trades push prices toward a more accurate reflection of the relevant facts, which The Author of A calls good for everyone in the market. Keep the mechanism straight, since it is the load-bearing claim: trading transmits information into price, so restricting trading keeps prices wrong for longer.

The close offers a comparison meant to expose an inconsistency. Consider insider nontrading, meaning purchases or sales a person would have made but refrains from making because of what they know from inside the company. This happens constantly, The Author of A says, and properly so, and nobody proposes jailing anyone for it. The implication left for you to draw is that if acting on inside knowledge by not trading is unobjectionable, the line the law draws around trading looks arbitrary.

Passage B opens from the opposite premise, building on transparency rather than information flow. The Author of B defines a transparent market as one where information affecting trading decisions reaches every participant simultaneously, so the only route to success is skill at analyzing that information and choosing well. The consequence stressed is fairness of opportunity: everyone gets the same chance, and outcomes track individual merit. Note that this is the same market both authors are describing, but B treats equal access as the foundational value where A treated price accuracy as the goal.

The middle paragraph applies that standard to insider trading and finds it damaging. When some participants trade on information others cannot obtain, those outsiders simply cannot make comparably informed decisions. The Author of B calls this an unfair compromising of the market, and the stated harm is concrete rather than abstract: insiders can act far ahead of everyone else, which makes it difficult or impossible for other people to make money. This is the direct answer to The Author of A, treating asymmetry itself, not just fraud, as the injury.

The final paragraph traces the consequences outward into a chain. Unfairness costs investors their confidence, and confidence is what brings them in, since people invest expecting to make money over time. If they conclude they cannot, they stop investing, and companies then lose access to the capital they need to grow, with the possibility of widespread financial damage. Watch the escalation: B ends by arguing that the practice A defends as good for everyone in the market could destroy the market itself.
overall_html: Both passages ask whether insider trading should be prohibited and reach opposing conclusions. The Author of A argues that trading on superior information is what markets normally reward, that insider trades push prices toward accuracy, and that the accepted practice of insider nontrading exposes the law's line as arbitrary. The Author of B argues from transparency instead, holding that simultaneous access to information is what makes success a matter of merit, and that informational asymmetry unfairly disadvantages outsiders, erodes investor confidence, and could ultimately choke off the capital companies need. The disagreement is fundamental and turns on which value defines a healthy market: price accuracy or equal access.

passage_html:
There are some basic conceptual problems hovering about the widespread use of brain scans as pictures of mental activity. As applied to medical diagnosis (for example, in diagnosing a brain tumor), a brain scan is similar in principle to an X-ray: it is a way of seeing inside the body. Its value is straightforward and indubitable. However, the use of neuroimaging in psychology is a fundamentally different kind of enterprise. It is a research method the validity of which depends on a premise: that the mind can be analyzed into separate and distinct modules, or components, and further that these modules are instantiated in localized brain regions. This premise is known as the modular theory of mind.

It may in fact be that neither mental activity, nor the physical processes that constitute it, are decomposable into independent modules. Psychologist William Uttal contends that rather than distinct entities, the various mental processes are likely to be properties of a more general mental activity that is distributed throughout the brain. It cannot be said, for instance, that the amygdala is the seat of emotion and the prefrontal cortex is the seat of reason, as the popular press sometimes claims. For when I get angry, I generally do so for a reason. To cleanly separate emotion from reason-giving makes a hash of human experience.

But if this critique of the modular theory of mind is valid, how can one account for the fact that brain scans do, in fact, reveal well-defined areas that "light up" in response to various cognitive tasks? In the case of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), what you are seeing when you look at a brain scan is actually the result of a subtraction. The fMRI is usually interpreted as a map of the rate of oxygen use in different parts of the brain, which stands as a measure of metabolic activity. But what it actually depicts is the differential rate of oxygen use: one first takes a baseline measurement in the control condition, then a second measurement while the subject is performing some cognitive task. The baseline measurement is then subtracted from the on-task measurement. The reasoning, seemingly plausible, is that whatever remains after the subtraction represents the metabolic activity associated solely with the cognitive task in question.

One immediately obvious (but usually unremarked) problem is that this method obscures the fact that the entire brain is active in both conditions. A false impression of neat functional localization is given by differential brain scans that subtract out all the distributed brain functions. This subtractive method produces striking images of the brain at work. But isn't the modular theory of mind ultimately attractive in part because it is illustrated so well by the products of the subtractive method?
explanation_html:
The opening draws a distinction that governs everything after it. Used medically, a brain scan is essentially an X-ray, a way of looking inside the body, and its value is not in dispute. Used in psychology, though, neuroimaging is a different sort of enterprise, because its validity rests on an assumption rather than on simple seeing: that the mind divides into separate modules and that each module sits in a particular brain region. The Author names this the modular theory of mind and treats it as a premise to be examined, not a finding.

The premise is then attacked. Uttal is brought in to argue that mental processes are probably not discrete entities but properties of a general mental activity spread across the brain. The Author supplies the illustration: the popular claim that the amygdala houses emotion while the prefrontal cortex houses reason cannot hold, because getting angry usually involves having a reason to be angry. Separating emotion from reason-giving, in the passage's phrase, makes a hash of experience. Note that The Author is not merely reporting Uttal but arguing alongside him.

A fair objection is now raised against the critique, and answering it takes up the paragraph. If modularity is wrong, why do scans show defined regions lighting up during particular tasks? The answer is that an fMRI image is the product of a subtraction. It is usually read as a map of oxygen use standing in for metabolic activity, but what it actually shows is a difference: a baseline reading in the control condition subtracted from a reading taken while the subject performs the task, on the assumption that the remainder is the activity belonging to that task alone.

The closing paragraph converts that technical fact into the payoff. Because the subtraction removes everything common to both conditions, it hides the point that the whole brain is active in each, and the tidy localization the images display is an artifact of the method rather than a discovery about the brain. The Author ends on a pointed question rather than a flat assertion, suggesting that the modular theory owes part of its appeal to being illustrated so vividly by the very technique that presupposes it.
overall_html: The passage argues that using brain scans as pictures of mental activity in psychology rests on the questionable premise of a modular, localized mind, and that the neat functional localization such images display is largely produced by the subtractive method used to make them rather than found in the brain. The Author's purpose is critical, moving from a contrast with unproblematic medical imaging, to Uttal's case that mental processes are distributed, to an explanation of how fMRI subtraction works, and finally to the suggestion that the modular theory is attractive partly because the method illustrates it so well. The Author and Uttal share the skeptical position, set against the popular press and the modular theory's proponents.

passage_html:
The following passage is adapted from an article published in 1981.

Chinese is a language of many distinct dialects that are often mutually unintelligible. Some linguists have argued that a new dialect of Chinese has evolved in the United States, which is commonly used in the Chinatown section of San Francisco. The characterization of this "Chinatown Chinese" as a distinct dialect is based primarily on two claims: first, that it is so different from any other dialect used in China that a person newly arrived from that country might have a difficult time communicating with a Chinese American in San Francisco who speaks nominally the same language as the newcomer, and, second, that no matter which of the traditional Chinese dialects one speaks, one can communicate effectively with other Chinese Americans in San Francisco so long as one is proficient in the uniquely Chinese-American terminologies.

Regarding the first claim, much of the distinctive vocabulary of Chinatown Chinese consists of proper names of geographical places and terms for things that some people, especially those born and raised in villages, had never encountered in China. Some are transliterated terms, such as dang-tang for "downtown." Others are direct translations from American English, such as gong-ngihn ngiht ("labor" plus "day") for "Labor Day." However, the core of the language brought to the U.S. by Chinese people has remained intact. Thus, the new vocabulary has supplemented, but not supplanted, the traditional language in the traditional dialects. In fact, normal conversations can be conducted fairly readily between Chinese-speaking Chinese Americans and new arrivals from China, provided that they speak the same traditional Chinese dialect as each other. Terms not familiar to the newcomer, most of which would name objects, places, and events that are part of the local experience, can easily be avoided or explained by the speaker, or their meaning can be inferred from the context. The supposed language barrier is, therefore, mostly imaginary.

The second claim—that the sharing of a uniquely Chinese-American vocabulary makes possible communication among Chinese Americans no matter what their basic dialect of Chinese may be—is a misleading oversimplification. While many Chinese-American speakers of other Chinese dialects have become familiar with Cantonese, now the most common dialect of Chinese spoken in the U.S., through watching Cantonese movies and by hearing that dialect in Hong Kong, Guandong, or the U.S., this is not the same thing as sharing a single unique dialect. Moreover, the dialects of Chinese can differ markedly in their systems of sounds and, to some extent, in grammar and vocabulary, and these differences persist among Chinese-American speakers of these various dialects. Hence, even a common vocabulary for such things as names of U.S. cities, street names, and non-Chinese items does not guarantee mutual intelligibility because these words constitute only a minute percentage of each dialect and are generally peripheral to the core vocabulary.
explanation_html:
The passage sets up a claim it will spend the rest of its length dismantling. Chinese comprises many dialects that speakers of one often cannot understand in another, and Some Linguists hold that a new one has emerged in the United States, spoken in San Francisco's Chinatown. Their case rests on two specific claims, and you should number them as you read, because the structure of the passage tracks them exactly. First, that Chinatown Chinese differs so much from any dialect in China that a newcomer would struggle to communicate with a Chinese American speaking nominally the same language. Second, that whatever traditional dialect you speak, proficiency in the distinctively Chinese-American terminology lets you communicate with other Chinese Americans there.

The first claim is taken up and rejected. The Author observes that the distinctive vocabulary consists mostly of place names and words for things some speakers, especially those from villages, never met in China, some transliterated from English and some translated directly. The crucial point is that these additions supplement the inherited language rather than replace it, so the core brought from China remains intact. Speakers of the same traditional dialect can therefore converse readily, since unfamiliar local terms can be avoided, explained, or inferred from context. The Author's verdict is blunt: the supposed barrier is mostly imaginary.

The second claim gets a different objection, which the passage calls a misleading oversimplification rather than a straightforward error. The Author grants that many Chinese Americans who speak other dialects have picked up Cantonese, now the most common Chinese dialect in the country, through films and exposure in Hong Kong, Guandong or the United States, but insists that shared familiarity with Cantonese is not the same as sharing one unique dialect. Underneath, the dialects still differ in sound systems and somewhat in grammar and vocabulary, and a shared set of American city and street names is too small and too peripheral to guarantee mutual understanding.
overall_html: The passage rejects the claim that a distinct Chinese-American dialect has developed in San Francisco's Chinatown, answering in turn the two arguments offered for it: that newcomers from China cannot understand it, and that its shared vocabulary lets Chinese Americans of any dialect communicate. The Author's purpose is refutation, and the macro-structure is a two-part rebuttal that mirrors the two-part case laid out at the start, arguing first that the new vocabulary supplements rather than replaces the traditional dialects and second that a small shared stock of local terms cannot bridge genuine differences in sound, grammar and core vocabulary. The opposed viewpoints are Some Linguists and The Author.

passage_html:
In a typical Hollywood action movie, the hero skirts death to complete a mission. Bad guys shoot, cars explode, objects fall from the sky, but all just miss. If any one of those things happened just a little differently, the hero would be dead. Yet the hero survives.

In some respects, the story of our universe resembles an action movie. A slight change to any one of the laws of physics would likely have caused some disaster that would have disrupted the normal evolution of the universe and made life impossible. For example, if the strong nuclear force had been slightly stronger or weaker, stars would have forged very little of the carbon that seems necessary to form planets and living things. Indeed, it seems that in order for a universe to support life, the laws of physics must be so finely tuned that the very existence of such a universe becomes improbable.

Some cosmologists have tried to reconcile the existence of our universe with the seeming improbability of its existence by hypothesizing that our universe is but one of many universes within a wider array called the multiverse. In almost all of those universes, the laws of physics might not allow the formation of matter as we know it and therefore of life. But given the sheer number of possibilities, nature would have had a good chance to get the “right” set of laws at least once.

But just how exceptional is the set of physical laws governing our universe? The view that the laws of physics are finely tuned arises largely from the difficulty scientists have had in identifying alternative sets of laws that would be compatible with life.

The conventional way scientists explore whether a particular constant of physics is finely tuned is to tweak it while leaving all other constants unaltered. The scientists then “play the movie” of that universe—they do calculations, what-if scenarios, or computer simulations—to see what disasters occur. But there is no reason to tweak just one parameter at a time. By manipulating multiple constants at once, my colleague and I have identified numerous scenarios—hypothetical universes—where the physical laws would be very different from our own and yet compatible with the formation of complex structures and perhaps even some forms of intelligent life.

Fine tuning has been invoked by some cosmologists as indirect evidence for the multiverse. Do our findings therefore call the concept of the multiverse into question? I do not think this is necessarily the case for two reasons. First, certain models of the birth of the universe would lead us to expect the existence of something like the multiverse. Secondly, the multiverse concept may well prove to be the source of solutions to certain other long-standing puzzles in cosmology.
explanation_html:
An analogy opens the passage before any science appears. In the standard Hollywood action film the hero completes the mission while bullets, explosions and falling objects all narrowly miss; change any one of them slightly and the hero dies, yet somehow he lives. Nothing is being argued yet, so read this as a device rather than a claim. The improbable-survival structure is what the next paragraph will map onto the universe, and keeping the analogy in mind makes the physics that follows much easier to hold.

The analogy is now cashed out. Alter any law of physics slightly and some disaster would likely have derailed the universe's development and ruled out life. The example given is the strong nuclear force: nudge its strength either way and stars would have produced very little carbon, which appears necessary for planets and living things. The conclusion drawn is the fine-tuning claim, that a life-supporting universe requires laws calibrated so precisely that such a universe looks improbable. This is the puzzle the rest of the passage addresses.

One proposed solution comes from Some Cosmologists, who suggest our universe is one member of a much larger collection called the multiverse. In nearly all of those universes the laws would forbid matter as we know it and therefore life, but with enough universes on offer, nature had a decent chance of landing on the right set of laws at least once. Notice how this dissolves the improbability rather than denying it: an unlikely outcome stops being surprising when there are enough trials.

Rather than accept or reject the multiverse directly, the passage steps back to question the premise both sides share. How exceptional are our laws really? The Author points out that the fine-tuning view rests largely on scientists' failure to find alternative sets of laws compatible with life. That is a claim about what researchers have managed to identify, not about what exists, and flagging the difference is what sets up the methodological objection in the next paragraph.

The objection is that the standard procedure is too narrow. Conventionally, scientists adjust one physical constant while holding all others fixed, then run the calculations, what-if scenarios or simulations to see what goes wrong. The Author notes there is no reason to change only one at a time, and reports that by varying several constants together, he and a colleague found numerous hypothetical universes whose laws differ sharply from ours yet still permit complex structures and perhaps intelligent life. Fine tuning, on this showing, may be an artifact of method.

The close handles the obvious follow-up question with unexpected restraint. Since fine tuning has been cited as indirect evidence for the multiverse, does this work undermine the multiverse? The Author answers no, not necessarily, and gives two reasons: certain models of the universe's birth independently predict something like a multiverse, and the concept may turn out to solve other long-standing puzzles in cosmology. Watch this move carefully, since The Author weakens one argument for a hypothesis without rejecting the hypothesis itself.
overall_html: The passage takes up the claim that our universe's physical laws are finely tuned for life and argues that the apparent fine tuning may be an artifact of how scientists test it, since varying constants one at a time hides the alternative universes that emerge when several are varied together. The Author's purpose is to challenge that premise while remaining measured about its consequences, moving from an action-movie analogy, to the fine-tuning puzzle, to the multiverse response offered by Some Cosmologists, to a methodological critique, and finally to a refusal to conclude that the multiverse itself is thereby discredited. The viewpoints in play are Some Cosmologists and The Author, who reports his own research.

passage_html:
Passage A

Comedians are not amused when their jokes are stolen, and for that reason we might expect joke-stealing disputes to ripen into lawsuits occasionally. Copyright is the most relevant body of law; formally, it applies to jokes and comedic routines. Yet copyright infringement lawsuits between rival comedians are all but unheard of, despite what appears to be a persistent practice of joke stealing among stand-up comedians. The nonexistence of such lawsuits is a product of both practical considerations that render the cost of enforcing the formal law prohibitively expensive, and legal hurdles that make success difficult and uncertain in lawsuits relating to joke stealing. In the end, copyright law simply does not provide comedians with a cost-effective way of protecting their comedic material.

Conventional intellectual property wisdom holds that absent formal legal protection, there would be scant production of creative works, as potential creators would be deterred by the unlikelihood of recouping the cost of their creations. If there is no effective legal protection against joke theft, then why do thousands of comedians keep cranking out new material night after night?

The answer to this question is that, in stand-up comedy, social norms substitute for intellectual property law. Taken as a whole, this norms system governs a wide array of issues that generally parallel those ordered by copyright law. These norms are not merely hortatory. They are enforced with sanctions, including simple badmouthing and refusals to work with an offending comedian. These sanctions, while extralegal, can cause serious reputational harm to an alleged joke thief, and may substantially hamper a comedian's career. Using this informal system, comedians are able to assert ownership of jokes, regulate their use and transfer, impose sanctions on transgressors, and maintain substantial incentives to invest in new material.

Passage B

Accomplished chefs consider their recipes to be a very valuable form of intellectual property. At the same time, recipes are not a form of innovation that is effectively covered by current intellectual property laws. Recipes are rarely patentable, and combinations of ingredients cannot be copyrighted. Legal protections are potentially available via trade secrecy laws, but chefs very seldom use them. Instead, three implicit social norms are operative among chefs, and together these norms function in a manner quite similar to law-based intellectual property systems.

First, a chef must not copy another chef’s recipe innovation exactly. The function of this norm is analogous to patenting in that the community acknowledges the right of a recipe inventor to exclude others from practicing his or her invention, even if all the information required to do so is publicly available. A second norm mandates that, if a chef reveals recipe-related secret information to a colleague, that colleague must not pass the information on to others without permission. This norm gives a chef a property right similar to that attainable via a contract under trade secrecy law. A third norm is that colleagues must credit developers of significant recipes as the authors of that information. This norm operates in a manner analogous to copyright protection.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a puzzle rather than a thesis. Comedians resent having jokes stolen, and copyright formally covers jokes and routines, so you would expect lawsuits. Yet suits between rival comedians are essentially unheard of even though joke theft persists. The Author of A gives two reasons for the gap: enforcing the formal law costs more than it is worth, and legal obstacles make winning such a case difficult and uncertain. The conclusion is that copyright offers comedians no cost-effective protection, which leaves an obvious question about why they keep writing.

That question is now made explicit and sharpened against received theory. Conventional Intellectual Property Wisdom holds that without formal legal protection creative output would dry up, since creators could not expect to recover what their work cost them. Set that against the situation just described and a contradiction appears: thousands of comedians produce fresh material every night despite having no effective legal shield. Notice the paragraph does not answer the question, it only frames it, which is a common setup for a passage that will supply an alternative explanation next.

The answer is that social norms take the place of intellectual property law. The Author of A describes a system that covers roughly the same ground copyright would, and stresses that these norms are not just polite advice. They carry sanctions such as badmouthing and refusals to work with an offender, and although extralegal, those penalties can damage a reputation and set back a career. Through this informal machinery comedians claim ownership of jokes, control their use and transfer, punish violators, and retain real incentives to keep producing new material.

Passage B opens on the same structure applied to a different trade. The Author of B notes that accomplished chefs treat recipes as valuable intellectual property while current law barely protects them, since recipes are rarely patentable and ingredient combinations cannot be copyrighted. Trade secrecy law is technically available but chefs almost never invoke it. In its place operate three implicit social norms which, taken together, do work quite similar to a formal intellectual property system. Watch for the deliberate pairing of each norm with the legal device it mimics.

The three norms are then set out with their legal analogues attached. A chef must not copy another's recipe innovation exactly, which functions like a patent by letting the inventor exclude others even when the information is publicly available. A chef told a colleague's recipe secret must not pass it on without permission, which mirrors the protection a trade secrecy contract would give. Finally, colleagues must credit the developer of a significant recipe, which parallels copyright. Together these give chefs, like comedians, ordered property rights without the law.
overall_html: Both passages describe creative professions in which formal intellectual property law is effectively unavailable and informal social norms perform its work instead, so their relationship is one of agreement applied to parallel cases. The Author of A explains why copyright suits over stolen jokes essentially never happen, poses the puzzle of continued creative output that Conventional Intellectual Property Wisdom cannot explain, and answers it with a norms system enforced by reputational sanctions; The Author of B describes chefs, whose recipes law scarcely protects, and identifies three norms that mirror patent, trade secrecy and copyright. Each author's purpose is descriptive and explanatory rather than critical, and B supplies a second instance of the pattern A theorizes.

passage_html:
The novelist and social theorist Charlotte Perkins Gilman, whose writings were widely read and discussed in the early twentieth century, played an important role in the debate about the theories of Charles Darwin and their application to society. Darwin's theory of evolution did not directly apply to social ideology, but various intellectuals translated his ideas of natural selection into social language and argued about their interpretation. Some of these Social Darwinist theorists held that the nature of human social interactions is strictly determined by the process of biological evolution, and that it is futile to try to meddle with the competitive struggle for existence and the survival of the fittest. Another, more activist group of Social Darwinists held that although changes in human societies, like those that occur in biological species, do constitute a sort of evolution, this evolution at the level of a human society need not be competitive, but can emerge through collective action within society.

Gilman identified herself with this latter ideological camp and applied evolutionary theory in the movement for social change. The central thesis of this group of Social Darwinists was that although people, like all life, are the products of natural evolutionary forces, the principles of change that determine the development of organisms have brought humans to the point where it is possible for us to contribute consciously to the evolutionary process, to redesign and mold our societies in appropriate ways. This, for Gilman, was not simply a descriptive observation about humanity but was also a source of ethical responsibility. She argued that since a prime source of social evolution is human work, whether in crafts, trades, arts, or sciences, one of the primary ethical responsibilities of a person is to identify and engage in work that is societally relevant and that makes the best use of that person's talents.

Gilman was not merely engaged in an intellectual debate. Motivated by her ethical vision and convinced of the plasticity of human nature, Gilman vehemently sought to break the molds into which people, especially women, had been thrust. In both her fiction and her social theory she urges women to further social evolution by collectively working toward a reorganization of society. A central goal of the reorganization she envisioned would be the abandonment of gender-specific work roles and hierarchical relationships. Gilman believed that at one time such arrangements had been necessary for evolution because what she felt were male traits of assertiveness, combat, and display were essential for the development of a complex society. Future progress, she believed, now required the restoration of a balance that would include what she saw as female qualities of cooperation and nurturance.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by placing Gilman, a widely read novelist and social theorist, inside a specific intellectual argument, then spends most of its length mapping that argument. Darwin's evolutionary theory said nothing directly about society, but intellectuals translated natural selection into social terms and then disagreed about what it meant. Two camps emerge, and you should keep them apart. The Determinist Social Darwinists held that social interaction is fixed by biological evolution and that interfering with competitive struggle and survival of the fittest is pointless. The Activist Social Darwinists agreed that societies evolve but denied the process must be competitive, arguing it could proceed through collective action.

Gilman is then assigned to The Activist Social Darwinists, and their central thesis is spelled out. People are products of natural evolutionary forces, but those same forces have brought humanity to a point where we can consciously participate in evolution and reshape our societies deliberately. The important turn is what Gilman adds to this. For her the claim was not just a description of the human situation but the ground of an ethical duty, and since human work in crafts, trades, arts and sciences drives social evolution, each person is obliged to find socially useful work that suits their particular talents.

The closing paragraph moves from theory to Gilman's practice, which is the passage's real destination. Convinced that human nature is malleable and driven by that ethical vision, she attacked the fixed roles people, and especially women, had been forced into, urging women in both fiction and social theory to work collectively toward reorganizing society. The specific target was gender-specific work roles and hierarchical relationships. Her reasoning is historical rather than dismissive: she thought traits she regarded as male, assertiveness, combat and display, had once been necessary to build complex societies, and that progress now demanded restoring balance through qualities she saw as female, cooperation and nurturance.
overall_html: The passage presents Charlotte Perkins Gilman as a Social Darwinist of the activist rather than determinist kind, explaining how she took evolutionary theory to imply that humans can consciously direct their own social evolution and turned that claim into an ethical obligation to do socially useful work and to reorganize society. The Author's purpose is expository, situating Gilman within a debate, identifying her camp and its thesis, and then showing how she applied it in campaigning against gender-specific roles and hierarchy. The competing viewpoints to keep apart are The Determinist Social Darwinists, The Activist Social Darwinists, and Gilman's own extension of the latter position into ethics and advocacy.

passage_html:
The following passage was written in the mid-1990s.

Evidence that the earth's atmosphere has warmed has become quite compelling, in part because it has been reinforced recently by the development of accurate profiles of average annual temperatures throughout the last 1,000 years. These data, inferred from studies of geological patterns and samples of ice deposits, tree rings, and coral growth layers, indicate that the recent increase in average temperature—a rise of about one half of a degree Celsius over the last 100 years—is unprecedented in the previous 1,000 years. At the same time, other recent studies have strengthened the controversial link between this increase and the "greenhouse effect." Proponents of the greenhouse effect claim that the increase was caused by elevated levels in the atmosphere of certain gases that prevent heat from radiating back into space.

Early models charting the greenhouse effect were somewhat inconsistent with observed data; they estimated that the increase in the earth's atmospheric temperature over recent decades should have been higher than the increase observed in actuality, which led opponents to question the validity of the greenhouse theory. But new methods have enabled scientists to gauge the effect of greenhouse gases more accurately by taking into account an important factor that earlier studies overlooked: airborne sulfates. Sulfates from natural sources such as volcanoes as well as from human technological sources tend to counteract the heating effect of greenhouse gases by reflecting solar energy back into space. Taking into account the varying levels of airborne sulfates indicated by the concentration of sulfates in successive ages of glacial ice, these scientists have calculated theoretical temperatures for recent decades that are consistent with observed temperatures.

Another question for proponents of the greenhouse theory comes from scientists who have attempted to tie changes in the earth's atmospheric temperature to variations in solar energy. From observations of cycles in several types of solar phenomena, these scientists have developed models that chart variations in the sun's heating effects, and the models do show a strong decade-by-decade correspondence between solar activity and atmospheric temperature fluctuations. But the models cannot account for the entirety of the recent rise in atmospheric temperature. While researchers have found that the average annual atmospheric temperature fluctuates from one year to the next, its temperature over the long term has been relatively stable—deviations from the long-term average atmospheric temperature have inevitably reverted to this average, or equilibrium, temperature. But the current rise in temperature surpasses the most extreme fluctuations in temperature consistent with the models based on variations in solar energy. In light of all this, it seems reasonable to conclude that changes in the earth's atmosphere have raised its equilibrium temperature, and that greenhouse gases represent the best explanation of that shift.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by separating two things that are easy to run together: that warming happened, and what caused it. The first is presented as well established, strengthened by temperature profiles reconstructed for the past thousand years from geological patterns, ice deposits, tree rings and coral growth layers, which show that the roughly half-degree Celsius rise of the last century has no precedent in that span. The second is flagged as contested. Proponents of the Greenhouse Effect attribute the rise to raised atmospheric levels of gases that trap heat instead of letting it escape to space, and the passage notes only that recent studies have strengthened this controversial link.

Two objections to the greenhouse theory now get answered in turn, and this paragraph handles the first. Early greenhouse models predicted more warming than actually occurred, a discrepancy The Opponents used to question the theory. The resolution is a factor the early work left out: airborne sulfates, produced by volcanoes and by human technology, which reflect solar energy back to space and so offset the warming from greenhouse gases. Using sulfate concentrations preserved in successive layers of glacial ice to estimate past levels, scientists recalculated the theoretical temperatures and got figures matching what was observed. The mismatch was an omission, not a refutation.

The second challenge comes from The Solar Scientists, who tie temperature change to variation in solar energy and have built models, from cycles in solar phenomena, showing a strong decade-by-decade correspondence with temperature fluctuations. The rebuttal concedes the correspondence but denies it is sufficient. Long-term average temperature has been stable, with deviations always returning to an equilibrium value, and the current rise exceeds the most extreme swing those solar models allow. The Author then draws the conclusion the whole passage has been building toward: something has raised the equilibrium temperature itself, and greenhouse gases best explain that shift.
overall_html: The passage argues that recent atmospheric warming is real, unprecedented over the past thousand years, and best explained by greenhouse gases, defending that explanation against two challenges rather than presenting it as uncontested. The Author's purpose is to evaluate and ultimately endorse the greenhouse theory, and the macro-structure is a claim followed by two objections answered in sequence: the early models' overprediction, resolved by accounting for the cooling effect of airborne sulfates, and the solar-variation account, which matches short-term fluctuations but cannot cover a rise exceeding its most extreme predictions. Proponents of the Greenhouse Effect, The Opponents and The Solar Scientists appear as positions, with The Author siding with the first.

passage_html:
When interviewing witnesses to a crime, police interviewers seek to maximize the amount of information that a cooperating eyewitness can give them so that they can generate leads to follow, confirm or disconfirm alibis, and so forth. One method for eliciting information over and above what a cooperative witness might otherwise provide is the cognitive interview.

Developed by psychologists and adopted by police forces around the world, the cognitive interview combines cognitive techniques known to improve recall, such as multiple retrieval attempts, with communication strategies developed by social psychologists, such as conversation-management skills and techniques for building rapport between interviewer and interviewee. The general consensus is that this package has proven successful in increasing the number of details recalled by witnesses, with little impact on the number of incorrect details reported (neither increasing nor decreasing overall accuracy). However, a problem associated with the cognitive interview is that it is a complex procedure, requiring substantial training to learn and a long time to conduct. Because of this complexity, not all officers receive this training, and even trained officers often deviate from the procedures specified in the cognitive interview training.

An alternative to the cognitive interview is hypnosis. Indeed, hypnotic investigative interviewing was a precursor to the cognitive interview. However, even though the techniques involved are much less complex, the evidence suggests that overall accuracy, as determined by the proportion of correct to incorrect responses, is not generally improved with hypnosis; in fact, sometimes it may deteriorate. Hypnosis may also give rise to a "false confidence" effect, whereby witnesses are more confident in their reports generally, including reports of incorrect information. There are other practical difficulties, most notably that not all witnesses are susceptible to hypnosis.

For police interviewers, the ideal method for eliciting additional information from an eyewitness would be one that requires no special training for the interviewer, that can be applied to the entire population of potential witnesses, and that has a positive effect on correct memory reports, with no corresponding increase in false details reported. Research suggests that such a method may in fact be available. Encouraging eyewitnesses to close their eyes during recall attempts is a technique that is common to both hypnosis and the cognitive interview. Recent studies demonstrate that instructed eye-closure can benefit recall for both visual and auditory materials, for events witnessed on video, and for events witnessed through live interactions. These studies indicate an improvement over hypnotic interviewing, with no problems of participant dropout because of lack of hypnotic susceptibility. More significantly, instructed eye-closure by itself appears to improve witness recall to a degree equivalent to that demonstrated by the cognitive interview. And the benefits of eye-closure are achieved with no increase in errors, no specialist training, and no greater complexity of interviewing technique.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by establishing the practical goal that will serve as the yardstick for everything after it. Police interviewing a cooperative eyewitness want as much information as possible, because details generate leads and let alibis be confirmed or ruled out. One technique for pulling out more than a witness would otherwise volunteer is named here, the cognitive interview, but not yet explained. Read this as a problem statement: a method will be described, then a second, then a third, and each will be judged by how well it serves this aim.

The cognitive interview is now unpacked and assessed evenhandedly. Built by psychologists and used by police internationally, it pairs recall-boosting cognitive techniques such as repeated retrieval attempts with communication strategies from social psychology, including conversation management and rapport building. The consensus is that it works, raising the number of details recalled without changing how many are wrong, so overall accuracy stays where it was. The drawback is practical rather than scientific: the procedure is complex, demanding heavy training and considerable time, so many officers never learn it and even trained ones drift from the protocol.

Hypnosis is presented as the alternative and, historically, as the cognitive interview's forerunner. Its advantage is simplicity, but the evidence goes against it on the measure that matters, since the ratio of correct to incorrect responses generally fails to improve and can even worsen. Two further problems follow. Hypnosis can produce a false confidence effect, leaving witnesses more sure of everything they report, mistaken details included. And not every witness can be hypnotized, which limits how widely the method can be applied. Notice that each drawback names a criterion the closing paragraph will reuse.

The final paragraph states the ideal explicitly, then argues that it exists. What police want is a method needing no special training, usable on every potential witness, and raising correct recall without raising false details. The candidate is instructed eye-closure, a step already shared by hypnosis and the cognitive interview. Recent studies show it helps recall of visual and auditory material, for video and live events alike, with no dropouts for lack of hypnotic susceptibility, and on its own it matches the cognitive interview's benefit while adding no errors, no training burden and no complexity.
overall_html: The passage argues that simply instructing eyewitnesses to close their eyes during recall may be the best available interviewing technique, since it matches the recall gains of the cognitive interview while avoiding the drawbacks of both established methods. The Author's purpose is comparative and recommending, and the macro-structure is a survey in which each option is measured against the same criteria: the cognitive interview raises recall without harming accuracy but is too complex to train and apply consistently, hypnosis is simpler but fails to improve accuracy and breeds false confidence in some witnesses while excluding others, and eye-closure delivers the benefit with no training, no added errors and universal applicability.

Passage A

In a 1978 lecture titled "The Detective Story," Jorge Luis Borges observes that, "The detective novel has created a special type of reader," and adds, "If Poe created the detective story, he subsequently created the reader of detective fiction." For Borges, this "special type of reader" confronts literature with such "incredulity and suspicions" that he or she might read any narrative as a detective story. Borges’s interest in this particular genre, of course, inspired a good deal of his own fiction, but his account also draws our attention to an insight into the general nature of literature.

Literature, according to Borges, is "an aesthetic event" that "requires the conjunction of reader and text," and what the detective story highlights, he suggests, is the way in which the reader forms the conditions of possibility for this "aesthetic event." Borges imagines that the participation of the reader is not extrinsic to but instead essential to the literary text. Thus, what unites works belonging to the same genre is the way those works are read, rather than, say, a set of formal elements found within the works.

Passage B

One can, if one wants, define genres of fiction as sets of texts sharing certain thematic similarities, but the taxonomic difficulties of such an approach are notorious. The problem of "borderline cases"—especially in science fiction—arises so often that the definition fails to demarcate genres entirely. A more fruitful way to characterize the distinction between genres is to view it as a distinction between reading protocols: between ways of reading, responding to sentences, and making various sentences and various texts make sense. We are free to read any text by any reading protocol we wish. But the texts most central to a genre are those texts that were clearly written to exploit a particular protocol—texts that yield a particularly rich reading experience when read according to one protocol rather than another.

Our major critical effort must therefore be an exploration of the specific workings of many of the individual rhetorical configurations that contour, exploit, or even create a specific reading protocol. Here—to give an example outside of fiction—is a general description of one aspect of the reading protocols associated with poetry: with poetry, we tend to pay more attention to the sound of the words than we do with prose. Therefore we look for rhetorical figures that exploit, among other things, the phonic aspects of the words making up the text. With science fiction, much of the significance of the story will manifest itself in the alternative workings of the world in which the characters maneuver. Therefore we will pay particular attention to the rhetorical figures by which differences between our world and the world of the story are suggested.
explanation_html:
Passage A begins with a claim borrowed from a 1978 lecture. Borges argues that the detective novel produced a distinctive kind of reader, so that Poe, in inventing the detective story, also invented its audience. What defines that reader is an attitude rather than a preference: such suspicion and disbelief that any narrative at all might be approached as a detective story. The paragraph notes that this interest shaped Borges's own fiction, then signals the real destination, which is not the genre itself but a wider insight about how literature works.

That insight is now drawn out. Borges treats literature as an aesthetic event requiring reader and text together, and the detective story matters because it makes visible how the reader supplies the conditions under which that event can happen. The reader's participation, on this view, is not something added from outside but part of what the literary text is. The conclusion to hold onto, since Passage B will develop it, is that what groups works into a genre is the manner in which they are read, not shared formal features inside them.

Passage B opens by rejecting the alternative Passage A set aside. The Author of B grants that one may define genres as sets of texts sharing thematic similarities, but calls the taxonomic troubles notorious, pointing to borderline cases in science fiction that appear so often the definition stops marking boundaries at all. The proposed replacement is a distinction between reading protocols, meaning ways of reading and of making sentences and texts make sense. A useful qualification follows: any text may be read by any protocol, but a genre's central texts are those written to exploit one particular protocol.

The closing paragraph turns that definition into a research program. If genres are reading protocols, criticism should investigate the specific rhetorical configurations that shape, exploit or even create them. Two illustrations show the method. With poetry we attend more to the sound of words than in prose, so we look for figures working on the phonic level. With science fiction, meaning lives largely in how the story's world operates differently from ours, so we watch for the figures that signal those differences. Notice the practical payoff: the protocol tells the critic what to look for.
overall_html: Both passages argue that genre is properly defined by how texts are read rather than by formal or thematic features they contain, so the relationship is one of agreement in which the second develops and applies what the first establishes. Passage A presents Borges's view that the detective story created its own kind of reader and that literature is an aesthetic event requiring the reader's participation, making reading itself the unifying principle of a genre. Passage B rejects thematic taxonomies as unable to handle borderline cases, redefines genres as reading protocols, and then converts that definition into a critical program of studying the rhetorical figures that particular protocols exploit.
