It might reasonably have been expected that the adoption of cooking by early humans would not have led to any changes in human digestive anatomy. After all, cooking makes food easier to eat, which means that no special adaptations are required to process cooked food. However, current evidence suggests that humans today are capable of living on raw food only under unusual circumstances, such as a relatively sedentary lifestyle in a well supported urban environment. Important theoretical obstacles to living on raw food in the wild today include both the low digestibility of much raw plant food, and the toughness of much raw meat. These points suggest that humans are so evolutionarily constrained to eating foods that are digestible and easily chewed that cooking is normally obligatory. Furthermore, the widespread assumption that cooking could not have had any impact on biological evolution because its practice is too recent appears to be wrong. (Various European and Middle Eastern sites that go back more than 250,000 years contain extensive evidence of hominid use of fire and apparent “earth ovens.”) The implication is that the adoption of cooked food created opportunities for humans to use diets of high caloric density more efficiently. Selection for such efficiency, we suggest, led to an inability to survive on raw-food diets in the wild.

Important questions therefore arise concerning what limits the ability of humans to utilize raw food. The principal effect of cooking considered to date has been a reduction in tooth and jaw size over evolutionary time. Human tooth and jaw size show signs of decreasing approximately 100,000 years ago; we suggest that this was a consequence of eating cooked food. Subsequent population variation in the extent and timing of dental reduction is broadly explicable by regional variation in the times when improvements in cooking technology were adopted. It is also possible that the earliest impact of cooking was the reduction of tooth and jaw size that accompanied the evolution of Homo ergaster approximately 1.9 million years ago. If so, the decrease in tooth and jaw size that started around 100,000 years ago may prove to result from later modifications in cooking technique, such as the adoption of boiling.

The evolution of soft parts of the digestive system is harder to reconstruct because they leave no fossil record. Human digestive anatomy differs from that of the other great apes in ways that have traditionally been explained as adaptations to a high raw-meat diet. Differences include the smaller gut volume, longer small intestine, and smaller colon. All such features are essentially adaptations to a diet of relatively high caloric density, however, and may therefore be at least as well explained by the adoption of cooking as by eating raw meat. Testing between the cooking and raw-meat models for understanding human digestive anatomy is therefore warranted.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up an expectation and then knocks it down. You might assume cooking changed nothing about human digestive anatomy, since cooking makes food easier to handle and so demands no special adaptation. Evidence points the other way. People today can live on raw food only in unusual conditions, such as a sedentary life in a well supplied city, because much raw plant matter digests poorly and much raw meat is tough to chew. The Authors also dismiss the objection that cooking is too recent to matter, citing European and Middle Eastern sites over 250,000 years old with fire use and apparent earth ovens. Their proposal is that cooked food allowed efficient use of calorie-dense diets, and selection for that efficiency cost us the ability to survive on raw food in the wild.

Having established that cooking mattered, the passage asks what specifically limits our capacity to use raw food, and turns to the hard tissue evidence first. The best studied effect is shrinkage of teeth and jaws. Human teeth and jaws begin decreasing about 100,000 years ago, which The Authors attribute to cooked food, and later variation between populations in how much and how early this happened tracks regional differences in when better cooking technology arrived. A second, bolder possibility is floated: cooking's first effect may have been the tooth and jaw reduction accompanying Homo ergaster roughly 1.9 million years ago, in which case the change 100,000 years ago reflects later refinements such as boiling.

The final paragraph shifts to soft tissue, and flags why it is harder ground: these structures leave no fossils. Human digestive anatomy differs from that of other great apes in having smaller gut volume, a longer small intestine and a smaller colon, differences traditionally credited to a diet high in raw meat. The Authors make a careful move rather than a sweeping claim. Every one of these features is an adaptation to food of high caloric density, and cooking raises caloric density too, so the cooking explanation fits at least as well. They therefore call for testing the two models against each other rather than declaring a winner.
overall_html: The passage argues that the adoption of cooking exerted real evolutionary pressure on human anatomy, contrary to the assumptions that cooked food requires no adaptation and that cooking is too recent to have mattered, and that humans are now unable to live on raw food in the wild as a result. The Authors' purpose is to advance and support their own hypothesis, moving from the case that cooking is effectively obligatory for humans, to the fossil evidence of reduced teeth and jaws, to the soft tissues of the digestive tract, where they contend that features usually credited to a raw-meat diet are equally consistent with cooking and call for the two models to be tested against each other.

This passage was adapted from an article published in 2003.

For two decades, Wynton Marsalis complemented his extraordinary gifts as a jazz trumpeter with persuasive advocacy of the importance of jazz history and jazz masters. At his peak, Marsalis ruled the jazz universe, enjoying virtually unqualified admiration as a musician and unsurpassed influence as the music's leading promoter and definer. But after drawing increasing fire from critics and fellow musicians alike for his neotraditionalism, the biggest name in jazz faces an uncertain future, as does jazz itself.

In 1999, to mark the end of the century, Marsalis issued a total of fifteen new CDs. In the following two years he did not release a single collection of new music. In fact, after two decades with Columbia Records—the prestigious label historically associated with Duke Ellington, Thelonious Monk, and Miles Davis—Marsalis has no record contract with any company. Over the past few years Columbia has drastically reduced its roster of active jazz musicians, shifting its emphasis to reissues of old recordings. Atlantic Records folded its jazz catalog into the operations of its parent company, Warner Music, and essentially gave up on developing new artists.

For this grim state of affairs in jazz, Marsalis, the public face of the music and the evident master of its destiny, has been accused of being at least partly culpable. Critics charge that, by leading jazz into the realm of unbending classicism and by sanctifying a canon of their own choosing, Marsalis and his adherents have codified the music into a stifling orthodoxy and inhibited the innovative impulses that have always advanced jazz. As a former executive with Columbia noted, "For many people, Marsalis has come to embody some retro ideology that is not really of the moment—it's more museumlike in nature, a look back."

Indeed, in seeking to elevate the public perception of jazz and to encourage young practitioners to pay attention to the music's traditions, Marsalis put great emphasis on its past masters. Still, he never advocated mere revivalism, and he has demonstrated in his compositions how traditional elements can be alluded to, recombined, and reinvented in the name of individualistic expression, taking the nature of that tradition and trying to push it forward. However, record executives came away with a different message: if the artists of the past are so great and enduring, why continue investing so much in young talent? So they shifted their attention to repackaging their catalogs of vintage recordings.

Where the young talent saw role models and their critics saw idolatry, the record companies saw brand names—the ultimate prize of marketing. For long-established record companies with vast archives of historic recordings, the economics were irresistible: it is far more profitable to wrap new covers around albums paid for generations ago than it is to find, record, and promote new artists.
explanation_html:
The opening establishes a rise-and-reversal shape you should hold onto. For twenty years Marsalis was both a gifted trumpeter and an effective champion of jazz history and its old masters, admired as a player and unmatched as the music's promoter and definer. The 'but' turns the paragraph: criticism from the Critics, meaning reviewers and other musicians, has mounted against his neotraditionalism, and now his future is uncertain. Note the final clause, which quietly widens the stakes from one career to the art form itself, and tells you the passage will be about jazz's condition, not just Marsalis's reputation.

Rather than argue, the second paragraph piles up facts. Marsalis released fifteen CDs in 1999 to mark the century's end, then nothing new for two years, and after two decades at Columbia, the label of Ellington, Monk and Davis, he now has no contract anywhere. The industry numbers point the same way: Columbia cut its active jazz roster sharply and turned toward reissuing old recordings, while Atlantic absorbed its jazz catalog into Warner Music and stopped developing new artists. Read this as evidence establishing a decline, with no explanation offered yet.

Now the passage supplies an accusation and, importantly, attributes it rather than asserting it. Because Marsalis is the public face of jazz, he has been blamed for at least part of the decline. The Critics' specific charge is that he and his followers pushed jazz into rigid classicism, canonized a body of work of their own choosing, hardened the music into stifling orthodoxy and suppressed the innovation that always drove jazz forward. A former Columbia executive's remark sharpens the image, describing Marsalis as embodying something museumlike and backward-looking rather than current.

Watch the concession-then-correction move here, because this is where the Author's own position emerges. It is true that Marsalis stressed past masters, wanting to raise jazz's public standing and push young players toward the tradition. But the author denies he preached simple revivalism, pointing to compositions in which traditional material is alluded to, recombined and reinvented as individual expression that moves the tradition forward. The damage came from misreading: the record executives heard the praise of past greatness and concluded that investing in young talent was pointless, so they turned to repackaging vintage catalogs.

The final paragraph names the real culprit by lining up three readings of the same tradition. Young musicians saw role models, the Critics saw idolatry, and the record executives saw brand names, which is what marketing prizes most. For companies sitting on deep archives, the arithmetic settled it: putting new covers on albums whose costs were paid generations ago beats the expense of finding, recording and promoting unknown artists. Notice the author's implicit verdict, that economics rather than Marsalis's aesthetic is what drained investment out of jazz.
overall_html: The passage argues that although Marsalis has been blamed for stifling jazz by enshrining its past, his actual practice reinvented tradition rather than merely reviving it, and the music's commercial decline owes more to record companies who saw in that tradition a cheap supply of marketable brand names than to his aesthetic. The author's purpose is corrective, moving from Marsalis's rise and reversal, through evidence of industry retreat, to the critics' accusation, and finally to a concession that becomes a reassignment of blame. Three viewpoints matter: Marsalis, the critics who charge him with orthodoxy, and the record executives whose profit calculation the author treats as the decisive factor.

Common sense suggests that we know our own thoughts directly, but that we infer the thoughts of other people. The former process is noninferential and infallible, while the latter is based on others' behavior and can always be wrong. But this assumption is challenged by experiments in psychology demonstrating that in certain circumstances young children tend to misdescribe their own thoughts regarding simple phenomena while nonetheless correctly describing those phenomena. It seems that these children have the same thoughts that adults have regarding the phenomena but are much less capable of identifying these thoughts. Some psychologists argue that this indicates that one's awareness of one's own thoughts is every bit as inferential as one's awareness of another person's thoughts. According to their interpretation of the experiments, thoughts are unobservable entities that, among other things, help to explain why we act as we do. It follows from this that we are wrong to think of ourselves as having noninferential and infallible access to our own thoughts.

Recognizing an obligation to explain why we cling so tenaciously to an illusory belief in noninferential and infallible knowledge of our own thoughts, these psychologists suggest that this illusion is analogous to what happens to us when we become experts in a particular area. Greater expertise appears to change not only our knowledge of the area as a whole, but our very perception of entities in that area. It appears to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them. For instance, chess experts claim the ability to see without calculation whether a position is weak or strong. From a psychological perspective, we become so expert in making incredibly fast introspective inferences about our thinking that we fail to notice that we are making them. This failure leads naturally to the supposition that there is no way for us to be wrong in our identification of what we ourselves think because we believe we are perceiving it directly.

In claiming that we have only inferential access to our thoughts, the psychologists come perilously close to claiming that we base our inferences about what we ourselves are thinking solely on observations of our own external behavior. But, in fact, their arguments do not commit them to this claim; the psychologists suggest that we are somehow able to base our inferences about what we are thinking on internal cognitive activity that is not itself thought—e.g., fleeting and instantaneous sensations and emotions. The frequent occurrence of such internal activities explains why we develop the capacity to make quick and reliable inferences. Their internality makes it impossible for anyone else to make an inference based on them that contradicts our own. Thus, they are crucial in creating the illusion of noninferentiality and infallibility.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the commonsense picture it means to unsettle: we know our own thoughts directly and cannot be wrong about them, while our knowledge of other people's thoughts is inferred from behavior and always fallible. The challenge comes from experiments in which young children misdescribe their own thoughts about simple phenomena while describing the phenomena themselves correctly, suggesting they have the adult thought but cannot identify it. Some Psychologists read this as showing that awareness of one's own thoughts is just as inferential as awareness of anyone else's, since thoughts are unobservable entities posited partly to explain behavior. The commonsense picture of direct, infallible access therefore fails.

Having overturned the intuition, Some Psychologists take on a debt they explicitly acknowledge: explaining why the illusion is so hard to shake. Their answer is an analogy with expertise. Becoming expert in a domain seems to change not only what you know but how you perceive the things in it, so that entities and relations you once had to reason about now appear to be simply seen, as chess experts report telling a strong position from a weak one without calculating. On this account we grow so practiced at making lightning-fast introspective inferences that we stop noticing they are inferences, and that unnoticed speed breeds the sense that error is impossible because perception is direct.

The final paragraph identifies a danger in the position and then shows how it is avoided, which is where The Author becomes audible. Saying that access to our thoughts is merely inferential comes uncomfortably close to saying we read our own minds only from our outward behavior, an implausible result. The Author notes the psychologists are not committed to it, since they hold that the inferences rest on internal cognitive activity that is not itself thought, such as fleeting sensations and emotions. Because these occur constantly we get fast and reliable at using them, and because they are private nobody else can contradict our inferences, which is precisely what sustains the illusion.
overall_html: The passage examines the psychological claim that our knowledge of our own thoughts is inferential rather than direct and infallible, presenting the experimental basis for it, the account it offers of why the contrary intuition persists, and a clarification that saves it from an implausible consequence. The Author's purpose is largely expository and mildly sympathetic, laying out the view of Some Psychologists in three steps: children who hold adult thoughts yet misidentify them, an analogy with expertise in which fast unnoticed inference feels like direct perception, and the appeal to private internal sensations that both makes such inference reliable and shields it from contradiction by others.

passage_html:
This passage is based on an article written in 1995.

Dowsing is the practice of detecting resources or objects beneath the ground by passing handheld, inert tools such as forked sticks, pendulums, or metal rods over a terrain. For example, dowsers typically determine prospective water-well drilling locations by walking with a horizontally held forked tree branch until it becomes vertical, claiming the branch is pulled to this position. The distance to the water from the surface and the potential well's flow rate are then determined by holding the branch horizontally again and either walking in place or backwards while the branch is pulled vertical again. The number of paces indicates the distance to the water, and the strength of the pull felt by the dowser correlates with the potential well's flow rate.

Those skeptical of dowsing's efficacy point to the crudeness of its methods as a self-evident reason to question it. They assert that dowsers' use of inert tools indicates that the dowsers themselves actually make subconscious determinations concerning the likely location of groundwater using clues derived from surface conditions; the tools' movements merely reflect the dowsers' subconscious thoughts. Further, skeptics say, numerous studies show that while a few dowsers have demonstrated considerable and consistent success, the success rate for dowsers generally is notably inconsistent. Finally, skeptics note, dowsing to locate groundwater is largely confined to areas where groundwater is expected to be ubiquitous, making it statistically unlikely that a dowsed well will be completely dry.

Proponents of dowsing point out that it involves a number of distinct techniques and contend that each of these techniques should be evaluated separately. They also note that numerous dowsing studies have been influenced by a lack of care in selecting the study population; dowsers are largely self-proclaimed and self-certified, and verifiably successful dowsers are not well represented in the typical study. Proponents claim that successful dowsers may be sensitive to minute changes in Earth's electromagnetic field associated with variations in subsurface conditions. They also claim that these dowsers have higher success rates than geologists and hydrologists who use scientific tools such as electromagnetic sensors or seismic readings to locate groundwater.

The last two claims were corroborated during a recent and extensive study that utilized teams of the most successful dowsers, geologists, and hydrologists to locate reliable water supplies in various arid countries. Efforts were concentrated on finding groundwater in narrow, tilted fracture zones in bedrock underlying surface sediments. The teams were unfamiliar with the areas targeted, and they agreed that no surface clues existed that could assist in pinpointing the locations of fracture zones. The dowsers consistently made significantly more accurate predictions regarding drill sites, and on request even located a dry fracture zone, suggesting that dowsers can detect variations in subsurface conditions.
explanation_html:
Before the passage proper, a dating note tells you the article comes from 1995. That matters only for calibration: when the final paragraph calls a study recent, recent means recent as of that year, and the instruments mentioned for locating groundwater are the ones available then. Nothing in the argument turns on the date, but treat it as a reminder to judge the evidence by the standards of its own era rather than by what has been established since.

The opening definition is deliberately plain and value-neutral. Dowsing means hunting for buried resources by walking over ground holding a passive tool — a forked branch, a pendulum, a metal rod — that supposedly moves on its own. The water-well example spells out the procedure: the branch swings vertical over a promising spot, and the dowser then converts a second pass into numbers, counting paces to estimate how deep the water lies and reading the strength of the pull as the well's likely flow rate. No verdict is offered yet; the author is simply laying out what will be argued about.

Objections arrive next, from the skeptics. Their first move is intuitive: the tools are crude and inert, so nothing in them could be responding to water, and any movement must come from the dowser's own hand, driven by subconscious guesses read off surface conditions. Their second is statistical, since studies show a scattering of consistently successful individuals but an unreliable success rate for dowsers as a group. Their third is a base-rate point worth holding onto: dowsing is mostly practised where groundwater is expected everywhere, so a dowsed well is unlikely to come up dry by chance alone.

The proponents answer on each front. Dowsing is not one technique but several, they say, so testing the mixture as a single thing proves little. The study populations are also contaminated: because dowsers certify themselves, the demonstrably good ones rarely turn up in a typical sample, which would drag down the group success rate the skeptics cite. Then come two positive claims to keep separate from the defensive ones — that skilled dowsers may be sensitive to tiny variations in Earth's electromagnetic field caused by subsurface conditions, and that they outperform geologists and hydrologists working with instruments.

The final paragraph is where the author stops reporting and starts endorsing, and the hinge is the phrase about the last two claims: it is the electromagnetic sensitivity and the outperformance that the study corroborated, not the earlier procedural complaints. Notice how the design closes the skeptics' loopholes — arid countries, unfamiliar terrain, water hidden in narrow tilted fracture zones in bedrock, and agreement from every team that no surface clues were available. The dowsers predicted drill sites significantly more accurately and, on request, located a dry fracture zone, which undercuts the base-rate objection directly.
overall_html: The passage lays out the dispute over dowsing and comes down, cautiously but clearly, on the side of its defenders: a controlled study in arid regions found that the most successful dowsers outpredicted geologists and hydrologists on terrain offering no usable surface clues, supporting the claim that they detect genuine variations in subsurface conditions. The author's purpose is to weigh a contested practice rather than merely describe it, moving from a neutral definition of the technique, to the skeptics' three objections, to the proponents' replies and their two testable claims, and finally to the study that corroborates those claims. Keep the skeptics, the proponents, and the author's own late endorsement distinct.

passage_html:
Passage A

Why do some trial court judges oppose conducting independent research to help them make decisions? One of their objections is that it distorts the adversarial system by requiring an active judicial role and undermining the importance of evidence presented by the opposing parties. Another fear is that judges lack the wherewithal to conduct first-rate research and may wind up using outlier or discredited scientific materials.

While these concerns have some merit, they do not justify an absolute prohibition of the practice. First, there are reasons to sacrifice adversarial values in the scientific evidence context. The adversarial system is particularly ill-suited to handling specialized knowledge. The two parties prescreen and compensate expert witnesses, which virtually ensures conflicting and partisan testimony. At the same time, scientific facts are general truths not confined to the immediate cases. Because scientific admissibility decisions can exert considerable influence over future cases, erroneous decisions detract from the legitimacy of the system. Independent research could help judges avoid such errors.

Second, a trial provides a structure that guides any potential independent research, reducing the possibility of a judge's reaching outlandish results. Independent research supplements, rather than replaces, the parties' presentation of the evidence, so the parties always frame the debate.

Passage B

Regardless of what trial courts may do, appellate courts should resist the temptation to conduct their own independent research of scientific literature.

As a general rule, appellate courts do not hear live testimony. Thus these courts lack some of the critical tools available at the trial level for arriving at a determination of the facts: live testimony and cross-examination. Experts practicing in the field may have knowledge and experience beyond what is reflected in the available scientific literature. And adverse parties can test the credibility and reliability of proffered literature by subjecting the expert witness to the greatest legal engine ever invented for the discovery of truth—cross-examination. The trial judge may even participate in the process by questioning live witnesses. However, these events can only occur at the trial level.

Literature considered for the first time at the appellate level is not subject to live comment by practicing experts and cannot be tested in the crucible of the adversarial system. Thus one of the core criticisms against the use of such sources by appellate courts is that doing so usurps the trial court's fact-finding function. Internet sources, in particular, have come under criticism for their potential unreliability.

When an appellate court goes outside the record to determine case facts, it ignores its function as a court of review, and it substitutes its own questionable research results for evidence that should have been tested in the trial court. This criticism applies with full force to the use of outside-the-record texts and treatises, regardless of the medium in which they are found.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by putting the objection first rather than the thesis: why do some trial judges refuse to research a scientific question on their own? Two worries are attributed to the objecting judges. The first is structural — a judge who investigates becomes an active participant, which unbalances the adversarial system and demotes the evidence the two sides actually put in. The second is practical: judges are not trained researchers and could end up leaning on fringe or discredited scientific material.

The concession in the first clause is doing real work. Author A grants the worries some merit, then narrows the target to an absolute prohibition, which is far easier to defeat. The first affirmative reason attacks the premise that adversarial values must always win. Specialized knowledge is where the system performs worst, since each side screens and pays its own expert, so partisan and conflicting testimony is near guaranteed. And because scientific facts are general truths, an admissibility ruling reaches beyond the case at hand, so errors cost the system legitimacy.

The second reason answers the competence objection, and notice how modest it is. Author A does not claim judges are good researchers; the claim is that the trial itself constrains what they can do with research. Any inquiry is guided by the issues the trial has framed, and it supplements the parties' presentation rather than displacing it, so the parties still set the terms of the debate. That containment is what makes an outlandish result unlikely.

Passage B opens with its conclusion in a single sentence, and the opening clause is the key to the whole comparison: whatever trial courts do is set aside deliberately. The argument is aimed only at appellate courts, which should not go digging through scientific literature themselves. Read this as a change of level rather than a direct contradiction of Passage A, and everything that follows will read as an explanation of why the appellate level is the special case.

The reason turns on what appellate courts structurally lack. They do not hear live witnesses, so two fact-finding tools are missing. Practising experts often know things the published literature has not caught up with, and that knowledge only surfaces when someone testifies. More important to Author B is cross-examination, praised in the strongest possible terms as the engine for discovering truth, since it lets opposing parties probe whether a source is credible. The trial judge can even question witnesses directly. None of this exists on appeal.

Now the consequence. Material introduced for the first time on appeal has never been commented on by a live expert and never run through adversarial testing, and the resulting criticism is jurisdictional rather than merely evidentiary: the appellate court takes over fact-finding that belongs to the trial court. Internet sources draw particular fire for unreliability, but keep that in proportion, because it is offered as one instance of the problem rather than its core.

The closing paragraph restates the objection at full strength and then widens it. Leaving the record behind means abandoning the reviewing role and swapping untested research for evidence that should have been tested below. Author B's last sentence forecloses the obvious escape route, insisting the criticism applies with full force to treatises and printed texts too, so nobody can treat this as a complaint about the internet that better-quality sources would solve.
overall_html: Both passages ask whether judges may research scientific questions on their own, and they differ in scope rather than clashing head-on: Author A argues that trial judges should not face an absolute ban, since adversarial expert testimony handles science badly and the trial structure keeps any independent inquiry in check, while Author B argues that appellate judges must not do it, precisely because the appellate level has no live testimony or cross-examination to test what the judge finds. Author A's purpose is to rebut the objecting judges' two worries in turn; Author B's is to condemn a practice as a usurpation of the trial court's fact-finding role, extending the condemnation from internet sources to texts and treatises alike.

The United States Supreme Court’s 1948 ruling in Shelley v. Kraemer famously disallowed state courts from enforcing racially restrictive covenants. Such covenants are, in essence, private legal obligations included in the deed to a property requiring that only members of a certain race be allowed to occupy the property. Because it prohibited the enforcement of these covenants, the Court’s decision in Shelley v. Kraemer is justly celebrated for overturning a key instrument of housing discrimination. However, while few would deny that racially restrictive covenants are unjust, the stated legal rationale for the Shelley decision has nevertheless proven to be problematic.

The Shelley Court relied on the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which grants equal protection under the law to all U.S. citizens. This amendment had long been held to apply to state actors but not individuals. Shelley did not purport to alter this. But where, then, was the state action that is necessary for invoking the Fourteenth Amendment, given that the restrictive covenants were private contracts? The Court’s answer was that although the restrictive covenants themselves were perfectly legal, judicial enforcement of the covenants violated the Fourteenth Amendment because responsibility for a contract’s substantive provisions should be attributed to the state when a court enforces it. According to this "attribution" rationale, courts could enforce only those contractual provisions that could have been enacted into general law. Because the Fourteenth Amendment would not have allowed a law that banned members of a certain race from purchasing property, it followed from Shelley's analysis that judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants also was unconstitutional.

Shelley's attribution logic threatened to dissolve the distinction between state action, to which Fourteenth Amendment limitations apply, and private action, which falls outside of the Fourteenth Amendment’s purview. After all, Shelley's approach, consistently applied, would require individuals to conform their private agreements to constitutional standards whenever, as is almost always the case, the individuals want the option of later seeking judicial enforcement. Primarily for this reason, neither the Supreme Court nor lower courts later applied Shelley's approach. Courts routinely enforce contracts whose substantive provisions could not have been constitutionally enacted by government. For instance, courts regularly enforce settlement agreements that limit the settling party’s ability to speak publicly in various respects, despite the fact that statutory limitations on the identical speech would represent an unconstitutional violation of free speech.

Additionally, there is a particularly noxious aspect of the Shelley Court’s analytics—namely, the Court’s conclusion that racially restrictive covenants themselves were perfectly legal. The legal rationale behind the Shelley decision thus failed to target the genuine problem with racially restrictive covenants: what was troubling was not the covenants’ enforcement but their substantive content.
explanation_html:
The opening does two jobs at once, and separating them is the whole passage. First the facts: a racially restrictive covenant is a private clause written into a property deed limiting occupancy to members of one race, and in 1948 the Supreme Court barred state courts from enforcing such clauses. Then the split that the author will maintain throughout — the outcome deserves its celebration and the covenants really are unjust, but the legal reasoning offered for that outcome is defective. Watch for a critique of rationale, never of result.

The middle of the passage reconstructs the reasoning the author means to attack. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees equal protection, but it binds government, not private individuals, and the Shelley Court did not claim otherwise. That creates a puzzle, since a covenant is a private contract, so where is the government conduct that the amendment needs? The answer was to locate it in the courtroom: the covenant is legal, but a court that enforces one makes the state responsible for its terms. This attribution rationale implies a general rule — a court may enforce only terms that could lawfully have been passed as legislation — and since no statute could bar a race from buying property, enforcement fails too.

The first objection is that the rationale proves far too much. Almost nobody signs a contract meaning to give up the option of enforcing it, so if attribution were applied consistently, every private agreement would have to satisfy constitutional standards, and the line between state action and private action would collapse. The author's evidence that this is a real defect rather than a theoretical one is behavioral: neither the Supreme Court nor lower courts have used the approach since. Settlement agreements are the illustration, routinely enforced even though they gag parties in ways a statute imposing the same silence could never do.

The closing objection is moral rather than doctrinal, and the author flags it as the more offensive of the two. To reach its result, the Shelley Court had to declare the covenants themselves perfectly lawful and place the constitutional fault solely in their enforcement. That inverts what was actually wrong with them. On the author's reading, the trouble was never the machinery that gave the covenants effect but the racially exclusionary content written into them, which the decision's logic leaves formally untouched.
overall_html: The passage praises the result in Shelley v. Kraemer while arguing that the reasoning behind it was unsound, on two counts: the attribution rationale, which treats judicial enforcement of a private contract as state action, would subject virtually all private agreements to constitutional scrutiny and erase the state-action distinction, and it also required the Court to pronounce racially restrictive covenants themselves perfectly legal. The author's purpose is critical and diagnostic rather than revisionist, moving from the celebrated holding, to a careful reconstruction of the Court's Fourteenth Amendment logic, to the doctrinal overreach that later courts quietly declined to follow, and finally to the moral misidentification of what made the covenants objectionable. The viewpoints to keep apart are the Shelley Court's and the author's.

Through years of excavations and careful analysis of her finds around Krasnyi Yar in Kazakhstan, archaeologist Sandra Olsen has assembled what may be evidence of the earliest known people to have domesticated and ridden horses, a momentous development in human history. In remains of pit houses of the Botai people, who inhabited this area some 6,000 years ago, are large numbers of bones, 90 percent of them from horses. It is not immediately evident whether the horses were wild or domesticated, because unlike other animals such as dogs and sheep, domestic horses' bones are not morphologically different from those of their wild counterparts. So Olsen relies heavily on statistical tabulations of the Botai horses by sex and age at death, looking for mortality patterns that might correlate with expectations regarding domesticated herds or wild victims of hunting.

Herders of domesticated animals used for meat or milk typically kill off all but a few males before they are fully mature, but not the females, and archaeologists have evidence of a similar pattern for prehistoric goat herding. At the Botai sites, however, Olsen has found that most of the male horses were fully grown and slightly outnumber the females. One might suppose, then, that they were wild rather than domesticated animals; with many large animal species, hunters would preferentially target adult males so as to maximize size and meat yield. However, it is different with horses. Wild horses live in two types of groups: families consisting of one stallion, six or so adult females, and their young; and bachelor pods consisting of a few males. The families stick together when attacked, but the male groups tend to scatter, so to maximize success in hunting horses, one would target the families. Thus, if the Botai had merely hunted horses, Olsen argues, the proportion of adult male bones should be lower. But if they were in domesticated herds, why were the young males not culled, as would typically occur with, say, herds of goats? Olsen reasons that if the Botai had indeed begun riding, they would likely have kept males alive to ride.

Another clue that at least some of the horses may have been domesticated and that some may have even been ridden is in the fact that their remains include full skeletons, entire vertebral columns, and pelvises. It is unreasonable to suppose that hunters dragged whole 1,000-pound carcasses back to their dwellings. Olsen reasons that these were probably domesticated horses, together with, perhaps, some wild ones hunted and transported using the power of domesticated horses. A number of these nearly whole horse skeletons were discovered buried in a carefully arranged pattern with some of the only human remains yet found in the area, which further suggests a relationship to horses beyond that of merely hunting them as a source of meat.
explanation_html:
The opening sets up a detective problem and tells you why it is hard. Olsen, digging at Krasnyi Yar in Kazakhstan, thinks she may have found traces of the first people to tame and ride horses, which would be a major moment in human history. Her material is bone: the pit houses of the Botai, occupied roughly six thousand years ago, are full of animal remains, nine tenths of them equine. The obstacle is stated plainly and matters for everything that follows. Dogs and sheep were physically reshaped by domestication, so their bones betray it, but a domestic horse's skeleton looks like a wild horse's. With direct anatomical proof unavailable, Olsen has to work indirectly, tallying the sex and age at death of the horses and asking whether the resulting mortality pattern looks like a managed herd or a pile of hunted animals.

A chain of inferences follows, and tracking the turns is the real work. Start with the herding signature: people raising animals for meat or milk kill most males young and spare the females, a pattern already documented in prehistoric goats. The Botai bones fail that test, since the males are mostly adult and slightly outnumber the females, which at first glance suggests hunting, because hunters chasing big game usually pick adult males for the meat. Olsen's counter is that horses do not behave like other big game. Wild horses form families of a stallion, several mares and their young, plus separate pods of bachelor males; families hold together under attack while bachelors scatter, so an efficient hunter targets families and brings home few adult males. That leaves domestication, and the leftover puzzle of why the young males survived is where riding enters: males kept alive are males kept to ride.

A second and independent line of evidence closes the case. The deposits contain complete skeletons, intact spinal columns and pelvises, and Olsen's argument here is one of sheer practicality, since no hunting party is hauling half-ton carcasses back to the settlement whole. Animals that walked home are animals under human control, and she allows that some genuinely wild horses may also be in the assemblage, hunted and then carried back using domesticated horses as transport. The final detail pushes past subsistence altogether. Several near-complete horse skeletons were buried in a deliberate arrangement alongside the only human remains recovered from the area, which suggests the Botai related to horses as something other than a food supply.
overall_html: The passage presents Sandra Olsen's case that the Botai people of Kazakhstan may have domesticated and ridden horses six thousand years ago, built entirely from indirect evidence because domestic and wild horse skeletons are anatomically indistinguishable. The author's purpose is expository, laying out a chain of reasoning rather than judging it: first the obstacle and Olsen's statistical workaround, then the age and sex profile of the bones, which fits neither ordinary herding nor ordinary hunting once wild horse social behavior is taken into account and which points toward animals kept for riding, and finally the whole skeletons and the deliberate burials alongside human remains. Olsen is the only viewpoint developed; the author reports her inferences without endorsing or contesting them.

Passage A

Music does not always gain by association with words. Like images, words can excite the deepest emotions but are inadequate to express the emotions they excite. Music is more adequate, and hence will often seize an emotion that may have been excited by images or words, deepen its expression, and, by so doing, excite still deeper emotion. That is how words can gain by being set to music.

But to set words to music—as in opera or song—is in fact to mix two arts together. A striking effect may be produced, but at the expense of the purity of each art. Poetry is a great art; so is music. But as a medium for emotion, each is greater alone than in company, although various good ends arise from linking the two, providing that the words are subordinated to the more expressive medium of music. What good could any words do for Beethoven's Fifth Symphony? So too an opera is largely independent of words, and depends for its aesthetic value not upon the poetry of the libretto (the words of the opera), or even the plot or scenery, but upon its emotional range—a region dominated by the musical element.

Passage B

Throughout the history of opera, two fundamental types may be distinguished: that in which the music is primary, and that in which there is, essentially, parity between music and other factors. The former, sometimes called "singer's opera"—a term which has earned undeserved contempt—is exemplified by most Italian operas, while the latter, exemplified by the operas of German composer Richard Wagner, depend for their effect on a balance among many factors of which music is only one, albeit the most important. Theoretically, it would seem that there should be a third kind of opera, in which the music is subordinated to the other features. While the earliest operas were of this kind, their appeal was limited, and a fuller participation of music was required to establish opera on a secure basis.

In any event, in any aesthetic judgment of opera, regardless of the opera's type, neither the music nor the poetry of the libretto should be judged in isolation. The music is good not if it would make a good concert piece but if it serves the particular situation in the opera in which it occurs, contributing something not supplied by other elements. Similarly, the poetry is good not because it reads well by itself but primarily if, while embodying a sound dramatic idea, it furnishes opportunity for effective musical and scenic treatment. True, the elements of music and poetry may be considered separately, but only for purposes of analyzing their formal features. In actuality these elements are as united as hydrogen and oxygen are united in water. It is this union—further enriched and clarified by the visual action—that results in opera's inimitable character.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a claim that sounds counterintuitive and then explains it. Author A holds that adding words to music is not automatically a gain. The reasoning runs through expressive capacity: words and images can stir deep feeling but cannot fully express what they stir, whereas music can, so music takes an emotion that words have raised, expresses it more completely, and thereby deepens it further. Read the last sentence carefully, because it fixes the direction of benefit for the rest of the passage — words gain from music, not the reverse.

Now the argument turns evaluative. Setting words to music blends two arts, and Author A treats that blending as a cost: each art is diluted, and each is more powerful as a vehicle for emotion on its own than in partnership. The concession is narrow and conditional, since good things can come of the pairing only where the words stay subordinate to the more expressive medium. Beethoven's Fifth is offered as a rhetorical clincher, the point being that no text could improve it. The conclusion extends this to opera: its aesthetic worth rests on emotional range, which is musical territory, and not on libretto, plot or scenery.

Passage B begins descriptively rather than argumentatively, sorting opera into kinds instead of ranking the arts. Author B identifies two real types: one where music dominates, the Italian tradition often dismissed as singer's opera, a label Author B says is unfairly scorned, and one where music remains the most important element among several that must balance, exemplified by Wagner. A third type is logically possible, with music subordinate to everything else, and it briefly existed in the earliest operas, but its appeal proved too narrow, and opera only became secure once music took a fuller part.

The closing paragraph states the evaluative principle, and it applies to every type. Nothing in an opera should be assessed on its own terms: music is not judged by whether it would work in the concert hall but by whether it does something for the dramatic situation that no other element supplies, and a libretto is not judged by how it reads but by whether it carries a sound dramatic idea and opens room for music and staging. Author B allows that the parts can be separated for formal analysis, then insists that in practice they are bound like hydrogen and oxygen in water, and that this union, with visual action added, is what makes opera unique.
overall_html: Both passages concern the relation between music and words in opera, and they disagree about how tightly the two belong together: Author A argues that music is the more expressive medium and is weakened by mixture, so an opera's value lies in its musical emotional range while the libretto, plot and scenery matter little, whereas Author B classifies operas by how far music dominates and insists that in any of them neither music nor poetry may be judged in isolation, since each is good only insofar as it serves the whole. Author A's purpose is to argue a hierarchy of the arts; Author B's is to lay out a typology and then a standard of aesthetic judgment grounded in the inseparability of opera's elements.

According to the generally accepted theory of plate tectonics, the earth's crust consists of a dozen or so plates of solid rock moving across the mantle—the slightly fluid layer of rock between crust and core. Most earthquakes can then be explained as a result of the grinding of these plates against one another as they collide. When two plates collide, one plate is forced under the other until it eventually merges with the underlying mantle. According to this explanation, this process, called subduction, causes an enormous build-up of energy that is abruptly released in the form of an earthquake. Most earthquakes take place in the earth's seismic "hot zones"—regions with very high levels of subduction. Contrary to expectations, however, global seismic data indicate that there are also regions with high levels of subduction that are nonetheless nearly free of earthquakes. Thus, until recently, there remained a crucial question for which the plate tectonics theory had no answer—how can often intense subduction take place at certain locations with little or no seismic effect?

One group of scientists now proposes that the relative quiet of these zones is tied to the nature of the collision between the plates. In many seismic hot zones, the plates exhibit motion in opposite directions—that is, they collide because they are moving toward each other. And because the two plates are moving in opposite directions, the subduction zone is relatively motionless relative to the underlying mantle. In contrast, the plate collisions in the quiet subduction zones occur between two plates that are moving in the same general direction—the second plate's motion is simply faster than that of the first, and its leading edge therefore becomes subducted. But in this type of subduction, the collision zone moves with a comparatively high velocity relative to the mantle below. Thus, rather like an oar dipped into the water from a moving boat, the overtaking plate encounters great resistance from the mantle and is forced to descend steeply as it is absorbed into the mantle. The steep descent of the overtaking plate in this type of collision reduces the amount of contact between the two plates, and the earthquake-producing friction is thereby reduced as well. On the other hand, in collisions in which the plates move toward each other the subducted plate receives relatively little resistance from the mantle, and so its angle of descent is correspondingly shallow, allowing for a much larger plane of contact between the two plates. Like two sheets of sandpaper pressed together, these plates offer each other a great deal of resistance.

This proposal also provides a warning. It suggests that regions that were previously thought to be seismically innocuous—regions with low levels of subduction—may in fact be at a significant risk of earthquakes, depending on the nature of the subduction taking place.
explanation_html:
Everything here is setup for a puzzle. The accepted account of the earth's crust has roughly a dozen rigid plates drifting over the mantle, a semi-fluid rock layer beneath them, and it explains earthquakes as the product of those plates grinding together. Where two meet, one is driven beneath the other and eventually absorbed into the mantle, a process called subduction, and the energy stored up in that struggle is let go suddenly as a quake. So earthquakes cluster in hot zones where subduction is heaviest. The trouble, and the reason the passage exists, is that the global record also shows heavily subducting regions that stay almost silent, which the standard theory could not account for.

The answer proposed by one group of scientists is that what matters is not how much subduction occurs but how the plates are moving, and specifically how fast the collision zone travels across the mantle underneath. In a typical hot zone the plates approach head-on, so the zone where they meet stays roughly fixed relative to the mantle. In a quiet zone both plates head the same way and the faster one overruns the slower, dragging the collision zone along at speed. The oar image carries the mechanism: a blade dipped from a moving boat meets heavy resistance, and the overtaking plate is likewise shoved down at a sharp angle. A steep plunge means the two plates touch along only a small surface, so there is little friction to generate quakes. Head-on collisions produce the opposite, a shallow descent with a broad contact plane, the two surfaces gripping like sandpaper.

The short closing paragraph converts the explanation into a practical consequence, and it is the kind of turn worth watching for. If the driver of seismic risk is the geometry of the collision rather than the sheer amount of subduction, then the reassurance offered by low subduction totals is worth less than assumed. Areas written off as seismically harmless could in fact face substantial danger, depending on how the plates involved are moving. Notice the hedge: the proposal predicts risk in some such places, not all of them.
overall_html: The passage takes an anomaly that plate tectonics could not explain — regions with heavy subduction but almost no earthquakes — and presents one group of scientists' proposed solution, which attributes the difference to the direction of plate motion: head-on collisions leave the subduction zone nearly stationary over the mantle and produce a shallow descent with broad, high-friction contact, while a plate overtaking another drags the zone rapidly across the mantle, meets resistance, and plunges steeply, reducing contact and friction. The author's purpose is expository, moving from accepted theory and the puzzle it left open, through the proposed mechanism with its oar and sandpaper analogies, to the warning that seemingly quiet regions may carry real seismic risk.

Along with Egypt and Sumer, the third major early Bronze Age civilization was the Indus Valley civilization, which flourished from 2600 B.C. to 900 B.C. In geographic size, the Indus Valley civilization was the largest ancient urban civilization, bigger than pharaonic Egypt. Centered on the Indus River and the now dry Ghaggar-Hakra River, it comprised about 1,400 settlements across what is now Pakistan, Afghanistan, and northwestern India. The Indus Valley civilization was long considered archaeologically uninteresting because of its ordinary urban architecture and lack of palaces or citadels, but recent excavations show the civilization to be without parallel in history, displaying characteristics not elsewhere united in a single civilization.

The Indus Valley people, masters of urban planning, built brick cities on flood-proof terraces with grids of long, straight streets and the first urban sewer systems, made of masonry. No signs of dominant rulers have been found, and the cities' living quarters show little sign of class distinction, suggesting that their system of government was, at least in part, democratic. The civilization also apparently thrived without armies—there is, for example, no evidence of weapon production.

The Indus Valley people were the first to cultivate rice and cotton, and they developed a carefully organized agricultural system to produce and distribute food. In addition, the Indus Valley civilization was one of the ancient world's top traders. Examples of its standardized weights have been found in many harbors around the Arabian Sea, and Sumerian tablets inscribed in 2300 B.C. provide evidence that the Indus Valley people maintained trade with Mesopotamia.

The causes of the civilization's decline, however, are not certain, and this has produced the most contention among scholars. A long-standing theory, one that today still inhabits history books, was proposed by British archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler in the 1920s and points to a final massacre by marauding Indo-Aryan invaders. But, in addition to a lack of written evidence of such an event in any ancient Indian records, there is no archaeological evidence of battles within the cities. In fact, new excavations show that Indo-Aryans were not even in the region at the time the massacre was alleged to have taken place. Archaeological evidence also shows a later resurgence of the civilization a substantial distance to the south of its original location. This suggests that the Indus Valley people most likely relocated for catastrophic environmental reasons, with the large empire disintegrating into many regional cultures. Severe drought, of which there is evidence, may have made some lands unfarmable. Without enough grain to feed the large urban populations, many of the Indus Valley civilization's large cities would probably have been abandoned. Or, a massive earthquake in this seismically volatile region may have changed the course of rivers and disrupted many cities, spurring a migration of refugees to the countryside.
explanation_html:
The first paragraph places the subject and then reverses an old judgment about it. Alongside Egypt and Sumer, the Indus Valley civilization was one of the three great Bronze Age societies, lasting from 2600 to 900 B.C. and covering more ground than pharaonic Egypt, some fourteen hundred settlements spread over what is now Pakistan, Afghanistan and northwestern India, clustered along the Indus and a Ghaggar-Hakra river that has since dried up. The pivot comes at the end. Because its buildings looked plain and it left no palaces or fortresses, archaeologists long found it dull; recent digging has shown instead that it combined features no other civilization brought together.

What follows is the evidence for that claim, and this paragraph supplies the first cluster of it. These were planned cities: brick-built, raised on terraces above flood level, laid out on grids of long straight streets, and equipped with masonry sewers, the earliest urban sanitation known. The social inferences are the part to hold carefully, because they rest on absences rather than discoveries. Nothing indicates powerful rulers, and housing shows little difference in wealth, which suggests some measure of democratic government. Nor is there sign of an army, the supporting detail being that no weapon manufacture has turned up.

The second cluster covers how they fed themselves and whom they dealt with. They were the first people to grow rice and cotton, and they ran a deliberately organized system for producing food and moving it where it was needed. They also traded on a scale matching anyone in the ancient world, and two concrete proofs are given: their standardized weights turn up in harbors ringing the Arabian Sea, and Sumerian tablets from 2300 B.C. record dealings with Mesopotamia. Together with the previous paragraph, this is what the opening meant by an unparalleled combination.

The final paragraph shifts from description to dispute, since the end of the civilization is where scholars disagree most. Mortimer Wheeler argued in the 1920s that invading Indo-Aryans massacred the population, a story that still survives in textbooks. Three findings dismantle it — no ancient Indian text records such an event, no city shows archaeological traces of fighting, and newer excavation indicates the Indo-Aryans had not yet reached the region. The author favors a different account: evidence of the civilization reappearing well to the south points to migration driven by environmental catastrophe, with the empire fragmenting into regional cultures. Two candidate causes are offered, severe drought emptying cities that could no longer be fed, or a major earthquake rerouting rivers.
overall_html: The passage argues that the Indus Valley civilization, once dismissed as archaeologically dull, was in fact unique in combining planned brick cities with sewers, apparently egalitarian and partly democratic government, no army, pioneering rice and cotton agriculture, and long-distance trade, and that its collapse was environmental rather than military. The author's purpose is to revise the received picture on both fronts, first assembling the achievements that make the civilization without parallel, then dismantling Mortimer Wheeler's enduring invasion-and-massacre theory with three pieces of counterevidence before proposing drought or earthquake as the likelier trigger for a southward migration. Wheeler's theory is the only rival viewpoint developed; everything else is the author's own reading of the excavations.

Film scholar David Bordwell refers to the years 1917–1960 as the classical era of filmmaking in Hollywood. Bordwell defines the era's style as being governed by straightforward narrative considerations, i.e., the need to follow well-defined characters through a chronological sequence of events, or plot. The technical elements of filmmaking—camera movement, lighting, editing, and sound—are all employed to tell a realistic story, one in which the world of the story is self-sufficient and recognizably related to our own. Devices that draw attention to the film as film rather than to the story are avoided.

Within this definition, the musical films of the 1930s are anomalous in that they interrupt narrative to present musical performances only tangentially related to the plot. In one film directed by Busby Berkeley, for example, a scene begins with a shot of an audience watching a singer. The singer's face then fills the screen—a natural enough transition—but this image soon dissolves into a fanciful sequence consisting of various aerial views of city life. Although the sequence illustrates the song being sung, it does not contribute to the story Berkeley tells between musical numbers. In such sequences, filmmaking techniques are used not to advance a narrative but as a respite from narrative; the people we see are not characters in a plot but rather are abstracted figures; editing and camera movement function not to help tell a story but to manipulate images into intricate patterns. Can the musical—in which such differently motivated and constructed sequences abut so closely—fit comfortably within Bordwell's definition of the classical style?

Bordwell's response is that the musical, no less than comedy or melodrama (two other staples of the classical era), evolved from popular live theater. The musical's conventions, Bordwell argues, cue viewers to expect a different structure—alternating narrative scenes and self-contained performances—from that of other genres, a structure that audiences are prepared for and thus accept as "realistic." But raising the issue of genre does not disguise the fact that Bordwell stretches the definition of the term "realism," for there is still the problem exemplified in films such as Berkeley's by the fact that the musical performances are not merely self-contained but self-absorbed—the selfish aesthetic of the interlude isn't intended to advance the plot but instead to draw attention to its own artistic expertise. Even the viewer aware of the film's genre cannot remain entirely unfazed by the break in the film's "reality." Bordwell too quickly dismisses the fact that watching a film is a perceptual act and not an academic exercise in pigeonholing genres. Because knowledge of genre is acquired, it would be worthwhile for scholars like Bordwell to first consider how viewers process cinematic images and eventually come to accept them as conventions before generalizing about the realism of certain film styles.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by handing you a definition it will later test. Bordwell, a film scholar, labels 1917 to 1960 Hollywood's classical era and says its style is ruled by storytelling: clearly drawn characters followed through events in time order. Everything technical — how the camera moves, how a scene is lit, how shots are cut together, how sound is used — is put at the service of a realistic story, meaning one whose world holds together on its own and looks like ours. The last sentence is the one that will cause trouble, since it rules out anything that reminds the viewer they are watching a film rather than living a story.

Enter the counterexample. Musicals of the 1930s stop the story dead to stage numbers with only a loose connection to it, and the Busby Berkeley scene is walked through so you can see exactly where the break happens. It starts plausibly, an audience watching a singer, then the singer's face in close-up, but the face dissolves into invented aerial views of a city that illustrate the lyric while contributing nothing to the plot running between numbers. Note the inventory of reversals: technique now offers relief from narrative instead of advancing it, the people onscreen become abstract shapes rather than characters, and cutting and camerawork arrange images into patterns. The paragraph closes by putting the challenge as an open question, which signals that an answer is coming.

Bordwell answers by appealing to genre. Musicals, like comedy and melodrama, grew out of popular live theater, and their conventions train audiences to expect alternating story scenes and standalone performances, so a prepared audience takes that structure as realistic. The author finds this unpersuasive and says why in stages. It stretches the word realism past its meaning; the Berkeley numbers are not merely separate from the story but absorbed in themselves, showing off their own artistry; and knowing the genre does not stop a viewer from feeling the rupture. The deeper complaint is methodological — watching a film is an act of perception, not an exercise in sorting works into categories — and it yields the closing recommendation that scholars investigate how viewers actually take in images and learn conventions before making claims about realism.
overall_html: The passage uses the 1930s musical to challenge David Bordwell's account of classical Hollywood style as narrative-driven realism, arguing that his appeal to genre convention stretches the meaning of realism rather than resolving the problem, since a Busby Berkeley number is self-absorbed spectacle that a viewer feels as a break in the film's reality whatever they know about the genre. The author's purpose is critical, laying out Bordwell's definition, pressing the musical against it as a counterexample, then reporting and rejecting his defense before recommending that scholars study how viewers perceive and learn conventions before generalizing about style. Two viewpoints are in play throughout: Bordwell's and the author's.

Passage A

The legal system rests on the assumption that people use conscious deliberation when deciding how to act—that is, in the absence of external duress, people freely decide how to act. But behaviors—even high-level behaviors—can take place in the absence of free will. For example, someone with a neurological disorder might form a facial expression without choosing to do so.

The crucial legal question is whether all of our actions are fundamentally beyond our control or whether some little bit of you is "free" to choose, independent of the rules of biology. After all, as neurologists tell us, there is no spot in the brain that is not densely interconnected with—and driven by—other brain parts. And that suggests that no part is independent and therefore "free."

One thing seems clear: if free will does exist, it has little room in which to operate. It can at best be a small factor riding on top of vast neural networks shaped by genes and environment. In fact, free will may end up being so small that we eventually think about bad decision-making in the same way we think about any physical affliction.

Blameworthiness should thus be removed from the legal argot. It is a backward-looking concept that demands the impossible task of untangling the hopelessly complex web of genetics and environment in order to isolate a factor of free will that may or may not exist. Instead of debating culpability, the legal system has to become forward looking, and address how an accused lawbreaker is likely to behave in the future.

Passage B

Here is a paradox: if people lack free will, then how can the law be moved away from what seems to be a deeply entrenched reliance on blame-related concepts? Rational arguments will only get you so far.

Clinical research indicates that people will often continue to make moral judgments even when they are conditioned to think that human behavior is determined by physical processes. The blaming urge is deeply rooted in the human psyche, and I have considerable doubt that any amount of scientific evidence can remove it from our criminal justice processes.

We have, of course, tried this before. Rehabilitation was widely accepted by criminal justice experts in the mid-twentieth century. But public support waned, and a retributive backlash occurred in the 1970s and 1980s. Criminal behavior may be a matter of biology, not choice, but the public seems unwilling to incorporate this idea into the law.

My sense is that blaming performs some useful social function, even if it is in some way "false." Blaming seems too intrinsically a part of the social life of human beings for me to see it as a worthless appendage that can be harmlessly amputated. As the criminal justice system confronts the challenges of brain science, it should also seek a better understanding of why people blame and try to continue to respect the underlying social needs.
explanation_html:
Passage A starts by naming an assumption buried inside the law: that people think things over and, unless someone is forcing them, choose freely how to act. Author A immediately puts pressure on it with a counterexample rather than an argument, noting that a neurological disorder can produce a facial expression nobody decided to make. The point of the example is scope — even complicated behavior can happen without any act of choosing — which is what makes the legal assumption vulnerable.

The question is then sharpened into the form the passage will answer. Is every action of ours outside our control, or does some fragment of a person get to choose in a way that biology does not govern? Author A leans on neurology for the answer, and the reasoning is about wiring: every region of the brain is densely linked to and driven by other regions, so no region stands apart, and without independence there is nothing that could count as free.

Notice the concession here, because it is what keeps the argument careful. Author A does not declare free will nonexistent; the claim is that even if it exists, it has almost nowhere to work, amounting at most to a thin layer sitting on huge neural systems built by genes and environment. The paragraph then extends the thought forward, suggesting we may come to treat poor decision-making the way we treat any bodily ailment.

Now the payoff, which is a proposal about legal language. Blameworthiness should be dropped, and the reason given is that it looks backward and requires something nobody can do, namely picking apart an impossibly tangled mix of genetics and environment to find a free-will component that may not be there. Author A's replacement is prospective: rather than arguing about guilt, courts should ask how the accused is likely to act in the future.

Passage B opens on the practical problem Author A left untouched, and framing it as a paradox is deliberate. Grant that free will is absent; the law's attachment to blame is still deeply entrenched, and something has to explain how it could ever be pried loose. The short second sentence is Author B's thesis in miniature, warning that reasoned argument has limited power here. Read what follows as an answer about feasibility, not about the science.

Evidence for that limit comes first from the clinic. Studies show people go on making moral judgments even after being conditioned to believe behavior is physically determined, which means accepting determinism intellectually does not stop the blaming. Author B generalizes from this to a claim about human nature, calling the urge deeply rooted, and then states a personal doubt that any volume of scientific evidence could drive blame out of criminal justice.

History supplies the second kind of evidence, and the phrasing signals that this has been tried before. Rehabilitation, essentially a forward-looking approach, won broad expert backing in the mid-twentieth century, and then public support drained away and the 1970s and 1980s brought a swing back to retribution. Author B grants the underlying science in passing, allowing that crime may be biology rather than choice, while insisting the public will not let that idea into the law.

The final move turns a limitation into a value. Blaming probably does useful social work, Author B suggests, even if it rests on something false, and it is too woven into how humans live together to be cut away without cost. The recommendation follows directly and stands as a counterpart to Author A's: as brain science presses on criminal justice, the system should study why people blame and keep honoring the social needs behind it.
overall_html: Both passages accept that neuroscience undercuts the law's assumption of free will, but they draw opposite practical conclusions: Author A argues that blameworthiness is an unworkable backward-looking notion that should be dropped in favor of predicting an offender's future behavior, while Author B contends that the urge to blame is too deeply rooted to be argued away, citing clinical findings and the retributive backlash against mid-century rehabilitation, and that it serves a real social function worth understanding rather than amputating. Author A's purpose is to press a scientific premise into a reform proposal; Author B's is to question whether such a reform is achievable, granting the science while doubting the public and psychological ground for it.
