Organic chemist Larry Koskan's inspiration arrived in the mid-1980s, when he read a report by marine biologists describing how oyster shells grow. It was known that oysters secrete calcium carbonate as an essential constituent of their hardened exteriors, but the biologists discovered that they also produce a special protein-based agent that molds the mineral into their shells' characteristic shape.

At the time, Koskan was studying the properties of water-soluble polyacrylates. Among other things, these widely used additives help to stem the buildup of damaging mineral-scale deposits (carbonate and sulphate compounds) on the surfaces of industrial water-treatment equipment. What Koskan realized was that the agent produced by the oysters—polyaspartate—inhibits the formation of calcium carbonate and could also therefore control scale. Polyaspartate mimics the scale-inhibiting activity of polyacrylates because it has a similar chemical structure. But because the backbone of polyaspartate is made of peptides (chains of amino acids) rather than the hydrocarbon compounds that constitute polyacrylates' backbone, it is subject to bacterial action (i.e., it is biodegradable).

Polyacrylates, inexpensive and versatile chemicals, are easy to manufacture and process. In laundry detergents, they act as dispersants that keep dirt suspended in the wash water. As a recent alternative to phosphates, which, via wastewater, pollute surface waters, some half a billion pounds of polyacrylates are used in detergents worldwide every year. Additionally, some polyacrylates have chemical configurations with a tremendous affinity for water, making them ideal in superabsorbent materials for disposable products like baby diapers, which currently account for around 2 billion pounds in annual production of polyacrylates. The trouble is, polyacrylates last virtually forever, and these vast quantities of the highly stable substance are being discarded in landfills.

With requests by consumer products companies for environmentally friendly products growing rapidly, Koskan started his own small company and began researching cost-effective ways of producing polyaspartate for industrial use. Soon, leading chemical companies also began researching the issue, with the consensus being that polyaspartate was the most suitable replacement for polyacrylates. Unfortunately, as with many emerging technologies that lack a supporting infrastructure, polyaspartate's price was estimated to be four to five times that of the high-volume-production alternative. Given this, the consumer products industry lost interest in the technology, and the chemical industry shelved it. Koskan's company, however, believing that polyaspartate could nonetheless be market-competitive on its own merits, decided to persevere and focus on specialty application niches. Polyaspartate has since shown unparalleled success at eliminating scale in offshore oil production equipment and is being used by the farming industry to keep chemical fertilizers in the soil longer, reducing pollution of groundwater by the fertilizers. If Koskan's company can show continued success, it may yet help enliven an environmental chemistry sector saddled with a reputation for ineffectiveness and high cost.
explanation_html:
A single moment of borrowed insight sets the passage going. In the mid-1980s the organic chemist Larry Koskan read marine biologists' account of how oyster shells grow. Oysters were already known to secrete calcium carbonate as an essential part of their hard exteriors; what the biologists had newly found was that the animals also make a special protein-based agent that molds that mineral into the shell's characteristic shape. Nothing is evaluated yet. Read this paragraph as the setup for a transfer of ideas from biology into industrial chemistry, and keep the molding agent in view, because it is the hinge of everything that follows.

The transfer happens here. Koskan was then studying water-soluble polyacrylates, common additives that among other things hold back the buildup of damaging mineral-scale deposits, meaning carbonate and sulphate compounds, on industrial water-treatment surfaces. His realization was that the oysters' agent, polyaspartate, inhibits calcium carbonate from forming and so could control scale as well. It works like polyacrylates because its chemical structure is similar, but one difference is decisive: its backbone is built of peptides, which are chains of amino acids, instead of the hydrocarbon compounds in polyacrylates, so bacteria can break it down. Polyaspartate is biodegradable.

Before pursuing the substitute, the author establishes why a substitute is wanted. Polyacrylates are cheap, versatile, easy to make and easy to process. In laundry detergents they act as dispersants that keep dirt suspended in the wash water, and as a recent replacement for phosphates, which pollute surface waters through wastewater, they account for roughly half a billion pounds of worldwide detergent use each year. Some also have configurations with an enormous affinity for water, which makes them ideal in superabsorbent goods such as disposable diapers, another two billion pounds annually. The catch is durability: they last virtually forever, and those quantities end up in landfills.

The closing paragraph turns the science into a business story with a mixed ending. As consumer products companies asked for environmentally friendly materials, Koskan founded a small company to find cost-effective ways of making polyaspartate industrially, and leading chemical companies agreed it was the most suitable replacement for polyacrylates. Cost decided otherwise: like many emerging technologies without a supporting infrastructure, it was estimated at four to five times the price of high-volume production, so the consumer products industry lost interest and the chemical industry shelved it. Koskan's company persisted in specialty niches instead, succeeding against scale in offshore oil equipment and helping farmers keep fertilizer in the soil longer, which reduces groundwater pollution.
overall_html: The passage traces how a biological discovery about oyster shells led Larry Koskan to identify polyaspartate as a biodegradable substitute for polyacrylates, the durable additives used by the billion pounds in detergents and disposable products and then left permanently in landfills. Its purpose is explanatory rather than argumentative, following a chronological arc from the initial insight, to the chemistry that makes the two compounds interchangeable except in biodegradability, to the scale of the pollution problem, and finally to the cost obstacle that made large industry abandon the technology while Koskan's own company pursued profitable specialty applications. No competing viewpoints are developed; the author reports the episode in a neutral voice.

The late 1950s and early 1960s were a time of profound growth for the civil rights movement in the United States. Although racial segregation in the public schools had been outlawed in 1954, the ruling applied only to this one category of discriminatory practice in U.S. society. But it furthered within the African-American community the anticipation of broader changes. It was in this climate that the student sit-in demonstrations of the early 1960s were born. The technique of the sit-in was simple—African Americans occupying "whites only" seats in racially segregated establishments—but this new type of student activism galvanized established civil rights organizations, brought about the creation of new ones, and generated support for the civil rights movement among many new segments of the populace.

Initiated by four students of the North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College, the first sit-in occurred at a lunch counter in February 1960. Sit-ins then spread rapidly through the southern U.S., involving over 70,000 participants by August 1961. The sit-ins provided an important model for nonviolent protest and showed students that they could affect the political process. The influence of these demonstrations on the determination of the student activists was particularly visible in two events: the formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and the birth of a second form of sit-ins called Freedom Rides.

The formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee followed the first sit-in by just a few months and not only solidified student involvement in the civil rights movement but also placed students in leadership roles for the first time. It operated independently of other civil rights organizations and relied on strong local leadership, helping to transform student involvement from participation in small-scale protests into a sustained effort to challenge discrimination throughout the U.S. But the development that marked the clearest turning point for the civil rights movement was the Freedom Rides. The goal of the rides, which were organized in 1961 by the already well-established Congress of Racial Equality, was to challenge segregation through the occupation of "whites only" seats on interstate buses and in facilities at the various terminals at which the buses stopped. Because the rides inspired violent reprisals in some regions, the U.S. government began using force to protect the safety of the Freedom Riders; this was the first government action taken explicitly in support of the cause of desegregation outside the public schools. The Freedom Rides thus helped take the civil rights movement to a new level by underscoring to the U.S. government, and to U.S. society generally, the harsh realities of the segregation system, and by providing, for students and their elders alike, examples of the methods they might use to achieve a more equal society.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph supplies the conditions that made the sit-ins possible. Racial segregation in public schools had been outlawed in 1954, but the author is careful about the limits of that ruling: it reached only one category of discriminatory practice, while everything else stood. Its real effect within the African American community was to raise the expectation of broader change, and it is in that climate of anticipation that the student sit-ins of the early 1960s appear. The technique was simple, African Americans taking "whites only" seats in segregated establishments, but the consequences listed at the end are large — established civil rights organizations were galvanized, new ones were created, and new segments of the public came over to the movement.

Facts and figures follow, converting the general claim into a documented sequence. Four students from the North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College staged the first sit-in at a lunch counter in February 1960; the tactic spread rapidly through the southern United States and had drawn more than 70,000 participants by August 1961. Two results matter to the author: the sit-ins gave the movement an important model for nonviolent protest, and they showed students that they could affect the political process. The last sentence is a roadmap, naming the two developments that demonstrate this new determination and that the final paragraph will take up in order.

Both promised developments are delivered, and they are ranked. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee formed within months of the first sit-in, solidifying student involvement and placing students in leadership roles for the first time; operating independently of other organizations and drawing on strong local leadership, it turned scattered small-scale protest into a sustained national challenge to discrimination. The Freedom Rides, though, are called the clearest turning point. Organized in 1961 by the already established Congress of Racial Equality, they contested segregation on interstate buses and in terminal facilities, and the violent reprisals they provoked pushed the government into using force to protect the riders — the first federal action explicitly supporting desegregation beyond the schools.
overall_html: The passage argues that the student sit-in demonstrations of the early 1960s transformed the American civil rights movement, both by proving that nonviolent student activism could move the political process and by generating the two developments that extended it, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and the Freedom Rides. The author's purpose is explanatory and historical, and the structure moves from the post-1954 climate that produced the sit-ins, to their spread and their two most important consequences, to a closer look at each, ending with the Freedom Rides as the clearest turning point because they forced the first federal action for desegregation outside the public schools. The account is delivered in the author's neutral historical voice.

Grammarians of the prescriptive school take it as part of their task to distinguish correct from incorrect usage in language and thereby to encourage the former. They believe that in so doing they play an essential role in preventing a constantly changing language from falling into disarray. In contrast, descriptive grammarians are so called because they are content to describe the way language is actually used by members of a community. In their eyes, those who seek to preserve some forms of usage while preventing others from gaining a foothold are being unscientific and are, moreover, doomed to almost certain failure. Descriptivists point to numerous examples of usage that were once judged by prescriptivists to be incorrect but that over time and through continual use have come to be almost universally accepted. One example is the use of "data" as a singular noun in English: prescriptivists have typically regarded the phrase "the data is incomplete" as ungrammatical, on the grounds that "data" is the plural of the Latin noun "datum" and should continue to be treated as a plural in English out of respect for the word's origins. Descriptivists argue that "data," in addition to its use as a plural, has acquired a widespread use as a singular mass term, like "water." It would be pointless, they say, to try to reverse this trend.

This example illustrates the two main objections of descriptivists to prescriptivism. The first is the scientific objection: the transformation of language is governed by laws not unlike the laws of nature, and those trying to hold back linguistic change might as well attempt to defy the law of gravity. The second is the egalitarian objection: the prescriptivists are simply trying to impose their own linguistic practices, which are usually those of an educated and affluent elite, upon other members of society. The suggestion is that the attempted imposition is somehow immoral.

With regard to the scientific objection, it should be noted that while many attempts to regulate language have failed, some have succeeded. Descriptivists may respond that in the latter cases the usages favored by prescriptivists were in accordance with the laws governing linguistic change and would have prevailed without their assistance. But this is in large measure an article of faith. In the end it must be acknowledged that the laws governing the transformation of language are not like the laws of physics. Language usage depends on choices made by individuals, who are subject to persuasion. In response to the egalitarian objection, prescriptivists point to the importance of standard language usage for the free exchange of ideas. Those to whom preservation of the standard is entrusted inevitably possess some of the attributes of an elite, but their aim is one of inclusion rather than exclusion.
explanation_html:
Two camps are defined before any argument begins. The Prescriptivists take it as their job to separate correct usage from incorrect and to encourage the former, believing this keeps a constantly changing language from falling into disarray. The Descriptivists simply record how a community actually uses language, and they regard the other side as unscientific and almost certain to fail, pointing to usages once condemned that continual use has made near-universal. The worked example is "data": prescriptivists reject "the data is incomplete" because data is the Latin plural of datum and should be treated as plural out of respect for its origins, while descriptivists reply that data has also become a singular mass term like water, and that reversing that trend would be pointless.

The example is then converted into two labelled objections, and keeping them apart is the key to the passage. The scientific objection holds that language changes according to laws not unlike the laws of nature, so resisting change is like defying gravity. The egalitarian objection holds that prescriptivists are imposing the linguistic practices of an educated and affluent elite on everyone else. Notice how the last sentence is worded: the immorality is described as a suggestion carried by the objection rather than a claim the author makes, which is the first hint that the author does not stand with The Descriptivists.

The final paragraph answers both objections in the same order, and the author is arguing now, not reporting. Against the scientific objection: some attempts to regulate language have in fact succeeded, and the descriptivist reply that those usages would have prevailed anyway is called an article of faith. The deeper point is that linguistic laws are unlike physical laws because usage rests on choices made by individuals, and individuals can be persuaded. Against the egalitarian objection the author gives the prescriptivist reply directly: a standard usage matters for the free exchange of ideas, and though its custodians inevitably have some attributes of an elite, their aim is inclusion rather than exclusion.
overall_html: The passage sets out the quarrel between prescriptive grammarians, who try to enforce correct usage, and descriptive grammarians, who only record how people actually speak, and then defends prescriptivism against the two objections descriptivists raise against it. The author's purpose is evaluative rather than merely expository: the structure runs from a definition of both camps and the illustrative dispute over singular "data," to a naming of the scientific and egalitarian objections, to a point-by-point rebuttal arguing that linguistic change is not law-governed the way physics is and that maintaining a standard serves inclusion. The Descriptivists supply the objections, and the author sides with The Prescriptivists.

Passage A is from a newspaper article. Passage B is from UNESCO's 1999 Draft Convention on the Protection of Underwater Cultural Heritage.

Passage A

A North American company that found what is believed to be the HMS Sussex during expeditions in the Mediterranean from 1998 to 2001 has signed an agreement with the British government, which owns the Sussex, to raise what may be history's richest sunken treasure and to split the proceeds. The agreement is a legal breakthrough that could allow the recovery of perhaps US$4 billion in gold coins lost with the Sussex in a storm in 1694.

As robots, sonar, and other technologically advanced gear have opened the deepest oceans to exploration and recovery, governments have begun asserting ownership over their sunken vessels. But governments often lack the money and skills to retrieve cultural riches and, until now, there had been no legal precedent for a private company to join with a government to salvage the government's treasure. This agreement could end the days of freelance treasure hunting and allow nations to oversee the recovery of their lost fleets.

The company, which is funding the venture, agrees with British historians that the ship carried coins, most likely gold, worth £1 million in 1694. The US$4 billion figure is the coins' theoretical value if sold to collectors. The agreement calls for archaeological integrity—a difficult technical feat at such depths and a goal that critics of for-profit archaeology are likely to doubt. Many archaeologists abhor the sale of recovered artifacts, arguing that this inhibits scholarly analysis and public display. The agreement, however, draws a distinction between different classes of artifacts, recognizing that cultural items have greater archaeological value than coins, which it allows to be sold to help pay for the project.

Passage B

"Underwater cultural heritage" (UCH) means all traces of human existence that have been partially, totally, or periodically situated underwater for at least 100 years.

1. The protection of UCH is best achieved through in situ (original site) preservation, which should be considered as the first option. Accordingly, activities directed at UCH shall be authorized by the competent authority of the concerned State only when they make a significant contribution to knowledge, protection, and/or enhancement of UCH.

2. The commercial exploitation of UCH for trade, sale, barter, or speculation...is fundamentally incompatible with the protection and proper management of the UCH.

3. Activities directed at UCH shall not adversely impact UCH more than is necessary for the objectives of the project;

4. must use nondestructive techniques and prospection and limited sampling in preference to recovery of objects. If excavation is necessary for the purpose of scientific studies, the methods and techniques used must be as nondestructive as possible and contribute to the preservation of the remains;

5. shall avoid the unnecessary disturbance of human remains or venerated sites;

6. shall be strictly regulated to ensure proper recording of historical, cultural, and archaeological information.

7. Public access to conduct activities relating to UCH that are nonintrusive (such as photography) should, where practicable, be encouraged.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens as a news report on a deal. A North American company that located what is believed to be the HMS Sussex during Mediterranean expeditions between 1998 and 2001 has signed an agreement with the British government, the wreck's owner, to raise the cargo and split the proceeds. The ship sank in a storm in 1694, and its gold coins are called possibly history's richest sunken treasure. Notice the word breakthrough: the arrangement is presented as an achievement, and the rest of Passage A defends it.

Why it counts as a breakthrough comes next. Robots, sonar and similar gear have opened the deepest oceans, and governments have responded by asserting ownership over their sunken vessels. That creates a gap, since governments often lack the money and skill to retrieve cultural riches, and no legal precedent existed for a private company to join with a government to salvage what the government owns. The claimed payoff is twofold: freelance treasure hunting could end, and nations could oversee recovery of their own lost fleets.

Objections are anticipated and answered here. The company funds the venture and accepts historians' estimate that the coins were worth one million pounds in 1694, the four billion dollar figure being only their theoretical value to collectors. The promised archaeological integrity is technically hard at such depths and doubted by critics of for-profit archaeology. Many archaeologists object to selling artifacts at all, saying sales block scholarly analysis and public display; the agreement answers by sorting artifacts, treating cultural items as more valuable than coins, which may be sold to fund the work.

Passage B changes genre completely. Instead of reporting an event it lays down rules, beginning with the definition that fixes their scope: underwater cultural heritage means every trace of human existence partially, totally or periodically underwater for at least a hundred years. Do the arithmetic quietly rather than hunting for argument, because a ship lost in 1694 falls inside that definition. Read the numbered principles that follow as a standard against which the Passage A arrangement can be measured, though Passage B never mentions the Sussex.

The first principle sets a presumption. Preservation in situ, at the original site, is best and should be the first option considered. Anything else requires authorization from the concerned state's competent authority, granted only for activities making a significant contribution to knowledge, protection or enhancement. The default is to leave a wreck where it lies; disturbing it is the exception and must be justified by what the disturbance adds. That is a very different starting point from the recovery Passage A celebrates.

The second principle is the sharpest collision with Passage A. Commercial exploitation for trade, sale, barter or speculation is declared fundamentally incompatible with protection and proper management. Note the strength of that wording: not a caution about excess or a call for supervision, but a claim that the two purposes cannot coexist. The Sussex agreement rests on exactly such exploitation, since it splits proceeds and licenses coin sales, so under this principle its financing is not merely risky but disqualified.

The third principle governs how permitted work is done rather than whether it happens. Activities must not damage the heritage more than the project's objectives actually require. This is a proportionality test, and it assumes the objectives themselves already pass the earlier principles. Applied to a salvage operation it would ask not only whether recovery succeeded but whether every disturbance along the way was necessary, a standard more demanding than a general promise of archaeological integrity.

Method is specified in the fourth principle, and the preference is explicit. Nondestructive techniques, prospection and limited sampling come ahead of recovering objects at all. If excavation is genuinely necessary for scientific study, the methods must be as nondestructive as possible and must themselves help preserve the remains. Recovery is therefore the disfavored last resort, worth registering carefully, since raising objects from the seabed is the entire point of the project described in Passage A.

A narrower and more solemn restriction follows: activities must avoid unnecessary disturbance of human remains or venerated sites. The concern shifts from objects and information to the dead and to places treated as sacred, protected by the same test of necessity applied elsewhere in the list. For a warship lost with its crew in a storm this is hardly abstract, though Passage B keeps to the form of a general code and draws no connection to any particular wreck.

The sixth principle addresses record-keeping: activities are to be strictly regulated so that historical, cultural and archaeological information is properly recorded. Underlying it is the assumption running through the whole list, that a submerged site's value lies in the knowledge it carries rather than in the objects, and that such knowledge survives only if the work is documented. This is where the archaeologists quoted in Passage A rest their objection, since artifacts dispersed to collectors carry their information out of scholarly reach.

The list closes on permission rather than prohibition. Nonintrusive public access to activities relating to this heritage, photography being the example, should be encouraged where practicable. Ending here matters for the shape of Passage B: after a run of restrictions it names a way the public may still engage, by looking rather than taking. Set against Passage A, where public benefit arrives through recovered treasure and eventual display, that is a competing account of what access should mean.
overall_html: Passage A reports and defends an agreement between a salvage company and the British government to raise the treasure of the HMS Sussex, presenting the public-private partnership as a legal breakthrough that lets governments oversee recoveries they could not fund themselves and permitting the sale of coins to pay for the work. Passage B, a code of principles rather than a narrative, defines underwater cultural heritage and sets out rules favoring preservation in place, minimum necessary damage, nondestructive method and full documentation, and it declares commercial exploitation fundamentally incompatible with proper management. They conflict directly on the central point: the very financing that makes the Sussex project possible is what Passage B rules out.

Some environmentalists claim that the higher the international debt a nation carries, the more likely it is that the quality of life in that nation will suffer. These environmentalists argue that in a variety of ways the effort a nation must expend to pay its debt hastens the depletion of its natural resources, increases pollution, or hampers domestic spending. The most common reason given by the environmentalists is known as the exports promotion hypothesis. According to this hypothesis, in order to increase foreign trade in a way that better allows it to repay international debt, a nation must divert resources away from sectors generating domestic goods and toward the production of export goods. Partly because of the greater volume involved, this causes more environmental damage than does production of goods for domestic consumption. One possible scenario frequently cited by environmentalists is that a nation might raze its forests for timber or to open up land on which to plant cash crops. Another reason the environmentalists give for their claims is that domestic spending can fall when a nation shifts money toward repayment of its debt. A nation may take funds away from health care, education, or improvements in such public services as water quality or sanitation. It can also adjust its economy in other potentially harmful ways in order to cut costs—for example, through the elimination of government subsidies for practices that reduce pollution or conserve natural resources.

But the evidence for the environmentalists' claims is weak. With respect to the exports promotion hypothesis, one recent study does suggest a positive correlation between international debt and deforestation, but also indicates that other factors besides debt may play a stronger role. Another study found only a slight positive correlation between debt and deforestation; in fact, in one nation the correlation was negative, contrary to the environmentalists' expectations. The impact of debt on environmental indicators such as pollution or depletion of other resources has not yet been studied. Similarly, with respect to the domestic spending argument, while debt-saddled nations might shift money away from programs designed to enhance quality of life, it is just as likely that they would shift the money from plans that, if implemented, would have a negative impact on the environment. For example, they might abandon plans to build new dams or roads, or eliminate subsidies that promote fertilizer or pesticide use. The extent, then, to which a nation's quality of life is connected to the size of its international debt must be considered unknown. Indeed, a case could be made that at least some of the fiscal discipline or economic restructuring imposed by debt may rein in potentially harmful spending.
explanation_html:
The whole first paragraph belongs to one side. The Environmentalists claim that the higher a nation's international debt, the more its quality of life is likely to suffer, because repayment depletes natural resources, increases pollution, or squeezes domestic spending. Their leading reason is the exports promotion hypothesis: to expand foreign trade enough to service its debt, a nation shifts resources out of production for the home market and into export goods, and the volume involved makes that more damaging than producing for domestic consumption. The scenario they cite most often is a country razing forests for timber or for cash-crop land. Their second reason concerns budgets rather than production, since money moved toward repayment can come out of health care, education, water quality or sanitation, and cost-cutting may also mean scrapping subsidies that encouraged conservation. Notice the author is only reporting so far.

The reversal arrives in the first sentence: the evidence is weak, and the Author answers each argument in the order it was given. On exports promotion, one recent study does find a positive correlation between debt and deforestation, but suggests other factors may matter more; another finds only a slight positive correlation, and in one nation the correlation ran the wrong way. Effects on pollution and on other resource depletion have not been studied at all. On domestic spending, the author grants that a debt-burdened nation might cut quality-of-life programs, then observes it is just as likely to cut projects that would have harmed the environment, abandoning dams or roads or ending fertilizer and pesticide subsidies. Be precise about the conclusion: the connection is called unknown, not absent, with only a suggestion that debt-imposed discipline may restrain harmful spending.
overall_html: The passage sets out the environmentalist claim that heavy international debt degrades a nation's quality of life, through the exports promotion hypothesis and through cuts to domestic spending, and then argues that the supporting evidence is too weak to sustain it. The author's purpose is critical rather than constructive, and the structure is a simple two-part case-and-rebuttal: one paragraph builds the environmentalists' position in full, the next answers each of its two supports with contrary or missing studies and with the observation that budget cuts may fall on environmentally harmful projects. The conclusion is deliberately modest, that the link between debt and quality of life must be considered unknown.

In 1959, Hitsville, USA—the company better known as Motown Records—was founded in Detroit, Michigan by Berry Gordy, Jr. Several factors contributed to Motown's rapidly becoming one of the most successful record companies in the United States. Gordy's entrepreneurial skills and his belief in economic independence played a great role in Motown's success, as did the artistic situation in Detroit in the 1960s. Capitalizing on the rich musical talent of Detroit's African American community, Motown moved quickly into the vanguard of the popular music industry.

Motown's status as an independent company allowed Gordy considerable freedom to oppose recording industry convention. He rejected the practice that was common in the late 1950s and early 1960s of having established recording stars remake songs originally produced within and for limited markets. Gordy insisted that the musical performances recorded by Motown artists would appeal not just to African American audiences, but to a much wider market, and that there would thus be no need to engage high-priced major-label artists to produce alternate versions of Motown's songs. Gordy believed that maintaining the highest possible technical quality in Motown's recordings was an essential part of this appeal, and he devoted the necessary resources to this endeavor.

Another crucial factor in Motown's success was Detroit's well-developed public school music-education program, which provided the company with a deep and talented pool of artists and technicians. The roots of this program reached back to the turn of the century, when a trained soprano and Detroit native named E. Azalia Hackley adopted the musical education of African American youth as her personal mission. From Hackley's tutelage to that of locally renowned public school music teachers, Detroit's African American youth had been educated in a vibrant musical atmosphere. Nearly all of Motown's session musicians, arrangers, and producers were trained in this program. Moreover, many of the performers who would become famous exemplars of the Motown sound received musical training and exposure to diverse musical styles in Detroit schools. Motown's three major early groups—the Supremes, the Temptations, and the Miracles—came together and originally rehearsed at their high schools.

In addition to Gordy's business acumen and the talent produced by the local school system, the invention and growing popularity of electric instruments also played a noteworthy role in Motown's rise to prominence. African American musicians were among the first to use the electric bass, for example, crafting a distinctive sound that inspired other musicians to experiment with this new musical technology. This experimentation ultimately led to a revolution in popular music, helping to broaden both its sound and its audience. In this way, too, Motown Records helped to initiate, and simultaneously benefited from, landmark shifts in popular music culture.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph is a roadmap disguised as a founding story. Berry Gordy, Jr. established Hitsville, USA — better known as Motown Records — in Detroit in 1959, and the passage immediately names the factors behind the company's rapid rise: Gordy's entrepreneurial skill and his belief in economic independence, together with the artistic situation in Detroit during the 1960s. Drawing on the musical talent of the city's African American community, Motown moved quickly into the vanguard of the popular music industry. Expect each of these causes to be taken up in turn, and note that the author is explaining a success rather than arguing about it.

Independence is the first cause, and its payoff was freedom from industry convention. In the late 1950s and early 1960s it was standard practice to have established recording stars remake songs first produced within and for limited markets; Gordy rejected it. His reasoning was commercial as much as artistic: Motown's own recordings would appeal well beyond African American audiences to a much wider market, so paying high-priced major-label artists to cut alternate versions was unnecessary. Because that broad appeal depended on sound quality, he treated the highest possible technical standard as essential and committed the resources it required.

The second cause is institutional rather than personal, and the author traces it back further than the company itself. Detroit's well-developed public school music-education program gave Motown a deep pool of artists and technicians. Its roots run to the turn of the century and to E. Azalia Hackley, a trained soprano and Detroit native who made the musical education of African American youth her personal mission; locally renowned public school teachers carried the work forward in a vibrant musical atmosphere. Nearly all of Motown's session musicians, arrangers and producers came through it, and the Supremes, the Temptations and the Miracles first formed and rehearsed at their high schools.

Technology supplies the third cause and the passage's closing turn. The invention and growing popularity of electric instruments mattered to Motown's rise, and African American musicians were among the first to take up the electric bass, crafting a distinctive sound that prompted other musicians to experiment with the new technology. That experimentation eventually produced a revolution in popular music, broadening both its sound and its audience. The final sentence makes the relationship reciprocal rather than one-directional: Motown helped set these landmark shifts in motion and benefited from them at the same time, which is how the author ties the three causes together.
overall_html: The passage explains why Motown Records rose so quickly after its founding in Detroit in 1959, attributing that success to three converging factors rather than to any single one. The author's purpose is expository, and the structure is straightforwardly enumerative: an opening paragraph names the causes, then each is developed in turn, beginning with Berry Gordy's independence and his refusal to let established stars remake Motown songs, continuing with Detroit's public school music-education program and the talent pipeline it created, and closing with the rise of electric instruments and the broader revolution in popular music that Motown both helped start and profited from. No competing viewpoints appear; the account is delivered in the author's neutral voice.

Passage A

Markets, such as stock exchanges, distill the collective wisdom of millions of individuals into a single number, and they do so with amazing efficiency. In contrast to other information-gathering institutions, such as committees and polls, markets require participants to put hard dollars behind their opinions. What's more, markets reward people who are right, not those who lie convincingly or are loudest or most aggressive or who have the most degrees after their name.

Some markets have been engineered for the purpose of providing forecasts. For over a decade, an academic project called the Iowa Electronic Markets has predicted the outcomes of certain elections better than 75 percent of the polls did. Investors put money into a pool. If there are two candidates, each dollar invested purchases two contracts, one paying $1 if candidate A wins, and one paying $1 if candidate B wins. Participants can then buy and sell those contracts at a website. If the going rate for candidate A is 53 cents, then the market as a whole thinks candidate A has a 53 percent chance of winning.

Markets are highly "efficient," in the sense that the market as a whole learns—lightning fast and very accurately—what informed people know. In one experiment, a dozen participants were permitted to trade a fictional stock, having been told that it was worth one of three possible amounts. Two of the participants were then told which amount had been selected, giving them "inside knowledge." Participants couldn't communicate with each other; they could only buy and sell on the market. But everyone watched the movements of the market price, and within seconds, everyone was acting as if they were insiders.

Passage B

Markets are not infallible. To many people, this statement is a form of economic blasphemy. I suggest those people should get over it.

In a recent election, the Iowa Electronic Markets had the eventual winner trading far lower than an opponent up until a few days before the event. For almost a solid year leading up to it, this market's "prediction" was that the opponent would win easily.

Think of markets as racetracks: you get paid lower odds the better the horse looks before a race. When the nag appears ill, old, or tired, the odds are highest, and buyers get the greatest potential payoff. When the steed starts to look healthier, the odds slide lower as a win starts looking more and more likely.

If "prediction markets" do not actually predict the future, then what do they do? I suggest they merely reflect the majority opinion at a given moment. That does not imbue them with any special omniscience. Think of them as polls that avoid random spoofing because the polled must pay an entry fee to participate. That generates more serious responses than other polls—but the answers are just as potentially wrong as any other future guess. Like the majority, sometimes they are right, and sometimes they are wrong.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with a claim, not a hedge: markets such as stock exchanges distill the collective wisdom of millions of individuals into a single number, and do it with remarkable efficiency. The comparison class is deliberate. Unlike committees and polls, markets make participants put hard dollars behind their opinions, and they reward people for being right rather than for lying convincingly, shouting loudest, pressing hardest, or carrying the most degrees. Keep that contrast with polls in mind, because the second passage will return to it and use it the other way.

Evidence follows, from a market built specifically to forecast. The Iowa Electronic Markets, an academic project, has for over a decade predicted certain election outcomes better than 75 percent of polls did. The mechanism is worth holding onto because both passages rely on it. Investors pool money; in a two-candidate race each dollar buys two contracts, one paying a dollar if candidate A wins and one paying a dollar if candidate B does, and participants trade them online. A going rate of 53 cents means the market collectively puts A's chances at 53 percent.

A second supporting idea is efficiency, meaning that a market learns what informed people know, quickly and accurately. The experiment illustrating it is small but pointed: a dozen people traded a fictional stock known to be worth one of three amounts, and two were told which amount had actually been selected, giving them inside knowledge. No communication was allowed, only buying and selling, yet everyone watched the price move and within seconds all of them were trading as though they too were insiders. Price, on this account, transmits private information.

Passage B answers with a flat denial and a change of tone. Markets are not infallible; the author acknowledges that many people treat saying so as economic blasphemy, and tells them to get over it. Notice the shift in form as well as content, from measured exposition to short, combative, first-person assertion. This is not a qualification of Passage A's argument but a rejection of its central claim, and the paragraphs that follow will supply a counterexample, an analogy, and an alternative account of what these markets actually do.

The counterexample is aimed at Passage A's own showcase. In a recent election the Iowa Electronic Markets had the eventual winner trading far below an opponent until just a few days before the vote, and for almost a solid year the market's prediction was that the opponent would win easily. Watch what this does argumentatively: rather than dismissing prediction markets in general, the author takes the single institution Passage A offered as proof of accuracy and shows it sustaining a wrong answer for a very long stretch.

An analogy supplies the alternative explanation. Think of markets as racetracks, where the better a horse looks before the race the lower the odds you are paid. A nag that appears ill, old or tired carries the highest odds and the greatest potential payoff, and as the animal starts to look healthier the odds slide down while a win looks likelier. The point being made is about what prices track: they register how things appear at the moment, adjusting continuously to present impressions rather than reporting a future outcome.

The conclusion states the alternative directly. If prediction markets do not predict, they merely reflect majority opinion at a given moment, which carries no special omniscience. The author's own comparison is to polls, but polls that avoid random spoofing because participants must pay to take part, and the entry fee produces more serious responses. Concede that much and the deciding point still stands: the answers remain as potentially wrong as any other guess about the future, right sometimes and wrong sometimes, exactly like the majority whose opinion they record.
overall_html: The two passages disagree about what prediction markets accomplish. Passage A argues that markets aggregate dispersed knowledge into a single accurate number, supporting this with the Iowa Electronic Markets' record against election polls and with an experiment in which prices transmitted insiders' private information within seconds; its purpose is to defend markets as superior forecasting institutions. Passage B denies that markets are infallible, uses that same Iowa project's year-long backing of a losing candidate against it, and offers a racetrack analogy to argue that prices merely register present appearances, making these markets nothing more than polls with an entry fee. The disagreement is direct, and it turns on shared evidence read in opposite ways.

Political arguments about biodiversity and the preservation of endangered species generally assume we know what a species is. Yet answering the question of what constitutes a "good" species has long been a confusing and controversial exercise. Within ornithological circles, the debate over the "species question" has often been described as being between "lumpers" and "splitters," between those who group separate but very similar populations of birds into a single species and those who divide such populations into full species. Generally, the lumpers employ what is known as the biological species concept, which until recently was the dominant approach to species classification. Its proponents define a species as a group that is reproductively isolated from other groups, which means that there is no substantial interbreeding in the wild between members of the groups. Splitters, on the other hand, tend to use the increasingly popular phylogenetic species concept, which defines a species as a "diagnosable" population, among which there is a pattern of ancestry and descent. A phylogenetic species is a population in which members share a distinctive, genetically traceable feature that distinguishes it from other populations.

The late Charles G. Sibley, a prominent ornithologist and one of the fomenters of a controversial revolution in avian taxonomy, could be called a splitter. He used a process known as DNA-DNA hybridization—which compares DNA from different species—to determine the relationships of the various families of birds. From his studies he concluded that many earlier classifications of the relationships of bird families were wrong. For instance, he said that vultures found in North and South America were more closely related to storks than to European vultures, and that loons and grebes, which many taxonomists had argued were closely related, were not.

Sibley's work has not been widely accepted. "What the DNA data can give you is an approximation of how different the genes of two isolated populations are," one critic has written, "but how you interpret those differences is basically arbitrary, as arbitrary as any decision made in any species concept." Sibley might not have disagreed, at least not entirely. In 1996 he wrote that "Evolution produces all degrees of genetic differences between populations of organisms, but, for practical reasons, we must limit the number of degrees we choose to 'recognize' by names. We assign names of populations and proposed definitions of taxonomic categories based on various criteria, but the 'species concept' is slippery because there are so many examples in nature of populations that refuse to fit our limited set of definitions and names."

Whatever the merits of each position, the species question undoubtedly has political and economic stakes. For example, increasing the number of species would probably increase the number needing protection as well.
explanation_html:
A political question turns out to rest on an unsettled scientific one. Debates about biodiversity and endangered species assume we know what a species is, yet deciding what makes a good species has long been confusing and controversial. Among ornithologists the dispute runs between the Lumpers, who group separate but very similar bird populations into one species, and the Splitters, who divide them into full species. Each camp has a concept behind it. Lumpers generally use the biological species concept, until recently dominant, which defines a species as a group reproductively isolated from others, with no substantial interbreeding in the wild. Splitters prefer the increasingly popular phylogenetic species concept, on which a species is a diagnosable population sharing a distinctive, genetically traceable feature and a pattern of ancestry and descent.

The abstract dispute now gets a face. Charles G. Sibley, a prominent ornithologist and one of the instigators of a controversial revolution in avian taxonomy, counts as a splitter. His method was DNA-DNA hybridization, which compares DNA drawn from different species, and he used it to work out how the various families of birds are related. His conclusion was that many earlier classifications had it wrong: vultures in North and South America turned out to be closer kin to storks than to European vultures, while loons and grebes, long assumed by many taxonomists to be closely related, were not.

Reception is the subject here, and it is mixed rather than hostile. Sibley's work has not been widely accepted, and a Critic puts the objection sharply: DNA data can approximate how different the genes of two isolated populations are, but interpreting those differences is basically arbitrary, as arbitrary as any decision made under any species concept. The author then complicates the disagreement by noting Sibley might not have entirely disagreed. Writing in 1996, he observed that evolution produces every degree of genetic difference between populations while practical necessity forces us to recognize only some by name, which leaves the species concept slippery because so many real populations refuse to fit our definitions.

The short closing paragraph pulls back to the frame set in the first sentence. Whatever the merits of either position, the species question carries political and economic stakes, and the example given is concrete: raise the number of recognized species and you probably raise the number needing protection as well. Notice what the author does not do. No verdict is delivered between lumpers and splitters, and no claim is made that the stakes should influence the science; the point is simply that a taxonomic decision has consequences beyond taxonomy.
overall_html: The passage explains why biologists cannot agree on what counts as a species, framing the dispute as one between lumpers, who rely on the biological species concept of reproductive isolation, and splitters, who rely on the phylogenetic concept of a diagnosable population, and then illustrating it through Charles G. Sibley's DNA-based reclassification of bird families and the criticism that interpreting genetic differences is inescapably arbitrary. The author's purpose is expository rather than partisan, moving from the definitional problem, to a representative splitter and his results, to the critical response and Sibley's own concession, and closing by returning to the political and economic stakes raised at the outset.

This passage was adapted from an article published in 1991.

Because it is relatively easy and inexpensive to produce copycat computer programs, most people believe that some form of legal protection should be extended to creators of computer software. Without a legal deterrent to copycat programming, the resources expended by an individual or a company to develop an innovative software program could be unfairly exploited by rivals who develop a similar product and rush it to market at a lower price. The occurrence of such exploitation would leave software developers with little financial incentive to develop innovative products. While most legal commentators agree that copyright has generally proven to be an effective means of preventing this exploitation, some contend that patent protection is also needed to combat copycatting.

In essence, every piece of software is an encoding of one or more algorithms. An algorithm is simply defined as a series of steps to be followed in carrying out a task; to be usable in computer applications, an algorithm must be expressed in terms that can be processed by a computer. Proponents of software patents assert that in providing a specific way of achieving a desired result, the encoding of algorithms is analogous to the design of a process. Process designs (for example, an innovative way of inducing a series of chemical reactions) do, in fact, fall under the scope of patent protection. However, in order for any design to be patentable, it must be genuinely a product of invention (rather than, say, a law of nature or a logical axiom). For example, while a particular innovative windmill design might be patentable, the principle that wind can be harnessed to produce energy would clearly not be. On similar grounds, software algorithms, because they represent generic principles underlying the specific processes by which tasks are to be carried out by computers, should not be considered patentable.

Issuing patents for computer programs would extend protection to software developers beyond that afforded by copyright when there is really no compelling justification for doing so. Insofar as software programs constitute the expression of ideas in the form of specific texts (i.e., sequences of computer code), they fall more appropriately within the established domain of copyright law. Whereas patents protect the underlying design of an invention, even if it is never actually executed, copyright protects only the particular way in which the underlying ideas are expressed. Because the value of software lies in its form of expression, protection should be given only for particular applications—expressions of algorithms in an encoded form. Such protection could be more effectively afforded with only slight modification to existing copyright laws, and the financial incentive to develop innovative software could thereby be preserved.
explanation_html:
The opening lays out common ground before any dispute begins. Copying software is cheap and easy, so almost everyone accepts that developers deserve some legal protection; otherwise a rival could imitate an expensive innovation, undersell it, and destroy the incentive to invent anything new. Having secured that much, the paragraph narrows to the actual disagreement. Most legal commentators hold that copyright already prevents this exploitation effectively, while the proponents of software patents insist patent protection is needed as well. The question for the rest of the passage is not whether to protect software but which legal tool fits.

The middle paragraph builds the proponents' argument fairly and then dismantles it. First the technical vocabulary: a piece of software encodes algorithms, and an algorithm is just a sequence of steps for performing a task, written so a computer can process it. The proponents' analogy is that encoding an algorithm specifies a way of reaching a result, much as a process design does, and process designs like a novel method of triggering chemical reactions are genuinely patentable. The Author accepts that premise but attaches the limit that defeats it: patents cover inventions, not laws of nature or logical axioms. A clever windmill is patentable, the principle of harnessing wind is not, and algorithms are generic principles of that second kind.

The conclusion converts the objection into a positive recommendation. Patenting programs would hand developers protection beyond copyright without any compelling reason, and the author explains why copyright is the better fit by drawing the distinction the argument turns on. A patent protects an underlying design even if that design is never built, while copyright protects only the particular expression of an idea. Since a program's value lies in its expression, a specific sequence of code, protection should attach to particular encoded applications rather than to the algorithm itself. Slight amendments to existing copyright law would do the job and keep the incentive to innovate intact.
overall_html: The passage argues that although software developers plainly need legal protection against copycats, patents are the wrong instrument, because algorithms are generic underlying principles rather than inventions, and copyright, which protects a particular expression rather than an underlying design, already fits the way software's value actually resides in its specific code. The author's purpose is to settle a legal dispute by recommending one form of protection over another, moving from shared premises, to the patent proponents' analogy with process design and its refutation by the invention requirement, to a proposal that existing copyright law be modified slightly. The positions to track are the patent proponents' and the author's own, alongside the commentators who already favor copyright.

A major problem facing industrial societies is their exponentially increasing production of toxic waste. Environmental regulations and expenses for landfills and incinerators have increased significantly in recent years. In an effort to save time and money, many industries have turned to alternative methods of hazardous-waste disposal, including increased use of deep-well injection. In this method, wells are drilled into porous and permeable rock strata that are already saturated with salt water. Liquid wastes are then injected into the rock strata. Most of these wells are drilled to a depth of at least 300 meters—the minimum depth that generally puts the injected waste at a safe distance below any aquifer, in this case a rock stratum containing drinkable water. Such wells are rarely deeper than 1,800 meters, because below this depth it is more cost-effective to consider an alternative method of disposal. Deep-well injection, which has been used to some extent since the 1930s, has become a matter of controversy as growing numbers of communities come to rely on underground sources of drinking water. The controversy arises because there are three serious problems with this method of waste disposal.

Under the best conditions, wastes are injected into rock strata saturated with salt water and separated by impermeable rock strata from aquifers containing drinkable water. However, injection wells may leak, allowing significant amounts of noxious chemicals to mix with supplies of drinking water. In other cases, mistakes by personnel working on the wells may lead to the pollution of aquifers. In one such case, workers installing a 500-meter-deep well left a gap along approximately 30 meters of its steel casing. This allowed waste to escape at a depth of only 200 meters, threatening a regional aquifer supplying water to 100,000 people. Because such accidents take place deep within the earth, people may be exposed to dangerous levels of waste materials for long periods of time before the problem is even discovered.

The third problem associated with deep-well injection arises from the fact that it is nearly impossible to predict how the injected wastes will be acted on by the geological features of the injection area. Unlike surface water, the water in underground rock strata does not flow entirely under the influence of gravity. Moving along subterranean pressure gradients, it can flow in any direction and, in some cases, can be transported thousands of meters per year through geologic faults, porous rock, or other geologic formations.

The significant uncertainty about where injected wastes will flow, along with the possibilities of mechanical failure and human error, makes deep-well injection a risky means of managing hazardous wastes. Unfortunately, as societies produce more toxic waste, industry will rely increasingly upon this relatively cheap, efficient means of disposal.
explanation_html:
Everything the argument needs is loaded into the opening. Industrial societies produce exponentially more toxic waste, and because regulation and the cost of landfills and incinerators have risen sharply, industries have looked for cheaper disposal, deep-well injection among them. The method is explained plainly: wells are drilled into porous, permeable rock already saturated with salt water, and liquid wastes are pumped in. The depth range has reasons attached — at least 300 meters, the minimum that generally keeps waste safely below an aquifer, meaning a stratum holding drinkable water, and rarely past 1,800 meters, below which other methods become more cost-effective. The last sentence is the roadmap, promising three serious problems.

Two of the three arrive here, and both concern failure rather than design. Under the best conditions waste goes into salt-water strata sealed off from drinkable aquifers by impermeable rock. But wells can leak, letting significant amounts of noxious chemicals reach drinking supplies, and mistakes by personnel working on the wells can pollute aquifers directly. The case supplied is concrete: workers left a gap along roughly 30 meters of the steel casing on a 500-meter well, so waste escaped at only 200 meters and threatened a regional aquifer serving 100,000 people. Because the failures happen deep underground, people can be exposed for long stretches before anyone notices.

The third problem is announced explicitly and is the most fundamental, since it survives even when nothing breaks. It is nearly impossible to predict how the geology of an injection area will act on the wastes put into it. The reason is that underground water does not behave like surface water: rather than flowing entirely under gravity, it moves along subterranean pressure gradients, which means it can travel in any direction at all, and in some cases thousands of meters a year through geologic faults, porous rock or other formations. Waste can therefore end up somewhere no one intended.

The closing paragraph delivers the verdict and then undercuts it. Combining the deep uncertainty about where injected wastes will travel with the possibilities of mechanical failure and human error, the Author judges deep-well injection a risky way to manage hazardous waste. What makes the ending pointed rather than merely conclusive is the forecast attached to it: as societies generate more toxic waste, industry will rely on this method more, not less, precisely because it is relatively cheap and efficient. Notice that the author offers no alternative and no remedy, which leaves the passage closing on an unresolved warning.
overall_html: The passage explains how deep-well injection disposes of hazardous liquid waste and argues that the method is dangerously unreliable, identifying three problems: wells that leak, errors made by the personnel who build and service them, and the impossibility of predicting where underground water will carry the injected wastes. The author's purpose is critical, and the structure is announced in advance, with an opening paragraph that describes the technique and promises three problems, two paragraphs that deliver them with a concrete case of faulty casing threatening a regional aquifer, and a closing verdict that the method is risky yet will be used more heavily as toxic waste increases.

Native American stories often feature a character called the trickster, a comic figure who has both mortal weaknesses and supernatural powers. Recently, the term "trickster" has also appeared in criticism of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century European literature, particularly in reference to the picaresque novel and its central character, the picaro (Spanish for "rogue"): both the picaro and the trickster are heroes of episodic adventures, and both live on the peripheries of society and are morally flawed.

Yet closer examination reveals that applying the term "trickster" to both characters obscures essential differences between them. The picaro—typically a male character—operates primarily as an agent of satire. Most commonly, the picaro's adventures begin when he spontaneously yields to his own roguish, though innocent, impulses. The picaro indulges in vices and follies with relish and freedom, much to the outrage of other members of society, who often secretly indulge in similar pastimes out of a habitual compulsion. Thus the picaro's authenticity serves as a foil to the perceived hypocrisy of conventional society. To such a society, the picaro can represent a dangerous, disruptive freedom, and it reacts by marginalizing him. It is in that distance—between the ostensibly disreputable freedom of the picaro and the hypocrisy of the safely ensconced social being—that the satire occurs.

But the trickster, usually an animal acting as a human agent, does not serve a satiric function. For while the picaresque novel takes place in and satirizes human society, the trickster operates in the ahistorical world of myth; where the targets of the picaresque novel are the idiosyncrasies and inconsistencies of a historical human society, trickster stories seek, using the trickster's negative example, to instruct listeners about moral behavior of individuals. In fact, whatever flaws the trickster reveals are thoroughly the trickster's own. They are not a foil to a corrupt society; they are instead essential to who the trickster is. The trickster is a comic figure precisely because of these somewhat irrational, compulsive, and foolish—in short, mortal—actions. Similarly, the trickster is a socially peripheral character not by being forced to the periphery by a hypocritical society, but rather because the trickster's thoroughly flawed character makes the trickster fundamentally antisocial, even anarchic, all the while helping listeners to avoid these flaws.

It is this combination of mythic setting and mortal weakness that determines the particular targets of the trickster's comic high jinks: the eternal and unchanging foibles of mortal beings. In one story, for example, a coyote trickster falls in love with a star. The trickster is quite tenacious and human, even though the object of desire is beyond reasonable mortal possibility. In the end the star takes the trickster up into the sky, only to let the trickster fall back to Earth; the story's listeners realize that the trickster has gotten a comeuppance for reaching beyond proper limits, but all the while they recognize in themselves the trickster's extravagant hopes.
explanation_html:
A borrowed label sets up the comparison the passage will take apart. In Native American stories the trickster is a comic figure combining mortal weaknesses with supernatural powers. Critics of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century European literature have recently begun applying the same term to the picaresque novel and its central figure, the picaro, Spanish for rogue. The grounds offered are real enough: both are heroes of episodic adventures, both live on the peripheries of society, and both are morally flawed. Register that the author is reporting this critical usage, not adopting it, since the next sentence of the passage begins dismantling it.

The picaro is analyzed first, on his own terms. Closer examination shows the shared label obscures essential differences, and the difference that matters is function: the picaro, typically male, works as an agent of satire. His adventures begin when he spontaneously gives in to roguish but innocent impulses, and he indulges vices and follies with relish and freedom, outraging members of society who secretly do much the same out of habitual compulsion. His authenticity is therefore a foil to their hypocrisy. Society reads his freedom as dangerous and disruptive and pushes him to the margins, and the satire lives in exactly that distance.

Every element of that account is now matched and reversed. The trickster, usually an animal acting as a human agent, serves no satiric function at all. The picaresque novel is set inside human society and satirizes it, while the trickster inhabits the ahistorical world of myth; the picaresque targets the idiosyncrasies of a particular historical society, whereas trickster stories use the trickster's negative example to teach listeners about individual moral behavior. His flaws are not a foil to anything corrupt outside him but essential to who he is, and their irrational, compulsive, foolish, in a word mortal, quality is what makes him funny. He is peripheral because that character is fundamentally antisocial, not because a hypocritical society expelled him.

The consequences of that contrast are drawn out and then illustrated. Because the trickster combines a mythic setting with mortal weakness, his comedy takes aim at the eternal and unchanging foibles of mortal beings rather than at one society's particular failings. The example is a coyote trickster who falls in love with a star, tenacious and recognizably human even though the object of desire lies beyond reasonable mortal possibility. The star carries him into the sky only to drop him back to Earth. Notice how the ending works on two levels: listeners see a comeuppance for reaching past proper limits, and simultaneously recognize their own extravagant hopes in his.
overall_html: The passage argues that applying the term trickster to the picaro of the European picaresque novel obscures essential differences between the two figures, since the picaro operates within a historical society and functions satirically, as a foil exposing that society's hypocrisy, while the trickster inhabits the ahistorical world of myth and instructs listeners through the negative example of flaws that are entirely his own. The author's purpose is corrective, and the structure is a controlled comparison: the shared label and its apparent justification, then the picaro analyzed in full, then the trickster matched against him point by point, and finally the coyote and star story illustrating how mythic setting and mortal weakness together fix the trickster's targets.
