Passage A is adapted from an essay by historian Christopher Ricks; passage B is from the introduction, by historian Paulina Kewes, to a book in which Ricks's essay appears.

Passage A

In her 1996 history of plagiarism in English Renaissance drama, Laura J. Rosenthal tells us that her purpose is to "question differences between plagiarism, imitation, adaptation, repetition, and originality." But such rhetorical questioning invariably leads to the required postmodern answer: that there is no difference between these things—other than that those in power use the opprobrious term "plagiarism" when the work in question emanates from those whom they dislike.

Though the book is animated by a political fervor that is clearly moral, the author writes as if a political approach has to extirpate all moral considerations from any discussion of plagiarism. What in moral terms is a matter of honesty or dishonesty—plagiarism being dishonest—is instead reduced to "the cultural location of the text and the position of the author."

The consequence of a historical approach that seeks to "delegitimize" the distinction between imitation and plagiarism is that it demeans and degrades moral thought. That no moral standard is universal does not of itself entail that moral standards are nothing but expressions of power. Moral conventions, though not universal, may be valuable, indispensable, worthy of respect. The extirpation of moral considerations from political histories such as this one is a sad loss to political history.

Passage B

The idea of plagiarism, like all ideas, has a history. To earlier generations it had semantic inflections and resonances different from those we recognize today. The varied impulses behind these varying views—which have themselves evolved in response to commercial circumstances, new theories of artistic creation, and developments in copyright law—have repeatedly complicated judgments of plagiarism. Despite an abiding sense that plagiarism is morally wrong, there has been much fluidity in the way the charge has been applied, and virtually identical acts of illicit appropriation have been sometimes denounced, sometimes excused, and sometimes praised.

Christopher Ricks is suspicious of historical approaches to ethical issues; to him, emphasis on change across generations produces an extenuating moral relativism that shields the evil of plagiarism from its due obloquy. But there are historical approaches, and there are historical approaches.

Ricks is rightly dismissive of the postmodern reduction of moral standards to expressions of power. And it is also true that there has been some shoddy scholarship that anachronistically projects modern-day ideologies having to do with gender, race, or class onto historically remote controversies. Yet bad history is no argument against history itself. To reconstruct the attitudes of the past is not necessarily to vindicate them. It is merely to acknowledge that whatever we might think is the correct way of apprehending plagiarism—and there is hardly a consensus on the matter even today—our predecessors may not, and often did not, share our perspectives.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens as a hostile review. Laura J. Rosenthal's 1996 history of plagiarism in English Renaissance drama says its purpose is to question the differences between plagiarism, imitation, adaptation, repetition and originality. The Reviewer treats that framing as rhetorical, insisting such questioning invariably produces the required postmodern answer, that no difference exists except that those in power apply the word plagiarism to work by people they dislike. The word required is doing the work here, since it accuses the book of reaching a conclusion fixed in advance rather than discovered.

The central charge follows, and it is about moral vocabulary. The Reviewer grants that the book is animated by a political fervor which is itself clearly moral, then objects that its author writes as though a political approach must strip every moral consideration out of any discussion of plagiarism. What is properly a question of honesty or dishonesty, plagiarism being dishonest, gets reduced instead to the cultural location of the text and the position of the author. Notice the parenthetical insistence, because it states the reviewer's own commitment rather than reporting the book's.

The objection is now generalized into a principle, and the reasoning is worth following closely. A historical approach that sets out to delegitimize the distinction between imitation and plagiarism demeans and degrades moral thought. The Reviewer accepts the premise but denies the inference drawn from it: that no moral standard is universal does not by itself entail that moral standards are nothing but expressions of power. Conventions can be less than universal and still be valuable, indispensable, worthy of respect. Removing moral considerations from political histories is a loss to political history itself.

Passage B begins from the very premise Passage A distrusts. Plagiarism, like all ideas, has a history, and earlier generations heard semantic inflections and resonances in it that we no longer recognize. The impulses behind those changing views have themselves evolved in response to commercial circumstances, new theories of artistic creation and developments in copyright law. The result, despite an abiding sense that plagiarism is morally wrong, is fluidity in how the charge gets applied, with virtually identical acts of illicit appropriation sometimes denounced, sometimes excused and sometimes praised.

Here the second passage turns to a named opponent, Ricks, whose position lines up closely with the argument Passage A made. His position is restated accurately rather than caricatured: he is suspicious of historical approaches to ethical issues because stressing change across generations produces an extenuating moral relativism that shields the evil of plagiarism from the condemnation it deserves. Then comes the pivot, the deliberately repetitive remark that there are historical approaches and there are historical approaches, promising a distinction between the kind he rightly fears and the kind being defended.

That distinction is drawn by conceding first. Ricks is called right to dismiss the reduction of moral standards to expressions of power, and right that some shoddy scholarship anachronistically projects present-day ideologies of gender, race or class onto remote controversies. But bad history, the author answers, is no argument against history itself. Reconstructing the attitudes of the past is not the same as vindicating them; it only acknowledges that whatever the correct understanding of plagiarism may be, and there is hardly consensus even now, our predecessors often did not share our perspectives.
overall_html: Both passages address how plagiarism should be studied, and they partly overlap before parting. Passage A is a review attacking a historical study for dissolving plagiarism into a question of cultural position and power, and arguing that moral standards can be non-universal yet still valuable, so that stripping moral thought out of political history impoverishes it. Passage B, written with Ricks and his objection explicitly in view, agrees that reducing morality to power is wrong and that some historical scholarship is anachronistic, but insists that bad history is no case against history, since reconstructing past attitudes acknowledges difference without endorsing it. The relationship is partial agreement on principle with disagreement about method.

The use of criminal sanctions against corporations is well established, but the practice has recently come under fire from legal theorists who maintain that corporations should be held civilly rather than criminally liable for wrongdoing. Civil liability, these theorists argue, shares important features with criminal liability: both impose punishment on a company, both aim at deterrence, and both degrade a company's reputation. Yet, they claim, civil liability is better able to determine appropriate levels of damages. Furthermore, because criminal liability causes a greater loss of reputation, its overall cost to corporations is far higher than that of civil liability; this additional cost is borne by society at large in the form of higher product prices. Finally, civil liability is also more cost-effective from the point of view of the government: the greater procedural protections of criminal law make deterrence through criminal prosecution extremely expensive.

Even if it is less economical, however, criminal liability is a much stronger deterrent. The considerable enforcement powers involved, including the ability to detain and question corporate officials, are themselves significant deterrents. Furthermore, the fact that private civil litigation requires an identifiable victim with the necessary resources to commence litigation weakens its deterrent impact. Most importantly, the main function of criminal law is to censure wrongdoing and to emphasize that society forcefully rejects such conduct. Civil liability is ill suited for this purpose.

Other legal theorists who do not object to criminal sanctions per se argue that individuals within corporations, rather than corporations themselves, are the appropriate target of criminal prosecution in cases involving corporate wrongdoing. They maintain that individuals within corporations are more responsive to deterrence because they generally fear prosecution and the loss of employment that can result from it. Additionally, they say, punishment of a corporation, in the form of a fine, essentially punishes shareholders, creditors, employees who may be laid off, and ultimately the public, which is forced to absorb higher prices.

However, this approach is also misguided. Corporations often bury responsibility within complex hierarchies, with the result that no individual responsible for corporate misdeeds can be identified. Another problem is that under this approach, a corporation will often find it cheaper to designate and compensate an internal scapegoat to face prosecution than to refrain from wrongdoing. The most effective way to ensure that corporations improve their practices is to hold corporations themselves criminally liable for their conduct. Indeed, criminal liability works on shareholders as well as corporate officers and employees: because criminal punishment of corporations decreases their wealth, it can motivate shareholders to push for better corporate practices. Arguments that shareholders and employees need economic protection are outweighed by the greater societal interest in ensuring the safety of employees, the public, and the environment.
explanation_html:
The first position is laid out in full before anyone answers it. Criminal sanctions against corporations are well established, but the Civil Liability Theorists hold that corporations should face civil rather than criminal liability. Their case begins with similarity: both forms punish a company, both aim at deterrence, both damage its reputation. From there come three advantages, worth tracking separately. Civil liability determines appropriate damage levels better; criminal liability inflicts a greater reputational loss and so costs corporations far more, a cost society absorbs through higher product prices; and criminal law's greater procedural protections make deterrence by prosecution extremely expensive for government.

The Author answers on the one ground the previous paragraph never contested. Grant that criminal liability is less economical; it is nevertheless a much stronger deterrent. Three reasons follow in ascending order of importance. The enforcement powers involved, including the ability to detain and question corporate officials, deter by themselves. Private civil litigation needs an identifiable victim with resources enough to sue, which blunts its deterrent force. Most important is a claim about purpose rather than efficiency: criminal law exists to censure wrongdoing and to mark society's forceful rejection of it, and civil liability cannot do that.

A second and narrower opposing view now enters, and the distinction matters. The Individual Liability Theorists raise no objection to criminal sanctions as such; they argue that the right targets are individuals inside corporations rather than the corporations themselves. Their reasoning is partly about incentives, since individuals respond better to deterrence because they fear prosecution and the loss of employment it can bring, and partly about who actually bears a corporate fine, which falls on shareholders, creditors, employees who may be laid off, and ultimately a public paying higher prices.

The refutation and the author's own conclusion close the passage together. Corporations bury responsibility inside complex hierarchies, so often no individual responsible for a misdeed can be identified at all, and where one can, a corporation may find it cheaper to designate and compensate an internal scapegoat than to stop the wrongdoing. Hence the author's position: hold corporations themselves criminally liable. That reaches shareholders anyway, since punishment decreases corporate wealth and can motivate them to press for better practices. The final move is a weighing rather than a denial, setting economic protection for shareholders and employees below society's interest in the safety of employees, the public and the environment.
overall_html: The passage defends holding corporations themselves criminally liable for wrongdoing against two rival proposals, arguing that criminal liability deters more strongly than civil liability and that prosecuting individuals inside a corporation fails because responsibility is buried in complex hierarchies and scapegoats can be cheaply arranged. The author's purpose is to argue for a position by refutation, and the structure alternates: the civil liability theorists' economic case, then the author's reply that criminal law uniquely censures wrongdoing; the individual liability theorists' case, then the author's reply and conclusion, which weighs shareholder and employee protection against the greater societal interest in safety.

For decades, there has been a deep rift between poetry and fiction in the United States, especially in academic settings; graduate writing programs in universities, for example, train students as poets or as writers of fiction, but almost never as both. Both poets and writers of fiction have tended to support this separation, in large part because the current conventional wisdom holds that poetry should be elliptical and lyrical, reflecting inner states and processes of thought or feeling, whereas character and narrative events are the stock-in-trade of fiction.

Certainly it is true that poetry and fiction are distinct genres, but why have specialized education and literary territoriality resulted from this distinction? The answer lies perhaps in a widespread attitude in U.S. culture, which often casts a suspicious eye on the generalist. Those with knowledge and expertise in multiple areas risk charges of dilettantism, as if ability in one field is diluted or compromised by accomplishment in another.

Fortunately, there are signs that the bias against writers who cross generic boundaries is diminishing; several recent writers are known and respected for their work in both genres. One important example of this trend is Rita Dove, an African American writer highly acclaimed for both her poetry and her fiction. A few years ago, speaking at a conference entitled "Poets Who Write Fiction," Dove expressed gentle incredulity about the habit of segregating the genres. She had grown up reading and loving both fiction and poetry, she said, unaware of any purported danger lurking in attempts to mix the two. She also studied for some time in Germany, where, she observes, "Poets write plays, novelists compose libretti, playwrights write novels—they would not understand our restrictiveness."

It makes little sense, Dove believes, to persist in the restrictive approach to poetry and fiction prevalent in the U.S., because each genre shares in the nature of the other. Indeed, her poetry offers example after example of what can only be properly regarded as lyric narrative. Her use of language in these poems is undeniably lyrical—that is, it evokes emotion and inner states without requiring the reader to organize ideas or events in a particular linear structure. Yet this lyric expression simultaneously presents the elements of a plot in such a way that the reader is led repeatedly to take account of clusters of narrative details within the lyric flow. Thus while the language is lyrical, it often comes to constitute, cumulatively, a work of narrative fiction. Similarly, many passages in her fiction, though undeniably prose, achieve the status of lyric narrative through the use of poetic rhythms and elliptical expression. In short, Dove bridges the gap between poetry and fiction not only by writing in both genres, but also by fusing the two genres within individual works.
explanation_html:
The opening states the situation to be explained. In the United States, and above all inside universities, poetry and fiction have been held apart for decades, with graduate writing programs training a student as one or the other but almost never as both. Writers on both sides have largely endorsed the split, and the passage attributes that to a prevailing assumption about what each genre is for: poetry is supposed to be elliptical and lyrical, tracking inner states and the movement of thought and feeling, while character and narrative events are treated as the property of fiction.

A question drives the second paragraph, and it belongs to the author. Granting that these are genuinely distinct genres, why should a distinction produce separate training tracks and literary territoriality? The author offers a cultural explanation rather than a literary one, suggesting that American culture regards the generalist with suspicion, so anyone competent across several areas risks being called a dilettante, as though skill in one field must be diluted by accomplishment in another. The explanation is put forward tentatively, but it relocates the cause of the divide away from anything intrinsic to either genre.

Evidence that the bias is fading arrives next, concentrated in a single figure. Several recent writers are respected in both genres, and Rita Dove, acclaimed for her poetry and her fiction alike, is the passage's chief example. Speaking at a conference on poets who write fiction, she expressed gentle disbelief at the habit of segregating the two, recalling that she grew up reading and loving both and never suspected any danger in mixing them. Her study in Germany sharpens the contrast, since there poets write plays and novelists compose libretti, and the American restrictiveness would strike people as incomprehensible.

Why Dove thinks the division makes little sense occupies the close, and this is the most technical stretch of the passage. Her claim is that each genre already shares in the nature of the other, and her own poems demonstrate it as lyric narrative. The language is lyrical in the ordinary sense, evoking emotion and inner states without forcing the reader through a linear sequence, yet it simultaneously plants elements of a plot so that clusters of narrative detail keep surfacing within the lyric flow, and the poem accumulates into fiction. Her prose performs the reverse through poetic rhythm and elliptical expression. She therefore bridges the gap twice, by working in both genres and by fusing them inside single works.
overall_html: The passage explains the long-standing separation of poetry and fiction in American literary culture, attributes it less to any real difference between the genres than to a national suspicion of the generalist, and presents Rita Dove as evidence that the division is both weakening and unnecessary. The author's purpose is to diagnose the separation and then to challenge it, moving from the institutional split and the conventional wisdom supporting it, to a cultural explanation for its persistence, to Dove's incredulity and her German counterexample, and finally to an analysis of her lyric narrative, in which poems accumulate plot and prose takes on poetic rhythm. The viewpoints are the author's and Dove's, and they align.

The two passages discuss recent scientific research on music. They are adapted from two different papers presented at a scholarly conference.

Passage A

Did music and human language originate separately or together? Both systems use intonation and rhythm to communicate emotions. Both can be produced vocally or with tools, and people can produce both music and language silently to themselves.

Brain imaging studies suggest that music and language are part of one large, vastly complicated, neurological system for processing sound. In fact, fewer differences than similarities exist between the neurological processing of the two. One could think of the two activities as different radio programs that can be broadcast over the same hardware. One noteworthy difference, though, is that, generally speaking, people are better at language than music. In music, anyone can listen easily enough, but most people do not perform well, and in many cultures composition is left to specialists. In language, by contrast, nearly everyone actively performs and composes.

Given their shared neurological basis, it appears that music and language evolved together as brain size increased over the course of hominid evolution. But the primacy of language over music that we can observe today suggests that language, not music, was the primary function natural selection operated on. Music, it would seem, had little adaptive value of its own, and most likely developed on the coattails of language.

Passage B

Darwin claimed that since "neither the enjoyment nor the capacity of producing musical notes are faculties of the least [practical] use to man . . . they must be ranked amongst the most mysterious with which he is endowed." I suggest that the enjoyment of and the capacity to produce musical notes are faculties of indispensable use to mothers and their infants and that it is in the emotional bonds created by the interaction of mother and child that we can discover the evolutionary origins of human music.

Even excluding lullabies, which parents sing to infants, human mothers and infants under six months of age engage in ritualized, sequential behaviors, involving vocal, facial, and bodily interactions. Using face-to-face mother-infant interactions filmed at 24 frames per second, researchers have shown that mothers and infants jointly construct mutually improvised interactions in which each partner tracks the actions of the other. Such episodes last from one-half second to three seconds and are composed of musical elements—variations in pitch, rhythm, timbre, volume, and tempo.

What evolutionary advantage would such behavior have? In the course of hominid evolution, brain size increased rapidly. Contemporaneously, the increase in bipedality caused the birth canal to narrow. This resulted in hominid infants being born ever-more prematurely, leaving them much more helpless at birth. This helplessness necessitated longer, better maternal care. Under such conditions, the emotional bonds created in the premusical mother-infant interactions we observe in Homo sapiens today—behavior whose neurological basis essentially constitutes the capacity to make and enjoy music—would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens with the question the whole set addresses, whether music and human language originated separately or together, and begins assembling the case for together. The similarities offered are functional rather than historical: both systems use intonation and rhythm to communicate emotion, both can be produced by voice or with tools, and both can be produced silently inside one's own head. Nothing has been concluded yet, but the direction of travel is clear, and each parallel is chosen to make a common origin look plausible.

Neurological evidence deepens the parallel and then introduces the wrinkle that will decide the argument. Brain imaging suggests that music and language belong to one large, vastly complicated system for processing sound, with fewer differences than similarities between them, an idea the passage captures with the image of two radio programs broadcast over the same hardware. Then comes the asymmetry to hold on to: generally speaking, people are better at language than at music. Anyone can listen easily enough, but most people perform poorly and many cultures leave composition to specialists, whereas nearly everyone actively performs and composes language.

The conclusion of Passage A draws on both preceding paragraphs at once. Shared neurology suggests that music and language evolved together as brain size increased over hominid evolution, while the observable primacy of language indicates that language, not music, was what natural selection actually operated on. Music, on this account, had little adaptive value of its own and most likely developed on the coattails of language, making it a by-product rather than a target of selection. That last claim is precisely what the second passage sets out to overturn.

Passage B opens by quoting Darwin, who ranked musical capacity among the most mysterious human faculties precisely because it seemed to serve no practical use. This author treats that as a problem to be solved rather than as a verdict, and answers with a thesis about one particular relationship: the enjoyment and production of musical notes are of indispensable use to mothers and their infants, and the evolutionary origins of human music lie in the emotional bonds their interaction creates. Notice what is and is not being disputed, since B says nothing against the neurology in A and everything against the claim that music lacked adaptive value.

Evidence for the thesis comes from observed behavior rather than from theory. Lullabies are set aside deliberately, since those are songs a parent chooses to sing, leaving the ritualized sequential exchanges of voice, face and body that mothers and infants under six months engage in on their own. Filmed at twenty-four frames per second, these prove to be jointly improvised, with each partner tracking the other, and they last from half a second to three seconds. The crucial claim is what they are made of, namely musical elements: variations in pitch, rhythm, timbre, volume and tempo.

The closing paragraph supplies the adaptive mechanism the thesis requires, and it does so by chaining physical changes together. Hominid brain size increased rapidly while growing bipedality narrowed the birth canal, so infants were born ever more prematurely and thus more helpless, which made longer and better maternal care necessary. Under those conditions the emotional bonds created in premusical mother-infant interaction would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage. Catch the definitional move planted mid-sentence, that the neurological basis of this behavior essentially constitutes the capacity to make and enjoy music, since that is how a claim about bonding becomes a claim about the origin of music.
overall_html: Both passages ask how human music originated, and they reach incompatible conclusions about whether it was ever selected for in its own right. Passage A infers from shared neurological processing that music and language evolved together, but concludes from the present primacy of language that selection operated on language alone and that music, having little adaptive value, developed on its coattails. Passage B answers Darwin's puzzle about music's apparent uselessness by locating its origins in mother-infant interaction, whose improvised exchanges are built from musical elements and whose emotional bonds would have been advantageous once narrowing birth canals and expanding brains left infants helpless. B thus grants music the independent adaptive value that A denies it.

The World Wide Web, a network of electronically produced and interconnected (or "linked") sites, called pages, that are accessible via personal computer, raises legal issues about the rights of owners of intellectual property, notably those who create documents for inclusion on Web pages. Some of these owners of intellectual property claim that unless copyright law is strengthened, intellectual property on the Web will not be protected from copyright infringement. Web users, however, claim that if their ability to access information on Web pages is reduced, the Web cannot live up to its potential as an open, interactive medium of communication.

The debate arises from the Web's ability to link one document to another. Links between sites are analogous to the inclusion in a printed text of references to other works, but with one difference: the cited document is instantly retrievable by a user who activates the link. This immediate accessibility creates a problem, since current copyright laws give owners of intellectual property the right to sue a distributor of unauthorized copies of their material even if that distributor did not personally make the copies. If person A, the author of a document, puts the document on a Web page, and person B, the creator of another Web page, creates a link to A's document, is B committing copyright infringement?

To answer this question, it must first be determined who controls distribution of a document on the Web. When A places a document on a Web page, this is comparable to recording an outgoing message on one's telephone answering machine for others to hear. When B creates a link to A's document, this is akin to B's giving out A's telephone number, thereby allowing third parties to hear the outgoing message for themselves. Anyone who calls can listen to the message; that is its purpose. While B's link may indeed facilitate access to A's document, the crucial point is that A, simply by placing that document on the Web, is thereby offering it for distribution. Therefore, even if B leads others to the document, it is A who actually controls access to it. Hence creating a link to a document is not the same as making or distributing a copy of that document. Moreover, techniques are already available by which A can restrict access to a document. For example, A may require a password to gain entry to A's Web page, just as a telephone owner can request an unlisted number and disclose it only to selected parties. Such a solution would compromise the openness of the Web somewhat, but not as much as the threat of copyright infringement litigation. Changing copyright law to benefit owners of intellectual property is thus ill-advised because it would impede the development of the Web as a public forum dedicated to the free exchange of ideas.
explanation_html:
The opening frames a conflict rather than a phenomenon. The Web is a network of linked pages, and because those pages carry documents somebody wrote, it raises questions about intellectual property. Two positions go on the board immediately. The Owners, the people who create documents for Web pages, warn that without stronger copyright law their material will not be protected from infringement. The Web Users counter that reducing access to pages defeats the whole point of an open, interactive medium of communication. Notice that the author has not taken a side yet; keep both positions available, because the final paragraph comes down firmly on one of them.

The second paragraph explains what actually generates the dispute: linking. A link works much like a footnote citing another work, with one decisive difference, since the cited document is retrievable the instant a user activates the link. That matters legally because copyright law lets an owner sue whoever distributes unauthorized copies, even a distributor who never personally made a copy. The paragraph closes on the precise question the passage exists to answer: if person A posts a document and person B links to it, has B committed infringement? Read this as setup rather than argument, with the problem defined carefully so the analogy that follows can dissolve it.

Now the author's own answer, and the reasoning turns on who controls distribution. Posting a document is like recording an outgoing message on an answering machine, and linking to it is like giving out the phone number. Anyone who calls hears the message, because that is what the message is for. B may make access easier, but A, simply by posting, is the one offering the document for distribution, so a link is not a copy. The author adds that A already has a remedy, password protection, much as a phone owner keeps an unlisted number and shares it selectively. That costs some openness, though less than the threat of litigation would. Hence the verdict: strengthening copyright law is ill-advised.
overall_html: The passage argues that creating a link to someone else's Web document is not copyright infringement, since the person who posts a document is the one offering it for distribution and can restrict access by other means, so changing copyright law to favor intellectual property owners would be ill-advised. The author's purpose is to resolve a dispute rather than merely report it, moving from the clash between The Owners, who want stronger protection, and The Web Users, who want open access, to the legal question raised by instant linking, and finally to an answering-machine analogy that supplies the answer. Only the author reaches a verdict; the two opening positions are reported, not endorsed.

In tracing the changing face of the Irish landscape, scholars have traditionally relied primarily on evidence from historical documents. However, such documentary sources provide a fragmentary record at best. Reliable accounts are very scarce for many parts of Ireland prior to the seventeenth century, and many of the relevant documents from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries focus selectively on matters relating to military or commercial interests.

Studies of fossilized pollen grains preserved in peats and lake muds provide an additional means of investigating vegetative landscape change. Details of changes in vegetation resulting from both human activities and natural events are reflected in the kinds and quantities of minute pollen grains that become trapped in sediments. Analysis of samples can identify which kinds of plants produced the preserved pollen grains and when they were deposited, and in many cases the findings can serve to supplement or correct the documentary record.

For example, analyses of samples from Long Lough in County Down have revealed significant patterns of cereal-grain pollen beginning by about 400 A.D. The substantial clay content of the soil in this part of Down makes cultivation by primitive tools difficult. Historians thought that such soils were not tilled to any significant extent until the introduction of the moldboard plough to Ireland in the seventh century A.D. Because cereal cultivation would have required tilling of the soil, the pollen evidence indicates that these soils must indeed have been successfully tilled before the introduction of the new plough.

Another example concerns flax cultivation in County Down, one of the great linen-producing areas of Ireland during the eighteenth century. Some aspects of linen production in Down are well documented, but the documentary record tells little about the cultivation of flax, the plant from which linen is made, in that area. The record of eighteenth-century linen production in Down, together with the knowledge that flax cultivation had been established in Ireland centuries before that time, led some historians to surmise that this plant was being cultivated in Down before the eighteenth century. But pollen analyses indicate that this is not the case; flax pollen was found only in deposits laid down since the eighteenth century.

It must be stressed, though, that there are limits to the ability of the pollen record to reflect the vegetative history of the landscape. For example, pollen analyses cannot identify the species, but only the genus or family, of some plants. Among these is madder, a cultivated dye plant of historical importance in Ireland. Madder belongs to a plant family that also comprises various native weeds, including goosegrass. If madder pollen were present in a deposit it would be indistinguishable from that of uncultivated native species.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a limitation. Scholars tracing changes in the Irish landscape have leaned mainly on historical documents, and The Historians who do so are working from a record the author calls fragmentary at best. Reliable accounts barely exist for much of Ireland before the seventeenth century, and the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century documents that survive tend to be written with military or commercial concerns in mind, so they notice selectively. Nothing here attacks any particular conclusion yet; the paragraph is clearing space for a second kind of evidence.

That second source arrives immediately: fossilized pollen grains preserved in peats and lake muds. The idea is simpler than the terminology suggests. Plants shed pollen, sediments trap it, and the kinds and quantities of grains lodged at a given depth record what was growing and when, whether the change came from human activity or a natural event. Analysis can name the plants and date the deposit. Note the author's careful claim about what this buys you, since pollen evidence can either supplement the documentary record or correct it. The two examples that follow give you one of each.

The first example does the correcting. Samples from Long Lough in County Down show cereal-grain pollen appearing by about 400 A.D. Growing cereals means tilling, and the soil there carries heavy clay that primitive tools struggle to break. The Historians had therefore assumed such land went largely untilled until the moldboard plough reached Ireland in the seventh century. The pollen puts grain in that ground centuries too early for the assumption to hold, so the inference is that these difficult soils were in fact being tilled successfully before the new plough arrived.

The flax case works in the opposite direction, deflating a guess rather than revising a technological assumption. County Down was one of the great linen regions of eighteenth-century Ireland, and linen comes from flax, yet the documents say little about growing the plant there. Knowing that flax cultivation was established in Ireland centuries earlier, The Historians surmised that Down must have grown it before the eighteenth century too. Pollen analysis says otherwise, since flax pollen appears only in deposits laid down from the eighteenth century onward. Same method, opposite service.

The closing paragraph is the author's own qualification, and it keeps the passage from reading as pure advocacy. Pollen cannot always be resolved to species; for some plants it identifies only the genus or family. Madder, a cultivated dye plant of real historical importance in Ireland, belongs to a family that also contains native weeds such as goosegrass, so madder pollen in a deposit would be indistinguishable from the pollen of plants nobody planted. Carry this forward as a limit on resolution rather than on reliability, since the author still treats the pollen record as a genuine supplement to documents.
overall_html: The passage puts forward pollen analysis as a corrective supplement to the documentary sources that scholars of the Irish landscape have traditionally relied on, illustrating with two County Down cases in which preserved pollen revised what historians believed about early tilling of clay soils and about when flax cultivation began there. The author's purpose is to recommend a method while marking its boundaries, and the structure follows that aim: the shortcomings of documents, an introduction to the pollen record, two supporting examples, then a closing qualification about pollen identifiable only to genus or family. The viewpoints to keep apart are The Historians, whose inferences get revised, and the author, who is measured rather than triumphant.

Dos de las expectativas que tenemos acerca de la ley generan un difícil conflicto que contribuye a que a menudo no se dé el resultado que imaginamos debería tener la aplicación de la ley. Por un lado, ambicionamos un sistema de ley formalista —es decir, un sistema racional, fundamentado en reglas claras y con aplicación coherente y razonada, protegiéndonos así de la arbitrariedad, la irracionalidad y el puro capricho—. Presumimos que el sistema legal ha de ser comprensible para todos los ciudadanos y confiable en términos generales, en el sentido de que cada cual puede estar tranquilo de que puede ordenar sus asuntos conforme a la ley, sabiendo que no está en desventaja frente a ningún otro ciudadano respecto a la misma. En otras palabras, tenemos la expectativa de que la ley ha de proveer un principio universal de orden, cuya aplicación se hará de manera racional, coherente e imparcial; la ley y su aplicación deben ser totalmente neutrales respecto a las diversas situaciones sociales y económicas de los ciudadanos.

Sin embargo, por otro lado tenemos una segunda expectativa respecto a la ley: pensamos que la ley no puede estar desconectada de la realidad social; en efecto, entendemos que la ley debe ser sensible a los pormenores de los distintos contextos de donde surgen los casos individuales. Después de todo, el aparato legal sería de poca utilidad si generara una justicia meramente procesal, en contraste con una justicia sustantiva —es decir, si la ley fuese incapaz de generar resultados que la gente pueda reconocer como justos y válidos en casos individuales—. Esto no significa, claro está, que el resultado ha de ser el que uno, como parte individual, desearía. Siempre hay alguien que pierde en un sistema adversativo. No obstante, el resultado de la aplicación de la ley al menos debe ser tal que cualquier ciudadano razonable, como parte u observador, lo pueda acoger como legítimo y justificable según las nociones vigentes de equidad y justicia. Nadie sostendría, por ejemplo, que un caso ha de resolverse única y estrictamente con base en la aplicación de reglas absolutas e inalterables, sin considerar la equidad o la sensatez del resultado de dicha aplicación de la regla. Un formalismo legal extremo, aplicado neutralmente y sin prejuicio, pero también sin sensibilidad respecto a los contextos sociales de las partes concernidas, tiene muy poco que ver con la sustancia de la justicia. Y es imperativo que el sistema legal haga justicia sustantiva en casos individuales —que surja y se nutra tanto de la experiencia subjetiva como de la razón objetiva—.

Parecería por ende que estamos ante un conflicto insoluble ocasionado por los dos imperativos contrapuestos del formalismo y de la justicia sustantiva. Todo intento de hacer caber ambos principios dentro del sistema legal está abocado al fracaso, por razones sistémicas: el formalismo es incapaz de producir justicia sustantiva hasta tanto no se haya logrado un grado razonable de equidad social. Sin equidad social, el formalismo muy bien podría perpetuar la injusticia; no existen reglas universales que puedan garantizar lo contrario. Ahora bien, si no es asequible el alto nivel de equidad social y económica requerido para conciliar el formalismo con la justicia sustantiva, entonces hemos de dejar a un lado el formalismo, para que así la ley pueda adaptarse plenamente a la realidad social. Así pues, todo intento de armonizar el formalismo con la justicia sustantiva, cuando se trata de un sistema legal erigido en condiciones de desigualdad social, es un proyecto desatinado.
explanation_html:
A conflict between two things we want from law is announced at the start, and the first demand fills this paragraph. Formalism means a rational, rule-based system that rescues us from arbitrariness, irrationality and caprice by deciding matters in a coherent, reasoned way. The practical value claimed for it is predictability: a system we can understand and depend on when ordering our affairs, confident that no one will be individually disadvantaged before it. The paragraph then compresses the demand into a single requirement, that law supply a universal ordering principle that is rational, consistently applied, and blind to the differing social and economic situations of those who come before it. Hold on to that blindness, since it becomes the problem later.

The competing demand enters on the other hand, and the contrast is exact. We also want law connected to social reality and sensitive to the particular contexts individual cases arise from, because merely procedural justice is of little use if the results in specific cases cannot be recognized as fair and equitable. The Author is careful about the standard being set: it is not that each party gets the outcome they would prefer, since somebody must lose in an adversarial system, but that parties and observers alike can accept the outcome as legitimate under some common understanding of fairness. Extreme formalism, neutral and unprejudiced yet insensitive to social context, is said to speak little to the substance of justice.

The conclusion is framed as an irreconcilable tension, then pushed well past a stalemate. Any attempt to honor both imperatives inside one legal system is bound to fail for systemic reasons, and the reason given is specific: formalism cannot produce substantive justice until a reasonable degree of social equality already exists, and without that equality neutral universal rules may actively perpetuate injustice. That diagnosis yields a recommendation with real bite. If the required social and economic equality is beyond reach, formalism should be abandoned so the law can adapt to social reality, and trying to reconcile the two ideals under conditions of inequality is dismissed as a misguided project.
overall_html: The passage argues that two demands we make of law, formalism's rational, consistently applied and context-blind rules on one side and substantive justice responsive to the circumstances of individual cases on the other, cannot both be met in a society marked by inequality, and concludes that formalism should be given up so law can adapt to social reality. The author's purpose is to diagnose that conflict and then take a side, presenting each demand sympathetically in turn before showing that formalism depends on a degree of social and economic equality that does not exist and may entrench injustice in its absence. The only viewpoint developed is the Author's own, offered as an expectation we all share about what law should do.

El pasaje A es una adaptación de una reseña de un libro realizada por el físico Freeman Dyson. El pasaje B es una adaptación de una respuesta a esa reseña.

Pasaje A

Existen dos perspectivas extremas acerca del rol de las ciencias en el conocimiento humano. La perspectiva reduccionista sostiene que todo tipo de conocimiento, desde la física hasta la ética, puede reducirse a la ciencia. La perspectiva tradicional sostiene que la ciencia es sólo una de muchas fuentes independientes de conocimiento. Casi todo el mundo ocupa una posición intermedia entre estos dos extremos. Los escépticos en torno a los fenómenos paranormales generalmente están cerca del extremo reduccionista, mientras que yo me ubico cerca del extremo tradicional.

El tema de los límites de la ciencia está íntimamente relacionado a la existencia posible de fenómenos paranormales. Los esfuerzos científicos por estudiar la percepción extrasensorial y la telepatía han sido un fracaso. Los escépticos concluyen por ello que los fenómenos paranormales no son reales. Como yo no soy un reduccionista, no acepto tal conclusión. Es posible que los fenómenos paranormales existan, pero que sean inasequibles para la metodología científica. Esta posibilidad es tan sólo una hipótesis, per es una que considero válida y plausible.

Dicha hipótesis está sustentada por abundante evidencia (relatos de personal comunes y corrientes que aparentemente poseen habilidades paranormales) que han recopilado la Sociedad para la Investigación Psíquica y otras organizaciones análogas. La evidencia en cuestión es anecdótica más que científica, ya que no puede reproducirse bajo condiciones controladas. Sin embargo, las organizaciones mencionadas han entrevistado concienzudamente a testigos presenciales justo después de los eventos relatados y han documentado cuidadosamente los testimonios de estas personas. Los testimonios dejan claro que, si ocurren eventos paranormales, es sólo cuando los sujetos están bajo estrés y experimentando fuertes emociones. Esto explixaría por qué los fenómenos paranormales no son observables en experimentos científicos debidamente controlados. Las emociones fueres y el estrés son incompatibles con los procedimientos científicos.

Entiendo que los fenómenos paranormales y el método científico podrían se complementarios. "Complementarios" es un término técnico en la física cuántica que significa que, aunque dos descripciones de la naturaleza son válidas, las mismas no pueden observarse simultáneamente. El ejemplo clásico de complementariedad es la naturaleza dual de la luz. La luz se comporta como una onda en un primer experimento y como párticulas en un segundo, pero es imposible observar ambas cosas en el mismo experimento.

Pasaje B

Freeman Dyson hace un llamamiento ridículo a adoptar una actitud abierta ante lo paranormal debido a que él no es reduccionista y porque la evidencia anecdótica lo convence de que bajo ciertas condiciones (p. ej., el estrés), algunas personas exhiben poderes paranormales, a menos que se sometan a condiciones científicas controladas, en cuyo caso los poderes desaparecen misteriosamente. Un científico de calibre de Dyson debiera saber que anécdotas no constituyen ciencia. La única forma de averiguar si las anécdotas representan fenómenos reales es conduciendo pruebas experimentales controladas. Lo fenómenos paranormales se han sometido repetidamente a experimentos científicos rigurosos y los resultados son inequívocos: el poder psíquico es una quimera. Dyson reconoce que su apertura a la posibilidad de que existan fenómenos paranormales está en conflicto con su óptica científica, pero reacciona invocando el principio de complementariedad. Lamentablemente dicho principio no aplica a lo paranormal. O bien las personas tienen la habilidad de leer la mente de otros, o bien no la tienen. La ciencia ha demostrado que no hay tal habilidad. Ser holístico en vez de reduccionista, o leer sobre situaciones extrañas que le suceden a la gente, en nada altera este hecho científico.

En las historiografías convencionales sobre los inicios del bebop —el primer estilo de jazz "moderno", originado en la década de los 40 por Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker y Thelonious Monk, entre otros— la comercialización juega un papel importante, aunque indirecto. Para los comienzos de la década de los 40, según estas historiografías, el jazz estaba estancado. Estos análisis plantean que el estilo de jazz dominante en aquel momento, el swing, se había vuelto algo "desgastado"; que era un "callejón sin salida armónico y melódico", una música popular formulaica que estaba pasando por una "muerte por entropía”; y que se había convertido en un "atolladero multimillonario".

Estas metáforas, tomadas de diversos escritos sobre el jazz, hacen eco a la "teoría de la crisis" sobre la música clásica europea del siglo veinte. A principios de siglo veinte, la música clásica dio un giro radical hacia un estilo "moderno" caracterizado por la atonalidad. Las referencias académicas comúnmente atribuyen este giro al uso excesivo y poco original en el siglo diecinueve del sistema tonal. Algo similar se insinuaba sobre el jazz a principios de la década de los 40. El nuevo estilo moderno se debió, según los escritos mencionados, a la incapacidad por parte de los músicos de la época de extender el lenguaje rítmico, armónico y melódico del jazz en direcciones claramente indicadas por la misma música.

No obstante, la utilización de frases como "atolladero multimillonario" claramente sugiere que, para estos autores, la verdadera causa del desgaste del jazz lo fue la comercialización —es decir, la fusión de arte y lucro que, por cierto tiempo, permitió que el swing se convirtiera tanto en una auténtica expresión del jazz como en una moda pasajera nacional estadounidense—. Según la teoría de los autores, aun cuando la popularidad del swing ya había menguado considerablemente, la industria musical seguía empujando este género raído, brindándoles a los músicos un pretexto económico para continuar explotando lo que era una fórmula comprobada, mucho después de que hubiese alguna razón artística legítima para producir más swing. En otras palabras, el capitalismo de mercado masivo fue un escollo en la evolución del jazz, un obstáculo que sólo logró eliminarse mediante la irrupción súbita y arrolladora de otro estilo distinto, el bebop. En esta narrativa sobre el desarrollo del jazz, percibimos una teleología implícita respecto a la progresión del género —desde el jazz inicial, pasando luego por el swing, hasta llegar entonces al bebop—. Tal teleología apunta al abandono paulatino del vínculo que tenía el jazz con el baile, con la canción popular y con el entretenimiento. El bebop representa entonces la culminación lógica de este proceso: con el bebop, el jazz finalmente se convierte en "arte", rompiendo para siempre sus lazos con lo comercial.

Ahora bien, la insistencia de que el bebop es anticomercial puede que se ajuste a las narrativas actuales sobre el jazz, pero no sirve como base historiográfica. Tal postura idealiza las condiciones en las que se da toda creación artística y suprime la realidad, quizás molesta, de que hay una dimensión comercial en todo tipo de entretenimiento musical. Para los músicos que originaron el bebop, el capitalismo de mercado masivo no fue una prisión de la cual el auténtico artista tenía la obligación moral de escaparse. Era más bien el sistema de intercambio en el que estaban inmersos, que definía la música como profesión, y que hizo posible sus logros artísticos. Para el 1945, Parker, Gillespie y Monk habían en efecto engendrado una nueva subcultura musical. Sin embargo, ellos no buscaban desvincularse de la escena musical "comercial", sino más bien hallar un nuevo punto de encuentro con dicha escena —uno que les proporcionara cierto grado de autonomía y reconocimiento—.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the story it plans to correct. In the standard accounts of how bebop began — the first modern jazz style, originated in the 1940s by Gillespie, Parker, Monk and others — commercialism plays an important but indirect role. The standard histories hold that jazz had reached an impasse by the early 1940s, with swing degraded into a formulaic popular music: threadbare, a harmonic and melodic blind alley, dying of entropy, a billion-dollar rut. Register that these judgments belong to those writers rather than to the author, and note the loaded vocabulary, because the author will later mine it for what it gives away.

Next comes the intellectual pedigree of that story. Those metaphors, gathered from various jazz writing, echo the crisis theory applied to twentieth-century European classical music, where textbooks blame the eruptions of modernity in the early 1900s on classical music's refusal to move past a tonal language exhausted by nineteenth-century overuse. The same shape is imposed on jazz: musicians failed to extend its rhythmic, harmonic and melodic language in the directions the music itself supposedly indicated, pressure built, and a new modernism erupted. The author is identifying a borrowed template here, not endorsing it.

Here the author extracts what the standard histories really believe. A phrase like billion-dollar rut points at commercialism as the true culprit, the mingling of art and commerce that briefly let swing be both authentic jazz and a national fad. On this theory the popular music industry kept propping up the exhausted idiom after it had run its course, seducing musicians into going through the motions with no artistic reason left. Mass-market capitalism becomes a logjam that only explosive force could clear, and bebop is that force. Notice the teleology the author draws out: jazz progressively sheds dance, popular song and entertainment until bebop turns it into art by severing its ties to commerce.

The final paragraph is where the author speaks in his own voice, and he rejects the whole framework. Insisting that bebop was anticommercial may serve present-day jazz discourse, but it makes poor history, idealizing the circumstances of artistic creation and repressing the fact that commercial relations run through every part of musical entertainment. For the musicians who actually made bebop, mass-market capitalism was not a prison to escape but the system of transactions that defined music as a profession and made their achievements possible. They had willed a new musical subculture into being by 1945, yet what they wanted was a new point of engagement with the commercial world, on terms granting them autonomy and recognition.
overall_html: The passage attacks the received account of bebop's origins, which treats the style as an explosive break with a commercially corrupted swing era and therefore as the moment jazz became autonomous art; the author argues instead that bebop's originators sought not escape from the commercial music world but a new and more rewarding point of engagement with it. The purpose is corrective, and the structure builds the target before dismantling it, moving from the standard narrative of swing's exhaustion, to the crisis-theory template borrowed from classical music history, to the anticommercial teleology hidden inside that narrative, and finally to the author's own historical objection. Keep the standard histories separate from the author throughout.
