El ingeniero químico Larry Koskan, especialista en química orgánica, tuvo su idea más importante a mediados de la década de los 80, al leer un informe realizado por biólogos marinos sobre la formación de conchas de ostras. Era de conocimiento común en ese entonces que el carbonato de calcio que secretan las ostras es un componente esencial del caparazón exterior duro de las ostras. Sin embargo, los biólogos descubrieron que las ostras también producen un agente especial a base de proteínas que moldea el carbonato de calcio para producir la forma característica del caparazón.

En aquel momento, Koskan se encontraba estudiando las propiedades de los poliacrilatos solubles en agua. Los poliacrilatos son aditivos de uso bien amplio que, entre otras cosas, contribuyen a reducir la acumulación de depósitos minerales en las superficies de los equipos industriales de tratamiento de agua. En particular, los poliacrilatos disminuyen la acumulación de depósitos compuestos de carbonato y sulfato que, de no tratarse, forman costras que pueden dañar el equipo. Koskan se dio cuenta que el agente producido por las ostras —el poliaspartato— inhibe la formación de carbonato de calcio y que por ende, también podía usarse para controlar la formación de costras. Él se percató que el poliaspartato detiene la formación de costras de manera similar a los poliacrilatos porque tiene una estructura química similar. Sin embargo, a diferencia de los poliacrilatos, cuya estructura es a base de hidrocarbonos, el poliaspartato tiene una estructura compuesta principalmente de péptidos, es decir, de cadenas de aminoácidos. Esto significa que el poliaspartato es susceptible a la degradación bacteriana, y, por consiguiente, que es un material biodegradable.

Los poliacrilatos son químicos baratos y versátiles, y son fáciles de manufacturar y procesar. En los detergentes de ropa actúan como dispersantes que mantienen la mugre suspendida en el agua de lavado. Aproximadamente quinientos millones de libras de poliacrilatos se usan en detergentes cada año a nivel mundial. Representan una alternativa desarrollada recientemente a los fosfatos, los cuales contaminan los cuerpos de agua a través de las escorrentías de aguas usadas. Por otro lado, la composición química de ciertos poliacrilatos los hace extremadamente afines al agua, por lo que son ideales para usarse en materiales superabsorbentes. Por ejemplo, son idóneos para la elaboración de productos desechables tales como los pañales de bebé, que por sí solos representan al presente una producción anual de poliacrilatos de alrededor de dos mil millones de libras. Un problema, sin embargo, es que los poliacrilatos son compuestos muy estables —y esto quiere decir que las enormes cantidades antes mencionadas terminan en los vertederos, donde permanecerán básicamente por el resto de la eternidad—.

En las últimas décadas ha habido un aumento vertiginoso, por parte de empresas productoras de artículos de consumo de todo tipo, en proveerle al consumidor productos eco-amigables. Motivado por esta tendencia, Koskan fundó su propia pequeña compañía de químicos, y empezó a desarrollar formas costo efectivas de producir el poliaspartato para uso industrial. Poco después, algunas de la grandes compañías químicas también empezaron a auscultar la posibilidad de producir poliaspartato para fines industriales. Existía un reconocimiento general de que el poliaspartato era el reemplazo más adecuado para los poliacrilatos. Desafortunadamente, como sucede con muchas nuevas tecnologías sin una infraestructura de apoyo, se determinó que el precio del poliaspartato sería de cuatro a cinco veces mayor que el del poliacrilato, el cual se produce a bajo costo en grandes cantidades. Ante esta situación, el sector de ventas de artículos de consumo perdió interés en el material y la industria química dejó de desarrollarlo. La compañía de Koskan, sin embargo, optó por seguir adelante, concentrándose en ciertas aplicaciones especializadas. La empresa tenía la convicción de que el poliaspartato iba a poder competir en el mercado por sus propios méritos.

Y en efecto, el poliaspartato ha demostrado poder eliminar con un éxito inigualable las costras que se forman en el equipo de producción petrolera en alta mar. Además, la industria agrícola está usando el compuesto para aumentar la efectividad de los abonos químicos utilizados en los terrenos de cultivo, lo cual reduce la contaminación producida por estos abonos en los acuíferos y las aguas subterráneas. Si la compañía de Koskan logra mantener una trayectoria de éxito, puede que ayude a reactivar el sector de química medioambiental, el cual carga con la reputación de ser ineficaz y de alto costo.

Torchy Brown, in "Dixie to Harlem", de Jackie Ormes, es una tirilla cómica que se publicó de 1937 a 1938. La tirilla es muy singular, y no meramente porque se trata —casi con total certeza— de la primera tirilla cómica escrita y dibujada por una mujer afroamericana. En 53 episodios publicados semanalmente, Ormes narra las experiencias de una glamorosa heroína que se muda del Sur de los Estados Unidos a la Ciudad de Nueva York, donde inicia una vida y una carrera nueva en el afamado Cotton Club de dicha ciudad.

A primera vista, las aventuras de la protagonista, Torchy, parecerían sacadas de un cuento de hadas, por lo increíbles que son. Los primeros episodios se enmarcan en la comunidad rural sureña de dónde es oriunda Torchy. En este lugar tranquilo y casi idílico, un tío y una tía amorosos crían a Torchy, que se desplaza despreocupadamente en un ambiente pastoral. En los episodios subsiguientes, Torchy emprende su viaje al Norte, y, en la mejor tradición de los cuentos de hada, la vemos amenazada por personajes siniestros pero también apoyada por aliados misteriosos. Una vez llega a Nueva York, Torchy alcanza el éxito instantáneamente como artista en el Cotton Club. Ahí, muy segura de sí misma, interactúa de tú a tú con leyendas musicales afroamericanas como Duke Ellington y Cab Calloway.

A pesar de los elementos fantásticos que contiene Torchy Brown, es claro que la tirilla hace referencia a problemáticas culturales importantes. La historia de una joven artista que arriba al casi mítico Cotton Club es un dispositivo que le permite a Ormes engrandecer y amplificar el éxito de afroamericanos reales, reconocidos en aquel momento como profesionales trabajadores y talentosos. Son tantos los episodios que giran en torno al Cotton Club, donde observamos a Torchy evolucionando como artista, que en efecto el Club ha de interpretarse como un símbolo del reclamo de que los afroamericanos se consideren por sus méritos, y, por consiguiente, que el público blanco los reconozca como talentos dignos de admiración, en lugar de pasarlos por alto o de mirarlos sin verlos. Además, en varios episodios, Ormes asemeja explícita e ingeniosamente la improvisación característica de la música swing y del baile claqué a la forma de su propia tirilla cómica. Así pues, la tirilla cómica de Ormes provee no tan sólo un testimonio de una coyuntura notable en la evolución del jazz, sino también una comparación entre dos tipos de arte popular, la música jazz y la tirilla cómica.

Es claro que Ormes se gozaba los triunfos de su personaje Torchy en el Cotton Club, triunfos que reflejaban los suyos propios como caricaturista. Sin embargo, Ormes no obvia otras posibilidades menos felices; de hecho, el éxito de Torchy es aún más significativo porque es fácil imaginar que todo pudo haber sido muy distinto. Pese a los aspectos "fantásticos" e inverosímiles del trayecto de Torchy a Nueva York, se impone la realidad de la segregación racial de la época; Torchy debe abordar un vagón de tren para personas de color. Aquí vemos que Ormes estaba muy consciente de los peligros para viajeros primerizos. Insertando de este modo al personaje en situaciones reales, en las que mucho depende del coraje de la persona, Ormes suplementa el contenido social de la tirilla con lecciones de la vida real para beneficio del lector.

Los dos pasajes a continuación se basan en artículos publicados en 2005 y 2002, respectivamente.

Pasaje A

En los países en vías de desarrollo, se han dado dos modalidades importantes para facilitarles crédito a personas de escasos recursos que trabajan por cuenta propia. La primera es mediante bancos gubernamentales instaurados por estos países; tales bancos se han enfocado particularmente en ofrecer financiamiento a personas pobres de zonas rurales, y, en gran medida, han sido un fracaso. La segunda modalidad, que ha resultado mucho más exitosa, es a través de organizaciones que conceden préstamos sin fianza a prestatarios de muy escasos recursos. Una de estas organizaciones, el Banco Grameen de Bangladés, inició sus operaciones en 1976 y pronto se volvió famoso por su modelo comercial de "microcréditos".

Para cualificar para un préstamo del Banco Grameen, el solicitante debía ser muy necesitado —usualmente era alguien que ganaba menos de un dólar al día—. En vez de requerir una fianza o basarse en el historial crediticio para otorgar el préstamo, el banco ponía como condición que el cliente se uniera a un pequeño grupo de personas vinculadas al banco y que asistiera a las reuniones semanales del grupo. Los miembros del grupo se monitoreaban los unos a los otros, y ejercían presión para garantizar el pago. De este modo, el grupo desempeñaba la función de la fianza. Y, a medida que el cliente iba saldando el préstamo, se le permitía coger prestado más dinero. El modelo financiero del Banco Grameen no es perfecto, pero tiene virtudes considerables y se ha extendido por todo el mundo.

Ahora bien, ¿por qué se limitaron inicialmente las organizaciones de microfinanzas, tales como el Banco Grameen, meramente a conceder crédito? Supusieron que las personas de escasos recursos no tenían la capacidad de ahorrar, y que sólo acudirían a un banco para obtener acceso a crédito. Sin embargo, es probable que ésta haya sido una suposición errada desde el principio. Considérese el caso del BRI, una entidad prestamista rural fallida, vinculada al estado indonesio. En 1984 se transformó en un banco dirigido principalmente al cliente de escasos recursos; BRI pasó de brindar productos prestamistas normales a ofrecerle al cliente además una cuenta de ahorro sin depósito mínimo y garantizada por el gobierno. Esto ha sido un éxito rotundo: BRI ahora tiene sobre 30 millones de estas cuentas de ahorro.

Pasaje B

SafeSave es una institución financiera que opera en las comunidades más pobres de Dhaka, Bangladés. Con menos de 5,500 clientes, SafeSave sigue siendo una organización pequeña, pero está atrayendo atención debido a los productos interesantes que ofrece. Estos productos están diseñados para que el cliente urbano de escasos recursos maximice sus ahorros; los productos ponen a disposición del cliente muchas maneras convenientes de convertir el dinero ahorrado en montos grandes que le sean útiles a éste.

Básicamente, SafeSave ofrece a sus clientes la gama completa de servicios bancarios, a la puerta de su casa y sin exigirles que formen grupos. Los empleados de SafeSave, denominados recolectores, visitan a cada cliente diariamente, seis días a la semana. En cada visita, los clientes pueden depositar dinero en ahorro, retirar fondos o pagar préstamos en cualquier monto que deseen. También pueden solicitar préstamos cuyas cantidades se determinan con base en el historial de ahorro y pago del cliente. Debido a la gran flexibilidad de los servicios que ofrece SafeSave, un número considerable de clientes realiza transacciones con mucha regularidad; de hecho, el volumen de transacciones de SafeSave excede por mucho el de otros bancos más convencionales dirigidos al cliente de bajos recursos. Esto sirve para explicar por qué los clientes de SafeSave tienden a saldar préstamos más prontamente que los clientes del Banco Grameen.

Los costos operacionales de SafeSave son bajos, en parte porque el banco ha implementado varias medidas de reducción de gastos, tales como ampliar el uso de la informática y reclutar a recolectores provenientes de las mismas comunidades pobres que atiende el banco. Por consiguiente, las bajas tasas de interés que cobra SafeSave son suficientes para cubrir los costos operacionales de la empresa. A medida que siga creciendo, SafeSave habrá de tornarse completamente rentable como negocio.

Desde 1929, se tiene conocimiento de que el universo está expandiéndose. Hasta recientemente, se pensaba que la expansión iba desacelerando, porque la gravedad del universo tendría el efecto de contraerlo. A finales de la década de 1990, los astrónomos se dieron a la tarea de medir la desaceleración, calculando las distancias entre la Tierra y estrellas en proceso de explosión, conocidas como supernovas. Para la sorpresa de los astrónomos, las supernovas más lejanas estaban mucho más distantes de lo que se esperaba. El hallazgo implica que la expansión del universo de hecho se está acelerando.

Se han propuesto dos explicaciones para la aceleración; ambas desafían la concepción actual del universo. La primera explicación, que es la más ampliamente aceptada, postula la existencia de cierta "energía oscura" que causa que el espacio se estire. Estudios recientes del resplandor residual del Big Bang sustentan el concepto de energía oscura, y plantean, además, que la energía oscura podría representar dos terceras partes del universo. Según la versión más sencilla de la teoría, la energía oscura es un componente inherente al vacío del espacio y ejerce una presión constante. La noción básica en cuestión se remonta a 1917, cuando Einstein estipuló la existencia de una cantidad fija de presión —que él denominó "la constante cosmológica"— para explicar por qué el universo no se encoge por su propia gravedad. Einstein posteriormente abandonó esta noción, por considerarla innecesaria, al determinarse empíricamente que el universo en efecto se está expandiendo. Sin embargo, esta idea huérfana de Einstein podría ser la clave para identificar la causa de la aceleración.

Algunos cosmólogos proponen que la energía oscura que provocaría la aceleración se genera por cierto tipo de partículas subatómicas, llamadas "virtuales". Como corolario de la mecánica cuántica, se sabe desde hace décadas que el llamado "vacío" del espacio en realidad está repleto de partículas subatómicas virtuales, las cuales surgen y luego desaparecen; este proceso causaría una "energía del vacío" con presión constante. Según los teóricos de la energía oscura, dicha energía del vacío efectivamente constituye la energía oscura que propone la teoría. Desafortunadamente, sin embargo, existe una discrepancia considerable entre el valor que la teoría le asigna a la energía del vacío y la cantidad de energía requerida para explicar la expansión acelerada.

Tal discrepancia no representa problema alguno para la segunda explicación, ya que ésta no depende del concepto de energía oscura en lo absoluto. La segunda explicación sostiene que, cuando se trata de distancias bien grandes (de millones de años luz, por ejemplo), la fuerza de gravedad ya no se acopla a la teoría general de la relatividad de Einstein. Claro está, tal cambio a la teoría de la gravedad es bien radical y presuntamente tendría implicaciones significativas incluso para distancias cortas. Pero esto podría representar una ventaja para la segunda explicación, porque las presuntas implicaciones sobre la gravedad a distancias cortas podrían corroborarse en nuestro propio sistema solar, lo que hace a la segunda explicación más fácil de probar que la primera.

Durante la mayor parte del siglo pasado, los estudiosos de la tradición jurídica angloamericana cuestionaron la idea de que la propiedad privada se fundamenta en algún derecho específico. Defendieron la posición alterna de que la propiedad se deriva de un "conjunto de derechos", el cual emana de decisiones judiciales particulares en ámbitos bien diversos (por ejemplo, los derechos de arrendamiento, venta, subdivisión e imposición de impuestos). Por consiguiente, el concepto de propiedad, en sí mismo, no puede limitar al juez a la hora de decidir un pleito sobre el uso de bienes, dado que el conjunto de derechos que define lo que es propiedad proviene de decisiones judiciales anteriores y no es un asunto terminado.

Esta perspectiva ha sido criticada por los proponentes recientes de una teoría legal alterna y más antigua, según la cual la propiedad privada es un derecho básico que excluye a otros de una cosa particular. Esta "teoría de los límites" implica que el concepto de propiedad constriñe al juez si apela en su razonamiento al derecho de excluir a otros de la cosa, ya que así es precisamente cómo se define la propiedad privada.

Si bien la teoría de los límites reconoce correctamente que existe un concepto de propiedad privada que limita las decisiones judiciales, ésta no explica ciertas características clave de la propiedad privada. Tan es así, que la teoría podría considerarse una teoría de la no-propiedad. La teoría se centra en la posición de los no-propietarios, una posición definida en términos de la obligación general de no traspasar los lindes de cosas que no le pertenecen a uno. En efecto, esta perspectiva se basa en un proceso de eliminación para distinguir a los propietarios de los no-propietarios: el propietario es el último que queda luego de separar de la cosa a todos los demás. Pero ésta es la descripción más exigua posible de la relación especial entre el propietario y la cosa: simplemente y por defecto, el propietario es el único con la libertad de usar la cosa luego de haberse excluido a todos los demás.

Es claro que hay algo de verdad en la teoría de los límites, puesto que la propiedad privada es un derecho excluyente. No obstante, la teoría presume erróneamente que el carácter excluyente de la propiedad privada estriba únicamente en que el no-propietario tiene la obligación de separase de la cosa. Es preciso distinguir dos sentidos de "derecho excluyente". En el primer sentido, excluyente significa que el no-propietario ha de separarse de la cosa; en el segundo sentido, excluyente significa que el dueño de la cosa ocupa un sitial especial con relación a la cosa que ninguna otra persona ostenta.

Una tercera teoría, la "teoría del establecimiento de la agenda", concibe la propiedad privada como un derecho excluyente en el segundo sentido, pero no en el primero. Según esta perspectiva, el carácter excluyente de la propiedad implica que el propietario es quien "establece la agenda" para la cosa, el que decide cómo ha de usarse la cosa. Por ejemplo, el propietario de una granja es quien determina los usos específicos de sus terrenos. Así pues, se desprende de la teoría que la ley reivindica el carácter excluyente de la propiedad, no al excluir a los no-propietarios, sino al armonizar los intereses de éstos con la autoridad que posee el propietario de dictaminar la agenda para la cosa. Tal convergencia es la esencia de la propiedad privada, y no la exclusión del no-propietario, como plantea la teoría de los límites.

The 50 million sheep of New Zealand outnumber its people 13 to 1, the highest such ratio in the world. At the wool industry's peak, in the 1950s, the wool growers of New Zealand delivered well over a third of that country's total export revenues. Yet this figure has declined drastically, as has the industry's profitability. New Zealand is second only to Australia in total wool production and is the world's largest producer of "strong wool," a relatively coarse wool characteristic of crossbred sheep that is used mostly for carpets. But for the past 20 years, competition from synthetics has inexorably driven down the price of clean strong wool, causing annual production to drop by 65,000 tons as farmers switch land to other uses. Thus wool has fallen behind beef, lamb, milk, butter, cheese, fish, fruit, and wood and pulp as an agricultural export earner.

Rather than raising wool prices, the only reliable route to profitability lies, as in any agricultural enterprise, in improving productivity. New Zealand's commercial sheep farmers need to achieve the same kind of annual productivity gains that manufacturers of synthetic materials have recorded. This goal could readily be achieved if the industry as a whole were to adopt the management and breeding practices of the country's leading (and comfortably profitable) wool growers.

Gains on the order of those achieved by the world's cotton growers—who on average have been improving productivity at several times the rate of wool growers—can come wholly through better farm management. At present, wool growing in New Zealand, like agriculture everywhere, is deeply divided. On the one side are professional operations that exceed market returns, with 30 percent of farms achieving double the average profitability and the top 10 percent achieving 3 to 4 times the average. On the other side are family farmers willing to receive a substantially lower return to maintain their lifestyle.

To encourage increased overall productivity, the establishment of a commercial genetic research company (which would concentrate on genetic selection for crossbreeding sheep, not on the artificial manipulation of genetic material in individual sheep) is recommended. This would represent a shift in spending away from industry efforts to improve the efficiency of wool processing (for example, by lowering spinning costs) and toward efforts to cut the cost of producing a given unit of raw wool or to increase the quality of raw wool produced. Enormous gains in overall productivity could be made through genetic improvement. The best of New Zealand's sheep produce wool worth significantly more than the wool of the country's average sheep, and these superior sheep can be identified and kept as breeding stock.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with the state of a struggling industry, and the numbers all point one way. New Zealand has thirteen sheep per person, more than anywhere else, and in the 1950s wool brought in over a third of export revenue, but both that share and profitability have fallen sharply. The country still ranks second worldwide in wool output and first in strong wool, the coarse crossbred fiber used for carpets. Synthetics have undercut its price for two decades, output has dropped by 65,000 tons a year as farmers repurpose land, and wool now trails many other agricultural exports.

Having laid out the problem, The Author rules out one solution and commits to another. Pushing prices back up is not the answer; as with any farming business, profit has to come from productivity, and the target is the kind of steady annual gain that synthetic manufacturers have managed. Notice that the proposed remedy requires no new discovery. The author claims the goal is within easy reach if the industry simply copies the management and breeding methods already used by the country's best and reliably profitable wool growers.

Evidence and a diagnosis follow. Cotton growers have been raising productivity several times faster than wool growers, and the author insists those gains come purely from better farm management, not from anything exotic. The obstacle is a split that runs through agriculture everywhere. On one side sit professional operations beating market returns, with thirty percent of farms doubling average profitability and the top tenth reaching three or four times it; on the other sit family farmers who accept much lower returns because they value the way of life.

The closing paragraph turns analysis into a specific recommendation. Set up a commercial genetic research company, and note the boundary the author draws around it: the work would be selecting which sheep to crossbreed, not manipulating genetic material inside individual animals. This also means redirecting money away from making wool processing more efficient, such as cheaper spinning, toward lowering the cost or raising the quality of the raw wool itself. The justification is straightforward, since New Zealand's best sheep grow wool worth far more than average, and those animals can be identified and used as breeding stock.
overall_html: The passage argues that New Zealand's declining wool industry cannot recover through higher prices and must instead pursue productivity gains, chiefly by spreading the management and breeding practices of its most profitable growers and by funding a commercial genetic research company focused on selective crossbreeding. The author's purpose is diagnostic and prescriptive, opening with statistics on wool's fall against synthetic competition, identifying productivity as the only reliable route to profit, using cotton growers and the gap between professional and lifestyle farmers to show how much room for improvement exists, and closing with a concrete proposal. The argument runs in the author's own voice throughout, with no competing viewpoints developed.

In filmmaker Woody Allen's Deconstructing Harry, the writer Harry Block is presented as extremely neurotic and narcissistic. Block uses his experiences as fodder for his work, no matter how embarrassing the result may be for the other people in his life. And while Allen exaggerates Block's narcissism for comic effect, the effect is not simply comic: the film is emblematic of Allen's career precisely because of its extravagantly exaggerated censure of a life dedicated to and obsessed with art. Deconstructing Harry may be the most unequivocally peevish of Allen's depictions of artists, but it is less a new direction for Allen than a concentrated reprise of a theme present throughout his career.

For instance, a film producer in Stardust Memories, Allen's sourest portrait of artists before Harry, articulates a particularly cynical view of cinematic art after a screening of a film-in-progress by Stardust Memories' main character, Sandy Bates. The producer says of Bates, "His insights are shallow and morbid. I've seen it all before. They try to document their private suffering and fob it off as art." The producer, like all the figures in this film, often seems less a distinct individual than a projection of Bates's personal self-recriminations. This effectively reinforces the charge of solipsism with which Bates, the unstable and demoralized artist, indicts himself. Indeed, the possibility that artists are merely "documenting their private suffering and fobbing it off as art" appears sufficiently often in Allen's films to seem an unresolved personal issue.

In Manhattan, the ex-wife of a television writer and aspiring novelist offers a denigratory take on the artistic enterprise that is similar to the producer's in Stardust Memories. Her book documenting the collapse of her marriage punctures her ex-husband's artistic pretensions by revealing that he "longed to be an artist but balked at the necessary sacrifices. In his most private moments, he spoke of the fear of death, which he elevated to tragic heights when, in fact, it was mere narcissism."

It is also significant that in Allen's films, the less artistic the characters, the more likely their narrative is to result in a happy ending. Thus, the filmmaker in Crimes and Misdemeanors, the novelist in Husbands and Wives, and the screenwriter in Celebrity all wind up desolate and solitary, largely because of the egocentric and exploitative attitudes embodied in their art and the effects of those attitudes on those around them. On the other hand, the unpretentious, thoroughly inartistic title character in Zelig dies an untroubled, even happy, death, only slightly compromised by his failure to finish reading Moby-Dick. And the title character and talent agent in Broadway Danny Rose is the beneficiary of the most gratifying resolution Allen has scripted, primarily due to altruistic devotion to his utterly talentless nightclub performers.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph introduces one film and immediately turns it into a thesis about a whole career. In Deconstructing Harry, the writer Harry Block is neurotic and self-absorbed, mining his own life for material regardless of the humiliation it causes people around him. The Author grants that Allen overstates the narcissism for laughs but insists the point is not only comic, since the film condemns a life given over to art. The claim to track is the last one: this is not a departure for Allen but a distilled version of something running through his work.

Support begins with the film the author calls Allen's next harshest treatment of artists. In Stardust Memories a producer, reacting to an unfinished film by the main character Sandy Bates, dismisses his insights as shallow and morbid and accuses artists of passing off private suffering as art. The interpretive move worth noticing is what the author does with that speech: because the producer, like everyone in the film, functions less as a separate person than as a projection of Bates's self-reproach, the accusation is really Bates indicting himself. The recurrence of that charge suggests an unresolved concern of Allen's own.

A second, briefer example reinforces the pattern by showing the same criticism delivered from a different vantage point. In Manhattan the ex-wife of a television writer who wants to be a novelist has written a book about their marriage collapsing, and it deflates his artistic self-image. Her verdict is that he wanted to be an artist but would not make the sacrifices, and that the fear of death he treated as tragic profundity was only narcissism. The wording echoes the producer's charge closely, which is precisely the author's point about consistency across the films.

The final paragraph shifts from what characters say to how their stories end, and the correlation is the strongest evidence offered. Allen's artists finish alone and wretched, as the filmmaker in Crimes and Misdemeanors, the novelist in Husbands and Wives and the screenwriter in Celebrity all do, undone by the self-centered, exploitative outlook their art embodies. The unartistic fare better. Zelig, unpretentious and talentless, dies content apart from an unfinished novel, and the talent agent in Broadway Danny Rose earns Allen's most satisfying ending through selfless loyalty to hopeless performers.
overall_html: The passage argues that Deconstructing Harry's savage portrait of a self-absorbed writer is not new ground for Woody Allen but a concentrated version of a censure of artistic life that pervades his career. The author's purpose is interpretive, establishing the thesis with the most extreme case and then accumulating evidence: the producer's accusation in Stardust Memories read as the protagonist's self-indictment, the ex-wife's parallel charge of narcissism in Manhattan, and finally the pattern by which Allen's artists end desolate while his least artistic characters, Zelig and the agent in Broadway Danny Rose, receive happy endings. The single developed viewpoint is the author's reading of Allen, with the films' characters supplying the evidence.

In the early 1900s, most astronomers mistakenly believed that 66 percent of the sun's substance was iron. As a graduate student at Harvard University in the 1920s, Cecilia Payne—later a professor of astronomy there—argued pioneeringly that the sun is instead composed largely of hydrogen and helium. Her claim, though substantiated by the evidence and later uniformly accepted, encountered strong resistance among professional astronomers.

The orthodox view that the sun was mainly iron was buttressed by the knowledge that Earth and all known asteroids contain iron. Also, the evidence from spectroscopy—a technique used to identify chemicals by the distinctive spectral properties of the light patterns they emit when heated to incandescence—was generally taken to show that iron was the predominant element in the sun. But how could a body composed largely of iron generate the huge energy output of the sun? The eminent British physicist Lord Kelvin had hypothesized that the sun was continuously contracting and that the resulting compression had raised the temperature of the sun's materials sufficiently to account for its enormous heat. But, given the usual assumptions about the sun's size and rate of contraction, it followed that the sun's age would be about 20 million years; evidence from the fossil record, however, strongly suggested that the sun had warmed Earth for billions of years. For Payne, this meant that the "iron" hypothesis had to be reexamined, together with the extensive spectroscopic data alleged to support it.

Preliminary examination of the spectroscopic data convinced Payne that they lent themselves to multiple readings. She suspected that preconceptions about the sun's makeup as being mainly iron might have led to skewed interpretations of that data, and this led her to subject the data to rigorous critical scrutiny and review. Analyzed without preconceptions, she found, the data could be consistently read as indicating that, while it does indeed contain iron (along with other elements found on Earth), 90 percent of the sun is hydrogen and most of the remainder is helium. Most astronomers at the time dismissed Payne's interpretation, and some sought to explain it away simply by claiming that what she had examined was data about the sun's outer surface rather than its interior.

Absent a generally accepted explanation of how hydrogen and helium could produce the sun's energy, Payne's findings could not easily override her contemporaries' preconceptions. We now know that the sun's heat is generated through nuclear fusion: the sun's gravitational force compresses together atoms of hydrogen, causing a nuclear reaction. This reaction produces enormous amounts of energy, while forming helium and other elements. But this process—so well charted today that even elementary physics textbooks discuss it—was inadequately understood in the 1920s. The emergence of that understanding—which relied on Einstein's equation governing the relationship between mass and energy—eventually provided strong confirmation of Payne's results.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by setting a mistaken consensus against a lone correct challenger. In the early 1900s Most Astronomers held that iron made up two thirds of the sun. Cecilia Payne, then a Harvard graduate student in the 1920s and later a professor there, argued instead that the sun is mostly hydrogen and helium. Note how the first paragraph frames what follows: her claim had the evidence behind it and was eventually accepted without dissent, yet professional astronomers resisted it strongly. The passage will have to explain both why they were wrong and why they held on.

The case for the orthodox position comes next, and it was not baseless. Iron turns up in Earth and in every known asteroid, and spectroscopy, which identifies chemicals by the distinctive light patterns they give off when heated, was read as showing iron predominant in the sun. The paragraph then exposes the weak point: an iron sun struggles to explain the sun's energy. Lord Kelvin's proposal that steady contraction compressed and heated the sun implied an age of roughly twenty million years, while the fossil record pointed to billions. That contradiction is what prompted Payne to revisit both the hypothesis and its spectroscopic support.

Her actual method occupies this paragraph, and it is a lesson in how evidence gets misread. A first look showed Payne that the spectroscopic data admitted of more than one interpretation, and she suspected that assuming an iron sun in advance had bent earlier readings toward that answer. Approaching the data without those assumptions, she found a consistent reading in which the sun does contain iron and other terrestrial elements but is ninety percent hydrogen with most of the rest helium. Most astronomers rejected this, some brushing it aside by claiming she had only measured the sun's surface.

The closing paragraph explains the resistance rather than merely condemning it, then delivers the vindication. Without an accepted account of how hydrogen and helium could produce so much energy, Payne's findings were never going to dislodge entrenched assumptions on their own. The missing mechanism was nuclear fusion, in which the sun's gravity forces hydrogen atoms together, releasing enormous energy while forming helium and other elements. Routine in physics textbooks today, that process was poorly understood in the 1920s, and the understanding that arrived later, built on Einstein's mass-energy relation, confirmed her conclusion.
overall_html: The passage recounts how Cecilia Payne overturned the early twentieth-century consensus that the sun was mostly iron, showing that spectroscopic data read without preconceptions indicated ninety percent hydrogen with most of the remainder helium, and how astronomers resisted her until nuclear fusion supplied the missing explanation of the sun's energy. The author's purpose is expository and appreciative, moving from the orthodox view and the age-of-the-sun problem that undermined it, to Payne's critical reanalysis of the data and its dismissal, to the later understanding grounded in Einstein's mass-energy relation that confirmed her. The two positions to keep apart are the iron orthodoxy of most astronomers and Payne's hydrogen and helium conclusion.

Passage A discusses the views of the economist and political thinker Thomas Sowell. Passage B is adapted from an article by Sowell.

Passage A

"Cosmic justice," as Sowell uses the term, refers to the perfect justice that only an omniscient being could render—rewards and punishments that are truly deserved when all relevant things are properly taken into consideration. Inherent human limitations, however, make it impossible to achieve this type of justice through human law, even though many times it seems that people are arguing for such justice and promote policies they think will render it through our human laws. But our human legal systems should not try to dispense cosmic justice since we do not know all the critical relevant facts or understand all the complex causal interrelationships involved or even know definitively what cosmic justice really is.

Whether somebody truly deserves something is a very difficult thing for us to determine. For one thing, we are not knowledgeable enough about the person and situation, or smart enough, even if we knew what all the critical factors were, to perform the complicated calculus necessary to understand how the complex interrelationships among the various variables should affect our ultimate conclusions. Deservedness necessarily focuses on a consideration of inputs. An omniscient being is capable of perfectly considering all these things, but we are not. With all the limitations that we face as mere humans, the best we can reasonably do is judge primarily based upon outputs, or consequences, rather than inputs.

Passage B

Cosmic justice is not simply a higher degree of traditional justice; it is a fundamentally different concept. Traditionally, justice or injustice is characteristic of a process. A defendant in a criminal case would be said to have received justice if the trial were conducted as it should be, under fair rules and with an impartial judge and jury. After such a trial, it could be said that "justice was done"—regardless of the outcome. Conversely, if the trial were conducted in violation of the rules and with a judge or jury showing prejudice against the defendant, this would be considered an unfair or unjust trial—even if the prosecutor failed to convince the jury to convict an innocent person. In short, traditional justice is about impartial processes rather than either results or prospects.

On the other hand, cosmic justice foolishly seeks to correct, not only biased or discriminatory acts by individuals or social institutions, but unmerited disadvantages in general, from whatever source they may arise. In criminal trials, for example, before a murderer is sentenced, the law permits his traumatic childhood to be taken into account. Seldom is there any claim that the person murdered had anything to do with that traumatic childhood. It is only from a cosmic perspective that it could have any bearing on the crime. If punishment is meant to deter crime, then mitigating that punishment in pursuit of cosmic justice presumably reduces that deterrence and allows more crime to take place at the expense of innocent people.
explanation_html:
Passage A begins by defining its central term through Sowell. Cosmic justice is perfect justice, the kind only an omniscient being could deliver, in which rewards and punishments are genuinely deserved once everything relevant has been weighed. The Author of Passage A grants that people often seem to be demanding exactly this and to back policies meant to produce it through ordinary law, but argues human limits make that unreachable. The reasoning is epistemic rather than moral: we lack the critical facts, cannot grasp the tangled causal relationships involved, and do not even have a settled definition of what cosmic justice is.

The second paragraph develops that limitation and draws a practical conclusion from it. Judging whether someone truly deserves something is extremely hard, because we know too little about the person and the situation and, even given a complete list of relevant factors, could not perform the intricate reckoning needed to see how they interact. The key distinction arrives here, between inputs and outputs. Deservedness is necessarily a matter of inputs, which only an omniscient being could assess properly, so the author concludes that human beings should judge chiefly by outputs, meaning consequences.

Passage B attacks the same target from a different angle, insisting that cosmic justice is not merely traditional justice pursued more ambitiously but something categorically different. On the traditional understanding, justice describes a process. A criminal defendant received justice if the trial followed fair rules before an impartial judge and jury, whatever the verdict; a trial conducted in violation of the rules with a prejudiced judge or jury was unjust even if an innocent defendant went free. Both examples are chosen to make one point stick, that traditional justice concerns impartial procedure rather than results or prospects.

The closing paragraph states what cosmic justice does instead and why The Author of Passage B objects, and the language is openly hostile. Beyond correcting biased acts by individuals or institutions, cosmic justice tries to correct undeserved disadvantages of every kind, whatever caused them. The illustration is sentencing, where a murderer's traumatic childhood may be weighed even though the victim plainly had nothing to do with it; only a cosmic outlook makes it relevant. The consequence alleged is practical, since softened punishment weakens deterrence and leaves innocent people exposed to more crime.
overall_html: Both passages reject the pursuit of cosmic justice through human legal systems, but they argue from different grounds and with different tempers: Passage A objects on epistemic grounds, holding that only an omniscient being could assess the inputs that determine desert, so humans should judge by consequences instead, while Passage B argues conceptually that cosmic justice differs in kind from traditional procedural justice and warns that correcting general disadvantages, as when a murderer's traumatic childhood mitigates sentencing, undermines deterrence. The purposes differ accordingly, A being definitional and cautionary while B is comparative and openly critical, with Sowell's notion of cosmic justice serving as the shared reference point both reject.

Until recently, many biologists believed that invertebrate "schools" were actually transient assemblages, brought together by wind, currents, waves, or common food sources. Jellyfish groupings, for example, cannot be described as schools—cohesive social units whose members are evenly spaced and face the same way. However, recent research has found numerous cases in which crustaceans and other invertebrates form schools as fish do. Schooling crustaceans such as krill regularly collect in such massive numbers that they provide abundant food for fish, seabirds, and whales.

Like schooling fish, invertebrates with sufficient mobility to school will swim in positions that are consistent relative to fellow school members, and are neither directly above nor directly below a neighbor. The internal structure of such a school changes little with external physical disruption but dramatically with the advent of a predator.

Since schooling is an active behavior, researchers assume that it must bring important benefits. True, schooling would appear to make animals more visible and attractive to predators. However, schooling leaves vast tracts of empty water, thereby reducing a predator's chances of picking up the school's trail. A large group maintains surveillance better than an individual can, and may discourage predation by appearing to be one massive animal. And although an attacking predator may eat some of the invertebrates, any individual school member has a good probability of escaping.

In addition to conferring passive advantages, schooling permits the use of more active defense mechanisms. When a predator is sighted, the school compacts, so that a predator's senses may be unable to resolve individuals, or so that the school can execute escape maneuvers, such as freezing to foil predators that hunt by detecting turbulence. If the predator attacks, the school may split, or may employ "flash expansion"—an explosive acceleration of animals away from the school's center. When large predators threaten the entire school, the school may attempt to avoid detection altogether or to reduce the density of the school at the point of attack; when small predators threaten the margins, school members may put on dazzling and confusing displays of synchronized swimming.

Schooling may also enable invertebrates to locate food—when one group member finds food, other members observe its behavior and flock to the food source. On the other hand, competition within the school for food may be intense: some mysids circle around to the back of the school in order to eat food particles surreptitiously. Schooling can facilitate the search for mates, but as a school's numbers rise, food may become locally scarce and females may produce smaller clutches of eggs, or adults may start to feed on the young. Thus, circumstances apparently dictate the optimal size of a school; if that size is exceeded, some of the animals will join another school.
explanation_html:
A superseded view opens the passage and gives the new findings something to correct. Many biologists once held that invertebrate groupings were only temporary assemblages, thrown together by wind, currents, waves, or a shared food source. Jellyfish clusters make the point, since they lack what defines a real school: a cohesive social unit whose members keep even spacing and face the same direction. Recent research overturned that assumption by finding crustaceans and other invertebrates that school just as fish do. Krill are the striking case, collecting in numbers large enough to feed fish, seabirds, and whales.

Two structural facts confirm that these are schools rather than crowds. Any invertebrate mobile enough to school keeps a consistent position relative to its fellow members, and never sits directly above or directly below a neighbor. More telling is how the arrangement answers to disturbance, since external physical disruption barely alters the internal structure while the appearance of a predator changes it dramatically. That contrast carries the paragraph's real point, because it shows the formation is actively maintained by the animals themselves rather than imposed on them by the water.

Since schooling takes active effort, researchers infer that it must bring important benefits, and the passive ones are weighed here against an obvious cost. Grouping does make animals more visible and more attractive to predators. Set against that, a school leaves vast stretches of water empty, so a predator is less likely to pick up its trail at all; a large group keeps watch better than any individual can; and the mass may deter attack by looking like one enormous animal. Even a successful attack takes only a few members, leaving any given individual good odds of escape.

Beyond those passive advantages the school can act, and the responses are matched to the threat. On sighting a predator the school compacts, either so the hunter's senses cannot resolve individual bodies or so the group can execute escape maneuvers, including freezing in place to defeat predators that hunt by detecting turbulence. Under attack it may split, or use flash expansion, an explosive acceleration of animals away from the center. Threat size shapes the tactic: large predators menacing the whole school prompt attempts to avoid detection or to thin the school where the attack lands, while small predators nibbling at the margins are met with dazzling synchronized swimming.

Costs and benefits are balanced in the closing paragraph, which arrives at a limit. Schooling helps with finding food, since one member's discovery is watched by the others, who flock to the source, though competition inside the group can be intense and some mysids circle to the back of the school to feed unobserved. Finding mates gets easier too. But as numbers rise, food grows locally scarce, females produce smaller clutches, and adults may begin feeding on the young. Circumstances therefore set an optimal size, and once it is exceeded some animals leave to join another school.
overall_html: The passage establishes that many invertebrates genuinely school, correcting the older belief that their groupings were transient assemblages produced by currents or shared food, and then explains what schooling does for them. The author's purpose is explanatory rather than argumentative, moving from that corrected assumption and the structural criteria that identify a true school, to the passive antipredator benefits of grouping, to the active defensive maneuvers such as compacting, splitting, and flash expansion, and finally to the mixed effects on feeding and reproduction that impose an optimal size beyond which members depart. No competing viewpoints are developed beyond the superseded belief noted at the start.

Many of us can conceive of penalties that seem disproportionate to the crimes they are intended to punish. A sentence of probation for a person convicted of a brutal murder is one example of such an imbalance. At the other extreme is a sentence of twenty years in prison for shoplifting. But what is the source of these commonsense intuitions about the appropriateness of punishments?

There are two main rationales for punishing criminals. The first rationale justifies a punishment in terms of its benefit to society. Society is said to benefit whenever the fear of punishment deters a person from committing a crime, or when a convicted criminal is removed from contact with society at large. The second rationale is that a punishment is justified by the severity of the crime, independent of any benefit to society. This rationale is controversial because some find it difficult to see how a punishment can be justified if it brings no societal benefit; without such benefit, punishment would appear to be little more than retribution. But from the retributivist point of view, the question to be asked about punishment is not whether it is beneficial, but whether it is just—that is, appropriate.

One problem with the social-benefit rationale is that it is possible that very harsh penalties even for minor offenses may have great benefit to society. For example, if shoplifters faced twenty-year jail sentences, shoplifting might be deterred. Yet something leads us to say that in such cases the penalty far outweighs the crime. That is, there appears to be something intuitively wrong, or unjust, about these punishments. And it would seem that this intuition can only find support in a retributive conception of punishment, under which certain types of punishments are inherently more appropriate than others. The notion of appropriateness is absent from the first rationale, which could conceivably allow for any sort of punishment as long as it benefits society. Retributive considerations, on the other hand, allow for proportionality between punishments and crimes. This is what fuels our notion of just (as opposed to beneficial) punishment.

However, it can be argued that our intuition of the injustice of an overly harsh punishment is based on our sense that such a punishment is more harmful to the criminal than beneficial to society; and, similarly, that our intuition that a punishment is just is based on our sense that this punishment fairly balances societal benefit against harm to the criminal. In this way the second rationale can be seen as grounded in the first and its retributive nature disappears. Thus it seems that even our so-called intuitive notions of the appropriateness of punishments have their basis in the concept of benefit.
explanation_html:
A puzzle is posed before any theory arrives. Most of us can recognize a penalty that fails to fit its crime, whether it is probation for a brutal murder at one extreme or twenty years in prison for shoplifting at the other. Nothing here resolves those reactions; the paragraph simply names them as commonsense intuitions and asks where they come from. Treat that closing question as the passage's organizing problem, since everything after it attempts to trace the intuitions to a source, and the answer does not settle until the passage's final sentence.

Two justifications for punishment are laid out, and the distinction between them governs everything that follows. The first grounds punishment in benefit to society, delivered when fear of punishment deters someone from offending or when a convicted criminal is removed from contact with the public. The second grounds it in the severity of the crime alone, with no reference to benefit, which is why it attracts controversy: punishment that helps no one starts to look like plain retribution. The Retributivists reply that the right question is not whether a punishment is beneficial but whether it is just, meaning appropriate to what was done.

Pressure now falls on the social-benefit rationale, and the shoplifting example does the work. Very harsh penalties for minor offenses might well serve society, since twenty-year sentences would presumably deter shoplifting, and yet the punishment still strikes us as wildly out of proportion. Where can that judgment come from? Only, it appears, from a retributive conception in which certain punishments are inherently more appropriate than others, because benefit by itself contains no notion of appropriateness and would license anything that worked. Proportionality between crime and penalty belongs to retribution, and proportionality is what our sense of just punishment rests on.

Everything just concluded is reversed here, so read the previous paragraph as a position being built up rather than endorsed. The counterargument reinterprets the same intuitions: judging a harsh punishment unjust may simply express a sense that it harms the criminal more than it helps society, and judging a punishment just may express a sense that it balances the two fairly. On that reading the retributive rationale turns out to rest on the social-benefit rationale, and its distinctly retributive character dissolves. The passage ends deliberately at this point, with even our intuitions about appropriateness traced back to benefit.
overall_html: The passage asks where commonsense intuitions about proportionate punishment come from, entertains the retributive answer, and concludes that those intuitions rest on the concept of social benefit after all. The author's purpose is to work through a philosophical problem rather than to survey a debate, opening with penalties that plainly do not fit their crimes, distinguishing the social-benefit rationale from the retributive one, arguing that only retribution seems able to explain why a harsh but effective deterrent feels unjust, and then overturning that argument by recasting the same intuitions as judgments about harm to the criminal weighed against benefit to society. The retributivist position and the author's own conclusion are the two to keep apart.

Despite the great differences among the cultures from which we spring, there is a trait shared by many Hispanic-American writers: the use of a European language, Spanish, transplanted to the Western hemisphere. This fact has marked our literature profoundly and radically. We Hispanic Americans who write in Spanish have attempted from the beginning to break the ties of dependency that linked us with the literature of Spain. We have pursued this goal of ever-increasing independence through a twofold movement, seeking to adopt the literary forms and styles in vogue in other European and North American literatures, and endeavoring to describe the nature of the United States and give voice to the Hispanic peoples who live there. These often conflicting tactics can be described as cosmopolitanism and nativism, respectively.

The opposition between cosmopolitanism and nativism has divided the Hispanic-American literary consciousness for generations. For example, the work of one Mexican-American novelist was praised by some Hispanic-American critics for its skillful adaptation of European literary techniques but criticized for its paucity of specifically Mexican-American settings or characters. On the other hand, a Cuban-American novel was admired by other Hispanic-American critics for the vivid portrayal of its characters' daily lives but faulted for its "roughness" of form and language.

Cosmopolitanism is the venturing forth into the public or mainstream culture; nativism, the return to the private or original culture. There are periods in which the outward-oriented sensibility predominates, and others in which tendencies toward self-absorption and introspection prevail. An example of the former was the rich period of the avant-garde between 1918 and 1930. This was a time of searching and experimentation, when successive European movements from expressionism to surrealism—movements that were also inspiring other North American writers—had a profound influence on many Hispanic-American poets and novelists. This phase, which produced a number of outstanding works of exceptional boldness of expression, was followed by another characterized by a return to our peoples and our colloquial dialects, by the creation of works less indebted to current trends in the mainstream culture. Throughout our history, a concern for novelty and experimentation has been followed by a return to origins.

We contemporary Hispanic-American writers who write in Spanish live somewhere between the European tradition and the reality of the Americas. Our roots may be European, but our horizon is the land and history of the Americas. This is the challenge that we confront each day: in order to appreciate the value of one's own culture, one must first venture forth into the public sphere; in order not to disappear into the mainstream, one must return to one's origins. In this way, we attempt to reconcile the opposing tendencies of cosmopolitanism and nativism.
explanation_html:
The passage opens with a shared inheritance rather than a shared culture: Hispanic-American writers spring from very different places but write in Spanish, a European language carried across the Atlantic. The Author writes from inside this group, using 'we' throughout, and frames its whole history as a push to break literary dependence on Spain. Two tactics serve that single goal — importing the forms and styles in vogue in other European and North American literatures, and turning outward to describe the United States and give voice to the Hispanic peoples living there. Notice he names them at once as cosmopolitanism and nativism, and flags that they often conflict.

Two contrasting receptions show the split doing real work. Hispanic-American critics praised a Mexican-American novelist for skillfully adapting European literary techniques, then faulted the same work for offering few specifically Mexican-American settings or characters; other critics admired a Cuban-American novel for its vivid picture of daily life but objected to the roughness of its form and language. Watch the symmetry, because it is the point: each book earns credit on one axis and a penalty on the other. The author supplies these as illustration of a divided consciousness, not as a judgment about which side is right.

Here the two terms get proper definitions and a history. Cosmopolitanism is the venture outward into the public or mainstream culture; nativism is the return inward to the private or original one, and Hispanic-American writing has swung between them in alternating periods. The avant-garde years between 1918 and 1930 are the outward example, when European movements from expressionism to surrealism, which were also shaping North American writers, pressed hard on Hispanic-American poets and novelists and produced work of unusual boldness. The inward swing followed, rooted in the writers' own peoples and colloquial dialects. The rhythm is cyclical: experimentation, then a return to origins.

The close converts the opposition into a resolution rather than a choice. Contemporary Hispanic-American writers working in Spanish live between the European tradition and the reality of the Americas — European roots, but a horizon made of American land and history. The Author's own position is that the two tendencies require each other: you must venture into the public sphere before you can appreciate the value of your own culture, and you must return to your origins to avoid disappearing into the mainstream. That reciprocity, not a victory for either tendency, is how he claims Hispanic-American writers reconcile cosmopolitanism and nativism.
overall_html: The passage argues that Hispanic-American literature written in Spanish has been shaped by a long oscillation between cosmopolitanism, the outward turn toward European and North American forms, and nativism, the inward turn toward local peoples and speech, and that the two tendencies are finally complementary rather than exclusive. The Author's purpose is explanatory and reconciling: he identifies the shared linguistic inheritance and the drive for independence from Spain, illustrates the split through contrasting critical receptions, traces its alternating historical phases, then argues that each tendency depends on the other. The viewpoints to keep apart are The Author, writing as a member of the group, and the Hispanic-American critics whose divided verdicts dramatize the tension.

In the past, students of Renaissance women's education extolled the unprecedented intellectual liberty and equality available to these women, but recently scholars have presented a different view of Renaissance education and opportunity for women. Joan Gibson argues that despite more widespread education for privileged classes of women, Renaissance educational reforms also increased restrictions on women. Humanist education in the Renaissance was based on the classical division of the liberal arts into seven categories, including the three language arts: grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric. Although medieval monastic education, also based on the classical division, had stressed grammar and languages in preparation for a life devoted to meditation on religious literature, humanist education revived the classical emphasis on rhetoric—the art of persuasive and declamatory speech—in the context of training for public service in legal and political debate. All students began with elementary study of grammar and progressed to stylistics and literary criticism. But rhetorical training, which was increasingly undertaken only at the university level, could lead in different directions—to study of composition and oral expression or to study of persuasion, in conjunction with a dialectic concerned with broad principles of logic and argumentation. Male students routinely learned material through rhetorical, argumentative role-playing, and although many Renaissance authors expressed horror at their aggressive wrangling, such combativeness was thought still less appropriate for women, who were not supposed to need such preparation for public life.

Thus, humanist education for women encompassed literary grammatical studies in both classical and vernacular languages, while dialectic and rhetoric, the disciplines required for philosophy, politics, and the professions, were prohibited to women. Even princesses lacked instruction in political philosophy or the exercise of such public virtues as philanthropy. The prevailing attitude was that girls needed only a generalist education conducted in a family setting and directed toward private enjoyment and the eventual teaching of very young children. Unlike either dialectic or rhetoric, grammar training cast students in the role of an audience, striving to understand authors and teachers. Women were to form an audience, not seek one; for them, instruction in speaking was confined to books of courtesy.

The coupling of expanded linguistic and literary education for women with the lack of available social roles for educated women led to uneasy resolutions: exceptionally learned women were labelled as preternatural or essentially masculine, or were praised as virtuous only if they were too modest to make their accomplishments public. Some Italian humanist women gave fashionable oratorical performances, but these were ceremonial in nature rather than designed to influence public affairs. Renaissance women educated along humanist lines did not tend to write works of philosophy; instead they became most notable for literary achievements, particularly translations, poetry, and tales in the vernacular or correspondence and orations in Latin.
explanation_html:
The opening sets a revision against an older consensus. Earlier students of Renaissance women's education celebrated an unprecedented intellectual liberty and equality, while recent scholars, and Joan Gibson in particular, argue that the reforms which widened access also tightened restrictions. The rest of the paragraph supplies the machinery behind that claim. Humanist education kept the classical seven liberal arts, three of them language arts: grammar, dialectic and rhetoric. Where medieval monastic schooling had stressed grammar and languages as preparation for religious meditation, humanism revived rhetoric, the art of persuasive public speech, as training for legal and political service. Everyone began with grammar, but advanced rhetorical work, increasingly a university matter, ran on aggressive argumentative role-playing thought unsuitable for women, who were not expected to enter public life.

'Thus' signals consequence, and the consequence is a hard boundary. Women's humanist education stopped at literary and grammatical study in classical and vernacular languages, while dialectic and rhetoric — the disciplines that opened philosophy, politics and the professions — were closed to them. Even princesses went untaught in political philosophy or in public virtues such as philanthropy. The prevailing attitude held that a girl needed only a generalist education conducted at home, aimed at private enjoyment and at eventually teaching very young children. Keep hold of the distinction the paragraph turns on: grammar casts a student as an audience receiving an author, while dialectic and rhetoric train a student to command one.

The final paragraph traces what happens when learning outruns opportunity. The resolutions were uneasy, as Gibson's argument predicts: an exceptionally learned woman was labelled preternatural or essentially masculine, or was credited with virtue only if she stayed modest enough to keep her accomplishments out of public view. Some Italian humanist women did give fashionable oratorical performances, but those occasions were ceremonial and were not meant to influence public affairs. Output followed training. These women produced not philosophy, which required the forbidden disciplines, but translations, poetry and vernacular tales, along with correspondence and orations in Latin.
overall_html: The passage lays out the revisionist case, associated with Joan Gibson, that Renaissance humanist education broadened women's literary learning while simultaneously narrowing their prospects, because dialectic and rhetoric, the disciplines that led toward public life, were withheld from them. The author's purpose is expository rather than polemical, presenting the mechanism in three steps: the contrast between older celebratory scholarship and the newer view alongside the structure of humanist training, then the specific curricular boundary drawn around women, then the social awkwardness and the literary rather than philosophical achievements that followed. The viewpoints to keep separate are the earlier students of Renaissance women's education and the recent scholars represented by Joan Gibson.

Naturalists have long studied the ability of North American forest birds to survive extremely cold overnight temperatures in winter. For example, nuthatches sleep in cavities such as tree hollows or holes dug into snowdrifts, retaining heat closer to the body and thus saving energy by reducing the need for shivering. Chickadees induce torpor, saving energy by allowing their body temperatures to decline drastically. Grosbeaks stay close to trees whose seeds contain sufficient fat to fuel shivering. But the survival of one species, the kinglet, remains something of a mystery.

There are two reasons for this. First, although kinglets are tiny—about 9 cm long including the tail—they maintain extremely high body temperatures at conditions well below freezing. According to the physical laws of heating and cooling, kinglets would lose heat at a rate about 75 percent faster than birds twice their mass—chickadees, for example—and so would have to consume and burn 75 percent more food per unit of body mass than the larger birds to maintain the same body temperature. The insulation provided by feathers, which, similarly to other northern birds, make up about 25 percent of the kinglet's mass, accounts for some of its heat-retaining capability but does not explain how kinglets manage to survive as well in cold climates as do the larger birds. Because smaller birds have a lesser absolute amount of insulation than larger birds, they would cool even faster than predicted by body mass alone.

The second reason kinglet survival is so remarkable is that, unlike most bird species that remain in cold climates during winter, their diet consists exclusively of insects. Researchers wonder how it is possible for kinglets, birds that do not cache food and are known not to forage at night, to gather and consume the necessary amount of insects each short winter day. The question is more vexing considering that a kinglet's stomach when filled to capacity contains only enough food to keep it warm for one hour.

A partial explanation is that kinglets store fat; kinglet body fat can triple in the course of a day. Nevertheless, this increase accounts for only about half the energy needed to maintain the kinglet's body temperature overnight. Researchers once theorized that torpor might make up the difference, but found no evidence of torpor in kinglets. Another theory, which is still untested but which may be borne out by a recent study of goldcrests, a related species, is that kinglets cluster together at night. Kinglets flock in groups of twos and threes during the day; while such small groups alone could not maintain such high body temperatures, it is hypothesized that after nightfall several groups in a region may find each other by means of calling and consolidate in a central location.
explanation_html:
The opening supplies solved cases before introducing the unsolved one. Naturalists have long asked how North American forest birds get through bitterly cold winter nights, and three answers are offered in quick succession: nuthatches sleep inside cavities such as tree hollows or holes in snowdrifts, which holds heat near the body and cuts the need to shiver; chickadees let their body temperature fall sharply, entering torpor to save energy; grosbeaks stay near trees whose seeds are fatty enough to fuel shivering. The last sentence pivots to the kinglet, whose survival is still a mystery, and that mystery organizes the rest of the passage.

The first half of the puzzle is a mismatch between size and body temperature. Kinglets run very warm in conditions well below freezing despite measuring only about nine centimeters, tail included. Physics makes this expensive: a bird that small sheds heat roughly seventy-five percent faster than one twice its mass, a chickadee for instance, and would therefore need to eat and burn seventy-five percent more food per unit of body mass to stay equally warm. Feathers account for about a quarter of a kinglet's mass, as in other northern birds, and help, but note the twist at the end, since less total insulation means cooling faster still.

The second half of the puzzle concerns fuel rather than heat loss. Most birds wintering in cold places eat something other than insects, but kinglets eat insects and nothing else, and they neither store food for later nor hunt after dark. That leaves one short winter day in which to find and eat everything they need. The detail that sharpens the difficulty is worth holding onto: even a stomach filled to capacity carries only about an hour's worth of warmth, so daytime feeding cannot simply be banked for the night.

Answers arrive, but the paragraph is honest about how incomplete they are. Kinglets do lay down fat, tripling their body fat within a day, which still covers only about half of what an overnight requires. Researchers once proposed torpor, the chickadee's solution, and then found no sign of it in kinglets. The remaining idea is nighttime clustering, untested but perhaps supported by recent work on the closely related goldcrest: kinglets travel in twos and threes by day, groups too small to hold that much heat, so several may call to one another after dark and gather in one place.
overall_html: The passage sets out a natural-history puzzle, asking how the kinglet survives freezing winter nights when its tiny body loses heat far faster than that of larger birds and its insect-only diet cannot be cached or hunted after dark. The author's purpose is expository, opening with the well-understood strategies of nuthatches, chickadees and grosbeaks as a contrast, then laying out the two dimensions of the kinglet's anomaly, and finally reviewing partial explanations: fat storage that covers about half the need, torpor that was ruled out, and an untested clustering hypothesis. The only perspective in play is that of the researchers investigating the question.
